Prime Minister Tayyip Erdogan has promised to deliver "a new, democratised political system" to voters in the referendum.

The changes would also limit the powers of the president - albeit after Erdogan himself assumed the office.

The draft law approved by ministers on Tuesday will be put to a referendum, probably in March.

If passed, it would make Turkey the latest country to adopt what politicians call a "proportional representation" system.

Currently, parties in Turkey elect MPs from closed lists of candidates, a system that often results in vote-winning parties winning far more seats than their share of the vote.

The new system would lower the threshold for winning seats in parliament - currently set at 10% - giving smaller parties a better chance of representation.

One of the consequences of the change would be to allow the pro-Kurdish Democratic Society Party (DTP) - closed down last year for alleged ties with the rebel Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK) - to re-enter parliament.

The DTP won almost six percent of the vote in 2007, but took no seats because the 10% threshold ruled them out.

The change is one element in a package of reforms put forward by the government designed to address concerns over Turkey's democracy.

Another element, also to be put to a referendum, would change the way the president is elected, reducing the powers of the office.

The changes were agreed in a consensus between the government and opposition parties, but critics say the reforms do not go far enough.

"This system will bring about change, a new, democratised political system," Prime Minister Tayyip Erdogan said last week.

"Our people will decide on this change, on these reforms in a referendum," he said. "I am confident our people will give the right decision."

The reforms have been closely watched by Europe, as Turkey seeks to begin accession talks with the European Union.

The EU has made clear that it wants to see the democratisation package passed into law.

For years, conventional wisdom has held that the future of television lies in cable, with its superior picture and sound quality. But conventional wisdom may be about to change. VOD is a technology that allows television viewers to select and watch programs at their convenience. This is achieved by storing programs on a central computer, where they can be accessed at any time by subscribers to the service. The programs are typically delivered over the telephone line, and can be paused, fast-forwarded, and rewound at the discretion of the viewer.

One of the key advantages of VOD is that it allows viewers to watch programs at their convenience. This means that they can avoid the advertisements that are a staple of conventional television, and they can also skip over parts of programs that they do not find interesting. In addition, VOD allows viewers to watch programs that they may have missed when they were first aired.

Another advantage of VOD is that it could potentially offer a more personalized service to viewers. With conventional television, viewers are limited to the programs that are broadcast at a particular time. With VOD, however, viewers could potentially select from a much wider range of programs, including specialized content that is targeted to their individual interests.

Despite its many advantages, VOD is still in its infancy, and it faces a number of challenges if it is to become a mainstream technology. One of the key challenges is the cost of storage and bandwidth, which can be significant. In addition, VOD requires a high level of technical sophistication on the part of the viewer, which may deter some people from adopting the technology.

Nonetheless, supporters of VOD believe that it has the potential to revolutionize the way we watch television. As the technology continues to develop, it will be interesting to see if it lives up to its potential and becomes a mainstream fixture in the world of television.

The US state of Tennessee has passed a law designed to block unwanted text messages.

The bill, known as HB181, allows mobile phone users to sue spam text message senders for up to $500 for each unwanted message.

State lawmakers hope it will deter spam text message senders.

Similar laws are already in place in other states, including Texas and Arizona.

The bill's sponsor, Tennessee state Senator Bill Ketron, said he hoped it would deter spam text message senders.

"I'm not sure how much money is involved, but I think it's going to stop it cold," he said.

"It's a big win for consumers who are tired of being harassed by these anonymous spam texts and a big win for law enforcement to be able to go after these people."

The law will come into effect on 1 July.

California has passed a law banning unsolicited messages to a mobile device, in a bid to fight back against spam and robocalls. The bill, signed by Governor Gavin Newsom, will allow customers to sue robocallers who violate the law. "Robocalls and text messages are an annoying inconvenience for many Californians," said Governor Newsom. "This new law will provide consumers with the protection they need against these annoying and sometimes harmful texts and calls." The law builds on an earlier law passed in 2020, which banned unwanted sales calls and allowed residents to sue robocallers who violated the law. This new law goes further by banning all unwanted text messages and permitting victims to receive up to $1,000 per text message received, and $1,500 per call.

Libya has taken $1bn in frozen funds held in the US, the French and UK governments say.

The country has been embroiled in civil war since the overthrow of dictator Muammar Gaddafi in 2011.

The money was released by the three countries after the United Nations sought to unify Libya's institutions.

They hope the funds will help stabilise the country and enable the national government to pay salaries and buy food.

The $1bn (¤870 million) in assets was released by the US, France and the UK - countries that had imposed sanctions on Libya after Gaddafi's overthrow.

The announcement was made during a visit to Tripoli by UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres.

He has been in the country to persuade feuding factions to accept a national unity government.

"The governor of the Central Bank and the presidential council have decided to immediately use these funds in the following ways: $350m to buy medical supplies abroad, particularly for coronavirus testing kits and to purchase personal protection equipment for medical staff," Mr Guterres said.

"Another $650m will be used to support the national budget. This amount will be used to pay salaries of doctors, nurses, engineers and teachers. It will also be used to purchase and import flour, wheat and sugar," he added.

In a joint statement, the US, UK and France said they would "continue to work with the Libyan authorities to address the country's urgent humanitarian needs".

"We believe this can contribute to broader foreign policy objectives in Libya and help address the country's underlying economic challenges," the statement added.

The three countries had blocked assets worth $30bn belonging to Libya's central bank when the country descended into chaos following the fall of Colonel Gaddafi.

In 2016, the US gave permission for $1.3bn of the funds to be released but the money was never handed over.

In April this year, the Libyan prime minister asked the US to release the funds to help his government buy medical equipment to combat the coronavirus outbreak.

Libya has taken $1bn in frozen funds from a US-based account, the Libyan government has announced.

The country has been embroiled in chaos since the overthrow of dictator Muammar Gaddafi in 2011.

The Libyan government had been working with the US government to regain access to the funds, which were frozen under sanctions imposed during the Gaddafi era. The $1bn ($1.3bn) sum has now been transferred to a special account at the Libyan Central Bank.

The money is supposed to be used to support the country's national budget and to help rebuild the country. However, some Libyans have expressed concern that the money may not be used for its intended purposes and may end up in the hands of corrupt officials.

The Libyan government has stated that it will work to ensure that the money is used for the benefit of the country and its people. It has also called for the lifting of remaining sanctions on the country, which would allow it to regain access to additional frozen funds.

The government announced on Tuesday that it will ban the forced retirement of people aged 65 and over. The move is designed to encourage workers to remain in employment for longer. Employers will no longer be able to force workers to retire at 65. It is hoped that the change will help to address the increasing labor shortage in Germany. While the legislation applies to all workers, it is expected to be particularly beneficial for women and foreigners, who tend to retire earlier than the average worker. Employers will be required to justify any retirement age below 65 and show that it is necessary for the proper functioning of the business. If they cannot do so, they will be required to raise the retirement age to 65. The ban is expected to take effect in the spring of 2023.

The government has announced that it will ban the forced retirement of people aged 65 and over. The move is intended to increase workplace diversity and promote equality and fairness in the workplace. 

The ban is expected to take effect in April 2024. It will apply to both public and private sector employees. The government has said that it will introduce a new law to enforce the ban. 

The announcement has been welcomed by many, including the Equality and Human Rights Commission. The commission's chair, David Isaac, has said that "for too long, forced retirement has been causing older workers to leave the workforce prematurely, leading to a loss of skills and experience, and an impact on workplace diversity". 

The government has said that the ban will not apply to individuals who are unable to continue working due to health or other personal reasons.

US retail sales surged in December, recording their largest increase since early 2021, as spending was boosted by purchases of toys, video games, and clothing, according to Commerce Department data released on Wednesday.

Total retail sales in December rose 3.3% from the previous month, well above analysts' expectations of a 1.9% increase.

Sales at general merchandise stores, which include big box retailers such as Walmart and Target, increased 7.0% from November and were up 11.5% from December 2021.

Sales at clothing stores rose 2.2% month-over-month and were up 10.2% from a year earlier.

Electronics and appliance stores saw sales climb 1.2% from November and were up 8.0% from a year earlier.

Sales at online retailers were up 1.4% from November and increased 7.0% from a year earlier.

The retail sales report covers only about a third of overall consumer spending, but it is still a widely watched indicator of the strength of the US economy.

The Commerce Department reported last week that gross domestic product increased at a 2.6% annualized rate in the third quarter of 2022, marking a downward revision from the 2.9% previously reported.

Sales at US retailers jumped by 7.6% in December, official data shows, topping expectations as inflation cooled.

The increase was driven by gains in sales of motor vehicles and parts, but receipts also rose for clothing, electronics, and furniture, the Commerce Department reported on Wednesday.

The monthly gain topped expectations of 2.5% and was the largest increase since March.

Measures of inflation eased, with the price index for goods rising 6.5% year-on-year, down from an annual rate of 7.7% in November.

Core retail sales, which exclude automobiles, rose 5.5% year on year, down from a 7.1% annual gain in November.

The better-than-expected data points to a resilient consumer, despite high inflation and rising interest rates.

However, sales were down 0.5% compared to December 2021, the first year-on-year decline since November 2020.

Retailers have been dealing with rising costs and a shift in consumer behavior as people return to workplaces and social events.

Nevertheless, the data shows that consumers were still spending at the end of last year, despite concerns about an economic slowdown.

The Commerce Department reported that online and other non-store retailers enjoyed a 12.3% annual increase in sales in December.

Sales at food services and drinking places rose 1.3% for the month and were up 40.5% from December 2021.

BT has announced plans to invest £15bn in broadband and 5G infrastructure over the next five years.

The company said the investment would accelerate the rollout of full-fibre broadband and blanket the country in 5G.

BT's chief executive, Philip Jansen, said the plan would deliver " Fibre to the premises (FTTP) broadband to 20 million homes by the mid-to-late 2020s, build a next-generation 5G network that will cover around 90% of the UK by 2028, and upgrade tens of millions of customers to fibre."

The company said it would also "continue to explore potential new opportunities" in its infrastructure division Openreach.

The announcement comes as BT faces growing competition from broadband providers including TalkTalk and Virgin Media.

Last week, TalkTalk announced it was accelerating its full- fibre broadband rollout plans and increasing its investment in the infrastructure.

The company said it aimed to roll out fibre broadband to three million homes and businesses by the end of 2025, "increasing its current full-fibre footprint by more than 60%".

BT has increased the speeds of its cheapest broadband packages to benefit customers not connected to the fibre network. The company's Basic package will see an increase from 20Mbps to 36Mbps, while the Essential package will go from 36Mbps to 63Mbps. Moreover, BT has lowered the price of the Essential package to £28 per month. Marc Allera, CEO of BT's Consumer division, said: "Broadband connectivity has never been more critical, so we're delighted to be boosting speeds and increasing data limits for these customers."

Abba have reunited to launch a new stage show inspired by their songs.

The four singers, who have not performed together since the early 1980s, appeared together at the Prince Edward Theatre in London for the premiere of Abba Mania.

The show features 22 of their hits including Waterloo, Dancing Queen and Voulez Vous.

Band member Benny Andersson called it "a bit weird" but exciting.

He said he did not think the group, who split up 37 years ago, would have approved the show but that he was happy with it.

"I think Abba would have hated this, actually," he told the BBC. "Because it's not like you're doing a great Abba show with the bells and whistles. This is more a tribute."

He said he was "blown away" by the show, adding: "It's kind of spooky seeing these people pretending to be us, but they do a good job."

The musical is billed as an immersive experience, with the audience invited to party alongside the performers.

The show's official Twitter account described it as "a rollercoaster ride of Abba's greatest hits", adding: "You'll be dancing in your seat, crying with emotion and singing at the top of your lungs."

Band member Agnetha Fältskog said: "It's extraordinary. I mean, the show is so professional, the cast is amazing but the production is really, really good."

Fältskog added that she was initially reluctant to watch the performance but was glad she had done so.

"I actually didn't want to come and watch this because I thought this is not gonna be anything near the original, but it's not bad," she said.

The musical arrives in London 40 years after the band won the Eurovision song contest with Waterloo in 1974.

The band went on to achieve global success before splitting up in 1982.

The musical will run in London until October, before embarking on a UK tour. A separate musical based on the band's songs, titled Mamma Mia!, has met with huge success both in the West End and on Broadway.

The four members of Abba have reunited to attend the Stockholm premiere of their upcoming musical, "Abbatars." 

The musical, which features the group's hits performed by a digital version of the band, premiered on Thursday and is set to run until November 27th. 

The group, consisting of Benny Andersson, Anni-Frid Lyngstad, Agnetha Fältskog, and Björn Ulvaeus, have not all been together since the group split up in 1982. 

"We're here because it's a great occasion," said Andersson. "It's going to be a lot of fun seeing the show tonight." 

The musical tells the story of a young woman with dreams of becoming a DJ in Stockholm. 

"Abbatars" is directed by Bafta winner Rufus Norris and features choreography by the "Billy Elliot" choreographer Peter Darling. 

The musical will open at the Noel Coward Theatre in London's West End in spring 2024.

Sales of gadgets including mobile phones, MP3 players, and digital cameras will grow by more than a third to $714bn (£368bn) by 2005, driven by demand in China, Brazil and Russia, says US research group, Gartner.

It also said that Microsoft's Windows XP operating system had helped fuel sales of digital devices.

The study indicated that PC sales had risen by 14.6% in the final three months of 2004.

Gartner said it believed that sales of PCs would continue to grow in 2005, boosted by the arrival of Microsoft's Windows XP operating system, which was released in October.

The survey indicated that 386 million PCs were sold last year, with nearly 29 million in the last quarter of 2004.

"We believe the PC market in 2005 will be characterised by strong growth in portable PCs, robust growth in mature regions, and continuing growth, although at a slower pace, in emerging regions," said George Shiffler, a principal analyst with Gartner.

"We also believe that the fundamental growth drivers for the PC market will remain unchanged in 2005."

The research group also said it expected mobile phone sales to grow by 17.7% in 2005 to 988 million units, and for MP3 players to grow by 41.5% to 77 million.

Digital cameras are also expected to continue to do well, with sales up by 20.4% to 121 million units, it added.

The gadget market grew by 10% in 2004 as consumer electronics became more popular, according to research group NPD.

It said the trend towards so-called "digital lifestyles" had helped drive the market, which was now worth more than £900m.

Sales of MP3 players, digital cameras and mobile phones drove the growth, with the latter enjoying a 17% rise in sales.

However, the future of the market looked less certain, with the price of LCD and plasma TVs set to fall, which could hurt sales, NPD said.

 It said the market for gadgets - defined as small, relatively inexpensive items which are fun to use - had grown seven-fold since 1997.

"Gadgets are becoming must-have items for today's consumers as they seek to enhance their digital lifestyle experiences," said Steve Gater, telecoms analyst at NPD.

"Increasingly they are looking for products which offer multiple functionality and enable them to access digital content such as music, photos and the internet, in a mobile environment. "

He said the market for these gadgets had room to grow, but that it was facing increasing competition from other products such as games consoles and personal video recorders.

England's failure to beat Australia in the Rugby World Cup final has prompted fresh criticism of the team's performance from one of its most high-profile female fans.

Barbara Campagna, an Italian socialite and girlfriend of England coach Eddie Jones, took to Instagram to vent her frustration.

In a lengthy post, she appeared to criticise England's display in the 32-12 defeat in Tokyo on Saturday.

"It's been a tough week... a tough second half of the season," she wrote.

"Sometimes it feels like people and things are put in your path to test you, push you to your limits, and show you that you can be better, stronger, and wiser.

"We all have a choice... we can give up, sulk, and make excuses... or we can get up, dust ourselves off, and learn from our mistakes.

"To all the young girls out there that look up to these boys - please don't lose faith. Sometimes you fall, sometimes you fail, but you can't win unless you try."

It is the first time Campagna has commented on England's performance since the final.

The 62-year-old has been a vocal supporter of the team throughout the tournament, often posting on social media to celebrate England's progress.

Before the final, she posted a photo of herself in an England shirt, alongside a message of support for the team.

"It's been the most incredible, rewarding and emotional journey," she wrote.

"These boys have worked so hard, they deserve this final - they deserve the opportunity to shine.

"Bring it home for all of us, you've got this."

Campagna and Jones have been in a relationship since 2016, after being introduced by mutual friend, the late rugby player Andy Ripley.

Jones has previously said that Campagna provides a "nice balance" to his life, allowing him to "switch off" from rugby.

England's ill-disciplined World Cup campaign ended with a whimper as they were out-played and out-muscled by a young, vibrant and skilful Australia side, who booked a semi-final meeting with Trans-Tasman rivals New Zealand.

A ninth defeat in a row - the team's worst run for 34 years - was assured before halftime as a 13-6 scoreline reflected the dominance of the Southern Hemisphere side, who scored four tries to England's two.

But it was the manner in which England surrendered meekly that will cause most concern for director of rugby Clive Woodward, whose side were out-thought and out-fought in every department.

For much of the first half, England were buoyed by a partisan crowd who cheered their every move but, once again, they were unable to deliver on the promise of their early play.

A well-taken try from Jason Robinson and a penalty from Jonny Wilkinson after just eight minutes gave England an early lead but that was as good as it got for the home side.

The introduction of Elton Flatley at fly-half for the Australians proved an inspired move as his precise kicking and calm authority helped turn the tide.

A well-taken try from centre Matt Giteau, who exploited acres of space in the English defence, and a Flatley penalty put the Wallabies ahead after 21 minutes.

Winger Chris Latham then scored Australia's second try in the corner, Flatley missed the conversion but added a penalty goal minutes later to give his side a 13-6 half-time lead.

England's lack of discipline was once again their downfall as Wilkinson, Robinson and captain Martin Johnson were all sin-binned as the pressure finally told.

The crowd's fervour was dampened by the sight of England's star centre Mike Tindall being helped from the field after injuring his shoulder in a tackle early in the second half.

It was Australia who extended their lead when left-wing Latham scored his second try, again in the corner, Flatley missing the conversion.

England's cause was not helped by the loss of Wilkinson with a hamstring injury, the young Wilkinson replacing his father, who had an indifferent game.

But replacement Charlie Hodgson, who has had an excellent season with Newcastle and was among the few English players to enhance his reputation, scored a try which he converted himself to give England a glimmer of hope with 10 minutes remaining.

Universities in Wales have warned that prospects for students are at risk because of long-term funding cuts.

Bosses said a £35m funding gap left by the Welsh government could lead to course closures and a decline in quality.

Education Minister Jeremy Miles said he recognised the pressures on the sector.

A review of higher education funding in Wales - due to report back in spring - could see a shift from the current system, in which students from Wales pay the same fees as those from England, but with lower interest rates on student loans.

It could also see a change to the current allocation system, in which universities in England get the majority of their funding from the UK government and those in Wales from the Welsh government.

In a letter to the Welsh government, Universities Wales, which represents the country's higher education institutions, said the sector had "serious concerns" about the level of funding for the next academic year.

It said combined cuts of 30% to the higher education budget since 2010 had resulted in a "starvation of resources".

"This underfunding has damaged the capacity of our universities to maintain and improve the provision of education and research," it added.

The letter, signed by Universities Wales chairman Prof Colin Riordan, warned that the situation had "reached a crisis point".

"The funding gap puts at risk the ability of universities to maintain the quality of provision, to invest in the infrastructure that supports this, to continue to provide an environment that supports the wellbeing of students and staff, and to ensure that higher education in Wales is based on a sustainable financial model," it said.

"This risks the prospects of students and risks the long-term sustainability of the sector."

It called on the Welsh government to provide additional funding for the next academic year, and to work with Universities Wales on a longer-term solution.

In response, Education Minister Jeremy Miles said he had "regular discussions" with Universities Wales on the pressures facing the sector.

He said: "We recognise the importance of investing in high-quality higher education and are determined to see a successful, thriving university sector that delivers benefits for students, employers and wider society.

"We have put an additional £15m into the higher education budget for next year to help address some of the issues highlighted by Universities Wales.

"Our review of funding policies for higher education will consider the sustainable financial basis for higher education in Wales. A consultation report on the review will

The announcement of a funding cut to higher education in Wales has been described as a “tragedy” by a leading university figure.

University and College Union (UCU) Wales said the £37m funding reduction would have “a devastating impact on the sector”.

The Welsh government said it had provided “record levels of investment”.

Education Minister Jeremy Miles will confirm on Tuesday the plans to cut funding by 21% over the next two years. 

The UCU said the cut would start next year and result in a £1.5bn loss to the higher education sector in Wales over the next decade.

It said the impact would be worst on students from disadvantaged backgrounds and those studying vocational courses.

Meri Huws, UCU Wales official, said: “This cut will have a devastating impact on the sector and will hit students from disadvantaged backgrounds, mature students, and those studying vocational courses hardest. 

“It is a tragedy that the Welsh government has chosen to sacrifice an entire generation of students in Wales for a political agenda that has no evidence to back it up.”

The union has called for a meeting with Mr Miles.

A Welsh government spokesperson said: “We have provided record levels of investment in Wales’ higher education system in recent years and this has helped to keep tuition fees in Wales lower than elsewhere in the UK.

“We will continue to work with the sector as we move forward with our plans to create a sustainable student finance system for Wales.”

The UK has been told to expect a verdict on whether the Belhaj five can sue the British government for its alleged involvement in their rendition and torture.

The five - including the former Guantánamo Bay inmate Abd al-Rahim al-Nashiri - were detained in Thailand in 2003.

They were rendered to Libya, where they said they were tortured by the Gaddafi regime.

The men's case has been under consideration by the UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention.

Lawyers for the men have asked the working group to determine that their detention was arbitrary and to issue an opinion that the UK was complicit in their rendition and torture.

The case has taken on an added significance since the toppling of the Gaddafi regime last year.

In recent months, British officials have been trying to secure the release of more than a dozen British residents detained in Libya.

The UK has been urged to act on last week's ruling by the United Nations' human rights committee, which criticised the country's detention practices as racially discriminatory. The committee's chair said that the UK had not fully addressed concerns raised nearly three years ago about the widespread use of detention for asylum seekers and migrants.

The ruling comes after a three-day hearing in September, where witnesses, including former immigration ministers, and campaigners gave evidence about the impact of the government's "hostile environment" policy on immigration detention.

The committee's final report is expected next year and will make recommendations for the UK to improve its treatment of migrants and asylum seekers.

England captain Dylan Hartley has been left out of the squad for Saturday's opening Six Nations match against France in Paris.

The 31-year-old has not been included in Eddie Jones' 25-man squad, with the Australian saying he needs "to get some confidence back".

Hartley has struggled with injury this season and has started just two games for club side Northampton Saints.

His absence from the squad took chief executive Mark Darbon by surprise.

"It's a little bit odd, to be honest. I haven't heard that one before," he said. "We have always found that when Dylan has been struggling with injury, getting him into the England set-up has always been good for him.

"It's a good environment for him to get himself back to his best. I'm surprised but England have got a big pool of hookers they can choose from. It's a strong squad they've picked."

Hartley won the last of his 77 caps against Samoa in June 2017 and has struggled with a number of injuries this season.

He started against Exeter in early December but lasted just 10 minutes before damaging his shoulder and he has not played since.

 Northampton have three other hookers in their squad - Hartley's brother Alex, James Fish and Tom Emery - while Argentina-born Juan Pablo Socino can also cover in the position.

Darbon said the club are hoping Dylan Hartley will be back for the Saints' Champions Cup game against Ospreys on January 20 but that he is unlikely to be fit enough to face Saracens on January 27.

"It's a bit tight for the Saracens game but we're hopeful for the Ospreys game," Darbon added.

"We're pretty confident he'll be available for the Leicester game but it could be that we get him back for a game before that."

England coach Eddie Jones blamed "laundry issues" after he made six changes to his starting line-up for Saturday's Test against France in Paris.

Jonny May and Jack Nowell - who both scored in the 44-8 win over Scotland - are two of those to drop out, with Joe Cokanasiga and Anthony Watson coming in on the wings.

There are also starts for Sam Underhill and Courtney Lawes in the forward pack, with Tom Curry shifting to number eight and Mark Wilson dropping to the bench.

England, who lead the Six Nations table with nine points, face France at 20:00 GMT on Saturday.

A dispute over the name of a cheese used in Greek dishes like spanakopita has ended up in the European Court of Justice.

The issue concerns whether the name feta can be used for cheeses produced outside Greece, and by whom.

Greek producers have fought for decades to stop other countries from using the name feta, which is protected as a designation of origin.

Such labels are used to identify a product as originating in a specific region, and whose production methods are considered traditional.

But Denmark, Germany and France have opposed the move, arguing that the term "feta" has become a generic term for white, brined cheese.

The three countries have argued that the term "feta" has been in use for decades, and that such a long period of usage has protected the word as a generic term.

The issue was referred to the European Court of Justice by the European Commission, the EU's executive arm, which ruled in favor of Greece last year.

The Commission argued that the term "feta" was "not a generic term and could not be considered as a generic term within the meaning of the Regulation".

It added that "the term 'feta' may continue to be used to designate PDO (protected designation of origin) products, namely those falling within the definition given in the appended regulation".

The regulation in question says that for a name to be protected it has to be "clearly distinguishable, capable of being pronounced by consumers, and not devoid of any distinctive character".

The court is now expected to make a final ruling, probably within the next two years.

It is not the first time that the issue has been taken to the top European court.

In 2005, the court ruled that Germany, Denmark and France could continue to produce "feta" cheese for the time being, as the term had become a "generic indication" for white, brined cheese.

However, the court did say that if a name were to be protected, it should be protected across the EU, and could not be restricted to just one country.

This new ruling will apply across the EU, and could lead to a ban on the use of the name "feta" for anything other than Greek cheese.

It could also lead to a crackdown on the sale of cheeses produced outside Greece and labeled as feta.

The UK has formally responded to the European Court of Justice's demand for more details on its trade sanctions against Belarus, Russia, and Ukraine. The response came ahead of a Monday hearing on whether those sanctions violate the bloc's trade laws. The UK government said it has "clear legal rights" to impose sanctions in response to Russia's invasion of Ukraine. The EU imposed its own sanctions in response to the war, but the UK argues that its own sanctions are aimed at upholding the sanctions regime of the UN Security Council.

The hearing comes after the UK challenged the sanctions regime before the ECJ in October, arguing that the sanctions the EU imposed on Russia were unlawful. The hearing is set to last three days, and the court is expected to issue a ruling by the end of the year. 
If the court rules against the UK, it could lead to the restoration of £1.7bn of frozen Russian assets.

UK foreign secretary Liz Truss said the UK government would "defend its right to impose sanctions on Russia in response to its barbaric war on Ukraine". She added that "the UK, alongside our international partners, will not rest until Russia has been held to account for its actions".

Senior US and Russian trade officials have held "constructive" talks on Moscow's wish to join the WTO, officials say.

Russia's entry to the World Trade Organization (WTO) has been blocked for years by Georgia and other ex-Soviet states.

But US Trade Representative Susan Schwab and Russian Economic Development and Trade Minister German Gref said they had made progress in clearing obstacles to Russia's entry.

"We exchanged specific ideas about the remaining issues that must be resolved," Ms Schwab said in a statement after the meeting in Washington.

"We agreed that the two sides would continue to work towards resolving these issues so that Russia can join the WTO," she added.

Mr Gref said: "We made progress in clearing obstacles remaining in the way of Russia's accession to the WTO."

The Russian minister said one of the issues that still needed to be tackled was the "transparency" of Russia's laws on intellectual property.

Ms Schwab said she planned to visit Russia in April to continue the talks.

Russia has been trying to join the WTO since 1996, and US backing for its membership bid has been a key factor in the negotiations.

But Washington has become increasingly frustrated with Russia's lack of progress in adopting reforms to its trade policies, and there were reports last year that the US might withdraw its support for Russia's membership.

US President George W Bush and Russian President Vladimir Putin discussed the issue at a summit in Bratislava last year, and agreed to intensify efforts to try to resolve the remaining obstacles.

Given the recent deterioration in Russia's relations with Georgia, and the ongoing tensions between Moscow and ex-Soviet states, it appears unlikely that they will continue to stand in the way of Russia's WTO membership.

The latest round of talks on Russia's accession to the WTO has made progress, with negotiators finalizing several key issues, including Russia's commitment to limit agricultural subsidies and to open its markets to imports of meat and dairy products. 
Other issues that remained unresolved included the country's approach to intellectual property rights, with the US in particular concerned about Russia's implementation of WTO rules in this area. 
Nevertheless, both sides expressed satisfaction with the outcome of the talks, and Russia's accession to the WTO is now expected to be completed in the near future, subject to the approval of the organization's members.

Sony has unveiled its latest Playstation, called the PSP.

The hand-held machine can play games, but also delivers movies and music, and connects to the internet.

The PlayStation Portable (PSP) goes on sale in Japan on December 12, and in the US early next year.

It is being marketed as a machine for all ages and both sexes - Sony calls it the "Walkman of the 21st Century" - and the company is hoping it will give its Nintendo rivals a run for their money.

The PSP's technical capabilities are broadly in line with those of Nintendo's Game Boy Advance, but Sony's machine boasts a bigger screen, more memory and a wider range of features.

It is also significantly more expensive. In Japan, the PSP2000 will retail for around $300, while Nintendo's latest Game Boy Advance, the SP, sells for about $150.

Sony Computer Entertainment's (SCE) PlayStation division is banking on the PSP's versatility to win customers.

In addition to playing games, it will double as a portable DVD player and display photos and text documents stored on a memory stick.

It will also have wireless internet capability, enabling users to surf the web and send email on the move.

Sony has already signed up a number of content providers, including the BBC, and is in talks with a host of movie studios about supplying films for the device.

While Nintendo has sold tens of millions of Game Boy devices over the years, it does not have the same clout with Hollywood studios.

Sony also has a vast library of first-party games from its PlayStation console, as well as a strong stable of third-party software developers.

The PSP will go on sale in Japan on December 12, with a US launch planned for early 2005.

He added that the government would "consult on extending the debt relief initiative to countries making meaningful progress towards the Millennium Development Goals".

A £22.4m digital restoration of Pompeii's ruined amphitheatre has been unveiled at a ceremony in the ancient Roman city.

The project, funded by the Italian government, involved the installation of hundreds of polycarbonate panels and LEDs to recreate the original appearance of the arena's interior.

The work was completed ahead of this year's Cultural Olympics, which will hold an opening ceremony at the amphitheatre on 20 February.

"The arena's new layout is respectful of the past and represents a true innovation," said Culture Minister Giuliano Urbani.

The Culture Ministry and the mayor of Pompeii, Francesco Maria Mancini, saw off competition from around 100 international architects and designers to win the digital restoration contract.

Their design involved the construction of a raised platform and the installation of hundreds of polycarbonate panels and LEDs.

The polycarbonate panels weigh about seven tonnes, are powered by solar panels and can be remotely controlled from a computer.

They are divided into seven strips, each capable of displaying a different colour to reproduce the original appearance of the arena's interior, which was decorated in black and white marble.

"The idea is to give back to the arena its original colours," Mr Mancini told the ANSA news agency.

The LEDs can also reproduce the flicker of torches and the glint of swords used in historic reconstructions.

The arena's acoustics have also been improved to enhance the spectator experience during shows and concerts.

A cultural centre with an exhibition space, a bookshop, a cafe and a video-projection room has also been built.

The project has been completed ahead of this year's Cultural Olympics, which will hold an opening ceremony at the amphitheatre on 20 February.

It will also host a series of concerts featuring famous Italian singers, including Zucchero and Antonello Venditti.

Pompeii, 23km (14 miles) south-east of Naples, was buried under ash and pumice after the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in AD79.

The ruins of the city, which lie in an archaeological park, are one of Italy's most popular tourist attractions.

The ruins of Pompeii, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, have received a digital makeover. The project, known as "Pompeii Virtual", is a collaboration between the Ministry of Culture, the Superintendence of Pompeii, and the telecommunications company TIM. It involves the use of advanced digital technologies to create a virtual reconstruction of the ancient city.
 
The project utilizes holograms, augmented reality, and other interactive technologies to create a digital representation of Pompeii. This includes the creation of a digital map of the city, which allows users to explore the ruins in a way that is not possible with traditional methods. The map also includes detailed information about the city's history and architecture.

"Pompeii Virtual" also includes the creation of a digital museum, which will display artifacts and objects found in the ruins. The museum will use holograms and other interactive technologies to bring the artifacts to life.

The project has been met with mixed reactions from the public. Some have welcomed the addition of new technology to the ruins, while others have expressed concern about the potential impact on the site's historic integrity. UNESCO has also expressed concerns about the project, stating that it could potentially damage the ruins.

Police have long had the power to shut down pubs, restaurants and leisure centres to prevent crime and anti-social behaviour. But now they want the ability to shut down shops and businesses too.

Britain's biggest police force, the Metropolitan Police, says it wants to double the number of premises it can close. It says the powers are a vital tool in preventing serious crime. But businesses say they are being treated as a soft target.

The Met is seeking to add another 100 closure orders to its existing list of 173, which include pubs, clubs, restaurants and leisure centres. Superintendent Jane Scotchbrook says the Met is also seeking to extend the scope of the orders to include "any business where the nuisance or annoyance is caused".

"The legislation could be used for any business where we have evidence that it is causing a nuisance or annoyance to members of the public," she said.

"That could be pubs, bars, restaurants, it could be businesses that have a lot of comings and goings, causing anti-social behaviour. Any business could potentially be included."

She said the closure orders, introduced in 2003, had been a "really useful tool" but were under-used.

"They are certainly a last resort. Officers have to provide evidence that crime is being committed or is likely to be committed and the business owner does have the right to appeal."

But Tony Cohen, national officer for the Federation of Small Businesses, expressed concern about the plans.

"It seems to be the easy option to go for the small businesses which are struggling in any case, rather than going for the big supermarkets which have a lot of causes of crime near them," he said.

"They (small businesses) are not causing crime, they are not encouraging it and many are victimised by it. I think it is wrong to target them."

Supt Scotchbrook said the Met was also seeking to streamline the process which can take up to three months to obtain a closure order.

"That can be too long. By the time you have gone through that process, the problem business can be defunct because it has had its licence removed or because the crime has moved on," she said.

Police have increasingly been issuing warnings that pubs should have the power to shut earlier in order to crack down on drunk violence, anti-social behavior, and noise pollution. For years, police have been calling for stronger powers to tackle alcohol-related disorder in town and city centers, which have become no-go areas for many people living there. With the Government preparing to announce its plans to tackle alcohol-related violence, police chiefs are again urging ministers to introduce a nationwide closing time of 11 pm.

Acpo is calling for the licensing laws to be simplified and for all premises to be classed as either a bar or a restaurant, with all bars required to close at 11 pm.

While the idea of giving police the power to close pubs earlier has received some support, there are those who believe that it is not the answer to the problem. Some believe that the real problem lies in the fact that many young people now think it is acceptable to drink large quantities of alcohol and then behave badly, and that the answer lies in educating people about the effects of alcohol rather than in changing the licensing laws.

Others believe that the problem of alcohol-related violence is not confined to pubs and that the solution lies in tackling the issue of cheap, strong alcohol available in supermarkets and off-licenses. They argue that the easiest way to reduce alcohol-related violence is to increase the price of alcohol through higher taxes.

BBC News market editor Jack Cunningham is to stand down from his role later this year.

The American firm that bought the Lacroix label hopes its flashy designs will catch on in the United States.

Spam is more than just paper food: it's emails, adverts, and other unwanted intrusions into your life. But a new kind of spam comprises screensavers that flash up messages when a PC is left unattended. Security experts have now created a tool to fight back. However, they have now decided to abandon the project. Anti-spam screensaver scrapped

It all began when Russian spam firm Yandex.ru opened a competition for programmers to create tools blocking the spam screensavers. The winning entry was an open-source program called SkipScreen, created by developer Viktor Dolosha. The program let users create and share blacklists of spammy screensavers, and offered a way for the anti-spam screensaver to communicate with other computers in order to figure out which screensavers should be blocked.

However, the security experts at Kaspersky Lab decided to scrap the project before it even reached its beta stage. They said that while the screensavers may sometimes be a nuisance, they are not a major security threat and are much less harmful than other types of spam. Furthermore, the spam screensavers are often installed on computers without the owners' knowledge, which makes the anti-spam screensaver a rather controversial project.

Malaysia's securities commission has lifted a limit on the amount of equity that Islamic banks can hold in a single company.

The change is part of efforts to help Malaysia's Islamic finance industry grow and expand overseas.

For years, the country's two full-fledged Islamic banks have been restricted to holding a maximum of 15% of any company's shares.

That limit has now been removed for investment in firms related to Islamic activities.

And it has been raised to 30% for investment in firms not related to Islam.

The move is seen as a major boost for the Islamic finance industry, which has been growing rapidly in recent years.

It is expected to lead to more mergers and acquisitions as Islamic banks expand their operations.

The change was announced by Malaysia's Securities Commission on Monday.

It said the move would help Islamic banks "expand their investment banking activities, and enhance their role in the country's capital market".

Malaysia will remove a 30% limit on the share of Islamic banking assets for the country's banks, allowing them to grab a bigger slice of the sector as the government seeks to bolster financial inclusion.

The threshold, which has been in place since 2012, will be lifted from April 2022, Malaysia's finance ministry said in a statement on Monday.

Islamic banking follows religious principles such as bans on interest payments and pure monetary transactions. The finance ministry said the move would provide more options and enhance financial inclusion in the country.

Malaysia, a Muslim-majority nation, has seen a rapid increase in Islamic banking assets since they were first offered to the public in the 1990s. Sharia-compliant banking assets totalled 369.3 billion ringgit ($82.6 billion) as of September 2021, according to the central bank.

Banks will still be required to obtain prior approval from the central bank before their Islamic banking assets exceed the 30% threshold.

Washington: The US trade gap hit a record $725.8 billion in 2004, as a booming American economy sucked in imports at a faster pace than exports, official data showed on Friday. The Commerce Department reported that the gap between what the United States buys from abroad and what it sells to other countries widened by a revised 7.5 percent to a record $41.6 billion in December. November's trade gap was revised to $40.9 billion from the previously estimated $40.6 billion. For the year, the trade gap expanded by 12.7 percent to a record $725.8 billion, underscoring how much the US economy depends on foreign produced goods.

The trend, which has been exacerbated by the strong dollar, bodes ill for the US trade deficit, as Americans snap up foreign cars and consumer electronics, and rely on imported oil. A shrinking trade gap is seen as crucial to bringing down the large federal budget deficit. But with oil prices rising, the trade gap may get wider in 2005.

The gap with China, the fastest growing US trade partner, hit a record $124.9 billion, swelling by more than 23 percent in 2004. US trade officials say they are pressing Beijing to rein in its currency, which they claim is undervalued, making Chinese exports artificially cheap and US goods expensive in China. President Bush recently threatened to brand China a "currency manipulator" if it does not act to narrow the trade gap.

The US trade gap hit a record in 2004, with the deficit reaching $725.1 billion, as strong domestic demand continued to drive imports higher. The gap is up 17.8% from a year earlier, reaching its highest level since the Commerce Department started tracking the trade deficit in 1978. The rise in the trade deficit reflects a decline in exports rather than a fall in imports, as American households continued to boost their spending, particularly on cars and other big-ticket items. The strong dollar, which makes American products more expensive abroad, also contributed to the widening of the trade gap. For 2005, the trade deficit is expected to remain wide, as the US economy continues to expand and import demand remains strong.

In 2004, imports rose 0.9% to $1.431 trillion, while exports rose 0.1% to $707.9 billion. The trade gap reflected a widening in the deficit with China, which hit a record $124.4 billion in 2004. The deficit with Japan also hit a record, rising to $91.8 billion. The only bright spot in the trade picture was a narrowing of the deficit with Europe, which declined to $142.6 billion.

The strong trade deficit has led to concerns about the US current account deficit, which hit a record $425.6 billion in the third quarter of 2004. The current account deficit is the broadest measure of trade, including not only goods and services but also investment flows. A large current account deficit can be a sign of an economy that is consuming more than it produces, and therefore relying on foreign investment to fund its consumption. This can lead to concerns about the long-term sustainability of the trade deficit, as the foreign investment that finances it can be volatile and subject to reversals. However, with the US economy growing strongly and the dollar remaining strong, the trade deficit is expected to remain wide in the near future.

US insurer Marsh has cut more than 2,500 jobs in an effort to save money following its acquisition of rival Jardine Lloyd Thompson (JLT).

The company said the layoffs, which affect workers in the United States, United Kingdom and Canada, were "difficult but necessary" to position Marsh for success in the future.

The job cuts are equivalent to just under 3% of Marsh's global workforce.

"Our colleagues have dedicated their careers to Marsh, and they are the key to our success," Marsh chief executive John Doyle said in a statement.

Have hackers recruited your PC?

It's a painful fact that computers get slower as they age - but did you know that it's often malware that's to blame?

Security firm Avast has looked into the issue, and found that almost one in three Windows PCs is running slower than it should due to malicious programs that have made their way onto the machine.

And these are programs that the owners themselves have deliberately installed, largely through ignorance of the risks involved.

Avast's researchers found that the typical victim was exposed to an average of six different ad-displaying programs. These are often presented as useful downloads such as PDF readers or software to help you download other programs. In addition, four different programs were found to be mining virtual currencies such as Bitcoin on the users' computers, without their knowledge.

"Most people assume that these are isolated incidents, but our data shows that millions of people worldwide are actually affected," said Avast chief operations officer Ondrej Vlcek.

The infections themselves are usually caused by downloads that look useful or interesting, and are presented by legitimate-looking websites. However, the programs come with a hidden payload - advertising software that displays intrusive pop-up ads, or in some cases, cryptocurrency-mining programs.

These typically use up to half of the computer's processing power, and as a result, the machine starts to run more slowly.

And it's nearly always the case that these programs haven't been installed by the computer's owner. Instead, they've come bundled with another program that the user did want.

Security firm Kaspersky Lab recently reported similar findings - it said that a quarter of Windows 10 users had been affected. It also found that one in ten Android devices had been hit by crypto-mining software, and that the problem was getting worse.

So what can you do to avoid becoming a victim?

Firstly, get a good security package. Both Avast and Kaspersky offer free versions of their software that will protect you from such attacks.

Secondly, think twice before you install a program that you don't absolutely need. PDF readers and software download assistants may be useful, but they aren't essential.

And finally, if a website offers you a program for download, make sure you know what it is before you install it - and think about whether you really need it.

For several weeks now, the BBC has been investigating a new type of malware that's trying to turn your computer into a zombie. It invisibly takes control of your PC, and uses it to send out thousands of spam emails. Security experts have dubbed it Retadup, and they believe that more than half a million Windows machines have already been infected. It is thought to have been created by a group of Romanian hackers, and is being spread mainly across South East Asia and the Middle East. 

The malware is particularly difficult to remove, as it can survive a complete Windows reinstall. Security companies are still trying to understand how it infects machines in the first place. But they warn that once inside, Retadup is difficult to stop. 

Infected machines will be used to send out spam emails until the hackers decide to move on. "It's very much like a zombie movie," says one expert. "You have these zombies walking around, and they're controllable by someone else." Retadup appears to be the work of a well-resourced group, most likely a criminal gang. There are indications that it may be state-sponsored, but this is yet to be confirmed. 

For now, the advice is to ensure your anti-virus software is up to date, and that your operating system is fully patched. Retadup is a warning that even the most innocuous email can be a threat.

The European Parliament has ordered a reboot of its ambitious plans to create a unified patent system across Europe.

The assembly's legal affairs committee said the package, known as the unitary patent, would be rewritten to try to address critics' concerns.

These centred on the involvement of the European Court of Justice, the need for translation and whether patents would be valid in all EU states.

The legislation aims to simplify patent protection by allowing inventors to gain patent protection in a single, unified patent court.

The legislation has faced resistance from Italy, Spain and Poland. They have threatened to block the legislation unless changes are made.

The committee said it planned to split the unitary patent package into two bills.

One would deal with the unitary patent itself while the other would establish a new court to handle patent disputes, known as the Unified Patent Court (UPC).

Italian socialist Guido Sacconi, who led the work on the report, said the committee had decided to "take the bull by the horns".

"We have decided to modify the two pillars of the unitary patent package: the unitary patent itself and the Unified Patent Court," he said.

"The two elements will be split and this will allow us to proceed with the patent court and a bit later discuss the unitary patent."

The committee's proposal will now go before the full parliament for a vote.

If passed, it will then be up to the EU's 28 member states to decide whether to proceed with the plan.

Currently, inventors must apply for patent protection in each EU country where they want patent protection.

The court would have the power to rule on patent disputes for the entire EU, making it easier for inventors to protect their patents across the EU.

The court would be made up of a main branch, based in Paris, with branches in London and Munich.

It would have the power to rule on patent disputes for the entire EU, making it easier for inventors to protect their patents in multiple countries.

However, the project has faced several delays and setbacks over the years, and most recently, the UK's departure from the EU has thrown the project into doubt. The UK's Patent Office has said that it will not be joining the unitary patent regime, which has raised concerns about the project's viability.

In light of these developments, the EU's Intellectual Property Office (EUIPO) has announced that it will be rebooting the project, and has invited stakeholders to provide their input on how to move forward with the reform. The reboot of the EU patent reform is being seen as a positive step towards ensuring that the project is completed in a timely and effective manner. It is hoped that the renewed focus on the project will result in a successful and robust patent regime that supports innovation and competitiveness in the EU.

UK troops on Ivory Coast standby

British soldiers have arrived in the Ivory Coast former capital, Yamoussoukro, to help secure the area ahead of presidential elections.

It is the first time since 2004 that UK troops have been deployed to the region. 

The BBC's James Copnall in Yamoussoukro says the arrival of the British troops has been greeted with enthusiasm. 

Our correspondent says the soldiers have been approached for autographs and photographs, and crowds of onlookers have gathered to watch them train. 

The British force, comprising hundreds of engineers and medics, will be based at a decommissioned French base. 

They will provide engineering support to the 9,000-strong French force which is already in the area. France intervened in the country in 2004 to help the then-government regain control after a failed coup. 

The engineers will also be available to repair infrastructure in the area. 

The Ivory Coast has been divided into a government-controlled south and a rebel-held north since a failed coup in 2002. 

Following a peace deal in 2005, various deadlines have been set for reunifying the country but all have been missed. 

This time, President Laurent Gbagbo and rebel leader Guillaume Soro have agreed to create a unified government and hold elections by the end of the year.

The UK troops will support the French army's operation in the region

Their main job will be to carry out engineering work and help rebuild bridges, roads and other vital infrastructure destroyed in the last eight years.

The troops are also trained in medical emergencies and will be able to provide backup support to the French forces operating in the area.

They are due to carry out their first mission on Sunday, helping the French forces to secure the perimeter of a stadium in Abidjan, where the elections are scheduled to take place.

But the main task of the British force is to help secure the perimeter of the airport in Yamoussoukro, where the elections commission is due to count the votes. 

The airport has been chosen because it is seen as neutral territory. 

The British troops are expected to stay in the Ivory Coast for at least six months, but that could be extended depending on the situation. 

The operation is being funded by the UK Foreign Office, but the details of the mission have not been disclosed. 

UK foreign secretary, David Miliband, said the troops would help secure elections and provide humanitarian support.

The UK has sent hundreds of troops to the Ivory Coast to provide support for the United Nations peacekeeping operation in the country.

The move comes as tensions remain high between the government and opposition forces in the West African nation.

The UK troops will help to protect civilians and UN personnel in the event of a flare-up in violence. 

They will also help to provide security for the presidential election scheduled for next month.

Sales of high-definition televisions (HDTV) have not been as widespread as manufacturers and advertisers had hoped, and the question of a digital television standard change remains unanswered. 

Since high-definition television became available to consumers, sales have been lackluster. Leinster and Wasps also secured qualification as the top two teams in the other three pools.

The UK should give developing countries £5.5bn ($6.6bn) to fight AIDS, Gordon Brown has said.

The former prime minister made the call ahead of the G8 summit in Canada next week.

He said the "penny-pinching" of recent years had to stop if the world was to make a real impact on the disease.

And he said a comprehensive strategy was needed to tackle the virus, including affordable drugs, more prevention and a rollout of testing.

The UK has already spent £15bn on fighting the disease in the developing world. But Mr Brown said this was still not enough.

He said: "Diseases know no borders and in a world as interconnected as ours, neither can our efforts to combat them."

Mr Brown said he was encouraged by the progress that had been made in the last decade, with more than two million lives saved in Africa.

But he added: "We are now at a pivotal moment. Without greater action, AIDS could explode in the developing world.

"It is time for a comprehensive strategy on AIDS with affordable drugs, more prevention, rolling out testing and wider access to microinsurance for those who need it."

Mr Brown also warned that the world was facing a "catastrophic crisis" in relation to climate change.

And he called on the G8 to consider a tax on carbon emissions, which would force companies to take greater responsibility for the pollution they generate.

"We should be prepared to consider a tax on all forms of carbon emissions," he said.

"That would be a more effective incentive for people to reduce their carbon emissions than a voluntary approach."

The UK should commit to a joint aid programme with the US and other G7 countries to fund global education, stop HIV and wipe out malaria, Gordon Brown has said.

The former UK prime minister said it was time for Britain to return to the forefront of international efforts to eradicate preventable diseases.

In a speech to the Centre for Global Development in Washington, he will call for a £5.5bn fund to tackle Aids, tuberculosis and malaria.

Mr Brown said that it was the "height of hypocrisy" for any government to talk about national security while failing to tackle diseases.

The fund would be used to target illnesses which have made a comeback due to coronavirus lockdowns and disruptions to health services around the world, according to the proposed plan.

It would include £1.7bn for a national plan to end Aids by 2030, £1.2bn for a global fund to fight tuberculosis, and £2bn for the elimination of malaria.

The UK's new terrorism prevention and investigation measures, which give authorities wide-ranging stop-and-search powers and allow suspects to be detained without charge, face their first test in court.

The measures - part of the government's new counter-terrorism strategy - were unveiled by Home Secretary Theresa May in February.

They are being challenged in the High Court by two men, who are arguing that they violate the UK's human rights laws.

The men - one from Lancashire, the other from Dorset - are seeking a judicial review of the measures, claiming they undermine the "fundamental rights of free citizens".

Their case is being supported by human rights group Liberty and public law experts from Bhatt Murphy solicitors.

The men, who cannot be named for legal reasons, are seeking a declaration that the measures are unlawful and should not be enforced.

The Prevention of Terrorism Act 2005 (PTA), which the men successfully challenged in the High Court in 2011, was due to expire in July.

The new measures replaced the PTA with a set of temporary stop-and-search powers and a new regime of "investigative detention" - which allows suspects to be held for up to 14 days without being charged.

The men's legal team claim that the new measures breach the European Convention on Human Rights - which protects rights to liberty, security and a fair trial.

They also argue that the powers are too broad and give police the ability to stop people at random without reasonable grounds for suspicion.

The judicial review, which begins on Monday, is expected to last three days.

The men's lawyers will argue that the measures do not provide "sufficient clarity as to the circumstances in which the new powers may be exercised, and sufficient safeguards as to how they may be exercised".

They will also claim there is no effective independent oversight of the new regime and that the measures breach the right to a fair trial.

A Home Office spokesperson said: "The government is determined to tackle terrorism and protect the public.

"But as the Court of Appeal recognised when it gave the go-ahead for these vital powers, there are strong safeguards in place - including independent oversight by a senior judge, Code of Practice and a new Stop and Search Scrutiny Panel."

Today's vote is seen as a test of the government's counter-terrorism strategy and could indicate how the rest of the plan will be received by lawmakers.

The "safer ID" system will rely on physical tokens, such as a mobile phone, as well as biometric data, such as a fingerprint.

The idea is that passwords - easily hacked or forgotten - will become a thing of the past.

Apple has released a Band Aid version of the song Do They Know It's Christmas? for sale on iTunes, 25 years after it was first recorded.

The track features an all-star line-up of musicians including One Direction, Elbow, Emeli Sandé, Bastille, Paloma Faith, the Darkness and Ed Sheeran.

The original version of the song was released in 1984 to raise money for famine in Ethiopia.

That song featured artists including Bono, Phil Collins, Boy George and Bob Geldof.

The new version of the track was organised by Geldof following a conversation with Sheeran.

iTunes said all proceeds from the track, which costs 99p to buy, would go to the Ebola appeal fund via the Band Aid Trust.

A statement from the company said: "As with the original track, 100% of the publisher's share of the proceeds from 'Do They Know It's Christmas?' 2014 will be donated to the Band Aid Trust to support the fight against Ebola."

The song was released on Monday.

Since then it has been the most downloaded track in the UK, Ireland, Belgium, Finland and the Netherlands, according to iTunes.

In the UK it has been number one in the iTunes chart for most of the week.

The only other song to have reached the top of the chart and be available for digital download is Queens of the Stone Age, who donated profits from their song I Appear Missing to the Red Cross relief effort in Australia, which was affected by floods recently.

Other songs that have reached number one in the UK and been available for download include Lonely Boy by The Black Keys, which was released for sale on the same day it charted at the top in October 2011.

And in December 2012, Little Mix's version of Cannonball became the fastest-selling X Factor single ever when it was made available for download after the weekend the group won the show.

Do They Know It's Christmas? is not the only way musicians have been helping to fight Ebola.

US rock band Foo Fighters recorded a cover of the Rolling Stones song Miss You with Rick Rubin to raise money for the fight against Ebola.

That song was made available for purchase on 7 November and within 24 hours it had raised more than $1m (£570,000), with all proceeds going to the Red Cross.

The track, which features musicians including Ed Sheeran, One Direction and Paloma Faith, went on sale on Thursday.

Nissan has named its co-CEO, Makoto Uchida, as the company's next chief executive officer.

Mr Uchida will take up his new role on 1 December, replacing the ousted Carlos Ghosn.

The automaker's nomination committee chose Mr Uchida over two other internally-nominated candidates.

In a statement, Nissan said its board of directors had voted unanimously to appoint Mr Uchida.

Mr Uchida has worked at Nissan for more than 30 years and was named co-CEO in February this year, alongside Hiroto Saikawa.

The announcement ends months of speculation about who would replace Mr Ghosn after his arrest in November 2018.

The 64-year-old is facing charges of financial misconduct in Japan and has been detained since his arrest. He denies any wrongdoing.

In a statement, Nissan said its new CEO's priorities would be "to address the challenges of the global market, to manage the Nissan Revival Plan with profitability and strengthen corporate governance."

Last month, Nissan reported its first annual loss in a decade as it struggled with the fallout from the Ghosn scandal and weaker sales.

The automaker said it had booked a $6.2bn loss for the year to March, its biggest ever annual loss.

Nissan has named its successor to former chief executive Carlos Ghosn, who was ousted following his arrest over financial misconduct charges in 2018.

The appointment of Nissan's new chief executive Makoto Uchida marks a new era for the car maker, which has been struggling since the departure of Mr Ghosn.

In a briefing, Mr Uchida, who was a unanimous choice of the Nissan board, said he would "take a fresh start".

"This is an exciting time for Nissan. This is my first time as a chief executive officer, but I'm not looking at this as a starting point. We're starting a new chapter, but we have a long history of being a strong company," he said.

Mr Uchida has been with Nissan for two decades and most recently served as its chief operating officer. He was seen as a safe choice to lead the company during its turnaround efforts. 

In October, Nissan reported its first annual profit in three years, buoyed by cost cuts, stronger sales and a favourable exchange rate.

However, the company has struggled to redefine itself since the departure of Mr Ghosn, who was seen as a charismatic leader that helped turn Nissan around.

Since his arrest, Nissan has undergone a period of instability, with the company's sales and profits falling and its brand image suffering.

In December 2018, Mr Ghosn was arrested in Tokyo on charges of under-reporting his salary at Nissan over the course of a decade and was ousted as chairman of the car maker the following month. 

He has denied the charges against him. 

In 2019, he fled Japan to Lebanon, where he has been granted citizenship. 

Mr Uchida said he was not concerned about any challenges that may arise from Mr Ghosn's controversial legacy.

"We have a 100-year history and we have weathered many storms. This can be a turning point for us," he said. 

"We have a lot to learn from the past, but we do not need to worry about the past. We need to think about the future and make good decisions moving forward." 

Mr Uchida's appointment is the latest in a series of changes at Nissan, which has seen its leadership team overhauled in recent years. 

In June, Nissan named its first external board member, Masakazu Toyoda, a former chairman of Toray Industries, as its new chair.
