Rory McIlroy won the indoor 800m title for St Patrick's Academy in Armagh on Wednesday.

The BBC Sport NI reporter Ryan Sidley tweeted a video of the event, with the caption "Rory McIlroy wins indoor 800m title for St Pat's Armagh!!"

McIlroy, who is from Holywood in County Down, is better known for his prowess in golf.

The 29-year-old is a four-time major winner, most recently securing the Wells Fargo Championship in May 2021.

He has 19 PGA Tour titles to his name and has won three European Tour titles, too.

On Tuesday, McIlroy pulled out of the Abu Dhabi HSBC Championship as he recovers from a hairline fracture to his rib.

Rory McIlroy produced a sparkling final round to win the BBC Sports Personality of the Year's 800m indoor title by a street at the Arena Birmingham on Saturday.
The world number two from Northern Ireland was in a class of his own as he raced to victory in a superb time of one minute 46.07 seconds.
The 27-year-old's time was the fourth fastest in the world this year and fastest in Europe as he beat England's Andrew Pozzi into second by 1.21 seconds.
"I am a bit rusty so to get out there and run sub-48 seconds is great," McIlroy told BBC Sport.

"I wanted to get into the 45-second range but I haven't run that fast since 2016."
McIlroy, who described himself as "rusty" after his opening heat on Friday, was keen to stress that he did not travel to Birmingham for the event just to make up the numbers.

"I don't want to be a also-ran and come down and run slow times," he added.
"I am competitive and even more so when I feel I am not in shape. I want to try to execute the races and get the most out of myself.

"I have played golf competitively for 15 years and know how to deal with that pressure but this is different. I feel like I am learning and it is exciting."

Rescue hope for Borussia Dortmund

Borussia Dortmund have been boosted by the news that midfielder Mo Dahoud has signed a new contract with the club until 2025.

Dahoud, 26, was out of contract at the end of the season and had been linked with a move to Premier League clubs Chelsea and Manchester United.

But the former Wolfsburg and Monchengladbach player has signed a deal that includes an option for an additional year.

"Borussia Dortmund are a huge club, we have an incredible team and fantastic supporters," said Dahoud.

"I've been at the club since 2015 and have always felt at home here. I'm happy to be part of this family for two more years and, beyond that, I hope that we will achieve a lot together."

Dortmund chief executive Hans-Joachim Watzke said: "Mo Dahoud has been with the club for six-and-a-half years and, together with Marco Reus, is the longest-serving player in the team.

"He has developed fantastically since joining the club as a young player and has become an absolute mainstay in central midfield. We are delighted that he will continue to be available to us in the coming years."

Dahoud has made 215 appearances for Dortmund, scoring 15 goals and providing 25 assists.

This season he has struggled for game time under new manager Edin Terzic and has made just six appearances in the Bundesliga.

But he has been ever-present in the club's successful run in the Champions League, starting all five matches so far.

The midfielder signed a three-and-a-half-year contract when he joined the club in January 2015 from Monchengladbach for a fee of about £12m.

He has also been linked with Paris St-Germain and Napoli in recent months.

Dortmund are fifth in the Bundesliga, four points behind Bayern Munich, who occupy the last qualification place for the Champions League.

They are also through to the last 16 of this season's Champions League, where they will face Chelsea.

Borussia Dortmund have been given hope that they may be able to rescue the season after reaching the last 16 of the Europa League and moving up to third in the Bundesliga.

A 1-0 win at Mainz on Saturday was their sixth successive league victory, meaning they are now nine points behind leaders Bayern Munich, who drew 0-0 at home to Cologne.

And on Thursday, a 1-0 win in Italy over Lazio means they go through to the last 16 of Europe's secondary competition as Group F winners.

"We have our goals in the Bundesliga and the DFB-Pokal, and now we've achieved our first goal in the Europa League," said Dortmund captain Marco Reus, who scored the winner in Rome.

Manager Edin Terzic added: "It wasn't easy today, we were without Jude Bellingham, Mahmoud Dahoud and Dan-Axel Zagadou. We had a lot of young players in the squad. It was an important step for the team."

Dortmund's hopes of retaining their title looked over in early November after losing to Bayern Munich, with the champions 11 points clear after 14 games.

But since then they have kept four clean sheets in six games, with goalkeeper Marwin Hitz, 35, playing every minute of that run.

"The team in front of me doesn't concede many chances in a game and that's why we've been able to keep so many clean sheets," said Hitz, who was voted man of the match after the win in Mainz.

"We're on a good run at the moment but we're not getting carried away. We've got a tough game coming up next weekend and we're focusing on that now."

That tough game is at home to second-placed Union Berlin on Saturday, with the capital club two points ahead of Dortmund having played two games more.

Spain's Carlos Moya became emotional after his side won the Davis Cup in Madrid on Sunday.

The 41-year-old former world number one, who was making his comeback to the Spain team after a 10-year absence, was seen fighting back the tears as he celebrated.

Spain defeated Canada 2-0 in the final, winning their sixth title overall.

Moya, who won the tournament three times with Spain in 2000, 2004 and 2008, was a late replacement for Rafael Nadal, who missed the event through injury.

The world number six sustained a abdominal muscle injury during his semi-final loss to Denis Shapovalov at the Rogers Cup in Montreal last month.

"It's been a difficult week, the emotions are amazing," Moya told reporters after the match.

"It's the public here, the energy of this place. We have a great team, incredible players. We knew it would be a difficult task without Rafa, we had to rally together."

Moya was handed a wildcard by Spain captain Sergi Bruguera to make his comeback and played a key role in his country's success, winning all eight of his singles and doubles rubbers.

The Spaniard teamed up with Nadal in a thrilling doubles victory over Shapovalova and Vasek Pospisil in the semi-final, which lasted almost five hours.

Moya was also a crucial calming influence on Nadal during his tense victory over Shapovalova in the singles rubber.

Britain's Cameron Norrie and Dan Evans sealed the team's victory against Australia after defeating Nick Kyrgios and Alex de Minaur in the doubles decider.

Evans fought back from a break down in the first set against De Minaur before winning seven straight games to take the tie to a deciding rubber.

Norrie and Evans secured the decisive break in the third set to wrap up a memorable victory.

Britain's victory came after Australia's John Peers and Luke Saville defeated Joe Salisbury and Neal Skupski 4-6 6-7 (5-7) 6-3 6-4 6-7 (4-7) to take the tie to the final day.

Earlier, Evans defeated De Minaur 6-2 7-6 (7-3) after Norrie had beaten Kyrgios 6-2 6-4 in the day's opening singles rubbers.

Belle and Sebastian have been named the best Scottish band in a poll of music retailers. The Glasgow group - who released their first album, Tigermilk, in 1996 - received the most votes in a poll of 70 Scottish music retailers, conducted by Scottish music magazine, The List. The magazine's editor, Rory Foster, said all the bands in the top 20 have had an impact on the Scottish music scene. "The fact that the poll was conducted by the people who know most about Scottish music, the retailers, makes me very confident that we have got it right," he said. "And the good news for everyone is that all of these bands are still going strong, with new albums in the pipeline."

Foster said it was encouraging that the poll's top 20 included several newer acts, such as Glasgow indie rockers, Franz Ferdinand, and that no band had dominated the top of the chart since the days of eclectically-inspired rockers, Travis. "There's no doubt that Belle and Sebastian are revered by the dealers, but so are a lot of other bands," he said. "There isn't one band that the dealers think are brilliant and are selling in huge numbers. "  

Travis topped the chart in 1997 and 1998, and came second last year. This year the Glasgow band came sixth with their recent album, The Man Who, while Dundee's Gomez came second, down from first place last year. Glasgow's Idlewild came third, with Moby, who recently opened a restaurant in Edinburgh, in fifth place. Foster added that female-fronted bands were well represented in this year's chart. "There are lots of great female musicians out there at the moment and quite a few featured in our poll," he said. "Helene Rohner from the Delgados is possibly the most influential female musician in Scotland at the moment."

Rohner, who writes the group's lyrics and plays the guitar, emerged victorious in a recent battle with the group's record label, Warners, after complaining that the label were not doing enough to promote her as a songwriter. She recently signed a new deal with Warners and is currently working on the follow-up to the Delgados' 1998 album, The Great Eastern.

The four-piece, comprising Martin Keena, Gerard Black, Mick Slaven and Stuart Kidd, only play exclusive shows and private events. This is absolutely brilliant and just testament to the strength of the band, the musicianship, the songs and the performances.”

Second place in the poll was taken by Biffy Clyro, who have recently been nominated for the 2022 Mercury Prize for their album ‘The Myth of Happily Ever After’. England coach Steve McNamara has welcomed the return of James Beattie to the Great Britain training camp ahead of this week's Test against New Zealand.

Beattie missed Saturday's tour opener against France - which Britain won 22-18 - because his wife gave birth to a baby boy on Friday.

Beattie could feature in a much-changed side, with McNamara considering making as many as 14 changes to his team.

Britain's three-match tour concludes on Saturday with a Test against Australia in London.

The Sound of Music, one of the world's best-loved musicals, is returning to its roots.

The Salzburg Festival in Austria will host a production of the show, starring real-life sisters Maria and Elisabeth von Trapp.

It will be the first time the musical has been performed in the city where it is set.

The show will run from July to September 2024.

The von Trapp family story, on which the musical is based, is an Austrian institution.

Captain von Trapp married Maria Augusta Kutschera – the woman who inspired the role of Maria – in 1927.

The musical was written by Rodgers and Hammerstein, and premiered in 1965 on Broadway. It is one of the most successful musicals of all time.

It was turned into a highly successful 1965 film, starring Julie Andrews as Maria.

The musical will be performed at the Salzburg Festival, which runs from July through September each year, and is one of the most important festivals in the world for classical music and opera.

"She had taken the substance on a doctor's recommendation and had given all the medical documentation to do with this," said Alexander Djabirov.

According to the Russian Anti-Doping Agency (Rusada), two-time Grand Slam champion Svetlana Kuznetsova has failed a drugs test. 

The Rusada executive committee confirmed the news on Tuesday, with the committee stating that the presence of a prohibited substance had been found in a sample given by the Russian tennis star. 

In a statement, Rusada said the detected substance was trimetazidine, a medication used to treat angina and other heart conditions. It is a substance listed as a S4 stimulant, and as such, it is prohibited by the World Anti-Doping Agency (Wada). 

Kuznetsova was informed of the adverse analytical finding on 9 March, but the results have only recently been released by Rusada. Through her lawyer, Kuznetsova claimed the violation was due to her ingestion of medication prescribed by her doctor to help with a respiratory infection she was suffering from at the time. 

The lawyer stated that Kuznetsova gained no sporting advantage from the use of the substance, and that a confidential settlement had been offered by Wada, which was accepted by the Russian tennis star. 

As a result of the violation, Kuznetsova has been banned from tennis for two years, starting from the date of her sample collection on 25 January 2023. 

The ban will see Kuznetsova miss the French Open, Wimbledon, and the US Open in 2023, as well as the 2024 French Open. 

The Russian tennis star has won two Grand Slam singles titles during her career, the 2004 US Open and the 2009 French Open, as well as achieving a doubles Grand Slam title at the 2016 French Open. 

Kuznetsova's ban is one of several doping-related scandals to have affected the world of tennis in recent years. Other players to have been found guilty of doping violations include Novak Djokovic, Marin Čilić, and Maria Sharapova.

Worldcom's former chief executive has told the BBC that he did not know about false accounting practices at the company before they were revealed in 2002.

Bernie Ebbers said he had left the company's books alone after selling its telecommunications division four years earlier.

Mr Ebbers is serving a 25-year prison sentence for his part in the $11bn (£7bn) accounting scandal.

He spoke to the BBC's Panorama as part of a documentary on the scandal, which will be aired on Monday.

Last week, former Worldcom accountant Troy Normand told Panorama that he had warned Mr Ebbers that the company was using fraudulent accounting practices to inflate its profits, but that the executive had ignored him.

"I met with Bernie Ebbers in December 2000 and I told him that I thought that the company was doing some creative accounting," he said.

"He laughed out loud and he told me that he didn't know anything about that. He said 'You know, I sell multi-million dollar businesses all the time and I've never had to doctor the books to make a sale.'"

In an exclusive interview from prison, Mr Ebbers told the BBC that Mr Normand's claims were not true.

"I had nothing to do with the accounting. I sold the operating company four years before all this happened," he said.

"The operating company had nothing to do with the accountants. I didn't deal with the accountants - I never even saw the books."

Mr Ebbers admitted that he had signed off on some of the accounting practices, but said he had not looked at them in detail or questioned them because he had trusted the people who had presented them to him.

He said he had only found out that something was wrong when Worldcom's shares crashed in 2002.

"I was stunned. I couldn't believe it," he said.

"I thought, 'How could anybody manipulate the stock market like this?' I was shocked. I was devastated."

The £24.4m ($32.5m) documentary, entitled The Fall of Worldcom, will be aired on BBC One at 2100 GMT on Monday.

Bernie Ebbers, the former boss of collapsed telecoms firm Worldcom, has claimed he left accounting books alone in the years leading up to the firm's collapse.

Mr Ebbers, who is serving a 25-year prison sentence for his part in the fraud that brought down the firm, said he did not interfere with the work of accountants.

Speaking to the Wall Street Journal, he said "I didn't touch the books", and that he had trusted senior accountants. 

The former boss, who was once ranked as the second best-paid boss in the US, said he was "comfortable" with how much he was paid.

Prosecutors said he took home $408m ($512m in today's money) in salary and stock options during his time at the firm. 

Mr Ebbers protested his innocence up until he was sent to prison and continues to do so, despite being found guilty in 2005 of engineering a $11bn accounting fraud.

The Journal interviewed him at Louisiana's Angola prison, where he is serving his sentence. 

He argued that he has served enough time behind bars - more than three times what white-collar criminals typically get for fraud. 

Mr Ebbers claimed he should be released immediately with residence and reporting requirements, akin to probation.

Hanna Valickova and Martin Klizan defeated the United States' Coco Gauff and Jack Sock in the deciding doubles to send Slovakia through to the final of the Hopman Cup in Perth.

It was the second year in a row that Gauff and Sock had gone down in the mixed doubles, having been beaten by Switzerland's Belinda Bencic and Roger Federer 12 months ago.

Slovakia will face either Switzerland or Spain in Saturday's final after their group encounter ended in a thrilling 3-3 tie.

Valickova and Klizan, who had combined to win the opening singles rubbers against the US on Monday, proved too strong in the deciding doubles, winning 6-3 7-6 (7-4).

That sealed a come-from-behind 2-1 victory for Slovakia, who were facing elimination after Gauff had defeated Valickova in the women's singles.

The 18-year-old American, who is ranked 23rd in the world, was too strong for her 93rd-ranked opponent, winning 6-1 6-3 to level the tie having lost the opening singles against Gauff.

Earlier, Sock had got the US off to a winning start with a comprehensive 6-3 6-4 victory over Klizan in the men's singles.

New training aid could help golfers improve their swing by enabling them to see and feel the correct movements.

To achieve a better golf swing, you need to maintain flexibility and strengthen the right muscles. However, it can be difficult for beginners to coordinate the movements needed for a perfect swing.

Now help could be at hand thanks to a new training aid that has been compared to having a second pair of hands.

The Moving Mobile helps golfers coordinate the sequence of movements needed for a perfect swing and offers immediate feedback on their posture and position.

 Tested by BBC London's golf enthusiast Justin Webb, the device could help frustrated golfers who are struggling to master the moves needed to hit the ball long and straight.

Initially, it looks like an ordinary club but closer inspection reveals a flexible shaft about two-thirds of the way down.

This moves like a fishing rod, allowing you to feel a slight resistance as you hit imaginary balls.

The heavier end of the shaft must be held firmly with the left hand and the movement of the shaft then helps get the feel of the correct swing motion.

"It's about getting the sensation of the correct move and feel for a better swing," said Peter Dawson, the director of the Golf College in Hertfordshire, who demonstrated the device to BBC London.

"It helps get the feeling of the weight and the timing of the backswing and helps get the transition going from the backswing to the downswing."

The Moving Mobile can help improve a golfer's swing tempo, ensuring it is not too fast or too slow. It can also be used as a warm-up tool before playing a round of golf.

"It's a way of getting that feeling of tempo and rhythm back into the hands," said Mr. Dawson.

"It's a bit like having an extra pair of hands to help you."

The concept is similar to shadow swinging - where you pretend to hit balls to get the correct muscle memory - but offers more feedback on any mistakes.

And unlike a normal club it does not feel unnatural as you can actually feel the shaft bending as you make a swing.

Mr. Dawson said it was particularly useful for helping with the transition phase of the swing - the point where many beginners go wrong.

A new device, which attaches to a golf club, can help improve your swing by providing real-time feedback on speed, tempo, and angle of the club. The mobile phone-sized tool, called the "Swing Catalyst," could help golfers fix their swing and lower their score on the green. 

The catalyst is a device that attaches to the end of a golf club, where the clubhead and shaft meet. After a swing, the golfer can view the results on their smartphone or tablet. The device sells for about $399 and is available for preorder. 

The Swing Catalyst works using a combination of sensors. First, a 3D sensor that measures clubhead speed as well as face angle and path. Second, an HD video system allows golfers to see their swing in action. Third and optionally, a pressure mat which captures the golfer's weight shift, centered on the ball, throughout the swing. 

Together, the club attachment, video, and pressure mat provide golfers with information to help them improve their swing. For example, the device might tell a golfer that their club is slowing down as it makes contact with the ball or that their swing is off-center. Video footage of the swing combines with the sensor data to show what the golfer is doing wrong and offers tips on how to fix it.

The Swing Catalyst is not the only device available to help golfers fix their swings. Other devices include the GolfSense and the Zepp Golf, which both attach to a golfer's glove. These devices cost considerably less than the Swing Catalyst, but according to Golf.com, the Catalyst "appears to be the first device to combine such a high-speed camera with the other metrics." 

Phil Akers, the managing director of GolfGear, the UK distributor for Swing Catalyst, said the device could help any golfer, regardless of ability. 

"It's a great tool for golfers to understand their own swings and for coaches to be able to explain to their students what is happening and how to improve it," said Akers.

The men's champion at the 2019 US Open - who had been scheduled to play in Melbourne on Monday - said the clot had been "triggered by a recent medication for a liver condition that I have been treating".

Liverpool manager Jürgen Klopp has said he is not concerned by the club's recent poor form, with the team winning just one of their last six matches in all competitions.

The Reds were beaten 3-0 by lowly side Leicester City in the Premier League on Tuesday, with the Foxes scoring all three goals in the last 16 minutes.

It has cut Liverpool's once-commanding lead at the top of the table to four points, with Manchester City now having a game in hand.

"Would I be concerned if we had not had these kinds of problems in the past? Maybe," said the German.

"But we have had problems in the past and we solved them. Not immediately, but eventually we solved them.

"We are now in a situation where we have to solve them again and that is what we will do."

Klopp said the team's struggles were part of a "development" and that he was not worried about their title chances.

"I am completely relaxed, because I know that we have 18 games to go and lots of points to get," he added.

"I know how the players feel, I know about the squad and I know we have space to improve."

Liverpool face Bayern Munich in the last 16 of the Champions League, with the first leg taking place at Anfield on Tuesday.

The Reds beat the German champions 3-1 at home in September, but went on to lose the return match 5-0.

Klopp said he was expecting a tough game, adding: "They are in a good moment and they are an experienced team."

Liverpool manager Jürgen Klopp admitted his side were not at their best after they scraped into the last 16 of the Champions League despite a 3-1 defeat away to Napoli on the night. 

The Reds won the tie 4-2 on aggregate, thanks to their thrilling 4-0 win in the first leg at Anfield last month but they struggled in Italy, despite taking the lead through Mohamed Salah's early penalty. 

Napoli substitute Lorenzo Insigne scored twice in the second half – the second from the penalty spot – before Diego Demme's late free-kick squeezed in at the near post to seal the Italians' victory. 

"We needed luck for the result and we didn't get it," Klopp said. "We should have been more confident on the ball, we didn't do enough to get the result we needed. 

"We were not really brilliant tonight but we got through and that is all that counts. I am happy for the boys that we are through but the performance could have been better." 

The German added: "I think we felt the intensity of the situation and wanted it not to be intense any more by trying to keep the ball or whatever, just try to play through the lines and stuff like this. 

"It didn't work out and made the game even more intense. We were not calm enough to get through this. It was a difficult game, they played like Italians usually play, very committed, good organisation, good structure, and then quick transitions." 

Group winners Liverpool will discover their last-16 opponents when the draw is made on Monday, with the first leg to be played on February 16.

The bank held the rate at 4.75% today. But it hinted that a cut was likely in the coming months, if the economic outlook deteriorates.

At midday, the bank's monetary policy committee announced its decision.

It said the outlook for UK inflation was "broadly in line" with its projection in May.

Since May, the pound has fallen by more than 5% against the dollar, partly due to the uncertainty over the Brexit deal.

That would usually suggest that the Bank of England might raise interest rates to keep a lid on inflation.

But the Bank said the drop in the value of the pound had helped keep inflation lower than expected. It said it was "reasonable" to expect that softer growth would mean softer inflation.

It also said that global trade tensions had intensified since May, which was likely to affect UK financial conditions.

"The Committee therefore judges that the current stance of monetary policy is appropriate," it said.

"But the Committee will continue to monitor the incoming data, and stands ready to adjust monetary policy accordingly to meet its remit."

In other words, the Bank is keeping its options open.

The Bank of England has held interest rates at 4.75% today, despite speculation in recent weeks that it could rise. The decision comes as a surprise to most economists, as the consensus was that the bank would increase rates in order to combat rising prices. However, the bank has decided to hold rates in order to assess the impact of previous rate hikes on the economy. 

The Bank of England's decision comes as a relief to many homeowners and businesses, as it will keep borrowing costs down. However, it may also come as a disappointment to those who were hoping for a further increase in rates in order to curb inflation. 

The bank has said that it will continue to monitor the economy and make further decisions on interest rates based on incoming data. This could suggest that further rate hikes are still on the table, and that the bank is not done in its efforts to curb inflation.

US employers added 233,000 jobs in May, according to the country's Bureau of Labor Statistics.

The figure was well above most economists' expectations.

And job growth for the previous two months was higher than first thought, the bureau said.

The data showed that the number of unemployed people looking for work decreased by 342,000 to 6.1 million.

The unemployment rate remained unchanged at 3.6% percent, near a 50-year low.

Average hourly earnings increased by 5.2% year-on-year, unchanged from April.

Price increases appear to be moderating, raising hopes that the Fed might pause its interest rate increases.

The jobs figures are good news for President Joe Biden, whose approval ratings have risen in recent months.

The number of people in the US who are employed or looking for work rose unexpectedly in September, official data shows. The labour market was expected to weaken after a burst of hiring in August as coronavirus cases surged, but data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) showed further gains in the unemployment rate. The rate rose to 4.8% in September from 4.5% in August, according to the BLS data released on Wednesday. Meanwhile, the number of non-farm payrolls increased by 194,000 in September, beating estimates of about 155,000. 

In the report, BLS noted that there was a decline in government jobs last month, with state and local education seeing job losses. But the worst of the layoffs appeared to be over, as most school districts have started the new academic year and hired staff. The report also showed that the number of jobs in the food services and drinking industry declined, as well as in the arts, entertainment, and recreation industry. 

The report was released as Federal Reserve officials concluded their latest two-day policy meeting. The central bank said it would soon start reducing its monthly bond purchases, but held off on raising interest rates, saying it was still assessing the impact of the Covid-19 pandemic on the labour market. 

The yield on the 10-year US Treasury note rose following the jobs data release, reaching 1.6% ahead of the Fed's decision.

Middlesbrough chairman Steve Gibson has received a "verbal offer" to buy a controlling stake in the club from an investor group fronted by former Brazil international midfielder Juninho.

The offer, revealed by Gibson at Boro's annual general meeting on Thursday, is thought to be in the region of £16m.

And, such is the urgency of the offer, that Juninho wants to meet with outgoing chairman Gibson as soon as possible.

Gibson revealed that he had received a letter from the 37-year-old, who is currently sporting director at French club Lyon, on Wednesday - 24 hours before the AGM.

"It was a verbal offer to buy the football club. That's as far as it has gone," Gibson told BBC Radio Tees.

"They are looking to come into the football club sooner rather than later. I have told them that I have up to 27 June and they want to meet as soon as possible.

"They are an investor group, Juninho is the front man, and they are looking to make their money work for them.

"They are serious people, they are not speculators, and that is from our lawyers' advice."

This latest development comes in the wake of Gibson confirming that he has had a £25m offer for the club from an Arab consortium.

The Tees Valley native, who saved the club from liquidation in 1986 and has been at the helm ever since, confirmed he had received the approach last week - and that it was "too big an offer to turn down".

But he revealed that the consortium had insisted on doing business with the incoming chairman, and not him.

That led to him tendering his resignation, along with the rest of the board, which was accepted by the club's shareholders at the AGM.

But Gibson, while no longer chairman, will remain on the board pending the conclusion of talks with both parties.

"There is no doubt the offer from the Arab consortium is a good offer, it's a serious offer and it's one that has to be considered seriously," he added.

"There is no doubt that the offer that has come in from Juninho and his group is also one that has to be considered seriously.

"I have a duty to explore both these options for the long-term future of the football club. This club has been my life and will continue to be my life for as long as I'm involved in it."

Middlesbrough chairman Steve Gibson has received a "verbal offer" from former England manager Steve McClaren to return to the Championship club as coach.
  
McClaren, who has been out of work since being sacked by QPR in April, is keen to team up with former Middlesbrough captain Jonathan Woodgate, who was appointed head coach on a three-year deal last week. 

It is understood that Woodgate has been keen to bring McClaren in since being appointed and that the former Nottingham Forest and Derby County manager would be happy to work under him.

The 57-year-old fell out with Gibson during his first spell as Middlesbrough manager, but the chairman has always maintained that he did not want to get in the way of McClaren furthering his career.

McClaren won promotion to the Premier League with Middlesbrough in 05-06, finishing the season as runners-up to Champions League qualifiers Fulham.

He left the following season with the Teessiders lying seventh in the top flight, but subsequently had spells with FC Twente, VfL Wolfsburg, Nottingham Forest and Derby County before joining Queens Park Rangers in 2018.

The EU's competition commissioner, Neelie Kroes, has given the go-ahead for an investigation into whether Italy has given Alitalia illegal state aid.

The probe follows the Italian government's announcement that it is to pump another €300m ($430m; £260m) into the loss-making airline.

Ms. Kroes said there were "serious doubts" about the investment being compliant with the EU rules on state aid.

She said the decision to open the investigation did not prejudge the outcome.

Alitalia has been losing about €1m a day, but the government has insisted the airline will not be allowed to fail.

The commissioner's decision on Tuesday to open the investigation follows a complaint by the Association of European Airlines (AEA), which claimed that the Italian government had not demonstrated that its plan for Alitalia complied with EU state-aid rules.

These require a government to demonstrate that any injection of public funds does not distort competition in the single market.

In a statement on Tuesday, Ms. Kroes said that she agreed with the association's assessment that there were "serious doubts" about the investment being compliant with state-aid rules.

"Consequently, the commission will open proceedings pursuant to Article 88(2) of the EC Treaty [the basis of EU state-aid rules]," she said.

"This decision does not prejudge the outcome of the proceeding."

The commission has given Italy 20 days to respond to its concerns.

Last week, Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi defended the government's decision to inject more funds into Alitalia, despite the airline making successive losses.

"Alitalia is a national interest," he said. "We will not allow it to collapse."

The government has said that it wants to draw a line under the various bail-outs of the past, and has appointed advisers to help find a partner for the airline.

The European Union will launch a probe into whether a planned injection of state capital into Italian flag carrier Alitalia constitutes illegal state aid, a EU official said on Wednesday.
  
 The announcement comes days after Rome said it would pump $3.35 billion into the struggling airline to save it from bankruptcy, with the government funding coming on top of a $2.4 billion rescue package in 2021.
  
 "The European Commission will open tomorrow an in-depth investigation into the public financing of ITA Airways," a Commission official said, referring to Alitalia's new owner. 
  
 "The Commission suspects that this public financing by Italy could give an unfair competitive advantage to the newly created ITA Airways, allowing it to gain market share and destabilise the level playing field in the airline market," the official said.

The controversial £1.4bn Crossrail link to Heathrow Airport is expected to get the go-ahead after months of delay.

Ministers were expected to approve the project - which has been hit by funding problems and delays - at a meeting on Friday.

The link, connecting the western hub of Heathrow with Reading, Slough and Maidenhead in the east, is seen as vital to the airport's future development.

But it has also been criticised for the use of public money and the impact on local residents.

Business Secretary John Hutton said in June the project's "economic case remained strong" and the government was still committed to the scheme.

But he said the government was considering asking banks and other financial institutions to share the risk of the project, which is expected to attract about 18 million passengers a year.

The Department for Transport refused to comment on Friday's expected go-ahead for the project, which has been hit by a series of setbacks over the last year.

In July, Transport Secretary Ruth Kelly announced a review of all major transport projects in the wake of the successful campaign against the government's plan for a third runway at Heathrow.

And in April this year, the government was forced to give a £170m bail-out to the project, after it emerged that its costs had soared by more than a quarter to £1.76bn.

The project - dubbed the "Elizabeth Line" - will link Heathrow Airport, west of London, with stations in Reading, Slough and Maidenhead to the east, and as far as Paddington, Bond Street and Liverpool Street stations in central London.

The link faces strong opposition from local residents who say it will spark massive house demolitions and could cause house prices to plummet. 

A public inquiry into the project ended last year and Minister of State for Transport Tony McNulty announced in January that he planned to give the go-ahead for the scheme "as soon as possible".

The long-delayed London Crossrail project is expected to get the green light tomorrow, Wednesday, despite concerns over funding. The project, which will be known as the "Elizabeth Line", will connect Reading, Slough, Heathrow, central London, and Shenfield. It is expected that the new line, which should have opened in 2018, will boost the local economy by £42bn. However, questions remain about who will foot the bill for the estimated £1.6bn cost of fixing the flaws in the original work.

The project, which has been plagued by delays and budget overruns, was originally meant to open in December 2018, but it was pushed to March this year. Then in February, Transport for London (TfL) said it would not open for another two years, with a new opening date of autumn 2023.

TfL said it had agreed a £3.7bn grant and loan from the government to cover the cost of finishing the project. However, the deal requires TfL to meet a number of conditions, including finding a solution to the project's funding gap. The government has said it will not provide any more money for the project.

There are also concerns that the new line could be hit by further delays if the government does not agree to extend the opening date. The project's directors are expected to give more details about the plans for the line, including the opening date, at a meeting on Wednesday.

Disneyland Paris's management said it believed that the company's new financial plan would help it to return to profitability and continue operating as a major tourist attraction in France.

Among the many fees that banks in China have been accused of charging without proper disclosure, the most common by far is something called a "financial holding fee" — in essence, a penalty for having money in an account. 

In recent months, thousands of people have taken to social media to complain about being charged this fee, estimating that banks have taken billions of yuan from customers unfairly.

But in a country of 1.4 billion, where transparency on these charges is scarce, the exact number is difficult to ascertain.

Here's what little we know.

China's financial holding fees are essentially a way for banks to penalize depositors for holding above-threshold amounts of money in their accounts — in essence, a way to squeeze excess liquidity out of the financial system.

They were first introduced in 2013, and since then, the threshold — the amount of money that triggers the fee — has risen steadily.

This year, it stood at 123,000 yuan ($17,700) for urban banks and 87,000 yuan for rural banks, though the amount charged varies by bank.

China's central bank, the People's Bank of China (PBOC), has repeatedly urged banks to disclose these fees more clearly, warning that the lack of transparency could hurt the reputation of the financial system and undermine market confidence.

Giant pandas are mostly known for their distinctive black and white fur and for being one of the most endangered species on the planet. They also have a voracious appetite for bamboo – they can eat up to 38 kilograms a day – and they have a rather sluggish digestive system. Wild pandas typically defecate around 30 times a day, and their fecal matter can remain in their digestive tract for up to 38 hours, according to the World Wildlife Fund (WWF). As a result, they can produce up to 40 pounds of poop a day, or around 9,000 pounds a year. That's roughly the weight of a grand piano.

To address this issue, the China Conservation and Research Center for the Giant Panda, located in the mountainous bamboo forests of Sichuan Province in central China, has come up with a high-tech solution: a wireless sensor network that can detect the whereabouts of pandas, monitor their habits and even determine when they are pooping.

The sensors, which are powered by solar panels and have a battery life of up to three years, were developed by the Chinese company Huawei. They have a range of up to 50 meters and can be placed on trees or other objects in the forest. They collect data on the pandas' movements and send it to a base station, which then transmits it to researchers' computers.

The data is stored in the cloud and can be accessed by researchers in real time. It can also be used to predict the pandas' habits, such as when they will next need to poop, and to plan accordingly.

The system has already proved its worth. "Last year, our staff were able to locate a panda mother and her cub quickly, thanks to the sensors," Zhang said. "They were able to save the cub, which had become trapped in a ravine."

Many Irish firms have established bases in the UK in order to access the EU common market, and there are serious concerns in Ireland about the potential for a hard border between the two countries, which could lead to trade restrictions and tariffs.

One thing that's certain is that the issue will continue to dominate the headlines in the coming year.

No-deal Brexit aside, the Irish economy has continued to grow strongly in 2019, with GDP up by about 5% in the first three quarters of the year.

Unemployment is down to 4.8%, its lowest level in a decade, and wages are rising steadily.

However, there are some warning signs on the horizon.

Consumer spending is down, and business investment has been weak.

Friday 31 December marks one year since Ireland exited its longest-ever recession, but it has been a year to forget for many Irish people.

The economy is growing again, with an expected expansion of more than 7% in 2015, and the government is borrowing less, but recovery is still elusive for many.

Young people have borne the brunt of the recession and many feel that they are being left behind as the economy improves.

One in three under-25s are unemployed and nearly half of those in work are on temporary contracts, according to the Central Statistics Office.

Many have left to work abroad, with Australia, Canada and the UK popular destinations - more than 12,000 people left in the first three months of 2015 alone.

The Irish diaspora is vast with about 70 million people around the world claiming Irish ancestry, so it is no surprise that the trend of people leaving has continued for so long.

But emigration has changed.

"It used to be that people would leave for a few years and come back, now people are leaving and they don't know if they will come back," says psychologist and counsellor Susan Hegarty.

"The difference now is that people are emigrating because they have to, because they believe they have no other option."

Many of those who do return home find it difficult to settle back into Irish life.

"A lot of people who come back can't get a foothold back here again," says Ms Hegarty.

"They have lost their networks, their support systems, their friends and often their families have dispersed as well.

"They have lost their sense of belonging here, and it can take a long time to build that up again."

Ukraine has trimmed its target for privatisation revenues this year by more than half to $1.5bn (£1.2bn), according to the ministry of economy.

The aim had earlier been set at $3.7bn. There are few investors keen on Ukraine's state-owned enterprises.

The ministry said it had revised its targets lower, because plans to sell large state assets had failed to materialise. It is also looking to speed up the sale of smaller assets.

"We are not going to wait for the big privatisations. Small and medium-sized privatisations will speed up Ukraine's economic growth," said Economy Minister Yulia Svyrydenko.

Privatisation proceeds aimed at helping Ukraine recover from war

The ministry said it was retaining its goal of raising $281m from the sale of state-owned stakes in agricultural firms. That would include the sale of 100% plus one share in agricultural company Mriya.

The ministry said it was also aiming to raise $322m through the sale of other state assets, including aircraft engine maker Motor Sich and Ukraine's largest chemical plant, Azot.

However, Ukraine's previous attempts to sell state enterprises have largely failed because of investor wariness about corruption and the country's poor business climate.

Last year, a deal to sell Ukraine's largest lender, Privatbank, to the state fell apart because of legal challenges.

The war has also disrupted Ukraine's economy and industrial production has plummeted, making it difficult to find willing investors for state enterprises.

Many of Ukraine's state-owned enterprises were built up under former President Viktor Yanukovych, whose regime was ousted in 2014.

Mr Yanukovych amassed huge debts, leaving the enterprises indebted and in need of repair.

Ukraine's government has been trying to overhaul the state-owned sector since a debt crisis erupted in 2015. But progress has been slow.

Ukraine has trimmed plans to privatise its state-owned assets amid opposition from key allies including the US, the UK and the EU. The country had been expected to raise about $10bn from the sale of more than 700 state enterprises. But a draft law now going through parliament has dropped a list of assets to be privatised. The amended bill only mentions four state companies that would be put up for sale, raising about $233m. The amendment was supported by the president, Volodymyr Zelensky. 

In October, US secretary of state Antony Blinken said that Ukraine should not be in a hurry to sell state assets because corrupt officials could exploit the process to obtain them at undervalued prices. Ukraine's prime minister, Denys Shmygal, said the sale was necessary to plug a budget deficit, which hit 6.1bn hryvnia ($185m) in the first 10 months of 2022 and is expected to reach 7.5bn hryvnia ($224m) by the end of the year. The amended bill says the money raised from the privatisations will go towards servicing Ukraine's debt. 

The original draft had identified hundreds of state firms for possible privatisation, including Ukraine's biggest bank, Privatbank, several regional banks, energy company Ukrgazvydobuvannya and its rival, Ukrenergo. Also on the list were Motor Sich, the country's largest aircraft engine manufacturer and a key supplier to the Ukrainian military, and the state's stake in Ukraine's largest steel mill, Metinvest.

Auction house Graceland has put some of Elvis Presley's personal belongings and historic documents on sale, including the King's first ever recording. 

The item is among more than 1,000 lots offered as part of the Graceland Auctions' 2022 event, which runs until 11 November.

The recording, made when he was 18, features Elvis singing and playing guitar on the songs "Harbor Lights" and "Love of my Life". 

Auction house owner Josh Kincheloe said it was "the earliest known recording of Elvis Presley".

The auction also includes Elvis' personal Bible, a letter he wrote to President Richard Nixon and some of his military uniforms.

Elvis' grandmother, Minnie Mae Presley, bought the Bible for him in 1957. It features annotations in the singer's handwriting, and is expected to sell for between $50,000 (£43,000) and $70,000 (£59,000).

Elvis wrote to President Nixon in 1970, asking him to designate 22 November as "National Prisoners Day" so that "these men constantly reminded of their failure as men, and not of their possible rehabilitation".

The letter is expected to sell for between $15,000 (£12,300) and $20,000 (£16,600).

Mr Kincheloe said it was "extremely significant" as it revealed "a very different side of Elvis that we don't often get to see".

Elvis served in the US Army from 1958 to 1960.

Following his death in 1977, his wife Priscilla inherited his estate, including Graceland.

She said the auctions offered "a little bit of something for everyone" and encouraged people to bid on the items "for keepsake and collectible purposes".

"These are things that were used and loved by Elvis Presley and the Graceland family," she added.

The early recordings of Elvis Presley, including the original version of That's All Right, are being sold by his estate in an auction that includes items from other rock and roll legends. 

The recording, with the incorrect spelling of "That's All Righ't" on the label, is expected to sell for between $50,000 and $70,000. The song, originally recorded at the Memphis Recording Service in July 1954, was released by Sun Records. It was written by Arthur Crudup and was published by Southern Music as "That's All Right (Mama)". 

The auction will also include a guitar owned and used by Chuck Berry, a Gibson acoustic guitar owned by Johnny Cash, and an invitation to The Beatles' legendary 1969 rooftop concert.

Drinks group Diageo is to buy US wine company Beam Inc in a deal worth £13.4bn ($17.81bn).

The maker of Johnnie Walker whisky is paying £4.55bn ($6.4bn) in cash and shares for the maker of Jim Beam bourbon and Courvoisier cognac.

 Shares in London-based Diageo closed up 1.5% on the news.

The company said it would accelerate its expansion in key growth markets such as the US and China.

Diageo has been advised by Goldman Sachs, while JPMorgan and PJT Park Hill have worked with Beam on the deal.

The deal comes as the drinks industry faces slowing growth in Europe and increasing pressure from governments seeking to counter binge drinking.

Last year, Diageo held talks with Guinness maker Heineken over a possible merger of their drinks businesses. However, those discussions broke down over price and because of the complexity of merging the two firms.

At the end of 2013, Diageo had sales of £6.7bn and operating profits of £2.7bn. It employs about 30,000 people.

Beam, which is listed on the New York Stock Exchange, reported sales of about $4.3bn and operating profits of about $660m in the year to 31 March. It employs about 5,000 people.

Diageo's purchase of Aviation Gin is part of its strategy to expand its presence in the premium spirits market. The company has been focusing on premium brands, as consumers increasingly opt for higher-quality drinks. 

With the acquisition of Aviation Gin, Diageo will be able to offer a more comprehensive range of premium spirits to its customers. This could include a combination of gin and wine, as well as other spirits such as whiskey and vodka.

It seems obvious where the adverts are on Google - and indeed, where they are not.

Search for "holiday" on Google and the top of the search results are clearly marked as "ads" - paid-for links sold by Google to companies eager to catch people's eyes.

Yet a study suggests that many people still do not spot ads on Google - and that they increasingly do not realise when other information on the search results page is advertising either.

The study, by researchers at Columbia University, in the US, is based on experiments involving more than 1,000 Google searches.

They reached their conclusions by comparing the results of experiments involving Google with identical experiments involving a simpler search engine they created, called MobiliSearch.

In the MobiliSearch experiments, they deliberately inserted ads where users might not expect them, in an attempt to assess whether participants noticed the ads at all.

And they found that users were much better at spotting ads on MobiliSearch than on Google - even when the ads were in the same place on the page.

The results were the same, even when participants were given money to spend on the ads, and were told that the top results were ads.

"We were surprised that people were failing to notice the ads on Google," said Dr. Aaron Brown, who helped carry out the research.

"But given how ubiquitous Google is in people's lives, it makes sense that people have come to trust the platform, and that they are less sceptical of the results they get."

Google gave this response when asked about the study: "This study was not peer-reviewed, and conclusions drawn by the researchers about Google Search are inaccurate."

The company did not respond to requests for more detail about which conclusions it thought were wrong.

The researchers said that it was not clear whether the participants in their experiments had been searching on smartphones or computers. But they said that Google's search results pages were much the same on both devices.

Dr. Brown said that it was possible that on smartphones, which have smaller screens, users might be less able to spot where ads began and organic search results ended.

He also said it was possible that Google's algorithms pushed ads further down the page on smartphones, making them less visible.

Columbia University has made the results of its experiments - due to be presented at the ACM Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems in May - available on the university's website.

A study carried out by the University of Texas showed that people were unable to correctly identify the sponsored advertisements on search engine results pages (SERPs). When shown screenshots of Google search results, participants pointed out advertisements as fewer than 25% of the time, despite the presence of cues like "Ad" or "Sponsored." 

One of the authors of the study, Amanda Broderick, commented on the low number of participants able to discern between ads and search results, noting that "just because something is labeled 'Ad' doesn't mean that people will notice that it's an advertisement." This failure to identify advertisements relates to a concept from psychology known as inattentional blindness, which causes people to miss obvious facts when their attention is focused elsewhere. 

The authors of the study suggest that the low ability to recognize ads is due to the design of SERPs, which often place ads and search results in similar formats. Additionally, people may be more focused on the search results themselves rather than the ads that appear on the page. The authors suggest that search engine designers should make ads more distinct from search results to improve transparency and help users make more informed decisions. 

The study's findings highlight the need for search engine users to be more vigilant in identifying advertisements and interpreting information on SERPs. It is important to be aware of the potential for ads to influence search results and to consider the motivations of the companies behind the advertisements. 

Overall, the study suggests that people are unable to reliably identify advertisements on SERPs, which has implications for the credibility of information and the influence of advertising on search engine users.

Italian tennis player Francesca "Farina" Schiavone achieved one of the most surprising victories in Venus Williams' grand slam career when she knocked the American out of the French Open in the third round. 

Schiavone, who is unranked having not played since last year's Wimbledon Championships, took advantage of a error-strewn display from Williams to claim a 6-4 6-4 victory on Saturday and set up a fourth-round meeting with Kazakhstan's Elena Rybakina.

The Italian, who is celebrating her 42nd birthday this week, played the first set perfectly, dropping only one point on her serve, as Williams made a high number of unforced errors. 

The seven-time grand slam champion Williams, who had reached the last 16 in Paris on nine previous occasions, finally clicked into gear at the start of the second set, breaking Schiavone's serve to love. But the veteran Italian, who won the title here in 2010, broke back immediately and served out the match to love to seal a stunning victory. 

"It's not easy to play against a legend like Venus Williams. She's a great player, a great champion," Schiavone told Eurosport. "Today was my day, I played really well. It's impossible to describe this feeling. I just can say that I'm so happy."

Schiavone's last victory at a major was at the French Open in 2010, when she beat Samantha Stosur in the final for her first and only grand slam title.

The director of Rome's Museo Nazionale Romano has been accused of bypassing norms to fast-track the acquisition of a 2,000-year-old Egyptian mummy for €2.5m (£2.2m). Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera reported that the acquisition of the mummy – named Farina Elia – was approved by the museum's director, Francesco Prospere, despite criticism from the museum's scientific committee. According to the paper, the mummy was imported by Italian company Heritage Egypt, which was commissioned to create a replica of the mummy for the museum, with Farina Elia – a priest's daughter from the era of the pharaoh Ramses II – destined for a private client in Dubai. The acquisition has been criticised for allegedly bypassing the museum's usual procedures, with some accusing the museum of wasting public funds.

The Museo Nazionale Romano, which is dedicated to antiquities of the Roman Empire, did not respond to Corriere della Sera's requests for comment. However, in a statement sent to The Art Newspaper, Prospere said that "the acquisition of the mummy Farina Elia was carried out in full compliance with the existing norms and regulations. It was undertaken following a project conceived by [Museo Nazionale Romano] and developed together with Heritage Egypt, which was awarded the tender called by the museum last year". He added that "the choice [of Heritage Egypt] was made on the basis of the quality of the goods and the affordability of the offer".

The acquisition has renewed discussions around the trafficking of antiquities in Italy. The country is known for its strict heritage preservation laws, which dictate that all artefacts found on Italian soil belong to the state. However, the rising number of archaeological finds in Italy – largely due to the country's recent seismic activity – has put pressure on the nation's museums, with some critics arguing that restrictions on the number of staff and acquisitions have resulted in backlogs and the illegal trade of artefacts. In May, the Italian police seized 4,300 archaeological artefacts from a warehouse in Rome, which were believed to have been stolen from digs across the country. Those held included fragments of Roman and Etruscan amphorae, Greek and Roman coins, and the lower part of a statue believed to be of Apollo.

Top of the Pops 'last show on BBC One'

BBC One's flagship music show Top of the Pops is to end its run on the channel after more than 40 years.

The broadcaster has decided not to renew the programme's contract, which expires this month.

Presented by Reggie Yates, the final edition of the show will be broadcast on 30 July.

A BBC statement said: "Top of the Pops is a much-loved show and it's not surprising that BBC One wants to keep it."

The statement added: "We are in discussions about continuing the show in the future."

First broadcast in January 1964, Top of the Pops was shown every Thursday evening and at one point was the most-watched programme on British television.

However, audience numbers have declined in recent years and the programme's £150,000-a-week budget was described as "eye-watering" by a BBC source.

In May, BBC One controller Lorraine Heggessey defended the show, saying she was "very optimistic" about its future.

She said Top of the Pops would "continue to be part of BBC One's music offering".

A source close to the show said: "There have been cuts across the board at the BBC and music programmes have taken a particular pasting.

"Top of the Pops is seen as something that can go because it's not core to the BBC's music business.

"It's a real shame because it's such a brilliant show that reaches a huge audience."

The source added: "It is a real anomaly that a show that attracts millions of viewers each week is seen as dispensable.

"Ultimately the BBC wants to make programmes that are more 'worthy' like the One Show or Countryfile. That is the future of BBC One."

The show, which for many years was hosted by DJ Jimmy Savile, has undergone numerous revamps in recent years.

A weekly highlight show was axed in 2006 and replaced with a monthly edition, and last year the show was moved from BBC Television Centre in west London to the BBC's new studios in Manchester.

The programme, which will continue to air on BBC Radio 1, has also seen a number of presenters come and go including Yates, Jo Whiley, and John Peel.

It was announced in May that Yates would replace DJ Zane Lowe as the main presenter of the show.

The iconic music show Top of the Pops is to leave BBC One after 45 years. 

The programme, which has been a staple of the BBC's programming since 1977, will move to BBC Two as part of the corporation's efforts to "refresh" its offering. Top of the Pops will continue to air on the BBC Red Button and iPlayer, with the final episode on BBC One scheduled for August. 

The BBC has said it wants to create "a strong music offering on BBC Two", with other programmes such as Later... with Jools Holland and Live from the BBC moving to the channel. 

A BBC spokesperson said: "Top of the Pops is coming off BBC One, but it isn't going away - audiences will be able to enjoy the programme on BBC Two, Red Button, and iPlayer, as well as continuing to enjoy the best of the action on BBC Sounds. 

"We are committed to providing the best music programming on the BBC and refreshing our output to ensure we continue to serve all our audiences."

BT has announced it will be offering free internet phone calls to customers, the BBC reported. The UK's largest telecoms provider said calls would be free whether made to fixed-line or mobile phones, or even international numbers. However, calls will only be free if they are made via broadband and not via the mobile phone network, BT said. In its statement, BT said its customers would need to have an active subscription to BT Broadband and a compatible router to benefit from the offer. Once they had signed up, they would be able to make free calls anytime, anywhere, the company said. Landline and broadband customers will be able to sign up from November, while EE mobile customers can do so in January.

It comes as BT, which still boasts 12 million landline customers, recently reported a quarterly rise in profits, boosted by growth in its broadband and mobile services. The company said it wanted to "reward our loyal customers and attract new ones". A spokesman for BT told the BBC the company was "confident" the offer would not result in a "material decline" in the number of calls made via the landline network. Landlines continue to be used by many customers for regular phone calls, as well as taking advantage of offers such as free weekends and cheap evening calls, said Marc Allera, CEO of BT's consumer division.

Existing BT customers will be able to use the service immediately once they have updated their router. New customers will be given the latest router when they sign up for an eligible package.

The BBC's John Simpson in Shanghai says that, despite the warming of relations between the two countries, the Chinese are still very wary of foreign companies.

"It is understood that SAIC's due diligence inspections have discovered that MG Rover's books are in far worse condition than they had previously thought," says the Reuters news agency.

The company's administrators, Deloitte, have been trying to find a buyer for the company's assets since then.

It appears that the $230m price tag was partly made up of MG Rover's debts to Shanghai Automotive, which had been incurred when the Chinese company had supplied parts to the British car maker.

Now it seems that Shanghai Automotive may be trying to lower the price it is willing to pay for MG Rover.

On Thursday, SAIC confirmed that it had held "extensive" talks about a possible partnership with MG Rover's administrators.

A SAIC statement said the two sides were in "close communication and are working hard to finalise the details of the cooperation agreement".

The statement added: "SAIC is confident that the partnership with MG Rover will be beneficial to both sides and will also promote the technical exchange and cooperation between the Chinese and British automotive industries."

The delay follows concerns being raised in parliament about the suitability of Shanghai Automotive Industry Corporation (SAIC).

It is understood that the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) wants more time to assess SAIC's plans for MG Rover, which went into administration in April. 

The government wants to know how many of the company's workforce would keep their jobs, and where the cars would be built. 

It is believed that SAIC has asked the DTI to keep the details of its rescue package confidential.

The Chinese company made a formal approach to the administrators several weeks ago and is thought to be the only party still in talks with them.

It is believed that SAIC wants to buy the Longbridge plant in Birmingham and retain a workforce of about 2,000 - mainly engineers - to help design a new range of MG sports cars.

The company also intends to use the site to build its own range of saloon cars which will be sold in Europe.

It is not thought that SAIC has made a formal offer for the company, but administrators PricewaterhouseCoopers (PWC) have said they are confident that a deal can be done.

It is understood that SAIC has requested that the DTI does not make any announcement about the nature of its plans for MG Rover until after the Shanghai motor show at the end of this month.

"We have not been approached by SAIC asking for confidentiality on this matter," he added.

"We are confident that a deal can be done to save the company."

The future of MG Rover, which has been making cars at Longbridge for more than 80 years, has been uncertain since it stopped production in April.

More than 6,000 people have lost their jobs at the plant and at dealerships around the UK.

Japan's economy has slipped into recession after it contracted by an annualised 2.3% in the third quarter of 2022, official data shows.

The figure was worse than many analysts had expected and followed a 0.8% drop in the previous quarter.

Japan has been hit by soaring energy prices and a strong currency, and is struggling to attract tourists as borders remain closed.

The latest data will increase the pressure on the government to do more to help the economy.

Japan's Prime Minister Fumio Kishida said the data was "extremely disappointing".

"I am fully aware that the Japanese economy faces serious challenges including inflation and will take all possible measures to overcome them," he said.

Earlier this month, Japan's central bank warned that the economy was likely to shrink further in the current quarter. It also raised its inflation forecast, predicting that prices would rise by 3.0% this year, up from its previous forecast of 1.8%.

Japan has been hit by the same problems as other countries, including the war in Ukraine, but its response has been muted because it is a net importer of energy.

It has taken steps to try to cushion the blow to households by offering subsidies for electricity and natural gas, but economists say this has had little effect.

In addition, its export-heavy economy has been hit by the strong yen, which makes Japanese goods more expensive overseas.

And with its borders still closed to most foreign tourists, the country's service sector has been unable to benefit from the recent global tourism boom.

The latest data showing Japan's economy slipped into recession in the third quarter has put the spotlight back on the country's central bank to do more to shore up growth.

Japan's economy contracted by an annualised 1.2% in the three months to September, compared to a market forecast of a 0.8% contraction.

The figure, which covered the period from July to September, means Japan has now entered its second technical recession in less than two years. The economy also shrank by an annualised 1.9% in the second quarter.

"The Japanese economy contracted for a second consecutive quarter, putting it in a technical recession," said Yoshiki Shinke, chief economist at the Dai-ichi Life Research Institute.

"The gloomy outlook for the world's third-largest economy adds pressure on the Bank of Japan to take additional easing measures when it reviews its policy next month."

The central bank has been trying to spur growth for years by flooding the economy with cash, with little success.

Part of the problem is that the bank has been reluctant to take more aggressive steps due to concern about the potential impact on financial institutions' profits.

Britain will no longer tolerate the "chronic and systemic" failure of other countries to criminalize hijacking planes, the foreign secretary has said.

Dominic Raab said such action was needed to tackle a "startling" rise in hostage-taking and suicide bombings.

Writing in the Sunday Telegraph, he said the UK would "take the lead" in imposing sanctions on any state that failed to act.

Mr Raab said another seven countries had joined the UK and US in taking action since the start of the year.

The foreign secretary's comments come after the Manchester bombing trial heard that Islamic State (IS) had planned to target aircraft.

John Thompson, a member of the UK's Joint Terrorism Analysis Centre (JTAC), told the trial of eight people accused of plotting the Manchester Arena bombing in 2017 that IS had aimed to "gain leverage" by seizing aircraft.

The defendant Elshafee Elghnawni, who denies being involved in the plot, told the court he had been instructed to carry out a hijacking as part of his terrorist training in Syria.

Mr Raab said the UK had secured the cooperation of another seven countries - Australia, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands and New Zealand - in the last year, taking the total number of countries who have criminalized aircraft hijacking to 24.

Shredding in Whitehall has increased since 2005, according to a new report by the National Audit Office. The report, presented to Parliament, showed that central government departments spent £80m on shredding in 2005-06. The Department of Work and Pensions accounted for nearly half of that - £35.4m. The department said it was getting rid of 3 million cases of old paperwork each year. That figure has now risen to 4.5 million. The Department of Health spent £2.7m on shredding - £700,000 more than in 2005-06. Nearly two-thirds of the 26 departments increased their spending on shredding. The NAO said the overall increase may be due to departments shredding more material on site instead of sending it to commercial companies.

Shredding in Whitehall has increased under the Conservative government, according to a Freedom of Information request submitted by the Labour Party. The party obtained data from the Cabinet Office, which oversees the civil service, showing that the monthly amount of shredding across government departments has increased year after year since 2016. The data does not include the Prime Minister's Office.

In 2016, the monthly average of shredded documents was around 12 tonnes. This increased to over 13 tonnes in 2017, 15 tonnes in 2018, and 17 tonnes in 2019. Data for 2020 is unavailable, but in the first three months of this year, an average of 16 tonnes of documents were shredded each month.

The highest monthly amount of shredding in the past four years was in March 2019, when over 19 tonnes of documents were destroyed. April and May of this year saw similar levels, with just under 19 tonnes of paper being shredded both months. 

A Cabinet Office spokesperson said: “The Cabinet Office does not recognise these figures. Shredding is carried out on a bank basis by our clearing contractor and any paper that is shredded is recycled.”

The Labour Party has criticized the government for shredding documents that should be preserved for future generations. Shadow Cabinet Office minister Rachel Reeves said: “The shredding spree in Theresa May’s Downing Street reached new heights today. Shifting from denial to sarcasm, ministers now admit they shred policies and important documents but insist it’s all to save the planet. 

“Labour has uncovered a vast and growing culture of shredding within Whitehall. From Universal Credit to the 'no deal' Brexit papers, it seems this government is happy to destroy vital documents to hide their failures from the public.”

US transportation officials are to meet on Friday to discuss travel chaos over the Christmas period, which was blamed on a severe storm that disrupted flights and road travel.

The Biden administration is to launch a "full investigation" into the incident, a Transportation Department (DOT) spokesperson told the BBC.

Thousands of holiday travellers were left stranded at airports around the US amid delays and cancellations due to severe weather, including heavy snowfalls and icy conditions.

There have been calls from lawmakers for the federal government to investigate how the storm impacted travel, as well as the role that climate change may have played in the severity of the weather.

According to flight tracker FlightAware, more than 9,000 US flights were delayed and almost 1,600 were cancelled on Saturday alone. Five of the six busiest North American travel days of the year occur during the Christmas holiday season, according to the DOT.

A massive winter storm moved across the US ahead of Christmas, dumping snow from the Rocky Mountains to parts of the northeast. As the storm advanced, the National Weather Service (NWS) issued winter storm warnings from the nation's capital, Washington, to parts of Maine.

In a statement released on Saturday, the Biden administration said they were "working closely with airlines and airport authorities to move towards normal operations, and actively working to understand any underlying issues with the extensive disruptions".

The statement added that the Biden administration "will take any appropriate action" to support passengers.

On Thursday, Republican Senator Ted Cruz of Texas tweeted: "Perhaps a probe into how the winter weather was so poorly forecast & how best to prepare for future weather events?"

After thousands of flights were delayed and canceled, Cruz added on Sunday that "the Biden Administration's failure to adequately prepare for Christmas week's winter storm hurt American travelers."

The US Department of Transportation (DOT) has said it will investigate the travel chaos that occurred over the Thanksgiving weekend. This comes after the country's airlines canceled thousands of flights, leaving many travelers stranded.

The DOT said it would look into whether the airlines responded adequately to the situation, and whether their policies around flight cancellations and customer service were sufficient.

Thanksgiving is one of the busiest times of the year for US airlines, as people travel to visit family and friends. This year, however, a severe winter storm hit the country, disrupting flight schedules and leaving many airlines unable to recover.

The storm, which was the most significant Thanksgiving storm in a decade, left over 10 million people without power and caused over $7 billion in damage. Several people were killed by the storm.

US airlines canceled over 10,000 flights in the week leading up to Thanksgiving, with thousands more being canceled on the day itself. Many travelers were left stranded at airports, unable to reach their destination.

In a statement, the DOT said it would "examine the services and support that airlines provided to passengers during the holiday travel season and determine if airlines' policies and procedures lived up to the expectations of their customers."

The statement added that the DOT would "take appropriate action" based on its investigation.

Chester City's future has been thrown into doubt after chairman Steve Vaughan was refused permission to sell the club to a prospective new owner.

The Football League has turned down Vaughan's request to sell because he has not yet provided proof that the club can pay off its debts.

Chester face liquidation if they do not fulfil their final two matches of the season, against Carlisle United and Luton Town.

The League has told the club it must provide the required information before 1500 BST on Friday, 23 February.

That is when a period of exclusivity granted to one potential new owner expires.

Vaughan had asked the League if he could sell the club to the man, who wishes to remain anonymous, on 17 February.

But Football League chief executive David Burns said: "The board has asked for additional information in support of the proposal for the club to be sold.

"This was requested on Tuesday and, as yet, has not been provided. This information is essential to allow the board to make an informed decision as to whether it is in the best long-term interests of the club."

Chester's players and staff were paid on Friday, but first team coach Stuart Murphy has warned that the club cannot afford to pay them again on Monday.

The club have been given permission to postpone Sunday's match at Luton because of safety concerns.

A meeting between the Football League and the club on Friday will decide whether Chester's final game of the season, at home to Carlisle on Saturday week, will go ahead.

Carlisle have already said they may not travel if the club's future is not resolved by the time they are due to arrive in Chester on the day of the game.

The League has said it is "essential" that Chester complete their final two fixtures of the season.

And Burns added: "The board is aware that this is a difficult and complex situation for all parties and will give the matter its full consideration when all the information required has been provided."

Chester, who were relegated from the Football League last season, have debts of about £7m, with much of that owed to former chairman Stephen Vaughan senior.

The club have had several winding-up orders this season, but have always paid off their creditors before each hearing.

Chester's future as a racecourse is in doubt after the British Horseracing Authority (BHA) announced it would be suspending all racing at the venue from Wednesday.

Both courses are owned by the same company and are operated out of the same site. 

Six cases of equine flu were confirmed at trainer Donald McCain's stable last week.

Disney has given its support to Sony's new high definition DVD format, a move which is likely to give the format a huge boost.
