Disney's support will give the HD DVD format a huge lift, as the company controls some of the most popular films, including Star Wars and Pixar animations.

The format war has been going on for nearly two years, ever since Toshiba launched its HD DVD format, backed by Microsoft and Intel.

Sony later launched its own version, and now seems to be winning the battle, with a growing number of supporters.

Last week, US retailer Best Buy said it would stock the HD DVD players and movies in its stores.

This week, US director James Cameron said he had tested both HD DVD and Blu-ray and decided the HD DVD was superior.

"HD DVD is winning the format war, hands down," he said.

However, not all supporters of Blu-ray have given up hope.

Last week, a top executive from Samsung, a Blu-ray backer, said his company was "very confident" Blu-ray would win in the end.

Disney has decided to support Sony's new DVD format, known as Blu-ray Disc. The decision comes after Disney spent months weighing up the pros and cons of both Blu-ray and Toshiba's HD DVD. A "post-Christmas lull" in lending to British businesses has been described by a paint and varnish maker.

The managing director of Durham-based HMG Paints said he had applied for a £1m loan, but had been offered less than a quarter of that amount.

John Falder said the "lack of enthusiasm" from lenders left him worried about the health of the economy.

He said he had been told his firm's projections were "too optimistic".

It comes as official figures showed a sharp fall in approved lending to small and medium-sized firms.

According to the Bank of England, net lending rose by just £131m in November, the weakest growth since March.

The BBC has contacted the British Business Bank for comment.

Mr Falder said he had wanted to borrow £1m to invest in new technology, but that he had been offered less than £250,000 by his bank.

"I phoned up our bank manager and said 'what's going on?' and he said 'oh, it's that time of year - it's a post-Christmas lull'," he said.

"I said 'look, can you lend us some money?' and he said he'd see what he could do, and he went away and he actually came back and offered us less than a quarter of what we wanted.

"That does worry me in terms of the health of the economy… the fact that the banks aren't really enthusiastic at the moment about lending."

"I think they're being very, very cautious - they've been burnt with the property market, with Brexit and other things, and they're just holding back," added Mr Falder, who has run HMG Paints since 1987.

Figures from the Bank of England showed that net lending to small and medium-sized businesses rose to £131m in November from £1.38bn in October.

City analysts had expected a fall to about £1bn, but lending has been weaker than expected since the summer.

The Bank of England said that a slowdown in mortgage lending, as interest rates rose, had been offset by stronger consumer credit.

The annual growth rate of consumer credit, including credit cards and personal loans, rose to 10.4% in November from 9.7% in October, its highest since March 2016.

The Forum of Private Business said that the lending figures were "disappointing"

The British public's appetite for loans and credit cards continued to fall in December, new figures show.

Figures from the Bank of England show that consumers borrowed £1.2bn on credit cards and loans in December, down from £1.5bn in November.

It is the fourth month in a row that borrowing has fallen, and the slowest pace of growth in a year and a half.

Analysts said that after a boom in spending on credit cards ahead of Christmas, people appeared to be paying down their debts.

"The post-Christmas lull in lending is no surprise, as households focus on paying down credit card balances," said Samuel Tombs, chief UK economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics.

"Going forward, we expect a recovery in consumer borrowing, as households increasingly switch back to borrowing on credit cards, as opposed to their current preference for personal loans," he added.

Overall, consumer borrowing increased by £1.3bn in the three months to December, down from £6.7bn in the three months to November.

The figures also showed that households saved £4.7bn in December, the highest since March 2020, and £15.4bn in the three months to December.

The former Commons speaker, Betty Boothroyd, has called for peers to elect a speaker for the House of Lords, as the upper chamber goes through its biggest overhaul in history.

The former Labour MP, who was the first, and so far only, woman to hold the post of Commons speaker, said the election would help "reassert the authority" of the Lords following the ending of the hereditary principle.

In a piece for the Guardian, she suggested that peers should elect a speaker once the House has been reformed, and that the new speaker should be given the power to select fellow peers to sit on committees, now that most committees are elected by the whole House.

Her proposal is likely to be controversial as the government is determined that the reformed House of Lords will have no elected element at all. Ministers say this is meant to ensure the new second chamber differs from the Commons and does not rival it.

But Boothroyd said the absence of an elected element meant the new House would have "no legitimate authority".

"The only solution, it seems to me, is for the reformed House of Lords to elect its speaker," she wrote.

"A powerful speaker, elected by peers, would help reassert the authority of the House and command respect from the government of the day and the public."

Boothroyd argued that a powerful speaker was needed to guide the House through what she described as the "political minefield" of selecting fellow peers to sit on the new second chamber's committees.

"The speaker should be given the job of selecting the members of the committees, just as the Speaker of the House of Commons does," she wrote.

"That would dispel any suggestion of a stitch-up. It would be the best way of all of them experiencing the work of committees and for the committees to have the benefit of their knowledge and experience."

The former speaker also suggested that the new upper chamber should have a "provisional" term of office for its members - perhaps for 15 years - after which time they could be re-elected by their fellow peers.

Boothroyd argued this would "emphasise the need for continuing excellence in the work of the House and for continuing accountability to it by each peer".

The Labour MP and former Speaker of the House of Commons, Betty Boothroyd, has called for a return to the traditional system of selecting the Speaker. She said the current system, which sees the MPs elect the Speaker, introduced in 2005, reduces the likelihood of finding "the best person for the job".

Ms. Boothroyd, the first woman to be elected Speaker in the House of Commons in 1992, said the restoration of the old system where the Queen appoints the Speaker would be "much preferable". 

Her comments come as the House of Lords is expected to elect a new Speaker tomorrow, with the Labour peer Baroness Hayman widely expected to get the job.

Ms. Boothroyd told the BBC that the prospect of a Labour peer becoming Speaker was a "strong argument" for electing speakers in the House of Commons.

"It's important that the Speaker is appointed by the whole house and it shouldn't be a partisan appointment," she said. 

"The idea that the House of Lords has suddenly got itself a Speaker because they've got a vacancy and they've elected a Labour speaker - that's a strong argument, of course, for changing the system in the House of Commons."

Ms. Boothroyd served as Speaker from 1992 to 2000, during which time she was appointed by the Queen on the recommendation of the outgoing Speaker. 

The system changed in 2005 following the enactment of the Parliamentary Elections and Referendums Act, which transferred the power to elect the Speaker from the Crown to the House of Commons. 

Since then, MPs have elected the Speaker and the three deputy speakers from among their number, but Ms. Boothroyd said the new system had not served the country well.

"I think it is desirable to return to the former system," she said. "Clearly, it is for the government of the day to decide, and I realize that there are arguments on both sides. 

"But I think if you are going to have a fully elected House of Commons, then it does reduce the likelihood of getting the best person for the job if it is purely elected by the members of the House of Commons."

The government says its new plan will reduce net migration to the "tens of thousands" - a longstanding promise by Conservative MPs - by providing skills to the economy and controlling immigration better than the previous system. Smoking cost the lives of 800,000 people in Europe every year, health experts have told the European Court of Justice.

The court in Luxembourg was hearing arguments on whether the EU should have the power to regulate tobacco products.

The tobacco industry argued that such legislation would represent an illegal interference with their trade.

Judges were told that smoking caused 600,000 deaths in the EU every year, with another 200,000 people dying from exposure to second-hand smoke.

The court's ruling is not expected before the summer.

The case was referred to the court by the French government which wanted to know if its own laws, banning smoking in public places, breached the tobacco firms' trade mark rights.

In court, the tobacco giants argued that there was no scientific proof that their products were dangerous and that smoking was a matter of personal choice.

They also argued that any laws aimed at reducing the number of smokers would amount to an illegal interference with their trade.

"There is no scientific consensus on the harmfulness of tobacco smoke and on the accuracy of the methods of measurement usually applied," said an alliance of British American Tobacco, France's Imperial Tobacco and Altadis, a Spanish-French group.

The World Health Organization (WHO), which was invited to speak as amicus curiae (a legal term meaning 'friend of the court'), argued that tobacco products were uniquely dangerous and that the case against them was "overwhelming".

The WHO said that smoking caused 600,000 deaths in the EU every year, with another 200,000 people dying from exposure to second-hand smoke.

"There are very few substances with which tobacco can be compared," it said in its submission.

"Even nitric acid, the substance with which the tobacco industry compares its products, is not as harmful as tobacco."

The court's ruling on the legality of any future EU laws on tobacco products will not be delivered until the summer at the earliest.

Euronext has confirmed that it has held talks with the London Stock Exchange (LSE) about a possible counterbid for Refinitiv.

The LSE agreed to buy the majority of Refinitiv for $27bn (£16.8bn) last month.

But Euronext said in a statement it had made a "confidential proposal" to the LSE board.

It added that there was no certainty any firm offer would be made.

The LSE has until early July to firm up its offer for Refinitiv.

Refinitiv is currently owned by a consortium of investors including Blackstone, Thomson Reuters, and the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board.

They took over the company, formerly known as Thomson Reuters Financial & Risk (TRF&R), in 2018.

Euronext said its proposal included "a significant share component" for the LSE's shareholders.

The LSE has until 02 July to decide whether to make a firm offer for Refinitiv and until 19 July to table that offer.

Refinitiv's shareholders have until 01 August to decide whether to accept the LSE's offer.

If the LSE does not table a firm offer for Refinitiv by 19 July, it would have to wait until November, meaning its current takeover plan would likely fall apart.

Last week, Reuters reported that the LSE was looking at taking on more debt as a way of coming up with a counterbid.

At 1400 GMT, LSE shares were up 6.6% at £76.88.

The chairman of Euronext has reportedly written to the board of the London Stock Exchange (LSE) urging it to engage in discussions about a possible merger. 

The letter from Stéphane Boujnah follows interest from the LSE in acquiring Refinitiv, the financial data provider that is currently owned by a consortium including Blackstone. 

Blackstone has indicated it would prefer Refinitiv to be sold to a single buyer and sources close to the matter have said the LSE may be willing to sell its majority stake in Borsa Italiana to facilitate a deal. 

Euronext's move marks the latest development in the potential overhaul of the $14 trillion global foreign-exchange market. 

Refinitiv is the largest seller of market data to banks, providing stock market quotes, news and analytics. Its subsidiary, Tradeweb, is one of the biggest platforms for trading bonds. 

Sources close to the matter say that if the LSE pursued both Refinitiv and Borsa Italiana it would constitute a major step in the exchange's push to become a more global business. 

It comes after the LSE abandoned its pursuit of Deutsche Börse in 2017 following a lengthy battle and concerns raised by the UK's competition authority.

The money spent on Britain's new e-university could have been better spent on widening participation in higher education, according to the head of the country's largest university. In one of his first major speeches as head of the University of Warwick, Professor Nigel Thrift said that the £136m spent on the e-university could have paid for 30,000 extra students to go through the university system. "It is a disgraceful waste of money which could have been spent on widening participation," he said.

The e-university was announced in 1997 as part of the government's strategy for increasing the number of people with access to higher education. It was intended to be a "virtual" university, without a campus, offering courses predominantly through the internet. But the project has been hit by a series of problems and has been the subject of criticism from academics who said that it would not attract students because of the lack of face-to-face teaching.

Last month, the government's spending watchdog said that there was no clear business plan for the e-university and that value for money was not proven. The university's board is due to meet later this month to consider its future. Professor Thrift said that he did not believe that the e-university concept was "a bad idea in principle". But he added: "It is clear that it was conceived 11 years ago and that the world has moved on. "The sums of money involved, £100m of public money and £36m of private money, could and should have been spent on widening participation."

The University of Warwick, which has more than 12,000 students, received £121m in income last year. Professor Thrift said that the university intended to increase its intake of students from Britain's poorest backgrounds by 25 per cent over the next five years.

The head of one of Britain's biggest universities has criticised the planned online university, saying it is a "disgraceful waste" of public money.

London Metropolitan University's vice-chancellor, John Raftery, said the government's plans for an e-university were a "distraction" from the mainstream universities.

His comments come after the government awarded the consortium led by the Open University a £17m development grant.

The Open University (OU) said it planned to offer UK students the chance to gain a whole degree online by 2006.

But Mr Raftery said: "To spend £17m on a distraction from the mainstream is a disgraceful waste of public money."

His comments were reported by the Sunday Times.

The Department for Education and Skills (DfES) awarded the money to the OU-led consortium in July.

The consortium includes the University of London, City University, the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC), and the Science Museum.

The money will be used to develop the virtual learning environment and to establish the e-university's governing body.

The DfES has made available a further £140m for the running of the e-university in 2006-7 should the consortium's bid be successful.

A spokesman for the OU said the consortium's virtual learning environment would "revolutionise" home study.

"This is a major, imaginative and exciting initiative which has the potential to transform the way people learn," he said.

"Rather than simply providing a series of online lectures, the environment will enable students to learn through a variety of methods and activities that will provide a rich, varied and flexible learning experience."

The plan is to offer students the chance to study for a whole degree online by 2006. In the future, students may also be able to study for doctorates and other professional qualifications online.

The economic situation in Britain is likely to deteriorate over the next 12 months, according to a poll of economists carried out by the BBC.

Singer Courtney Love has avoided jail by pleading guilty to assaulting a former manager.

Love, 52, was accused of punching and kicking Barry Reinbolt several times in June 2020, in connection with claims that he had stolen jewellery from her.

She pleaded guilty to fourth-degree assault and was given a one-year deferred sentence in court on Thursday.

The singer was ordered to pay $350 (£268) to a women's shelter and participate in an anger management course.

"I want to say that I'm sorry for my behaviour," Love said during an emotional hearing in court, according to documents obtained by PA news agency.

The court heard how Love and Reinbolt were in a "loving relationship" when he began working for her, but that his behaviour had become "controlling" and she had tried to end the relationship.

On one occasion, Love said, Reinbolt had pushed her to the ground and taken her phone to stop her from calling her assistant.

The singer "felt scared and embarrassed" when police arrived at her home following an incident in June 2020, and claimed that Reinbolt had taken her phone and handcuffed her to a chair.

Love admitted that she had punched Reinbolt in the face and kicked him in the groin, but said that she had acted in self-defence because he had threatened to make explicit videos of her and distribute them.

Reinbolt, who the court heard has "sincerely apologised" to Love for his behaviour, testified that Love had handcuffed him to a chair and hit him in the face several times.

He said he had taken her phone to stop her from posting messages on social media and did not believe he had stolen any jewellery.

Love's lawyer said his client had experienced "trauma and abuse" in her relationship with Reinbolt.

He added that Love, who was not present for the hearing, had sought professional treatment for her mental health issues and wanted to "move on with her life".

The singer was ordered to undergo an assessment for domestic violence and was given a one-year deferred sentence.

If Love commits another offence in that time, she will be sentenced on the assault charge as well.

Several of Love's guitars were ordered to be returned to her, along with a gun and jewellery.

Liverpool chairman Tom Werner has warned the English game is "close to burning out" young players and says Academy chief Alex Inglethorpe has been asked to help protect against it.

Werner was speaking as Liverpool opened their state-of-the-art Academy on Friday.

The £50m complex, which sees the club return to Kirkby on a site close to Liverpool's old stadium, has been specifically designed to develop and nurture young players.

"One of the things we're concerned about is young players getting burned out," said Werner, who is also the Fenway Sports Group's chairman.

"We have discussions with Alex Inglethorpe, our academy director, all the time about weaning these young players so they can develop gradually, because that is what is required if they are to have long careers.

"It's pretty clear English football is close to burning out young players. You see the numbers that get played at a young age. The notion of 'super-sub' doesn't seem to exist in England. In Germany and Spain, players are much more developed when they get to the first team."

Liverpool manager Jurgen Klopp is among those to have expressed concern about the physical demands being placed on young players, who can struggle to cope with the expectation to perform well in their early games for the club while adapting to the step up in intensity from youth football.

Klopp has repeatedly called for reform of the schedule for young players in England to bring it in line with other countries.

Werner added: "It's not just Liverpool. I think it's a problem across England.

"You have a player like Raheem Sterling, who is a tremendous athlete, and he was playing games at the age of 15.

"Think about that. He's an extraordinary athlete but at 15 he was playing games for a big club.

"That doesn't happen in other countries. These are the discussions we have to have, because the game is about the players. It's our job to protect them so they can have long and successful careers."

Football: Player burn-out worries Robinson

Footballers are "breaking down" because of the volume of football they are expected to play, says Portsmouth manager Danny Robinson.

The 26-year-old former England Under-21 goalkeeper - who had a six-year spell at Tottenham - had season-ending knee surgery in August.

"There's no time off, no rest for the players, especially when you're going from a Saturday to a Tuesday," he said.

"That's not enough time for the body to recover and I think that's showing with a lot of the players, they are breaking down."

Ollie Watkins, who joined Aston Villa from Brentford for £28m in September, is the latest high-profile example, having been ruled out for up to three months with a hamstring injury.

Robinson said he "totally agreed" with Villa's head coach Dean Smith, who said this week that the Christmas period football programme was "crazy".

The festive schedule sees Villa play four games in 10 days, with two of those games coming in 48 hours.

The mobile phone has changed a lot in 20 years, from bulky devices that could only make calls and send text messages to the multi-functional smartphones of today.

They have gone from being a luxury to a necessity, and from a novelty to an everyday item. But one thing hasn't changed: the speed at which we upgrade them.

In the US, the average lifespan of a mobile phone is 22 months. In the UK it is 18 months.

And it is not just phones. In general, consumers upgrade their gadgets every three to four years.

This is having a big impact on the planet.

Electronic waste, or e-waste, is now the fastest-growing waste stream in the world, and it is increasingly ending up in landfills in developing countries.

The United Nations estimates that in 2016, the world produced 44.7 million tonnes of e-waste, and that this will grow to 52.2 million tonnes by 2021.

This is the equivalent of throwing away 800 laptops every second.

Most of this waste is not properly recycled, and the toxins in e-waste, such as lead, cadmium and brominated flame retardants, can pollute the air, water and soil.

And the carbon emissions produced during the manufacturing and disposal of electronic devices are significant.

One report estimated that the carbon footprint of the information and communications technology (ICT) industry is already equivalent to that of the civil aviation industry.

So what can be done to reduce the environmental impact of our love of gadgets?

One approach is to make them easier to repair.

A recent study in the US found that making smartphones easier to fix could significantly reduce the environmental impact of the gadget boom.

The study found that extending the life of a phone by just one year could reduce its carbon footprint by up to 30%.

This would have the biggest impact on the most-used devices, such as smartphones.

Another approach is to make phones using more sustainable materials, such as biodegradable plastics or fabrics made from recycled materials.

There are also many things we can do as consumers to reduce the environmental impact of our gadgets.

This includes buying devices that are more durable and longer-lasting, extending the life of our devices by taking care of them and repairing them when they break, and recycling our old devices when we upgrade.

With the right approaches, we could reduce the environmental impact of our gadgets while still enjoying the benefits

The mobile phone has changed a lot in the past 20 years, but one thing has remained constant: our reliance on them.

According to a recent study, the average person will upgrade their phone every 2.5 years, with some people keeping their devices for as long as five years. But no matter how long we keep our phones for, one thing is certain: we can't live without them.

In the early days of mobile phones, they were used primarily for making calls and sending text messages. But today, they're used for everything from browsing the internet to paying for groceries.

As mobile phones have become more and more popular, so too have the number of apps available for them. There are now millions of apps available for both iOS and Android devices, ranging from games to productivity tools.

While some people may argue that mobile phones are a distraction, there's no denying that they've become an integral part of our lives. Whether we're using them for work or play, they're here to stay.

Bayern Munich have been dealt a double injury blow ahead of Saturday's Bundesliga showdown with title rivals Borussia Dortmund.

Dutch full-back Jeremie Frimpong was already out with a thigh problem and now Arjen Robben has joined him on the sidelines.

The 35-year-old former Netherlands international has suffered a hairline fracture of his left foot in training.

The Conservative Party has published details of its policy to send asylum seekers to Rwanda.

The cost of the policy, which aims to deter people crossing the English Channel in small boats, would be about £1.4bn a year, the party says.

Under the scheme, announced earlier this month, arrivals would be given a choice of either being sent to Rwanda or leaving the UK for a "safe third country" where they would be granted asylum.

Those who chose to go to Rwanda would be processed there and, if successful, would be resettled in the east African country.

Unsuccessful applicants would be offered accommodation in Rwanda and encouraged to apply again, the policy says.

The cost of the policy would be about £1.4bn in the first full year, then £1.2bn a year afterwards, the party says.

About £106m of that money would be for accommodation for those waiting for decisions on their asylum claims.

The remainder would be for airline contracts and "support on the ground" in Rwanda.

The party says it has received advice from the Migration Advisory Committee on the cost of the policy and that the committee's members agreed with their calculations.

The policy has been widely criticised by churches, charities and opposition parties.

The Archbishop of Canterbury, Justin Welby, said it was immoral and unjust while the Prime Minister's wife, Carrie Johnson, said it was "unethical and dangerous".

The UN's refugee chief called the policy "catastrophic" and the US government described it as "wrong" and a "waste of human life".

The policy says the government could consider further "safe destination" agreements for asylum seekers in the future.

The government has unveiled plans to reform the asylum system, including a proposal to send some asylum seekers to a "third country" while their application is processed. 

The plan, which was announced by Home Secretary Priti Patel, would see applicants sent to countries such as Rwanda, Ghana, and Kenya. Under the plans, some asylum seekers could be charged up to £1,000 to fund their flight. 

The government says the scheme will cost £120 million in the first year and will "deter illegal entry" to the UK. 

The plans have been criticised by opposition parties and human rights groups, who have described them as "inhumane" and "unethical". They add that the government has not provided any details on how the scheme would work or how much it would cost.

Super Size Me, the documentary in which American filmmaker Morgan Spurlock eats only McDonald's food for a month, has won a writers' award.

The film, praised and damned for its investigation of the fast food industry, received a Christopher Award on Monday.

The awards, given for "excellence in communications that affirm the highest values of the human spirit," have been handed out by the Christophers, a Catholic organisation, for the past 50 years.

Super Size Me was named best television documentary.

Mr. Spurlock's film depicts the negative effects of eating the kind of food that is served at the McDonald's restaurant chain.

A crew from the BBC filmed Mr. Spurlock as he stopped eating nutritious food and exercised in order to determine what would happen if he lived on McDonald's food alone.

The film shows him gaining 25 pounds (11 kilograms) and having increases in his cholesterol and triglyceride levels.

At the end of the experiment, Mr. Spurlock goes to a doctor, who tells him he is on the road to obesity and possible diabetes.

The Oscar-winning documentary Super Size Me has won the Writers Guild of America award for best documentary screenplay.
The film, which examines the health effects of the fast-food industry, beat four other nominees to win the prestigious honour.
The writers of the best documentary nominees accepted their awards at a ceremony in Los Angeles on Sunday.
Super Size Me director and screenwriter Morgan Spurlock accepted the award on behalf of his colleagues.
Of the honour, he said: "Thank you for recognising the hard work that all of us did on Super Size Me.
"I share this award with my colleagues, my supervisors, my producers, and most importantly the participants of the film - the people that stood by me during this whole process."

Super Size Me follows Spurlock as he spends 30 days on a diet of McDonald's food, filming the effects on his health.
The film has earned more than $21m (£11.6m) at the US box office to become one of the most successful documentary films of all time.
It has also sparked a national debate about obesity and the fast-food industry.

The other nominees in the best documentary category were:

- Benjamin Button, written by Eric Roth
- The Cove, written by Mark Monroe
- Fahrenheit 9/11, written by Michael Moore
- Grizzly Man, written by Werner Herzog

Former MP John Hemming has told the BBC the death rate of children in custody in England and Wales "shocks and shocks" him.

His daughter Harriet, a probation officer, conducted a study on behalf of the Howard League for Penal Reform.

Her report reveals that between 1990 and 2020, 4,543 children were arrested and put in custody - and 293 died.

Mr Hemming said the figure "doesn't include the many who require hospital treatment".

Harriet Hemming's report is based on responses to Freedom of Information requests to each of the regional police forces in England and Wales, and to the British Transport Police.

The Freedom of Information requests asked for information on the number of children in each regional police force who had been arrested and taken into police custody, and on the number of child deaths in custody for each force, from 1990 to 2020.

The study found that 36 forces had recorded 239 child deaths of those in custody, while 46 forces did not provide a figure for how many children had died in their custody.

The report also found that more than half of the child deaths in custody occurred while the child was under the care of a police officer, on their way to a place of safety or in a cell.

Mr Hemming, who served as MP for Birmingham Yardley from 1987 to 2017, said his daughter had "done a very good report on it, which shocks and shocks me".

"It's an appalling record, frankly. Nobody seems to be accountable for it," he added.

The former MP added the rate of deaths of children in custody was probably more than 1 in 1,000 - as there were more than a million arrests of children every decade.

"It's probably about 1 in 2,000 or 1 in 1,000 - it could be higher than that," he said.

"These are children in custody who die - that is, they are in the custody of the police, in a cell, in a van taking them somewhere, or actually in the police station itself.

"Some of them die through suicide, some of them die through accident, some of them die through misadventure and some of them die because the police handle them in a really dangerous way."

Mr Hemming said no-one had been held accountable for the deaths, which were "totally unacceptable".

He added the rate of deaths would "shock the public" if they were made more aware of the

The government has been urged to act after a BBC News analysis found hundreds of people died within two years of being released from prison custody in England and Wales last year.

The BBC's analysis of Ministry of Justice data showed 325 deaths of people who were released from prison or police custody in 2021. 

This is an increase on previous years and the highest number since at least 2014. Of those, 174 died within two days.

A prominent human rights lawyer who defended some of the most high-profile defendants in recent terrorism cases has told the BBC he is ashamed of the anti-terror laws he helped create.

Clifford Chance partner Martyn Day was a member of the official committee that helped draft the Terrorism Act 2000.

But he says he is now horrified by the way the law is used, in particular the "draconian" Prevention of Terrorism Act 2005.

"I genuinely fear that we are creating a police state by degrees," he said.

Mr Day is so concerned that he is taking an active role in the campaign against the law, and is even calling for the arrest of Tony Blair for the part he played in introducing it.

The lawyer, who has been involved in many high-profile terrorism cases, said the legislation was having a "chilling effect" on the fundamental rights and freedoms in Britain.

He told the BBC News website that the laws created a "two-tier" legal system, with some people having more rights than others.

And he said that while the law was aimed at protecting the public, it was in fact endangering them.

"Because the consequence of the legislation is that the police are not investigating properly, and therefore there is a real risk that terrorism will be perpetrated," he said.

He added that he believed the law was being used to harass ethnic minorities and political dissidents.

And he said that the definition of terrorism was so broad it could be used to criminalise legitimate political activities.

"I think that the legislation is so broad and so draconian that it will catch legitimate political protest," he said.

"It's designed to catch terrorism but it's actually catching legitimate political dissent and that is unacceptable in any democratic society."

Mr Day added that he believed the law was being used to harass ethnic minorities.

"I think that the legislation is, unfortunately, in danger of being used to hound ethnic minorities, to hound dissidents in this country," he said.

"And I think that is substantially a result of guidance that has been issued by the Association of Chief Police Officers (Acpo)."

Mr Day is now actively supporting the campaign group Liberty, which is seeking to have the Prevention of Terrorism Act 2005 repealed.

He is also supporting a legal challenge to the law, which is due to be heard by the European Court of Human Rights later this year

Lawyer attacks anti-terror laws

A leading human rights lawyer has launched a scathing attack on the government's anti-terror legislation, describing it as "oppressive" and "unjust".

Ramby de Mello, who has represented a string of high-profile clients including Julian Assange and Wikileaks, accused the government of using the threat of terrorism to introduce laws that are "undemocratic and unlawful".

The government has said the legislation is necessary to protect the public from the threat of terrorism.

But Mr de Mello, who is the founder of the International Rights Advocate Group, argued that the laws were being used to restrict freedom of expression and freedom of association.

"The government is using the threat of terrorism as a pretext to introduce laws that are unjust and oppressive," he said.

"This is a classic example of using a sledgehammer to crack a nut. It is clear that the government is more interested in curbing dissent than in protecting the public from terrorism."

Mr de Mello said the government's attempts to crack down on terrorism were "worrying" and could have a "chilling effect" on freedom of speech.

"The government should be careful not to impose restrictions that are unnecessary and disproportionate," he said.

"The right to freedom of expression and association is a fundamental human right that should not be restricted except in exceptional circumstances."

Kraft Foods has announced it is no longer going to advertise its snack brands to children under the age of 12 in the US.

Kraft said it would define childhood as under 12 years of age based on the US Census definition.

CFBAI said the decision was "a significant step forward in the effort to improve the nutritional profile of food advertised to children". 

"Kraft's commitment serves as an example of the industry's ability to self-regulate and improve its practices to promote healthier dietary habits among children," said CFBAI president Lisa Gable. 

Kraft's pledge comes after a study by the University of Connecticut's Rudd Center for Food Policy and Obesity found that the three food companies most prominently advertising on children's television - McDonald's, Kraft and Hershey - could do more to ensure their ads met CFBAI's nutrition criteria. 

The study found that although the three companies had improved the nutritional quality of products advertised to children, in 2010, only 18% of the 3,000-plus ads met nutrition standards. 

In addition, the Rudd Center found that the three companies did not consistently follow best practices for advertising to children, such as advertising only healthier products and avoiding advertising during children's programming. 

"This latest study shows that the companies that spend the most on advertising to children have more work to do to fulfil the commitment they made to self-regulate their food advertising," said Jennifer Harris, director of marketing initiatives at the Rudd Center. 

"The fast-food industry, in particular, needs to do more to market healthier options to children and to limit marketing of unhealthy products," she added. 

Kraft said as part of its pledge, it would enhance its marketing practices to not directly target children under 12 in its snack advertising. 

"We will continue to advertise our snack brands in programming that is targeted to

Kraft, the maker of Oreo and Ritz crackers, is cutting back on advertising to children. The company's CEO, Irene Rosenfeld, said in a statement that too many kids were eating too many unhealthy snacks. "As a parent, I am deeply concerned by the unhealthy habits that are developing in our children," she said. Kraft will continue to advertise its cereals, which are generally healthier than its snacks. However, the company will no longer advertise snack foods during shows or programs aimed at children. It also pledged to cut the number of unhealthy ingredients in its snacks.

Schools in the UK will be teaching children as young as 11 years old about the  legality and ethical concerns around file sharing, as part of a government campaign.

The Intellectual Property Office (IPO) said file-sharing was "fast becoming a mainstream activity".

About 2,000 schools will take part in the year-long campaign to give legal advice to prevent copyright theft.

The IPO said teenagers were particularly at risk as they "often do not realise they are breaking the law".

The advisory programme will provide information to help pupils "distinguish between lawful and unlawful file sharing".

It aims to teach children how to "stay within the law" and will provide information on how to acquire films, music and other content online.

Young people's behaviour is under greater scrutiny as statistics released last month revealed that one in five 11 to 15-year-olds had copied music files from the internet, according to BBC News.

Intellectual Property Enforcement Director Edward Moseley said young people were often unaware that downloading or sharing copyrighted material without permission was illegal.

"The advisory programme... will make it easier for them to separate the lawful from the unlawful and understand the consequences of their actions," he added.

The programme will be available online and will become part of the curriculum in selected schools from September this year.

Britain's creative industries, worth more than £100 billion to the economy, are facing a crisis with the rapid rise of piracy. 

In a bid to combat the trend, pupils are to be given lessons in the importance of paying for digital content. 

The BBC, along with the UK's five other public service broadcasters, the Premier League, and the Creative Industries Federation, have devised a plan to educate children, and their parents, about the risks of piracy. 

The move comes after a Government green paper revealed that millions of people in the UK could be accessing content illegally.

The UK's national fraud and cyber crime reporting centre has issued an alert over an increase in the theft of card details.

The centre, run by the City of London Police, said criminals were targeting web browsers and passwords. 

It issued advice on how to reduce the risk of fraud, but no specific incidents had been reported. 

The warning came after months of similar alerts from banks.

In a statement, the centre said it wanted to make the public aware of "increasing reports" of a new technique being used by criminals to steal people's card details. 

"Fraudsters are targeting the computers of consumers, as well as businesses and retailers, by infecting web browsers with malicious malware," it said. 

"This malware is known to be difficult to detect, and allows criminals to capture card details as a customer enters them online."

It urged people to protect themselves when shopping online by using websites that were "secure and authentic". 

"We would also encourage people to be wary of clicking on promotional banners, pop-ups or attachments in emails - as these are commonly used as a vehicle to transmit the malware," it added. 

"Ensuring you have antivirus software installed on your computer and keeping web browsers up to date is also vital in combating this type of malware."

The centre said it had also alerted the banking and retail industry to the threat. 

A number of major banks have issued warnings about the threat of so-called "card-not-present" fraud - where a stolen card is used to buy goods or services over the phone or internet - in recent months. 

The warning came on "Cyber Monday", the busiest day of the year for online shopping.

Card fraudsters are increasingly targeting the web as the use of contactless payments increases, the banking industry says.

The UK's Payment Systems Regulator (PSR) said more fraud was moving online as the use of contactless cards increased.

In the first six months of 2022, £353.3m was lost to card fraud, up 26% compared with the same period in 2021.

Contactless fraud made up more than a quarter of that total, increasing 45% from the first half of 2021.

PSR strategy director Nick Pope said: "Contactless fraud has increased in every month since November 2021, reaching a record £39.1 million in June 2022."

The regulator said there was also a shift towards fraudulent purchases of goods, as opposed to the theft of card details for use in cloning cards.

Fraud involving the purchase of goods made up 56% of contactless fraud in the first half of 2022, up from 39% in the same period last year.

It said this reflected more stolen cards being used to buy goods, rather than being passed on to professional criminals to create cloned cards.

The PSR said "significant further work" was needed to protect customers from fraud.

Its interim report made 12 recommendations to the industry, including the establishment of a fraud data hub to improve the sharing of fraud data between payment firms.

It also called for better communication with customers on how to protect themselves from fraud.

The birthplace of music legend Ray Charles in Florida is set to reopen to the public on Friday after being closed for a year.

Folk singer and civil rights activist Miriam Makeba bought the studio in Gainesville, Florida, in 1986, three years after Charles' death. Makeba, who was known as Mama Africa for her role as an apartheid activist, died in 2008.

The studio, which is now a museum, is where Charles recorded his first record, "Confession Time," at the age of 18 in 1949.

The museum reopened for the annual celebration of his birth on Friday, with exhibits including the piano he used at the studio, a replica of the recording booth, and posters of his performances from the University of Florida's Gator Growl, the longest-running student-produced show in the US.

Charles grew up during segregation and went on to win 12 Grammy awards and sell more than 75 million records. He died aged 73 in 2004.

The studio where American musician Ray Charles created some of his most iconic works has opened as a museum. 

Charles, nicknamed the "Genius", was one of the most influential artists in the history of American music, blending rhythm and blues, gospel, and country into his signature style.

His recording studio in Atlanta, Georgia, has been transformed into a museum, showcasing items including original manuscripts, letters and photographs. 

Following his death in 2004, the space was purchased by entrepreneur and philanthropist Paul Allen, who is behind the transformation.

Greater Manchester's mayor has questioned why his constituents have received pre-recorded messages from the NHS encouraging people to get vaccinated, which feature Greater Manchester Police Chief Constable Stephen Watson.

Andy Burnham said using the force's head in that way was "not clever".

The NHS said the campaign was developed in partnership with police leaders.

The initiative sees recorded messages sent to the homes of people who have not yet had their booster jab.

They are played down the phone to people who answer, featuring Mr Watson, who urges them to get vaccinated.

The force said it had not been contacted about the campaign.

Mr Burnham said he had "never heard" of the initiative and knew nothing about it until people started contacting his office to ask if the communication was legitimate.

He said he had since made enquiries and been told the campaign used Mr Watson's recorded voice because the NHS had been unable to get hold of the mayor.

"Obviously I'm flattered they thought my voice was good enough but actually that's not clever using the chief constable in that way," he said.

"It's not been done in consultation with elected members or with local authorities.

"Using the chief constable in that way suggests the police are backing a vaccination campaign - that is not what I understand from discussions with the chief constable."

Mr Burnham said he had been "very clear" that he was supportive of the vaccine campaign but this should be "done in an appropriate way".

"I am not criticising the NHS directly because I don't know who has decided to do this and on what basis," he added.

An NHS spokesman said the campaign was developed in partnership with police leaders and featured recorded messages from a number of forces.

He said: "Voice messages were sent to households within the GM [Greater Manchester] area that did not answer their door to vaccination canvassers.

"Canvassers found that some people were not answering their doors because they were wary of strangers, so we sent these voice messages to ensure they had the chance to ask questions and book their appointments."

The campaign behind the so-called "cold calls" made to voters in the run-up to the general election has been questioned by the head of the UK statistics agency.

Prof Sir Ian Diamond said the practice of making unsolicited phone calls to voters "undermines" public trust in statistics.

The Labour Party has admitted making " overcautious" calls to voters to check their details were correct.

The Liberal Democrats and Conservative Party have both received reports of similar calls.

In an interview with the BBC News website, Prof Diamond, the UK Statistics Authority (UKSA) chair, said making such calls was "not acceptable".

He said: "This issue of making cold calls - which are not agreed with the recipient - to households to check their energy tariff or whatever is a very serious issue.

"It undermines that trust in official statistics and it's something that the Statistics Authority will be pursuing with the Office for Statistical Regulation."

"I think it is not acceptable to make these cold calls.

"They are not agreed with the people who are receiving them, they are receiving them unexpectedly. They are not able to check the source of the call or to know whether the person on the other end of the line is legitimate."

Labour said on Saturday that it had "reviewed our processes" following the furore over the calls.

"We have concluded that, in a small number of cases, our volunteer callers have overstepped the mark in their enthusiasm to get details correct," a party spokesperson said.

"In these cases, our volunteers have made additional calls to people who have already confirmed they are on the electoral register.

"This is not acceptable and should not have happened. In these cases, our volunteers have overstepped the mark. Labour's campaign has contacted those people to apologise and deleted their data."

The spokesperson added that the party had "reviewed our scripts, procedures and training" and that the campaign "will ensure our volunteers are better trained and better supported".

Earlier, a Liberal Democrat spokesperson said the party had received a "small number of complaints" about unsolicited phone calls.

"In some cases, volunteers may have inadvertently crossed a line, though our understanding is the vast majority of calls were entirely appropriate," the spokesperson said.

"All parties need to ensure their volunteers are trained and updated on the correct process. Liberal Democrats have taken this opportunity to remind all volunteers of the need to comply

The International Association of Athletics Federations (IAAF) has confirmed that it will rule on whether to ban the Greek sprinters Kostadinos Kenteris and Katerina Thanou for allegedly taking performance-enhancing drugs.

- Introducing a public interest test into whistleblowing law
- Strengthening the powers of regulators to act on whistleblowing
- Introducing compensation for workers who suffer detriment as a result of blowing the whistle

The TUC also called for a new independent public body to be set up to investigate whistleblowing complaints and support those who have suffered detriment.

Ms O'Grady said: "Whistleblowers need proper legal protection. They face reprisals from their boss, including dismissal, and bullying. This cannot be allowed to continue.

"Ministers have seriously undermined their own inquiries into Downing Street parties by failing to launch an independent investigation.

"Given the obvious conflict of interest, it is impossible for this government to be trusted to investigate itself."

Richest 1% of Colombia's population has grabbed nearly half the money set aside for the nation's anti-poverty programme, alarming officials in a country where wealth inequality is among the widest in the world.

The enriched families withdrew nearly $750m (£656m) from the so-called "solidarity dividend" over the past six years.

The dividend is paid by the government from taxes on the nation's largest banks and telephone and utilities companies.

It is meant to help some of Colombia's neediest citizens.

But the fund has instead become a windfall for the wealthy, according to the head of the national tax office, Juan Carlos Velez.

"This is unacceptable," he told local media. "We are going to implement measures to avoid this happening again."

The fund was set up more than 20 years ago as part of a landmark peace deal between the government and guerrilla group, the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc).

But in recent years the rules governing the programme have been loosened and the money is now used by some as an alternative pension scheme, or to pay for private education and healthcare.

The head of the tax office plans to restrict the use of the funds, and increase controls over them.

Several former directors of the fund have been accused of taking bribes in exchange for allowing wealthy Colombians to withdraw money.

One former official was arrested last week as part of the investigation.
The fund is officially called the Solidarity Intergenerational Savings Programme, and was modelled on a similar scheme in Chile.

It is funded by a tax on the largest local and foreign companies operating in Colombia. The money is meant to incentivise businesses to invest in the country.

Colombia has one of the highest rates of wealth inequality in the world, according to the World Inequality Report 2022.

The report found that the top 1% of earners in the country earn more than 20% of the total national income.

The very poorest people in Colombia are having their savings eaten away by inflation, forcing them to eat less and turn to child labour, the country's central bank has said.

The bank's survey - based on interviews with more than 17,000 people - found that nearly half of the country's poorest had lost money because of inflation.

Households earning less than 375,000 pesos (£63; $75) a month - around the minimum wage - lost an average of 13% of their savings in the past year, it found.

Many said they were eating less, or eating lower-quality food. Some reported having to send their children to work. The survey was carried out in October 2021.

"I want to eat three meals a day but I can't," said one respondent. "Sometimes I eat only once and that's in the morning. When I can I eat lunch, otherwise I don't."

The statistics are the latest to highlight the impact that decades of conflict, climate change and the pandemic have had on some of the country's most vulnerable people.

Colombia's statistical agency said that the country's poverty rate - which stood at 52% in 2019 - had likely increased during the pandemic.

And the country's National Planning Department said that 8.4 million people were living in conditions of extreme poverty, defined as living on less than $1 a day.

The central bank's survey found that poverty and inflation were higher in rural and urban areas than in small towns.

The bank's governor, Leonardo Villar, said that the findings showed that "price dynamics are affecting the poorest households the most".

"This tells us we have to redouble our efforts, not only to bring down inflation, but also to find mechanisms to protect the most vulnerable households," he told reporters.

The bank has been raising interest rates to try to reduce inflation, which currently stands at nearly 11%, one of the highest rates in the world.

But it has warned that inflation - which is also being hit by the war in Ukraine - is likely to remain high for some time.

Britain's most senior judge warned on Thursday that the government's planned identity cards scheme would undermine the fundamental right to privacy.

His comments came as Home Secretary Charles Clarke faced a rebellion from backbench Labour MPs over the plans.

One senior minister told the BBC that up to 40 Labour MPs were prepared to vote against the government when the matter is put to the vote in the House of Commons on Monday.

The BBC's political editor Nick Robinson said senior ministers had told him they now believed the vote would be lost - but they would have to wait until Monday to see if their MPs were prepared to defy the government.

On Thursday, in the final part of his daily campaign for the scheme, Mr Clarke told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that ID cards were "absolutely essential" in fighting terrorism.

But he faced immediate criticism from opponents - and even some supporters - who said the scheme was too expensive, too authoritarian and would not tackle terrorism.

David Cameron has been urged to drop plans to introduce national identification cards after the idea was backed by senior ministers. Home Secretary Charles Clarke faced the rebellion from MPs after announcing the details of the plan to parliament on Tuesday. So what is the government's plan, and why has it caused such controversy? The national identity scheme, as the government would have it, sounds innocuous enough. Individuals would be offered a "choice" of whether or not to sign up for a national ID card, which would be produced by a private company. Alongside this, everyone who wants a passport would have to apply for a new-style document, which would double as a national ID card. The former executives of two American companies went on trial in Milan on charges of murder and failure to protect the environment.

The trial of the former executives of mining companies Union Carbide and Dow Chemical got under way in Italy on Tuesday.

They are accused of failing to prevent the deadly explosion at the Bhopal plant in India in 1984, which killed thousands of people.

The defendants are also accused of failing to adequately dispose of hazardous waste at the site.

The seven executives include the chairman and chief executive of Union Carbide at the time, Warren Anderson, who has since died.
The others are ex-Union Carbide India chairman Kishore Kamdar, and former Dow Chemical CEO, Geoffrey H. Keys.

They all deny the charges.

The explosion of methyl isocyanate at the plant in the central Indian city released a toxic gas that killed thousands and injured more than 150,000.

The site had been owned by Union Carbide, but seven years before the disaster, the firm had sold it to Dow Chemical.

The long-awaited trial began after the Indian government finally handed over documents relating to the case that had been requested by Italian magistrates.

The defendants had been due to go on trial in Bhopal, but the Indian government failed to respond to requests for information about the incident.

That led the judges to issue an international warrant for the executives' arrest in 1992.

The warrant was executed in Switzerland five years later and the defendants have been on trial in Milan ever since, but the case was repeatedly delayed because the Indian government failed to provide documents relating to the incident.

David Waters and Francis Hatfield, former executives of the failed Anglo-Irish bank, face charges of fraud and false accounting at a trial that begins today. 

The long-awaited trial, which is expected to last for six months, represents the UK's largest prosecution of individuals connected with the global banking crisis. 

The charges against Waters, the bank's former finance director, and Hatfield, its ex-chairman, relate to a failure to inform auditors of a secret €3.2bn (£2.5bn) loan from the Irish government in 2008. 

The case against the men was brought by the Serious Fraud Office but passed to the Crown Prosecution Service earlier this year. 

Both defendants deny any wrongdoing.

Intel has built a breakthrough new laser that could finally help bring extreme high-speed internet access to your home.

The chip maker has demonstrated a technology called "terabit silicon laser" that can transmit data at a staggering rate of 1.02 terabits per second over a distance of 2km (1.24 miles).

That's 50 times faster than the fastest fibre optics connection available today and speeds that even quantum computing cannot hope to match.

The silicon laser could be used to upgrade the infrastructure of internet service providers (ISPs) to enable speeds of up to 1.6 terabits per second downstream from ISPs to homes.

Thereafter, the speed of data transmission would be dependent on the equipment inside consumers' homes.

Today, most homes in the UK have a broadband speed of 36Mbps, while those lucky enough to live in areas covered by Virgin Media's cable service can receive speeds of up to 1Gbps - less than 0.2% of the speed that the new silicon laser is capable of.

The technology relies on a new type of laser etching that allows data to be processed and transmitted using light, rather than electrical pulses.

Justin Rattner, Intel's chief technology officer, said: "For the data centre market, where optical interconnects are beginning to reach their limits, the terabit silicon laser demonstrates how scalable and compact optical I/O can be for future high-performance computing platforms."

He added that the technology could be used to connect computers within a data centre, connecting data centres themselves and providing internet access.

The silicon laser could also be used to provide the infrastructure for 5G networks and high-speed autonomous vehicles.

Intel has made a breakthrough in laser technology that could ultimately result in the development of computers that are hugely more efficient than today's machines.

The company has been working on a project, named "Snowflake", to build a silicon chip that produces a laser, rather than a standard electronic beam, to carry data.

The initial target for the technology is the data centre market, worth an estimated $50bn (£39bn) per year.

Intel unveiled the project at an event in San Francisco on Wednesday.

"This is a new way of thinking about computing," said Rob Crooke, a senior vice-president at the company.

"Instead of having separate electronic and optical pathways in our chips, we're combining them into one, by putting lasers in silicon."

What is silicon?

Why it is important

The chips that power computers, phones and other smart devices use electrical circuits to carry data. However, electrical circuits have a limited capacity, and so can be improved upon.

Optical beams, carried by lasers, have much greater capacity. This means that computers using light to carry data can be more powerful, and process information more quickly, than those using electrical circuits.

To date, lasers have been built separately to silicon chips, then fitted together. That can affect the performance of the final product.

By contrast, Snowflake chips will have lasers built directly into the silicon, creating a more integrated product.

"It gives us a much better chance of getting to that exaflop milestone," said Mr Crooke, referring to a measure of computing speed.

How fast can computers get?

What is a petaflop?

Who is competing?

Intel is one of several companies working to improve computing speeds. Its rivals in the so-called "race to exascale" include IBM, Microsoft and Nvidia.

All have been developing technologies based on quantum computing, which promises exponential increases in speed.

Intel's laser technology is more conventional, and the company does not claim it will deliver exponential performance improvements. However, it believes it can deliver significant gains.

The company said the Snowflake project was in the "research phase", with the first chips expected to be ready for testing within 18 months.

The magical nanny who swoops in to save the day has been a figure of fantasy for more than 50 years.

And now she is flying high in the West End in a £10m (£6.6m) musical extravaganza that has got off to a flying start.

The stage musical of Mary Poppins, starring former Royal Ballet principal ballerina Cynthia Erivo, has taken £450,000 in advance bookings alone.

It has been a long time coming for the famous nanny, who first appeared in a book by PL Travers in 1934 and on the big screen 16 years later in Walt Disney's classic animation.

The magical musical story of Mary Poppins will return to its original home in December, with a special charity performance of the show raising money for AIDS and HIV charity, Crusaid.

The special performance, which is hosted by Sir Trevor McDonald, will see the return of Stephen Mear, who played Bert in the original London production, and who will be flying back to London from his current job in Broadway to participate. Fiat's board has approved a deal to give GM a $2.8bn (£1.7bn) stake in its auto business, clearing a major obstacle to a merger of the two carmakers.

The deal had been delayed as Fiat's board debated GM's offer and fought off a rival bid from Ford.

The merger will create the world's third-biggest carmaker by sales.

The combined company will be called Fiat-GM and be headed by Fiat's CEO, Sergio Marchionne.

The deal must still be approved by regulators and shareholders.

If it goes through, GM will get a 20% stake in Fiat, while Fiat will get a 1.5% stake in GM.

The companies said the deal would save them $2.8bn a year by 2015.

The merger has been approved by the boards of both companies but still needs the go-ahead from regulators and shareholders.

If the merger is approved, the new company would be worth about $140bn, based on the companies' current market values.

By comparison, Toyota is currently the world's biggest carmaker with sales of 10.2 million vehicles last year, followed by Volkswagen with 8.3 million.

Fiat-GM would sell about 8.6 million cars a year.

The merger deal comes as the auto industry struggles to recover from a sharp drop in sales in the US and Europe.

The combined company will have about $132bn in debt, ranking it as one of the most indebted companies in the world.

GM sold a record 4.7 million cars and trucks in 2010 but analysts say it needs to expand to survive as sales growth slows in its main markets.

Shares in Fiat Chrysler rose on Monday after the company confirmed it is in talks to merge with France's Renault, but added there is no guarantee a deal would be reached.

The statement followed a report in the Financial Times on Friday that the two car makers were in advanced talks about a 10 billion euro ($11 billion) tie-up.

The newspaper said the companies could make an announcement as soon as this week, adding that the deal could create a company with eight billion euros in annual synergies.

Fiat Chrysler (FCA) shares were up 5.2% in Milan on Monday morning, while Renault's were up 5.1% in Paris.

FCA said in a statement on Sunday: "The relevant committees of both boards have been meeting regularly over the past few weeks, with the involvement of their respective advisers, to evaluate a possible combination of their respective businesses.

"While there is no guarantee that these discussions will conclude successfully, they are proceeding well."

The statement added that any deal between the two companies would be subject to "completion of such discussions and conclusion of mutually satisfactory transactions".

In Paris, Renault said: "Discussions are taking place with respect to a friendly transaction with FCA Group."

The company said its board of directors met on Sunday and "decided to pursue vigorously the project of a merger with FCA Group".

The potential merger would create a group with eight million vehicles sold annually, making it the third-biggest car maker in the world, behind Volkswagen and Toyota.

The combined group would be 50% larger than either Renault or FCA alone, and would save about five billion euros in purchasing costs.

Renault's alliance with Nissan has been rocked by the arrest last November of its chief executive Carlos Ghosn, who has since been charged with financial misconduct.

Mr Ghosn, who denies any wrongdoing, has blamed his arrest on a "plot" against him by Nissan and Japanese officials.

The Italian-American carmaker has been looking for an alliance to help it tackle the costs of meeting tougher emissions regulations and developing electric and hybrid cars.

Last month, FCA pulled out of talks with Peugeot owner PSA, saying the two companies had not been able to find enough areas of "substantial synergies".

Five US citizens have been convicted of running a pirate streaming site which allowed tens of thousands of people to watch film and TV shows for free.

The platform, known as Jetflix, had a library of more than 10,000 movies and TV series. It registered a million user accounts and earned estimated revenues of $1.5m.

US authorities described it as "one of the largest streaming services offering illegal movies and television shows".

The site was shut down in November 2020.

At a federal court in western Texas on Tuesday, Jetflix's five founders were found guilty of conspiracy to commit copyright infringement.

The evidence presented at the trial showed that the defendants were aware that copyrights were being infringed but took steps to conceal their involvement in the piracy, according to the US Attorney's Office for the Western District of Texas.

The defendants were also found guilty of laundering the money earned from the streaming service through bitcoin.

Each faces up to five years in prison and $250,000 in fines for the copyright charges and up to 20 years in prison and $500,000 in fines for the money laundering charges.

In a major breakthrough for the fight against software piracy, four Americans have been convicted of engaging in widespread copyright infringement by operating a pirate website. After a seven-day trial, a federal jury in Texas found Denelle Dixon, David Bodher, Jeff Lundqvist, and Matthew Smith all guilty of conspiracy to commit copyright infringement. 

The four defendants were the masterminds behind a popular peer-to-peer file-sharing website called "MegaUpload," which allowed users to store and share files, including copyrighted content such as movies, TV shows, music, and software, without permission from the copyright holders. The site was shut down by the FBI in 2012 following an investigation that revealed the massive scale of copyright infringement taking place on the site. 

The jury found that the defendants were aware of the widespread copyright infringement taking place on MegaUpload but took no meaningful action to prevent it. In a statement, the U.S. Attorney's Office said that the defendants "profited handsomely from promoting and providing access to copyrighted content without the permission of the copyright holders... the defendants enriched themselves while harming artists, filmmakers, musicians, authors, and other creators of copyrighted works." 

The conviction comes as a significant victory for copyright holders in the ongoing battle against online piracy. It is the first time that individuals have been held personally liable for copyright infringement committed through a peer-to-peer file-sharing website.

Former Germany striker Lukas Podolski has tipped his former team-mate Thomas Hitzlsperger to be a success in management.

The ex-Aston Villa and West Ham United midfielder has been linked with the vacant managerial post at Irish side Aston Villa.

German Podolski played with Hitzlsperger at club and international level.

"He's a guy who's very interested in the game, he knows a lot about the game, he's got the personality, he's got the will," Podolski said.

"He's already been a captain at Aston Villa, so he's got the experience. I think for him it's maybe the next step and I think he can do very well."

Hitzlsperger, who won 54 caps for Germany and played at the 2006 World Cup, has been without a job since leaving Villa in 2016.
The 38-year-old has been linked with the vacant manager's job at League of Ireland side Dundalk, but Podolski believes his friend would be better off waiting for a job in England or Germany.

"He knows the football, the players, the teams, the clubs, everything about England, and Germany as well," Podolski added.

"I think it's not easy to go to another country and another league and start from scratch.

"He's still young, he's only 38, so he can still wait a little bit and get a good job in England or in Germany and do a good job there."

German football legend Thomas Hitzlsperger is waiting on the Irish businessman Tony O'Leary to see if he is to remain on the board of the German Football Association (DFB), as allegations of sexual abuse continue to stain German football.

Former Germany international Hitzlsperger, who in 2011 revealed he was gay, has been threatened with expulsion from the DFB's executive committee if he does not resign from his role as a pundit for Sky Sport Germany. Hitzlsperger had been accused of "violating and disregarding" his DFB obligations because of the comments he made while working as a television analyst during the recent World Cup in Qatar.

It is understood that Hitzlsperger, who was appointed to the DFB's executive committee in 2019, has asked fellow executive O'Leary to release a statement in support of him. O'Leary, who was elected to the DFB's executive committee in April this year, is said to have refused to do so and has instead called for Hitzlsperger to resign. 

Hitzlsperger, who scored 15 goals in 79 appearances for Germany, has confirmed that he will not be stepping down and has described the demands as "silencing strategies". 

The DFB has faced increased scrutiny since last month's revelation that Germany's biggest-selling newspaper, Bild, had been secretly recording therapeutic conversations with young patients at its flagship football academy, the Bayern Munich youth academy. A culture of fear is said to have existed at the academy, where numerous sexual abuses are alleged to have taken place. 

Despite Hitzlsperger's refusal to step down, it is believed that the DFB is keen to avoid a public dispute with the former Aston Villa and Middlesbrough midfielder and is open to a compromise.

The Football Association of Wales has launched an investigation after Wales player Joe Allen suffered an injury in a hotel bed prior to flying out to face Belgium in a World Cup qualifier. Centre-back Ashley Williams also picked up a training ground injury which means he will not feature in Monday's game. Wales boss Chris Coleman said it was "not ideal" ahead of the crucial match. He said it was "not the same injury" as the one he sustained against Serbia in November, which cut his season short.

Wales face Belgium in Brussels on Monday in their final Group E game of World Cup qualifying, with both nations having already qualified for next summer's tournament in Russia.

Wales have been forced to field a weakened side in their opening 2022 FIFA World Cup playoff final against Ukraine, after a number of players picked up injuries. Palestinian economy in decline

Large budget deficit and growing debt burden compounded by coronavirus pandemic

The Palestinian economy is in decline with a large budget deficit and growing debt burden compounded by the coronavirus pandemic, the World Bank has warned.

The bank urged Israel to improve economic ties with the Palestinians, and for the international community to offer greater support.

It said that real GDP in the Palestinian territories is expected to shrink by 11.5% in 2020, but modest growth is expected to resume next year.

The World Bank's report said that the West Bank's economy has been growing at a slow rate in the past 15 years, and the Gaza Strip has experienced a prolonged economic crisis.

"Growth has been stagnant, unemployment has risen, and poverty has increased, especially in Gaza," the report said.

"Societal fragility, including trust in institutions, has declined, and the fiscal situation has deteriorated, with debt rising and fiscal space limited."

The coronavirus pandemic has hit the Palestinian economy hard, with lockdowns and restrictions disrupting businesses, and few resources available to help households and businesses weather the economic fallout.

In the first quarter of 2020, the West Bank and Gaza saw their economies contract by 7.6% and 11.2% respectively, with more than half of the active workforce in the West Bank and three-quarters in Gaza losing their jobs.

The World Bank is calling on Israel to carry out long-delayed reforms to ease restrictions on the movement of people and goods that harm the Palestinian economy. It also urged Israel to improve the business environment for Palestinian firms in Israeli-controlled areas.

The bank said that Israeli authorities have, over the years, taken some steps to ease restrictions, but more needs to be done.

It cited a World Bank report that said the Palestinian economy could grow by an additional 12% per year, and Israeli economy by 1.2% per year, if restrictions were lifted.

The bank also called on the international community to offer greater support to the Palestinian Authority, particularly in the form of budget support and debt relief.

It said that the PA's budget deficit is expected to reach 11% of GDP this year, and its debt could reach 190% of GDP by the end of 2022.

The report said that donors have been generous in their support for the PA, but budget support has declined since 2018 and debt relief is limited.
