The Palestinian economy is in decline. Despite some positive growth in recent years, driven largely by the telecommunications and construction sectors, poverty and unemployment have risen. The primary cause of this decline is the ongoing conflict with Israel, which has resulted in the occupation of Palestinian land and the restriction of movement and access for people and goods. This has led to a decline in private investment and limited economic opportunities. 

The occupation has also led to a decline in the quality of life in Palestine. The Israeli military has damaged or destroyed many homes, businesses, and public buildings. There are also significant restrictions on the freedom of movement for Palestinians, which makes it difficult for them to travel to and from work, school, and other places. The lack of freedom of movement also limits the ability of Palestinians to trade with other countries, which further limits economic opportunities. 

The Palestinian government has implemented various measures to try to stimulate economic growth, such as simplifying the process of starting a business and investing in infrastructure. However, these measures have had limited success due to the ongoing conflict and the restrictions imposed by the Israeli occupation. The future of the Palestinian economy remains uncertain, as the conflict with Israel shows no signs of resolution.

Georgia plans to pardon dozens of people convicted of hidden asset crimes committed during the Soviet era.

They were given prison terms of up to four years for illegally possessing gold or other valuables.

The move follows a recommendation by a governmental panel which ruled that the crimes were committed "in exceptional circumstances" and were "triggered by the urge to survive".

It also concluded that the convicts had already served enough time.

Georgia's Prosecutor-General's Office will soon announce the exact number of people who will be granted pardons.

They are expected to be among the hundreds of people who were sentenced after the government launched a crackdown on illegal possession of gold in 2004.

One of the people convicted at the time was former Georgian President Mikheil Saakashvili.

The former leader, who is now the governor of Ukraine's Odessa region, was sentenced in 2005 to a fine of $390 and a two-year suspended prison term for having a kilogram of gold in his possession.

He avoided serving the sentence because he was granted amnesty later.

During the Soviet era, it was common for people to hide valuables - such as gold, jewellery and antique carpets - to keep them out of the hands of the communist authorities.

But it was not until two decades after the fall of the Soviet Union that the government of Georgia - which became independent in 1991 - decided to address the issue.

Those who were convicted at the time argued that they had hidden the assets for many years to safeguard them from being nationalised or stolen by the country's turbulent political elite.

While the governmental panel accepted this explanation, it denied that there was a formal policy to encourage people to hide assets, as prosecutors had claimed.

The Republican governor of Georgia, Brian Kemp, has announced plans to introduce a bill that would allow people with a criminal record for possessing illegal firearms to avoid jail if they declare their weapons.

The move is an effort to reduce the state's severe prison overpopulation.

Under the proposed law, people who have served their sentence would be able to avoid prosecution by legally registering the weapons.

Governor Kemp said the bill, which will be introduced in the state legislature next year, would give people with criminal records a "second chance".

He said the current policy of prosecuting people who have served their initial sentence was unfair.

"I think that's the fair thing to do," he told ABC's Good Morning America on Thursday. "And again, we're going to work with the general assembly, if they're going to act on it, but I think it's the right thing to do."

The proposal has been criticised by Democratic representatives in the state, who said it would endanger the public by allowing people to own guns illegally.

"Governor Kemp's dangerous and irresponsible plan to allow felons to legally possess firearms without a permit is unacceptable," said State House Minority Leader James Beverly on Friday.

"One of the main priorities of our state should be to keep guns out of the hands of criminals, not give them a free pass to ignore the law and endanger our communities."

There are currently about 52,000 people in Georgia's prisons, which has a designed capacity of 38,000. According to the governor's office, prison populations have increased by more than 20% over the last decade.

Russian oil giant Yukos has announced it is returning to US courts in a last-ditch attempt to overturn a $50bn arbitration award handed to a former subsidiary.

The move comes after a French court upheld the award earlier this month.

Yukos, once Russia's biggest oil firm, filed for bankruptcy in 1999.

Its main asset was sold to state firm Rosneft in 2004.

The case dates back to the early 2000s, when Yukos defaulted on $27bn in loans from a group of Russian banks and bondholders.

The creditors brought arbitration claims against the energy firm, which were eventually settled for $9.35bn in 2014.

However, a trio of hedge funds – GML, Inc, Bro-Drift and Veteran Partners – allege they own Yukos' debt, and brought a separate lawsuit demanding $114bn in 2008.

They won a $50bn arbitration award against Russia in 2014, though Moscow has always denied any involvement in the case.

Last month, a French court upheld the award, and rejected Russia's appeal to have the matter reheard.

In a statement on Friday, Yukos said it welcomed the decision, but pointed out that other courts had "expressly reserved" the company's right to challenge the award.

"Yukos intends to utilise this jurisdiction to request the annulment of the award, having regard to, inter alia, the decision of the French court," the firm said.

"Given the significance of the award, Yukos is entitled to pursue all available legal remedies."

Yukos cited "substantial grounds" for requesting the cancellation of the award, without giving further details.

However, it may ask the court to take into account the fact that most of the firms' assets were sold to Rosneft in 2004, and therefore it could not pay the award.

Yukos has repeatedly rejected the charges levied against it, describing the case as an attempt to "instrumentalise" the firm for political purposes.

A judge has given the go-ahead for oil company Yukos to pursue $1.9bn in compensation from Russia in a Washington court.

The company was broken up and sold off after Russian tax authorities seized its assets.

The ruling in a Delaware court is the latest twist in a 15-year legal battle between Yukos and Russia.

The case will now proceed to trial unless the two parties reach a settlement.

Yukos was once Russia's largest oil producer. It filed for bankruptcy in 1999 and was broken up after Russian tax authorities seized its assets.

The company's former shareholders sued Russia in a Washington court, arguing that the country had expropriated their investment in Yukos.

They also alleged that Russian authorities had colluded with Yukos's management to divert assets from the company.

In 2014, a US court ruled that Russia had violated Yukos's investors' rights by seizing its assets.

The court ordered Russia to pay $50bn in compensation.

Russia appealed against the ruling, and the case went to the Supreme Court.

In 2018, the Supreme Court ruled that the case should be reheard by a lower court.

Now, a judge in a Delaware court has given the go-ahead for Yukos to pursue $1.9bn in compensation from Russia.

The case will now proceed to trial unless Yukos reaches a settlement with Russia.

800m runner Kelly Holmes has tipped her former training partner Jenny Meadows to succeed her as Olympic champion.

Holmes, who retired after Beijing 2008, said Meadows was "getting back to her best" after recovering from injury.

The 35-year-old is bidding to win her first global title at the World Championships, which start in Daegu, South Korea on 27 August.

She said: "I think Jenny will win a global gold medal. Whether that's this year or further down the line, I don't know."

Meadows, who won bronze at the 2005 Worlds and silver at the 2006 Europeans, missed the 2009 season after undergoing surgery on both knees.

She returned to win bronze for England at the 2010 Commonwealth Games before claiming the European indoor title in Paris earlier this year.

"She's got a great chance at the Worlds," added Holmes. "I think she'll run tactically really well. She's got a great finish when it comes to the last 80m. When she's in good shape, no-one can catch her."

Meadows, who runs in the 800m heats on Wednesday, said: "It's been a long time since I've been in the shape I'm in now. I'm running well and I'm looking forward to it."

Holmes, who won gold and bronze in the 800m and 1500m respectively in Beijing, retired aged 32, saying she lacked the motivation to continue.

The 38-year-old mother of two has had to juggle family life with the demands of elite sport. But it's a balance that seems to be working well for her.

In February, she took victory in the 3,000m at the British Indoor Championships in Birmingham. Then, at the European Indoor Championships in Torun, Poland, in March, she claimed a thrilling victory in the 3,000m final.

Pavey's success in Poland was a landmark moment for her - not only because it was her first major international title, but also because it proved to her that she was back to her best after her illness.

"To win the European indoor championships was amazing," Pavey said. "It showed that I was back where I wanted to be, which was really special after the last couple of years."

With the outdoor season now underway, Pavey is setting her sights on more success in the 5,000m and 10,000m. And with the World Championships in Oregon fast approaching, she's keen to make the most of the opportunities that come her way.

"I'm feeling really good," she said. "I've had a good winter of training, and I'm looking forward to the outdoor season.

"The World Championships are definitely a long-term goal. I'll just focus on getting ready for them, and see what happens."

Playing on a GameBoy sounds like a blast from the past, but Polish musicians are using the handheld device in their performances. The game has become so popular that there are now online communities dedicated to it. These communities allow players to share their creations and collaborate with each other.

Gareth Bale's former international teammate Ryan Giggs is the favourite to take over as Wales manager.

It follows the announcement that current boss Chris Coleman will leave at the end of his contract in November.

England left-back Ben Chilwell could be out for the rest of the season after undergoing knee surgery, his club Chelsea said.

People sent text messages related to New Year's celebrations to friends and family in record numbers this year, with nearly 360 million messages sent in the UK and Ireland, according to wireless carrier O2.

The company said the number was up by 25% on the previous record set in 2008.

Many people exchanged texts wishing each other a happy new year as they celebrated the start of 2023.

O2 said the peak time for sending messages was just before midnight on 31 December.

"This year's New Year's text message traffic was the highest we have ever seen," said Mark Evans, chief executive of O2's parent company, Telefonica UK.

"Reaching this level of traffic eight years after the previous record underlines what a important role text messaging plays in all our lives," he added.

Telefonica UK operates the O2 network as well as providing telephone and internet services.

People around the world welcomed 2022 with celebrations, despite many countries still reeling from the impact of the omicron variant of COVID-19. One notable exception was Australia, which saw fireworks explode over the Sydney Opera House and other cities despite a total ban on gatherings.

But as the clock struck midnight, many people took to their phones to send New Year's messages to loved ones, resulting in a surge of text messages that broke records.

According to the telecommunications company Vodafone, more than 36 million messages were sent in the UK between midnight and 12:01 AM on January 1. That number broke the previous record of 25 million messages sent in 2015.

The company also reported that the total volume of data used during the festive period was over two and a half times higher than usual.

"As people saw in the New Year with family and friends, it was the perfect time to check in and connect with loved ones," he added.

Brazilian stocks and currency have rallied in recent weeks, in a sign that markets are betting on the country's economic recovery.

The Bovespa stock index has risen about 8% since the start of September, with investors encouraged by the prospect of looser monetary policy.

And the real has strengthened 5% against the dollar over the same period.

Brazil's central bank surprised investors last week by cutting its key interest rate for the first time in six months.

It signaled that it would continue to do so, amid signs that the country's deep recession is easing.

The interest rate cut is a sign that policymakers are worried about economic growth, said Tom Nelson, an economist with UBS.

"Markets are looking at [Brazil's] fundamentals and saying 'growth is going to be pretty decent,'" he said.

In recent months, data has showed that the country's deep recession is easing, with economists predicting that growth will return next year.

There are also hopes that the new government, which takes over later this month, will push through much-needed structural reforms to boost growth.

"The market is pricing in the new government being able to push through reforms and getting the economy going again," said David Hauner, chief Latin America economist with Bank of America Merrill Lynch.

"If you look at the last couple of months, the economic data has not been bad - exports have been pretty good, the trade balance has improved, and the central bank's business climate index has improved significantly."

However, some investors are still wary of piling into Brazilian assets, as the country is still mired in its worst-ever recession and faces a series of political uncertainties.

The real is down more than 20% against the dollar this year, and analysts say it is too early to tell if the recent gains will last.

The Brazilian real has strengthened against the dollar, with experts suggesting the country's recession has come to an end.

The real gained more than 6% in October, reaching its strongest level in more than two years.

It came after the central bank raised interest rates to their highest level in more than a decade.

And government data showed that the country's inflation rate slowed for a tenth consecutive month in September.

Most economists agreed that the market-driven currency rally was a response to the central bank's resolute anti-inflation stance, rather than the recent change of government, with some even suggesting the real was undervalued.

Caption: Egypt to sell off state-owned bank - BBC News

Subcaption: A deal to sell a majority stake in the National Bank of Egypt (NBE) has been agreed, officials say.

The bank's chairman said a number of investors would buy a 51% stake. Details of the deal are expected to be announced later on Thursday. The government is selling state firms to help reduce its debt. The sell-off comes as Egypt battles inflation - which hit 18% in November - and a slump in the value of its currency.

The deal entails the participation of a number of strategic investors, the bank's chairman, Hisham Okasha, confirmed to Reuters news agency. He did not disclose the identities of the buyers. "It's a great day for the National Bank of Egypt," he was quoted as saying. "We are selling at a good price and we are selling to strategic investors."

The bank's sale has been on the cards for years. In 2017, the Egyptian government signed a memorandum of understanding with Saudi Arabian investors, but the deal never materialised. A number of other, unsuccessful attempts to sell the bank have also been made.

The NBE is the largest of Egypt's state-owned banks. It handles about half of the nation's banking transactions. The bank's assets were about 1.7 trillion Egyptian pounds ($119bn; £95bn) at the end of 2020.

The Egyptian government has been trying to reduce its debt, which stood at 108% of GDP in the second quarter of 2021. Last year, it sold its remaining stake in the Middle East's largest container handling company, Suez Canal Container Terminal, to the Dubai-based DP World.

This year, the government started selling state-owned enterprises in sectors including pharmaceuticals, chemicals and fertilisers. Late last year, it launched a programme to sell off state-owned property. In November, it sold a landmark government-owned property in Cairo.

The sale of state firms comes as Egypt battles inflation, which hit 18% in November - its highest level in 30 years. The country's currency has also slumped from about 15 Egyptian pounds to the dollar in 2019 to about 20 pounds to the dollar now.

The Central Bank of Egypt has raised its key interest rate by 3% to curb inflation. But it has faced criticism that its attempts to control rising prices have not been enough.

Speeches by Labour's deputy leader Harriet Harman and former foreign secretary Robin Cook attacking the budget have been welcomed by supporters of Gordon Brown.

The chancellor's allies also welcomed the Budget - although one said the prime minister should have given details of public spending plans in his speech.

And Conservative Party chairman David Cameron said the Budget speech "wasn't perfect" but would "do".

And she added that the "gloomy" chancellor had failed to "paint a vision" of Britain's future.

Mr Cook, also speaking in his south London constituency, said the Budget had "done nothing" to help low-paid workers and those on benefits.

And he added that the "thin" Budget speech had been a "disappointment" to those who wanted to see the end of the "boom and bust" economic cycle.

Our political editor Nick Robinson says both Ms Harman and Mr Cook have now put themselves in contention to be elected Labour leader should Mr Brown fall.

Our correspondent says both used almost identical language - "painting a vision", "budget for working families" - that Gordon Brown himself used in the past but no longer does.

And he says both used the word "missed", which is clearly a coded attack on the prime minister.

Supporters of the chancellor said Ms Harman and Mr Cook had "missed the point" of the Budget.

One ally said it had been clear the prime minister was going to set out details of public spending in the next few months.

And another said voters believed the Conservatives were still the party of the rich as none of their front bench had voted against the Budget.

But Tory leader David Cameron said: "I don't think it was a perfect Budget speech.

"But you know, this is the real world, we are not going to get everything we want every time.

"I think it was a good start and I think it was a good Budget speech that in the end will do."

In his own constituency, Chancellor Brown told supporters the Budget had "set out a vision for Britain for the future".

And he added that he had given details of public spending

Mumbai bombs movie postponed

The release of a controversial film on the 2008 Mumbai attacks has been postponed by Indian producers, who say they want to "respect the sentiments" of the victims' families.

The film, titled The Attacks of 26/11, was due to be released on 29 March.

Its trailer sparked anger among those affected by the siege, in which 164 people were killed.

The producer said the film would be revised following complaints.

Police say the film, which has been made by Indian-American director Anthony Maras, depicts the attacks accurately.

But survivors and relatives of the victims say it is a "disrespectful" portrayal of the events.

Police say the attackers - who were Pakistani Muslims - split into 10 teams, rampaging through the city for four days.

In November 2008, India accused Pakistan's intelligence services of being involved in the attack and said the assault was co-ordinated by the Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) group.

Pakistan denied the charges and said it was not involved.

Following the violence in Mumbai, India and Pakistan deployed additional military forces along their border.

"We have collectively decided to revise the script and change certain aspects of the film," he said.

He added that he had been "extremely disturbed" by the hurt caused to victims' families.

European Union and US officials are seeking to resolve a 16-year-old dispute over airline schedules to offer greater certainty to carriers, according to the EU.

The "capacity allocation" dispute began in 2004, when US airlines complained about increasing numbers of night flights and early morning arrivals by European airlines - mainly Irish - at US airports.

The two sides have been talking about the issue for several years, but have now "stepped up" negotiations, the EU said.

A deal could offer more than $1bn (£800m) in benefits to both sides, it added.

The dispute, which has been running since before the current Covid-19 pandemic, relates to the number of slots - or takeoff and landing spaces - that airlines can use at crowded airports.

US airlines complained in 2004 that a surge in flights by Air Lingus and Ryanair between the EU and the US was damaging their businesses.

The US Department of Transportation (DOT) subsequently limited the number of flights that could be operated by Air Lingus and Ryanair between the US and the EU.

The two Irish airlines responded by switching to flying to the US via Canada, with some flights stopping off in the Caribbean.

The EU said at the time that the move by the US breached its airspace rights.

Talks to resolve the issue have moved slowly. Under a tentative deal reached in 2014, the EU proposed that the number of flights by EU airlines would increase by 66% over a five-year period.

However, the DOT rejected the proposal, saying it would hurt US carriers, according to the AFP news agency.

On Thursday, the EU's aviation chief, Adina Valean, said the two sides were seeking an arrangement "on reciprocal access to the airspace of the parties".

"I welcome the intensified engagement between the EU and the US on this issue," she said in a statement.

"Resolving the long-standing airline slots issue would unlock benefits worth over $1bn for the air travel industry on both sides of the Atlantic and provide much-needed certainty for airlines and passengers."

The EU and US are seeking a deal to overcome a dispute over air traffic rights, which has been going on for 14 years. The two regions have the two biggest economies in the world and the most powerful aviation markets. 

The row over the rights dates back to 2004. The US claims the EU has not honoured its part of a 1992 agreement, which granted US airlines equal access to European skies. 

The EU argues that its airlines have not been able to operate as many flights as they would like to and that this is unfair. The two sides have been trying to reach an agreement for a long time, but they have not been able to do so. 

The dispute has caused a lot of tension between the EU and US. It has also caused a lot of inconvenience for passengers who have had to change their flights. It could cost US airlines alone $1.6 billion in lost revenue. 

The two sides are now seeking a deal that would allow EU airlines to operate more flights in the US and vice versa. They are also seeking a deal that would allow for more cooperation in the field of aviation. 

The two sides have made a lot of progress in the talks and they are hoping to reach an agreement soon.

The future of the Scottish fishing industry has been assessed by a group of MPs.

The Scottish Affairs Committee concluded that it did not support the UK government's plan to hand management of fishing quotas to an independent Scottish state.

The UK government plans to publish a fisheries bill within the next year, which would pave the way for the devolution of fishing quotas - a move supported by the Scottish government.

But the cross-party committee said there was a lack of evidence that divided management of fishing quotas would benefit the industry.

The committee's report also called for a clearer picture of the future UK-Scotland relationship in the wake of the Brexit deal.

And it recommended that the two governments reach an agreement that would allow Scottish fishermen to continue to access fishing grounds in Norwegian and Icelandic waters.

Committee chairman Pete Wishart said the report was concerned that the UK government's approach to fisheries management was "too narrowly focused" on the question of quota only.

"There is a lack of evidence to demonstrate that dividing up the management of fishing quotas between the UK and an independent Scottish state will deliver tangible benefits for the Scottish fishing industry," he said.

A campaign has been launched to help independent music retailers compete with larger rivals in the digital downloads market.

The tracks will be sold on a profit-share basis, with 50% going to the artist and 25% each to Bira and the retailer.

Bira chief executive Andrew Goodacre said the scheme would help smaller stores compete with larger rivals which sell downloads.

"It is increasingly difficult for independent retailers to compete against digital downloads from the likes of Amazon and iTunes which are sold below cost price," he said.

"This is particularly difficult for the independent retailer who cannot buy the downloads as cheaply as the multiples can.

"We are levelling the playing field by offering a digital download service to independent retailers at the same price as the multiples."

The downloads will be available from 150 independent stores around the UK, with more stores being added to the scheme soon.

Mr Goodacre said he hoped the scheme would encourage other independent retailers to sign up.

"Anything that helps level the playing field for independent retailers has got to be a good thing," he said.

"I think it is a great idea because we can make the same amount of money as the bigger stores like HMV by selling the downloads."

Mr Mercer said the scheme could also help to promote new artists.

"A lot of the downloads are by up-and-coming new bands who are just breaking into the market and need exposure," he said.

Bira said the initial response from its members had been positive and it expected take-up to be strong.

Can Yahoo dominate next decade?

The application also suggests users might be rewarded with cryptocurrency for using the service.

Yahoo already offers 1,000 Yahoo Coins for signing up for a Yahoo account, and filing the application shows the company continues to explore blockchain technology. 

The patent application outlines a system in which a blockchain would be used to encrypt and store email messages, with a cryptographic key held by the sender and recipient.

This would prevent the contents of emails from being revealed to anyone other than the intended recipients.

"Some embodiments may incentivise the use of the email platform," the application reads.

"For example, the email platform may reward users with a cryptocurrency for using the platform."

It goes on to explain that users might be rewarded for actions including "transmitting an email", "receiving an email", or "reading an email".

Yahoo CEO Marissa Mayer said during an investors' call in February that the company was "continuing to invest in blockchain", according to CNET.

Decentralised blockchain-based systems are commonly associated with the cryptocurrency Bitcoin.

But the technology has many other potential applications including the verification of transactions and the storage of data.

Yahoo is not the only major tech firm to have explored blockchain technology.

Microsoft launched a blockchain-as-a-service offering earlier this month, and Amazon introduced a similar service in November.

Microsoft has launched a new version of its Windows operating system in India, aimed at curbing software piracy.

Windows 10 "Core", as it has been named, is an edition of Windows 10 that contains minimal features. While users will be able to run apps, they will not be able to access Microsoft's Windows Store to download programmes.

The move aims to offer a low-cost alternative to Windows, making it easier for Microsoft to compete with cheap pirated versions of its software, which are widely used in the country.

It also hopes the new version will encourage users of pirated Windows to move towards legal versions, by offering a more affordable option.

"It has always been our endeavour to ensure that customers have the best possible experience on our platform, and as a part of this, we are bringing the Windows 10 'Core' edition to India," said Bhaskar Pramanik, chairman of Microsoft India.

"This edition offers a no-frills Windows 10 experience to our customers at an affordable price, and we believe this edition will be attractive to both desktop and mobile customers in the country."

The Indian computer market is currently dominated by software pirates, who buy a single copy of Windows and install it on multiple computers, rather than buying separate licences for each.

According to industry body National Association of Software and Services Companies (Nasscom), the rate of software piracy in India in 2016 was more than 59%, costing the country more than $1.7bn (£1.2bn) in lost revenue.

Microsoft has launched several initiatives in India to curb the practice. It launched a programme called "Digital-Life Alliance" in 2016, aimed at educating Indians about the dangers of downloading pirated software.

In addition, Microsoft's Indian subsidiary launched a website this year, Buy Genuine Software, which describes the risks of using pirated software, and offers alternatives.

According to Microsoft, users of Windows 10 Core will have the ability to "unlock" additional features in the future. However, the company has not detailed how this will be possible.

Microsoft has moved to intensify its anti-piracy efforts by introducing a new tool that prevents the unauthorised pre-installation of Windows 11 on computers. The company emphasised that it is prioritizing security and customer experience rather than device performance in this change.

The new tool, known as the Hardware Compatibility List (HCL), serves as a database that lists all the authorized PCs capable of running Windows 11. The database includes information such as the manufacturer, model name, and serial number of the devices.

According to Microsoft, the HCL aims to ensure that Windows 11 is only installed on compatible devices, reducing the risk of hardware malfunctions and security issues that can arise from unauthorized modifications. It believes that this measure is necessary to provide customers with a smooth and secure experience.

The HCL is a follow-up to Microsoft's Windows Genuine Validation (WGV) tool, which was launched in 2019. The WGV tool was designed to detect fraudulent or unauthorized Windows licenses and prevent them from being used. The HCL builds on this initiative by ensuring that only genuine devices can run Windows 11.

Microsoft has emphasized that the HCL is just one aspect of its broader anti-piracy strategy, which includes a range of measures such as Windows Update, Windows Defender, and the Microsoft Store. The company is committed to continuously improving its security measures and providing customers with the best possible experience.

While some users may view the HCL as a hindrance, Microsoft believes that it is a necessary step to ensure the safety and integrity of the Windows operating system. The company is encouraging users to purchase genuine Windows licenses and install the operating system on authorized devices to ensure they have a secure and smooth experience. 

This change reflects Microsoft's ongoing efforts to combat software piracy and provide customers with the best possible experience. The company will continue to prioritize security and customer experience in its future product offerings.

UK house prices have risen slightly, according to a survey by lender Halifax.

The average cost of a home was up by 1.3% in November, marking the fourth consecutive month of growth.

However, prices are still 7.4% below their level a year earlier, before the stamp duty holiday prompted a surge in demand.

"It remains true to say that the housing market has now weathered the storm of the pandemic," said Russell Galley, managing director of Halifax.

The stamp duty holiday, which ended on 30 September, helped to boost property prices as buyers rushed to complete before the deadline.

Since then, the market has cooled slightly, but builders' merchants have reported healthy demand from homeowners opting to improve rather than move.

According to Halifax, November's rise took the average UK house price to £272,992.

That was up from £268,285 in October, but still below the £297,546 recorded in November 2020.

Mr Galley said that prices were now rising at a pace of 0.8% per month, which was "similar" to the average rate since 2015.

He added: "With opportunities for overseas travel restricted last year, it is no surprise that demand for bigger homes has risen sharply as more people work from home and seek more space."

However, he said that it was still too early to assess the impact of the new Omicron variant on the housing market.

"New housing market activity and price growth is likely to be more subdued in the coming months as inflationary pressures bite, and with the Bank of England predicted to raise interest rates next year, higher borrowing costs will also exert a cooling influence," he added.

The UK's average house prices showed a slight increase in September, according to a report from the Halifax. The bank found that prices rose by 0.1% in September, following a 0.3% increase in August. This is the fourth consecutive month that house prices have risen, bringing the average price of a property in the UK to £261,922. This is still 2.3% lower than it was in February 2022, before the start of the economic crisis.

The data also showed that the number of mortgages approved for house purchases rose slightly in September, to 81,000. This is the highest level since March 2022, but still some way below the pre-pandemic average of 103,000.

Martin Ellis, the chief economist at Halifax, said that the housing market had 'weathered the financial storm' of the last few months. He said that low-interest rates and a shortage of properties for sale had kept the market stable.

However, he warned that the economic crisis was not over and that house prices could fall further in the coming months. 'We are entering a prolonged period of uncertainty, which will weigh on consumer sentiment and activity,' he said.

Many homeowners have decided to stay put as the cost of living crisis deepens, with rising energy bills and food prices. This has led to a boom in home improvements, as people invest in their current properties rather than trying to move up the property ladder.

At the same time, mortgage rates have fallen to record lows, with some lenders offering deals below 1%. This has encouraged some first-time buyers to take their first steps onto the property ladder.

Oil prices have risen above $50 a barrel for the first time in 2022, as investors bet the Omicron variant of Covid-19 will not derail the global economic recovery, and ahead of a meeting of Opec and its allies.

West Texas Intermediate (WTI), the benchmark for US crude, gained 2.1% to $50.60 a barrel early on Monday, while Brent crude, the international benchmark, rose 2.4% to $53.77 per barrel.

"While the new Omicron variant has resulted in renewed precautionary restrictions, early indications suggest that it is less severe than initially expected," said analysts at Commerzbank.

The rise comes ahead of meetings of the Opec+ group of producers on Tuesday.

The group decides how much oil its members will produce every month, with the aim of managing the price.

Last month, the Opec+ agreed to increase production by 400,000 barrels per day in January, despite the release of emergency reserves by the US and other nations, and concerns over the impact of Omicron.

As the group's meetings approach, analysts said the oil producers could decide to pause their output increases or even cut production.

"Together with a potentially declining oil demand due to the rapid spread of the Omicron variant, Opec+ might opt to pause its current planned output increase," said analysts at Rystad Energy.

Friday saw crude oil prices jump above the $50 per barrel mark, increasing more than 2% in the last session alone. This comes after data released showed that US crude stockpiles were falling, with concerns of a global economic slowdown seeming to fade. This marks a 13% increase in the price of oil over the past month, with prices now having nearly doubled since hitting a 2-year low in October. The rebound has come as a surprise to many, given the continued strength of the dollar and the harsh weather that has hit many parts of the world.

Amongst the factors contributing to the price increase are the ongoing Opec+ supply cuts, as well as the weakening of the dollar. The Opec+ group, which is made up of major oil producers including Saudi Arabia and Russia, has been cutting its output in an effort to boost prices. Meanwhile, a weakening dollar tends to make commodities priced in dollars more expensive for other countries to buy.

Consumers are likely to feel the impact of higher oil prices in the form of higher prices at the pump. However, with the US Federal Reserve expected to raise interest rates again next week, the dollar is likely to retain its strength, providing some support for oil prices.

For now, it appears that oil prices are on the rise and it remains to be seen whether they will continue to climb.

Former Tory minister Jonathan Djanogly attacks 'behaviour of Conservative MPs'
The senior Conservative MP Sir Nicholas Meyer has died aged 76.

He campaigned for the UK to stay in the EU - founding the group Business for New Europe - and later became a crossbench peer in the House of Lords.

Sir Nicholas was a leading figure in the Conservative Party for decades, serving as its deputy chairman and as a minister under both Margaret Thatcher and John Major.

But he was removed from the party's front bench over his opposition to Britain's entry into the Euro.

In recent years, he characterised the Conservative Party as a "stalking horse" for Brexit and urged peers to vote against the government in key votes.

Paying tribute, Tory MP and former minister Jonathan Djanogly said Sir Nicholas had been a "good friend and neighbour".

"His was a voice of reasoned argument on the EU and it never failed to make sense," he said.

"He was dedicated to the party, as shown by his recent comments. But it is sadly obvious that the behaviour of a large number of Conservative MPs and ministers has made his task harder."

Sir Nicholas was born in 1940 and attended Eton College and Trinity College, Cambridge.

He succeeded his father as the 2nd Baron Meyer in 1995, having begun his career as a journalist before moving into politics.

He was appointed Minister of State at the Foreign Office in 1989 and served in the Cabinet Office as Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster between 1995 and 1997.

In the Lords, he served as deputy leader of the Conservative Party from 1998 to 2001 before switching to the crossbenches.

Crossbench peer Lord Oakeshott said Sir Nicholas would be remembered as "a gentleman par excellence, charming, witty and kind".

"But he was also one of the most effective political operators of his generation," he added.

"His conduct of the referendum campaign of 1975 was one of the factors which led to the result - and it is a matter of some sadness that he felt unable to support the efforts of the current Prime Minister in the same cause."

The former Tory minister Jonathan Djanogly has died at the age of 67.

Mr Djanogly, who had been a minister in David Cameron's government, died on Friday night, his family said.

The Conservative MP for Huntingdon in Cambridgeshire was diagnosed with prostate cancer in 2017.

He stepped down from his post as a minister in 2018 and resigned as an MP in 2019.

In a statement, his family said: "It is with great sadness we have to announce that Jonathan Djanogly peacefully passed away on Friday night, surrounded by his family.

"Jonathan was not only a devoted husband, father and grandfather, but a loyal friend to so many.

"We would like to say thank you to all the NHS staff, particularly those at Peterborough Hospital, who cared for Jonathan with such warmth, diligence and professionalism over the past four years."

Bank of New York sued Parmalat on Monday, seeking $190m (£118m) for fraudulent transactions that took place 15 years ago. 

The bank claimed that it had been deceived by the Italian dairy company and asked a New York judge to dismiss the lawsuit. 

Parmalat filed the suit in 2007, claiming that the Bank of New York had failed in its duties as an administrator of its financial affairs. 

The dairy company claimed that the bank had diverted funds deposited with it and used them to cover up fraudulent activities by the company's management.

The Bank of New York was appointed by Parmalat to administer its $20m (£12.2m) cash account in 1994. 

It also provided foreign exchange services and managed a $150m (£89.4m) investment portfolio on behalf of the company. 

On Monday, the bank said it had been deceived by Parmalat and had been unaware that the company was engaged in any wrongdoing. 

It claimed that the dairy company had repeatedly lied to the bank about its financial health and had used money deposited with the bank to engage in fraudulent transactions.

The bank also said that it had been unaware of any wrongdoing by Parmalat until 2006, when the dairy company's management was arrested. 

Parmalat has always denied any wrongdoing and has said that it was the victim of a conspiracy by the bank and other parties.

If no settlement can be reached, the trustee will consider whether to drop the case, according to the document. 

The Bank of New York Mellon sued Credit Suisse in July, alleging that the Swiss bank misled it over the true financial state of Italian-listed conglomerate Parmalat. 

Parmalat collapsed in 2003 after an accounting scandal, leaving it $20bn (£16.4bn) in debt. 

The Bank of New York Mellon has said its losses from the collapse were $102m. 

At the time of the lawsuit, Credit Suisse said it "rejects these claims in their entirety".

China will overtake the US in the next few years as the country with the largest demand for Internet services, a report says.

By 2016, more than half of China's population will be online, compared with about two-thirds of the US population, says research firm McKinsey.

The report also said that India will rank as the second-largest Internet market in the world.

"Internet adoption in China continues to accelerate," McKinsey said. "Half a billion people will go online for the first time in the next decade."

By 2016, Internet usage in China will reach 866 million, the report said.

China already has more Internet users than any other country - more than 630 million, according to official figures.

But the US still has more Internet users than any other country, with more than 280 million, or about 80% of the population, according to the McKinsey report.

The report also noted that the European Union currently has about 490 million Internet users, which will increase to 705 million by 2016.

The report said that while the US and Western Europe led the initial surge of Internet adoption, "growth now is centred in Asia".

China will soon have more internet users than any other country involving more than one billion people. The official China Daily newspaper reports that more than one billion people in China, or about 75% of the population, will be online by the end of 2004. According to government data, the country had more than 680 million internet users at the end of 2003, the largest number of users in the world. The US has slightly more than 200 million users, or about 63% of the population.

China already has more internet users than any other country had at the same point in its internet development, according to Edward McCarrick, a senior analyst at the US-based Technology Research Bureau. He said that previous frontrunners in the number of internet users, such as the US, Germany, and Japan, had about 40% of their populations online when they reached the 680 million mark. "China has already surpassed that," he said. "They are doing it differently, and they are doing it faster."

Chinese internet users are increasingly accessing the web through mobile phones. The China Daily report said there were more than 590 million mobile phone users in China at the end of September, and about 310 million of them can access the internet through their phones. The popularity of internet-enabled mobile phones has helped drive the growth of China's online population. McCarrick said mobile phone users accounted for about 46% of China's internet users. "Any country that has a high growth of mobile phone use is going to have a high growth of internet use," he said.

A US federal judge has set a trial date for the Balco case, in which major league baseball players are accused of using steroids.

They include star names such as Jose Canseco, Juan Gonzalez and Jason Giambi.

Judge Harold Baer set the trial date after lawyers for the players and the Office of the US Attorney agreed to avoid a trial this year.

That would have clashed with the baseball playoffs and World Series, which finish in late October.

The players' lawyers had asked for a trial in February 2005 but the court rejected that proposal.

The players face evidence including secret recordings of conversations at the Laboratory for Athletic Performance, or Balco, in the San Francisco Bay area.

The US government filed charges in February, accusing the players of cheating, lying to officials and conspiring to cover up their doping violations.

They face potential fines of up to $250,000 (£150,000) and up to two years in jail.

- Former Oakland A's pitcher, Marvin McCorate

The case has been plagued with delays since it was first filed in 2003. The initial trial was set for 2005, but it was delayed multiple times. In 2018, the judge ruled that the four defendants would be tried separately. 

The upcoming trial dates are as follows:

The prosecution and defense have both agreed to the trial dates.

 Xavier Niel - a telecoms and technology entrepreneur who is also a minority shareholder in the LSE - held talks with the exchange's management on Thursday.

When another investor asked if he had visited the London Stock Exchange, Mr Rolet replied: "I spend most of my time in the office right next door to you."

The LSE's chief financial officer, Scott Evans, jumped in to clarify that Mr Rolet had in fact spent "a lot of time in this actual room".

"The LSE means a lot to me, it's a thrilling adventure, and I did not hesitate to make it official and public by moving to London," he said.

"I fell in love with the LSE, this is a true love, and you don't fall in love with the LSE and then try to destroy it."

Earlier this year, the LSE agreed to a £32bn takeover by the Franco-Dutch rival Euronext. Last month, the LSE's regulators cleared the deal, saying it did not harm the public interest.

"The young lads have been brilliant since I came in. They are good players and good lads - they want to learn and they want to get better and that's a great attitude to have.

Oxford's gameplan was clear - to use the athleticism and pace of forwards Kemar Roofe and Gavin Whyte on the counter-attack, while looking to frustrate their opponents and limit the space in wide areas.

It remained unchanged at the break with the game goalless, but Roofe almost gave Oxford the lead when his close-range shot was saved by Luke Southwood after Whyte had picked him out in the box.

Flynn responded by making three changes, introducing fresher legs in the form of Theo Wharton, Ryan Williams and Ben House, and within two minutes they almost paid dividends.

House turned his man and advanced into the box but saw his shot from 14 yards well saved by the feet of Simon Eastwood.

However, the opener came when Roofe was allowed too much space in the box to turn and smash a shot in off the underside of the crossbar from 18 yards.

That sparked a frantic final 15 minutes during which the hosts had chances to extend their lead through substitute Jonte Smith, while Ferguson went up the other end and headed just over from eight yards.

But the equaliser came when Ferguson's side finally made one of their attacking set-pieces tell, as sub Matt Taylor's delivery was perfect for the run of centre-half James Wilson, who powered in a header.

"It just doesn't work. It's as simple as that," said Rosenberg, a 44-year-old financial adviser.

Like many in this rapidly wired world, Rosenberg is fed up with his Internet service provider. But unlike most people, Rosenberg, along with his neighbors in the borough of Westminster, can do something about it: Choose another provider.

In fact, they can choose up to eight.

That's because Rosenberg lives in one of several London neighborhoods where telecommunications regulator Ofcom is testing a new concept in Internet access. In its bid to make broadband more widely available, Ofcom has taken the unprecedented step of designating these areas "open networks."

The idea behind open networks is simple: Instead of laying its own cables and wires, Ofcom has required Britain's largest telecom companies to allow other providers to use their infrastructure — ducts, telephone poles, and underground tunnels — to offer services of their own.

In the test areas, providers small and large — from British Telecom to small startups — are offering broadband packages, some including digital television and telephone.

The services are available in parts of London and in two other cities, Birmingham and Manchester. Ofcom plans to expand the trial to other parts of the country later this year.

Ofcom, which was set up by the government in 2004 to regulate the telecom industry, says it wants the entire country to have access to broadband by 2012.

"We are pushing the market as hard as we can to get as many people connected as quickly as possible," said Stephen Joseph, Ofcom's executive director of strategy. "This particular approach seems to be working well."

One alternative to traditional broadband that has been gaining popularity in recent years is satellite internet. Satellite internet providers, such as Elon Musk's Starlink, offer high-speed, reliable connections anywhere in the world, as long as there is a clear line of sight to the sky.

Another alternative is 5G internet, which offers speeds comparable to satellite internet but with the added benefit of not requiring a clear line of sight. 5G internet providers, such as EE and Three, are expected to see a surge in demand in the coming years as the technology becomes more widely available.

While alternative internet services may offer a solution to Britons' broadband woes, they come with their own set of challenges. Additionally, both satellite and 5G internet require a certain level of technical knowledge to set up and use, which may be a barrier for some consumers.

As the technology improves and becomes more widely available, it is likely that we will see even more Britons making the switch to these alternative services.

The Olympics were held every four years for nearly 12 centuries, until the Roman Empire conquered Greece in the mid-4th century AD. The Games continued to be held during the Roman period, but they declined in importance and eventually stopped after the Emperor Theodosius I banned them in 393 AD, considering them a pagan event.

The modern Olympics were revived in 1896 by Pierre de Coubertin of France. The Olympics have become the leading international sports event, with each occurrence of the Games being larger than the last. The Olympics have also grown to include a winter edition of the Games and have helped to popularize a number of sports, such as ice skating, bobsledding, and skiing.

The Olympics have also had a significant impact on the host cities and countries where they are held. The Games have often been used to promote economic growth and development in the host region, and many cities have used the Olympics as a way to improve their infrastructure and build new facilities. At the same time, the Olympics have also been criticized for being too expensive, causing traffic and pollution, and for promoting excessive commercialism and nationalism.

South Korean consumers are spending again on restaurants and travel as coronavirus restrictions ease, but fears of a third wave of infections are leading to a cautious approach to shopping.

Overall, household spending in April was up by a real 5.9% from a year earlier, according to the central bank - the fastest growth in a year.

But online retail sales, which have been a rare bright spot for the economy, fell back in April as consumers ventured out to the shops.

Department stores saw sales rise for the first time in a year, the central bank said.

"As Covid-19 got less serious, we saw people were willing to go out and spend money," said An Ki-jun, an economist at NH Investment & Securities.

However, he said that overall spending was still subdued and that the recovery would be slow.

"People are spending, but not excessively," he said. "Excessive spending is necessary for a meaningful recovery."

The government began easing social distancing rules in early May, but a slowdown in new infections has recently prompted concerns of a second wave of the virus.

New cases have also been reported from nightclubs that reopened in Seoul over the weekend.

More than 100 people were fined for failing to wear masks on public transport in Seoul on Monday, as the city stepped up its efforts to fight the spread of the virus.

The overall level of household debt has also made consumers cautious, said Kim Sang-jo, an economist at Kiwoom Securities.

"Confidence is not that high among consumers, with household debt much higher compared to their income," he said.

Household debt has been a major political issue in South Korea, and the government has implemented a series of measures to try to reduce the burden on consumers.

In recent months, authorities have forced banks to extend the terms of loans for households and small businesses and offered cheap loans to help consumers pay back debts.

South Korean consumers are spending again. Following a sharp decline at the end of 2022, retail sales rebounded in 2023, as consumers began loosening their purse strings after the government lifted COVID-19 restrictions.

Sales had been sluggish for the past few months as shoppers tightened their belts in the face of soaring living costs. Meanwhile, the lifting of COVID restrictions sparked a spending spree, especially in the service sector, with sales jumping 5.5% in January, year on year, the fastest pace since July 2022.

The recovery was driven by sales of cars and other big-ticket items as well as rising demand for restaurants and hotels. But analysts say the gains are likely to be short-lived as the interest rate hikes continue to weigh on consumer sentiment.

The government has been lifting restrictions on various businesses since November 2022, following a sharp decline in COVID-19 cases. Meanwhile, consumer price inflation has been moderating, easing pressure on households.

However, analysts say the rebound is likely to be short-lived. The interest rate hikes by the Bank of Korea are expected to continue for the rest of the year, which will likely weigh on consumer sentiment.

Court documents show that WorldCom executives gave themselves huge bonuses and stock options just before the company collapsed.

The revelations have emerged from previously sealed papers filed as part of WorldCom's bankruptcy proceedings.

They show that former Chief Executive Officer Bernie Ebbers received a $54m (£31m) payout, while two other former executives received $19m (£11.5m) and $14m (£8.5m) respectively.

The executives received the money despite WorldCom's admissions of fraudulent accounting that have brought the company to the brink of bankruptcy.

The documents also show that the three executives sold millions of dollars worth of WorldCom stock weeks before it admitted inflating its profits.

Revelations about the payouts are likely to raise questions about the ethics of executive compensation at a time when WorldCom is laying off thousands of employees and seeking creditor approval for a restructuring plan.

The document detailing the payments was filed on Friday in the US District Court in New York.

They were part of a larger set of court papers that included a list of more than 50,000 WorldCom shareholders.

Shares in the company have plummeted since it announced 14 months ago that it had inflated its profits by $3.8bn.

The company filed for bankruptcy protection in July, and announced last week that it plans to cut 20,000 jobs and exit from most of its international operations as part of its restructuring plan.

The court documents also show that WorldCom's former chief financial officer, Scott Sullivan, sold off more than $1m worth of WorldCom stock in March 2002, just weeks before the company admitted to its inflated profits.

And another former executive, Buford Yates, sold more than $7m worth of WorldCom stock in November 2001.

Both executives have been charged with fraud by US regulators.

Mr Ebbers has not been charged with any crime but has been called to testify before a congressional committee investigating the WorldCom fraud.

He has denied any wrongdoing.

All three executives have refused to return the money they received, saying they did nothing wrong.

Symantec discovered that during 2004, spam emissions from the US dropped from 61% to 54%, whilst spam emissions from China rose from 9% to 13%.

"Both the number of attacks and the level of sophistication are increasing," the report said, warning that phishing would be a major concern in 2005.

US trade gap narrows as exports rise

The US trade deficit narrowed in November for the third straight month, as exports of agricultural products and machinery rose, official data shows.

The gap between what the US sells and what it buys from other countries fell to $67.0bn, a decline of nearly 11% from $75.4bn in October, the Commerce Department said.

The improvement was driven by a 6.2% rise in exports to $224.9bn, with soybean shipments rising ahead of the harvest in Brazil, and an increase in exports of capital goods.

Imports were up 0.9% at $292.9bn, with increases in foreign-made cars and consumer goods.

The monthly trade gap is closely watched as it is considered an important barometer of the US economy.

But it also matters because the gap represents the difference between what the US buys from abroad and what it sells to other countries. 

When the trade gap is as large as it has been over the past year, it means the US is buying more from other countries than it is selling overseas, with the shortfall having to be financed by foreign capital.

That can contribute to a wider current account deficit, which means the US is paying out more money than it is taking in, increasing its need to attract foreign capital to finance the shortfall.

That can put pressure on the dollar, which fell after the release of the data on Thursday.

The improvement in the trade gap comes as central bankers and policymakers struggle to tackle inflation, which has been driven up by the supply chain problems and shortages caused by the Covid-19 pandemic and the recovery from the pandemic.

The Federal Reserve, which has kept interest rates low to support the economic recovery, has started to wind down its large-scale bond-buying stimulus scheme from November, and signalled that it plans to raise interest rates three times next year.

In the UK, the Bank of England raised interest rates for the first time in three years this month, and analysts expect the Fed to raise rates at its meeting next month.

The UK's trade gap narrowed in October as exports rose, according to official figures. The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said the gap between what the UK exports and what it imports narrowed by £2.4bn to £3.9bn in the latest month. The size of the trade gap has been hit in recent months by a surge in imports, which have been boosted by higher prices for goods and shortages of goods, such as semiconductors.

The ONS said that in the three months to October, the value of UK exports was up by £2.7bn compared with the three months to July, while imports were up by £2.2bn. Over the same period, the total trade gap widened by £5.8bn to £28.8bn. The ONS said that in October, the price of goods imported to the UK rose more slowly than the price of goods exported. It said the slowdown in the rise of import prices was driven by a reduction in the price of energy imports.

The ONS also released monthly figures for the amount of goods traded in October. It said that exports of goods rose by £1.9bn on the previous month, while imports of goods rose by £1.5bn. The ONS said that exports of machinery and transport equipment drove the rise in exports, while imports of machinery and transport equipment and chemicals drove the rise in imports.

The figures come as the government has been trying to promote the UK as a destination for foreign investment after a recent string of big announcements about investments in the UK's life sciences and renewable energy sectors. Last week, the government said that foreign direct investment in the UK had hit a record high in the first six months of the year, with investors attracted by the UK's strong trade links and its ability to tap into markets around the world.

LONDON — British Prime Minister John Major Wednesday denied a newspaper report that he had threatened to resign over the government's controversial identity card plan.

"There is no division on the issue of ID cards," Major told the House of Commons in answering a question from a lawmaker from his Conservative Party.

"I think that that issue is perfectly capable of being discussed without suggesting that the prime minister is on the point of resignation, which I most certainly am not," he said.

The prime minister's comments followed a report in the Daily Telegraph saying that Major had told lawmakers in a meeting Tuesday that he was ready to resign rather than implement the plan to issue ID cards to all British citizens.

The Telegraph said some of those at the meeting had leaked word of Major's comments.

The home secretary, Charles Clarke, faced calls yesterday to fire his adviser on civil liberties, Phil Shiner, after Mr Shiner declared that the government's plans for ID cards were "oppressive" and amounted to a "surveillance society".

The adviser's attack on the cornerstone of the government's law and order agenda will fuel speculation that the cabinet is divided over the plans, with Mr Clarke and the foreign secretary, Jack Straw, in favour while the prime minister, Tony Blair, and the chancellor, Gordon Brown, are said to have doubts.

Mr Shiner, who describes himself as "no friend of ID cards", described the scheme as "a solution in search of a problem". He added: "It is going to be incredibly expensive, it is going to be hugely invasive and it will change the relationship between the citizen and the state fundamentally, and not for the better."

His comments came as the government published a bill paving the way for the introduction of ID cards, which ministers say will help combat terrorism and other forms of crime. 

But the proposed law has been criticised by opposition parties and civil liberties groups for its potential impact on personal freedom.

Mr Shiner works three days a week as adviser to Mr Clarke on civil liberties, and is also director of the Public Interest Lawyers Union. He said that a recent briefing paper prepared for Mr Clarke by his advisers made it clear that the "great bulk" of the population would be required to obtain a card at a cost of £93, but that the real cost would be about £450 when the cost of updating the national identity register was taken into account.

He added that the "vast majority" of people would be required to verify their identity every five years at a cost of £56 a time.

Mr Shiner said that the government had produced no overall assessment of the cost of the scheme. "They have not done a benefit-cost analysis. They have just simply asserted that this is a good thing to do and it will cost X amount, but X is considerably less than the real figure," he said.

The adviser added that the government had also failed to explain how the scheme would combat terrorism. "If ever there was an example of a solution in search of a problem, this is it," he said.

Mr Shiner said the government should consider less intrusive ways of achieving its aims, such as making it compulsory for individuals to register their fingerprints with the police.

Search giant Google has asked users to help test a new toolbar which tracks what they search for online.

The move has sparked concern among privacy groups, who say the toolbar will monitor users' web activity.

The Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) said the software amounts to "spyware".

Google said the toolbar - which is in beta testing - was an experimental feature.

It is the second time this year that the company has caused controversy with a toolbar.

In September Google was accused of helping advertisers track users of its search engine, after it launched a toolbar tailored for advertisers.

This latest toolbar is aimed at all Google users. It will display a drop-down box whenever a user visits a website, showing them search terms they have used in the past that are related to the site they are visiting.

The toolbar also contains features found in the existing Google toolbar, including a pop-up blocker and features to help users download videos from popular video-sharing sites.

But the EFF said the new features raised "huge privacy concerns".

"It's stalking features - the idea that every site you go to, it's keeping track of where you've been and using that information to target advertising at you," the EFF's Peter Eckersley told the technology website CNet.

"It's using your own personal information against you, and that's just not right."

A Google spokesman said the new toolbar was an experiment and that the company was seeking feedback from users.

"From time to time we run experiments with new features to see whether they're useful to people," the spokesman said in a statement.

"This particular feature is an experiment to help people find relevant information from the web more easily, and we'll consider the feedback we get from users before deciding whether to launch it more broadly."

In a move that has surprised many industry experts, Google has released a new toolbar that tracks the user's web activity. The toolbar, which is available for download on the company's website, is designed to work with the user's web browser and collect data on their browsing habits. The data is then sent back to Google, where it is stored in a database.

While Google has always collected data on its users' browsing habits, this is the first time the company has released a toolbar specifically for this purpose. The move has sparked concern among privacy advocates, who worry about the amount of data Google is collecting on users and how it plans to use it.

"This is a serious invasion of privacy," said one privacy advocate. "Google is collecting data on users' browsing habits without their knowledge or consent. This data can be used to create detailed profiles of individuals, which can then be used for targeted advertising or sold to third parties."

Google has defended the toolbar, saying that it is a useful tool for users who want to track their web activity. The company has also stressed that the data collected by the toolbar is anonymous and that it will not be used to create targeted ads.

"The data collected by the toolbar is anonymous and will not be used to create targeted ads," said a Google spokesperson. "It is simply a useful tool for users who want to track their web activity."

Despite Google's assurances, many privacy advocates are still concerned about the toolbar and the potential impact it could have on users' privacy.

A helmet that reads people's brainwaves and lets them control a computer with their thoughts has been developed by Japanese researchers.

The "Brainwave" cap detects electrical activity in the brain caused by concentration and relaxation.

Users can perform simple tasks, such as turning a switch on and off, by thinking about it.

The device could be used to help people with movement disorders control equipment.

The researchers plan to trial the cap - dubbed "Brainwave" - on people with severe physical disabilities to see if it can help them to control computers.

"We were able to get some results that exceeded our expectations," said Dr. Tomoyuki Sato, who led the team at Yokohama National University.

"Using this device, we intend to continue research toward the realization of a new, interface that does not rely on the five senses," he added in a statement.

The device uses an electroencephalogram (EEG) to detect electrical activity caused by changes in brainwaves.

It then uses algorithms to analyze the brainwaves and activate the devices.

It has been programmed to recognize three different brainwave patterns:

1) When the user concentrates
2) When the user is relaxed
3) When the user is neither concentrating nor relaxed

Using these different patterns, researchers programmed the cap to turn on when the user was relaxed and turn off when the user concentrated.

In experiments, participants were able to use the cap to successfully switch a virtual light on and off, and to move a rising column of blocks up and down.

The device is currently attached to a computer by a cable, but the researchers want to develop a wireless version.

A brain-computer interface (BCI) that helps people with paralysis type on a computer just by thinking has been developed by US scientists. The new device uses a cap with 64 electrodes to sense neural activity, then translates these signals into text. 

The team presented the new BCI at the Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems in New Orleans, Louisiana. 

Lead researcher, Krishna Shenoy from the Howard Hughes Medical Institute, and the Stanford University School of Medicine, says the aim was to create a system that requires no training and is available to anyone. 

"We're approaching this from a totally different angle," he says. "Instead of having to teach the computer what thoughts mean, we're asking the computer to learn the mind of the individual."

The new BCI device uses a neural implant that goes over the scalp rather than being implanted under the skull. This makes it far more practical as an aid for paralysis.

When the electrodes pick up brain signals, they are sent to a small computer which decrypts the messages and sends them to a screen. 

The team has also developed a new way of decoding the brain signals that is more effective than previous techniques. This involves a two-step process that first identifies which brain signals are most useful, then traces them back to their source by looking at the timing of the signals. This has enabled the team to improve the speed of the BCI.

"We can decode some signals almost perfectly," says Shenoy. "And brain-computer interfaces are getting better all the time."

The current system has been tested on four people, and the team believes it can be expanded to work with other brain signals, and for other purposes, such as helping to improve the movement of prosthetic limbs.

"We're not limited to just moving a cursor on a screen," says Shenoy. "We can imagine more sophisticated things, like helping a person with paralysis move their arm."

Disney has agreed to pay $2.8m to settle charges it misled investors about the size of its streaming subscriber base.

The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) said Disney distributed inaccurate information about its subscribers to investors.

The SEC said Disney distributed inaccurate information about the number of subscribers it had for its Disney+ streaming service shortly after its launch.

Disney had stated that it had more than 100 million subscribers when it only had approximately 26 million, according to the SEC.

Disney+ launched in November 2019 and the SEC said Disney knew its subscriber numbers were not as high as it was telling investors.

The settlement with the SEC does not mean the company has admitted to any wrongdoing. Disney has not issued a comment on the settlement.

The SEC said its enforcement division found that Disney distributed inaccurate subscriber data in SEC filings and earnings releases between February 2021 and May 2021.

Disney+ launched in November 2019 and in early 2020 Disney told investors that its rollout had been highly successful, with nearly 34 million subscribers signed up.

The SEC said Disney knew its subscriber numbers after taking into account those who had received free promotional subscriptions were not as high as it was telling investors.

The regulator said Disney's filings inaccurately claimed that it had over 100 million total paid subscribers across its streaming services, when in fact it only had approximately 96 million.

The SEC said in a statement: "Disney misled investors by mistakenly including Disney+ Free Trial subscribers in its total subscriber count, when in fact Disney+ Free Trial subscribers do not provide Disney with any direct financial benefit, and were not counted as paid subscribers or as part of the total subscriber count pursuant to Disney's publicly-represented accounting policy.

"Disney's incorrect disclosures about the pace of Disney+ subscriber growth resulted from poor execution of a shift to a new subscriber reporting methodology, and not from any malicious intent or attempt to deceive investors."

Disney has recently been boosting its subscriber numbers through acquisitions such as its $73bn purchase of the bulk of 21st Century Fox in 2019.

It also owns cable sports network ESPN and recently launched a subscription based sports streaming service.

Hong Kong is among the unlikely candidates to stage the World Cup as the Asian metropolis joins the race for the right to host the tournament in 2018.

"We are not a mega-billion city like some others in the race, but we are a city with liveability.

"We are used to hosting major events. We are confident we can host a World Cup if given the opportunity."

Hong Kong is the second longest surviving British colony after the Falkland Islands and has a population of more than seven million.

Williams accepts that a World Cup in Asia would favour countries on the mainland, but he believes football's world governing body, Fifa, should consider the financial and commercial benefits of taking the tournament to a city like Hong Kong.

"It is a difficult decision for Fifa. They have to consider the political situation and also the geographical situation of where they place the World Cup," said Williams.

"We are confident that we can provide the infrastructure. We are not just a financial centre, we have a lot of history and culture. We are a city with a lot to offer.

"We have the experience of hosting major events. We have hosted the Olympic Games and we are regularly hosting top-level rugby and football tournaments.

"We are confident we can do it. It is a question of whether Fifa wants to take the World Cup to a new place, a new city."

The Asian Football Confederation (AFC) has nominated Australia as its candidate to host the 2018 tournament, but Williams says Hong Kong can bid independently if they wish.

"If we have to go it alone, we are prepared to do that. We have the backing of the government and that is a big plus for us," said Williams.

Police and crime commissioners (PCCs) are set to be given the power to suspend or fire senior officers if they are deemed to be failing. The proposal is contained in a new draft bill on criminal justice, published on Wednesday by the Home Office. It outlines plans to reinforce the role of PCCs, who were first elected in 2012. The draft legislation - the Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Bill - will be introduced to Parliament in the coming weeks.

The bill would also restrict the second jobs that police officers and staff can do. The bill would ban all but the most senior officers from working in the security industry or for an organisation that provides services to the police.
