Tech giants including Google and Amazon have welcomed "significant improvements" in a review of the body overseeing the web's domain name system.

The Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers' (Icann) new chief executive took over in March amid concerns about its transparency and accountability.

In a blog post, Icann said it was seeking comments on an initial plan for a "significant overhaul" of its governance.

"We are seeking to make substantial changes to virtually all aspects of Icann's structures, policies, and procedures," it said.

The overhaul includes the creation of an "independent accountability mechanism" to handle complaints about the body, as well as term limits for board members.

Icann also plans to increase the diversity of its leadership, including reaching out to parts of the world that are currently under-represented, such as Africa.

In a joint statement, Google, Amazon, Microsoft and Yahoo welcomed the progress, and said the next step should be to establish a "stable funding source" to ensure the long-term sustainability of Icann.

"To foster the kind of predictable, stable, and broadly supported funding source that Icann needs, we urge the US government to work with Icann, and the broader internet community, to determine the best method for unleashing the kind of funding that will support Icann's mission for the long term," they said.

Icann is currently largely funded by registration fees for web domain names, but has warned that this model is becoming unsustainable.

The tech firms also urged Icann to modernise its "outdated" bylaws, and said any new mechanisms should be "simple, clear, and easy for all stakeholders to participate in".

Icann is responsible for managing the web's address system, and has faced criticism in recent years about its handling of online piracy and the rise of malicious websites.

The body of a BBC news article titled "Progress on new internet domains":

For decades, the internet has functioned using the domain name system (DNS), which divides the digital universe into separate parts, or domains, each preceded by "www" and separated by periods. Examples include .com, .org, and .net. There are also country-specific domains, such as .ca for Canada. But despite the internet's rapid growth over the last three decades, the list of available domains has remained relatively stable. That is, until the summer of 2016, when the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers (ICANN), the non-profit organization that oversees the internet's DNS, announced that it would be expanding the list of available top-level domains (TLDs). ICANN's decision would open up the internet to potentially limitless new domains, ranging from .apple to .wine. 

This announcement has sparked excitement and intrigue in the tech community. Some believe that this expansion will lead to more innovation and creativity online. Others are concerned that it will lead to more cybercrime and online harassment. The change is certainly coming: in the first half of 2017 alone, ICANN received more than 1,900 applications for new TLDs, which came from a wide range of sectors, including banking, fashion, and agriculture. There are also nearly 200 applications for non-Latin script domains, including Arabic, Chinese, and Cyrillic. 

The process of reviewing and approving these new TLDs is rigorous. Each application must meet a specific set of criteria, including technical and operational capability, and must be supported by a $185,000 application fee. This means that the new domains are unlikely to launch anytime soon. 

Nevertheless, the question remains: how will this expansion of top-level domains affect the way we use the internet? Will it lead to a more diverse and inclusive internet? Or will it lead to greater fragmentation and chaos? Only time will tell. But one thing is certain: the internet is about to enter a new era.

Retail sales in the UK have risen for the fourth consecutive month, with clothing and computer sales driving the increase.

According to the British Retail Consortium (BRC), sales were up by 0.8% in December, compared with the same month in 2010.

The BRC said anecdotal evidence suggested it was the busiest Christmas for retailers since 2007.

However, it added that the rise in sales was also helped by mild weather and a later than usual Black Friday.

"Christmas featured heavily in October's sales, as retailers launched their campaigns earlier than last year, in response to the squeeze on consumer spending," said Helen Dickinson, the BRC's chief executive.

"The later-than-usual Black Friday also provided a boost in November, as consumers were able to make the most of the longer duration of Christmas offers."

She added that the mild weather had helped sales of seasonal clothing ranges.

The figures were compiled by the BRC's sales monitor, which tracks the sales performance of more than 5,000 shops.

Separate figures from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) show that overall retail sales were up 1.4% in November, compared with October.

However, the ONS also said the volume of retail sales was 0.2% lower in November than a year earlier.

The BRC's figures showed that shoppers spent more on clothing than any other category in December, with sales rising by 3.3% on a like-for-like basis compared with December 2010.

Sales of furniture and flooring increased by 4.1%, while food sales were up by 1.9% on a like-for-like basis.

However, the BRC said sales of household goods, such as furniture and electricals, were down by 1.8% on a like-for-like basis.

Ms Dickinson said 2013 had been a "challenging" year for retailers.

"A tough economic climate, compounded by extreme weather conditions, made for a difficult year for retailers, with many people holding back on spending," she said.

"We anticipate little change to this in the coming months, as consumer confidence remains fragile."

Retail sales jumped in December as a surge in Christmas spending raised hopes that the high street's troubles were easing, official figures show.

Sales volumes were up by 1.4% in December 2022 compared with the same month a year earlier, the Office for National Statistics said.

It marked the fastest growth since April 2022 and exceeded economists' forecasts for a 0.6% rise.

However, compared with before the pandemic, sales were down 2.1% in December, showing that shoppers have not returned to pre-Covid levels of spending.

Business groups warned that the figures were likely to overstate the strength of the high street as they included rising prices for consumers. Retailers also reported that trading remained weak in early January as households cut back on discretionary spending.

The ONS figures showed that retailers reported a boost in the run-up to Christmas, with clothing and footwear sales particularly strong as people splashed out on new festive outfits.

Food sales were also up, despite warnings from supermarkets that they faced higher chicken and turkey prices this Christmas. However, sales of electronics and furniture declined.

The figures showed an uptick in spending at restaurants and other hospitality venues just before Christmas as families caught up with friends and relatives they had not seen as often during the pandemic.

However, this was offset by a sharp fall in December as fears about the spread of the Omicron variant prompted people to cancel bookings.

Overall, retail sales in the final three months of 2022 were up by 0.2% when compared with the same period in 2021. However, they were down by 1.1% when compared with the pre-pandemic period in 2019.

Helen Dickinson, chief executive of the British Retail Consortium, said the figures showed that retailers had provided a "strong festive offering".

She added: "However, the current squeeze on household income is now clearly being felt in discretionary categories, with consumers limiting spending on items such as electronics, toys and furniture.

"With further interest rate rises expected this year, retailers will be hoping for a strong rebound in consumer demand in the spring to protect jobs and livelihoods."

The Santy worm, which has been around for years but was dormant for a while, has made an unwelcome visit to Android phones. Security experts have said that the worm, one of the first Android worms, is sophisticated and can bypass security defences. The discovery was made by researchers at Zimperium, an Arizona-based mobile security company. It affects "almost all Android 4 devices" which is around 95% of Android phones and tablets. The discovery was announced at the Black Hat security conference in Las Vegas. Ian Beer, from Google's Project Zero security team, said that the bug was "one of the worst I've seen in terms of potential impact". Google has released a fix for the vulnerability and is working with partners to get it to all users.

The worm was first seen in the wild in 2011 and is also known as Axiom, it targeted computers and networks in the Middle East and Korea. Antivirus firm Bitdefender says the Android version is a "near identical copy" of the Windows version, just under a different name - instead of Santy. It is hard to detect and very difficult to remove and, once one device is infected, it tries to spread to other devices connected to the same network. It does this by cracking the password used to secure the wireless network. It then harvests email addresses from the infected device and sends itself to all these addresses with a message containing a link to download a fake version of the Android operating system. Anyone clicking on the link would become infected.

Researchers at Zimperium found the worm when a customer in Germany asked them to investigate why many of his company's Android devices were crashing. The team was able to recreate the scenario and realised that the Santy worm was the cause. Zimperium has created a free app, zANTI, which can be used to detect if a phone is infected.

The Santa worm made an unwelcome visit to London this week. The city's transportation system was thrown into disarray as the worm made its way through the Underground. Trains were delayed and canceled, and many commuters were left stranded. The worm, which is known for its ability to chew through metal, has caused extensive damage to the tracks and signals. Engineers are working around the clock to repair the damage and get the transportation system back up and running. The Santa worm has also made an appearance in other parts of the UK, including Manchester and Glasgow. It is not known how the worm made its way to the UK, but experts believe it may have arrived on a ship from Asia.

The dollar has hit a new low against the euro, as its decline against other major currencies continued for a third day.

The euro broke through the $1.60 level for the first time, reaching a high of $1.6050 earlier on Wednesday.

The dollar has lost more than 6% of its value against the euro over the past year, as the US Federal Reserve has kept interest rates low to boost the economy.

Other major currencies including the pound and the yen have also gained against the dollar in recent months.

"The dollar is very weak, and it's not just versus the euro," said Jennifer Lee, an economist with BMO Capital Markets.

"It's reflective of the fact that the Fed has been extremely dovish, and that interest rates are low."

The euro has gained over the past year as the European Central Bank has gradually raised interest rates, in contrast to the Fed's moves.

However, some analysts say the euro's gains are beginning to slow as the currency reaches parity with the dollar.

"We are nearing the point where the euro is fully valued," said Joe Manimbo, an analyst with Western Union Business Solutions.

"The driver for the dollar's decline has been the Fed's dovish stance, but if the Fed is forced to become more hawkish, that would be a game changer."

Still, analysts say the dollar is likely to remain under pressure in the near future, as the US economy continues to improve and the Fed maintains its low interest rate policy.

The dollar hit a new low versus the euro on Monday, as concerns about the Federal Reserve's response to inflation continued to pressure the currency.

The euro rose to $1.1442, its highest level since July, while the dollar index fell to its lowest level since March. The pound also gained ground, rising to $1.3692.

Markets have been weighing the chances of the Fed raising interest rates at its meeting next week. Some policymakers have pushed for a more aggressive response to inflation, but others have warned that a hike could slow economic growth.

The euro has been gaining ground versus the dollar since the European Central Bank announced a more hawkish stance last week. The ECB said it would be "patient" in its approach to raising rates, but added that it would "not hesitate" to act if inflationary pressures increased.

The dollar's decline has also been driven by weakness in the Japanese yen and the British pound. The yen has been hurt by a weaker economy and lower interest rates, while the pound has been pressured by concerns about the UK's economic outlook.

The dollar's slide has been a significant trend in the past year, as concerns about the Fed's response to inflation and the US's growing debt have weighed on the currency. It has fallen by more than 12% since March, and by more than 20% since its peak in December 2016.

A clampdown on fraud and corruption throughout the European Union is being urged by the bloc's police agency.

In its annual report, Europol said organised crime was becoming more sophisticated, and warned that anti-fraud measures were struggling to keep up.

The Dutch government - which holds the EU's rotating presidency - has proposed a new fraud strategy.

But the UK - which has been criticised for not cooperating with other EU member states - has yet to sign up.

The report by Europol - the EU's law enforcement agency - warned that fraud was being committed by criminals operating from outside the EU, and that action was needed to counter the threat.

"Criminals don't care about borders and the Internet knows no boundaries - organised crime does not recognise the EU as a single jurisdiction," said Europol's executive director, Rob Wainwright.

"We need to react with the same level of co-operation and determination."

The agency's report highlighted fraud involving non-cash payment cards, and the dangers posed by sophisticated new techniques such as "skimming". This involves copying data from the magnetic strips of cards, which can then be used to create counterfeit cards.

The report also expressed concern at the growing threat to banks and businesses from "phishing" scams - in which criminals con people into revealing their passwords and personal details.

In addition, it warned that there was evidence of illegal immigration being funded by fraud, with immigrants' passports being used for identity fraud. This was being organised by criminal networks, the report said.

The Dutch government has proposed a series of measures aimed at tackling fraud, including a new "fraud action plan" aimed at improving co-operation between EU member states.

But the UK - which has been criticised for not doing enough to co-operate with other EU states - has not signed up to the plan. The UK says it has its own strategy for tackling fraud, and that this is already being implemented.

The Europol report said that although many EU countries had improved their anti-fraud measures, these were still "insufficient" overall.
It called for a strengthening of the EU's anti-fraud office, Olaf, which is responsible for co-ordinating the fight against fraud across the bloc.

The agency also called for a strengthening of Europol itself, to enable it to better monitor and analyse trends in organised crime.

The report's publication comes as the UK continues to debate its future

The BBC has learned that tens of billions of euros earmarked for helping the EU's economic recovery from the Covid pandemic have been lost to fraud. The scale of fraud and corruption risks derailing the EU's goal of a sustainable and inclusive recovery, and is also depriving citizens of much-needed support, according to a new report by Europol. The report calls on the EU to tighten up controls and to increase efforts to fight fraud. It warns that criminals are exploiting weaknesses in the EU's financial controls to steal funds on an "unprecedented" scale. The report's author, Europol's executive director, Catherine De Bolle, is calling on the EU to tighten up controls and increase efforts to fight fraud. 

"The European Commission, alongside member states, need to improve the overall control environment to prevent fraud, accelerate investigations and recover the proceeds of crime in order to make the EU budget more fraud resistant and future budgets harder to steal," she said. The call comes after the publication of a study by the European Court of Auditors, which found that weak controls and errors had led to possible fraud in projects worth €42bn (£36bn) - around 4% of the total value of projects funded by the EU's seven-year budget between 2014 and 2020. 

The audit found evidence of fraud in all of the EU's member states, with a particular concentration in Hungary, Italy and Bulgaria. It also revealed that the European Commission did not perform any checks on projects in member states deemed to be at high risk of fraud. The commission has welcomed the report, saying it takes the issue of fraud very seriously. 

A commission spokesperson said: "Fighting fraud is a top priority for the European Commission. We have put in place strong measures to prevent, detect and investigate fraud, and we are constantly seeking to improve our measures. "In parallel, and as part of our next long-term budget, we are stepping up checks and controls to prevent fraud from happening in the first place."

Roger Federer claimed his eighth title in the Dubai Duty Free Tennis Championships with a straight-set victory over Felix Auger-Aliassime.

The Swiss legend, playing in his fifth final in the UAE, beat the Canadian 20-year-old 6-2 6-7 (4-7) 6-4 to claim his 105th title.

It was also the first time Federer had dropped a set in the tournament.

The 20-time Grand Slam champion eased through the opening set in 33 minutes but was broken three times in the second as Auger-Aliassime forced a tie-break.

Federer, who turned 40 last month, took an early 2-0 lead in the tie-break but lost the next seven points as Auger-Aliassime levelled the match.

Both players broke each other's serve early in the deciding set but it was the veteran who earned the crucial break in the eighth game before serving out to love to seal the match in two hours and 21 minutes.

"It was tough, it was tough for me to play like this, especially after the year that I had," Federer said.

"The young guy is a terrific player with a great future ahead of him. I think for me, it's just about staying healthy, recalibrating everything and trying to play more this year."

It was Federer's first title since the Swiss Indoors in October 2019 and his first outdoor hard-court title since Shanghai in October 2017.

Auger-Aliassime, who reached the final without dropping a set, has still yet to win a title after seven final appearances.

The Canadian has lost all three of his meetings with Federer, including in the quarter-finals of last year's US Open.

Roger Federer claimed a "special" record eighth Dubai Championships title with a 3-6, 6-4, 6-4 defeat of Britain's Dan Evans in the final on Saturday.

The 20-time Grand Slam champion moved level with Novak Djokovic on 43 career titles with a determined display.

The Swiss legend carved out a decisive break in the penultimate game of the final set before closing out victory with a love service hold.

Evans, who knocked out top seed Stefanos Tsitsipas in the semi-finals, was unable to become the first British player to win the Dubai title.

Ad firm WPP posts rise in annual profits for the first time in four years - BBC News

WPP has posted its first annual rise in profits for four years thanks to cost cuts and increased revenue.

The advertising giant said pre-tax profits rose by 15% to £306m ($408m) for the year to 31 December.

It marks a turnaround for the firm, which has been hit by economic uncertainty and competition from digital rivals.

The world's biggest advertising agency said it had made a "solid start" to 2023.

WPP's shares rose more than 5% in morning trading in London.

The group said it had won new business, with net new bookings up by more than 50% compared to 2021.

Chief executive Mark Read said: "We are making good progress against our strategy, delivering meaningful growth for our clients and continuing to invest in creative capabilities and talent, despite a more difficult economic backdrop.

"We are making a solid start to 2023, with strong new business momentum and important client wins, and are well positioned to continue delivering for our clients as the global economy undergoes a transformation."

WPP's results come as rivals grapple with the impact of the economic downturn, although the industry has so far avoided major fallout from the conflict in Ukraine.

Last week, rival firm Omnicom reported its profits had fallen by nearly a third, while Publicis Groupe raised its profit forecasts on the back of "strong" demand.

At 09:00 GMT, WPP's shares were up 5.1% at 718p.

Ad firm WPP has reported a 15% rise in annual profits, boosted by a strong performance from its digital businesses and an economic recovery in parts of the world.

The group said it had seen a strong rebound in markets such as the UK, parts of Europe and Australia, following the lifting of Covid-19 restrictions.

Overall revenues at WPP were up 8.4% to £7.6bn for the year to 31 December.

It said it had seen a strong performance from its customer experience management and marketing business in North America.

WPP's chief executive Mark Read said the company was "back to normal" as the firm reported its first annual profit growth since 2018.

"We're back to normal against 2019 and actually ahead of 2019 in the UK," he said.

"There is a lot of talk about recession and maybe that will happen, but there is also talk about pent-up demand and consumers spending again as we come out of Covid."

Mr Read said the company was "well placed" to face any downturn, having pulled costs out of the business in recent years.

He also said the company was "seeing inflationary pressures" but added that it had so far not seen a "material impact" on its business.

"These are early days and it's difficult to predict how that will impact our clients and our company," he said.

Earlier this month, WPP made a series of senior promotions within its management team, as it looked to bolster its creative offerings.

The group said that Mark Hunter, global chief executive of its customer experience management division, Kantar, would be stepping down from the role.

Mr Hunter has served as CEO of Kantar since 2019. He will continue to work with the company as a senior adviser.

WPP - which owns several major advertising agencies such as Grey, Ogilvy and MEC - has faced a challenging few years as clients cut costs by reviewing their agency rosters.

Mr Read said that the company had won new business worth more than £3bn in the last financial year. That included work with Amazon, Starbucks and Samsung.

Conservative MP Christian Wakeford has defected to Labour, the party has announced.

Mr Wakeford, who represents Bury South, said he was "taking this decision now because I believe that Labour is the only party that can offer the ray of hope that the people of Bury South and Britain need".

He is the second Tory MP this week to switch to Labour, following the defection of Neil Coyle.

The Conservative Party has so far said nothing about Mr Wakeford's decision.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Mr Wakeford said he did not believe in the prime minister's sincerity about changes to the parliamentary disciplinary system, which has seen a number of MPs expelled from the Conservative Party.

He said he "didn't think" Boris Johnson would change "because of how it originated and the fact he didn't take any responsibility".

"I think we've all now witnessed Boris Johnson's brand of politics which is one of undermining and deceit and it's just not acceptable for the good people of Bury South," he added.

Around midnight on Wednesday, a car pulled up outside the house of Sir Keir Starmer, Labour leader, in Camden, north London. Daniel Kawczynski, a Conservative MP since 2005, got out and knocked on the door. Starmer was in bed, but his wife, Victoria, answered, and invited the MP in. He refused the offer of food and drink, and instead they sat in the kitchen, chatting.

Kawczynski had told his wife he was visiting a friend for "a drink and a chat", but in fact, he was moving MPs from the Conservative party to Labour. It is a remarkable act of political rebellion – and an indication of the turmoil in the Tory party following the election of Boris Johnson as leader.

For years, Kawczynski had been a loyal Conservative, first as a member of the European Parliament, then as a member of the Polish community in Britain. He was a strong supporter of Brexit and repeatedly attacked Labour as "the party of open borders".

But he became increasingly frustrated during the Tory leadership contest, as candidates veered to the right. Michael Gove, who ultimately came third, promised to lead the party out of the European Convention on Human Rights; Johnson gave only a qualified commitment to the Northern Irish backstop.

Kawczynski believes the Conservative party has abandoned the one nation tradition of Toryism, and become an instrument to promote the interests of the wealthy and the privileged. In Labour, he believes, he has found a party that reflects his beliefs, and those of many no-deal Brexiteers.

"The Labour party under Keir Starmer's leadership has changed dramatically," he told BBC News. "Keir Starmer has shown he is a man of principle, who has managed to unite his party, and who is offering the country a vision of hope, a vision of unity."

Starmer was keen to recruit MPs to his top team, but had expected any who defected to be from the Conservative party's One Nation wing. The arrival of Kawczynski, a committed Brexiteer, is a surprise, and a challenge.

The Labour leader has made clear he wants his MPs to represent all of Britain – Remainers and Leavers – and he hopes that Kawczynski will be able to talk to former Tory colleagues about the benefits of unity, and the dangers of Johnson's leadership.

Japanese authorities have arrested the chief executive of the country's biggest online fashion retailer for alleged wire fraud.

The Tokyo District Public Prosecutors Office said it had arrested Rakuten Inc's chief executive, Hiroshi Mikitani, along with seven others including Rakuten executives and employees of a subsidiary, on suspicion of falsifying documents to illegally gain $338m (£232m) from a client.

The prosecutors office and Rakuten did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The allegations centre on Rakuten's relationship with Japan Post, which in 2014 invested about $1.2bn in online retailer Rakuten Card, believing it had a stake of around 38% in the business.

It is alleged that Rakuten and Rakuten Card executives then manipulated accounting records to reduce Japan Post's actual stake in the subsidiary, which acts as the exclusive issuer of Rakuten Group's credit cards.

Rakuten is one of Japan's biggest e-commerce businesses and also operates online video and music streaming services, digital books and a bank.

It recently signed a deal with Netflix to distribute its library of shows and films in Japan and is expanding in the US after buying messaging app Viber for $900m last year.

Mr Mikitani, a Harvard University graduate who is worth $1.5bn according to Forbes, founded the business in 1997.

Rakuten's shares fell 12% after the allegations were made public and the company issued a statement saying it would "co-operate fully" with authorities.

Japanese police have arrested the CEO of one of the country's largest advertising firms on suspicion of padding his firm's books by at least $330m.

The Tokyo Securities Exchange ordered Dentsu to suspend trading in its shares last Friday.

The Japanese mogul, Tadashi Ishii, stepped down from his role after the company revealed it had found "serious" accounting irregularities. 

Ishii, who denies the allegations, is accused of having ordered the systematic faking of documents to make it look like the company had earned at least ¥44.6bn ($332m) from 2013 to 2015. 

The 83-year-old executive was detained on Tuesday night after questioning at Tokyo Metropolitan Police Department. 

Ishii has admitted to the reporting inaccuracy but claims it was not a deliberate act.

"I sincerely apologise again for causing a great deal of concern to a wide range of people, including shareholders and investors, through the false publication of the financial statements," he said in a statement. 

"It is true that there was a big mistake in management, but it is incorrect to say that it was a fraudulent act." 

Dentsu, one of Japan's most influential advertising agencies, has faced a string of scandals in recent years related to its ties with Japan's powerful Ministry of Finance.

Tory MPs say a planned rise in national insurance will break a 2019 manifesto promise not to raise taxes.

But Chancellor Rishi Sunak said it was a "fair" way to fund health and social care.

And Health Secretary Sajid Javid said without the tax rise the NHS was "going to feel this winter like it has never felt before".

The BBC's Laura Kuenssberg said she understood that a number of Conservative MPs were willing to submit letters of no confidence in Mr Johnson, with the total now at about 20.

That is despite the prime minister announcing a U-turn on the national insurance rise less than three days after it was introduced in the Budget, by agreeing to exempt the lowest earners.

 Tory MP Steve Baker, who is among those who submitted a letter, said he had confidence in Mr Johnson but that the tax rise was "not defensible".

The Chancellor, Philip Howard, has rejected suggestions that the Tories are putting off voters with their tough stance on tax.

The Conservative Party has promised to increase the threshold for the 40p income tax, but not until 2015. 

The party has also pledged to cut the top rate of tax from 50p to 40p, a move which Labour has said will cost the Treasury £3bn a year. 

Mr Howard said he was "not surprised" that voters were concerned about the issue of tax. However, he said the party was "not going to take lectures" from Labour on the matter.

The Chancellor said the Conservatives would continue to focus on their message of economic growth and "higher living standards". 

He added that the party was committed to "lower taxes" but would only deliver them once the economy had recovered.

Fit-again Sophie Betsen is included in France's squad for Saturday's Six Nations game against England.

The 27-year-old Montpellier back, who has recovered from a knee injury, has not played for her country since November 2012.

France coach Philippe Saint-Andre has named six uncapped players in his squad.

They include centre Coralie Serret, who will be aiming to make her debut against England.

France are looking to bounce back from their 41-16 defeat by Ireland in Dublin on Sunday.

England went into the weekend's games top of the table after winning their first two matches - against Scotland and Italy.

A fit-again Caroline Betsen has been named in France's squad for their Women's Six Nations clash with England.
Betsen, who has been out with a hip injury since the summer, is included in coach Francis Tourte's 28-strong group.
France, who defeated Scotland in their opening game, face England in Paris on Saturday.
England opened their campaign with a comprehensive 51-0 victory over Ireland.
Tourte has also called up Laure Sansus, who scored a try in France's victory over Scotland, and Laure Touye, who made her debut in that match.
England captain Sarah Hunter will win her 139th cap, which will be a new record for the Women's Six Nations. She currently shares the record with Italy's Sara Barattin.
Ireland coach Greg McWilliams has made three changes for his side's game against Wales in Dublin on Sunday.
McWilliams has brought in centre Jenny Murphy, number eight Aoife McDermott and full-back Emma Hooban.
Ireland were disappointed with their performance in the round-one defeat by England and are keen to show their capabilities this weekend.
"We were bitterly disappointed with the performance against England, and we've had some honest conversations about where we want to go as a group," said McWilliams.
"We know that Wales are going to be a very different proposition, and we need to be better across the board this week in order to win."

US fans of British band Duran Duran will get the chance to see the group in the world's first live virtual reality concert on a major network. 

The group will play live at London's Printworks venue on 27 November with the show made available to US television audiences on the CBS virtual reality platform, followed by a making-of festival version to be shown on Hulu the following day.

Duran Duran guitarist Rio Ferdinand said: "We've always been excited by new technologies - it's a way for us to connect with fans old and new."

Their show will be followed by an extended 90-minute cut of the concert, which will be available on Hulu the following day. 

The band will play some of their greatest hits including Hungry Like the Wolf, Rio and Ordinary World.

Duran Duran will perform their new album Future Past for the first time on US television, with a special set for NBC's The Today Show.

The British new wave band will play the 15-track record in its entirety during the set, which will be recorded on 27 January at the Roxy in Los Angeles. It will air on the Today Show on 31 January.

Beijing's government has cancelled a plan to charge drivers per entry into the city's central business district (CBD) after it sparked an angry response from the public.

The scheme, which was supposed to start on Friday, would have charged drivers of non-electric vehicles 3 yuan (£0.32; $0.43) each time they entered the district.

But it was suspended on Tuesday after online criticism and protests.

Many also questioned why two-wheeled motorbikes were not included in the plan.

"I thought Beijing was about to become a world city, but it turns out we're still living in a feudal society where the rich get special treatment," one person wrote on China's Twitter-like Weibo.

Beijing's CBD is home to many upscale shops, offices and government buildings.

BBC Sport's Paul Lewis on the TMO decision that cost Ben Cohen a try against France:

It was a try - simple as that.

There are times when technology in sport just leaves you scratching your head and this was one of them.

To the naked eye it was a try, and to the eye of the TMO as well because he took so long to make the decision.

Initially, he ruled it a try, then he went to check with his colleague and then they changed their mind.

It didn't affect the outcome of the match - England were going to win that game comfortably - but it was a pivotal moment in the sense it could have changed the whole mindset of the players.

They might have thought 'we'll just keep going, we'll keep attacking', rather than thinking 'right, we'll kick the points and make sure we're 13-8 up'.

I think it was a pivotal moment in the sense it might have set England on the path to a bigger score.

In terms of the TMO, you could see him scrunching up his face, initially looking at the try, looking at the grounding, looking at the player being tackled, then looking at the touch-judge, then talking to his colleague.

It was a confusing sequence of events.

To rule the try out - as he did - you're looking for definitive evidence, but there's nothing definitive here.

There have been a few tries disallowed this year on the basis the player's foot was on the line, but that's not the case here.

His foot was on the whitewash - that is indisputable. If the TMO is looking for definitive evidence to overrule that try, I'm not sure what he's looking at.

The try should have stood.

The League Against Cruel Sports has reported a drop in support for its campaign to ban hunting with hounds in England and Wales.

The charity, which is campaigning for a hunting ban, says its latest survey indicates public support is in decline.

The League said its survey showed 47% supported a hunt ban, with 35% against and 18% undecided.

In 2007, a similar survey found that 61% were in favour of a ban.

The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said it had no plans for a hunt ban.

The League's chief executive, Joe Duckworth, said: "The majority of the public don't want to see a return to the cruel and violent sport of hunting with hounds."

The issue of a possible ban has divided the Conservative Party, with Prime Minister Rishi Sunak opposing a repeal of the Hunting Act while some MPs and MPs supportive of the Conservative rural lobby voice support for a return to hunting with hounds.

Liam Neeson is in talks to revive a theatre in his hometown of Belfast. The actor has expressed an interest in developing the site of the old Odeon cinema in Donegall Street, which has been closed to the public since 1993. His production company, Kilmegan Productions, has had preliminary discussions with the Northern Irish government about a potential redevelopment.

The project would see the venue converted into a live music and theatre space, complete with a hotel, shops and apartments. Belfast City Council's deputy mayor, Mary Ellen Campbell, told the BBC that the actor's interest in the project "shows how much this city has to offer in terms of talent and creativity". She added: "It would be fantastic to see this iconic building restored to its former glory and I look forward to seeing how plans develop."

Neeson, who starred in a production of Arthur Miller's Death of a Salesman at the Old Vic theatre in London earlier this year, said he is "very excited" about the project. "It's a great space and it has been vacant for too long," he said. "We believe that it deserves to be restored to its former glory."

The actor Liam Neeson is leading a campaign to save his local theatre in Belfast from closure, promising to raise funds and attract celebrity supporters.

The Shaftesbury Theatre in Belfast has been threatened with closure just weeks after it reopened following a £1.2m refurbishment.

The actor said he was "shocked and saddened" by the decision of Arts Council Northern Ireland to withdraw funding.

He described the theatre as a "crucial hub for local actors and artists".

In a statement, he said he planned to reach out to "some famous faces that have performed there over the years" to help save the theatre.

Golden State Warriors coach Steve Kerr expressed his frustration with the team's recent performances, despite winning by a large margin in their latest game. The Warriors defeated the Memphis Grizzlies by a score of 113-95, but Kerr was not pleased with his team's lack of focus and energy. "I'm very frustrated," Kerr told reporters after the game. The Warriors have been on a roll recently, winning their last eight games and posting the best record in the NBA. However, Kerr is not satisfied with the team's recent play and is looking for them to improve going forward. "We're not gonna win a championship with the way we're playing," he said. "We're just not, so we've got to figure it out."

The Warriors will look to improve on their poor play when they take on the San Antonio Spurs on Monday.

Australia's Casey Dellacqua and Samantha Stosur have caused a massive upset against the top seeds on the third day of the WTA Finals in Istanbul. The Australian duo defeated the Chinese pair of Zhang Shuai and Zheng Saisai 2-6 6-4 10-5 and ended the year-long 26-match winning streak of top seeds Hsieh Su-wei and Elise Mertens.

Harry Potter actor Radcliffe yet to answer GB call

Daniel Radcliffe is yet to answer Team GB's call to be a torchbearer for the London 2012 Olympic Games.

The 19-year-old, who starred in the Harry Potter films, is "flattered" but has "prior commitments", says a spokesman.

GB rowing hero Redgrave told the BBC he would be "very surprised" if the actor had been approached.

Total Nonstop Programming turns to an Elvis impersonator to revive its fortunes. Terry Brock is not impressed.

Elvis has left the building, but only to make way for a new entertainment format.

The King may have been the ultimate pop idol, but even his talents and worldwide appeal couldn't save Total Nonstop Programming (TNP), the television production company that created the Popcorn channel.

So what's the answer? More pop corn, and lots of it.

It has been a tough year for TNP. Despite having three successful television shows in America - Melrose Place, 90210 and Dynasty - the company has been losing money.

Mr Spelling plans to put all his efforts into his new concept. "Elvis was a unique performer who appeals to all age groups and all over the world," he said.

The following year, TNP launched the country's first all-movie channel, the American Movie Classics network.

By 1995, the company was in financial trouble and began looking for a new direction.

The new channel was not a hit.

The one-time pad, an encryption technique invented nearly a century ago, relies on short key phrases. But a new study suggests that even when those phrases are nonsensical, their patterns can still be revealing. Benjamin Sparrey and Daniel Hughes of the University of Bristol in the U.K. examined four famously secure messages encoded using one-time pads. They found that, with enough contextual information about the authors and their backgrounds, they could guess at the content of the messages, despite having no knowledge of the key phrases used. For instance, they were able to infer the content of a message that Soviet spy John Cairncross sent to Moscow in 1943, despite having no knowledge of the keyphrase that Cairncross used. (They did have access to a 1987 book that gave six possible one-time pads that the author believed Cairncross might have used.)

The findings, presented last week at the IEEE European Symposium on Security and Privacy in Paris, underscore the importance of using appropriate one-time pads and cutting down on contextual information that might leak. In an email to The Register, Sparrey wrote that the one-time pad remains a secure encryption technique if used properly. "The reason why I performed this research is because I think it is important for people to realize just how secure the one-time pad is if used properly, and to understand the circumstances in which security may be broken," Sparrey wrote. "I hope that this research can be used to further educate people on the strengths and weaknesses of this beautiful and elegant encryption technique."

Asian stock markets have defied expectations and risen in the wake of last week's earthquake in Japan as investors looked through the current turmoil and focused on the longer term prospects.

Japan's Nikkei index closed up 1.2% after falling as much as 2.5% earlier in the day.

In neighbouring South Korea the Kospi index rose 1.1%.

In Australia, the ASX/200 closed up 1.4%.

In Hong Kong, the Hang Seng index ended the morning 0.3% higher.

And in China, where markets were closed on Friday for a public holiday, the CSI 300 index of the largest listed companies in Shanghai and Shenzhen rose 1.4% on Monday.

The resilience of Asian markets is in stark contrast to the reaction to the earthquake seven years ago.

After the earthquake in Tohoku, northern Japan, in March 2011, markets were jittery for months, said Yoshikiyo Shimamine, chief strategist at Daiwa Securities.

Back then, market participants were worried about the impact on the world's third biggest economy. This time, they are more worried about the rest of the world, given the strong economic ties between Japan and its Asian neighbours.

"Investors are looking past the earthquake and thinking about the recovery of the Japanese economy," said Mr Shimamine.

In a research note, analysts at Bank of America said there was a high chance that the economic disruption in Japan would be transitory.

"We are not concerned about the country's long-term economic outlook," they said.

Japan is a major exporter of cars and electronics and there are hopes that any slowdown in activity will be offset by a recovery in global demand as Covid-19 restrictions gradually get lifted.

The Bank of Japan's efforts to boost inflation are also likely to support the economy as it emerges from the shock, said Hiroaki Hashimoto, chief economist at Tokai Tokyo Research Institute.

"Looking at the bigger picture, there is no reason for the Japanese economy to be affected in the long term," he said.

And there is also hope that the planned $630bn stimulus package announced by the US government will give the global economy a big boost in the coming months.

But there are clearly risks. Disruption to supply chains could affect the region's export-oriented economies.

And worries about the security of nuclear power plants could weigh on the recovery in Japan, analysts say.

Asian share markets opened lower on Monday, but quickly turned positive as investors looked to buy into the dips, with optimism about a global economic recovery surpassing jitters over rising interest rates and the impact of a massive earthquake in Turkey.

Global markets have been rocked in recent weeks by central banks that have cranked up the pace of interest rate hikes as they try to tame inflation, and data last week showed US consumer prices remained elevated in September.

MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan was 0.2% higher, having swung from being down 0.5% at the open. Early in the session, the index had been dragged lower by declines in Chinese shares as the country resumed trading after a week off.

China's blue-chip index was 0.4% lower, with tech stocks weighing, but gains in materials and real estate companies limited the losses.

Hong Kong-listed shares in Alibaba jumped 10% after the company reported on Saturday that its Singles Day sales event had reached $84.5bn in the first 24 hours, up 8.5% from last year. 

Shares in other major Chinese tech firms listed in Hong Kong also rose, including Tencent, which gained 4.4%, and Meituan, which rose 6.1%.

In early European trades, the pan-European STOXX 600 was up 0.4%, having closed up 0.2% on Friday.

In currency markets, the Japanese yen fell as low as 147.95 to the dollar, its weakest since June 1995, as the dollar remained buoyant after last week's strong US consumer price index reading.

The quake in Turkey has also done little to dent the appeal of the lira, which has rallied around 5% over the past week.

While it did initially lose around 1% in the aftermath of the earthquake, the lira has since recovered those losses and was around 12% stronger against the dollar than where it was before last week's central bank meeting.

A popular Chinese lifestyle blogger known as "Sister Tao" has been grounded by her airline for posting a photo of herself wearing a bikini onboard a flight.

Tao Liang, who has more than 50 million followers on social media, posted the photo on June 25, posing in front of one of the plane's windows with the caption "summer vibe".

But it was the airline staff who were left feeling hot under the collar.

China's Hainan Airlines has banned Ms Liang from flying with the company for two years, and ordered her to undertake "corrective education" on air safety.

The company said in a statement that the move was made because the blogger had violated airline regulations on several occasions, including smoking in the plane's toilet, and not wearing a mask properly.

But Ms Liang hit back at the airline on China's Weibo social media platform, saying the bikini photo was taken after she had finished flying, and she was not wearing a swim suit on the flight.

"I never thought that my behaviour would be considered as not putting emphasis on civil aviation service morale, and I sincerely admit my mistakes," she said in a statement.

"I am willing to accept the punishment arranged by Hainan Airlines and promise to enhance my awareness of civil aviation services," she added.

The blogger has made headlines in the past for her controversial online content.

She shot to fame in 2016 for uploading videos of herself bragging about her wealth and buying expensive handbags.

But her online fame has not brought her happiness.

Ms Liang, from the southern city of Nanjing, has previously spoken about being bullied at school, and said in 2019 that she was being pursued by online trolls.

"I think at the very least, my happiness is taken into account," she said. "I don't want to continue with this facade, to keep smiling."

Samantha Brick's weekend began ordinarily enough. The journalist and newspaper columnist flew from London to Lisbon on Friday morning for a short break.

But by the time she arrived in the Portuguese capital, Ms Brick had become the centre of a social media storm. A tweet she posted in 2012 - in which she appeared to insult plus-size passengers - had resurfaced and was being widely shared.

"Why are fat people allowed on planes?" she had written. "I've put on a bit of weight recently and fear I will have to fly wearing a paper bag over my head."

By Saturday morning, the post had been shared thousands of times and attracted hundreds of comments.

Ms Brick, 57, responded by apologising "unreservedly", adding that she was "completely horrified" her comment had been resurfaced.

"I absolutely abhorred the post when I saw it," she told the BBC. "I thought - surely people aren't going to think I believe that.

"I fly a lot. I've flown a lot in the last year. I often wonder why there are so many overweight people on planes. It's a very uncharitable thought."

She added that she had not been embarrassed to make the initial tweet, but acknowledged that it was "absolutely disgusting" and that she was "horrified" at herself.

"I'm not proud of it," she said. "It's horrible, it's mean and it's unkind. I want to apologise to everybody for it."

By Saturday evening, Ms Brick had been suspended by The Sun, the newspaper where she has written a weekly column since 2004.

A Sun spokesperson said: "Samantha Brick's column last year was disgusting and deeply offensive. We unreservedly apologise to all those who were understandably horrified by it.

"Samantha has been suspended pending an investigation."

In a statement, EasyJet, which operated the flight on which Ms Brick travelled, said the tweet was "completely unacceptable… [and] does not reflect the values of EasyJet".

The airline added that it had "supported" Ms Brick's decision to cancel a second flight with the company on Saturday and offered her alternative travel arrangements.

Ms Brick said her decision to cancel the flight was a "precautionary measure"

She said she had been "inundated" with messages from people accusing her of being "horrible" and "nasty".

Microsoft has launched several new security tools, including one that it says can help protect people from malicious cyber activities by governments.

The software giant unveiled Microsoft Defender System Guard - a "new layer of defence" that works with the company's existing security products to provide "end-to-end protection" against various types of security threats.

It also includes new features to protect against so-called "zero-day" attacks, which exploit vulnerabilities that are either unknown or not yet fixed.

The company said the new security tools will be available as a "public preview" for some customers next month, with a full launch planned for later this year.

"As cyberattacks become more sophisticated and pervasive, cybersecurity needs to become more proactive, preventative and simple to implement," blogged Eric Doerr, vice-president of Microsoft Defender.

"Yet many organisations still struggle with basic security practices, and the complexity of security in the cloud era has only increased."

The company said the tools were designed to be easy to use and manage, in order to encourage businesses that do not have dedicated IT staff to adopt them.

"Cybersecurity is a journey, not a destination - and it's important to provide organisations with tools that are accessible and simple to use in order to foster adoption and mitigate risk," Mr Doerr wrote.

"It's important to us that customers can easily use, understand and adopt Microsoft Defender."

The news comes as businesses are increasingly seeking to protect themselves against cyber attacks, with many looking to cloud-based security tools as a way to do so.

According to a recent report by research firm Gartner, spending on cloud security services is expected to reach $5.6bn this year, up from $3.5bn in 2017.

Microsoft's move also comes as the company is facing increased competition from other cloud providers, such as Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud, which are both investing heavily in their own security offerings.

Microsoft's Security Manager provides companies with a comprehensive view of their security posture and recommendations on how to address potential issues. At the same time, the new Microsoft Defender product line will offer individuals and businesses alike protection for all their devices, including desktops, laptops, tablets, and mobile phones. 

The tech giant has also expanded its Microsoft Defender for Business product to more regions, and has added support for more platforms, including Linux and macOS. This tool is an endpoint security platform that helps companies protect their networks from cyber threats.

According to the company, Microsoft Defender for Business is now available in 42 countries and supports 19 platforms.

The UK's biggest civil service union will begin balloting members on strike action later this month.

The Public and Commercial Services (PCS) union said tens of thousands of civil servants could walk out in March over a pay dispute.

It said it would launch the ballot on 24 January.

The PCS has urged its members to back a strike in protest at a below-inflation pay rise offered by the government.

The ballot will close on 17 February. The first possible strike action would be on 1 March.

Civil servants at departments including Border Force, the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA), and HMRC, as well as courts and job centres, could strike.

The PCS balloted members on strike action last year but the vote did not achieve the threshold needed by law for action to go ahead.

Union bosses said this time they were "confident" of reaching the threshold.

The government has so far made no offer to improve on its pay rise proposal.

A government spokesperson said ministers had "already put forward a fair pay offer" despite the cost of living challenges".

Hundreds of thousands of civil servants in the UK are to be balloted on strike action in a dispute over pay, the Public and Commercial Services (PCS) union has said.

The ballot - the largest in a generation - will open on 11 January and close on 28 February.

It will open the same day as a strike by nurses, with the Royal College of Nursing (RCN) also in a pay dispute with the government.

PCS general secretary Mark Serwotka said the union was "going for broke" in its campaign for better pay.

He said the prime minister and chancellor could stop the strike by "opening their wallets".

The PCS, which represents workers in departments including HMRC, the Home Office and Ministry of Justice, as well as NHS admin staff, has asked for a 10% pay rise.

The union is also demanding a "cost-of-living adjustment" to all pay points, meaning all civil servants would receive a pay rise in line with the current rate of inflation - currently at 10.7%.

Mr Serwotka said the government was "forcing our hand" by "refusing to talk" to the union about pay.

He accused the government of "bare-faced cheek" in asking civil servants to accept a below-inflation pay increase at a time when ministers had given themselves a pay rise and a minister had been appointed to oversee a "pay rise for ministers".

"The prime minister and chancellor can stop this strike tomorrow by opening their wallets and putting some money on the table," he added.

The UK economy is facing "major risks" from spiralling costs and inflation, the Bank of England's governor has warned.

Andrew Bailey said the economy was facing a "very large" shock, as the price of goods rose much faster than people's wages.

His comments came as the Bank decided to raise interest rates to 1% - the highest level in 13 years.

The increase - widely expected following recent spikes in inflation - is designed to try to curb price rises.

Mr Bailey said the Bank expected inflation to peak at a higher level than previously thought, reaching 11% in the spring, up from a previous forecast of 10%.

The governor added that he also expected the UK economy to shrink by 0.25% in 2023, in comparison to previous estimates.

The decision to increase the cost of borrowing to 1% - the sixth consecutive rise - takes the Bank rate to its highest level since February 2009.

Inflation - the rate at which prices rise - is currently at its highest point in 40 years, mainly as a result of the pandemic and the war in Ukraine.

The Bank's decision comes as thousands of workers are striking in protest over pay, with rail workers, nurses, paramedics, and lorry drivers all walking out. Many unions have called for pay rises of around 10%.

Figures released on Wednesday showed that the cost of wholesale gas in the UK rocketed by more than 30% in just one day.

The price of oil has also jumped - rising above $100 a barrel for the first time since 2014.

The Bank's decision to raise interest rates is designed to increase the cost of borrowing money and reduce demand, which should help slow the increase in prices.

But it is expected that households will face further financial pressures with mortgage rates and borrowing costs set to rise.

Mr Bailey said that there was a risk that the Bank's actions "could end up being contractionary" - meaning that they could cause the economy to shrink.

He added that the Bank would "have to consider" whether to take further action at its next meeting in May.

The UK economy is facing a host of "major risks", the Bank of England's governor has said.

Andrew Bailey said the risks included high global inflation, rising interest rates and continuing supply chain problems.

He said the situation in Ukraine and China's Covid response were also among factors which posed a threat to the UK.

Mr Bailey's comments came as the Bank of England announced it was holding interest rates at their current record low of 0.1%.

New York's top financial prosecutor has opened an investigation into Citigroup's financial dealings with US equity traders, according to reports.

New York Attorney General Letitia James is said to be examining whether the bank misused its own money to gain an edge in the competitive world of equity trading.

The probe focuses on the activities of two Citigroup units, Citigroup Global Markets Inc and Citigroup Alternative Investments LLC, according to reports.

A spokesperson for Attorney General James's office declined to comment on the investigation.

"We are aware of the inquiries and are cooperating with regulators," a Citigroup spokesperson told the BBC.

The investigation is the latest trouble for the banking giant, which has faced several scandals in recent years.

In 2020, the bank reached a $400m settlement with the US Justice Department over allegations that it had defrauded investors who bought mortgage-backed securities before the 2008 financial crisis.

And in 2019, Citigroup was one of several banks to be fined $5.6bn for rigging interest rates.

The bank has also been criticised for its role in the opioid crisis, with many states suing major pharmaceutical companies.

Citigroup has said it is "committed to responsible banking and corporate practices" and that it is "focused on serving as a force for good".

Citigroup has been accused of providing lucrative deals to a number of high-profile customers despite being aware of allegations of corruption against them, according to a report by the BBC.

The bank is alleged to have offered deals worth hundreds of millions of pounds to customers it knew were being investigated for corruption by UK authorities, including a property development company controlled by the family of the former deputy chairman of the Conservative party, Lord Ashcroft.

In response to the allegations, Citigroup said it strongly rejects any suggestion that it has breached any laws or regulations. It added that it is committed to operating its business in a legal and ethical manner. 

The BBC's findings come after a three-year investigation into the bank's dealings with customers accused of corruption. As part of its investigation, the BBC spoke to former Citigroup employees who said they were pressured to offer deals to customers with a history of corruption. 

One former employee, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said: "It was very clear that we were offering deals to people who were being investigated for corruption. But we were told to ignore it and just do our jobs."

The BBC's "International Film Award" for 2022 has been won by Russia's submission, "Dear Comrades!" a somber retelling of real events, which the BBC calls a "searing depiction of abuse of power."

A decision by France's highest administrative court to reject all-black lists of candidates for parliamentary elections has sparked anger.

The Council of State ruled that the lists submitted by a leftist party and an anti-racism group were illegal because they did not represent "diversity".

The decision was described as a "slap in the face" to efforts to fight discrimination.

The lists, for elections to France's parliament in June, were submitted by the anti-racism group SOS-Racisme and the Revolutionary Communist League (LCR), which describes itself as "anti-capitalist".

They both put forward lists of candidates for the parliamentary seats in France's overseas territories, with the LCR list for French Guiana including only women from the local Amerindian community, and the SOS-Racisme list for the island of La Reunion being all-black.

But the Council of State, which regularly advises the government on legal matters, said the lists were illegal because they were not representative of the "diversity of the population concerned".

The ruling was immediately criticised by anti-racism groups.

Gerard Lauze, president of SOS-Racisme, said the decision was a "slap in the face to anti-racists and to all those who fight against discrimination".

"We are struggling to believe that in 2021, in France, there are still people who are so sensitive to the colour of people's skin," he told the AFP news agency.

The issue of discrimination in France has been in the spotlight in recent months, after a young black man, Adama Traore, was killed by police in Paris in July.

His death - which followed that of another black man, Michel Zecler, in November last year - has sparked a wave of protests under the slogan "Black Lives Matter".

A government commission is currently looking into racism in France, ahead of a planned visit by UN anti-racism envoy Felice Gaetano to France in March.

Mr Lauze said the Council of State's decision risked undermining the work of the commission, as it would discourage people from taking part in discussions.

The rejection of the all-black MP lists has caused a huge backlash from the public and politicians. The Speaker of the House of Commons, John Bercow, has said that the rejection is a "blatant example" of racism. Labour has called the decision "appalling" and demanded that Communities Secretary, Robert Jenrick, should reverse the decision. 

The Conservative Party has been accused of racism after it was revealed that all-black candidate lists for parliamentary seats in England were rejected by local associations.  The Conservative Party has said that the lists were rejected because they did not have enough female candidates on them. 
Sir Ed Davey, the leader of the Liberal Democrats, has called for an inquiry into the allegations. 
The controversy has led to calls for the Conservative Party to change its leadership. 
The Scottish National Party has also been accused of racism after it was revealed that Asian candidates were blocked from becoming MPs for the party.

The dollar's decline ahead of this week's G7 meeting in London prompted European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde to blame the US for not doing enough to bolster the world's primary reserve currency, whose global strength is seen as vital for economic stability.

"It is more reflective of the US economic situation and the US economic policy choices than it is on the international community and on the choices that have been made abroad," she said.

Ms. Lagarde, who will step down as ECB president at the end of her eight-year term in October, made the remarks in a question-and-answer session in the Dutch parliament.

Her comments come as central bankers and finance ministers from the G7 group of wealthy nations meet in London on Thursday and Friday.

The US dollar is widely regarded as a haven currency, and its decline has been accelerated by Russia's invasion of Ukraine. This has led to a marked increase in volatility across financial markets.

A weakening dollar can help US exporters and reduce imported inflation, but it can also lead to financial instability in some emerging markets that have borrowed in dollars.

It can also roil global markets as investors reassess what is supposed to be the safest asset of all. This creates problems for markets such as government bonds.

Interest rate differentials between the US and other major economies have been a key driver of the dollar's decline.

The US central bank, the Federal Reserve, is expected to raise interest rates by 50 basis points next month, but the ECB is not expected to raise rates at all this year.

In the Netherlands, Ms. Lagarde also spoke about the importance of the independence of central banks.

She said that political interference in central banking had led in the past "to disastrous consequences".

She cited the example of the Austrian central bank before the First World War and more recent examples of "political interference leading to outcomes that many would regret".

The dollar has fallen to its lowest level in 20 years against the euro, with other currencies also gaining ground.

The European Commission has warned that the weakening dollar could reignite the currency wars of the last financial crisis.

The dollar's decline accelerated after the US Federal Reserve last month signalled it was close to the end of its interest rate increases.

Many analysts think the Fed's move - which followed dovish signals from other major central banks - has triggered the dollar's fall.

But some see the start of a longer-term decline for the dollar, which would have serious implications for the US and the global economy.

The euro has risen above the key $1.20 level, hitting a high last seen in late 2002.

With the single currency now worth more than a dollar, holidaymakers travelling to the US are getting a bonus - their euros can buy more ice cream, burgers and beer than before.

But the European Commission, the EU's executive body, has warned that the dollar's decline is a cause for concern.

In its annual report on the international role of the euro, it said the euro's appreciation had been "particularly rapid" and warned that the "ongoing weakness of the US dollar" could have serious consequences for the global economy.

"The risk of competitive devaluations cannot be excluded," the report said.

Competitive devaluations are when countries deliberately reduce the value of their currencies in the hope of giving their exporters a price advantage. This can lead to a "race to the bottom" as countries try to undercut each other by devaluing their currencies further.

This dynamic can destabilise the global economy.

The report did not explicitly say the US was responsible for the dollar's weakness, but the clear implication was that the Fed's decision to pause its rate hike cycle had triggered the dollar's decline.

Other major central banks, including the European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan, have also shifted to more dovish stances, but the Fed's move was the most dramatic.

In effect, the report accused the US of deliberately weakening its currency to gain an economic advantage.

Over the years the US has frequently been accused of manipulating its currency, but it has always denied doing so.

The dollar remains the world's dominant currency, used in most international transactions. As such, any shift in its value has wide-ranging implications for the global economy.

US oil firm Kosmos Energy has admitted bribing ministers in the West African nation of Benin.

The Dallas-based company said it had paid $100,000 to Beninese customs and tax officials to obtain improper tax reductions.

In a filing to a US government agency, Kosmos said the payments had been made between 2007 and 2011.

Kosmos acquired an offshore oil block in Benin in 2008. It did not reveal its findings in the filing, made to the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC).

The company said it had launched an internal investigation into the payments after Benin issued an arrest warrant for its country manager in May.

It said the manager, who was not named, had admitted making the payments.

Kosmos said it was cooperating with Beninese authorities, and that it had alerted the US Department of Justice and the SEC.

It added that it was withdrawing as a defendant from a civil suit launched by Beninois citizens in the US in 2015.

The suit, filed in Texas, alleged that Kosmos and oil firm Addax Petroleum Corp had paid more than $110m in bribes to Beninese officials.

In a parallel development, the US Department of Justice said on Monday that Texas-based oil consultant Roger Jean-Pierre Malpasse had been sentenced to 30 months in prison for his role in the bribery scheme.

Malpasse, who has also been ordered to pay $1.8m in fines and restitution, had pleaded guilty in March to conspiring to violate the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, which bans the bribery of foreign officials.

According to the DoJ, between 2001 and 2012 Malpasse "paid approximately $394,931 in bribes to two ministers of petroleum and one deputy minister of finance" in Benin on behalf of Energy Infrastructure Services Inc.

It's not often that scientists get the chance to poke about inside the workings of the world's most sophisticated cyber-crime groups.

The team also discovered that the cyber-criminals had, on average, four different antivirus products on their victims' PCs - and that they had typically been there for over a year.

For £1.59 a month, UK users can now get ProtectSmart, a PC security package from a company called SmartProtect. The software, which is advertised on the radio and the internet, allegedly provides "trusted PC security" and "protection from viruses and malware". Sounds good, so what's the catch?

The small print reveals that this is a subscription service that will cost you nearly £20 a year. You have to provide a valid credit or debit card number in order to start the 14-day trial - and if you don't cancel within that time, you are automatically subscribed.

The eurozone economy slowed in January, a business survey has indicated, as firms struggled with inflation and the cost of energy.

The flash purchasing managers' index (PMI) for the euro area fell to 47.5 in January from 49.3 in December, according to data firm IHS Markit.

An index reading below 50 indicates contraction in the sector. The reading was lower than expected and mainly due to a decline in Germany, the EU's largest economy.

"Uncertainty related to the pandemic, higher prices, and a lack of pressure on capacity helped to keep a lid on optimism about the year ahead," said Andrew Kenningham, chief economist at IHS Markit.

This comes after the eurozone's economy contracted in the final three months of 2022, ending a period of eight consecutive quarters of growth.

However, economists said the fall - the first since the spring of 2020 - could be partly explained by a slowdown in Germany, mainly due to strikes in the manufacturing sector.

The European Central Bank has kept its main interest rate on hold at 2.5% but warned the economy was weakening more than expected.

In a statement, the bank said it was maintaining its rate "against the background of weaker economic activity".

The ECB had been expected to ease policy but economists predicted a cut might not come until July.

The eurozone's manufacturing and services sectors slowed in March, according to surveys released on Friday.

The ECB said interest rates were likely to remain at their current or lower levels until it saw inflation reaching its 2% target in a sustainable manner.

This is a change from its previous guidance, which said rates would remain low "for an extended period of time".

The ECB also said it would start buying euro-denominated securities issued by non-bank corporations on the secondary market. The so-called corporate sector purchase programme (CSPP) is due to start in June.

The bank also said it would provide further details of the CSPP at its next meeting on 4 June.

Like many others, I remember exactly where I was and what I was doing when I first heard about HIV and AIDS. I was in high school, and for myself and my peers, it was a crisis occurring among adults that felt very distant.

In the decades since, I've worked with a series of HIV/AIDS organisations, most recently the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria. From that vantage point, I have seen the crisis unfold and watched the remarkable progress that has been made to overcome it.

I remember speaking to a colleague working in Swaziland, one of the most HIV-affected countries in the world, about the fear that HIV causes, and how that thwarts efforts to fight it.

And yet, despite the terrible toll HIV has taken, the tide has turned. The number of new HIV infections has dropped by one-third since 2000; the number of AIDS-related deaths has fallen by one-half.

These achievements did not happen spontaneously. They are the result of long-term, well-funded, committed responses, both in terms of policy and funding.

But today, against the backdrop of the Covid-19 pandemic, that progress is at risk.

According to UNAIDS, the global response to HIV/AIDS has already been disrupted by Covid-19, with supply chain disruptions, access to antiretroviral therapy (ART) and HIV services, as well as interruptions in prevention programmes, including suspension of sexual education programmes and the cancellation of mass testing campaigns.

The fund has calculated that Covid-19 will reverse the progress against HIV/AIDS by at least seven years. Seven years of progress that has been painstakingly achieved through the concerted efforts of governments, private sector and civil society. That is unconscionable.

As the Covid-19 pandemic waxes and wanes, we must not allow HIV to stage a comeback. The fight against HIV/AIDS must not fall off the agenda. Instead, we must redouble our efforts to keep the momentum going - governments, the private sector, civil society and donors.

The Global Fund has just hosted its sixth replenishment conference where we asked donors to step up to ensure the fight against HIV/AIDS remains a priority. We are grateful to the United Kingdom for its increased pledge.

As the world refocuses on Covid-19, we must not forget the ongoing fight against HIV/AIDS.
