Search engine designers are constantly trying to devise ways of making their websites more appealing to users.

They want to ensure that people choose their search engine over their competitors'.

So it is not surprising that Bing, Google and Yahoo! are currently experimenting with placing links to their search services around the web - in the same way that they place advertisements.

Bing, Microsoft's search engine, has been the most aggressive in this respect, launching a preview of its Bing Smart Search application in November.

Bing Smart Search offers an alternative way of searching the web from a desktop computer by allowing users to highlight and right-click on any word or phrase on a webpage and quickly get search results from Bing, Wikipedia and other sources via a pop-up bubble.

"It is a unique way to get people into the Bing experience," says Stefan Weitz, senior director of Bing at Microsoft.

"It is a model that we believe will proliferate as people will want this kind of search experience wherever they are - on a desktop, a laptop, a tablet or a smartphone."

Google and Yahoo! are experimenting with similar applications.

Google Quick Search is an extension for the Chrome browser that allows users to highlight and right-click on any word or phrase on a webpage and quickly get search results from Google without leaving the page.

Yahoo! has launched Search Direct, an application that enables users to highlight and right-click on any word or phrase on a webpage and get search results from Yahoo! in a pop-up bubble.

"It is all about making search as accessible as possible," says Chris Tolles, a director of search at Yahoo!.

"Search Direct is all about making it easier for people to get the information they want as quickly as possible in the most convenient way."

Search engine experts believe that these new applications could represent the future of search.

"It used to be that search was all about the 10 blue links on a search results page," says Greg Sterling, an analyst with Sterling Market Intelligence.

"But that is no longer enough. To remain competitive, search engines need to expose their search tools and services across the web and make them as accessible as possible to users."

The battle for the future of search is heating up. As Google, the undisputed leader in the space, continues to fine-tune its algorithms and expand its reach, new players are emerging, looking to challenge the status quo. One of the most promising contenders is a company called Cuil (pronounced "cool"), which launched a beta version of its search engine earlier this year. Unlike Google, which relies on keywords and other traditional methods to rank search results, Cuil uses a technique called "relevance ranking," which takes into account the entire content of a website, as well as the context in which the search terms are used. This approach allows Cuil to produce more accurate and relevant results, which could give it an edge over Google in the future. 

Another company looking to make waves in the search space is Bing, Microsoft's new search engine. Bing offers several features that set it apart from Google, including a unique user interface and a focus on visual search. While it remains to be seen whether these features will be enough to convince users to switch from Google, Bing has already made some notable gains in the market. 

But it's not just these new players that are vying for a piece of the search pie. Google is also continuing to innovate, launching new services and features that aim to make search more intuitive and user-friendly. Its most recent offering, called "Google Squared," takes a new approach to search results, presenting them in a more organized and visually appealing way. 

As the competition heats up, it's clear that the future of search will be shaped by more than just Google. With new players and new technologies entering the market, users can expect to see more innovative search engines in the years to come.

Microsoft is urging computer users to patch a security vulnerability that could allow attackers to silently install malicious software onto their devices.

The tech giant said the flaw, discovered by researchers at CyberArk, was similar to one exploited by the US National Security Agency (NSA).

It allows hackers to take complete control of a machine, but it is difficult for security experts to analyse.

Microsoft said there had been no evidence that the vulnerability had been used by cyber-criminals.

But it urged customers to immediately install a patch it had developed for the flaw, which affects all versions of its Windows 10 operating system.

"We know that nation-state actors, cybercriminals, and other malicious actors will always look for new ways to gain unauthorized access to networks and systems," said Phillip Misner, Microsoft's security group manager.

"Our recommendation is to immediately install the updates provided here," he added in a blog post.

The NSA tool, called EternalBlue, took advantage of a flaw in Microsoft software to collect data on targets.

It was part of a cache of hacking tools leaked by a group called the Shadow Brokers in April 2017.

Microsoft said it had released patches for the vulnerability in March 2017, but many computers remained unpatched because the flaw was "cherry-picked" by the NSA to exploit.

The agency then lost control of the tool, which was used in the massive WannaCry ransomware attack that hit the NHS and hundreds of thousands of other computers around the world.

CyberArk, a security company, said the newly-discovered vulnerability was similar to, but not the same as, EternalBlue.

It is another example of a broader trend in which malicious actors take advantage of "dual use" vulnerabilities - flaws in software that can be used for both good and bad purposes.

"An attacker can use this vulnerability to gain access to an entire corporate network if they successfully exploit it on a single computer that has access to that network," said CyberArk researcher Ben Seri.

"It's just one example of many 'dual use' vulnerabilities, which can be used by both attackers and defenders, and illustrates why responsible disclosure and handling of vulnerabilities is so critical," he added.

Microsoft has released a security advisory detailing the technical aspects of the SysJoker trojan. The advisory states that the trojan is spread through a phishing email that contains a malicious attachment. When the attachment is opened, it installs the trojan on the victim's computer.

SysJoker is a highly sophisticated piece of malware that uses a variety of techniques to avoid detection. It is able to hide its presence on the victim's computer by using a rootkit, which is a type of software that allows the attacker to hide their files and activities on the system. The trojan is also able to use a process hollowing technique, which allows it to inject its code into legitimate system processes, making it harder to detect.

Microsoft has released a number of security updates to address the SysJoker trojan. These updates are available for download through the Microsoft website. It is important for Windows users to keep their operating system up to date in order to protect themselves from this and other security threats.

SysJoker is a serious security threat that has the potential to cause significant damage to Windows users. Ireland produced a magnificent second-half comeback to edge out South Africa 17-12 in a thrilling Autumn Nations Series clash in Dublin.

But Ireland, who welcomed back British and Irish Lions captain Johnny Sexton after a four-month lay-off because of a leg injury, improved after the break.

Another penalty from Sexton with two minutes left ensured the victory was safe, with South Africa having a late opportunity to level the match but they were off-target with their kick.

It was a memorable comeback from Andy Farrell's side, who were lacklustre in the first half and trailed for much of the match.

The result means Ireland, who also beat New Zealand 29-20 last week, have won their last 11 Tests at the Aviva Stadium.

South Africa scored three tries to Ireland's two but wasted too many chances in an error-strewn match.

South Africa went back in front when Sexton's cross-field kick was caught and touched down by Arendse.

Ireland hit back again when replacement centre Shane Daly scored in the right corner after a brilliant run by fellow replacement Jamie Osborne.

But South Africa secured the win with a penalty from Handre Pollard with two minutes left.

Failing to plan for staff being infected with HIV is costing British businesses millions of pounds, according to a leading charity.

Terrence Higgins Trust said employers were not providing adequate training on HIV and were paying out for unnecessary testing.

It said this was leading to inefficient use of NHS resources and infringement of HIV patients' rights.

The trust launched its HIV and Employment Guide for employers on World AIDS Day, 1 December.

The charity is concerned that because of a lack of knowledge, some employers demand that all applicants who are HIV-positive take a HIV test - something that is voluntary.

Those who are HIV-positive and who do disclose their status may face discrimination in the workplace, the charity said.

This includes being passed over for promotion or being unable to do their job properly because of a lack of understanding among colleagues and managers.

The trust is also concerned that some employers are not providing adequate training on how to avoid unnecessary risk of HIV transmission in the workplace.

This means employees are not always able to do their jobs safely, it said.

The guide advises employers on how to avoid unnecessary costs caused by HIV, including the cost of replacing staff who have contracted the virus and who need to take long-term sick leave.

It says inadequate planning for staff who are HIV-positive is wasting NHS resources because of unnecessary testing and follow-up treatment.

The guide also warns that employers who fail to carry out a proper risk assessment could face legal action.

Businesses are not doing enough to respond to the growing threat of HIV, with many failing to provide adequate health coverage for employees living with the virus, according to a report by the Business & Human Rights Resource Centre. The report, which surveyed more than 50 U.S. and E.U. firms, found that while most companies offer health insurance that covers HIV treatment, many do not provide comprehensive coverage for prevention and care. Additionally, the report found that few companies offer financial support or accommodation for employees living with HIV, such as flexible work schedules or the option to work from home. 

The report comes as HIV rates are on the rise in several countries, including the United States, due in part to a lack of access to prevention and treatment tools. "As HIV progresses, people are less able to work and need more health care, which can have significant costs for both the individual and employer," said Scott Pohlson, CEO of the Business & Human Rights Resource Centre. "But when employers take steps to address these needs, both the employer and employee benefit." 

While the report found that many companies are not doing enough to support employees living with HIV, it also identified some best practices, including providing comprehensive health coverage, offering financial support, and ensuring a safe and inclusive work environment. The report concludes that employers have a crucial role to play in addressing the HIV epidemic and calls for them to take action to improve support for employees living with the virus.

Ringtone sellers face tougher rules on what they can sell, following a spate of complaints from customers.

The Committee of Advertising Practice (CAP) has written to all major providers, telling them to stop selling ringtones as mobile content, and instead to treat them as premium rate telephone services.

The move follows a surge in complaints to the Advertising Standards Authority (ASA).

Customers have been unhappy with the cost and difficulty of getting refunds after they bought a ringtone by text message and did not receive it.

In one case a customer was charged £4,500 for ringtones they did not want after they mistakenly typed a number with many digits into their phone.

In most cases, customers who buy a ringtone are charged £3 plus a further £1.50 for a text message to send the ringtone to their phone.

The CAP said that because there had been so many complaints, it was taking immediate action on behalf of the ASA to ensure the ads were not misleading.

In a letter to ringtone providers, CAP said that all ads should make clear that customers will be charged for a telephony service and should not imply that the service is free or charged at a fixed rate.

The letter said: "Clearly, given the volume of complaints referred to the ASA and the seriousness of the issues raised, it would not be appropriate for the ASA to investigate individual cases prior to the implementation of the proposed changes.

"We understand that you will want to consider the details of the proposed changes and, if accepted, it will be for each of you to implement these as swiftly as possible."

CAP's proposals include a requirement that companies provide a free number for customers to call if they want a refund for a ringtone they did not want or receive.

In addition, customers should not have to go through more than one level of customer service to get a refund.

The letter said: "While we recognise that the cost of a ringtone is usually relatively low, the number of complaints indicates that there is clear public concern about the way these ads are currently being handled."

The Federal Trade Commission is cracking down on ringtone sellers that charge customers without their explicit consent. The FTC has issued a warning to companies that use text messages to gather phone numbers for ringtone downloads, telling them to get express consent from customers before charging them. The announcement comes after several cases were opened against companies accused of charging customers without consent. In one case, a company must pay nearly $50 million to customers who were charged for ringtones they did not want. 

The FTC's warning has shaken up the ringtone industry. Some companies are already complying with the new rules and are changing their policies to obtain express consent. Others are waiting to see how the situation plays out. The FCC is hoping that the warning will be enough to stop the unwanted charges. 

The case against the ringtone companies is just one of many the FTC is currently involved in. The FTC is cracking down on all types of companies that charge customers without their consent. As part of their effort, the FTC has issued warnings to several large companies, including a major social media platform.

Households across the UK are to be bombarded with up to 50% more junk mail from tomorrow, Saturday 1 April, thanks to changes in the law governing the posting of letters. From that date, postage costs for bulk mail will be reduced by up to 47%, resulting in an estimated extra 350 million items of junk mail every year. The new rules are part of a European Union (EU) wide reform of the postal sector which aims to create a more level playing field for all postal operators across Europe. But already some UK local councils are reporting that they are overwhelmed by the amount of junk mail they are receiving.

One council, in the London Borough of Richmond, says it is receiving up to 500 items of junk mail every day - equivalent to one delivery every six minutes. Similar stories are coming from councils in Bristol, Edinburgh, and other towns and cities across the UK.

The Direct Marketing Association (DMA), which represents the UK's direct marketing industry, says it is aware of the concerns raised by local councils and is seeking discussions with them to find a way forward.

The survey, for the local authority-backed website moneymagpie.com, found that two-thirds of respondents said they usually throw junk mail straight in the bin, without even opening it.

According to the new rules, postage costs for bulk mail will be reduced because the price of a second class stamp is being cut from 36p to 25p, and the price of a first class stamp falls from 46p to 31p. Prices have not changed since 2001. Last year, 6.8 billion items of bulk mail were posted in the UK. This figure includes junk mail. Of these, 1.2 billion were door drops. Almost all (99%) of local authorities report handling increased amounts of junk mail in recent years, according to the Local Government Association. Council tax bills and other important documents could get lost in the flood of junk mail.

The new pricing structure was approved by the EU last December, and all 27 member states were obliged to implement the changes from 1 April. Ireland and Greece have already introduced the new pricing structures, with Germany planning to do so later this year. In the UK, the new prices were announced by Royal Mail

Brussels has warned that mobile phone operators may be abusing their dominant position by charging for incoming calls.

The European Commission said it would investigate the practice, already criticised by consumer groups.

Mobile phone firms charge a fee for incoming calls while users are roaming outside their home country.

The commission said it would look at ways to "ensure a smooth and affordable use of mobile phones while travelling abroad".

The investigation could lead to changes in the fees European consumers pay when travelling within the EU.

Last year, the commission carried out a survey to find out whether there was cause to investigate the issue.

It found that 65% of respondents were in favour of abolishing the charge for incoming calls while they were abroad.

Currently, mobile phone operators can charge up to 19 euro cents per minute for incoming calls in the EU.

The commission's survey also revealed wide variations in the prices charged by different mobile phone operators. Incoming calls can cost between 6 and 19 euro cents per minute.

There are also big differences in the price of outgoing calls from one country to another. For instance, calls from Greece to Germany cost 19 euro cents per minute, while the equivalent call from Germany to Greece costs just 6 euro cents.

"We will look at the abusive practices which unfortunately still exist in the EU mobile phone market," said Viviane Reding, the EU's telecoms chief.

"Roaming charges should not be higher than at home, nor should they remain high when volumes increase."

The investigation could take a year.

The mobile phone industry has already been hit by a series of EU rulings on the cost of roaming.

Last month, the European Parliament voted for the complete abolition of roaming charges by 2015.

 Operators have also been forced to slash the cost of making calls while abroad.

Last year, the commission ruled that operators would have to cut the cost of outgoing roaming calls by more than half, to just 3 euro cents per minute, by July this year.

This summer, EU officials will also begin examining the cost of texting while abroad.

A recent survey by the British consumer group, Which?, found that UK mobile phone users were still often unaware that they were paying additional fees for incoming calls while abroad.

Last year, the Office of Fair Trading (OFT) in the UK expressed "serious concerns" about the practice.

The European Commission has told EU countries they must introduce a uniform mobile phone charging port to reduce environmental waste, despite resistance from the semiconductor industry.

Environmental activists have welcomed the move, arguing that it would reduce the mountain of electronic waste generated every year by Europeans.

The EU Commission said that mobile phone chargers were responsible for 11,000 to 13,000 tonnes of waste per year in the EU.

Indian company Reliance Industries has signed a $2.4bn deal to buy a majority stake in telecoms firm Reliance Communication.

The deal comes as the telecoms firm tries to reduce its debt.

It sold a 51% stake in its telecoms tower unit to a group of investors including Canada's Brookfield for $1.7bn.

The company has been hit by a price war in India's mobile market, which pushed it into debt.

"The transactions will help the company simplify its balance sheet and focus on the growth of its wireless, enterprise and digital services business," Reliance Communications said in a statement.

What's behind the deal?

Reliance Industries - owned by India's richest man, Mukesh Ambani - is buying the stake in Reliance Communication, which is owned by his younger brother, Anil.

Anil Ambani had owed the older Ambani brother $6.4bn as of the end of March, according to the most recent data available.

The two brothers had a falling out over the management of their assets in 2008, and their telecoms businesses have been locked in a price war ever since.

The deal does not include Reliance Communication's wireless spectrum and tower infrastructure, which will be transferred to a newly formed unit, Reliance Realty.

What are the implications?

It is expected to improve the financial health of Reliance Communication, which had about $7.4bn in debt at the end of March.

"It is a positive development for the company as it has resolved one of the biggest challenges it was facing," Hemant Minocha, an analyst at Sharekhan, said.

"From the Reliance Industries side, it makes sense to enter the telecom business again as the sector is up for consolidation," he added.

Reliance Industries quit the telecoms business in 2005, when it sold its telecoms arm to Anil Ambani.

Sales at Nike have risen by 11% compared with the same time last year, to $12.25bn, as the company continued to recover from the impact of the Covid pandemic.

The sportswear giant had suffered three months of falling sales in 2020 as lockdowns forced shops to close and sports events to be cancelled.

Overall, the company said it was now on track to achieve its goal of reaching $50bn in sales by the end of the fiscal year 2025.

"Our momentum continues despite supply chain challenges, and we are still on track to achieve our long-term growth goals," he added.

Nike, which is based in Oregon, said it was dealing with temporary shortages of key products, such as sneakers, due to supply chain problems, but that these were easing.

In recent months, the sportswear firm has been hit by a series of controversies over its production processes in Asia.

It has been accused of widespread labour abuses at factories in China and Vietnam which produce its shoes and clothing.

This week, Nike announced that it would launch a review of its global supply chains, in order to root out labour abuses.

The company said it would carry out audits of its suppliers and sub-contractors in China, Vietnam, Indonesia and Cambodia.

The move follows a series of warnings from investors about the risks of labour abuses in the company's supply chain.

Few names are as synonymous with comic books as Stan Lee. Yet, for all of his success, Lee remained grounded, and was known for his trademark wit, and an ability to connect with fans that transcended the page.

Born as Stanley Martin Lieber on December 28, 1922, in New York City, Lee grew up in a vibrant neighborhood filled with immigrants from around the world. As a child, he was fascinated by movies and books, and dreamed of one day becoming a writer.

Lee was also a pioneer in the realm of multimedia franchising. He saw the potential for his characters to thrive in other formats, and successfully expanded the Marvel Universe into television, film, and even video games.

As Lee's fame grew, so did his reputation as a pop culture icon. He made appearances in numerous Marvel films, and was beloved by fans for his trademark wit and charm.

"Big Brother" in the Age of Technology

With the rise of technology, particularly the internet and social media, the concept of "Big Brother" has become even more relevant. Today, vast amounts of data are collected and stored by companies and governments, often without our knowledge or consent. From our search histories and social media activity to our purchases and health information, our personal data is being used in ways we may not understand or agree with.

In conclusion, the phrase "Big Brother" has become a powerful symbol of the potential dangers of technology and the loss of privacy. The Conference Board's monthly consumer confidence survey points to improved confidence in the US during December, albeit at a slightly slower pace.

The index stands at 115.8, down from 117.5 in November, but above market expectations of 111.

"Consumers are entering 2023 with stout savings, the job market is robust, and inflation is moderating," said Conference Board chief economist Lynn Franco.

"Given these foundational factors, we anticipate that consumers will continue to spend, though perhaps at a slower pace than in 2022," she added.

The survey measuring current economic conditions stood at 144.4, down from 153.8 in November. The expectations index stood at 99.7, up from 96.4.

The numbers point to improved confidence in the US economy, with consumers more optimistic about the future, although inflation remains a concern.

However, the survey also showed that while confidence improved, consumer spending trends remained cautious.

The percentage of consumers planning to make a major purchase in the next six months fell to 12.1 percent, while those intending to purchase a car stood at 9.6 percent, down from 10.6 percent in November.

The survey also showed that consumer expectations for inflation over the next 12 months stood at 6.7 percent, down from 7.3 percent in November, but still high.

The Conference Board's survey is conducted monthly and measures consumer attitudes on the current economy and future expectations.

The latest report shows that while confidence improved, consumers remain cautious about their spending habits as they continue to feel the impact of high inflation.

Consumers were more optimistic about the labor market, with the percentage of respondents saying jobs are "plentiful" increasing from 18.3% to 20.3%. Meanwhile, those saying jobs are "hard to get" declined, from 13.6% to 12.5%.

Conference Board economist Lynn Franco said, "Consumers' assessment of current conditions improved, and their expectations for the next six months rose to their highest level since April 2021."

The increase in consumer confidence comes as the Federal Reserve continues to raise interest rates in an effort to tame inflation. However, the central bank has signaled that it may slow down the pace of rate hikes, which has been welcomed by investors and consumers alike.

German growth goes into reverse with economy contracting by 0.1% in second quarter

Germany's economy has shrunk by 0.1% in the second quarter of the year, according to official data.

It is the first time since 2015 that Germany has seen a quarterly decline in GDP and comes after six consecutive quarters of growth.

The Federal Statistics Office said a fall in exports and household spending were behind the drop.

There is concern that the German economy may be losing steam after a long period of expansion.

The data comes as concern about the German car industry mounts.

Last week, BMW cut its outlook for the rest of the year, saying that a slowdown in the car industry had affected its profits, which fell short of expectations.

Volkswagen, the country's largest car maker, last month reported its first quarterly loss in 15 years, as it struggled to recover from the diesel emissions scandal.

The German car industry is a major employer and contributes about 5% of Germany's GDP.

However, the statistics office said that the construction industry had helped to limit the decline in the second quarter.

Construction output increased by 1.6% compared with the first three months of the year, it said.

"The German economy halted its growth path in the second quarter of 2018," said Economy and Energy Minister Peter Altmaier.

"We have seen similar developments in some other major economies around the world."

He added that the government would "continue to pursue its stable course" and that it was "too early to assess the consequences of Brexit or the trade disputes".

In a separate release, the statistics office said that unemployment in Germany remained at 6.1% in July, the same as in June.

The number of people out of work fell by 4,000 to 2.37 million.

The German economy, the largest in the eurozone, has shrunk by 0.2% in the second quarter of 2023, according to preliminary data from the country's federal statistics office. This contraction follows a 0.1% decline in the first quarter and marks the beginning of a technical recession. A recession is commonly defined as two consecutive quarters of negative growth.

The German economy has been hit by a number of factors, including the war in Ukraine, rising energy prices, and supply chain issues. The country's manufacturing and construction sectors have been particularly hard hit, with decreases in output of 0.4% and 1.2% respectively.

The German government has announced a number of measures to support the economy, including a $60 billion package of measures aimed at helping households and businesses with the cost of living.

Despite the recent downturn, German officials have expressed confidence that the economy will recover in the second half of the year. However, many economists have warned that the country's economy could face further headwinds in the coming months, particularly as the central bank continues to raise interest rates in an effort to control inflation.

House prices in Britain have rebounded in the past month following a lull around the festive period, according to figures from mortgage lender Halifax.

The lender said that in January prices had risen by 0.3% month-on-month, the biggest monthly rise since March last year.

"Improved affordability, mainly due to falling real earnings, has helped to support demand," said Halifax's housing economist, Martin Ellis.

"Households' expectations of future house price growth have softened, which combined with a more constrained supply of new instructions, has helped to contain price growth," he added.

The figures chime with those of rival lender Nationwide, which reported a 0.4% monthly rise in January.

Both lenders report that house prices are now rising more slowly than wages, which grew at an annual rate of 2.9% in the three months to November, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

However, Halifax said that a shortage of properties on the market was helping to keep prices elevated.

The number of homes for sale per estate agent branch stood at 25 in January, unchanged from December but down from 32 a year earlier, Halifax said.

At the same time, would-be buyers are increasingly pessimistic about their chances of finding a home, with the number of people who thought it was a good time to buy falling from 42% to 35% in January, according to figures from the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors (Rics).

Many of those who did make the move appeared to be upgrading to more expensive properties, with 40% of moves being to a bigger home, according to separate research for estate agent Savills by NMG.

" upgraders are increasingly driving activity, with many having held back from moving over the past few years," said Lucian Cook, head of residential research at Savills.

Prices in the three months to the end of September were 2.5% higher than in the three months to the end of June, when prices fell by 0.1%.

It means that the average price of a UK home is now £294,606, the lender said.

"Improving labour market conditions, and the expectation that interest rates will remain lower for longer, have helped improve buyer confidence," said Halifax managing director Russell Galley.

Less than 3% of homeowners changed their mortgage in the three months to the end of September, according to banking group Lloyds. This is down from almost 6% in the same period of 2019.

Lockdowns and pandemic restrictions have also caused a shortage of properties for sale, which has pushed up prices.

However, a lack of stock is now limiting the number of potential buyers, Halifax said.

The lender said that first-time buyers now make up about half of all house purchases, compared with a ratio of about one in four before the financial crisis.

Mr Galley said that the average deposit put down by first-time buyers had increased to about 40%, as house prices had risen faster than wages in the past decade.

"This has implications for future generations, as home ownership delays could impact social mobility and mean that younger people's ability to build wealth through housing is affected," he added.

US gamers have voted Doom 3 as the ultimate game of 2005.

Id Software's sequel to the 1993 classic won the Readers' Choice award at the recent Game Developers Choice Awards.

The game - in which players battle demons from hell - was also named best action game at the recent Interactive Achievement Awards.

Doom 3 has sold more than 3.5 million copies since its release last August.

It was pipped for the overall Game of the Year award at the Interactive Achievement Awards by Shadow of the Colossus, a game in which players battle giant mythical creatures.

Colossus, from Sony's Japan Studio, also won the award for best visual design.

Guitar Hero, which challenges players to simulate playing rock guitar on a plastic peripheral, was named the best new franchise, and Best Selling Game went to Nintendo's Nintendogs, a game in which players train virtual dogs.

The Academy of Interactive Arts and Sciences gave out its 11th annual Interactive Achievement Awards at the Red Rock Casino, Resort and Spa in Las Vegas on Thursday.

The winners were chosen by members of the AIAS, with votes cast for nominees in 25 categories covering console, computer and handheld games.

When Doom 3 was released in 2004, it accelerated the first-person shooter's rise to prominence. To celebrate the game's 20th anniversary, it's finally getting the sequel it deserves.

Id Software's seminal shooter took the horror genre to a new level - and sped up the then-nascent FPS genre's ascent to the top of the gaming pile. It's since been ported to just about every platform under the sun and is now being celebrated with a special 20th-anniversary edition, along with a fourth sequel in the series.

Doom 3: Resurrection of Evil is a revamped version of the third game in the franchise, adding a new chapter and updating the 2004 original game with a fresh coat of paint. And following in the footsteps of Doom (2016), it adds multiplayer too.

The first is a revamped version of Doom 3's BFG Edition, which adds the "Lost Mission" - a brand-new chapter to the campaign, which was originally created for Doom 3's console release but never made it to PC.

It pits you, the sole survivor of the UAC facility on Mars, against the demons of Hell, and this time they're also bringing some zombies for good measure. The Lost Mission stars David Ashby, a member of the original Doom 3 development team, and has been slightly retooled for this new release.

The second is a spruced-up version of the base game, giving it a fresh coat of paint for 2022. Id has upgraded the graphics, added ray tracing, and introduced some quality of life changes to the gameplay.

It's a good looking game, and the original held up remarkably well - even on the ancient hardware of the time. 

The third and final part of Doom 3's 20th-anniversary package is the introduction of online multiplayer, a first for the series. You'll be able to play alongside three other teammates in classic modes such as King of the Hill and Capture the Flag, as well as a new mode called "Relic" - wherein you'll need to collect and hold onto a relic for as long as possible against opposing teams.

Whatever your feelings are towards the Doom series as a whole, it's hard to deny the importance of Doom 3. It took the franchise and stuck it in a horror setting, complete with a haunted house aesthetic and some seriously freaky demons. It also had a pretty decent story, some great set pieces, and some genuinely terrifying moments.

England's James Healey has said he is targeting a return to the international fold for the Six Nations, having recovered from a career-threatening knee injury. The centre suffered anterior cruciate and lateral collateral ligament damage in September 2022, but is expected to return to action in January.

Healey, who earned the last of his four England caps in July 2021, faces competition for a place in Eddie Jones' squad from the likes of Ollie Lawrence, Henry Slade and Elliot Daly.

"Every international player dreams of playing in the Six Nations," he told BBC Midlands Today. "That is my goal but it is a long way off. I'm not looking too far ahead. I'm looking to get back on the pitch for Worcester and then see where that takes me."

Healey, 25, has been sidelined since damaging his knee in a pre-season friendly against London Irish. The injury was worse than anticipated and required a second knee operation in October 2022.

"It's been a tough old road," said Healey, who signed a new deal with Worcester in July 2022. "There are times where you doubt whether you are going to get back to full fitness. "When you get to that low period, you get pretty depressed. You are bored, you are lonely and you are injured. There are a lot of ups and downs."

Healey, who joined Worcester from Gloucester in 2018, made his England debut against America in July 2021 and also featured against Canada and France that summer.

If he does return to action in January, it is likely Healey would receive a England recall for the Six Nations opener against Scotland on 4 February.

Apple has filed lawsuits against two people who allegedly shared copyrighted material, in what is believed to be the first time the technology giant has taken legal action against users of its operating system.

The file sharers were among a group of people who were monitoring the progress of the legal battle between Apple and Epic Games, the maker of Fortnite.

Apple said the two defendants, who live in Texas and Florida, had shared "trade secrets" and were in violation of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act.

The company filed the lawsuits in US district court in California on Tuesday, but did not file against the other members of the group, which monitored the Epic Games case on the online forum Reddit.

In a statement, Apple said the two defendants, who have not been identified, had "gained unauthorized access" to its "internal bounty system" for reporting bugs and security vulnerabilities.

It said the move was part of an effort to "hold individuals accountable for their intentional misconduct".

"Apple never alleged the defendants disclosed any information about the operating system," the company said.

"The defendants are charged with violating Apple's endpoint security policy, which applies to all Apple employees, because they were actively running an unprotected instance of Apple's in-house file sharing service, despite multiple reminders to protect their sensitive data," it added.

Epic Games sued Apple in 2020, accusing it of acting as a monopoly with its online marketplace for apps on its iPhones and other devices.

The lawsuit was filed in US district court in Northern California and is still ongoing.

In recent months, a group of people on Reddit who call themselves "fuqyes" have been live-streaming and posting videos of themselves watching the legal proceedings.

The two defendants who were sued were members of the group, and posted a link to a file-sharing app, according to Apple.

The lawsuit said the two defendants had been reminded of their obligation to keep confidential information secure, but had continued to use the company's file sharing system in an "unauthorized and irresponsible manner".

"In doing so, they have flagrantly violated Apple's policies and ignored multiple reminders to address their misconduct," the company said.

Music fans who use the "Tiger" file-sharing network could find themselves on the receiving end of a lawsuit from Apple Computer.

The creator of the iPod and iTunes, Apple is locked in a constant battle with those it accuses of digital piracy - so-called "copyright thieves" - as it tries to enforce digital rights management (DRM) technology built into many of its products.

Now the company has stepped up the fight, targeting those who use the fast-growing, Gnutella-based Tiger network to trade music files.

Apple has hired the Los Angeles law firm of Holzer, Holzer and Fistel to identify up to 25 Apple users in the US who have engaged in "unauthorised sharing" of music files using the Tiger network, according to a letter sent to the company by the law firm.

The letter gives users until 17 December to hand over their names and contact details, or face a lawsuit.

The five-seater pods, powered by electricity, have been developed by the British company Aurrigo.

The firm aims to make the "auto-pods" available for ride-sharing schemes by the end of the year.

It plans to operate them initially in a geo-fenced area, with trials planned at the O2 Arena and London's Excel centre.

The pods use sensors and cameras to navigate, avoiding any obstacles in their path.

A pilot operating the pods via a computer dashboard can override the vehicle's autonomous systems if necessary.

The pods are 8m (26ft) long, 2m wide and 2.8m high and weigh about 1,500kg (3,300lb).

They can travel up to 56mph (90km/h) and have a range of up to 124 miles (200km) on a single charge.

The vehicles are currently powered by petrol generators, but these will be replaced by lithium battery packs in the future.

Chris Harris, chief executive of the firm, said: "The auto-pod combines pioneering sensor technologies with the latest in computer vision to ensure that it operates safely on public roads and footpaths, without compromising the safety of pedestrians or other road users."

The pods could be used at airports, shopping centres, golf clubs and sports stadiums.

Mr Harris said the pods could "revolutionise" the way people travel around airports.

"The auto-pod can drive around airports without the need to ever expand the existing infrastructure, creating a fast, convenient and low-cost way of moving people around quickly and efficiently," he said.

And he accused the prime minister of a "panic-driven response" to the possibility of a Labour victory.

The pair were speaking after Mr Howard announced that Australians would be offered a referendum on changing the constitution to deny automatic Australian citizenship to anyone bearing foreign citizenship.

Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn said his Conservative rival Boris Johnson had lied to the public about his tax plans.

Mr Johnson insisted he was "utterly reasonable" and accused Sir Keir Starmer of wanting to raise taxes by taking Britain back into the European Union.

The BBC's political editor Laura Kuenssberg said the debate exposed clear divides on the economy and taxation.

JP Morgan has admitted for the first time that two of its predecessor firms owned slaves in the past.

The bank said its two largest antecedents, JPMorgan Chase and Chase Manhattan, had owned slaves prior to the Civil War and used discriminatory practices against them.

The admission came in a letter to Senator Ron Wyden of Oregon, who had queried the bank's ties to slavery.

The disclosure is extremely rare for a modern American bank, and reflects a growing willingness of companies to confront their historical ties to slavery.

Last year, New York Life, the nation's largest life insurance company, released a report on its historical ties to slavery, saying that many of its founders were slave owners and that the insurer profited from the slave economy through investments in slave-owning clients.

In its letter to Senator Wyden, JP Morgan said that its predecessor firms had owned at least 267 slaves, and that a pair of plantations the banks owned used the forced labor of slaves to produce cotton and rice. The bank said that many of the slaves were sold in order to keep the plantation running, a common practice at the time.

The letter also detailed the ways in which JP Morgan's predecessor firms used discriminatory practices against African Americans, including denying them mortgages and loans. The bank said it would donate more than $5 million to organizations dedicated to helping African Americans.

In a statement, JP Morgan said that the revelations were "extremely disappointing" but that the bank was "proud of the actions" it was taking to address them.

"We understand that our firm's history is linked to some shameful aspects of America's past," the bank said.

JPMorgan Chase has admitted that two of its predecessor firms benefited from slavery in the 19th century. The bank said its ownership structure was "consistent with" that of slave owners, in a statement accompanying its annual report. It comes after criticism from a UK-based campaign group, Spotlight on Slavery. The organisation had called for banks to investigate their historical links to slavery. Spotlight on Slavery's director, Christopher Brown, said the admission by JPMorgan was a significant step forward. "There are still thousands of people around the world who are impacted by the legacy of slavery, so it is crucial that financial institutions like JPMorgan Chase take responsibility for helping to address the systemic economic inequalities which are still present today," he added.

The bank did not specify whether it would offer compensation. It did, however, announce plans to allocate $350m towards a programme of initiatives addressing "systemic economic inequality" and "the legacy of slavery". These will include funding job training, education and entrepreneurship among communities of colour. 

The admission comes after increasing scrutiny of banks' historic ties to the slave trade. In March, an investigation by Guardian journalists revealed that nearly two dozen global banks had been founded, or had their early growth funded, by investors with links to the slave trade. These included Barclays, HSBC and Credit Suisse. 

The findings led to calls for banks to pay reparations for the slave trade. Earlier this year, a group of MPs and peers wrote to the Bank of England's governor, Andrew Bailey, urging the central bank to require banks to look into their historical links to slavery and make the results public.

The 29-year-old Leicester Tigers player, who has won 60 caps for England and three for the British and Irish Lions, has not been selected in head coach Eddie Jones' squad for the forthcoming tournament.

England begin their Six Nations campaign against Scotland at Twickenham on Saturday.

England centre Manu Tuilagi is out of the Six Nations after suffering an Achilles tendon injury.

Manchester City manager Pep Guardiola has called for the introduction of goal-line technology in the Premier League after Liverpool scored an injury-time winner against Everton from a clearly offside position.

Referee Anthony Taylor and his assistant on the near side were wrong to allow Mohamed Salah's 92nd-minute strike to stand, with the Egyptian forward inches offside as the ball was played forward by Trent Alexander-Arnold.

"It's not the first time and won't be the last time, that's the situation. We can talk about it for the next few weeks."

Everton's disappointment was compounded by the fact that they had scored a perfectly good goal of their own, through Richarlison, which was also incorrectly disallowed for offside shortly before Salah's strike.

Ask Jeeves has launched a new service which offers small businesses affordable and simple internet advertising.

The company said its new service, Ask Ad Solutions, fills a gap in the market.

"Many small and medium sized businesses have been left behind by the complexities and costs associated with online advertising," said Greg Sterling from the Interactive Advertising Bureau.

"While search engines, online directories and other web sites offer a range of advertising options, they are still difficult and too expensive for many small businesses," he added.

Ask Jeeves said it had developed its new service after research revealed many small businesses felt "left out" of online advertising.

"We saw a need to streamline and simplify the process, making it easy and cost-effective for local businesses to tap into the power of internet search and attract new customers," said Brian McAndrews, chief executive of Ask Jeeves.

"We believe this service will be particularly appealing to the vast majority of local businesses that do not have websites," he added.

Ask Ad Solutions allows businesses to create and place ads on the Ask Jeeves website, and appears alongside search results when users look for a particular product or service in a specific region.

The ads can be updated daily, to feature special offers or to announce new services.

Mr Sterling said small businesses had been "underserved" by the online advertising industry.

"Most local businesses don't have websites, and the cost and complexity of buying online ads has been a barrier for them," he said.

But other experts have warned that small firms could still be put off by the cost of maintaining a campaign.

"The reality is that maintaining a consistent and effective ad campaign, even with these simplified tools, requires time and money," said Kate Morris, chief executive of Buy.com.

The interactive search engine Ask Jeeves is set to make a comeback later this year, as the company behind it hopes to capitalise on the growing popularity of voice-activated technology.

DVD players equipped with Blu-ray's high-definition video will hit the US market on Tuesday, marking what many see as the final victory for the Blu-ray disc format in its two-year-long battle with HD DVD.

Britain's Regimental Associations – which represent hundreds of thousands of veterans – are to merge into a single organisation after more than a century of operating separately.

The 15 associations – each linked to a different regiment – have been a mainstay of Britain's military history, dating back to the 19th Century.

But they have struggled to attract recruits in recent years, with membership falling by more than 25% since 2018.

The vote to merge – expected to be approved – follows more than a year of talks between the associations.

It is hoped the move will save £1m a year in running costs and secure the future of the organisations.

More than 400,000 veterans are members of the Regimental Associations, which preserve the traditions and comradeship of their respective regiments.

They stage parades and other events, often with marching bands, to commemorate battles fought or deaths of former servicemen and women.

Most of the associations were formed in the 1880s and 1890s, following the Childers Reforms which merged and numberfied Britain's army regiments.

Members wear their regimental badges or tattoos to remember former comrades-in-arms and preserve the "esprit de corps" or spirit of their units.

But like many volunteer-led veterans' groups, the Regimental Associations have struggled in recent years with an ageing membership base.

Annual subscriptions are often waived for members aged 75 and over, while younger veterans are encouraged to join instead the Royal British Legion – a separate charity which also counts serving and former military personnel as members.

Six associations – those of the Rifles, the Royal Scots, the King's Own Scottish Borderers, the Royal Highland Fusiliers, the Black Watch and the Argyll and Sutherland Highlanders – voted against the proposal in Saturday's ballot.

The Soldiers, Sailors, Airmen and Families Association (SSAFA), a charity which offers lifetime support for veterans, is to take on the work of the Regimental Associations.

A spokeswoman for the SSAFA said the charity would "work with the associations that voted no, to discuss their concerns and explore the next steps".

Bank payout to Pinochet victims

Bank Julius Baer has agreed to pay former Chilean dictator General Augusto Pinochet $23.8m in a long-running case relating to money deposited in Swiss bank accounts.

The BBC's Sebastian Bell in Santiago says this is likely to be the final chapter in a historic case.

For years, thousands of victims of General Pinochet's military regime had demanded the return of $44m of state funds that were deposited in several Swiss banks.

In 2004, Swiss authorities ordered Bank Julius Baer to return $15m to the Chilean state, but the bank appealed, insisting that it had been advised by its lawyers that the funds deposited were legitimate.

The case has gone through several iterations. In 2010, a court ordered the bank to pay $50m in compensation, with $24m going to the Chilean state and $26m to 600 victims.

The victims then took the case to Switzerland, demanding that the bank return the full $44m. Last October, a Swiss court ruled that the bank had to pay $90m in compensation.

Now, Bank Julius Baer says it will pay a total of $23.8m to both the Chilean state and the victims. The bank said it had reached a "friendly agreement" with the victims.

It is not clear if this latest agreement will be the final chapter in the case.

Our correspondent says that even though Bank Julius Baer has agreed to pay $23.8m, more than half of the originally disputed amount, there is no guarantee this will be the end of the story.

He says both the Chilean government and the victims still have the right to appeal against the amount, although neither side has said yet if they will do so.

The BBC reports that a British court has ordered the freezing of £35 million ($46 million) in bank accounts owned by the family of former Chilean dictator Augusto Pinochet. 

The ex-dictator, who is now gravely ill, is himself subject to an order freezing £5 million ($6.5 million) of his own assets. 

Lord Justice Thomas, announcing the latest order, said it was designed to ensure that neither Pinochet nor his family would be able to evade the judgment won by victims of human rights abuses during his regime. 

The victims' lawyers said the order meant the victims could now "at last be compensated for the egregious crimes committed by Pinochet and his regime". 

Seventeen accounts in the name of Pinochet and his wife were frozen earlier this year. At the time the bank said it was acting on an order from the Home Office.

But lawyers for Pinochet argued that as a former head of state, he was entitled to immunity. 

They also claimed that freezing the accounts would cause "exceptional hardship" to his family.

However, at a later hearing, the Home Office said immunity did not apply in this case as Pinochet was accused of crimes against humanity. 

The judge said there was no evidence the ex-dictator had lived in the UK and therefore the Home Office had been correct to reject his claim for immunity. 

Lord Justice Thomas added that the £35 million frozen was "reasonable and proportionate" and would not cause exceptional hardship to the Pinochet family. 

About 3,000 victims of the Pinochet regime are expected to share a compensation payout. 

The Chilean dictator was arrested in Britain in 1998 while recovering from back surgery. He was held in custody for more than a year while a campaign developed for his extradition on charges of torture and murder.

Pinochet was never extradited, largely due to his poor health, but was indicted in Spain and Britain for crimes against humanity. 

Subsequent revelations about his human rights abuses have continued to shake Chile and led to the discovery of mass graves.

Small firms in the UK are being hit by rising costs due to inflation and increased energy prices, with some warning they are on the "verge of collapse", according to a new survey. The Federation of Small Businesses (FSB) said its research indicated that smaller businesses were particularly exposed to fluctuations in energy prices as they typically operate on thinner margins than larger firms.

The FSB's research, based on a survey of its members, found that small businesses were paying on average £4,418 a year on their energy bills - a rise of 46% compared with 2018. 

The organisation's national chairman, Mike Cherry, said: "Small businesses are on the verge of collapse due to energy costs, with many teetering on the edge of survival because of the worsening cost of doing business.

"The worst is yet to come in the next few months and thousands of firms could shut up shop unless urgent action is taken," he added. "Small businesses have been hit by a perfect storm of rising costs, falling consumer confidence, and dwindling margins.

The FSB has called on the UK government to take immediate steps to help small businesses, including by bringing forward the date of the next business rates review, introducing more grants and easing the burden of debt. 

The organisation also wants the government to work with the Bank of England to explore the possibility of a "small business emergency interest rate relief loan".

Mr Cherry said: "Small businesses have been neglected by this government. They are suffering because of the after-effects of the pandemic and need support if they are to survive and get through the next few months.

"We need the government to show small businesses the same love and support that it gives to big business."

Small firms across the UK are reporting higher costs and struggling to pass these on to customers, a survey has indicated. The Forum of Private Business said its research showed inflation was the biggest challenge for small and medium-sized companies. Forum spokesman Toby Marshall said many were "struggling to manage" increases in the cost of energy, fuel and raw materials. The forum's research showed 42% of firms had seen their energy bills rise in the past three months, while 36% had been hit by higher fuel costs.

Mr Marshall said: "Unfortunately, rising costs are now a fact of life for many small businesses. "This is a particular challenge for those who have barely recovered from the economic impacts of the pandemic and are still trying to get back on their feet. This comes amid expectations that the cost of living in the UK is set to rise further, with the price of energy expected to jump by as much as 50% in April.

About a third of the firms had put up their prices in the past three months, the research indicated. Of these, about 60% managed to pass on all or most of the increased costs to customers, while the rest absorbed the rises. The monthly survey by the forum is based on the responses of about 1,000 of its members. Mr Marshall said the government needed to do more to help firms facing higher energy prices. "We've long called for a permanent cut to VAT for the hospitality and tourism sector, which would help businesses manage higher energy costs," he added.

Microsoft is urging computer users to patch a security vulnerability that could allow attackers to silently install malicious software onto their devices.

The tech giant said the flaw, discovered by researchers at CyberArk, was similar to one exploited by the US National Security Agency (NSA).

"Our recommendation is to immediately install the updates provided here," he added in a blog post.

The NSA tool, called EternalBlue, took advantage of a flaw in Microsoft software to collect data on targets.

It was part of a cache of hacking tools leaked by a group called the Shadow Brokers in April 2017.

Microsoft said it had released patches for the vulnerability in March 2017, but many computers remained unpatched because the flaw was "cherry-picked" by the NSA to exploit.

The agency then lost control of the tool, which was used in the massive WannaCry ransomware attack that hit the NHS and hundreds of thousands of other computers around the world.

CyberArk, a security company based in Israel and the US, said the newly-discovered vulnerability was similar to EternalBlue, but was more dangerous because it was "totally silent and inaudible".

"This is the most serious vulnerability I have seen in many years," said CyberArk's security research manager, Ben Seri.

"It's a design flaw, which makes it impossible to detect by all known security products, so we have no way of knowing how many victims there are," he told the BBC.

CyberArk said it was difficult even for security experts to analyse because the malware was implanted directly in the kernel of the operating system - the part of the system that has the most access to its data.

A student who has been blind since birth can now see colours, following a groundbreaking surgery. The surgery involved a unique "tongue display" which stimulated the brain, enabling the patient to see colours.
The patient, who was born with a form of congenital blindness that affects 1 in every 10,000 people, underwent the experimental surgery in November last year.
The operation, which was led by Dr. Ron Pelias, assistant professor of ophthalmology at Stanford University, stimulated the tongue's nerve fibres, which in turn stimulated the brain's visual cortex, allowing the patient to perceive colours.
"We're trying to work out the neural mechanisms of colour vision by stimulating the brain in this very precise way," said Dr Pelias.
The patient can now see colours, but still does not have any form of visual acuity, meaning they can't see shapes or outlines.
The surgery was carried out on a patient with complete colour blindness and involves a small, 1.5mm square electrode, which is placed on the tongue.
The electrode is linked to a small, wearable computer, which transforms images from a camera into "tongue maps", consisting of eight different regions, each stimulated by a different colour.
When the patient looks at an object, the computer converts the image into a "tongue map", which stimulates the brain in such a way that the patient can perceive colours.
"We're trying to stimulate the brain so that it interprets stimuli as colour, by coaxing neurons in the brain to respond in a way that would normally only occur when a sighted person sees colour," said Dr Pelias.
The device needs to be calibrated against a "tongue colour chart", which the patient uses to tune the colours on the device, ensuring they are seeing the right colours.
So far, the patient has been able to identify colours in experiments, but the team is still working on improving the clarity of the images produced.
"This is a very early stage of the research. We're a long way from understanding how the brain encodes colour and even further from understanding how to restore that ability through electrical stimulation," Dr Pelias said.
"But it's a very exciting proof of concept that brings us a little bit closer to helping patients with congenital colour blindness."
The team hopes to carry out the procedure on other patients in the future and believes the technology could also be used to help people who have lost their sight to retinal degeneration.

A blind student from Bristol, UK, says he "hears in colour" after receiving a bionic eye. Tom Williams, 25, has only ever seen shadows and shapes – but now, after receiving the implant, he can identify colours in food and on clothes. The retinal implant goes over the top of his eye, with a video camera feeding information to a microchip which then sends signals to electrodes on the retina. It does not restore vision but allows Mr Williams to detect light and shade and determine the presence of motion.

The device was developed by the company Second Sight, and while it has been available in the US for some time, it is yet to be approved for use in the UK. It has been used in more than 300 people. The device was originally designed for people with a condition called retinitis pigmentosa, which affects the cells that detect light in the retina. However, it has also been tried with success in those with total blindness. 

Mr Williams has optic nerve hypoplasia, a condition where the optic nerves are underdeveloped. He hopes to gain even more sensation through training on the device. Currently, he uses a long cane to get around and listens to the sound of his footsteps to judge where he is.

"I knew it was going to be an extremely slow process, but I was willing to give it a go to help the next generation of visually impaired people," he told the BBC. "However, the sensations I experienced were much quicker and stronger than I expected. Being able to see motion and detect shades of grey has been amazing, but the colour is really something else."

Mr Williams is a classically trained musician and he immediately recognised the difference in colour on his piano keys.

"To be able to see the difference between my black and my white keys on the piano, and to see if my shirt is white or grey, is amazing," he said. "It's a whole new world." 

Mr Williams' bionic eye has a small video camera which is held on top of his eye by a magnetic clasp. This camera sends information to a microchip, which then transforms this data into signals that are sent to electrodes on the retina. The electrodes stimulate the retina's remaining cells, allowing the user to see. 

While the device does not provide the same vision as 20/20 eyesight, users can detect light and motion, differentiating between shades of grey and, in some cases, colour.

Glastonbury fans will be able to buy ID cards featuring images of the festival's stages. 

Organizers say the cards will be needed to gain entry to the 2023 event, following disruption caused by so-called "fake fans" last year.

The cards will be personalised and feature a photo and information about what the ticket-holder purchased.

Glastonbury 2023 will take place from 21 to 25 June. 

Tickets for the 2022 festival sold out in 33 minutes but many were then resold on sites like eBay for thousands of pounds.

Organizers say the photo ID cards will be introduced "to fight against theft" and "to make sure tickets get into the right hands".

They will also be needed to access "pre-sale tickets" for the 50th anniversary festival in 2024.

In a post on Instagram, Glastonbury Festival said: "Following disruption we saw from 'fake fans' last year - when tickets were purchased by people who hadn't any intention of coming to the festival, but instead resold them on secondary sites as soon as they got them - we are introducing personalised photo ID cards for all ticket holders in 2023.

"That means that every ticket holder will now need to have their photo taken when they collect their ticket, in order to receive their personalised photo ID card.

"These cards will be needed for entry into the festival, and will also be required to access any pre-sale tickets for the 50th anniversary festival in 2024."

The post adds the photo cards will fight theft and "make sure tickets get into the right hands".

It is not yet known whether you will be able to opt out of having your photo taken. 

In 2021, Glastonbury was one of the first big festivals to return after the lifting of coronavirus restrictions.

Headliner Paul McCartney had to appeal to fans to "look after each other" after a number of medical incidents were reported during the festival.

The following year, the festival introduced more measures to keep attendees safe, including setting up a "safe haven" area, where people could recharge their phone if they needed to contact friends or family, or charge a power bank. 

There were also increased medical facilities, including an on-site hospital, with more staff, equipment and treatment areas, as well as an increased presence of security and police.

Glastonbury fans will be able to buy ID cards recognising their vaccination status ahead of this year's festival.

Organisers of the event said the move, for the return of the festival after two years, would offer "a more seamless entry experience".

The cards will indicate whether the bearer has had a negative lateral flow or PCR test in the last 24 or 48 hours, or is fully vaccinated.

Glastonbury 2022, which will feature headline acts including Elton John, Billie Eilish and Kendrick Lamar, gets under way on 22 June.

In a statement issued on the festival's website, organisers said they were confident this year's event would go ahead, after being cancelled in 2020 and 2021 because of the coronavirus pandemic.

They said they were "working closely" with the government and local authorities to make this year's festival safe, "including the requirement for a negative LFT (lateral flow test) prior to arrival".

"There will also be the option of demonstrating proof of two vaccinations in the last 180 days," the statement added.

The NHS Covid Pass, which can be accessed through the NHS app, will change to allow people to demonstrate their vaccination status or test results.

Those who do not have access to the app, for example people without smartphones, will be able to order a paper NHS Covid Pass letter.

Glastonbury organisers said they were aware bearing "proof" of vaccination status or test results "may be tricky" for some people.

To address this, they said they were working with government departments to create a "Glastonbury NHS ID card" which would be sent to ticket holders "ahead of the festival".

"This will state your vaccination status or recent negative LFT test result directly on the card, to make things as simple as possible," the statement said.

It added that further details would be released at the end of March.

Boss of dairy group Parmalat says it will re-list on the Milan stock exchange as early as next year.

Parmalat collapsed in 2003 after an accounting fraud scandal.

The company's new chief executive, Jean-Claude Van de Rossum, said he wanted to return the firm to its "rightful home".

Mr Van de Rossum was appointed in August to help recover the company's fortunes.

He said a stock market flotation would help fund expansion and make the company more visible.

"We are working on a transaction that will enable us to return to the stock market in 2014," he said.

"We are working to make the company more visible, to make it more attractive for investors...  to be able to expand, also through acquisitions."

Parmalat was found to have cooked its books by overstating its profits and hiding billions of euros of debt.

The firm was snapped up for a token sum by the dairy group Lactalis in 2010.

Since then, Lactalis has rebuilt the company's fortunes and expanded abroad, particularly in Brazil.

The company now has revenues of €9.2bn and a presence in 33 countries.

Dairy group Parmalat will float on the Milan stock exchange next month, eight years after its biggest bankruptcy recovery in Italian history.

The company said shares would be sold in an initial public offering (IPO) at between €2.50 and €3 each, valuing the business at up to €8.5bn ($9bn).

The offering is expected to include a secondary sale of existing shares by its current owner, the Lactalis dairy group.

Lactalis bought Parmalat in 2011 for €1.5bn after it collapsed under the weight of a €14.3bn debt fraud.

The company was founded in 1961 by Sicilian entrepreneur Calisto Tanzi as a maker of stretched-curd cheeses, such as mozzarella. It grew rapidly in the 1980s and 1990s through a series of acquisitions, becoming a global dairy giant.

However, it collapsed in 2003 after an audit revealed that Mr Tanzi had been using fraudulent accounting practices to conceal a €14.3bn debt. The company was placed under administration and Mr Tanzi was sentenced to prison.

The administrator who oversaw the turnaround, Enrico Bondi, kept the company in private hands after Lactalis' purchase.

Parmalat returned to profit in 2013 and has paid off most of its debt.

The company's products include Lactalis' President brand of cheeses in France, as well as Parmalat-branded milk in Italy. It also makes yoghurts and other dairy products.

Parmalat's IPO would be the biggest in Milan for three years and the largest ever IPO on the Italian stock exchange, according to Reuters.

Mobile phones are destined to become the primary means of accessing the internet, offering users a "truly mobile" experience, according to the IT industry.

But the head of Microsoft's mobile technology division said it would be 2008 before mobile multimedia became a widespread service.

Chris Shaw said that, while some companies were rushing to provide mobile multimedia, the technology currently available was inadequate.

Mr Shaw, speaking at the 3GSM mobile phone conference in Cannes, said companies were in too much of a hurry.

His views echoed those of Franco Bernabè, chief executive of Telecom Italia Mobile (TIM), who said customers were "frustrated" by the current offer.

"We are in danger of getting ahead of ourselves. We are in danger of putting technology first rather than the customer," he said.

Mr Shaw said that in two years' time Microsoft would introduce a more sophisticated version of its Pocket PC, with improved email, web browsing and video capabilities.

He added that in five years all mobile phones would be multimedia devices that would become the primary means of accessing the internet.

"That is the vision - truly mobile, truly pervasive. The phone will become the centre of your communication experience, not just for voice but for all forms of communication," he said.

But he added that this would only be possible with the introduction of faster and more flexible networks.

The comments came as Nokia, the world's largest manufacturer of mobile phones, unveiled a new generation of phones with improved multimedia capabilities.

The Finnish group launched a new version of its popular 6110 phone, with a built-in camera, and the 6610, which can play video and audio clips and has a larger screen.

It also unveiled a new version of its smart phone, the 9210, with a larger screen for viewing multimedia messages and email.

Nokia chief executive Jorma Ollila said the company was committed to delivering a "wireless internet experience" but warned that networks needed to be improved.

"We are concerned that the networks are not ready for the data speeds that are required for a good internet experience," he said.

The existing network technology, known as 2G, is not designed to offer high-speed data transfer needed for internet access.

The study, conducted by consulting firm Accenture, found that although many consumers have access to broadband networks, they are not taking advantage of the faster data speeds and new multimedia services that are now available. The study found that only about 20% of mobile users have downloaded any multimedia content, such as ringtones, images, or videos. Furthermore, only about 6% of users download multimedia content on a regular basis. The study also found that users are hesitant to download multimedia content due to concerns about cost, privacy, and the overall usability of the services.

Accenture suggests that network operators work to improve consumer education about the availability and usability of mobile multimedia services. Additionally, the study suggests that network operators should focus on providing more compelling content and offers to encourage greater adoption. Accenture concludes that the slow uptake of mobile multimedia reflects the early stage of development of these services and predicts that adoption will increase as networks become more pervasive and as users become more comfortable with the technology.

But because increases in pension payments are linked to increases in average life expectancy, future increases in pensions could be less for men than for women.

This is due to a faster improvement in life expectancy for women, which means that the gap between the sexes is narrowing when it comes to how long they live.
