The former foreign secretary, Jack Straw, has told the BBC the House of Lords was wrong to argue in a landmark decision that it was always illegal to hold foreign nationals without trial.

And he predicted that the government would not accept the verdict - reached by a majority of three - and would seek to change the law.

The Lords ruled on Thursday that the Detention Authority Act 1994 meant that no minister could authorise the detention of foreign nationals indefinitely.

But Mr Straw said that when the legislation was passed, as well as when he used these powers when he was home secretary, it was assumed that it was legal to hold foreign nationals indefinitely.

He added that the then government believed that it would be impractical and foolish to have foreign nationals with no right to be in the UK - such as asylum seekers whose applications had been turned down - walking the streets at will. 

"That is the background against which this legislation was passed and it is entirely unreasonable for the House of Lords to make a judgment about the legislative intent against a background which they themselves have created," he said.

Mr Straw added that the decision would create huge practical problems because there were many foreign nationals who were currently unable to return to their own countries. 

He said the decision would also have serious consequences for the government's counter-terrorism strategy.

"I cannot believe that any government, any parliamentary democracy would allow the situation to develop whereby those suspected of involvement in terrorist activities, where evidence is scarce and it may take months to get hold of it, that they could not be held for the period of time necessary to enable the authorities to gather the evidence," he said. 

"The idea that they can simply be released, whether they are British or not, in the meantime seems to me to be a very dangerous development."

Mr Straw also said he did not think the decision would be respected in other commonwealth countries, adding that this was likely to affect the treatment of British nationals abroad.

The House of Lords was wrong to conclude that the UK government's policy on terrorist detainees was lawful, says the man who introduced it.

Jack Straw, the former foreign secretary, said the upper chamber had got it "wrong in law and wrong in fact" by supporting a court ruling that ministers had no duty to release terror suspects.

He told the BBC the ruling threatened the basic principle of British justice.

The Law Lords backed a Court of Appeal decision that the government had no obligation to release suspects detained under anti-terrorism laws.

Mr Straw introduced the policy in 2001, when he was home secretary.

He told the BBC that the Law Lords - the final court of appeal in the UK - had failed to understand the essence of habeas corpus, the ancient right to a fair trial and freedom from unlawful imprisonment.

And he said the Lords had mistakenly believed that the government had introduced a policy of "neither confirm nor deny" in order to avoid disclosure of sensitive information.

In fact, said Mr Straw, the policy had been designed to give effect to the government's view - that it would not specify matters relating to national security even if it were ordered to do so by the courts.

"The policy was not designed, nor did it have the effect, of preventing judicial scrutiny of the justification for detention," he said.

"The suggestion that the policy in some way undermines the fundamental liberty of habeas corpus is, frankly, absurd."

Mr Straw said the Law Lords had failed to take into account the "fundamental" distinction between national security and ordinary criminal cases.

And he said they had misunderstood the nature of the terrorist threat facing the UK, by suggesting that the threat had reduced since 2001 and that terrorism was "somehow... a less serious threat".

The former foreign secretary added that the Lords had been wrong to conclude that the government had been "attempting to manipulate the court" by disclosing sensitive information on the morning of the Court of Appeal hearing.

Downing Street said it welcomed the Law Lords' decision, and said it provided "clarity" on an important issue.

A spokesman for Prime Minister Gordon Brown said the government had always been clear that it had no intention of changing its policy on national security.

But the Liberal Democrats said the government had been "caught out misleading both the courts and Parliament" by attempting to introduce a policy of "neither confirm nor deny".

Business investment increased at a rate of 8.1%, while residential investment continued to drag on growth, decreasing at an annual rate of 3.1%.

Overall, this is the fastest pace of growth since the first quarter of 2015.

However, despite the upward revision, the picture of the US economy remains the same.

Growth has been fairly sluggish in the wake of the financial crisis, and there are few signs that a sustained acceleration is about to begin.

The ESL was launched on 18 April but collapsed within 72 hours due to widespread opposition.

United, Arsenal, Chelsea, Liverpool, Manchester City and Tottenham were the six Premier League clubs who signed up to the breakaway league.

Last month, the clubs faced heavy criticism after they were revealed to have signed 'letterheads' that would have seen them become founding members of the ESL.

United's involvement in the ESL proposal saw their plans for a £1.3bn ($1.7bn) float on the Singapore stock exchange delayed, while the Glazers received criticism for their involvement.

The family, who have been United owners since 2005, were understood to have been key players in the formation of the ESL.

In a statement, United said: "Independent advisers, supported by global legal firm Cleary Gottlieb Steen & Hamilton, will conduct a review of the club's involvement in the European Super League.

"The review will consider evidence gathered from fans, shareholders and other interested parties and will include input from independent advisers, supported by global legal firm Cleary Gottlieb Steen & Hamilton LLP, as well as from the club itself.

"All evidence will be scrutinised and considered as part of the review process and the advisers will be afforded access to senior executives and non-executive directors of the club, including executive co-chairman Joel Glazer."

United added that evidence can be provided until Wednesday, 21 July, with an online portal set up to allow fans to submit any evidence they feel is relevant.

The decision to allow the Glazer family to buy Manchester United was based on "inaccurate and flawed" information, according to a report published by the Independent Football Ombudsman (IFO). 

The IFO investigation into the process concluded that there were "multiple failures" in the system for ensuring that the purchase of football clubs by offshore trusts was transparent and in the best interests of the game. 

The report said there was insufficient scrutiny of the Glazers' ownership and suitability to own Manchester United. The panel found that the club's board had failed to carry out proper due diligence on the Glazers before the takeover went ahead and that the club had broken its own procedures.

The IFO has called for the introduction of stronger checks and balances to prevent a similar situation occurring in the future.

Danny Jones praised Ritchie Henson's "heroics" after the fly-half kicked 14 points to help London Irish end their 13-game Premiership losing streak with a deserved victory over Gloucester.

The Exiles had not won a top-flight game since beating Sale on 4 March, but they finally tasted victory again thanks to Henson's accurate kicking and a determined defensive effort.

Irish had to withstand a late Tigers onslaught but held on for a precious win.

"Ritchie's heroics won us the game," said Jones, who alongside Henson was one of Irish's two try-scorers.

"We always knew he had it in him. He's a top-class 10 and we're very lucky to have him.

"It was a team effort, though. The boys were outstanding and, while it was a poor kick to give away a try, I was happy with the way we responded."

Henson, who kicked 11 points as Irish drew with Exeter last weekend, was again his side's standout player as he scored 17 points.

His tactical kicking and game management were exemplary, while his goal-kicking was again faultless as he succeeded with all four attempts.

Irish's other try came from No 8 Steffon Armitage, who forced his way over in the second half following a powerful run.

Gloucester's only try came from a well-worked move early in the second half, with centre Bill Meakes touching down after good work from scrum-half Willi Heinz.

The visitors did not score again as Irish's defence held firm, with the home side winning the second half 6-3.

"It feels great," said Jones. "The boys have been working hard in training and in the games, but things weren't going our way.

"We've had a couple of close games but today everything went right. Credit to the boys, they worked hard and deserved it."

Irish's first victory since their return to the top flight leaves them seventh in the table, four points clear of bottom club Worcester, while Gloucester remain fifth.

"It was a typical Championship game," said Jones. "There were a lot of errors from both sides but we kept going and I'm glad we got the win."

The Bluebirds' resilience was eventually rewarded with a point, as they extended their unbeaten run to four matches and climbed up to 14th in the table.

It was a welcome result for Cardiff, who have struggled defensively this season, but Morrison said their display against Villa was just a sign of things to come.

"We have been working in training on our shape and I think it got better as the game went on," Morrison told BBC Sport.

"We have to work on our communication when we are in possession. We have gone away to work on that this week and it will get better.

"We have to adapt to the managers we have had this season. We have had a change now and I think you saw that with some of the things that happened in the game.

"We have just got to adapt to how the gaffer wants us to play. We have done that in previous seasons when we have had a new manager come in and I am sure it will be the same with the gaffer."

The father of a controversial play about Adolf Hitler has defended his right to a £20,000 arts grant - despite complaints that it glorifies the Nazi leader.

In January, the Arts Council of Wales gave the money to Jeff James for his play Führer, about the last days of Hitler's life.

The council received 34 complaints - 24 from the public and 10 from artists and academics.

One complainant, the historian Nigel Jones, has asked for the grant to be reinvestigated.

But Mr James, whose company is called No Fit State, said: "I think there's a kind of prurience about the way in which we approach the past."

He said the complaints were a form of censorship and that he was proud of his work.

"I think there's a very strong case for saying that this is a very important part of our recent past and that it deserves to be examined," he said.

"And if it is examined in a popular form, like a play, then I think that is a good thing."

Complainant Nigel Jones said he was "astounded" that the Arts Council gave over £20,000 to a play containing such "toxic" material.

"They are glorifying Hitler. It's madness," he said.

"You have got a situation where you have got a company called No Fit State, fronted by someone called Jeff James, who is apparently doing all sorts of things around the country, who have got very good at manipulating the system."

An Arts Council of Wales spokeswoman said the complaint would be "investigated through the appropriate channels" but said the matter was now with its independent adjudication panel.

The spokeswoman said the council had awarded £198,000 from its arts portfolio to No Fit State in the past.

Mr James said any criticism of his past work was "like comparing apples with oranges".

He said: "This is a new play, it hasn't been seen. How can you possibly censure something that doesn't exist?"

Führer will go on a national tour, starting at the Soho Theatre in London on 5 May.

Artist Robert Cohen died last week while awaiting the outcome of his legal challenge against the decision to give the grant to Mark Evans for his proposal using the name "Adolf" in the project.

Cohen, who originally applied for the grant, had argued that using the name would be inappropriate. The 58-year-old from Merthyr Tydfil said it would be a "contemptuous insult" to Helen Pennant, the girl who died at Bergen-Belsen, and her family. He launched an appeal against Arts Council Wales' decision to award the grant to Evans, but it was rejected by the High Court in July.

Despite the ruling, the row over the grant has continued. A petition calling on the Welsh government to stop the award has received more than 17,500 signatures. The grant, awarded as part of an arts programme named after the girl, was given to Evans, from Aberystwyth, to create the conceptual art piece using the name "Adolf" for a sculpture and performance piece.

The piece, entitled "The whole of Auschwitz was a sham", includes two stone tablets with the word "Adolf" carved into them. The tablets will be placed in a wooden crate and buried in the ground near a synagogue. Evans will then dig up and carry the tablets, wearing a uniform and holding a whip, towards the synagogue. 

The work aims to challenge "anti-semitic representations" of Hitler by "humanising" the dictator through the performance, according to Evans' proposal. The artist said the piece explores the "mythology" of Hitler and the "symbolism" of the tablets, which represent the "myth-making we see today in politics and the media".

British sprint great Chris Boardman has announced that he will extend his career as a professional cyclist and will compete in the team pursuit at the 2000 Sydney Olympics. 

The multiple world champion had said that the Sydney Games would be his last, but has now changed his mind after the British team finished second in the team pursuit at the track world championships in Italy. 

He will bring to an end a magnificent career, which has seen him win four Olympic medals, including gold in the individual pursuit at the 1992 Barcelona Olympics. 

Boardman, who will be 38 by the time of the Sydney Olympics, told BBC Sport that despite his previous statements, he "probably always knew" that he would continue his career if the team pursuit squad did well in Italy.

He said: "Whether I like it or not, I seem to be able to still contribute to the team. "With the benefit of hindsight, those comments weren't particularly clever. But I do feel that I can offer more to the team than just a good engine."

Boardman, who won the elite men's time trial road race in the World Championships yesterday, added that another factor in his decision was the likelihood of an Olympic medal. 

He said: "If we [the British team] turn up at Sydney as good as we are now, we are going to win a medal - that is a huge motivation." 

Boardman has won three Olympic golds, one silver and one bronze during his career.

BBC Sport football correspondent Mark Lawrenson on the challenges facing Liverpool manager Rafael Benitez.

When Liverpool appointed Rafael Benitez as manager in the summer of 2004, I thought they had got the best man for the job.

I still think that, despite the fact the Spaniard has not come close to delivering the Premier League title that everyone associated with Liverpool wanted so badly.

Benitez has not had the money to spend that his main Premier League rivals have - but that is no excuse.

In his first season at Anfield, he failed to mount a serious title challenge but did win a trophy - the European Champions League.

That success, and the manner in which Liverpool achieved it, justified the decision to give Benitez the job and tempered some of the disappointment at not being in the hunt for the title.

This season, however, Liverpool have been nowhere near the top of the Premier League and look certain to finish outside the top four.

So, just over two years into his five-year contract, Benitez is under pressure to deliver success - and quickly.

He has improved the team defensively but his purchases in that area - Jose Reina, Jamie Carragher, Steve Finnan and Daniel Agger - were already on the books.

Benitez got them playing as a more cohesive unit and that has been to the team's benefit - but it is still not good enough.

The new season offers Benitez the chance to make amends and he will be encouraged by the fact that Liverpool have made a promising start in the Champions League.

They have also been scoring goals for fun in the Carling Cup but, in the Premier League, they have already dropped 10 points.

Benitez knows he must convince the club's American owners, George Gillett and Tom Hicks, that he is the right man to deliver success.

And he will also be only too aware that the longer he goes without winning something, the more the pressure on him will increase.

Benitez can point to the fact that he has not had the money to spend that Arsenal, Chelsea, Manchester United and Manchester City have had in recent seasons - and he is right.

But he has spent about £60m on players since he arrived at Anfield and some of those purchases - like Peter Crouch and Dirk Kuyt - have not been successful.

Shares in the online marketplace operator fell more than 7% in after-hours trading.

The company warned that inflation was cutting into sales of non-essential items sold on its platform.

Quarterly earnings across eBay's businesses, including its marketplace and payments divisions, beat estimates.

But the company said challenges linked to higher prices on goods such as sneakers and trading cards - popular items on its platform - were affecting its marketplace business, particularly among sellers of non-essential items.

At the same time, eBay said it was facing inflation-related costs, with expenses including wages and payments processing fees climbing.

The company now expects first-quarter earnings to be between $0.76 and $0.77 per share, falling short of analysts' average estimate of $0.82 per share, according to Refinitiv estimates.

"Inflation is clearly having an impact on consumers' mindsets," said eBay CEO Jamie Iannone. "As inflationary trends continue, we are closely monitoring the impact on consumers as well as our business."

The results come as a key period for eBay begins, with the company gearing up to spin off its fast-growing payments division - a move expected later this year.

The spin-off would leave eBay focused on its online marketplace, where sales have been steadily increasing since the pandemic.

On Tuesday, eBay also announced the departure of two senior executives - Chief Financial Officer Scott Schenkel and Chief Product Officer RJ Pittman - as it streamlines its management structure ahead of the spin-off.

Mr. Schenkel will step down in April, while Mr. Pittman will leave at the end of the month, the company said.

Ms Lawder, 63, said she never stopped looking for her daughter.

"Finding her has answered a question that I've wondered about for so long," she said.

She made contact with Elizabeth, who lives in Australia, via the site and they arranged to meet in London earlier this month.

Some MPs are shocked at the return of a long-lost daughter. Sheila Smith discovered she had a daughter 17 years after donating her eggs to a stranger. Parliament's authorities were wrong to deny her a pass to attend a debate on her issue earlier this year. The MP for Shrewsbury and Atcham, Daniel Kawczynski, described the decision as "madness". The House of Commons' Speaker, John Bercow, has now given Mrs Smith a pass which allows her into Parliament.

Mrs Smith donated her eggs to American couples seeking fertility treatment between 1995 and 1997. At the time, she had no idea her eggs would be exported for use overseas. It is illegal to pay for egg and sperm donations in the UK. However, in the US, where donations are scarce, it is commonplace. Mrs Smith told the BBC she was not informed that her eggs would be sent abroad.

In 2014, Mrs Smith received a letter from the fertility clinic which arranged the donations. It said her eggs may have been used to create up to 12 children. Six years later, a young woman contacted her mother via Instagram. She said she had been given Mrs Smith's details by the fertility clinic. Mrs Smith said she welcomed the contact and a relationship developed. The woman, who is now 26, is planning to visit Mrs Smith in the summer.

Mrs Smith, a parliamentary pass holder, was shocked to be turned away from Westminster Hall earlier this year. She attempted to hear a debate on the issue of egg donation.  A Speaker's attendant told her she could not get in without a special pass. Mrs Smith felt "utterly devastated" at being turned away. She said: "I couldn't believe it. I explained I was a donor mother... and had been for many years... I couldn't believe it, I was in total shock."

The MP for Shrewsbury and Atcham, Mr Kawczynski, heard of Mrs Smith's predicament and offered his help. He wrote to John Bercow, the Speaker of the House of Commons. Mr Bercow then invited Mrs Smith to Parliament and apologised for the "misunderstanding". He presented her with a special pass, valid for one year, which allows her into Westminster Hall.

IBM has announced that it is to spend $1bn on developing its cloud and AI services.

The company said it would expand its global cloud data centre footprint to meet client demand for off-premises computing.

The centrepiece of its strategy is Linux, the open-source operating system, which will underpin its cloud offerings.

Notably, IBM will also increase its commitment to hybrid cloud, which enables customers to move data between their own data centres and cloud-based storage.

"Hybrid cloud is the dominant architecture of the future, and IBM is firmly positioned as the leading provider of hybrid cloud solutions and services to our clients," said IBM chief executive, Arvind Krishna.

"Linux is the glue that holds it all together," he added.

IBM's Linux push comes after it acquired Red Hat, a leading provider of enterprise open-source software, for $34bn last year.

The company said Linux would provide the "open architecture" that is needed to help its clients operate in multi-cloud environments.

Multi-cloud is the use of multiple cloud computing services in a single network.

IBM said it is currently the leading hybrid cloud provider and that its strategy had created a "clear and distinct competitive advantage" with revenue growing by 20% in the first quarter of this year.

"We are pioneering the hybrid cloud marketplace by enabling our clients to run their mission-critical workloads across their own data centres, public clouds and third-party data centres," said IBM's senior vice-president for global sales, John Teltsch.

"No other cloud provider has this capability," he added.

IBM has announced that it is to invest $1bn in Linux and open source technologies over the next three years.

It is the single largest investment in open source software in the company's history and reflects IBM's increasing emphasis on Linux and open standards.

The announcement came as IBM reported its third quarter financial results, which showed a 12% increase in year-on-year profits to $3.1bn.

At the end of 2002, IBM pledged to spend $1bn on Linux-related technologies over five years. Today's announcement represents a renewal and doubling of that pledge.

In a conference call with analysts, IBM's chief executive, Sam Palmisano, said that open standards were increasingly important to IBM's customers who did not want to be locked into proprietary software.

"There is a lot of excitement around open standards these days," he said. "Open and standards-based technologies are what's needed to solve complex business problems."

Linux, which was developed as an open source alternative to proprietary operating systems, has emerged as a major competitor to Microsoft.

According to market researcher IDC, Linux server revenue grew 32% in the second quarter of 2003, year on year, compared with 2% growth for Windows NT.

Mr Palmisano said that IBM planned to leverage its expertise in services to deliver Linux-based solutions to its customers.

At the same time, IBM will step up its development efforts, increasing the number of Linux developers it employs from 500 to 1,000. It will also establish Linux innovation centres in Asia, Europe and North America.

In related news, IBM also said it had formed a strategic alliance with Novell, a leading provider of Linux software, to better compete with Microsoft.

Under the agreement, Novell will work with IBM to improve the performance of Linux on IBM's mainframe computers.

Novell has already developed a version of its SuSE Linux operating system for IBM's eServer mainframe systems. The new agreement calls for the two companies to optimise the software so that it can take advantage of the unique capabilities of IBM's mainframe.

"By optimising Linux to run on IBM's eServer mainframes, we will provide customers with the benefits of open source and mainframe computing," said Jeff Jaffe, IBM's vice-president of strategy.

Entertainment giant Electronic Arts (EA) has outlined plans to create television and film content based on its video game franchises, principally around its sports titles but also including its action games such as Battlefield. 

The company has appointed EA Sports general manager Sean Ramjolesingh to lead its new initiative as executive vice-president of global television, film and immersive content. He will build a team to create “high-quality, narrative-driven content” based on the IP in EA’s portfolio.

The drive mirrors the strategy of gaming rival Microsoft, which has had success with its Xbox Game Pass subscription, and Netflix, in turning video games into television content. It also reflects the growing convergence of the video games, film and TV industries as audiences become less interested in traditional distinctions between them.

EA itself is no stranger to in-house video game adaptations. It previously created an unsuccessful TV series based on its popular FIFA football game. 

The company said it believed there was now “a golden opportunity” to reach a wider audience on streaming services and TV networks “by doing narrative-driven, character-focused stories with global appeal”.

“As the lines continue to blur between interactive and linear entertainment, there are more opportunities than ever to reach new audiences and tell stories in new ways,” said EA chief executive Andrew Wilson.

“Our goal is to build on our strengths to deliver new forms of entertainment and unlock new revenue streams, while preserving the integrity of our brands with stories that complement our existing franchises.”

Ramjolesingh will take up his new role on March 1, reporting to chief creative officer Chris Bruzzo. He will be responsible for working with EA’s studios “to help them identify and capitalise on opportunities to turn their franchises into TV and film properties”.

He will also work with external studios and producers to create and sell content based on EA’s IP, and identify opportunities for immersive content, including augmented and virtual reality.

Ramjolesingh has been with EA for nearly 20 years, most recently as executive vice-president of EA Sports. He has overseen the development and operation of the company’s sports titles including FIFA, Madden NFL, NHL, and UFC.

The chief executive of a US bank has heaped praise on the "genius" of Adam Smith, the 18th-century Scottish economist who pioneered modern capitalism.

Richard Davis, the boss of US Bancorp, said the writer of "The Wealth of Nations" was an "incredible thinker".

His comments came as he unveiled a bronze of Smith in his hometown of Kirkcaldy, in Fife.

Davis said the sculpture - the first of Smith to be erected in his home town - was a "fitting tribute".

He added: "Adam Smith was a massive, incredible thinker who changed the way that people think about free markets and what have you, so I think he was a genius."

Smith wrote "The Wealth of Nations" in 1776, promoting the idea that the selfish actions of individuals can lead to societal benefits.

The concept, now synonymous with capitalism, was an alternative to earlier economic theories that centred on the state's involvement in the economy.

Smith is thought to have born in Kirkcaldy in 1723, but there is no record of his birth or baptism.

He went to Glasgow University at the age of 14 and graduated in 1740, before moving to Oxford University.

He returned to Scotland and lived in Edinburgh, before moving to Paris in 1764 - where he met fellow philosopher David Hume - and then on to London.

It was while living in the British capital that he published "The Wealth of Nations".

Smith died in 1790 and is buried in Edinburgh.

Despite his legacy, there has never been a statue of him in his hometown.

Local councillor Neil Crooks said it was "fitting" that a statue of Smith was finally being put up, describing him as "one of Kirkcaldy's most famous sons".

"It is incredible that someone who is so famous worldwide, someone who has influenced millions of people around the world in terms of economic thinking, is not recognised in his home town," he said.

"We are all delighted that US Bancorp have decided to do this and put up a fitting tribute to Adam Smith in the form of a magnificent sculpture."

The bronze statue, created by Edinburgh-based sculptor Alexander Stoddart, was handed over to the local authority in a ceremony also attended by Smith's descendent, Gavin Hamilton.

Manchester United manager Jose Mourinho has been given a "final warning" by the club's former captain Bryan Robson.
Mourinho's side have made their worst start to a Premier League season, taking just 10 points from seven games.
Ex-United manager Robson said he would "100% definitely" be sacked if he was in Mourinho's position.
He told BBC Five Live: "The board have backed him tremendously. They gave him a contract last season knowing that they were going to have to spend an awful lot of money."
United signed three players for a combined £146.3m ahead of the current campaign.

Robson said he did not think there were many managers available who could improve the team's playing style, but believes the club need a "change of voice".
He added: "They need someone who can come in and give the players a different type of training, a different type of belief - get them running about and show lots of enthusiasm.

"I don't think there are many managers who can come in and do a lot better. At the moment you can look around Europe and there is nobody available who is better than Jose Mourinho."
United's poor start to the season has included a 3-0 home defeat by Tottenham and a 1-0 loss at promoted Wolves.
The Old Trafford club - who are 11th in the Premier League - also suffered a shock defeat by Derby in the EFL Cup third round.

Former England captain Robson, who won three Premier League titles and two FA Cups with United, said he did not see much improvement in the team's performances from last season to this.

He said: "There is no getting away from the fact that it has been a poor start to the season. You have to look at the manager and say: 'Have you got the right tools to do the job?'

"At the moment, 100% definitely, yes. But when you are at a club like Manchester United - especially when things are not going well - you are always going to be under pressure. The players look as if they are not playing for him."

Former England boss Robson warns current coach Mourinho about the dangers of burning out his career. Mourinho has won trophies at every club he has managed, but Robson says he should not be judged solely on his success. Mourinho was appointed Tottenham manager in November 2019 and although he led the club to a Carabao Cup final and a Europa League final last season, they finished in sixth place in the Premier League.

Robson said he did not believe the "maverick" Portuguese manager would end his career at Spurs. "They [Spurs] are a top, top club, but it's difficult to break that top four at the moment," he added. "That's where Jose wants to be - he wants to be winning league titles. "I think he would like to get back into the Premier League and have another crack at trying to win the title."

Mourinho succeeded Robson as manager of Porto in 2002 after he had guided the Portuguese side to a Champions League triumph a year earlier. He went on to win the competition again with Barcelona in 2006, Inter Milan in 2010 and Real Madrid in 2013.

Robson said it was important his old friend did not "rush into things" after leaving Spurs. "He's a serial winner, and he wants to win, but he needs to calm down a bit, and not rush into things," he added. "He can't keep moving every year or two. "I hope he doesn't burn out his career because he's a good manager."

Business confidence dips in Japan

Business confidence among Japan's biggest manufacturers has fallen for the first time in six months, a survey shows.

The Bank of Japan's (BOJ) quarterly "tankan" survey shows the headline confidence index, which measures sentiment among larger manufacturers, fell to plus eight in January from plus 19 in October.

The BOJ said uncertainty over the US government's handling of the debt ceiling and disruptions caused by the spread of the Omicron variant of coronavirus were among the reasons for the decline.

However, it also said manufacturers were more optimistic about the outlook for the next few months.

"The tankan results show that corporate Japan's mood has darkened," Marcel Thieliant, senior Japan economist at Capital Economics, said in a research note.

"The decline in the current situation index was driven by smaller manufacturers, suggesting that the hit to activity from Omicron has been fairly modest so far," he added.

Japan has not been hit as hard by the pandemic as many other countries, but it has been hit by supply chain problems, which have hurt manufacturing.

The country has also been hit by a fall in tourism and the decision by officials to impose restrictions on dining out.

Japan has recorded more than 18,000 deaths from COVID-19, but has avoided the kind of surge in cases seen in the US and some other countries.

Business confidence in Japan has dipped for the first time in six months, a Bank of Japan survey shows. The central bank's quarterly "tankan" survey shows the headline confidence index, which measures sentiment among large manufacturers, fell to 8 points from 10 in September. The figure was below economists' expectations and down from the 14 points recorded in June, shortly after the invasion of Ukraine began.

A sharp decline in the outlook for electronics and automobiles was a key factor behind the drop, the Bank of Japan said. The survey also showed that sentiment among large non-manufacturers fell two points to 22.

However, the dip in confidence was less severe than many had predicted, and the latest reading is still above the threshold of zero, which separates optimism from pessimism.

Many Japanese firms expect conditions to improve in the coming months, the survey suggested. About 43% of large manufacturers said they expected conditions to improve over the next three months, while only 12% said they expected them to worsen.

Broadband takes on TV viewing

TV viewing figures on all formats have fallen year on year for the first time since records began, official data shows.

The audience research body Barb said analogue and digital TV viewers watched an average of 3.4 hours of television a day in April, down from 3.6 hours in 2007.

But broadband usage - including web and video - soared, with uploads and downloads increasing by more than 40%.

The figures reflect the growing popularity of the internet as a source of news, entertainment and communication.

They also show the average UK adult now spends almost four hours a day using the internet, compared with less than three hours watching TV.

Of those, more than 80% use the internet daily compared with 60% who watch TV every day.

The data also reveals the average time spent online has increased by at least a quarter in the last year, with the average user spending 14.7 hours a week online, up from 11.8 hours in 2007.

"These figures confirm the directional shift of media consumption in the UK, away from linear broadcast TV towards on-demand TV and broadband," said Jane Ostler, lead analyst at media buyer Carat.

"However, it's too early to state that the age of TV is over, or that the future is solely online," she added.

TV still attracts the largest audiences, but the data does suggest that people are watching less television as they spend more time using the internet.

The research also shows that the way people watch TV is changing as they time-shift programmes using digital video recorders (DVRs) such as Sky Plus or Virgin Plus.

This allows them to watch what they want, when they want, and fast forward through the adverts.

Some 42.5% of TV sets in the UK are now connected to DVRs, an increase of more than a quarter in the last year, according to the data.

The average number of channels viewed by each TV set is also falling, from 26.1 in 2007 to 24.9 last month.

But TV still dominates the media landscape, attracting far larger audiences than the internet.

More than 28 million people - 90% of the UK adult population - watch TV every week, compared with 20 million who go online daily.

Sales of televisions are dropping as broadband takes over viewing, an industry report has suggested. The report, from the consultancy Deloitte, suggests that sales of "smart TVs" capable of connecting to the internet have risen by 28% over the past year. It claims that many people now regard streaming television shows and films as "a basic need", and that one in three households now has a smart TV, with no traditional TV service.

Traditional paid-for TV subscriptions have fallen by 400,000 in the past year, according to industry figures. Ben Perkins, head of telecoms, media and entertainment at Deloitte, said: "People no longer feel the need to be sat in front of the TV to watch their favourite shows, so we're seeing smartphones, tablets and computers being used more frequently for TV and video viewing."

The rise of streaming services such as Netflix, Amazon Prime and Now TV has been cited as the main reason for the shift. Perkins said that within the next five years, most TV viewing will be done on smartphones, tablets and computers.

India's second-largest state-owned oil firm is in talks to buy Russian oil assets owned by Yukos, the bankrupt oil company.

On Monday, Indian Oil Corp (IOC) announced it had signed a "non-binding letter of intent" to buy Yukos' core production unit, Yukos Enterprise, for $1.9bn.

The move comes as Indian firms are snatching up energy assets abroad because of domestic shortages.

Yukos went bankrupt last year after the Russian government seized its oil assets to pay off massive tax bills.

The deal, which still needs the approval of Russian authorities, would give state-owned Indian Oil access to Yukos' oil-producing unit, which has a daily output of 94,000 barrels of oil a day.

"There is no doubt that this acquisition will be a major step towards Indian Oil achieving its strategic mission of reaching a production level of 40 million tonnes of crude oil and equivalent hydrocarbons by 2011-12 and becoming a leading international oil and gas company," said Indian Oil Chairman M.S. Srinivasan.

Indian Oil said it expected the deal to go through by the end of the year, as long as "due diligence" inspections of Yukos' assets turned up no problems.

The Indian firm said it was also discussing the possibility of supplying gas to Russia's Far East region.

New Delhi has been trying to strengthen economic ties with Moscow.

Last year, Russia and India signed a nuclear co-operation agreement and an accord to set up a joint venture to extract titanium.

An Indian oil company is among the bidders for Yukos' former assets in Russia.
  
 India's Oil and Natural Gas Corporation (ONGC) is bidding for oilfields in Siberia previously owned by Yukos, the Russian oil company that owed billions in taxes and was broken up and sold off in 2004. 
  
 The company is bidding for a 49% stake in the Vankorneft consortium, which owns the Vankor oilfield in Siberia. ONGC is bidding against India's Vedanta and Russia's Rosneft for the stake. 
  
 The winner will own a half-share in the consortium, with Russia's Rosneft owning the other half. Rosneft has already bought a 20% stake in the field, and is expected to buy a further 30% stake. 
  
 The acquisition would be a further step in ONGC's strategy of acquiring foreign oilfields to supplement its fast-depleting domestic oilfields.

Ask Jeeves has joined the web log market with the acquisition of Bloglines.

The company has also launched Ask Blog, a custom search-powered weblog, and re-designed Bloglines to work more smoothly with the new service.

Bloglines boasts three million users who use the free service to track more than 300 million feeds.

It is the latest company to enter the blog search market, following Google's acquisition of Blogsearch.org, and Technorati's new blog search service.

Ask Blog and Bloglines are being promoted as a package, although they can be used separately.

The weblog comes with a choice of themes, and users can roll their own with HTML and CSS.

There is also an option to add Google AdSense so the owner can make money from the blog.

Ask Blog has a sidebar on the right with links to Bloglines, a to-do list, and a list of "hot" searches on Ask.com.

The searches are powered by Teoma technology, which Ask Jeeves bought last year.

"We believe there are going to be lots of niches in the weblog space, just like there are going to be lots of niches in the RSS (Really Simple Syndication) reader space," said Jason Shellen, co-founder of Bloglines, based in San Francisco.

"We feel there's going to be a place for simple, basic weblog services where you can get up and running quickly, and probably a place for much more elaborate, much more feature-rich products," he added.

Bloglines, which will remain a separate service, has also been re-designed with a greater emphasis on "search per feed", and each feed can be searched individually.

"If you look at weblog search today, it's really returning searches based on the meta-data of weblogs, the titles of weblogs, and the brief descriptions," said Mr Shellen.

"What we're trying to do is allow people to search the full text of every single feed that's in the system," he added.

Ever since US web giant Yahoo! bought search engine Ask Jeeves last March, the once-proud butler has been chained to a desk and made to work on the inventory, leaving his UK counterpart to face the technological tornado known as the web log or blog revolution on his own. 

But now GB Jeeves has finally been given the chance to join in. "The internet has become a vital medium for communications, but all the worthwhile blogs seem to be American," says the British Jeeves, polishing his bowler hat. "It's about time that a Brit offered a fresh perspective on the world." 

And so, from today, Ask Jeeves will provide a custom search portal for the blog entries of the day, as well as a hit list of the most popular blogs. The UK version of the site will also carry a round-up of the best blogs on a monthly basis. 

It is the first time Ask Jeeves has devoted such attention to the blog phenomenon. "Blogs are a fantastic source of information and opinion," says a spokeswoman for the company. "By highlighting topical blogs on our UK search portal, we are making it easy for consumers to find the information they need, when they need it." 

In recent months, blogs have begun to appear at the top of search engine rankings, pushing aside more established news sources. According to a recent study by the Pew Internet and American Life project, an astonishing 23 million Americans have begun publishing their own writings, an increase of 17 million since March last year. 

But until now, the blog explosion has been an exclusively American phenomenon. According to the statistical blog Technorati, only 5 per cent of the world's blogs are produced outside the US. Of these, only a handful are updated regularly, and even fewer are written in English. Britain supplies just 3 per cent of the world's bloggers. 

This may be about to change. According to the Internet trend-spotters at the Pew Centre, non-US bloggers are catching up with their American counterparts. The British are reportedly most enthusiastic, with nearly half of all surfers having looked at blogs, and a quarter saying they would like to become bloggers themselves. 

Ask Jeeves's new blog search service will concentrate on UK blogs, but users will also be able to read about such diverse subjects as gastronomy, showbiz and the US television series Lost, courtesy of the California-based Ask Jeeves Inc.

For decades, a mystery has swirled around a group of postcards sold to a British collector in the late 1940s.

Did the artist Paul Gauguin secretly create them?

For years, collectors and art experts have debated the authorship of the colorful images produced in the South Pacific island nation of Tahiti.

Now, a new study has provided some tantalizing answers.

Researchers at the University of Chicago and the Art Institute of Chicago say scientific analysis of the pigments used in the postcards correspond to those used by Gauguin.

They also discovered that some of the postcards were produced on paper watermarked with a distinctive "CV" symbol, which was used by a printer in Paris that had a business relationship with the artist.

"We believe this discovery is extremely significant," said Susan Alyson Stein, an assistant curator at the Art Institute of Chicago.

"These findings, combined with extensive archival research, add up to a compelling body of evidence that Gauguin made the postcards." 

The research was published in December 2022 in the academic journal Analytical Chemistry.

The story of the mysterious postcards begins in the years after Gauguin's death in 1903. 

According to the study, a woman who was living in Tahiti at the time came into possession of a group of postcards bearing Gauguin's signature and sent them to a friend in France. 

The recipient later showed the postcards to a French art dealer, who expressed interest in purchasing them. The woman sent him a batch of more than 100 postcards. 

Years later, the dealer sold the collection to a British collector who retained the postcards until his death in 1947. 

His estate put the collection up for sale, and it was purchased by a London art dealer who later sold individual postcards to collectors around the world. 

The Art Institute of Chicago purchased a collection of 14 postcards in 2013. 

Researchers spent years examining the postcards and conducting scientific analysis of the pigments and paper. They also traveled to Paris to examine documents from the printer that produced the postcards.

"Our research revealed that the same printer that collaborated with Gauguin also produced the postcards, including the 'CV' watermarked paper," said Alison Smiley, a research assistant professor at the University of Chicago.

The study also found that the postcards were produced using a type of paper that was not commercially available in Tahiti at the time, adding to the evidence that Gauguin was involved in their production.

Faced with the end of China's "golden economic period", some Beijing residents are reassessing their relationships and pursuing spiritual enlightenment.

China's breakneck growth has lifted millions out of poverty but it has also contributed to damaging the environment and many are now willing to pay the price for a greener tomorrow.

For freelance photographer Gao Shan, the surge in environmentally-friendly habits is partly a result of a mounting anxiety about the future.

"Many people are beginning to realize that the environment and our lives are connected," he says. "We're waking up to that.

"In the past, people only cared about making money and didn't care about environmental protection. Now, with the economy slowing, they're starting to realize that we must protect the environment for the sake of our children and grandchildren."

But challenges remain, he says. "Some people say that you can't live a good life if you don't own an apartment or a car, but I believe that we can have a happy life without these things if we have a healthy environment."

When Beijing was hit by coronavirus in early 2020, the city's notorious air pollution largely cleared, raising hopes that the pandemic might kickstart a green revolution.

But the return to "normal" also saw emissions rise again. And despite the recent boost in new renewable energy infrastructure, China is still heavily reliant on coal, which fuelled the boom years.

This is partly because China has pledged to achieve carbon neutrality by 2060 and reach peak emissions before 2030.

But the country is also grappling with the fallout of President Xi Jinping's signature Belt and Road Initiative (BRI), a multi-billion-dollar infrastructure scheme that has seen China lend to countries in return for commodities.

These loans have left China with a problem of its own, as recipient countries struggle to repay the money. This is thwarting China's attempt to open up new markets, and is likely to impact its trading capabilities as demand for its products wanes.

The country's "zero-COVID" policy has also hurt its economy, as lockdowns and travel restrictions snarl supply chains and leave exporters unable to fulfill orders.

Adding to this perfect storm is the US's pivot to Asia, which some experts believe will hamper China's economic ascent.

While the US is not the only country to be flirting with protectionism, it is increasingly clear that the superpower will use its economic might as a weapon, creating trading blocs that shut out China.

The prolonged period of historically low inflation appears to be ending, after more than a decade in most major economies.

Inflation is being driven up by the immediate knock to the economy from the Covid pandemic and the war in Ukraine, as well as the reversal of policy by major central banks.

For years, ultra-low interest rates and massive bond-buying schemes have helped drive down the cost of living. But with inflation now running at multi-decade highs in many countries, central banks are raising interest rates and putting their monetary policy tools on ice.

France has switched on its first digital television transmitter as part of a plan to improve broadcasting.

The transmitter at Tourves in the south of France was switched on at 09:00 local time (08:00 GMT) on Friday.

France's four existing TV networks will be broadcast digitally, alongside new free and pay-TV services.

Digital television requires a set top box to work, but TV sets with built-in digital receivers are also available.

The government expects half of all French households to have digital television by 2007.

Digital TV will offer better picture and sound quality than existing analogue signals and there will be more channels available, many of them in high definition.

It will also free up space for other uses, such as mobile phones and emergency services, because different signals can be used for different purposes.

France is one of the last European countries to adopt the new system

The UK completed its digital switchover in October 2012 and Spain finished earlier this year.

Italy has also started its switchover, while Germany and the Netherlands plan to complete theirs by 2022.

France will this week become the first country to require televisions to include digital tuners, in a move that could boost sales of LCD and plasma screens. The digital switchover, which begins on Tuesday, has been widely publicised in France for months and has prompted a surge in the sale of flatscreen TVs. From Tuesday, broadcasters will stop broadcasting on the country's four analogue channels, which for years have been able to be received anywhere in France. Full details of the digitisation process, and the names of the towns where analogue transmission will end, can be found on the website of France's public service broadcaster, France Televisions. Those who do not receive their television signal via satellite or cable, and who watch analogue broadcasts on a cathode ray tube TV, face having to buy a digital decoder or a new digital TV. 

Digital decoders, which cost about €100 (£65), are slightly cheaper than a basic LCD TV, which starts at about €150. Digital tuners are already included in all LCD and plasma TVs and sales have benefited from the run-up to the switchover. "This catalyst for digitising television has allowed us to regain market share in television sales, which had been slipping since the beginning of the year," said Patrice Brehmer, an executive at Fnac, the French high-street electronics retailer. About half of all French households already have digital television, either because they receive satellite or cable television, or because they have bought a TV with a digital tuner. 

According to the latest figures from GfK, a market research company, about 40 per cent of the French population plan to buy a digital TV or decoder in the next year. "The French have reacted reasonably to information campaigns conducted by broadcasters since the beginning of the year," said François Barrault, the director of the digital economy at the Ministry of Industry. "The French are aware of the digitisation process." The experience in France will be closely watched in Britain, where a digital switchover is due to take place in 2010. 

British broadcasters have already started to run information campaigns, but full-scale trials will not take place until next year. Michael Grade, the BBC's chairman, said last week that the corporation was working on the assumption that people would have digital television by 2010. "That is why we have consciously driven forward the take-up of digital television," he said. "Some 52 per cent of the population has already converted, and that will grow."

Ballot papers for the Northern Ireland Assembly have gone missing, just hours before people were due to start voting in local elections.

Returned papers from voters who opted to vote by post were due to be opened and counted on Saturday.

But election officers have revealed that papers sent by post from several polling stations have not arrived.

Party monitors are now seeking assurances that the missing votes will not affect the result of the election.

Election officer John Petrie said every effort was being made to locate the missing packets.

"We are carrying out an extensive search inside and outside of our buildings, in bins, and with our courier," he said.

"This is not a satisfactory situation and we will provide further information as soon as we can," he added.

The missing packets were from five out of the city's 80 polling stations.

It is believed the missing ballots were from a small number of polling stations in Belfast.

"There is no excuse, none whatsoever, this is absolutely unacceptable that ballot boxes have gone missing," he said.

"This is unprecedented, this has never happened before."

The SDLP's Alex Attwood said the situation was "unbelievable".

"Voters are entitled to believe that their vote will be counted, that votes are not going to disappear," he said.

"This is the most fundamental issue of democracy and it is an absolute requirement that every vote is counted."

The chairman of the UK's Electoral Commission, Roger Baker, said the commission was aware of the issue and was "looking into it".

"This is an operational matter for the local returning officer," he added.

Counting of votes begins on Sunday morning.

The Anglo-Nigerian writer Bernardine Evaristo has won the Booker Prize for her novel Girl, Woman, Other.

The novel tells the stories of 12 characters, mostly black women, living in Britain.

The 63-year-old reacted to winning the prize, worth £52,500 ($66,000), by lifting her arms in the air and laughing.

She described the book as "a celebration of heterogeneity".

The announcement was made at a dinner in London's Guildhall, with the shortlisted authors watching.

The previous winner was Anna Burns in 2018 for her novel Milkman.

They also wanted to encourage authors to enter their novels for the prize.

The Booker Prize is open to writers of any nationality, writing in English.

The prize money for the Booker has increased this year from £50,000 to £52,500.

The increase marks the first time the prize has risen above £50,000 in its history.

The veteran Nigerian author, Buchi Emecheta, has died at 74.

Her debut novel, Concubine, was published in 1966, and she went on to become one of the world's best-known female writers, with more than 20 novels and several short stories and essays.

She died in London on Monday, her family said, without giving details.

"Buchi was a great storyteller and her books will continue to be read and loved by readers all over the world," they said in a statement released by the United Kingdom's Guardian newspaper.

The novelist had been suffering from breast cancer.

Her most famous books include The Joys of Motherhood, published in 1979, and Double Yoke, published in 1973. The latter was adapted for a film in 1982.

She was appointed officer of the Order of the British Empire (OBE) in 2006 for services to literature.

Her novels, mostly set in Nigeria and featuring strong female characters, typically tackled issues such as polygamy and the role of women in society.

She once said of her writing: "If my books can help somebody, if they can make somebody understand somebody else's life better, then I have achieved something."

Born in Lagos in 1944, Emecheta moved to the UK with her husband in 1962. It was there that she began to write, following the breakdown of her marriage.

After the publication of her first novel, she would go on to publish at least a book a year.

One of her most recent novels, The New Tribe, was published in 2004. It told the story of a group of women who form a community in Nigeria, and their struggles with the traditions of marriage and family.

In a 2004 interview with the Guardian, Emecheta said she did not believe she had ever been properly recognised for her work.

"I don't think my books have been taken as seriously as they should be," she said. "Perhaps it's because I'm a woman. Perhaps it's because I'm black. I don't know."

Google, Microsoft, Amazon and other companies are joining forces to overhaul how people navigate the internet.

They are building a new system for the internet's naming system, which has remained largely unchanged since the 1980s.

The companies want to replace the "domain name system" with a more secure alternative.

It is hoped the change will make it harder for criminals to use the system to carry out cyber attacks.

The current system means that anyone can buy a domain name, such as "bbc.com", and use it to create a website.

This has led to the creation of many fraudulent websites, which have similar domain names to legitimate websites, such as "faceboook.com" instead of "facebook.com".

Asbestos is a material that was once widely used in construction, but can cause the lung disease mesothelioma.

Galliford Try said the provision related to allegations dating back as far as the 1960s, when its businesses were involved in construction and property development.

It said it had been contacted by about 650 claimants, but expected that number to rise to about 2,000.

It is a landmark moment in a long-running saga that has been marked by extraordinary courtroom scenes and revelations of corporate cover-ups. The Bank of England is set to keep interest rates on hold as it weighs up the prospects of a slowdown in the global economy and the impact of Brexit.

The Bank's rate-setting Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) is expected to keep the cost of borrowing at 0.5% when it announces its decision at midday on Thursday.

Since the MPC's last meeting in February, the mood in the global economy has changed markedly, with risks from mainland Europe, the US and China.

While the UK economy has continued to grow, analysts say the MPC is likely to want to see the impact of the Brexit negotiations on the UK's economic performance before making any moves.

At its last meeting, the MPC voted unanimously to keep rates at their current level, but two members, Ian McCafferty and Michael Saunders, voted to raise rates in February.

What's more, the MPC said that "some withdrawal of monetary stimulus was likely to be appropriate over the coming months" if the economy evolved as expected.

But since then, figures showing a slowdown in the economy towards the end of last year have raised questions about the strength of the UK's economic performance.

Some members are thought to want to curb inflation - which is running at more than double the Bank's target - by raising rates.

But others are thought to want to wait to see the impact of the new variant on the economy.

Economic data released on Friday showed that the cost of living rose by 4.2% in the year to October, down from a peak of 5.1% in July.

The MPC's decision will be announced at midday on Thursday.

Russian energy giant Yukos has lost a court battle with Deutsche Bank over $600m of debts.

Moscow's Arbitration Court ruled that Yukos must pay the bank the principal debt plus interest accrued, minus any proceeds from the sale of two Yukos subsidiaries.

The decision leaves the door open for further litigation between the two companies.

Yukos had sought to have more than $2.5bn of its debt to Deutsche Bank written off, claiming the bank pressured it into bad loans.

The energy firm declared bankruptcy in August and its main production unit was subsequently taken over by state-owned rival Rosneft.

Yukos has been battling a $3.4bn tax bill presented by the Russian government, which it says is politically motivated.

The case has pitted Russia's largest company against the German bank and concerned loans made in 2003 and 2004.

Yukos had claimed the bank pressured it into bad loans by threatening to withdraw credit lines, and that the bank had acted in collusion with the tax authorities.

But the court said in its ruling there was "no evidence" of this.

However, it did say that Deutsche Bank was in part to blame for the debt, because it had approved the loans after having been informed of the tax disputes.

The ruling suggested the bank would have been within its rights not to grant the loans at all, given the potential tax risks.

But the court ruled that Yukos had failed to prove its case for writing off the debt, and ordered it to pay up.

Yukos said it would study the ruling before deciding on its response.

Home phones face uncertain future as mobiles dominate communications

The demise of the landline in the UK is confirmed in a new study which shows it has dropped below 50% of households for the first time.

Industry regulator Ofcom said phones plugged into the wall were now in just under 50% of homes. It said this trend was likely to continue as mobile phone use exploded.

The study also revealed that the typical UK adult now owns 1.75 mobile phones.

Ofcom said this "exploding" use of mobiles had promoted a culture of "continuous connectivity".

The regulator's annual Communications Market Report found 47.7% of households only have a mobile phone and no landline.

That figure has jumped from 39% in 2012.

Ofcom said in 1998 - the first year it conducted the survey - that just 22% of households only had a mobile.

"Landlines are clearly becoming a thing of the past," said James Barford, author of the Ofcom report.

"In 1998, the majority of phones in the UK were landlines, with only 22% of households having mobiles as their only phone.

"Fast forward to today and the situation has radically changed - with nearly half of all households now relying solely on mobiles."

The study also revealed that 92% of people now own a mobile, a jump from 88% last year.

This proliferation of mobiles has helped fuel a 28% jump in the amount of time each day that people spend on phones - from 88 minutes to 114 minutes each day over the past year, Ofcom said.

The study also showed that texting is the most popular activity on mobiles - one in five texts are sent or received every day, with the typical mobile user sending 41 texts each month.

In contrast, the number of voice calls made on mobiles has fallen for the first time, dropping from 102 calls each month to 96.

Ofcom said this showed that voice calls were "becoming a less important part of the mobile experience".

The study also revealed that nearly three-quarters (71%) of people have a smartphone, while 4G coverage now reaches 90% of the UK population.

But the report warned that not everyone had benefited from the move to digital, with 10% of the UK's geographical area - land and sea - lacking 4G coverage.

It was once one of the most ubiquitous sights in Britain - a landline phone perched on a table, with a spiral cord stretching onto the sofa where someone sat, idly chatting away.

But the era of the home phone may be coming to an end - signalled by telecoms giant BT's decision to stop selling them altogether.

Landlines - once considered a vital component of the information superhighway - have been supplanted by mobile phones. The telecoms regulator Ofcom says that 65% of households now have a "phone-free" home, with adults and children communicating via mobile phones.

According to market research firm GfK, there were 16 million residential landlines in Britain at the end of 2021, down from 18 million two years earlier.

And Ofcom said last year that landlines were likely to disappear completely within the next decade. It found that even older people, who might have relied on landlines in the past, were turning to mobile phones.

The switch away from landlines has been rapid. Ten years ago, almost every home had one.

Since then, many have decided they do not need an additional phone socket in their homes, and have cancelled their landlines, or not taken one out when moving into a new property. Some have even ripped out the wiring altogether.

BT's decision to stop selling landlines - which Ofcom approved - is not expected to have an immediate impact on existing customers.

The company said landline connections were increasingly being used only for broadband, and that its focus would be on providing digital phone services, such as VoIP (Voice over Internet Protocol), which allows people to make calls over the internet.

But what does the disappearance of the home phone mean for Britain - and could it leave people behind?

Less socially inclusive

The end of the landline "may risk further isolating those who are already socially excluded", Ofcom warned last year.

It pointed to older people and those on low incomes as potentially being most affected, because they are less likely to own a mobile phone.

In 2019, Ofcom found that 8% of people did not have a mobile phone and 7% did not have home broadband, with low-income households significantly less likely to have access to the internet.

Although Ofcom does not link these figures directly to landlines, it says that for those who do not have internet access, "retaining landline connectivity will be important".

Last year, the Nigerian government announced that it would give cocoa farmers a boost of 50,000 tonnes of fertiliser.

The dollar has slid ahead of the new year, as investors bet that interest rates will go up less quickly in the US than hoped.

But it came under pressure again on Tuesday, as easing inflation and weaker-than-expected retail sales reinforced the view that the Fed could take its foot off the gas when it comes to rate rises.

"The dollar is crumbling… as the Fed is falling behind the curve," Joseph Capurso, a currency strategist at Commonwealth Bank of Australia, told Reuters.

"The market has priced out almost any chance of a 50 basis point hike in February and is pricing only about a 10% chance of a 25 basis point hike," he added.

The euro meanwhile has rallied and was trading at $1.0581 on Tuesday, a level not seen in six months.

Sterling also extended its gains to trade at $1.2346, a rise of more than 3.6% from its December low.

While the pound remains vulnerable to more volatility, it has been helped by data showing the UK is weathering the cost of living crisis better than expected.

The greenback was weighed down by thin holiday trade and the prospect of a more aggressive Federal Reserve, as markets priced in a policy interest rate hike of 50 basis points from the US central bank at its meeting next week.

The euro, meanwhile, held steady after advancing last week, as investors grew more confident that the European Central Bank will raise interest rates in March. That lifted the single currency to its highest level against the dollar since late November.

This resilience suggests that the worst of the euro's selloff – which began in September and intensified in the aftermath of the Bank of England's surprise rate hike – may be over, at least for now.

The pound also strengthened on Monday, with the currency benefiting from a more buoyant mood in global financial markets and firmer commodity prices.

But she always wanted to recreate the C64 - "as a kid it was my dream to have my own computer company and I never thought it would happen". And with the 30th anniversary of the C64 approaching, she decided it was time to fulfil that dream. "I finally just decided to go for it," she says. "It's been my hobby for the last two years."

Ms Ellsworth's new C64 is actually a hybrid computer. "It's not a pure C64, it's got a modern processor in there so you can run newer programs," she says. "But all the original peripherals work with it - you can use the original joystick, the original keyboard; it supports the original BASIC language. "It can do some modern stuff too, it's not just for playing old games. It runs Debian Linux, so you can do typical things you can do with a PC."

Once revered as a pioneer of personal computing, the Commodore brand now lives on through a quirky Canadian startup that is seeking to revive its legacy.

The company that once brought the world the Commodore 64 has been resuscitated multiple times by different owners since its original bankruptcy in 1994.

The most recent iteration is Toronto-based Commodore International Ltd., owned by former rock star and current businessman, Andy Ashfield.

Since acquiring the rights to the Commodore brand in 2020, Ashfield has been trying to breathe new life into the company by developing a line of modern PCs and laptops bearing the iconic name.

The most recent product announced by Commodore is the Commodore Extreme, a high-end gaming PC that starts at $2,495. It boasts some serious specs, including up to a 18-core Intel i9 processor, an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 graphics card, and up to 64GB of RAM.

The Commodore Extreme is certainly not cheap, but it is a powerful machine designed for gamers who need a lot of power under the hood.

Whether Commodore can succeed in its latest rebirth remains to be seen. The company has a long road ahead of it if it wants to recapture even a fraction of the success it found in the 1980s. 

It faces stiff competition from established players like Dell, HP, and Apple, not to mention a bevy of other gaming PC manufacturers like Alienware and Razer.

Still, Commodore enthusiasts remain hopeful that the brand can once again become a household name in the personal computing space.

Only time will tell if Commodore can find its way back to the top.

Everton's Scottish defender David Weir has played down his chances of making the cut for Euro 2008.

Weir, 33, was named the Scottish Football Writers' player of the year on Sunday.

The former Hearts man, who joined Everton in 2004, said: "It would be a dream come true but I'm not getting my hopes up."

Scotland have not qualified for a major tournament since the World Cup in France in 1998.

The Scots face Italy, France and Ukraine in Group B.

Weir was ever-present for David Moyes' side during the Premier League season, playing in all 38 matches as Everton finished in eighth place.

And he was delighted to pick up the award on Sunday, saying: "It's been a great week.

"To be voted the player of the year by your peers is a great honour - especially as the standard of Scottish football is so high just now.

"It was more difficult this year because players like Steven Fletcher and Kris Boyd had fantastic seasons."

Everton's young midfielder Tom Weir has cooled hopes of a quick return to European competition for the Toffees.

The 19-year-old, who made his senior Scotland debut in June, signed a new Toffees deal in July.

"Hopefully, we can get back there but I think that's maybe a hope for the future for me," he told the Liverpool Echo.

"This season, first and foremost, we need to get the basics right, dig in as a team and look from there."

Weir made his Everton debut last season and has made three further first-team appearances this term.

He was named on the bench for the Premier League trip to Manchester United in October and the Carabao Cup win over Manchester City last month.

Title: Bath faced with Tindall ultimatum

Subtitle: Sport: Rugby union: Bath have been given until Friday to resolve their dispute with England centre Mike Tindall.

If they can't reach an agreement the 26-year-old will leave the club.

Tindall wants to stay at The Rec but has been frustrated by the lack of a new contract offer.

He has been offered a deal by French giants Stade Francais.

The BBC's Jim Bear on Tindall: "He is one of the best centres in the country, if not the best. There is no doubt he is a world-class player. "He is also a local boy who has come through the ranks at Bath and is very popular with the fans. It would be a big blow to the club if he were to leave."

Bear on the offers Tindall has received: "There has been a lot of interest from France and even though Stade Francais are not one of the top clubs in France, the offer they have made to Tindall is worth around £350,000 a year. "That is about double what he is currently earning at Bath and the kind of money the club cannot really match. "You are also looking at the fact he is married to Zara Phillips, Princess Anne's daughter, and they have just had a baby son, so the attraction of staying in this country may not be as great for him as it once was."

Tindall was reportedly unhappy that he was not offered a new contract during the summer and, with less than a year left on his current deal, he is free to talk to other clubs.

The BBC's Bear adds: "There is a feeling that Tindall could have been offered a new contract during the summer to keep the peace and from the club's point of view they would have been happy for him to stay. But for whatever reason that offer never came. "Now he has basically said, if I don't get an offer by Friday, I am going."

If Bath do not offer Tindall a new deal, they will receive nothing if he moves to France but could receive up to £350,000 if he moves to another English club.

Bear concludes: "There is a feeling that his preferred option would be to stay at Bath but that possibility is looking less likely with every passing day."

The mayor of Bath has warned that the city could face an ultimatum over the future of the historic Royal Crescent. 

The crescent, a row of majestic Georgian houses built in 1767, is used as the setting for the hit Netflix series _The Crown_. 

The show rents accommodation from the local authority, Bath and North East Somerset Council, as a production base, and returns in the new year for series five. 

But mayor Kevin Guy says the council may have to choose between keeping the crescent as a tourist attraction, or renting it out as a location for _The Crown_. 

He said the council was considering applying for change of use planning permission, which could result in the city's iconic landmark becoming a tourist attraction and museum. 

The application would be likely to trigger a wave of objections from residents in the Royal Crescent who believe the council is exploiting its position as a freeholder of the property, and potentially putting it above its duty as a landlord.

Newcastle United are lining up a £3m bid for Chelsea's Nigeria international right-back Celestine Babayaro.

The Magpies' manager Graeme Souness sees the 24-year-old as the ideal replacement for injured England international Warren Barton.

Babayaro has struggled to establish himself in the Chelsea side since his move from Anderlecht two years ago.

He was linked with a move to Liverpool last season but stayed at Stamford Bridge - and has made just 12 starts for the Blues this season.

Ever since Newcastle's takeover by the Saudi Investment Fund, fans have been expecting big things. The Magpies have wasted no time in bringing in some big names, with the likes of Kieran Trippier, Chris Wood and Bruno Guimaraes all arriving for hefty fees. Now, they are linked with another exciting prospect in Dickson Etuhu's former teammate at Manchester City, Babayaro.

The 29-year-old is a versatile defender who can play anywhere across the back four. Babayaro is solid and reliable, and his experience could be vital for a Newcastle side looking to avoid relegation this season. The club has suffered a poor start to the season, and new manager Eddie Howe will be hoping to turn things around quickly.

The Nigerian international has struggled for game time at City this season, with John Stones, Aymeric Laporte and Ruben Dias ahead of him in the pecking order. With Newcastle in need of defensive reinforcements, Babayaro could be an excellent addition. It is yet to be seen if the Magpies can secure his signature in the current transfer window.
