UK retailer Next is to slow the rate of new store openings and the launch of its international websites after weak Christmas sales.

It said difficult trading conditions meant it would no longer reach its target of 650 stores.

Next currently has 540 stores and generates more than half of its £4.2bn sales online.

The retailer said sales in the 54 days since Christmas had been "strong" but added that the trading environment in the UK "remains challenging".

"In this environment we believe it is prudent to slow the rate of new space growth in the short term, and are today simplifying our store opening plans for the next financial year," the company said.

"We will open approximately 25 new stores during this period, compared to our original plan of c. 35.

"We will continue to open larger stores in our larger cities, but in the medium term will focus on meeting our customers' needs through our existing store estate, as well as enhancing our online offer."

Next also said the launch of its German website, planned for February, would be delayed.

It said the slowdown in store openings and the hold-up in the German launch were both "purely a result of the board's desire to maintain our strong financial position and to protect our profit margins".

The group said its full-year profit forecast of £790m remained unchanged.

 Shares in Next fell more than 8% in early trading on Thursday.

The update comes as retailers face challenging conditions on the High Street.

Last week, rival Marks & Spencer reported a 0.9% fall in like-for-like clothing and home sales in the 19 weeks to January 5.

However, M&S said its overall sales were up 3.1% in the same period, helped by growth in its food division.

In its update, Next said its total sales in the 54 days since Christmas had risen by 1.5% compared with the same period in 2018.

Within that, online sales were up 13.7% but in-store sales were down 5.2%.

The company said its clearance sale had been more successful than last year, with sales up by more than a third compared with 2018.

"We are pleased with our performance over the Christmas period," Next said.

"Our online business delivered growth in excess of our expectations whilst store like-for-like sales were in line with our planning.

"

Sales at Next fall in the first half of the year, as the cost of living crisis hits consumer spending.

The retailer said it was difficult to predict how its performance would fare in the second half.

Next said it had seen a slowdown in sales of higher margin, higher priced products.

The retailer added it was taking steps to mitigate the impact of the weaker demand by controlling costs. 

In recent months, it has seen a slowdown in sales in its retail stores.

Chief executive Lord Wolfson said: "We are not planning for a recession, but there are clear signs of consumer spending restraint."

He added that Next had not seen a "material impact" on full-price sales from the end of the government's windfall tax on oil and gas companies, which has resulted in lower energy prices.

The retailer said it had seen a "distinct change" in consumer behaviour in recent weeks with greater caution against rising prices.

Serena ends Sania Mirza's dream

World number one Serena Williams reached the fourth round of the Australian Open with a 6-2 6-3 victory over Hsieh Su-wei.

The American top seed has yet to drop a set in Melbourne as she chases a 20th Grand Slam title.

Williams, 33, has shown impressive form in her first three matches and she needed just over an hour to see off her Taiwanese opponent.

Mirza, who achieved a career-high ranking of 15 in 2009, is now ranked 65th in the world.

The Indian has won three Grand Slam titles - the 2005 US Open and the 2006 and 2010 Wimbledon women's doubles with Swiss great Martina Hingis.

Williams, who has won the Australian Open seven times, next plays Italy's Camila Giorgi, who beat Canada's Eugenie Bouchard 6-2 6-7 (5-7) 9-7 in the third round.

"I think I'm getting my rhythm and my fitness up for the next match," Williams, who is aiming to regain the world number one spot she lost to Romania's Simona Halep last year, said.

In a thrilling match, Serena Williams has ended Sania Mirza's dream of winning her first WTA title here at the Dubai Championships. Williams, who is the top seed here and ranked World No.1, survived a tough test from the talented Indian to win 6-2, 7-6(3).

Mirza, who had been suffering from a shoulder injury and only returned to the tour last month, showed no signs of rust as she served and volleyed her way to an early lead in the first set. However, the experienced American soon found her rhythm and started to dominate the match with her powerful groundstrokes.

Despite this loss, it has been a good week for Mirza, who had already exceeded her own expectations by reaching the semifinals. This was her best result on the tour since winning the Cincinnati Open in September 2012.

With this victory, Williams continues her good form ahead of the defense of her Australian Open title in January. Furthermore, the American has now won 14 consecutive matches since losing to Sloane Stephens in the semifinals of the US Open in September.

Williams will now face off against Carla Suárez Navarro in the final. This will be their second meeting within a week, as the American beat the Spaniard in the final of the Qatar Total Open in Doha last week.

Suárez Navarro, who is the fifth seed here, beat Czech player Lucie Šafářová 6-7(6), 6-3, 6-3 in the other semifinal today.

The dollar has hovered around 16-month lows against a basket of world currencies, as traders await the outcome of the Federal Reserve's meeting on interest rates.

The US central bank is widely expected to raise rates by 25 basis points to 0.5-0.75% as it begins to tighten monetary policy.

It comes as UK mortgage lending hits record highs, while the euro has gained against the dollar as investors bet on higher European interest rates.

Meanwhile, the dollar has slipped by more than 6% since the start of the year, with some investors betting that the Fed will not be able to raise rates because of concerns about the strength of the US economy.

Other investors are betting that, even if the central bank does raise rates, any increase will not last long as the Fed lacks the will to tighten policy sufficiently to drive down inflation.

Market players will be looking for clues as to how many times the Fed expects to raise rates this year, with estimates between three and seven times.

Any indication that the Fed will raise rates fewer times than investors currently expect would likely result in the dollar falling further, analysts say.

The dollar has hovered around record lows against a basket of other major currencies as markets brace for a pivotal Federal Reserve meeting on Wednesday.

The greenback slipped to a fresh two-decade low against the Japanese currency on Tuesday, as traders shifted to betting that the Fed will not raise rates this year, despite its recent hawkish signals.

The dollar index, which measures the currency against six major peers, traded just above 103, not far from last week's low of 102.93, which was the lowest level since December 2002.

The Japanese yen has been the main beneficiary of the dollar's weakness, as investors have flocked to the safe-haven currency in recent weeks amid growing concerns over the US economic outlook and geopolitical tensions.

The yen has rallied over 6% against the dollar since the start of the year, and traded at 129.85 to the dollar on Tuesday, not far from last week's high of 129.40, which was the strongest level since November 1998.

The euro has also benefited from the dollar's weakness, and the single currency traded at $1.08 on Tuesday, not far from last week's high of $1.09, which was the highest level since June 2020.

The British pound also traded at a fresh two-decade high against the dollar, as the currency benefited from bets that the Bank of England will raise interest rates again next month.

Soaring oil 'hits world economy'

The soaring price of oil has pushed up the rate of inflation in the world's biggest economies, forcing households to cut back on spending, according to a leading economic think-tank.

The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) said that high oil prices, partly due to the war in Ukraine, were the main reason for the jump in inflation.

It said the price of Brent crude oil would have to fall to around $88 a barrel to bring inflation back to the average level seen over the past decade.

The think-tank said that inflation was likely to be higher than predicted, and that central banks may have to raise interest rates even higher than expected.

The OECD's outlook for the world economy is gloomier than three months ago, with inflation expected to be higher and growth slower.

The organisation expects the global economy to grow by 3.1% this year, down from its forecast of 3.8% made in November.

It also expects inflation to be higher, at 6.3%, up from its previous forecast of 5.6%.

The OECD warned that the war in Ukraine was creating "additional uncertainty" for the world economy.

It said that the war, along with other factors such as the price of oil and the spread of Covid-19, were the key reasons for the downward revision of its growth forecast.

The organisation said it expected the US economy to grow by 2.4% this year, down from its previous forecast of 3.0%.

It also expects the UK economy to grow by 3.2% this year, down from its previous forecast of 4.0%.

High inflation has forced central banks to raise interest rates, which has hit economic growth.

The OECD said it expected the US Federal Reserve to raise interest rates to 5.1% by the end of 2022, up from its previous forecast of 4.1%.

It also expects the Bank of England to raise interest rates to 4.0% by the end of 2022, up from its previous forecast of 3.0%.

The price of oil has hit its highest level for years after Russia invaded Ukraine. For some countries this is proving to be a major problem. How is this affecting the global economy? And what can be done about it?

The price of crude oil has been increasing since Russia invaded Ukraine. It had already been rising before the war began, but the conflict has accelerated the process. On Monday, prices touched a record high of $139.13 per barrel.

This is hitting households across the world by pushing up the cost of living. The everyday products we rely on, from food to clothing, are all affected by oil price increases.

The cost of oil has a huge effect on the global economy. It affects the prices of raw materials, contributes to inflation, and increases the cost of trading. It also has a significant impact on the environment.

Many countries have called for an investigation into price gouging. The EU has been working to reduce its dependence on Russian oil. Both the US and the UK have announced plans to release oil from their strategic reserves, and the EU will hold talks on Tuesday about a coordinated release.

There are a few reasons for the price hike. One is that the war in Ukraine has caused a shortage of oil, as Russia is a major producer. This has caused the price of oil to increase.

The other is that the world economy is beginning to recover from the Covid-19 pandemic. As a result, there is a high demand for oil. Since the beginning of 2022, demand for oil has outstripped supply.

Hundreds of people have marched through the Scottish borders in a rally to save a railway line.

The Edinburgh-Carlisle line via Hawick is at risk of losing its direct rail link to Scotland's capital.

Campaigners say it is an important economic and social link for the region - they gathered in Hawick on Saturday to show their support for the line.

Scotland's Transport Minister Derek Mackay joined the march.

He said the Scottish government would continue to put pressure on UK ministers to save the line.

Mr Mackay said: "People in these communities rely on this line, whether it is to get to work, school or to visit family and friends.

"It is not just about the railway, it is about the future of these towns and these communities."

In June, a report into the future of the line by Scottish Affairs Committee said the decision on whether to keep the direct link should be taken in Scotland, rather than in Westminster.

The line via Hawick currently allows passengers from Scotland to travel south to Carlisle and on to Manchester, Birmingham and beyond.

If the direct link is scrapped, passengers would have to change at Edinburgh.

Campaign group Saving the Waverley Line said it was "essential" to the social and economic well-being of the Borders.

Spokesman Alan Dorans said: "People here feel very strongly about the issue. There is a great deal of anger about the way the line has been ignored.

"The march shows the level of support here in the Borders and also further afield. It is a great success."

Supporters of a new rail link between Borders and Edinburgh gathered for a rally in the region today, amid a fresh push for the project. Campaigners met at Carberry in the Scottish Borders, close to where an old railway line previously connected the region with the capital. The group, which included local politicians and business leaders, hope a new rail link could transform the local economy. 

The campaign has gained renewed momentum following confirmation that the Scottish Government is to hold an interim review of the transport links between Edinburgh and the Borders. Meanwhile, the Scottish Borders Council confirmed it had submitted an application for funding to examine the case for a new rail line. Council leader Mark Rowley said the region needed better transport links. "There is clear and mounting evidence of the huge benefits that electrified rail links to Edinburgh could bring to the Scottish Borders in terms of stimulating economic growth, getting people to work, and improving tourism," he added.

The campaign group, Campaign for Borders Rail, has argued that the region has been "left behind" due to a lack of investment in transport links. A feasibility study commissioned by the council last year found that a new rail link between Edinburgh and the Borders could lead to £322m in economic benefits. The study said the project would deliver net benefits of £1.2bn over 30 years. 

Supporters of the campaign have called for the Scottish Government to provide the necessary funding to deliver the project. Local businessman and campaigner Richard Richardson said: "We have heard a lot of warm words from the politicians down the years but now is the time for them to put their money where their mouth is and for Scottish Borders Council to submit a robust business case to win Phase 2 funding from the UK and Scottish governments."

Euronext has made an £8bn counter-offer for the London Stock Exchange, intensifying its battle with the Nasdaq for the exchange's ownership.

The offer of 4,325p per share is higher than the Nasdaq's proposed deal of 4,000p and values the LSE at about £24.2bn.

The LSE's board has already agreed to the lower bid from Nasdaq, but this remains subject to shareholder approval.

Nasdaq is expected to respond to the higher offer.

The LSE's independent directors have said they intend to engage with Euronext to understand the proposal before making any recommendation to shareholders.

They added that Nasdaq's offer was "reasonably fair" and in the interest of shareholders.

Charles Li, the chief executive of Nasdaq, said at the time of its offer that a merger of Nasdaq and the LSE would create a "global marketplace for capital".

But Euronext, which operates exchanges in Paris, Amsterdam, Brussels and Lisbon, said its offer would deliver "superior" shareholder returns and "near-term certain value".

Neil Campling, co-head of execution services at Mirabaud Securities, said the higher offer from Euronext was "going to turn this into a bidding war".

"It's a big step up from Nasdaq's offer and it's going to put a lot of pressure on Nasdaq to improve their offer," he added.

The chairman of the London Stock Exchange, Donald Brydon, has announced that he plans to step down from his role in 2022. 

In October, the exchange warned over fears that the takeover battle with Deutsche Börse could be delayed due to antitrust concerns. The LSE recently received another rival bid from Euronext, which is owned by Intercontinental Exchange. This came after months of the LSE's management advising shareholders to accept the Deutsche Börse offer.

The new Euronext proposal could lead to a situation where both offers are on the table at the same time. The LSE's board has already said it intends to engage with the Euronext proposal and that it would lead to a "substantial dilution" of the exchange's value.

A formal offer for the LSE could be made by Euronext by the end of the month, according to reports. This would trigger a lengthy takeover process.

The BBC reports that the Lib Dems have released their election manifesto, with a focus on three main policies. The first is a 1p income tax rise for those earning over £140,000 per year, which would be used to fund a £6 billion boost to the NHS and social care. The second is a pledge to plant 30 million trees per year. The third is to legalize cannabis for recreational use by adults. This final policy has been dubbed "bold" by the BBC.

The Liberal Democrats have unveiled the first of their election pledges, promising to "scrap" university tuition fees and lift the cap on student numbers if they win the general election.

The party, led by Ed Davey, is betting that the promise will appeal to graduates, young people and those from less well-off backgrounds, widening its voter base.

The pledge to scrap tuition fees, worth up to £9,250 a year, is one of the most expensive of the election so far. The Liberal Democrats say it will cost £1.3bn per year once implemented.

The policy would be paid for by a "wealth tax" on the value of people's homes, worth over £1m. The party says the tax would raise an estimated £4.4bn a year.

The commitment to lift the cap on the number of university places is aimed at creating a more "accessible" higher education system.

Manchester United's players have shown they have the character to go on and win the Premier League, says manager Alex Ferguson.

United maintained their challenge with a hard-fought 2-1 win over 10-man QPR at Old Trafford.

Ferguson said: "It is a great three points. It was not a great performance but it was one of resolve and a never-say-die attitude.

"We have shown we have got great character this season."

United led when Javier Hernandez fired home after 20 minutes but Djibril Cisse levelled just before the break with a penalty.

QPR were reduced to 10 men early in the second half when Karl Henry was sent off for a second bookable offence but United went back in front through Michael Carrick's free-kick seven minutes from time.

"It was difficult for both teams because of the heavy pitch but we got three points and that is important," added Ferguson.

"QPR are a good side and caused us problems in the first half but once we got the goal we controlled the game for long periods.

"It was a free header [for Djibril Cisse] for their goal and it was a great save from David de Gea for the penalty. He has been excellent recently and he had to be because of the conditions today."

Ferguson also confirmed that he will not be signing any more players in this transfer window, with the deadline approaching on Friday.

"We won't be bringing anyone else in, that is for sure," said the United boss.

"There are still two or three weeks left of the window and I have been asked the question a number of times and my answer is always the same - we have finished.

"We have got two or three young players here and we have got some great prospects - that is the way forward."

Ferguson hails Man Utd's resolve after Chelsea draw

Manchester United manager Alex Ferguson praised his side's spirit after a resilient display secured a draw at Chelsea.

United, who were reduced to 10 men when Robin van Persie was sent off just before the hour, earned a valuable point in their quest for a top-four finish.

Ferguson said: "It was a terrific performance and I'm really proud of them. It was a hard game for us but we dealt with it well."

United survived a barrage of Chelsea pressure after Van Persie's dismissal but created the better chances, with Javier Hernandez and Wayne Rooney going close.

Ferguson added: "I thought we might get a break, we certainly deserved it. We were the team trying to win the game in the last 20 minutes."

The draw maintained United's five-point advantage over Tottenham in fifth, although Arsenal, Chelsea and Liverpool all have games in hand.

The International Association of Athletics Federations (IAAF) says it is launching a "landmark" fight against doping.

It has created a new task force, which will attempt to establish whether there is a "culture of doping" in athletics.

The move comes in the wake of this year's Olympics, where many winners, including Britain's Mo Farah, faced accusations of doping.

The head of the IAAF, Lord Coe, has promised to leave "no stone unturned" in the hunt for drug cheats.

"Protecting the integrity of our sport is our number-one priority," he said.

"We want a level playing field for all our athletes."

The World Anti-Doping Agency (Wada) has also welcomed the creation of the IAAF's new task force.

It will be known as the Athletics Integrity Unit and have the power to impose life bans for doping violations. 

Once the unit is established, all past doping cases will be handed over to it, meaning any outstanding cases will be pursued. 

It will be funded by the IAAF and be independent from the governing body. 

"This is a significant moment for our sport," said IAAF president Sebastian Coe.

"The creation of this unit is something I am extremely passionate about for the benefit of our sport and our athletes."

The unit will be led by David Howman, who has been chief executive officer of Wada since 2003.

In a statement, he said: "This new unit will be a game-changer for athletics.

"It is imperative for the credibility of athletics that any alleged breaches of the anti-doping rules are investigated and adjudicated independently and with the utmost integrity."

The IAAF has been criticised in the past for failing to tackle doping.

A report by the World Anti-Doping Agency (Wada) and the Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU) last year said 28 national teams had failed drug tests provided by the IAAF over the previous decade.

The AIU also claimed more than 700 athletes who competed in London had "suspicious" drug tests between 2010 and 2015.

In a separate development on Wednesday, the IAAF said it was appealing the four-year ban imposed on Russia by Wada over alleged state-sponsored doping.

The International Association of Athletics Federations (IAAF) has launched an ambitious fight against doping, aiming to eradicate the use of performance-enhancing drugs from the sport entirely. The initiative, dubbed "Project Integrity", will introduce a range of measures designed to catch and deter drug cheats. 

The project will see the IAAF implement advanced testing techniques, including biological passport programs and targeted testing of high-risk athletes. The IAAF will also increase its collaboration with law enforcement agencies to investigate and prosecute doping violations.

In addition to these measures, the IAAF plans to increase awareness of the dangers of doping among athletes, coaches, and administrators. It will also work to improve the understanding of anti-doping rules and regulations among all stakeholders in the sport.

The IAAF's decision to launch Project Integrity has been welcomed by many in the sport, including Olympic champion and former world-record holder Michael Johnson. Johnson, who is now an athletics commentator, has long been an advocate for clean sport and has called for stronger action against doping.

"It's absolutely critical that action is taken to clean up the sport. I think this is a great start," said Johnson. "The IAAF is sending a strong message that they are serious about cleaning up the sport and taking action against those who cheat."

Project Integrity is seen as a bold and necessary step for the IAAF, as it seeks to restore trust and credibility in the sport. With this initiative, the IAAF hopes to create a level playing field for all athletes and ensure that the sport remains fair and honest. 

The fight against doping is one that requires the cooperation and support of all stakeholders in the sport, including athletes, coaches, administrators, and the public. The IAAF urges all members of the athletics community to join forces in this fight, to ensure that the sport remains clean and free from performance-enhancing drugs.

Oil prices have risen to their highest level since 2014 on the back of hopes for a swift economic recovery in 2021 and continued production cuts by OPEC and its allies.

West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures, the US benchmark, rose 2.5% to $63.37 a barrel on Tuesday, while Brent crude, the international benchmark, rose 1.5% to $67.83 a barrel.

Strong manufacturing data from China and the US, as well as an upbeat assessment of the US economy by Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell, have bolstered the case for a rapid recovery.

Mr Powell told the Senate Banking Committee on Tuesday that the US economy is poised to expand rapidly this year, adding that he expects inflation to pick up as the country reopens.

However, he said that any increase in prices would be temporary, and that the Fed would be patient in removing support from the economy.

Mr Howard said he did not support the "destructive" cloning of human embryos for research purposes and he wanted to ensure that any legislation introduced to allow research on spare embryos made that clear.

"I think it would be a mistake to try to legislate for cloning of human beings for research purposes," he said.

"I think that would be a step too far and, to be frank, I don't think the public would support that."

The Australian government has thrown its support behind a A$5 million (US$3.4 million) effort to lure the world's best stem cell researchers to the country. The move is being backed by Australian businessman and philanthropist Graham Tuckwell, who will donate A$50 million of his personal fortune to the cause. "Australia has lagged behind other nations such as the US, the UK and Canada in providing a supportive environment for this important area of medical research," said Tuckwell. The initiative will be guided by a seven-member advisory board, which includes Australian Nobel laureate Peter Doherty and US biologist Bruce Stillman.

Andy Murray's hopes of a fairytale finish at Wimbledon were ended by Marin Cilic, who fought back to beat the British favourite into retirement.

The Croatian world number nine produced a powerful display to win 6-7 (6) 4-6 6-3 6-4 6-2 and reach the final.

Defeat ended the hopes of a Murray win on his final Wimbledon appearance, with the roof closed on Centre Court to silence the crowd.

Cilic, who reached the Wimbledon final in 2017, hitting 51 winners and 18 aces on his way to victory.

He will face Nick Kyrgios in Sunday's final after the Australian beat Brandon Nakashima in the other semi-final.

It had been hoped Murray might be able to emulate his hero Fred Perry, who won his final match at Wimbledon, and then farewell the tournament with a lap of honour on Sunday.

But, despite a brilliant battle in which he produced moments of his old magic, the 39-year-old could not quite pull off his dream end.

Instead, it was Cilic who progressed to his first major final since the 2019 US Open, where he lost to Rafael Nadal.

Britain's Tim Hewitt fought back from a set down to beat Australia's Jason Kubler and reach the final of the ITF World Tennis Tour men's Futures tournament in Monastir.

The Briton, who is ranked 511th in the world, defeated the Australian top seed 3-6 7-5 6-4.

Hewitt, 29, will play Spain's Carlos Gimeno Valero in Sunday's final.

Valero, 34, beat Belgium's Zizou Bergs 5-7 6-4 6-2 in their semi-final. 


Hewitt returned to competitive tennis this year following a spell away from the game. He had spent 10 years as a tennis coach in the United States, where he honed his craft working with the likes of former world number one Jim Courier and Grand Slam champions Svetlana Kuznetsova and Samantha Stosur.

His progress this week has been impressive. Hewitt saved a match point in the second round before beating second seed Thales Turini from Brazil in the quarter-finals.

Athens 2004 silver medallist Konstantinos Kenteris has avoided a jail sentence for speeding but has been given a suspended fine of $1,200.

The Greek sprinter was caught driving at 162km/h (100mph) in his Mercedes on a road with a 60km/h speed limit.

He and his coach, Christos Tsekos, had been due to appear in court in Athens on Tuesday but the judge delayed the verdict until next month.

The 30-year-old runner, who also won 4x100m silver at the Sydney 2000 Olympics, had pleaded not guilty to the speeding charge.

His lawyer, Michalis Dimitrakopoulos, said he expected his client to be found guilty of breaking the speed limit but avoided a prison sentence as it was his first offence.

"I expect he will be found guilty of breaking the speed limit... and most likely he will not go to jail as it is his first offence," Dimitrakopoulos told Greek TV.

"Secondly, there are issues of statute of limitations on the charges against him so we expect for him a suspended fine of about $1,200."

Kenteris, who won a total of six Olympic medals, including two golds in the relay, retired from athletics after the 2012 Olympics in London.

The Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) will deliver its verdict on the appeal by Olympic 1,500m runners Nikki Kerppola and Iglesias Tsabounelis against their suspensions for doping on Monday. The Cas panel, whose decision is final, will announce its decision at 1600 GMT after a hearing on Monday. The two Greeks tested positive for the banned blood-booster EPO (Erythropoietin) in samples taken after their 1,500m heats at the Olympics in July. The IOC Disciplinary Commission originally gave the two Greeks a one-year ban, which meant they would miss the Athens Olympics. But Cas intervened after the Greek Olympic Committee (HOC) appealed to the international tribunal in Lausanne, Switzerland.

General Motors has warned it may post a rare quarterly loss as it offers customers hefty discounts to keep its vehicle sales afloat.

The world's largest automaker said it expected to lose up to $1.6bn in the first three months of 2005.

GM said it would take a charge of $600m to cover the estimated cost of health care for its retirees.

The announcement sent GM shares down 4.5 percent to $21.94 in after-hours trading.

"We are not satisfied with our performance in the first two months of this year," said GM's chief financial officer, John Devine.

"We are taking action to improve our performance for the remainder of the year," he added.

Mr. Devine said GM's vehicle sales were off by about 7 percent so far this year, and the company was being forced to offer higher incentives to move its vehicles off dealer lots.

GM has been struggling against a strong dollar, which has made its vehicles more expensive for overseas buyers, and a huge restructuring bill.

The company has also suffered from its reliance on sport utility vehicles (SUVs), which have fallen out of favor with consumers since the Iraq war began.

Mr. Devine said the company has been hit particularly hard in January and February by an increase in warranty costs and higher-than-expected health care costs.

GM is taking a charge of $600m this quarter to cover its estimated contribution to a new company being set up to take over its health care business.

Last month, GM's two rivals - Ford and DaimlerChrysler - reported lower-than-expected profits and were forced to cut their forecasts for the year.

Ford, the second-largest US automaker, reported a 44 percent drop in net income, which pushed its shares down more than 13 percent.

DaimlerChrysler, the third-largest US automaker, reported a 22 percent drop in quarterly profits, and warned that its earnings would continue to decline in the first half of the year.

General Motors (GM), the biggest US car maker, issues a profits warning for 2005 amid rising energy and commodity prices. 

The warning comes as GM reports a 6% fall in third-quarter profits to $1.6bn (£0.7bn), partly because of a $460m (£230m) increase in steel prices.  In July, GM raised its outlook for the year, saying it expected to post a profit of $2.70 to $2.90 a share. It now says it expects to earn $1.60 to $1.70 a share.

GM says the warning is also due to its reduced production volume, a decrease in pricing in North America, and increased costs in its international operations. The company says it has maintained its outlook for robust earnings growth in 2006 and beyond. 

GM's warning came as the company announced the next round of job cuts, with plans to eliminate 7,000 jobs in North America. The company has been cutting costs and jobs as it faces increasing competition from foreign automakers. 

In recent years, GM has closed several factories and laid off thousands of workers as it shifted its focus to making more profitable trucks and SUVs.  While those moves have helped GM's bottom line, they have also led to criticism that the company is abandoning its traditional car business. 

In a statement, GM Chairman and CEO Rick Wagoner says the company is taking actions to adjust to the changing dynamics of the automotive industry, which is moving toward higher fuel prices and increased competition. 

Wagoner says GM is confident that its business in North America is positioned to meet the challenges of the industry, and that its international operations are making good progress despite the current difficulties.

UK state pension should be overhauled to include a "good conduct" clause, The Pensions Advisory Service has said.

The government-backed pensions group said too many people still did not understand their retirement options.

Its report called for a simplification of the state pension, including the proposed "good conduct" clause.

This would see the government take into account people's lifestyles and contributions when working out their state pension.

Currently, the state pension is calculated on the number of years a person has worked and the amount they have paid in national insurance contributions.

But the report said this did not take into account whether people had taken active steps to save for their retirement or whether they had taken time out of work to care for children or elderly relatives.

It said the state pension should be "fairer" to these groups of people.

The report also called for a "default" retirement option to be offered to workers, to make sure they did not spend too long in low-return savings vehicles.

At the moment, too many people were staying in the same pension scheme throughout their career, when they would be better off moving to a different scheme, it said.

Default options would help people make better decisions about their retirement savings, it added.

The report's authors also called for the automatic enrollment into workplace pensions, which the government is planning to introduce in 2012, to be extended to the self-employed.

At the moment, the scheme is expected to cover only workers in large and medium-sized firms.

Small businesses will be exempt from the scheme, as will the self-employed.

But the Pensions Advisory Service said the self-employed would have to be included if the pension system was to be fair.

Its report said: "Automatic enrollment offers a real opportunity to increase pension savings, but this will only be successful if it is available to the self-employed as well as the employed.

"Without this, it could exacerbate the unfairness between the self-employed and employed in terms of retirement savings."

The report's authors also warned that the government's planned overhaul of the state pension, expected to be announced in the coming months, would not be enough on its own to make the pension system "fair and sustainable".

A spokesman for the Department for Work and Pensions said the government would consider the report's findings.

He added: "We are committed to ensuring that the state pension is

The state pension should rise in line with earnings rather than inflation after the next review, says a government-backed review. The move would help tackle the "gender pension gap", the intergenerational report says. It also recommends a "more coherent" state pension system. The review was commissioned by the government in 2019 and is led by former BBC trustee Richard Heaton. The current state pension is worth £185.15 per week and is indexed to inflation. 

The review suggests that if the state pension had increased in line with earnings since 2002, it would have been around 20% higher in 2021. Over the past decade, earnings have grown faster than price rises, meaning pensions have become less affordable for many, the review says. The state pension is a regular payment from the government paid to people who have reached the eligible age. 

In the review's words, the state pension is considered to be the "bedrock" of the pension system, and it is recommended that the government take active steps to ensure it remains "fair and sustainable". The triple lock guarantee - which promises the state pension will rise by the highest of earnings, inflation, or 2% - should be retained, the review says. 

But it says linking the state pension rise to earnings - as measured by the government's official measure of average earnings, known as the "nominal" measure - should be considered "as the next step" after the next state pension review, expected in 2024. The government already plans to scrap the triple lock guarantee for 2022, owing to the impact of the coronavirus pandemic on wages.

Britain's twin brothers Alistair and Jonathan Brownlee produced a thrilling finish to the triathlon as they took gold and silver for Team GB on Thursday.

The medal hopefuls started the 1.5km run segment together but it was Alistair, the 2008 champion, who powered away from his brother to defend his title.

It was not all plain sailing, though, as Spain's Javier Gomez looked set to take the gold at one point.

The 28-year-old was competing in his first Olympics after a career spent largely in triathlon's shadow.

Gomez was competing in his first Olympics after a career spent largely in triathlon's shadow

But he was unable to hold off a charging Brownlee, who produced a time of one hour 46 minutes and 25 seconds.

His brother Jonathan, who finished second in London four years ago, clung on for silver with a time of 1:46:40.

Gomez finished 11 seconds later to take the bronze.
The 26-year-old twins were always among the favourites in Rio and they lived up to the expectations in stifling heat that suited them.

Alistair said: "It's unbelievable. I knew the conditions were going to suit me. It's been a hard four years, but worth it."

And Jonathan added: "It's been a hard day. It's pretty brutal out there but I'm happy with the result."

The US has a two-goal advantage after the first leg of the playoff against England thanks to two incredible goals from the Bryan twins. After a goalless first half, the US scored two goals in quick succession as if the game plan had been planned. The first came from a fantastic strike from distance by the captain, Alex Bryan, who scored with an outstretched boot from the edge of the box. England now needs to score at least two unanswered goals in the second leg of the playoff to prevent the US from going to the World Cup.

Tom Hanks has braved the cold to attend the premiere of his new movie A Man Called Otto.

The 65-year-old actor arrived at the Empire, Leicester Square in London on Tuesday night for the debut of the film, which is based on the 2015 Swedish drama A Man Called Ove.

Hanks was greeted with cheers from fans as he arrived, with many trying to get photos of the Hollywood star.

He was joined at the event by his wife Rita Wilson, as well as his co-stars Mariana Treviño, Rachel Keller, and Manuel Garcia-Rulfo.

A Man Called Otto is set in the US and follows the story of Otto Anderson (Hanks), a grump who forms an unlikely friendship with his new neighbors.

It is based on the novel by Fredrik Backman, which was a bestseller in Sweden and has been translated into over 50 languages.

The film is directed by Marc Forster, who previously worked with Hanks on the 2004 film Finding Neverland.

Hanks has been promoting the film during his visit to the UK, having appeared on the BBC One show The One Show on Monday.

The stars of the new rom-com "Shotgun Wedding" hit the red carpet in New York for its world premiere as temperatures dropped below freezing.

The film's star and producer, Josh Duhamel, helped keep his co-star, Jennifer Lopez, warm as they arrived at the Brooklyn Academy of Music.

"This is nuts," he said. "This is cold. I've never felt cold like this in my life."

Despite the freezing temperatures, fans turned out to catch a glimpse of the stars.

Liverpool's injury nightmare has worsened with the news that striker Daniel Sturridge is now a major doubt for this Sunday's visit of Manchester United.
Sturridge joins Luis Suarez, Steven Gerrard and Jonjo Shelvey on the treatment table, with captain Gerrard ruled out for a month with a hamstring injury picked up in the win over United.
Midfielder Shelvey is out for at least three weeks with a thigh problem, while striker Suarez has not trained all week because of a knee injury and is rated as highly unlikely to be available.
That leaves Sturridge, who has already had surgery this season on his hip and a thigh injury, as the only senior striker available.

The news will be a huge concern to Liverpool boss Brendan Rodgers, who is already trying to cope with defensive injuries to Sebastian Coates, Martin Skrtel and Daniel Agger.
Coates is out for the rest of the season with a knee injury while Skrtel faces a fight to be fit for United after picking up a hamstring problem in the 2-1 win at Old Trafford.
Agger has been out for more than a month with a similar problem and is not expected back any time soon.

David Beckham's hopes of playing some part in London 2012 could hinge on the decision of Harry Redknapp whether or not to include him in the Queens Park Rangers party heading for Wales tomorrow for a friendly against Swansea.

The former England captain has not played since tearing his Achilles tendon against Bayern Munich in the Champions League last 16 second leg on 12 March.

Beckham has regularly trained with the QPR squad since joining the club in the summer of 2011 and Redknapp says he has no worries about selecting him.

Bayern Munich president Uli Hoeness has warned against the appointment of Laurent Blanc as the new France coach.

The former France captain has emerged as a leading candidate to replace Raymond Domenech after the national team's disastrous showing at the World Cup.

But Hoeness, a former Germany captain, believes Blanc's lack of top-level coaching experience would be a hindrance.

"It's a great shame that French football didn't look for a manager with real top-level experience," he told L'Equipe.

"Appointing Blanc would be a mistake in my view.

"He's done very well with Bordeaux, there's no doubt about that, but that doesn't necessarily mean he is ready to coach France."

Hoeness believes former England manager Sven-Goran Eriksson - who has also been linked with the job - would be a better appointment.

"Eriksson has experience of coaching a national team and that could be important for France," he said.

The former Bordeaux coach has reportedly agreed a deal to replace Domenech, although no official announcement has been made by the French federation.

Eriksson has also been suggested as a possible successor, although the former England manager has said he is not interested in the role.

Frenchman Thibaut Laporte got through a tough afternoon in Paris after being called up for the first time this season following an injury to Romain N'tamack.

The Sale scrum-half, who has been in fine form this season, was given a tough time by the French pack, especially at the scrum where the hosts took three against the head in the first half.

Sir Ian Corbett, the former director-general of the BBC, has attacked the "dumbing down" of television, arguing that the public service channels are in danger of "losing their way".

Corbett, who was director-general of the BBC from 1982 to 1987, was speaking at the launch of a new book about his predecessor, Hugh Greene.

"There are signs that some broadcasters are already moving in that direction [of dumbing down]," he said.

"I think they are misunderstanding their publics. I think they are doing themselves a disservice and, in the end, they will do the public a disservice."

He argued that the public service channels - BBC1, BBC2, Channel 4 and Channel 5 - were "in danger of losing their way".

"They should be providing alternative views," he said. "They should be providing stuff that isn't immediately accessible but which is worthwhile because it stretches your mind.

"I think they are in danger of forgetting that. They think their job is to satisfy as many people as possible of a certain level of intelligence."

Corbett said the BBC had "got much better" at reflecting the whole of the UK than when he was director-general.

But he added that it was still biased towards London and the south-east of England.

"I think the BBC reflects, far more than it did, the whole of the UK," he said. "But is it still London-oriented? Yes, it is.

"Is it as bad as it was? No, it's much better. But it is still the major problem for the BBC."

Corbett said the corporation still had too many senior managers and producers based in London.

"It is still the way the BBC works," he said. "It is still assuming that the centre of the universe is London and everybody else comes second.

"That's a pretty unhealthy approach for an organisation that is supposed to be supporting the whole of the UK."

He also had some advice for BBC director-general Mark Thompson, who is due to leave soon: "The most important thing is to have a really strong relationship with the government of the day.

"It's absolutely fundamental. If you haven't got that, it's very difficult to have the influence that you need."

Sir Anthony Corbett, the former controller of BBC Radio 2, has attacked the dumbing-down of television, arguing that it is misogynistic and favours the most stupid and coarse members of society.

Giving a lecture at Cambridge University, Sir Anthony, who was responsible for radio programmes such as Desert Island Discs and The Archers, spoke of his fears for the future of serious television.

He said television had taken a direction "completely contrary to the idea of an intelligent democracy".

The 83-year-old argued that there were some exceptions, such as Channel 4's coverage of the Iraq war, but that these were "becoming isolated islands in a sea of triviality".

"I worry about the future of serious television. I worry that it could disappear altogether," he said.

Sir Anthony criticised the trend towards reality shows and panel games, which he said allowed participants to behave badly towards each other, and the increasing use of sexualised female presenters in order to attract viewers.

"Is there any other explanation for the number of female presenters in mini-skirts presenting programmes about decorating your home or trying on clothes?" he asked.

"These are not role models for young women, nor for young men," he said. "They merely provide an excuse for more sexism and more exploitation."

The broadcaster argued that serious issues were being marginalised, saying that the BBC's flagship current affairs programme, Newsnight, had been pushed from its 10pm slot to midnight in Scotland.

And he claimed that an earlier generation of journalists would be "appalled" at the way news was presented now, with the emphasis on the visual rather than the story.

"In the old days, you had reporters who could write, and could describe what was going on. Now, the stress is on visual impact," he said.

"The priority is to get pictures, and the pictures are often shown repeatedly... with a voice-over which may have nothing to do with the pictures.

"I think the journalists of my generation would be appalled at the priorities, and the techniques, of many television journalists today."

Sir Anthony said he did not believe that television had been entirely taken over by "the stupid, the coarse and the venal".

But he added that it was difficult to attract large audiences for serious programmes, and that there was a danger that "the serious will disappear, and be replaced by the trivial".

Film composer John Williams is to be honoured at the Academy Awards for his work in the movie industry.

The 95-year-old has composed the music for more than 100 films including Star Wars and Jurassic Park.

He will be awarded the Academy's highest honour, the Irving G. Thalberg Award. The award is given annually to "a creative producer whose body of work has consistently reflected a devotion to excellence in film."

Williams has won five previous Oscars across a career that has spanned seven decades. He has received 52 Academy Award nominations, second only to Walt Disney.

"John Williams is one of the greatest composers in the history of film music," said Ray Beckett, conductor of the Chamber Orchestra of Ireland.

The composer has created many of the most recognisable film scores in history, from Jaws to Star Wars, Harry Potter to Jurassic Park.

His music has also been heard in many of the most popular movies of all time, including E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial, Superman, Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom and Schindler's List.

The composer retired from scoring film soundtracks in 2021.

The 64th Academy Awards will take place in Los Angeles on 27 March.

It's often the case that the type of lifestyle you lead will govern the choice of the mobile phone you require. 

For example, parameter such as; do you lead an active lifestyle and therefore require a robust phone? Or does you work in an environment that requires you to receive and make frequent calls, and therefore require a phone with a good battery life?

When choosing a mobile phone, there are many different factors you need to take into consideration. 

Do you require a phone that has high quality camera capabilities? Or does having the latest apps and games on your phone matter more to you?

The answers to these questions will help determine which phone is right for you. In recent years, smartphone developers have been innovative in developing phones that can survive underwater and drops from great heights, as well as making phones that are resistant to breakage.

These types of phones are ideal for people who lead active lifestyles. If you lead a less active lifestyle then a normal smartphone should be absolutely fine for you, as they are already designed to withstand the normal wear and tear of everyday life.

According to a recent study by the University of York, lifestyle choices are the primary determinant of the type of mobile phone one owns in Britain. The study found that there are six distinct mobile user groups in the country. These are:

- The Technophobes: They are typically unattached and often retired. This group tends to have little or no digital skills. Members are usually over 65 and tend to have lower incomes.

- The Traditionalists: They are usually over 45 and tend to be female. This group primarily uses their mobiles to make phone calls and send text messages.

- The Simplicities: This group uses their phones for calls, texts, and pictures. They tend to be female, over 65, and have middle incomes.

- The Communicators: This group sends more messages than the average user and more pictures than the Simplicities. This group's members are usually female and aged between 16 and 24.

- The Photographers: As the name suggests, the members of this group use their phones to take pictures and share them on social media. Over 55s tend to dominate this group.

- The Super Users: This group uses all the functions of a smartphone, particularly internet services and apps. This group is dominated by the 16 to 24 age group.

Children vote Shrek 2 best film

Children in the UK have voted Shrek 2 the best film of the last 30 years.

The sequel, featuring the loveable, swamp-dwelling ogre, secured a quarter of the vote in a poll commissioned by the BBC.

Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone was second with 10% and Star Wars: Episode One - The Phantom Menace came third with 9.5%.

The poll was answered by more than 3,000 people, all of whom were under the age of 15. They were asked to pick their favourite film from a list of 50.

Shrek 2 received 258 votes, with the Harry Potter film getting 152 and the first of the Star Wars prequels 138.

The rest of the top 10 was made up of Toy Story, Chitty Chitty Bang Bang, Home Alone, Hook, Cinderella, 101 Dalmatians and Frozen.

Beyond the top 10, other films to receive votes included Pretty Woman, La La Land and Brideshead Revisited.

No votes at all were received for A Passage to India, Secrets & Lies, The Cook, the Thief, His Wife & Her Lover, Dead Man's Shoes and The Comfort of Strangers.

"It is fascinating to see which films have stood the test of time and are regarded by this generation of film fans as the best ever," said Lauren Moss, BBC Breakfast's entertainment correspondent.

"Shrek 2 seems to tick all the boxes and is loved by children of all ages."

The poll was conducted by OnePoll.com ahead of this year's Bafta film awards.

Bafta's children's vote will be announced on February 18.

The classic 2001 cartoon Shrek has loyal fans but it is the 2004 sequel that has captured the hearts of a new generation of children, according to a poll published on Friday.

Shrek 2 was voted the best film of all time by a panel of 1,000 children aged six to 14 in a poll organised by the digital education platform Filmstro.

It topped a list of modern classics including Frozen, Lion King and Toy Story.

The survey was launched in September to celebrate the launch of Filmstro’s new education platform.

It was open to children in the UK and Ireland.

Shrek 2 follows the adventures of ogre Shrek and his friends as they attempt to rescue the princess Fiona from a dragon.

The survey was carried out before the death of Shrek star Eddie Murphy this month.

ABBA singer Agnetha Faltskog has entered the Sunday Times music rich list for the first time, with an estimated wealth of £26.2m.

The Swedish pop icon, 69, is the richest female musician in Sweden - ahead of Madonna and Beyonce.

Her fortune is largely due to her 50% share in ABBA's songs, which have enjoyed a revival thanks to the hit musical Mamma Mia! and the two films.

Her former husband and ABBA bandmate Bjorn Ulvaeus is the fifth richest musician in the UK, with an estimated £130m.

Agnetha, who lives in Stockholm, has not released an album since 2003's The Collection but has continued to tour with ABBA bandmates Bjorn, 76, Benny Andersson, 74, and Anni-Frid Lyngstad, 71.

They came second in the Eurovision song contest in 1974 with Ring and went on to become one of the most successful acts of the 1970s with a string of hits including Waterloo, Dancing Queen and Take A Chance On Me.

The Sunday Times Rich List is published on May 25.

ABBA singer Agnetha Faltskog has entered the Sunday Times music rich list for the first time, thanks to the success of the band's reunion tours and the hit musical Mamma Mia!

The United Nations has told the UK it "discriminated" against Roma migrants during the pandemic by failing to provide any accommodation or support for them.

The UK had argued such provisions would encourage others to make dangerous journeys.

The UN's anti-racism panel, CERD, made the ruling after examining evidence from the UK, which argued its policies were a proportionate response to the pandemic.

The UK's delegation to the committee in Geneva argued the government had "gone above and beyond" its obligations to protect the group.

But in a decision released on Monday, the UN's Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination (CERD) said the UK had "failed" to provide any accommodation or support to Roma during the pandemic.

It also criticised the government for its "overly broad" use of public health orders which allowed local authorities to close down campsites and evict Roma.

The UN said it was "particularly concerned" that such measures resulted in the forced eviction of Roma, "exposing them to great hardship and distress and impacting their right to health".

The government has said it is reviewing the UN's findings - the second time in a year the UK has been strongly criticised by UN racism experts for its treatment of Roma.

In July, the UN's human rights council (HRC) also found "discrimination" in the government's response to an outbreak of Covid-19 amongst Roma in Northern England.

The council's anti-racism envoy, Tendayi Achiume, said the government's failure to provide any accommodation for Roma during the pandemic reflected "structural racism".

The UK has discriminated against Roma people from Central Europe, breaching their human rights, the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) has ruled.

The complaint was brought by a Slovakian man, identified as M.H., who arrived in the UK in 2008 and claimed he faced discrimination when bidding to buy a plot of land in Yorkshire. He claimed this was due to his Roma ethnicity.

The ECHR ruled that the treatment he received amounted to discrimination "on the basis of race". 

The court ordered the UK government to pay M.H. €5,000 (£4,368) in damages for the discrimination, as well as €3,500 (£3,052) for costs.

Climate change protesters plan to gloat when they win their court fight against Heathrow Airport tomorrow.

DVD of shark tale most popular in US
A sequel to hit animated film Shark Tale has been given the go-ahead by the US company Dreamworks.
The original, about a fish who fibs his way through life, was the second biggest video release last year in America.
According to studio data, the DVD of Shark Tale was the number one rental and sell-through video for the week ending 20 March.
Shark Tale 2 is to be developed by the same team including Oscar winner Roger Deakins, who will again serve as executive producer.

"We're excited to collaborate with them again," said Jeffrey Katzenberg, chief executive of Dreamworks.
Shark Tale, which starred the voices of Will Smith and Jack Black, pulled in more than $321m (£176m) at the global box office.
It followed the adventures of Oscar, an angelfish who inhabits the fictional Reef City, where sharks rule the waters.
Oscar dreams of becoming a hero by defeating the dangerous shark, Don Lino, but he keeps getting into trouble due to his lies.

Voice actor Smith had been expected to return for the sequel but it is not known if he will be back for the second instalment.
No release date for Shark Tale 2 has been given.

The DVD of shark tale kicked off its US release at the top of the charts. The computer-animated comedy, featuring the voices of Will Smith, Jack Black and Robert De Niro, sold a whopping 210,000 copies in its first week, making it the biggest children's DVD launch ever, according to its distributor, Paramount Pictures. It left behind Shrek 2, which sold 165,000 copies in its first week in May 2004. Shark Tale features Smith as a timid fish who dreams of being a great shark, and Black as a self-centered, ultra-cool shark who teaches him some tough lessons about life and survival.

Car sales in the US have fallen for the sixth consecutive month, new data has shown, pushing overall retail sales down.

Vehicle sales in November were down 4.4% from a year earlier, following a decline in October, according to data from Commerce Department.

Overall, retail sales were down 0.6% from October to November. Analysts had expected a flat reading for the month.

Besides cars, sales of building materials also fell. But there were gains in sales at restaurants and bars, as well as online.

Retail sales for the October-November period were up 5.7% from the same period a year ago.

The data showed that consumer spending, which accounts for more than two-thirds of US economic activity, was unchanged in November.

Analysts said the data was further evidence that the US economy was slowing, and that a recession was a growing possibility next year.

"The consumer is tapped out," said Joel Naroff, president of Naroff Economic Advisors.

"With wages not rising and inflation eating into their spending power, consumers can't keep spending at the same pace."

The figures come a day after data showed that US industrial production had declined in November for the first time in eight months.

And last week, the Labor Department said that the number of Americans filing new claims for unemployment benefits had risen last week.

"The trifecta of weaker [manufacturing], housing and retail activity… does not bode well for the economy as we head into 2023," said Greg Daco, chief economist at EY Parthenon, the global strategy consulting arm of Ernst & Young.

Sales of cars and light trucks in the U.S. fell nearly 18% in September, compared with a year ago. It was the biggest decline since March 2020, when the pandemic started to hit the U.S. economy. 

Industry analysts say automakers are struggling with falling demand as financing costs rise and shoppers worry about affordability. On top of that, the semiconductor shortage that has plagued production all year long continues to impact sales. 

Toyota, the world's biggest automaker, said Thursday that its September sales were down by nearly 15% from a year ago. Honda reported an almost 30% drop. 

General Motors, the largest U.S. automaker, said its sales were down almost 19% for the month. Ford reported a 22% decline. 

Despite the recent drop in sales, automakers have managed to maintain strong profits this year thanks to higher prices and reduced incentives. But analysts say the market is cooling off. 

Jessica Caldwell, an industry analyst with Edmunds, said automakers may have to rely less on pricing and more on sales volume to make up for the expected decline in production.

The Producers has scooped three stage awards.

The musical, starring Sheridan Smith and Jack Black, was named best new musical at the Evening Standard awards.

Its stars also picked up two other prizes apiece.

James Dreyfus, who plays the narrator in the show, won best performance in a supporting role, and Sheridan Smith was named best actress.

The show's director and choreographer Susan Stroman said she was "thrilled and honoured" by the Standard award.

Best new play went to John Hodge's Collaborators, which appeared at the National Theatre towards the end of last year.

The Producers ' 12 awards included wins for stars Bette Midler and Nathan Lane, as well as a creative team award for Brooks himself. Midler won best actress in a musical, Lane won best actor in a musical, and Brooks won best score.

The show's director, Susan Stroman, won three awards including best direction of a musical.

"It's been said that happiness isn't meant to be buried. Happiness is meant to be shared," Stroman said.

The UK government has published details of its new immigration points-based system which comes into effect on 1 January 2021.

It aims to attract the "brightest and the best" from around the world and end free movement from the EU.

A points system will determine whether migrants will be granted entry to the UK.

Applicants will need to achieve a minimum score of 70 points in order to qualify.

They will need to fulfil at least one "skilled" job in a specific list of occupations.

These range from architects to veterinarians.

There will be no cap on the number of people coming to the UK.

But there will be a salary threshold - migrants will need to be paid at least £25,600.

Those who achieve the required number of points will be given either a skilled worker visa or a temporary worker visa.

This will depend on how long they are planning to stay in the UK.

The scheme will be piloted from 1 November, when the free movement of people from Europe will end.

The government said the scheme would "transform the way in which all migrants come to the UK".

"It will give us a skills-based immigration system that brings the earnings and salaries of immigrants in line with the rest of the population, and which allows us to attract the brightest and the best from around the world," it added.

But the Scottish government said the scheme would damage its economy.

"Despite repeated requests for flexibility from the Scottish government, it is clear they have ignored Scotland's interests yet again," said Migration Minister Jenny Gilruth.

"Employers in Scotland will now face the daunting prospect of hiring overseas workers under a complex new system from January."

And the Liberal Democrats said the salary threshold was too high and would prevent many key workers, including nurses, from coming to the UK.

"This derisory offer does nothing to reassure the millions of Europeans living in limbo in the UK that they are welcome here," said Home Affairs Spokesperson Christine Jardine.

"It's another massive own goal for this government, which has failed to show the leadership and certainty our economy needs."

The minimum salary threshold will not apply to those coming to the UK to fill a vacancy on the "shortage occupation list", which includes but is not limited to:

• nurses
• paramedics
• veterinarians
• poultry workers.

The UK government has been criticised for its plans to send some migrants to a processing centre in Ascension Island thousands of miles away in the Atlantic.

The scheme - part of tougher immigration measures announced by Home Secretary Theresa May - is designed to discourage migrants from making dangerous journeys across the English Channel.

Ministers say the centre on the island, which is a British overseas territory, will be used to process migrants' claims "fairly and efficiently".

But Labour called the plan "inhumane".

Ascension Island is a volcanic island halfway between Africa and South America, with a population of fewer than 1,000 people and temperatures reaching up to 40C (104F).

It is part of the British overseas territory of Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha - best known as the location of the former prison camp where Boer prisoners of war were held during the Boer War in the early 20th Century.

The island has a naval base - long attached to the UK's interests in the South Atlantic - and is a stopping-off point for Royal Navy ships, as well as an important satellite ground station.

Building work is already under way to transform an abandoned US airbase on Ascension - which is twinned with Saint Helena - into a migrant processing centre.

The exact location has not been disclosed, but it is understood to be on the island's sweltering coastline.

The plans, first reported by The Times, have been criticised by politicians and charities.

Labour's shadow immigration minister, Stephen Kinnock, said the party was "urging the government to scrap this inhumane plan".

He added that Labour would "work with the government to find a humane alternative".

And the chief executive of the Refugee Council, Enver Solomon, said sending people "even further away from their families and support networks" was "not the answer".

The Home Office said the centre would "provide a safer environment for processing than the cramped conditions [migrants] are currently subjected to during their perilous journey".

The announcement came as part of a broader strategy aimed at limiting illegal migration after record numbers of people arrived in the UK across the Channel last year.

Mrs May announced the government would introduce legislation making it a criminal offence to enter the UK illegally and "obstructing removal" - with a maximum sentence of 12 months.

She also wants to make it easier to return illegal migrants to mainland Europe and improve immigration detention.

A catering firm at the centre of the Wembley stadium fiasco has revealed it will not make a profit from its £2.3bn lottery contract.

Serious fraud office (SFO) investigators are looking into why Sports Interactive, the lottery's operating company, paid £43m to Wembley National Stadium Limited, the firm building the stadium.

The lottery's auditors, Deloitte and Touche, have already been fined £2.5m by the accounting watchdog for their part in the affair.

In a statement to the stock exchange, Sports Interactive said it had always anticipated it would not make a profit from the national lottery contract.

The statement came as the firm published its results for the year to 31 December 2004.

They show that the firm made an operating loss of £25.9m, compared with a profit of £40.2m the previous year.

The company added that it had always known that its investment in the lottery would be "significantly loss making".

"The national lottery is a high profile contract and a prestigious addition to the company's activities," the statement said.

"Whilst the board has always expected the company to invest significantly to establish the lottery business and create a platform for future profitability, it has always anticipated that the national lottery would not itself be profitable."

Sports Interactive signed the lottery contract in 2001, since when it has paid £43m to the stadium company.

The payments were made despite an internal audit at Sports Interactive which warned that the payments were "not in accordance with normal commercial practice".

The SFO is examining why the payments were made and is expected to report back to the government later this year. A decision on whether to bring any charges is likely to be made next year.

Sports Interactive is jointly owned by Sir Rodney Walker, former chairman of Wembley National Stadium Limited, and his brother, Sir David Walker.

The firm has previously said that the payments were a "commercial decision" and that Sir Rodney had no hand in them.

Brent Council has told a Wembley firm it must not make a profit from a planned homeless shelter next to Stonebridge Park Station. The authority has been under increasing pressure to allow a site to be used for a temporary overnight shelter after a string of high-profile cases of rough sleeping in the borough. 

It identified an unused building near Stonebridge Park Station as a potential site but has now received a legal letter warning that a planning condition preventing profit cannot be enforced. The condition was included in plans approved in 2015 for the site, which is owned by a firm called Project Urban. 

In summer, the council served the owners with a notice ordering them to open the doors to homeless people, arguing that a lack of suitable hostel beds in the borough was a special circumstance that overrode the condition. The letter, sent by Project Urban's lawyers last week, argues that the planning condition is valid and should be enforced. 

"There is no credible evidence... that the application would result in an unacceptable windfall profit," it says. "There is no justification for the council's attempt to override the condition... and its attempt to do so is an unlawful interference with Project Urban's rights." 

The letter, sent on October 7, adds that the council has not provided any evidence to support its case and that its notice is "an unlawful decision and should be withdrawn". 

A Brent Council spokesperson said: "The council stands by its decision and remains confident that its approach is both legally and morally right. "We have a duty to provide accommodation and support to all rough sleepers in the borough and have been working tirelessly with our partners to bring this to fruition. "We have been talking with the site owners for several months about using the premises as a night shelter and remain open to discussions."

Liverpool manager Rafael Benitez has defended goalkeeper Jerzy Dudek after the Reds keeper was blamed for Manchester United's winning goal in Sunday's FA Cup final.

Dudek came for a cross shortly before the interval, but missed it and Cristiano Ronaldo headed United ahead.

Benitez said: "Everyone has to take their share of the blame, not just the goalkeeper - it's a team game.

"We didn't defend well and they scored a goal from a set piece. We had chances to score and didn't take them."

The Liverpool manager said Dudek had been the victim of a miscarriage of justice following his costly mistake.

"People seem to want to hunt him down but he made some fantastic saves and I am happy with him," added the Spaniard.

Benitez believes the goal, which gave United a half-time lead they never surrendered, was avoidable.

"It was a set piece we had analysed and we knew what they would do," he said.

"We had talked about that and we made mistakes. It was an important goal because at half-time we were still in the game, we had chances in the second half but you could see the players were tired."

Benitez, whose side finished the Premier League season in third place, said he would now focus on strengthening his squad during the summer in a bid to make a stronger challenge on all fronts next term.

"We have to improve if we want to compete with Manchester United and Chelsea," he said.

"We have to realise we made mistakes in both games against them this season and we have to learn from our mistakes."

Benitez praises goalkeeper Dudek
Benitez said: "I am happy with the effort of the team, we knew it would be difficult. "In the first half we were doing well and had a few chances, in the second we had control of the game and could have scored another goal or two. 

"They had one chance and scored but the team was doing well, it was difficult for them to create chances.

"We were defending well, we have a good goalkeeper and good defenders, and I am happy with the point because it could have been worse."

Dudek praised
Dudek said: "I am happy, I made a couple of good saves and did not expect to play so well in my first game.

"The manager told me I would play against Charlton and I was happy, I have been working hard in training and it paid off. 

"This is the best league in the world, the training is different and I am learning all the time, the players have helped me a lot."

Mexicans tracking unhappy Juninho

Mexican football fans have been given permission to hire a private detective to tail their national team's unhappy star, Juninho, in a bid to persuade him to return to the country.

The Brazilian-born midfielder has been closely followed since he arrived in Mexico last month for a friendly, and has so far refused to answer calls from his club Monterrey.

The fans have raised about $8,500 to pay for the private detective, and delivered a letter to Juninho, copying in the Mexican Football Federation, which they also sent to the player's wife in Brazil.

In the letter, the Federation promises to help the player resolve his work permit problems in Mexico, while the fans ask him to think of the excitement his presence has brought to the game.

The intrigue surrounding the player deepened at the weekend when he failed to show up for training, with reports in the Mexican media claiming that he had again gone missing.

The 25-year-old, who has been capped once for Brazil, joined Monterrey last year after spells in Portugal and Turkey.

He became a naturalised Mexican in March and has expressed a desire to play for the country of his wife, actress Giselle Monserrat, despite being named in Brazil's squad for last month's friendly against Argentina.

The enigmatic forward known as Juninho, one of Mexico's most famous and popular footballers in the last 30 years, is reportedly unhappy with his current situation after a summer of uncertainty and little playing time, igniting a debate regarding his future. 

The legend of Juninho began when he was just 17 years old and debuted for Mexico's most popular club team America. Over the course of two decades, playing for Club America, Monterrey, and Santos, he became a fan favorite due to his skills, humility, and work ethic even though he never achieved the success of winning championships. 

In recent years, his career took a turn after he left Santos to join the Club America reserve team. This summer, after a brief stint in the Mexican second division with Atletico San Luis, he returned to Club America, but has failed to make any appearances under new head coach Fernando Ortiz. 

Ortiz recently commented that the club was working to find a solution for the player's future, which has led to many speculating that the forward could be transferred in the upcoming winter window. However, at 37 years old, options for the player may be limited. 

Regardless of what the future holds for Juninho, there is no doubt that he has had a long and successful career and remains a beloved figure in Mexican football.
