The prize, the brainchild of author Sophie McKenzie, is searching for a 16-25-year-old writer whose work could be turned into a successful novel.

The winner will receive £5,000 and their book will be published by HarperCollins.

Entrants must submit a 3,000-word crime fiction sample by 30 April. A shortlist will be announced in July. 

The competition is described as the "X-Factor for books". 

McKenzie said she wanted to "find the next generation of talented writers".

She said: "Writing a book is a dream that so many people have, and Literature Idol will give young people across the UK the chance to have their work recognised and turned into a real book."

Judges include authors Mark Billingham and Lucy Christopher, agent Clare Alexander and BBC radio presenter Simon Mayo.

The search for the next big thing in British literature has begun with the launch of a new award for unpublished authors.

Lit Idol, which describes itself as "Britain's search for new literary talent", is accepting submissions of novels, short story collections and works of non-fiction from anyone over the age of 16 who has not previously had a book published.

The submissions will be winnowed down by a panel of publishers, agents and authors, led by Lit Idol founder and literary agent Julia Kingsford, with the final round judged by a panel of readers.

The winner will receive a consultation with Kingsford and £5,000.

Kingsford said: "I'm really excited to be launching Lit Idol, which is a unique competition in the UK.

"It's a chance for unpublished writers to get valuable feedback on their work and to really get their names out there."

The number of homes with access to ultra-fast broadband has increased by more than 230,000 in the past three months, a new report shows.

By March this year, 5.6 million homes and businesses were able to access speeds of 1 gigabit per second (Gbps), according to industry body UK Broadband.

That means about 60% of UK households are within reach of ultra-fast broadband, compared with 55% three months earlier.

The numbers are presented in UK Broadband's annual report.

What is broadband?

Broadband internet is a high-speed internet connection that can handle a large amount of data and multiple demands at once, such as streaming movies, music and TV, and playing video games.

According to Ofcom, the UK's communications regulator, average download speeds for fixed-line broadband connections increased from 67.1Mbits per second (Mbps) to 84.7Mbps between November 2021 and February 2022.

This is an increase of more than 27% in just three months, and the fastest annual growth in at least a decade.

What are the different types of broadband?

There are several types of broadband connections, including:

Fibre optic - This type of broadband uses fibre optic cables to send and receive data, resulting in extremely fast internet speeds. Fibre optic broadband can reach speeds of up to 1Gbps.

Cable - Cable broadband uses the same cables as cable TV to provide internet service, typically resulting in faster speeds than ADSL.

ADSL - Asymmetric digital subscriber line is the most common type of broadband in the UK. It uses existing phone lines to provide internet service, but speeds tend to be slower than fibre optic and cable broadband.

Mobile - Mobile broadband uses mobile phone networks to provide internet service. It's often used as a backup or temporary internet connection, and speeds tend to be slower than fixed-line broadband.

How fast is my broadband?

You can check the speed of your broadband connection using an online speed test, such as those available from Speedtest, Ookla or Fast.com. These tests measure the speed of your internet connection by downloading and uploading sample files.

BBC News has learnt that Aston Villa manager Steven Gerrard is set to be named the new head coach of Premier League club Everton, with the Toffees' hierarchy confident they have found their primary target to replace Rafael Benítez.

Sources told BBC Sport that Gerrard had informed Villa of his decision on Thursday and that an announcement on his appointment at Everton could be made as early as Friday.

Gerrard has made an impressive start to his managerial career since leaving Liverpool's Under-18s setup in November 2018 to take charge of Rangers. Benítez was appointed as Everton's manager in the summer of 2021 but after a bright start to his tenure, the team's form declined. The United States has agreed to delay a new set of tariffs on some imported products from Europe, following an announcement that both parties had agreed to start talks early next month. 
The tariffs, which were due to come into force on Tuesday, have been postponed for up to six months. They would have hit a range of products, from large aircraft to dairy products and wine.
The move comes after the US and EU agreed to start talks later this month aimed at resolving a 17-year dispute over state subsidies for aircraft manufacturers Airbus and Boeing.
The US announced in May that it was imposing tariffs on imports of aluminium and steel from the EU, along with imports of a range of other products, including gouda cheese, single-malt whiskey and large aircraft. 

The EU responded with its own tariffs on more than $3.2bn worth of US goods, including corn, peanut butter, motorcycles and denim.

The two sides have now agreed to "pause" the tariffs for six months, according to a joint statement released by the US Trade Representative (USTR) and the EU on Friday. 

If talks to resolve the dispute over aircraft subsidies are not successful within six months, the US will move forward with the tariffs on the $7.5bn worth of EU goods. The EU will also do the same with its tariffs on more than $4bn worth of US goods.

It also follows the US government's decision to impose further sanctions on Russia last week, targeting the country's largest bank and several other key financial institutions.

Musical future for phones

Smartphones could replace MP3 players and be used to listen to music in new ways, thanks to a new breed of accessories.

At the Consumer Electronics Show (CES) in Las Vegas, phone-clip accessories that turn handsets into multi-directional stereo speakers were among the most popular products.

Another new type of accessory - a "dockless" charger - can boost a phone's battery without needing to plug it in.

And one manufacturer even showed off a smartphone with an embedded pico-projector.

The idea is that all these accessories will help release the phone's potential as a digital media device, as it replaces MP3 players and other devices.

"Phone manufacturers are trying to turn their phones into digital media hubs," said Avi Greengart, a phone analyst with Current Analysis.

"The phone has the CPU [central processing unit], the screen, the network connection and increasingly digital cameras.

"But the experience isn't as good as on a dedicated device, because the phone's speakers are weak and its screen is small. "So they are opening up the hardware to let accessory-makers fix that."

One of the most popular types of accessories at CES was the phone-clip speaker, which typically clips on to the back of a phone and uses its internal accelerometer - a device that measures acceleration - to determine which way is up.

This then allows the speakers to deliver true stereo sound, no matter how the user holds the phone.

Other similar devices simply deliver more powerful sound.

For example, the Bass Egg is a egg-shaped speaker that can plug into a phone or MP3 player and dramatically boost the volume.

It uses a technology called "acoustic resonance" which amplifies the sound coming out of the phone's speakers by vibrating the inside of the egg.

Another popular accessory was the "dockless" charger, which charges a phone's battery without needing to plug the phone itself into a socket.

Instead, the phone sits on a pad that uses a magnetic field to transfer electricity.

These pads can either be attached to a wall or embedded in furniture.

When the phone is placed on the pad, the magnetic field creates a conduction connection that charges the battery.

The advantage is that there is no need to plug the phone in every night, as it automatically charges just by being placed on the pad.

The future of smartphones could be a lot louder, thanks to a new technology that can turn them into speakers. U.S. company Noveto has unveiled the Noveto N1, a processor the size of a human thumb nail that can be attached to the back of a phone. It uses a technology called "beaming", which uses ultrasound to create audible sound from the vibrations in the phone itself. When held up to the ear, it allows the user to hear music, videos and calls directly from their phone, without the need for headphones. The technology is still in its infancy, but Noveto hopes it will eventually be built into all smartphones, allowing users to share music and videos with others, without the need for separate speakers.

Noveto isn't the only company looking to make phones louder. A growing number of devices, from smartphones to smart home devices, are now being designed with built-in speakers. And audio technology company, Sonarworks, has developed software that can optimise the sound of headphones and speakers, so that they produce the best possible sound for the user. These advances in audio technology are making it easier for people to share their favourite tunes with others, and could transform the way we listen to music and other media on our phones.

The stage musical based on the Ring cycle of operas will not be coming to London, its creators have said.

They said they hoped to stage the production in the UK at a later date.

A statement from the producers said: "Given the complexity and scale of the show, more time is needed than initially planned."

They said they had made "a strategic decision to postpone the premiere in London" and that they were "eager to find an opportunity to bring the show to the UK".

Ring, which features cutting-edge technology, tells the story of a cursed golden ring that passes from owner to owner, bringing death and destruction in its wake.

The original cycle of four operas - Der Ring des Nibelungen - is one of the most celebrated works in classical music, composed by Wagner in the late 19th century.

The musical had been due to run at the Palladium in London for a month before opening in Munich in 2020. It will now receive its world premiere in the German city at the start of 2020, with its German premiere set for spring 2021.

In a joint statement, Jones and director Gordon Davidson said: "Ring is an ambitious undertaking... [O]ur teams in Germany and the UK are working hard on this exciting production and we look forward to sharing more news with you soon."

The world premiere of the new musical based on the works of JRR Tolkien will not take place in the UK.

Instead, the show will have its debut in Chicago in June 2022 before arriving on Broadway in New York.

The musical's producers said there were " complexities" involved in staging such a " colossal" show in London.

They said plans for a UK run would be announced later, but stressed that it would not be a world premiere.

The show has music and lyrics by Oscar-winning Lord of the Rings composer Howard Shore, and book by Oscar-winning screenwriter John Logan.

It is being produced by the same team who created the Harry Potter and the Cursed Child parts one and two, which are currently running in London.

They include Warner Bros, Broadway producers Kevin McCollum and Neal Street Productions' Nicholas Hytner and Sonia Friedman. 

The show is not expected to arrive in the UK until at least 2024, with dates yet to be finalised.

The human rights group said in a new report that Russia's invasion had caused "horrific" suffering, with Ukraine facing a "serious threat" of genocide.

It also said that by not sending the weapons, Western leaders had sent the message that "they did not take Russia's invasion and war crimes seriously".

"But the longer the conflict continues, the greater the danger that he will stumble into a catastrophic confrontation with NATO that neither side wants," he added.

The Irishman called for Russia to declare a humanitarian ceasefire to allow the evacuation of residents in Ukraine's eastern Donbas region, which has seen some of the most intense fighting.

He said that both Russia and Ukraine had committed war crimes, but that the investigation into the alleged crimes by either side should be carried out by an international tribunal.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said last week that Moscow's conditions for talks were "unacceptable" but that he was open to negotiations.

People aged between 18 and 20 will be able to stand as MPs in the next general election, the Speaker's Committee has confirmed. 

The change - affecting the next election, due by 2024 - was announced last year.

The committee's decision confirms the details of the plan and says the change is "reasonable".

MPs aged 18-20 would be entitled to salaries, allowances and office costs.

The committee - which makes rules for the House of Commons - also recommended allowing 16-year-olds to take part in select committee inquiries.

Its report said the change would mean "a more diverse range of people" would be able to take part in scrutiny of the government.

The plans, which are subject to approval by MPs, would not reduce the minimum age for voting, which is 18.

The committee's report said there was a "wide range of views" on the issue of lowering the voting age but that the decision had been made to "take a cautious approach".

It said "the crucial factor in the selection of the minimum age for candidacy is that the candidate should have the capability of being an effective member of Parliament".

The current minimum age of 25 for MPs was set in 1695, with the original reason being that MPs needed to be mature and experienced.

The plans for the next general election were announced by the then Prime Minister Boris Johnson in July 2022.

The proposal was among a number of measures aimed at improving access to politics, after the UK's first minister with learning difficulties, Deputy Prime Minister Dominic Raab, appointed a panel to advise on how politics could become more accessible.

The UK government has announced that teenagers aged between 18 and 20 will be allowed to stand as MPs in the next general election, planned for 2024. The change forms part of the government's Youth Charter, which aims to give young people more say in the political process. 

"This is a crucial step towards a more diverse and inclusive parliament," said Cabinet Minister Julia Lopez. "Young people are underrepresented in our politics, both in the Commons and in the Lords. That needs to change, and it's going to change."

The move has been welcomed by some, but others have argued that it will not do enough to make politics more accessible to young people. "This is a small step in the right direction, but it doesn't go far enough," said Liam Kerr, the Scottish Conservative leader. "We need to see more meaningful action to make sure that our politics is accessible to people from all walks of life."

The changes are set to be implemented for the next general election, but it is not yet clear whether they will be made permanent.

Police in China have detained the chairmen of two dairy companies at the centre of a scandal over milk powder contaminated with industrial chemicals.

The general manager of Sanlu Group - the firm at the centre of the crisis - has also been taken into custody, police said.

It follows revelations that milk powder producers have been adding the chemical melamine to give false high protein readings.

Six children have died and more than 300,000 fallen ill from drinking milk and milk products laced with the chemical.

Police in the northern city of Shijiazhuang, where the Sanlu Group is based, made the arrests after the men volunteered to hand themselves in, state news agency Xinhua reported.

They have been charged with "endangering public security", which can carry the death penalty.

The scandal, which first emerged last week, has already seen 22 people arrested, including those working for three dairy companies implicated in the scam.

Yili is based in the northern city of Hohhot and describes itself as China's biggest dairy producer.

Police in the capital said they had also arrested two people working for the Xiabu Xiabu dairy firm, which is based in the eastern city of Tianjin.

The scandal has raised concerns over the safety of China's food production industry as demand for dairy products has soared amid growing wealth.

Many Chinese mothers prefer to use milk powder because of perceived purity questions over domestic milk supplies.

The Chinese government has ordered all dairy products to be tested nationwide and has halted exports of milk powder, infant formula and yoghurt.

On Thursday, New Zealand announced that it was suspending all imports of Chinese milk powder and other dairy products as a precaution.

And in Hong Kong, supermarkets and pharmacies have pulled Chinese-made milk powder and infant formula off their shelves.

Police in China have detained the heads of several milk powder producers amid fears that a supply of infant formula made by one company may have been contaminated with lead. 

The public security ministry said four people were detained over the incident, including the chairman of baby formula producer Biostime and the heads of three dairy companies in provincial regions. 

Milk powder is a sensitive issue in China after a scandal in 2008 when six babies died and nearly 300,000 were hospitalised after drinking milk powder laced with melamine.

The public security ministry said the Biostime products were not bound for the domestic market but for overseas. 

Milk powder produced by three dairy firms in Liaoning, Hebei and Shaanxi provinces were found to contain mercury, cadmium and lead above the allowable limit, the General Administration of Market Regulation (GMR) said on Sunday. 

The GMR has since then ordered companies to stop production and sales, and recall products. 

The Biostime formula, produced by a subsidiary called Ausnutria China, was found to contain lead at a concentration of 2.74 parts per million, exceeding the allowable limit of 2.5 parts per million. 

The batch of product, consisting of 223 cans, was manufactured on Aug. 29 this year and sold in Hong Kong with production codes ranging from 23082010204 to 23082010224, the Hong Kong government's Center for Food Safety said in a statement on Saturday. 

The center has requested the company to immediately stop the sale of the affected products and is conducting further investigation with the trade department and the food authority in Guangdong province, where Ausnutria China is based. 

The Biostime formula is being sold in Hong Kong under the brand name of Beingmate. 

The company, which has apologized over the incident, said the affected product accounted for about 0.08 percent of its total production in China this year.

Parchment suffered a horrific injury at the London Olympics when he crashed into a hurdle in the 110m hurdles final and twisted his knee.

He needed surgery to repair damage to his knee and hamstring and many thought he would never race again.

But the 25-year-old made an astonishing recovery and returned to training just seven months after the accident.

He made his return to competition earlier this year and managed to qualify for the World Championships in Moscow, where he won bronze in the 110m hurdles.

"I am very, very surprised to win this award," he said. "There are a lot of other athletes who could have won this and I am very happy to have received it.

The BBC's news website has launched a version specifically for mobile phones using the 3G wireless internet standard.

The BBC's executive producer for multimedia news, Emma Nagraba, said she was "delighted" by the launch.

"We're offering a rich, multimedia experience, with the same mix of news, sport, entertainment and information as the website," she said.

The mobile site will enable users to access the same information as the website, but it has been redesigned for the smaller screen of a mobile phone.

Ms Nagraba said the redesign would ensure the service was easy to use on the "smaller screen and limited navigation" of a phone.

The mobile site includes stories from the BBC's international, UK, and technology news sections, and users can also access the sports, entertainment and lifestyle sections.

They can also contribute their own content, including pictures and video.

"We're aiming to engage people by providing the tools for them to contribute, so we will be encouraging users to upload their content," said Ms Nagraba.

"We want to make it easy for people to use the BBC's mobile services, and we will be promoting the site through our other outlets, such as Radio 1 and BBC TV."

The mobile site also offers access to BBC Sounds, the corporation's digital radio station, and users can watch video footage and catch up on BBC Three programming.

The launch of the mobile service follows the BBC's recent decision to make its news output "digital first", meaning that its website will be the first place that BBC news stories appear.

The 3G (Third Generation) mobile phone is taking the UK by storm. Verizon seals takeover of MCI

Rory McIlroy warmed up for his Masters title defence with a comprehensive four-shot victory in the Honda Classic in Florida.
The 28-year-old world number two went into the final day one shot off the lead but fired a six-under-par 64 to finish on 11 under, with Japan's Yoshihisa Hasegawa and American Webb Simpson sharing second place.
McIlroy, who won the Genesis Open in Los Angeles last week, kicked off the final round with four straight birdies.
And he will now head to Augusta National confident of adding to the Green Jacket he wore last year after becoming the first Northern Irishman to win the Masters.
"It's great to get into that winning rhythm and get a couple of wins under my belt heading into the first major of the year," said McIlroy, who will play the first two rounds of the Masters with Tiger Woods after the pairings were announced on Tuesday.
"I get asked all the time about my preparations for Augusta and this is as good as it gets."
McIlroy, who won the Honda Classic in 2012 and 2016, began the day one off the lead but moved level with Japan's Hasegawa with a birdie on the second.
Another followed on the next and he fired three more on the back nine, despite a double bogey on the par-three 15th, to set the clubhouse target at 11 under.
Hasegawa and Simpson both birdied the last to set the target at nine under but it was not enough to stop McIlroy from claiming his 23rd PGA Tour title.
"I got off to a great start, four birdies in a row, and I never really looked back from there," added McIlroy, who recorded his first successive wins since 2014.
"To shoot 64 on a Sunday with a double bogey is pretty impressive and I took advantage of the par-fives on the back nine, which are tough.
"I got it to 13 under for a while but double bogeyed the 15th. I missed a short putt for par and that started the momentum going the other way.
"But I got a good up-and-down for par on the next and then finished with two birdies."

Rory McIlroy secured a record-tying victory at the HSBC Championship in Abu Dhabi to continue his winning streak. The former world number one began the day two shots off the lead but produced a six-under-par 66 - the lowest round of the day - to finish top of the leaderboard on 22-under. 

It was his 15th victory on the PGA Tour, moving him level with Dustin Johnson and Jim Furyk. I hit a lot of fairways, a lot of greens and holed some nice putts here and there," said McIlroy, who won the FedEx Cup in September 2022. McIlroy won the Abu Dhabi HSBC Championship in 2009, 2010 and 2011. It is the first time he has successfully defended a title on the PGA Tour. Im, who will be defending his Genesis Invitational title in Los Angeles later this month, finished second in Abu Dhabi last year and third in 2020. England's Tommy Fleetwood was in a three-way tie for third place with American Collin Morikawa and Norway's Viktor Hovland.

Arthur Hailey has made a fortune from fiction. His books have sold more than 170 million copies worldwide and have been translated into 40 languages. He is the author of a string of bestsellers, including Hotel, Airport and Wheels.

The success of these books saw him dubbed "the king of the bestseller".

The one thing his readers could rely on was that Arthur Hailey would never surprise them.

His formula was simple. Take a large organisation oozing with ambition, cynicism and greed. Throw in a ruthless businessman as protagonist. Add a strong female character as the moral compass.

Mix well and place in a container. Then take a large pinch of suspense, a generous scoop of romance, and a heap of insider information about the workings of the organisation concerned.

Bake until the plot is thick and juicy, and serve in small portions. A chapter a night is about right.

Some authors have admitted emulating Hailey's recipe for success. Stephen King, for one. "Hotel was one of the books that made me want to be a writer," he said. "I thought, 'I can do this. This is not rocket science.'"

Others have criticised Hailey for making writing look easy. Michael Crichton, creator of Jurassic Park, described Hailey as "a lazy writer".

"He works occasionally," he said, "but not hard."

The son of a police officer, Hailey was born in Luton in 1920. After leaving school at 14, he had a variety of jobs - including as a vacuum cleaner salesman and a touring actor with the BBC's repertory company - before joining the RAF during World War Two.

After the war he worked as a journalist in London and, in 1951, moved to Canada where he wrote for the Toronto Star. It was there that he started to write novels.

His breakthrough came with the publication of his seventh novel, Hotel, in 1965.

The book became an instant hit, turning Hailey into a millionaire.

He wrote a string of bestselling novels in the same vein - using real-life locations such as airports, railways and hospitals as the backdrop to his stories of big business and ambitious men.

His method was to carry out extensive research until he knew more about his subject than anyone else.

"I'm not a very bright fellow," he once said. "But I stay with it until I know as much as anybody about it."

The novelist Arthur Hailey could hardly have hoped for a more lavish tribute than the five-part television adaptation of his 1977 bestseller, Airport. It was the most expensive movie made up to that time, starred an array of major movie stars including Burt Lancaster, Dean Martin, George Kennedy and Helen Hayes, and was directed by the veteran master of suspense, George Seaton. The film was a huge hit, and its success helped make Hailey one of the bestselling authors of the late 20th century. By the early 1990s, his novels had sold more than 170 million copies worldwide, and had been translated into 40 languages. Hailey died in 2004, aged 84, but his work has not been forgotten. In the words of the writer Peter James, himself no slouch when it comes to popular crime fiction: "Arthur Hailey is the father of us all."

Hailey was born in Luton in 1920, the son of a wholesale jeweller. When the depression hit, the family fortunes changed dramatically, and Arthur found himself expelled from grammar school and sent to live with his aunt in Toronto. He mastered touch-typing and landed a job as a court reporter, and later as a journalist on the Toronto Star. His first novel, Dangerous Weapons, a suspense thriller about a nuclear missile hijacking, was published in 1959, when he was 40. But it was the novel Airport, published 14 years later, that really catapulted him to success.

According to the writer Robert Barnard, the secret of Hailey's success was his ability to make a thrilling story out of the banal. In Airport, he took the everyday scenario of an airport and made it the setting for an edge-of-your-seat drama that combined the threat of terrorist violence with more personal stories of romance and betrayal. The book was adapted for the screen by Hailey himself, in collaboration with the screenwriter Stirling Silliphant, and there was little scope for improvisation when it came to the script. The huge cast included Burt Lancaster as the managing director of Chicago's O'Hare airport, and Dean Martin as the pilot of the doomed flight. George Kennedy played the tough, no-nonsense airport chief, who managed to convey a great deal of information about aircraft procedures while issuing forth a steady stream of four-letter words. And Helen Hayes, fresh from her success in the stage and screen versions of Hello, Dolly!, played the grieving mother of a murdered girl, whose son is taken in by a religious sect.

The UK government should deliver tax cuts before the next general election, the Tory chairman said. Oliver Dowden said the government should "keep delivering" for voters ahead of 2024. He said Prime Minister Boris Johnson had delivered on an "ambitious agenda" amid challenges posed by the pandemic. The chancellor is due to deliver a third budget this year, with expectations of tax cuts for businesses.

Mr Dowden's comments came as the prime minister launched a plan to boost the number of police officers in England by 20,000 - with the aim of recruiting an extra 6,000 officers annually.

The PM said on Thursday that it was "absolutely right" to make sure the police "have the resources they need" to keep the public safe.

But the Labour Party said the prime minister was "giving with one hand and taking with another", with the tax rises introduced in the last budget used to pay for the plan.

What's Mr Dowden's point?

The Conservative Party chairman said the government should "keep delivering" on the agenda set out in the 2019 general election campaign.

"I think people voted for us to keep delivering on that ambitious agenda we set out," he told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

Why's the chancellor preparing a third budget?

Rishi Sunak will deliver his third budget on 15 March, as the government continues its support for the economy following the pandemic.

The chancellor has been keen to stress that any future tax cuts will be "fiscally responsible".

Tory MP Sayeeda Warsi is to stand down at the next general election.

The former cabinet minister announced her decision to step down as MP for Batley and Spen in West Yorkshire following discussions with her family.

The 51-year-old said it had been a "great honour" to serve her constituency.

Warsi became the first Muslim woman to serve in a British cabinet in 2010.

She was appointed by former prime minister David Cameron as minister without portfolio and shadow minister for faith and communities.

"I have decided not to stand at the next general election, although that is some years away," she said.

"That's a decision I have taken in conjunction with my family, particularly as my son is now 10 years old and they should not grow up solely with the weekends as the time they can see their mum."

Warsi was elected to Parliament in 2010, and became the first Muslim woman to serve in a British cabinet, as minister without portfolio and shadow minister for faith and communities.

She stepped down from the frontbench after voting against the government on the issue of airstrikes in Syria in 2015.

She was among several Tory MPs to criticise Boris Johnson over his handling of the partygate scandal earlier this year.

In January, she called for him to resign, saying she was "deeply disturbed" by the behaviour on display in Downing Street.

Warsi said she did not know what the future held for her, but that she was "excited" by the possibilities.

England centre Emily Scarratt will become the women's game's highest ever Test scorer as she sets her sights on breaking the 5000-point mark in the Six Nations.

Scarratt, 34, currently has 3,527 points and needs just 23 points in this year's Six Nations to pass Katy Daley-Mclean's mark.

She will reach the milestone if she scores two tries and kicks seven conversions in England's first two matches.

"It's a honour," said Scarratt. "When you look at the calibre of players that have come before, it's a proud moment.

"It's something I if hadn't have thought about, never mind something I probably wouldn't have imagined would happen when I started playing rugby.

"I feel incredibly lucky."

Before this year's Six Nations Scarratt needed 35 points to overtake Daley-Mclean's mark, but having been involved in England's recent Quilter Internationals against the USA and Canada, the centre has scored 60 points so far this season.

The England men's record is held by Jonny Wilkinson, who scored 1,246 points in his 95 Tests between 1998 and 2011.

If Scarratt reaches the 5000-point mark it will be thanks to her formidable penalty and conversion rates.

Of her 3,527 Test points, 2,577 have come from penalties and conversions.

Scarratt made her England debut in 2007 and has gone on to win 134 caps. She has appeared at six World Cups and was named player of the match in the 2017 final, which England won.

England captain Owen Farrell paid tribute to his "good friend" and former teammate Maro Itoje after Billy Vunipola's injury against Japan ruled him out of the rest of the November Tests.

The leader of the Scottish National Party (SNP) has warned Labour MPs in Scotland that they face being deselected if they do not back independence.

In an interview with the BBC's Political Editor, Laura Kuenssberg, Ms Sturgeon said the SNP would prefer to work with Labour in an independence referendum.

The PM's official spokesman said on Monday that "taxpayers expect their money to be spent on things that will benefit the whole country".

The former leader of the Scottish Labour Party has warned "centrist" MPs they will be kicked out of the party if they do not change their minds on key issues.

Mr Murphy, who served as Scottish Labour leader from 2015 to 2017, spoke to BBC Scotland as the party launched its local election campaign in Scotland.

"There are still far too many MPs, even after the last few years, who basically think we can be a centrist party and win a general election.

"That is not going to happen. We have to be a radical, transformational party and if those MPs disagree with that, then they should leave the party."

It is one of the world's biggest technology firms, but Microsoft has revealed that its customers are still being affected by bugs in its Windows operating system.

The US software giant issued an emergency fix for a vulnerability that allows hackers to remotely take control of any Windows computer - desktops, laptops, servers, and even smartphones.

The vulnerability, known as BadTunnel, allows hackers to take control of a machine despite no action by the user.

Microsoft said there was no evidence that the vulnerability, in the way Windows verifies security certificates, had been exploited.

But the software giant issued a fix for the bug on Tuesday after researchers discovered it.

Security experts said the discovery highlighted how difficult it was for software companies to secure their products.

The researchers who discovered the bug are demonstrating their findings at the Black Hat security conference in Las Vegas.

BadTunnel takes advantage of a feature in Windows that allows users to connect securely over the internet, using a technology called VPN (virtual private networking).

VPNs are used by companies to allow employees to connect securely to private corporate networks from outside; but the technology has also been offered to consumers by companies like AT&T in the US and BT in the UK.

The researchers found that by manipulating data packets, a hacker could cancel out the private encryption key normally used to secure data transmitted over a VPN.

That would allow a hacker to see all the data passing between a Windows device and its VPN server - including usernames, passwords and other sensitive information.

And because the hack takes advantage of how Windows verifies security certificates, there is nothing a user could do to stop it.

"The user doesn't have to do anything - just using the computer is enough to be vulnerable," said Marc Maiffret, who discovered the bug along with his colleague, Aaron Portnoy.

The researchers said the vulnerability was likely to affect all versions of Windows, including Windows 7, the soon-to-be-released Windows 8, and Windows Server 2003, 2008 and 2012.

And because VPN features are also built into Windows Phone, the vulnerability also affects Windows smartphones.

"We haven't tested it on phones, but there is no reason why it wouldn't work," said Mr Maiffret.

Microsoft issued a fix for the bug on Tuesday, and said it had not seen any evidence that hackers had exploited the vulnerability.

Share prices of some of the biggest gaming companies have been hit by rumours of a crackdown in China on the sector, which has ballooned in recent years.

It was one of the most popular video games of 2020. But today, "Cyberpunk 2077" has been removed from digital storefronts run by Sony, Microsoft and the game's developer CD Projekt Red. It's been a spectacular fall from grace for a game which once seemed set to take the crown for the biggest new IP launch of the last decade.

Yet this apparent disaster has had one surprisingly positive effect.

"Cyberpunk 2077" may have flopped as a game, but it's been a major success as a gangsters' paradise.

But for one particular type of gamer, even an empty city is better than no city at all.

Gangs of gamers have been using "Cyberpunk 2077" to stage massive multiplayer riots, races and shootouts - and it's led to a boom in popularity for the game.

 Multiplayer mods have brought new life to "Cyberpunk 2077"

"Cyberpunk 2077" may be a single-player game, but that hasn't stopped gamers from forming their own gangs and clans to take on the city's virtual criminals.

Brazil's president, Jair Bolsonaro, has signed a law allowing companies in the country to seek bankruptcy protection without the risk of executives being imprisoned.

The new law is aimed at helping companies hit by the coronavirus pandemic.

Bolsonaro signed the law days after the country's Supreme Court ruled that bankruptcy reform was constitutional.

The law had been approved by the Brazilian Congress in March 2020, but it was blocked by the country's top court shortly after it was signed by the president.

The pandemic hit Brazil at a time when the country's economy was already in recession.

Many companies have faced financial difficulties, and thousands have filed for bankruptcy protection, with hundreds of others having already gone out of business.

Prior to the new law, companies that had accumulated debts of more than BRL 260,000 ($39,250; £29,836) for three months or more could be prosecuted for fraud.

That could lead to executives being banned from serving as company directors for up to five years or even facing prison time.

Researchers at Brazil's Getulio Vargas Foundation, a think tank, estimate that the country's economy could contract by more than 5% this year, compared with a 0.5% drop in 2019.

Brazil's parliament has approved a controversial reform of the country's bankruptcy laws, aiming to simplify and speed up the process of reorganizing debts. The move is a part of Brazil's economic reforms aimed at boosting investment and growth. However, the reform has been criticized for favoring creditors over workers and consumers, who could face job losses and higher prices as a result. 

The new law will allow companies to seek bankruptcy protection before their debts become unpayable, allowing them to restructure their finances more quickly and avoid lengthy court battles. This is intended to encourage more companies to seek help when they are struggling, rather than waiting until they are on the brink of collapse. 

The reform has been praised by business leaders and economists, who say it will help to boost investment and economic growth in Brazil. However, labor unions and consumer groups have criticized the law, saying it will prioritize the interests of creditors over those of workers and consumers. They argue that it will lead to more job losses and higher prices, as companies will be able to restructure their debts without taking into account the impact on their employees and customers.

Eminem has scored his tenth number one album in the UK, making him the artist with the most chart-topping albums in history.

His new release, Curtain Call: The Hits, shifted more than 157,000 units in its first week on sale.

The album beat the record set by Elvis Presley, who scored his ninth number one album in 2005, with The Wonder of Elvis.

Curtain Call: The Hits is a compilation of Eminem's hits from The Slim Shady LP to Eminem Presents: The Re-Up.

It also includes two new songs, one of which features Elton John.

Impressively, Curtain Call has become the rapper's tenth number one album in just eight years.

His previous highest-charting album, 2005's Curtain Call, peaked at number two.

Curtain Call: The Hits will be officially released on 5 November.

In the meantime, Eminem is set to perform at the MTV Europe Music Awards in Lisbon on 6 November.

He is up for three EMAs - best song, best video and best act - and will perform his new single, Kiss Kiss.

Kiss Kiss features on Curtain Call: The Hits, as does the rapper's collaboration with Rihanna, Love The Way You Lie.

That song was number one for four weeks earlier this year and was the UK's biggest hit of 2010.

Reviewing the hits collection, the Daily Telegraph said that Eminem's "verbal ingenuity...is quite astonishing".

"The rhymes are multi-syllabic, witty, sometimes surreal and often vulgar," said the paper.

"There is something both awe-inspiring and exhausting about listening to Eminem spew out endless streams of syllables at breakneck speed."

Eminem has made chart history by becoming the first artist to score ten consecutive number-one albums in the UK. 

The musician's latest record, entitled "Curtain Call 2", a compilation of his hits, entered the charts at the top spot, pushing the Beatles' "Abbey Road" to second place. 

The "Curtain Call" album celebrated Eminem's 50th birthday and marked 25 years since the release of his debut major-label album, "The Slim Shady LP". 

The 47-year-old rapper boasts a total of 15 UK number-one albums. Only three other musicians have achieved more: the Beatles (with a total of 17), Elvis Presley (16) and Robbie Williams (14). 

Eminem, born Marshall Bruce Mathers III, burst onto the scene in 1999 with the release of "My Name Is". 

His debut major-label album, "The Slim Shady LP" (released in early 1999 in the US and the following year in the UK), became the fastest-selling solo rap album in history. 

Despite Eminem's chart success, his albums have not always been well received by music critics. 

His best-selling album, "The Eminem Show" (2002), was praised by the New York Times as "bold and cunning". However, other records were described as "mediocre" and "lazy" by Rolling Stone. 

Nevertheless, Eminem has sold more than 220 million records worldwide, making him one of the best-selling music artists of all time.

House prices have fallen for the sixth month in a row, according to figures from the Halifax.

The mortgage lender said prices dropped by 1.5% in November, following a 1.6% fall in October.

It said the market had seen a slowdown in activity in recent months, with the number of properties for sale falling by 5% between September and October.

Halifax said the average UK house price was £274,311 in November, which was just £1,613 higher than a year earlier.

"In recent months we have seen evidence that buyer demand has started to wane in response to the expiry of tax breaks designed to support the market, coupled with rising interest rates and a natural tapering of demand as we move into the quieter winter months," said Halifax managing director Russell Galley.

"Looking ahead, there is a combination of factors which could lead to a slowdown in house price growth, including the potential for higher interest rates, the winding down of government buyouts and increasingly stretched household budgets," he added.

However, Galley also said there was still a shortage of properties for sale, which he thought should continue to support prices.

According to Halifax, prices are still rising much more quickly than average wages, with average house prices now seven times average salaries, compared with about five times two decades ago.

Earlier this month, rival lender Nationwide reported that UK house prices fell by 2.3% in November, leaving them 3.2% higher than a year earlier. It said the slowdown reflected "a natural lull" in activity after the end of the stamp duty holiday in September, and the withdrawal of government support for the housing market.

However, it said the outlook for the market remained uncertain, with inflation and interest rates set to rise further, and tax hikes expected in the spring.

House prices fell for the sixth month in a row in November, according to a survey of estate agents.

The average price of homes sold through estate agents was £296,000, down by 1.5% compared with October, said property website Rightmove.

It said the market had "definitely cooled" in the past month, with buyer demand falling to its lowest level since January.

Rightmove's house price index tracks the asking prices of property advertised on its website.

It is a closely watched measure of the health of the UK property market, but does not capture the entire market.

The figures come after Bank of England figures last week showed that mortgage approvals had fallen to their lowest level since June 2020.

Approvals for house purchases in October were 67,000, down from 71,000 in September, according to the Bank.

That was below the 12-month average of 72,000, and the lowest figure since June 2020, when the housing market was shut down for part of the month due to the Covid pandemic.

Martin Beck, senior economic adviser to the EY Item Club, said: "Households are increasingly worried about the rising cost of living, and this is starting to impact the housing market."

He said that higher interest rates and inflation, which is currently at a 40-year high, had "increased the squeeze on household budgets", meaning that people "have less money to spend on big-ticket items like homes".

But he said that it was not all "doom and gloom" for the property market, as there was still a "significant number" of people looking to buy a home.

"While the number of property sales has slowed, this will not be reflected in house prices until next year, as it takes time for transactions to work their way through the system," he said.

Separate figures from the Government's Land Registry, which records the final sale price of properties, showed that average UK house prices rose by 5.8% in the year to September, down from 7.3% in the year to August.

The US Department of Energy said its new Summit supercomputer at Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Tennessee took the top spot in the Top500 list, with a computational speed of 200 quadrillion – or 200,000,000,000,000 – calculations per second.

But the US has caught up thanks in part to a $500m (£380m) investment in the Summit machine, which is powered by IBM POWER9 chips and NVIDIA GPUs.

It is also the first system to break the exaflop barrier, meaning it can perform 200,000,000,000,000,000 (200 exaflops) floating point operations per second. An exaflop is a measure of a computer's processing speed.

What is a supercomputer?

Supercomputers are extremely fast and powerful machines. They are designed to do complex calculations and work that requires a lot of number-crunching.

They are used by scientists to predict the weather, by engineers to design aircraft and by mathematicians to try to crack encryption.

Although they are incredibly powerful, supercomputers are generally not as flexible as a desktop computer or a smartphone.

And despite their name, they are actually fairly common. There are supercomputers in many countries around the world.

What are they used for?

Supercomputers are often used by scientists to run complex simulations. For example, they can be used to simulate how a new drug might work in the human body.

They are also used by engineers to design new aircraft and to figure out how to build bridges and other structures.

In the same period, Japanese exports to China reached $51.1bn, up 8.5% and also a record high, thanks to strong demand for cars and machinery.

Japan's trade surplus with China widened to $206.3bn, up 29% from a year earlier, according to the data.

By comparison, Japan's trade surplus with the US reached $100.4bn in the same period, down 4.9% from a year earlier.

"The main reason [for the change] is that the US economy recovered relatively early from the pandemic and its growth rate is very strong, while China's economy still lags behind due to its zero-Covid policy," said Takahide Kiuchi, a former Bank of Japan board member who now serves as chief economist at the Nomura Research Institute.

Former football coach Jimmy Jones has filed a lawsuit against Conte Sports, a sports marketing firm. Jones claims that the company failed to pay him for work done under his former contract with the company. The lawsuit seeks compensation for the unpaid wages, as well as damages for breach of contract.

Jones was contracted to provide coaching services to Conte Sports' football team, as well as to assist in the development of the company's training facilities. According to the lawsuit, Jones performed all of the services required under the contract, but Conte Sports failed to pay him for his work. The lawsuit also claims that the company breached the contract by failing to provide the agreed-upon compensation.

Conte Sports has yet to comment on the lawsuit.

LONDON - The former footballer, Alan Jones, has filed a lawsuit against the Italian manager, Antonio Conte, alleging unfair dismissal. 

The 58-year-old UK resident claims he suffered discrimination and was wrongfully terminated as an assistant coach of Tottenham Hotspur Football Club in July 2020.

Mr. Jones, who has worked with renowned football clubs like Chelsea and Liverpool, was hired by Tottenham Hotspur in 2019 as part of Conte's coaching staff. However, after just one season with the club, the Italian manager fired him without notice.

The former footballer claims that Conte unfairly favored his own staff members over him and that the decision to fire him was based on discriminatory grounds. Further details about the allegations are expected to emerge during the trial.

Tottenham Hotspur has denied any wrongdoing and stated that the decision to fire Mr. Jones was based on his performance. The club has expressed its full confidence in Conte's management.

The lawsuit is set to be heard in the UK's High Court, with a preliminary hearing scheduled for later this month.

Gareth Bale and Ethan Ampadu have been left out of the Wales squad for September's World Cup qualifiers against Czech Republic and Estonia.

Bale has not played since injuring his knee in May and his club side Tottenham have said the forward is unlikely to be fit enough to feature before October.

Ampadu has been omitted with Chelsea concerned about his fitness, while Ryan Bennett and Joe Rodon have been left out with their clubs happy to give them time to recover from injuries.

Wales boss Robert Page says he is "hopeful" Liverpool's Neco Williams will recover from a knee injury to link up with the squad.

The 20-year-old full-back has not featured for the Reds this season after picking up an injury in pre-season and last played for Wales in March.

Williams reported for training with Liverpool on Wednesday but is still some way off a return to action.

"It's great news that Neco is back on the grass but he's still a way off," Page told BBC Sport Wales.

"We're hopeful that he might get some game time before the international break."

Page has called Swansea defender Ben Cabango into his squad for the first time.

The 20-year-old has started the season well after an impressive debut campaign last time out.

"He's been excellent since the start of last season when he came in [for Swansea] and has carried that form on," Page said.

"We've been monitoring him for a long time, he offers something different and is versatile as he can play in a back three or four.

"There is competition for places which is what we want."

Wales face Czech Republic in Prague on 1 September before hosting Estonia in Cardiff three days later.

Wales have been boosted by the return of Liam Williams for their Autumn Nations Series finale against Australia on Saturday.

The full-back missed the wins over Fiji and Argentina after suffering an injury in Wales' opening 33-19 loss to New Zealand.

Centre Jonathan Davies is also included in the 39-man squad after missing the games against Argentina and Fiji through injury.

Wales have won their last nine home Tests and a tenth victory would equal their best home run of 11 successive wins between 1907 and 1910.

Sir Sean Connery's widow has made an "impassioned plea" to the Scottish government to help recover a sculpture bought by the late actor which has been missing for over 40 years.

Michelle Connery lent the 7ft (2.1m) bronze statue of her husband - created by Scottish artist Alan Snell - to a gallery in Edinburgh in 1976.

But the work of art went missing from a warehouse in 1978 following an exhibition at the city's Botanic Cottage.

Snell died in 2014 but Mrs Connery has asked Scotland's culture minister Jenny Gilruth to help find the statue, saying its "disappearance remains a sore point".

She said she did not think the art work had been destroyed, as it would be "almost impossible" to get rid of "something that size".

Snell's family has also asked for the statue's return.

Mrs Connery said she believed the sculpture "will surface" one day.

She added: "It's precious to me, of course, because it's the only portrait sculpture that was done during my husband's lifetime."

Culture minister Jenny Gilruth said the sculpture is not believed to be in any Scottish museum or gallery.

Ms Gilruth said: "I understand the importance of the sculpture to Michelle Connery and Alan Snell's family and can confirm that officers from National Galleries of Scotland have been in touch with Michelle Connery's representatives to discuss the matter further."

"National Galleries of Scotland has made clear it is willing to investigate any viable leads in relation to the current location of the sculpture," she added.

The minister said there had been "several unverified claims" about the statue's whereabouts since it went missing.

"All of these have proven to be unfounded," she added.

"I understand that the police have previously investigated the disappearance of the sculpture and exhausted all viable lines of inquiry at the time.

"However, I have asked National Galleries of Scotland to keep me updated should any new information come to light."

Sir Trevor Howard, one of Britain's most distinguished actors, was best known for his roles in the movies 'Brief Encounter' and 'The Third Man'. At the time of his death in 1988, aged 77, he was working on a memoir about his experiences during World War II. Nearly 35 years later, his daughter, the actress Emily Howard, has completed and published it – revealing, among other things, how her father inadvertently helped the Nazis.

Howard maintained a determinedly modest public profile, but his daughter describes a driven, complex man behind the scenes. 'His ambition was limitless,' she writes. 'He was never satisfied, never believed he had reached his goal. There was always another role to be played, another challenge.'

She also depicts a physically and emotionally abusive father who subjected her mother, actress Leslie Howard, to 'nightly humiliations'. He would crash out of parties and screenings, often after too much drinking, and become pathologically jealous if his wife was paid more than him or if she received good reviews for her acting. On one occasion, he attacked her after she touched the actor Peter Ustinov in what he perceived as a flirtatious way.

Leslie died in 1965, when Emily was just 12. 'I don't remember ever being hugged by him,' she writes. 'Nor did I ever see him express physical affection towards my mother… There is nothing of which I am more proud than being my mother's daughter.'

She was made a Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire in 1949 and was also awarded the Queen Elizabeth II Coronation Medal in 1953.

But Boris Johnson said he thought the memorial should focus on "busting the myth" that slavery was "some kind of side-issue".

The UK's fastest broadband is being trialled in Aberdeen, with speeds of up to 20 gigabits per second (Gbps).

The city is one of the UK's "smart cities" and is seen as an ideal location to test the benefits of very high-speed internet.

The trial is part of a programme run by a UK company called CityFibre. 

It is due to be completed by summer 2024.

What does it involve?
The company has created a network of more than 100 "spines" - small, sealed units filled with optical fibre and electronic equipment.

These are being installed around the city, never more than a few hundred metres away from each other.

Once turned on, each spine has the potential to provide internet speeds of up to 20Gbps. This is faster than any other current broadband network in the UK.

CityFibre said the spines would be able to offer "near infinite bandwidth" and would never need to be upgraded.

How is it being used?
The network has already been used to film a live performance of a ballet at the city's Music Hall, which was then streamed over the internet in ultra-high definition 3D.

It has also been used to connect schools, universities and hospitals in the city.

CityFibre said the network would be capable of streaming hundreds of Netflix movies to thousands of homes simultaneously, or every game from a major football tournament such as the Euros or the World Cup, to every screen in people's homes, all at the same time.

The company's chief executive, Greg Mesch, said the network could eventually be used to power all kinds of new technologies.

"From smart transportation and traffic systems to digital healthcare, ultra-high definition video, and even augmented and virtual reality," he said.

Why is it being trialled in Aberdeen?
Aberdeen has been named as a "smart city", as part of a project run by the UK government.

The project aims to make cities more efficient, using the internet of things - a network of internet-connected objects or devices.

CityFibre has been working in Aberdeen since 2019, and the city was chosen as the first to trial the new network.

The company said it planned to expand the network to other cities in the UK, including Edinburgh, Glasgow, Newcastle, Leeds and Manchester. But it has not yet said when this might happen.

Ultra fast wifi has been a tantalizing prospect for years now, with numerous experiments and trials underway – and it seems London could be next in line to get a signal that is "up to 100 times faster" than existing connections.

The UK capital is set to join the trial of a new multi-billion pound project dubbed "Airways". It is reportedly set to provide lightning-fast download speeds of up to 1 gigabit per second, and upload speeds of up to 150 megabits per second.

This would represent a significant upgrade on current top speeds in the UK of up to 1,300 megabits per second for downloads, and up to 50 for uploads.

It is understood that the system will be based on a mesh of small satellites orbiting the Earth at a height of 20,000 miles – an approach that could help millions of people who live in rural or remote areas, as well as those in densely populated cities, to get faster internet speeds.

The system would work by receiving signals from 5G phones and other wireless devices, then redirecting them to the satellite, which would then connect them to the internet.

It is claimed the system will be able to provide coverage in places that current satellite-based systems do not reach, as it will not be restricted by the signal strength of the device.

While the project is still in its early stages, and the speeds promised are only a fraction of those touted by other ultra fast wifi projects, it is a further sign that the era of ultra fast, satellite-enabled internet may be closer than many realise.

Drivers for the disabled can hit speeds of up to 180mph (290km/h), which is why British racing driver Billy Monger carries a parachute.

The 19-year-old, from Surrey, was born with a lower leg deficiency, had his legs amputated when he was a baby, and has been using prosthetic legs ever since.

He is currently competing in the British F3 championship, and aims to be the first disabled driver to race in Formula 1.

"I've always approached my disability as a challenge, not as a limitation," he says.

Monger competes against able-bodied drivers on equal terms, and says his disability gives him a competitive edge.

"There are lots of times when I'm more able than somebody with two legs," he says.

"I can run faster on crutches than most people can walk. I'm used to adapting and I can turn my disability into my ability."

As a high-profile athlete with a disability, Monger is proof of what can be achieved, says Mark Edwards, from Dare to Dream.

The charity was founded in 2004 by Edwards, a former Royal Marine who became a double leg amputee in 2001 after an IED exploded under his feet in Afghanistan.

"There's a huge amount of ability within disability, and that's what we're trying to prove," says Edwards.

"We want to challenge perceptions.

"A lot of people look at disability and see the can't, and we look at it and see the can."

While there are no reliable figures for the number of disabled people in the UK who want to participate in motor racing, Edwards says he receives about 50 enquiries a year from people with a disability wanting to give it a go.

"It's very physical, and it's very much about your upper body," says Monger.

"As a disabled person, you become even more focused on your arms, and using your arms to the best of your ability."

Monger began karting when he was just five years old, and has never let his disability get in the way of his career.

He has even modified his car to accommodate his prosthetic legs.

The newest movement in adaptive motoring is getting more disabled people on the road—and letting them do so at exhilarating speeds.

For most people, getting behind the wheel of a car and going fast is a thrilling experience. There is an indescribable sense of freedom on the open road, and for able-bodied drivers, the possibilities are endless.

But for those with disabilities, driving can be a more complicated affair. Some disabilities may make it difficult to control the steering, or to reach the pedals. Fortunately, with the help of new technologies, the world of adaptive motoring is opening up, allowing people with a wide range of disabilities to get behind the wheel and hit the road. And for some, that means going fast.

One of the pioneers in the world of adaptive motoring is Alex Zanardi, a former Formula One driver who lost his legs in a crash during a race in 2001. Zanardi has since gone on to become a world champion in Paralympic handcycling, and has developed a line of prosthetic legs specifically designed for driving.

Zanardi's legs, which are fitted with special pedals and mounts, allow him to control the throttle and brakes with his feet, while also providing the necessary stability and support to control the car. And despite his disability, Zanardi has not given up on his love of speed. In fact, he has become a champion drag racer, setting world records and winning competitions.

But Zanardi is not the only one redefining the world of adaptive motoring. There are now a number of organizations and companies dedicated to helping people with disabilities get behind the wheel. From modified steering wheels to voice-activated controls, the world of adaptive motoring is making it possible for more people than ever before to experience the thrill of the open road.

So whether you're a speed demon like Zanardi, or just looking to get from A to B, the world of adaptive motoring is making it possible for everyone to hit the road.

The UK has fallen to 14th in a table of average earnings for young people across Europe, according to Eurostat.

The statistics agency said 18- to 34-year-olds in Italy and France earned the most on average at the end of 2021.

The UK ranked among the top ten as recently as 2017, but has fallen down the table since.

Young people's average earnings in the UK were £415 per week, compared with £461 in Italy and £448 in France.

The Netherlands and Austria also featured in the top five countries where young people earned the most.

Young people's earnings in Germany and Denmark were the lowest among those recorded, where they earned about £350 per week.

These are the average earnings of people at the end of their education and entering the job market.

Compared with the previous year, young people's earnings increased in most European countries, but decreased in eight, with the biggest falls in the Czech Republic, Finland and Denmark.

Overall, across all age groups, UK earnings were the seventh highest in the EU.

Britain's youth are leading the way in Europe's gig economy, according to a study of people who share their earnings on the Bolt ride-hailing app.

Those in the UK median age bracket of 26 to 35 made the most on the Estonian-founded platform per hour on average - ahead of their Dutch and French counterparts, the study found.

The app has seen a surge in usage since the pandemic, particularly among younger people seeking flexible work.

The study covered March 2021 to February 2022.

In the UK, the median hourly earnings for a driver on Bolt was £17 ($21.60) compared with £14 in France and £12 in the Netherlands.

The average British driver on the platform was 30 years old, while the average Dutch driver was 41 and the average French driver was 36.

The study said British drivers were more likely to work longer hours, with their weekly average of 30 hours higher than the 25 hours worked by Dutch drivers.

It also found UK drivers were more likely to live in urban areas than their European counterparts.

Bolt carried out the study to mark the expansion of its services in the UK, which began with London in 2019 and has now rolled out to 30 British cities.

The company said it had seen a surge in drivers in the UK, with the number of active drivers growing by more than 530% in 2021.

Spokesman Paddy Doyle said: "In the UK, drivers using Bolt can now earn up to £250 a day - and this, alongside our fast-growing green footprint, is why so many drivers are switching to Bolt."

The company said 50% of its UK drivers were under 30, while in the Netherlands it was 20% and in France it was 15%.

Please note that this study is limited to Bolt drivers in the specified European countries. Different results may occur for other ride-hailing platforms or in other geographical areas.

A US composer has created a new score for Bach's Well-Tempered Clavier, using artificial intelligence (AI).

Ryan Neave created the music based on what he believes Bach might have written, given the same ingredients.

The tune for Book 1's Prelude in C was fed into an AI system, which generated a new score.

Neave then spent months refining that, using Bach's original keyboard music as a guide.

"I didn't want it to be a pastiche, I wanted it to be something that could stand on its own," he said.

The new score was performed at the Boston Early Music Festival over the weekend.

Bach wrote Well-Tempered Clavier – a set of 48 preludes and fugues in each major and minor key – in the 1700s. It is regarded as some of the most important works in the classical music canon.

Neave is a pianist and composer who graduated from Boston's Berklee College of Music, and is currently artist in residence at the University of Arkansas.

He said he first had the idea of using AI to recreate Bach's music in 2016.

"There was a lot of trial and error, but eventually I found the right process and the right collaborators to make it work," he said.

The process began by feeding a computer algorithm Bach's original melody for the Prelude in C from Book 1 of the Well-Tempered Clavier.

Neave then worked with a group of PhD students at the University of Arkansas to use AI to generate a new score by turning Bach's original tune into a set of numbers.

"We'll take a melody, assign some numbers to it, and then the computer will generate thousands of responses based on those numbers," he said.

The team then worked to refine the results, balancing the desire to use AI with making sure the new music sounded like something Bach could have written.

"There were a lot of wrong turns, but eventually we got something where I felt like it captured the spirit of what Bach might do, if he had been given infinite amounts of time, and used this technology," Neave explained.

The resulting piece is a solo piano work, 22 minutes long. It was premiered by pianist Samantha Bennett-Smith at the Boston Early Music Festival on Friday.

"It was a little bit intimidating, because it's so monumental," Bennett-Smith said of learning the new piece.

American composer and pianist Jeremy Denk has rewritten J.S. Bach's score for solo piano to include the composer's modern-day thoughts, feelings and quirks. The resulting composition, "These Words Are Yours", is being performed by Denk on a US tour. The show features video projections including handwritten scores by Bach and Denk, and even a grocery list. "There is a tremendous amount of excitement, frustration and glee that I feel when I play Bach," said Denk. "The piece became an excavation of all the different emotions that Bach's music elicits." 

The show has been performed several times since its debut in 2016. After one performance, a reviewer wrote that the experience of watching Denk perform the piece was akin to "watching someone recite a poem in another language and, without knowing it, finding it rolls off your tongue, too". 

Denk, a Pulitzer Prize finalist, is a well-known interpreter of Bach. "These Words Are Yours" is part of his ongoing project to perform and record Bach's complete piano music.

Voters in Britain are increasingly likely to vote for candidates who are not members of the two main parties, according to a new poll which suggests that the country is heading for a "tidal wave" of change.

The survey by polling organisation Ipsos MORI suggests that 54% of voters would be willing to back a candidate who is not a member of the Conservative or Labour parties, with just 46% saying they would not.

It follows recent local election successes for the Liberal Democrats in London and the SNP in Scotland, with both parties making gains at the expense of Labour and the Conservatives.

The polling organisation's managing director, Emily Gray, said the results suggested that the country was heading towards a "tidal wave" of change.

"This represents a significant shift in recent years in how voters perceive the options open to them at the general election," she said.

"With so many voters open to backing parties other than the two main parties, the risk for Labour and the Conservatives is that a significant chunk of the electorate will not be listening to their messages, or indeed will hear messages that chime with their view but will not feel that they have a safe option to vote for."

The poll also found that just 22% of voters believe that the country is heading in the right direction, with 46% thinking it is on the wrong track.

By contrast, voters were more positive about the direction of travel in their own local area, with 39% saying it was heading in the right direction and 35% believing it was on the wrong track.

The poll was based on interviews with more than 1,000 people across Britain, and has a margin of error of plus or minus 3.1%.

Brits' voting habits are in flux as traditional parties see a significant drop in support, a survey suggests.

The finding comes in a study of voters in England, Scotland and Wales just over a year before the next general election.

It found more than a third of people (37%) said they did not trust politicians in the UK to tell the truth.

And 64% of those who selected the Labour Party as their first choice on the survey did not trust the Tories - the highest level of distrust among any group of voters for any other party.

The analysis suggests the voting landscape has changed - with the traditional "big two" parties losing supporters to rivals on the left and right, and to independent candidates.

The survey suggests that in the 2005 general election, 67% of people voted for the Labour Party or the Conservative Party. That figure is now just 51%.

At the same time, the study indicates the proportion of people who voted for the Liberal Democrats, the Scottish National Party and Plaid Cymru has increased.

The survey suggests that the Labour Party is currently the most popular party in Britain, with 38% of people saying they would vote for Sir Keir Starmer's party if there were an election tomorrow.

The Conservatives have seen their support increase since the autumn, when the party was chosen by 31% of people.

But the study suggests support for the Tories is not as high as it was in the spring of this year, when 42% of people said they would vote for Boris Johnson's party.

The findings also indicate there could be a close race between Labour and the Conservatives as the two largest parties in Britain.

Just three points separate the parties, with the Liberal Democrats on 19%, the Scottish National Party on 8% and Plaid Cymru on 4%.

The BBC has learned that an increasing number of internet users are being diverted to scam web pages due to a flaw in the online domain name system (DNS). 

DNS is often compared to an address book, pointing web browsers to the right location on the internet.

Oil prices have dropped to their lowest level in three months, with demand slowing as China's latest coronavirus surge disrupts the country's economy.

China's daily crude oil processing last month dropped to its lowest level since September 2020, according to government data. This trend has been accelerating in recent days.

On Sunday, Tianjin authorities ordered a city-wide testing of nearly 14 million people following an outbreak of COVID-19.

In the meantime, global oil output is rising, with the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) boosting production by 278,000 barrels per day in November, month-on-month.

"There is not a lot of resistance until we get to the $70-75 per barrel area, so there is plenty of room for further downside," he added.

US crude futures fell below $80 a barrel, reaching their lowest level since early November.

The BBC's flagship technology show, Click, recently ran a story about the MP3. They rightly pointed out that "whatever happened to the MP3?" The answer is simple: almost everything. Today, MP3 technology is everywhere. It's in your phone, your car, your home, your fridge, your watch, and your fitness tracker. There are billions of MP3-playing devices around the globe. Chances are, you're listening to an MP3 file as you read these words.

The MP3 story is an interesting one and worth retelling. The technology that delivers music to your phone or PC has a rich history and a bright future.

In the early 1980s, the Fraunhofer Institute in Germany developed a way to compress audio files. The idea was to reduce the size of audio files to enable faster transmission over the internet while retaining acceptable quality. At the time, there were many competing audio formats, but the MP3 stood out. It was developed by MPEG, the same group that gave us the MPEG video standard.

The first MP3 player was unveiled in 1997. It was a portable music player that could hold enough music to rival the Sony Walkman. The Apple iPod launched in 2001 and quickly became the world's most popular MP3 player.

Since then, MP3 has become the de facto standard for digital audio. It's used in every device that plays digital music, from your phone to your car. There are billions of MP3 files stored on devices and computers worldwide.

But the MP3 is more than just a file format. It's a technology that has changed the way we listen to music. It has made it possible for us to carry our music collections with us wherever we go. It has made it possible for us to share our music with friends and family. It has made it possible for us to discover new music.

The MP3 is here to stay. Thanks to ever-improving audio technology, the MP3 continues to evolve. We can expect to see higher-quality MP3 files and more features that enable us to do more with our music. That's why the BBC was right to ask, "whatever happened to the MP3?"

For more than a decade, the BBC's Marc Settle has been worrying about the security of the many Wi-Fi networks he's been forced to connect to.

They're not just in coffee shops, but also in hotels, conference centres, and on trains.

"Some are completely wide open, and some have a flaky password that you can quickly glean from the guy at the front desk when you check in," he says.

So, what can be done to improve the situation?

"You basically have two choices," says Mr Settle.

"You can either stuff the network in a box, by using a VPN [virtual private network] app, or you can operate your own router as a firewall.

"The stuff-it-in-a-box solution is the easiest thing to do, but it's also pretty unsatisfactory," he says.

Once you're connected to the VPN, you have to be careful which websites you access, because your IP address is now hidden and you're effectively operating in secret online.

"VPNs are a little bit like the old days of Tor, when you had to carefully choose your browser to access the internet safely," says Mr Settle.

"It's better than nothing, but it's not a great solution."

Operating your own router as a firewall is technically challenging, he says, and you also need an internet connection that's stable enough to support it - which can be a problem on trains, for example.

So what can be done about the poor state of Wi-Fi security in public places and hotels?

The industry is slowly waking up to the problem, says Mr Settle, but change is slow.

"In the meantime, I'd like to see people thinking more carefully about security when they set these things up," he says.

"If you're running a network, please don't set the password on the front desk. And if you really must do that, make it a long password using all sorts of weird characters, not just 'hotelwireless'.
