Liverpool manager Rafael Benitez has warned his players not to get involved in "dirty games" after criticism from opposition managers this season.

The Reds have had more players booked this season than any other team in the Premier League.

Benitez's side have also been criticised for their style of play by managers like Arsenal's Arsene Wenger and Manchester United's Sir Alex Ferguson.

But the Liverpool manager said his players were not guilty of any wrong-doing.

"We are not involved in dirty games. Sometimes the players from the other teams are more clever than ours," said the Spaniard.

"Maybe we have more bookings because we play in the same way every week and the other teams adapt to play against us."

Benitez also defended the style of play that has been criticised by other managers.

"We can play in different ways but the main thing for us is to get the three points and to win the game," he said.

"If we were just kicking the ball in the air as some people have said, it would be very easy for the other teams to play against us.

"But it's not like that. We are playing our normal game, trying to pass the ball and trying to be successful."

Liverpool travel to Reading on Tuesday night looking to maintain their push for a top-four finish in the Premier League.

Liverpool manager Rafael Benítez has issued a warning to his former player Steven Gerrard, who is currently in charge of Aston Villa. Benítez says Gerrard has to be "careful" about the challenges he faces in managing a Premier League club and says he would like to see Villa do well, but recognises that his former club is currently in a far more fortunate position.

Speaking at his press conference ahead of Liverpool's game against Southampton on Saturday, Benítez said, "I think he is aware of the expectations, he is aware of the job that needs to be done, he is an experienced guy and he will know how to approach every game and he will try to get the best out of his players.

"For me it is a great challenge, because I know him very well, I worked with him when he was very young and he was a player who always wanted to learn and wanted to improve and wanted to win. So I am sure he is the same now as a manager and he will be trying to do his best."

When asked if he had any advice for his former player, the Liverpool manager said, "I think he is aware, he knows the league, he has experience, so I don't think he needs advice. Maybe just be careful with some of the expectations, because always in this country when you are doing well everyone is happy, but you need to be consistent and improve every day."

Benítez also spoke about the challenge of managing a team in the Premier League, saying, "I think it is different when you are a player and when you are a manager. "It is more challenging, because you have to manage the egos, you have to manage the players, you have to manage the staff, you have to manage the club, and then you have to manage the expectations of the fans and the owners. The IMF has cut its forecast for German economic growth this year because of the war in Ukraine.

It now expects Germany's GDP to grow by 2.6% in 2022, down from its forecast of 3.6% made in January.

The institute said Europe's largest economy was being hit by rising energy prices, which were affecting industrial activity.

The IMF also trimmed its global growth forecast to 3.6% this year, down from the 4.4% it predicted in January.

It said the war in Ukraine, surges in commodity prices, and the partial lockdown in China had influenced its decision.

The IMF expects the US economy to grow by 2.3% this year, down from its January forecast of 2.9%. It raised its UK growth forecast from 3.5% to 3.7% despite the economic hit from Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

It said the UK's economic performance had been "remarkably robust".

The IMF's global economic forecasts are closely watched by policymakers.

The fund's latest World Economic Outlook will be published on Tuesday.

According to the report published in January, 90% of the global economy resumed growth in 2021, but the war in Ukraine has reduced growth prospects this year, especially in Europe.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has cut Germany's growth forecast for this year, reflecting the impact of supply chain disruptions and the country's gas supply crisis.

The IMF now expects Germany's economy to grow by 1.7% in 2023, down from its previous forecast of 2%. This is significantly lower than Germany's estimated growth of 3.3% in 2022.

The fund attributed the cut to a severe contraction in Germany's manufacturing sector, which has been hit by supply chain disruptions and shortages of key components such as semiconductors. The IMF also noted the impact of the Russian gas supply crisis on Germany's energy sector.

This comes as Germany's economy minister, Robert Habeck, warned that the country's economy was likely to shrink by 1.5% in 2023, as high energy prices and supply chain issues continue to take their toll.

The IMF's cut to Germany's growth forecast is a further sign that the country's economy is facing significant headwinds in the coming months.

Microsoft is launching a tool to help computer users keep track of their favourite blogs and make their own postings.

The software, to be released as a free download on Wednesday, is the latest sign that Microsoft wants to position itself in the fast-growing "blogging" field, where it faces competition from Google and other companies.

Blogs are websites where people post thoughts, observations and links to other sites.

Microsoft's new software, Windows Live Writer, allows people to write postings, and to add graphics and pictures easily.

It also provides a single place to manage multiple blogs, offering features for creating and editing posts, and for publishing them.

"Live Writer makes posting faster, and provides a choice of powerful tools, and an intuitive interface," said Scott Moore, who heads Microsoft's community efforts.

Microsoft also plans to offer a "widget" - a mini-program that can be attached to blogs to show a person's music favourites from the Microsoft-owned website, Last.fm.

The software will be available as a free download to users of Microsoft's Windows XP and Vista operating systems.

While Microsoft has offered various pieces of blogging software before, this is the first time that the company has offered a single, simple tool for writing and tracking blogs.

The move comes as Microsoft is trying to compete with Google's popular Blogger service, as well as other offerings from companies like America Online and Six Apart.

Blogging has gone mainstream in the past year, with dozens of celebrities - from politicians to movie stars - maintaining their own blogs.

While Microsoft's Windows Live Writer will compete with software from other companies, it also has the potential to boost the Microsoft-owned blogging site, MSN Spaces.

Users of the software will be able to publish their blogs on a number of sites, but will get extra features if they publish on MSN Spaces.

For example, they will be able to drag-and-drop videos from Google's YouTube or Microsoft's own Soapbox video-sharing site into their blog postings.

They will also be able to add a "map" of where they took pictures by dragging-and-dropping Microsoft's Virtual Earth mapping software into their postings.

Microsoft is set to launch a blogging service on Tuesday, in an attempt to attract users who want to write longer-form content than the short text messages favoured by the Twitter microblogging service.

The software giant will unveil Windows Live Spaces, which will be integrated with its existing Windows Live services, at a launch event in New York.

The move comes as Microsoft continues to try to expand its social-networking offerings, a category of internet services that has grown enormously in the past year.

Windows Live Spaces is not a revolutionary new service. Instead, it is based on the Moveable Type publishing system, developed by a company of the same name. Microsoft struck a deal with Moveable Type to develop a custom version of its software for Windows Live users. 

Like most blogging services, Spaces will offer users the ability to publish text, photos and other media. It will also have built-in support for RSS feeds, a technology that allows internet users to subscribe to a blog or other information outlet, and then read the content using software called a newsreader.

What is more, Spaces will be integrated with Microsoft's other Windows Live services, such as the Windows Live Messenger instant-messaging software and Windows Live Mail email service. This means that Spaces users will be able to communicate with and read emails from their friends who are using other Live services, all from within the blogging interface.

"We believe this is going to be a very popular service," said Brian Hall, Microsoft's general manager of Windows Live, about Spaces. "It's a great way for people to express themselves."

However, industry experts have warned that Microsoft faces an uphill struggle to attract users to a new blogging service, given the popularity of existing blog hosts such as Blogger, owned by Google, and Movable Type's own publishing platform.

"It's going to be challenging for them to convince people to move from the blogging platforms they are using," said Susan Mernit, an internet consultant and veteran blogger. "People are going to want to know what is so special about Spaces."

Kevin Spacey's first leading movie role since being fired from House of Cards over sexual assault allegations will receive its UK debut this month. 

The Renaissance actor will play a grieving father in the drama All Access. It will screen at this year's Edinburgh film festival. The festival's director, Ed Strachan, described the film as "raw" and "very powerful". 

All Access will be shown on 20 June, about two months after its debut at South By Southwest in Austin, Texas. The film's UK distributor, Dogwoof, decided to give the movie its UK premiere at Edinburgh. 

All Access is about a father who loses his daughter in a car crash. He meets the occupants of a neighbouring cabin on a trip to the mountains to try to cope with his grief. 

The film's director, Randall Miller, pleaded guilty in 2012 to charges relating to the death of an passenger in a car crash. He was sentenced to two years in prison. 

Dogwoof said the film had been completed before Miller's arrest. It described All Access as an "unflinching, emotional and intimate story, told with gripping clarity".

The UK debut of the Kevin Spacey movie, "House of Cards", took place on Friday. The film, which was written and directed by David Fincher, premiered at the 61st BFI London Film Festival. It was inspired by the BBC series of the same name, which was created by Michael Dobbs. The movie tells the story of Democratic Congressman Stephen Underwood (Spacey), who decides to pursue a life of politics after being talked into it by his wife, Claire (Robin Wright). A restored copy of what is thought to be Dutch painter Vincent Van Gogh's last film has made its debut at a festival in France.

The artist filmed the landscape of France in the early 1890s using a lenticular camera - a precursor to the modern-day flip book.

The film was discovered in 2014 in the Netherlands and recently restored by the National Film Board of Canada.

It was shown at the Van Gogh exhibit at the Auvers-sur-Oise festival, outside Paris.

Museum official Emilie Gordenker told AFP news agency it was "exciting" to think it might be the final film Van Gogh made.

"We know he wanted to make a movie with moving images of peasants working in the fields," she said.

"We hope we will discover some day that there is another film... but for now this is the only existing one."

The 55-second long film shows peasants walking through a field and digging up potatoes.

It was shot in the French town of Auvers-sur-Oise, where the artist spent his final months and is buried.

The camera used to make the film rotates between two lenses, creating an effect similar to that of a flip book.

It was likely that Van Gogh had to stop and change the lens, meaning the filming process was probably quite slow, Ms Gordenker said.

Van Gogh is known to have made one other film, also using a lenticular camera, which showed his friend and fellow artist Paul Gauguin, though some experts have questioned whether that can really be classed as a movie.

The restored film was shown at the festival on Friday and again on Saturday.

For the first time in over a century, anyone can watch a newly restored version of the only existing film that legendary artist Vincent van Gogh ever made. It was commissioned by the painter's brother, Theo, for the Paris-based firm of Goupil & Cie, for promotional purposes. 

The film, which is just under two minutes long and shot in Paris in 1887, will be available to watch on the BBC website in the UK until the end of March. Sadly, it offers only an artist's impression of the swift-moving river and the city's skyline, as van Gogh himself only appears briefly in the background of one shot, walking along a path.

Despite its flaws, the restoration of the film is a valuable opportunity to see one of a handful of surviving films from the era of silent movies, and offers a unique insight into the life of one of the world's most influential artists.

Format wars between Blu-ray and HD DVD have "already damaged" the high definition DVD market in the UK, according to a retail study.

A survey by Retail Eyes found that the confusion among consumers over which format to buy caused sales of HD DVDs in the run up to Christmas to be "well below" expectations.

The study said that shoppers were put off buying machines capable of playing either Blu-ray or HD DVD, in case the format war ended up favouring the rival format.

"The format war has damaged consumer confidence in the whole category," the study said.

"Many consumers are reluctant to invest in a format that may become obsolete in the future."

The study found that just one in 200 UK shoppers purchased a high definition DVD player or recorder in the six weeks before Christmas.

Retail Eyes said that stock levels of the format were "generally good" but added that retailers should consider the impact of the format war when planning ahead for this year's Christmas season.

The study found that one in three shoppers would not buy any HD products because of the uncertainty surrounding the format war.

Last week, Japanese electronics giant Sony announced that it would buy out its rival Toshiba's share in a joint venture to produce HD DVDs.

The move all-but-ends the battle between Blu-ray and HD DVD to provide the next-generation optical disc for high definition movies and games.

Music fans should prepare for "years of confusion" as the industry moves towards making albums available in a range of formats, according to BBC radio DJ Jo Whiley.

The presenter of Radio 2's weekday evening show said continuing format wars between music companies risked alienating consumers.

She told the BBC's Music Week that the industry was "heading for confusion".

Last month, Sony announced that from 2022, it would make nearly all new albums available in three formats - CD, vinyl and streaming.

Universal announced a similar strategy in March, with vinyl sales continuing to grow. 

Whiley said: "People don't know what they're doing anymore. There's no cohesion, nobody is steering the ship.

"We're heading for confusion, we're heading for years of confusion and it's not going to be easy to resolve."

The BBC has contacted Sony and Universal for comment.

Whiley's concerns come as the British Phonographic Industry (BPI) announced that vinyl sales are at their highest level since the 1990s.

Almost 5 million vinyl records were sold in 2021, a rise of 23% on the previous year.

It marks the 15th consecutive year in which vinyl sales have grown, with nearly 100 million records sold since 2007.

Geoff Taylor, chief executive of the BPI, said the figures showed the "depth of love" that British people have for vinyl.

"Thanks to the dedication and ingenuity of vinyl makers and sellers, this most traditional of formats continues to attract a new generation of fans," he added.

Taylor also said the growth in vinyl sales showed the power of physical music sales alongside digital.

"In an age of streaming, vinyl remains a robust and healthy format for fans and artists alike," he said.

Clara Amfo, Radio 1's drivetime host, said she believed there was a place for both vinyl and streaming in the music industry.

"I think we're in an age where we use music in different ways, and that's OK," she said.

"We don't have to pit one against the other, especially if we want to continue to champion emerging artists and new music.

"Music is music, and as long as we continue to support all corners of the industry, I think we'll be alright."

London-listed shares in Oracle Co. fell after the U.S. business software company reported disappointing earnings and said it would lay off thousands of workers as part of its acquisition of healthcare tech firm Cerner.

Oracle said the layoffs were part of its integration plan for the $28 billion acquisition, which is the company's biggest deal to date. The company did not specify the number of jobs that will be lost.

The news comes as Oracle reported fiscal second-quarter earnings that missed expectations. The company reported earnings per share of $1.11, compared to the expected $1.14. It also reported revenue of $11.25 billion, compared to the expected $11.26 billion.

Oracle said it expects the Cerner deal to close this year, and that it will contribute to its growth in the coming years. The company also said it is confident in its ability to integrate Cerner and deliver value to customers and shareholders.

However, analysts were cautious about the company's outlook, with some pointing to the slowing cloud business as a concern.

"The core business is still growing at a healthy clip, but investors were hoping for more from Oracle's cloud unit," said Bob Peck, an analyst at SunTrust Robinson Humphrey. "The Street is concerned about the company's near-term outlook as cloud growth is decelerating."

Overall, Oracle reported that its cloud services and license support segment revenue grew by just 6%, down from 20% growth a year earlier. The company's total revenue grew by just 2% to $11.25 billion.

"Our overall revenue growth was impacted by the strengthening of the U.S. dollar index," said Oracle Chairman and CTO Larry Ellison. "We expect currencies to stabilize at these new levels."

Oracle is to cut 1,700 jobs, around 6% of its global workforce, as part of a restructuring process following its acquisition of electronic health record company Cerner. 

The company said that the redundancies were a "difficult but necessary step" in order to create a "more efficient" business. 

Consultancy firm McKinsey & Company is also set to cut a further 700 roles, although Oracle has said that this is not part of the restructuring process. 

In a statement, Oracle said that it had "made the difficult decision to eliminate a number of roles across our global business". 

"This decision was taken after careful consideration and analysis of our operations, and it is not a reflection of the quality of the work performed by our colleagues in the eliminated roles", the company added.

Oracle also said that it was "committed to ensuring that every affected employee receives our full support during these transitions".

While the Trump administration filed the case, the Biden administration has maintained it and sought the $280bn in damages, a figure that reflects amounts the US already has spent on terrorism victims.

US officials cited attacks ranging from the 1983 bombing of the US Marine barracks in Beirut, Lebanon, to last year's drone attack at the military airport in Abu Dhabi, UAE, which killed three people and wounded others.

Smartphone cameras are "must-haves" - but they could be so much better.

That is the view of ex-Apple designer Jony Ive, who has designed phones including the iPhone.

Ive said smartphones were the most important photographic innovation in a century. But he said their cameras were "terrible" and "embarrassing".

The designer, who now runs his own firm LoveFrom, said manufacturers were not trying hard enough.

LoveFrom is working with a charity that trains African photographers.

Ive said the firm would donate revenue from an upcoming product to the charity, which trains photographers in Nigeria, Kenya and Uganda.

"We have this extraordinary facility in our pocket which is the most important photographic innovation in a century, and yet the camera is terrible, it's embarrassing," he said.

"When you consider how this tool, the camera, is used worldwide today, it's primarily used for social approval. How do I look? How do I appear? Who's with me? Where am I? What am I doing?

"The use of the tool is primarily about social approval. And in that context, the quality is actually irrelevant."

Ive was giving a talk at the Royal Academy of Arts in London to promote a new book about his career.

The book features some of the products he designed alongside text written by the designer himself. It is billed as "a visual autobiography" and all the profits will go to charity.

In a wide-ranging interview, Ive also discussed virtual reality, a technology he said he was "fascinated" by.

He said it had the potential to be "profoundly important" and compared it to the invention of the wheel.

But he said VR had been held back by the lack of a "defining" application, such as the telephone.

"I think VR has the opportunity to be that next important chapter," he said.

"Ultimately, it is the complete suspension of disbelief. And it could be profoundly important."

Ive was also asked if he had any regrets about his time at Apple.

He said he felt "fantastic" about the products he had helped to create, but added: "I think we all in some way feel we could have done better.

"I don't think any designer at any point in any project thinks they've done enough."

Camera phones are must-haves for photography enthusiasts who don't want to carry a separate camera and phone. The latest smartphone models have advanced camera features that can take high-quality photos and videos, as well as edit and share them easily.

One of the main advantages of camera phones is their convenience. They allow users to capture moments anytime, anywhere, without having to carry a separate device. This is especially useful for those who want to take photos on the go, such as travel photographers or those who want to document their daily lives.

Another advantage of camera phones is their accessibility. They are relatively affordable, especially compared to traditional cameras, and are widely available. This makes them a great option for those who want to get into photography without having to invest in a separate camera.

However, there are also some drawbacks to camera phones. One of the main concerns is their image quality. While they have come a long way in recent years, camera phones still cannot match the image quality of dedicated cameras, especially in low-light conditions. In addition, the small size of camera phones can make it difficult to stabilize them, leading to blurry photos.

Despite these drawbacks, camera phones have become a popular choice for photography enthusiasts due to their convenience and accessibility. As technology continues to improve, it is likely that camera phones will continue to become more advanced and capable of taking even better photos and videos.

Three-time Olympic champion Asbel Kiprop will face an in-form Jake Wightman in the 3,000m at the Great City Games in May.

The announcement of the fields for the event, which takes place in Manchester on 7 May, was slightly premature as Kiprop has yet to confirm participation. However, the man who has won three Olympic titles - including successfully defending his 1,500m crown in Tokyo last year - is expected to confirm soon.

Kiprop, who turned 35 on Wednesday, will be up against a 25-year-old Wightman, who has already set the fastest indoor time in the world this year in the mile and last weekend broke the British record for 5km.

Another notable addition to the fields is triple jumper Tornike Kakhidze, who has been added to a strong men's long jump lineup that already included Olympic champion Miltiadis Tentoglou and Olympic bronze medallist Juan Miguel Echevarria.

Kakhidze, who finished fourth in Tokyo, has only recently returned to action after a car crash in January left him with multiple fractures.

There are also entries from 2020 Olympic finalists in the women's long jump, such as Serbia's Milica Gardašević and Canada's Christabel Nettey, as well as Olympic 400m bronze medallist Marileidy Paulino of Cuba in the 150m.

The women's 100m will see Daryll Neita, who finished fourth in the Olympics last year running into a -10.7m/s headwind, up against Arthur Cissé, who finished fifth in the 100m for Senegal in Tokyo.

Great City Games director Andy Brooks said he was "thrilled" with the entries.

"Every single person who watched the Olympics will have recognised the quality of those athletes, so to have them competing in Manchester is a massive boost," he said.

Reigning marathon world champion and Olympic bronze medallist, Edna Kiplagat, has been confirmed among the list of elite athletes set to race at the 2023 Edinburgh Marathon. 

The Kenyan runner, who won the London 2012 Olympic marathon bronze medal and took gold at the 2011 and 2013 World Championships, will be among the headline names when she takes to the start line in Scotland's capital on Sunday 23rd April. 

She will be joined by fellow Kenyan and two-time New York City Marathon champion, Mary Keitany. The race will be Keitany's first marathon in Scotland.

"I am excited to come to Scotland for the first time and race against such a high-quality field in Edinburgh," said Keitany.

"I have heard a lot about the Edinburgh Marathon and I am looking forward to racing in such a beautiful city."

The pair will be part of a world-class field assembled by the organisers, The Great Run Company, for the 2023 edition of the marathon, which will also include thousands of runners taking on the challenge from across the globe.

Army chiefs in the UK have been told to "think the unthinkable" and consider removing the names of colonial-era figures from regiments.

The Defence Committee said it recognised the names were an important part of regimental traditions.

But it added some names were "difficult to defend" in the modern day and it was a "reasonable question" to ask if they should continue.

The cross-party committee said it had "heard a variety of viewpoints" on the issue.

The report comes after a Ministry of Defence (MoD) review into the names of the regiments.

The review was ordered after Black Lives Matter protests in June 2020 and growing pressure from some soldiers.

The Defence Committee said it agreed with the decision to delay the publication of the MoD's review until all regiments had been consulted.

"It is important that the views of veterans, serving personnel and the wider public are heard in this process," the committee said.

"The names of the regiments are an important part of their identity and history, and many names reflect the long and gallant history of the regiments, or the local links they have developed over many years.

"However, some names do not have an obvious modern-day relevance and it is a reasonable question to ask whether they should continue in an increasingly diverse Britain."

The report said there were a number of ways to update the names, including introducing more recent names of "national heroes" or finding ways to reflect the "multiple heritages" of the regiments.

The committee said it recognised any changes would need careful handling and should not be rushed.

First Sea Lord Admiral Tony Radakin told the committee's hearing earlier this year the names were an "incredibly important" part of military history and any changes would have to be handled carefully.

"If you start going down that route, removing names, removing history, removing heritage because of the difficulty of where some names came from, you'll end up with nothing," he added.

The decision on whether to cut the number of British Army regiments has been described as “risky” by the Defence Select Committee.

The government is to reduce the number of infantry battalions from 82 to 72, with an announcement on which units are to be lost expected on Thursday. 

Committee chair Tobias Ellwood said there was a “real risk” that the reductions would undermine the Army’s adaptability and resilience. He added that the committee “remained to be convinced” of the military’s case for change. The MP warned that the committee “will be watching closely to see what the impact on interoperability is, and whether this risks the Army’s ability to fulfil its duties under future scenarios”. 

The Army has said the changes – due to be in place by 2040 – are designed to make the service more adaptable and agile.

MPs to debate 'euthanasia laws'

Parliament will hold a debate on "euthanasia laws" on Thursday.

The debate will be led by Labour MP Lucy Powell, who says it is time for parliament to "catch up" with public opinion.

She said a recent ComRes poll indicating that 79% of the public supported the legalisation of euthanasia "demonstrated that this is an issue the public believes should be dealt with by this Parliament".

"It is incumbent on MPs to consider this issue and determine whether the time is right to provide assistance to those who have concluded that they do not wish to continue living," she added.

Ms Powell, who is retiring at the next election, added that she had "no firm view on the issue" and would listen to the arguments before coming to a decision.

The term "euthanasia" refers to circumstances where a doctor assists a person to die.

It does not include palliative care, or the removal of life-saving treatment or food and water from someone who is dying naturally.

The debate will be held in the main chamber of the House of Commons, rather than in a committee room, and will therefore be broadcast.

It will be chaired by the Conservative MP Harriet Harman.

The term "euthanasia" refers to an act of doctor-assisted suicide, and usually involves a lethal injection. Euthanasia is different from assisted suicide, because doctors play a bigger role in euthanasia. Assisted suicide is usually performed through a lethal prescription, prescribed by a doctor, but with the person performing the act solo. The debate over euthanasia has long divided people and will likely divide MPs as well. Some argue it's time for the UK to consider changing the law, to let those with terminal illnesses end their lives on their terms. Others feel the law shouldn't change, to prevent vulnerable people from being pressured to end their lives.

The announcement came after a long-awaited report into the project said it could bring benefits to the UK.

Napster has launched a subscription service offering access to millions of songs for a monthly fee.

The service, Napster Unlimited, is priced at $5 a month for broadband subscribers.

Napster, originally a free music file-sharing service, was shut down in 2001.

It was bought by Roxio, now known as Roxio/Napster, which hopes the new service will help it compete with market leader iTunes.

The service was announced at the Consumer Electronics Show (CES) in Las Vegas.

Napster Unlimited offers unlimited access to Napster's library of more than eight million songs. Users will be able to play songs on up to three computers and burn up to three songs a day onto CDs.

The service will be available in the US before the end of January, with a UK launch to follow shortly afterwards, a Napster spokeswoman said.

Roxio competitor iTunes offers a subscription service in conjunction with phone company Verizon, but it is only available to Verizon broadband subscribers and is more expensive than Napster Unlimited.

iTunes is the market leader in legal digital music sales. It sold more than 70 million songs in 2004 and accounts for more than 70% of online music sales, according to media analyst firm Nielsen SoundScan.

Roxio has struggled to compete. It sold only about five million tracks last year, according to Nielsen SoundScan.

The new Napster service does not allow users to burn songs onto CDs without restrictions.

That is a marked difference from the original Napster, which made it easy for users to copy songs and gave the company its reputation as a piracy hub.

To burn more than three songs a day onto a CD, users will have to buy unlimited burning privileges for $5 more per month.

Roxio is hoping the new service will attract a large number of subscribers.

In a statement, Chris Gorog, chief executive of Roxio, said: "We think this is the right model at the right time.

"Given the choice, we believe that consumers prefer to rent their music on a monthly basis, with the ability to cancel their subscriptions at any time, rather than having to purchase their music collections."

To encourage users to sign up, Napster is offering a free 14-day trial.

The new service will be available in the US through all major broadband providers, including Comcast, Earthlink, and AOL Time Warner.

Music fans will soon be able to rent downloads from Napster, the digital music service that is being rebuilt by Best Buy.

The service has launched a range of rental options in the US, offering downloads from its eight million track strong catalogue for between two and 30 days. Rentals will initially be offered on a promotional basis, but could become a permanent feature if the trial is successful.

Napster chief executive Chris Gorog said the service would "add a new dimension to the way people experience and enjoy music".

Users will be able to rent albums for a day, week or month, and can rent music videos for up to 30 days. They can also rent a la carte tracks for two days, or for a month for the price of two downloads.

Industry observers said the rental strategy made sense because it answered the problem of what do once the download has been bought and was lying on a computer somewhere.

"Once you've bought a download it doesn't offer much unless you have an unlimited subscription to listen to it as often as you like," said Mark Mulligan, a media analyst with Forrester.

"This is an attempt to bring some of the flexibility of the old rental model to digital music and give people more options."

Napster, which was launched in 1999 and popularised digital music, has struggled in recent years in the face of competition from Apple's market-leading iTunes service.

Best Buy, the US electronics retailer, bought Napster for an undisclosed sum in September.

The Liberian economy is starting to recover after more than seven years of severe depression caused by the Ebola crisis and the Covid pandemic, the country's central bank says.

The West African country's economy is expected to grow by more than 4% this year, and 4.5% in 2023, according to a forecast by the Central Bank of Liberia (CBL).

Liberia's government says it is committing about $100m (£85m) to road construction and port upgrades to boost growth.

The CBL said that positive growth in the mining and panning, water and electricity, telecommunications and agriculture sectors would drive the expansion.

It also said that growth in the tourism and hospitality sectors was held back because of the impact of the Covid pandemic.

The Liberian economy is starting to recover after the country's civil war, with growth driven by its booming mining industry. The country's main export, iron ore, has increased in price, leading to higher revenues for the government. This has allowed the government to make investments in infrastructure and education, which has helped to reduce poverty levels.

The mining industry has also created jobs and increased economic activity in the country. This has helped to reduce unemployment levels and increase wages for workers.

The government has also implemented policies to help improve the business environment in the country. This has included simplifying the tax system and improving access to credit for businesses.

There is still room for improvement, however. The country's infrastructure is still lacking, and the government needs to do more to improve access to basic services. Additionally, the country's education system needs to be improved to help create a more skilled workforce. 

Despite these challenges, the Liberian economy is on the right track, and growth is expected to continue in the coming years.

Saudi Arabian shares jumped the most in almost three weeks on Sunday amid growing hopes for an economic recovery, but most other Middle Eastern markets dipped.

The Saudi stock exchange was the region's standout performer, with the main Tadawul index rising 3.0%.

Technology, retail and petrochemical stocks were among the best performers.

Most other Middle Eastern markets were in the red, with Dubai's main index falling 0.6% after a strong rally on Thursday.

The Abu Dhabi index fell 1.1%, hit by a 1.4% fall in the United Arab Emirates' biggest lender, First Abu Dhabi Bank.

Egypt's main index was a rare bright spot, rising 0.5% after the central bank lowered its key interest rate by a substantial 150 basis points to 12.75% on Thursday to support the economy amid the coronavirus crisis.

The Saudi index has gained 4.0% so far this year, outperforming most other stock markets in the region.

The kingdom has been easing restrictions on movement and travel ahead of an expected further reopening of the economy after the fasting month of Ramadan ends at the beginning of May.

The UAE has also been gradually easing restrictions. But in Iran, which has been the region's worst-hit country by the coronavirus, the death toll passed 3,000 on Sunday.

The Saudi Stock Exchange ended in the green on Sunday, supported by banking and petrochemical stocks, as the market reacted positively to the announcement of the kingdom's inclusion in the MSCI index.

The All Share Index (TASI) closed 1.5% higher at 11,634 points, after hitting a session high of 11,663 points.

The NCCI index, which comprises the largest and most liquid stocks, rose 1.7%. Saudi Basic Industries Corp (SABIC) jumped 3.1%, while National Commercial Bank (NCB) surged 4.1%.

The banking sector rose 2.1%, with Al Rajhi Bank climbing 3.1%. The petrochemical sector added 1.5% after Saudi Aramco raised the November official selling prices (OSP) for Arab light crude shipments to Asia.

Telecommunications firm Saudi Telecom jumped 7.4% after reporting a major increase in quarterly profits.

MSCI's decision last week to upgrade Saudi Arabia to emerging market status from frontier market is expected to attract billions of dollars of foreign investment to the kingdom's stock market.

"It is a historic day for Saudi Capital Market," said Khalid Al-Hussan, CEO of the Saudi Stock Exchange.

"Today's inclusion in the MSCI Emerging Markets Index is the result of hard work and the success of the many initiatives launched to develop the depth and liquidity of the market," he added.

Scottish actor Gavin Mitchell, who played the role of Billy Simpson in the hit sitcom Still Game, has died at the age of 62.

His death was announced by fellow actor Ford Kiernan, who starred alongside him in the show.

Kieran took to Twitter to pay tribute to his friend, saying he was "devastated".

"Gavin was a funny, talented and lovely man and he will be sorely missed," he wrote.

"It broke my heart this afternoon to hear that my great friend Gavin Mitchell has died," he added in a follow-up post.

Fellow actors and comedians also paid tribute to Mitchell, with Gregor Fisher writing: "Sorry to hear about the sad loss of Gavin Mitchell. A genuinely lovely guy. Thoughts with all his family and friends."

And fellow Scot Tony Roper said he was "devastated" at the news of Mitchell's death.

"I was so lucky to work with him all those years and we became great friends," he said.

"He was a brilliant actor and a hilarious and gorgeous human being. It was a joy to work with him."

Mitchell - who was born in Glasgow in 1959 - studied at the Royal Scottish Academy of Music and Drama and began acting in the early 1980s.

Along with his role in Still Game, he also appeared in numerous other TV shows and films, including Tutti Frutti, Dear Frankie and The House of Mirth.

The actor was also a keen musician and a member of the Scottish folk band The Whistlebinkies.

Notorious for his versatility and emotional range, actor Sir Sean Connery forged a reputation as one of Britain's most recognisable stars, receiving plaudits and an Oscar for his performance in the title role of the 1962 adventure film Dr No.

He passed away on 31 October 2020, at the age of 90.

Allan Stewart paid tribute to Connery, saying he was "the greatest actor of all time", with Kenneth Branagh describing him as "my greatest mentor and inspiration".

The son of a cleaning lady and a factory worker, Connery was born in Edinburgh and raised in the city's Fountainbridge area.

He went to school at Royal High School in the city, but was expelled at the age of 13 and despatched to the National Defence Corps, where he remained until he was 16.

Connery then served in the Royal Navy, principally in the boiler room of a destroyer, before being discharged after three years due to a stomach ulcer.

He moved to London in 1953, working first in the building trade and then as a lifeguard, before becoming a model.

Connery's acting career began in the theatre, where he performed in a number of amateur productions and then several professional appearances in Shakespearean plays, including Macbeth and Richard III.

He then joined the Royal Shakespeare Company, where he gained positive reviews for his performances in a number of productions, including All's Well That Ends Well, Antony and Cleopatra and Henry V.

Connery's big break came when he was cast as James Bond in Dr No, a role that he would go on to play in five films, winning an Oscar for his performance in the 1983 film Never Say Never Again.

The late actor was considered a sex symbol, with his carousing, womanising, and hard-living persona making him an archetypal Bond.

His other film credits include The Name of the Rose, The Untouchables, and Robin and Marian, a film that marked his retirement from acting in 1981.

Connery received a knighthood in July 2000.

He was married to Diane Cilento from 1962 to 1973 and had a son, Jason.

He later married actress and former model Micheline Roquebrune, and had a stepson, Stefan.

Brits return Keane to number one

Keane have made it a hat-trick of UK number ones with their latest offering, "Perfect Symmetry".

The band scored their first number one in 2004 with "Somewhere Only We Know", followed by "Is It Any Wonder?" in 2006.

"Perfect Symmetry" has now held on to the top spot for a second week, becoming the fastest-selling release of 2008, the BBC has reported.

The album saw off competition from Leona Lewis, who slipped to number two with her debut, "Spirit", and Muse, who entered at three with "The Resistance".

Keane's achievement marks the first time in a year that the same artist has held the top spot for two consecutive weeks.

The last artist to do so was Cascada with "Everytime We Touch" and "What Hurts the Most".

Keane, who released their debut, "Hopes and Fears", in 2004, said they are "delighted" with the news.

The group released "Perfect Symmetry" in October after a five-year break.

Frontman Tom Chaplin recently told the BBC that the album's title summed up the album's content.

"It's about finding perfect symmetry within your own life, and that can apply to love, to friendship, to family - any kind of relationship you have," he said.

Keane are currently touring the UK. They play the SECC in Glasgow on 11 February and London's Wembley Arena the following day.

Brits return Keane to number one with 'Fine Line': The veteran British pop band Keane scored their third number-one album in the UK on Friday with their latest release, “Fine Line.” 

The group, composed of Tim Rice-Oxley and Tom Chaplin, released their debut, “Hopes and Fears,” in 2004. The record went platinum and produced what remains the group’s biggest hit, “Somewhere Only We Know.” Three years later, their sophomore album, “Under the Iron Sea,” also hit number one. 

Keane took a hiatus in 2013 and came back in 2020 with “Cause and Effect,” which peaked at number two. Their new release, “Fine Line,” earned 44% of its sales from physical copies, with vinyl making up 75% of that figure.

Japanese banking battle at an end

Japan's biggest lender has reached a settlement in a long-running legal battle over compensation for customers who were wrongly charged for financial advice.

The bank said it would pay 101bn yen ($900m; £600m) to about four million customers.

It also agreed to establish a fund of about 50bn yen to handle future claims.

The move ends more than three years of legal battles with consumers and a powerful government regulator.

The Bank of Japan (BOJ) said the cost of the settlement was "huge".

But it said the move would help restore public confidence in the nation's banking system, which has been rocked by a series of scandals over the past year.

The central bank had been trying to get other banks to help pay for the settlement, but they have so far refused.

The bank has already set aside reserves for the settlement, which is expected to cost about 130bn yen.

The BOJ said it would work to improve its financial advisory services and strengthen its internal controls.

The long-running dispute between Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group and Mizuho Financial Group over a failed merger has come to an end, with the latter expected to offload its stake in the former.

Mizuho has agreed to sell its 5% stake in Mitsubishi UFJ to Japan Industrial Solutions, a subsidiary of Mitsubishi Corporation, for around $900m. The sale will reduce Mizuho's holding in Mitsubishi UFJ to less than 5%, which will result in it no longer being subject to a cap on its voting rights under Japanese law.

The dispute began in 2018 when Mitsubishi UFJ attempted to block Mizuho's plan to merge with Sumitomo Mitsui Financial Group, arguing that it would create a rival too big to compete. The merger was called off the following year, and Mitsubishi UFJ subsequently made a number of acquisitions to counter any potential threat from Mizuho. 

The ending of the dispute comes as both Mitsubishi UFJ and Mizuho have been hit by scandals in recent months. Mitsubishi UFJ was found to have manipulated its computer system to conceal large sums of money lent to a customer, while Mizuho is facing allegations that it allowed its customers to engage in margin trading without their knowledge.

Celtic have asked Uefa to consider moving their Europa League group game against Ludogorets Razgrad because of coronavirus travel restrictions.

The Scottish club had asked for their game on 9 December to be switched to a neutral country given the current guidelines in place.

But Uefa has decided the game will go ahead in Bulgaria - a country on Scotland's red list - with Celtic given just over a week to prepare.

The Scottish government has confirmed that players would have to quarantine on return from Bulgaria.

That would rule any travelling players out of the following league game, at home to Hibernian on 12 December.

In response, Celtic manager Ange Postecoglou said: "It's a really tricky situation. We are following the guidelines put in place by the government."

The game is the third in Group H, with Celtic having already played Real Betis away and Ferencvaros at home, picking up a win and a defeat.

Ludogorets, who have already played both of their opening games, are currently top of the group on four points.

Europa League rules state that the venue of a match moved by Uefa "should, in principle, be located in a neutral country".

However, in September Uefa president Aleksander Ceferin said that ruling could be relaxed to avoid an excessive number of games in a short period of time.

At the time, Celtic were contemplating whether to ask for their opening Europa League match against Ferencvaros to be moved from Hungary - then on the amber list - to Scotland.

The game went ahead in Budapest, resulting in Celtic flying to and from Hungary rather than staying there before the return game a few weeks later.

Celtic have requested that their Europa League group game against Bulgarian side Ludogorets be moved due to a lack of preparation time.

The clubs are due to meet in Sofia on Thursday, 9 November, with the game being played just four days after the Old Firm clash with Rangers.

And Celtic have asked Uefa to respect “the integrity of the competition” by finding a solution to the problem.

In a statement, the club said they had “attempted to find a solution that would mitigate against our players being deprived of preparation time and recovery time between these important matches”.

They added they had been “unable to reach a satisfactory resolution” with Uefa and had therefore requested that the game be moved to a different date.

Ludogorets, who beat Celtic 2-1 in Glasgow earlier this month, apologised to the Scottish club for any “inconvenience”.

In a statement on their website, they said they had offered for the game to be played at a neutral venue or for it to be postponed due to “exceptional circumstances”.

However, they stressed that they had been informed by Uefa that the game would go ahead as scheduled.

The paper reports how bloggers set up a Web site to help speed along recovery efforts. Bloggers for Relief, a collaborative effort of three blogging organizations, uses satellite photos and other images to pinpoint areas of damage and where help is most needed. The information is posted on Google Maps. "They're taking information that would have taken days and weeks to disseminate and putting it out in a real-time fashion," Brian Smith, a blog specialist with the American Red Cross, told the Picayune.

The blogging groups also are using their connections to get the word out about where money and supplies are needed, and to encourage people to donate. "It's a very grassroots kind of effort that's happening through the blogosphere," Smith said. The bloggers have been sharing information with the Red Cross and other aid organizations, he said.

Blogs also have played a key role in the evacuation and rescue efforts ahead of Hurricane Rita. The blog of the state of Texas lists all of the state's evacuation routes and has been updated every time a road is closed, the newspaper reported.

It was spring 1995, and a team of us at the BBC were charged with creating the corporation's first web page. My colleague Richard Taylor and I were put in charge, and we set up a skunkworks lab to investigate this new phenomenon.

We were lucky. Despite the vast reach of the BBC, the organisation had, in those days, a relatively small number of people involved in new media. So our team of about 12 was able to control the agenda. We were joined by Martin Freethy, a brilliant young programmer who had been recruited from Oracle, and Anthony Howard, a designer who instantly understood what we were trying to do.

We were not trying to do anything very grand. All we wanted to do was make sure the BBC had a web presence. But we were fortunate in having an enlightened manager, Alan Chesters, who understood this new medium and gave us pretty much free rein.  

We were also lucky that the web was so new that nobody really understood it fully, which meant we could pretty much make it up as we went along.

And so we did. We took all the things we liked about the emerging web landscape – the things that seemed to make the most sense – and built a site that had most of the elements you would recognise in the BBC's web presence today: a top menu, a sidebar of links to internal pages, and a big promotion on the homepage to a major news story. We added some other things that were novel at the time, such as a site-wide search engine and a daily updated list of "what's new".

And that was about it. We weren't trying to "design" the site, because the idea of "user experience design" hadn't been thought of yet. Nor were we trying to produce a "brand" experience, because again, that idea was still far in the future. In fact, the word "brand" wasn't even used much in the BBC.

But despite this lack of design thinking, and working with incredibly primitive tools, it seemed to us that the site we were producing had a certain something. In fact, looking back at it now, it seems pretty clean and crisp, and not that far off what we produce today.

And that, really, is the secret to the BBC's web success. We got there first, and have remained there pretty much ever since. The principles that guided us then – that less is more, that nothing should be unnecessary – have remained unchanged

It's 2023, and we're now well past the tenth anniversary of the introduction of the iPhone by Apple in 2007. That device, more than any other, was the catalyst for the mobile revolution. It seemed to appear out of nowhere, yet simultaneously felt like it had been around forever. The same is true of the way we interact with the web. It now feels like second nature to reach for our phones instead of our laptops when we want to visit a website. Yet, it's easy to forget that the first iPhone was only released ten years ago.

In the previous decade before the iPhone's arrival, web design had already gone through one major revolution. In the 1990s, websites became much more sophisticated and interactive, with the introduction of HTML tables, which allowed web designers to move beyond the constraints of HTML's original layout techniques and create more visually appealing pages. The industry saw an explosion of websites using these new techniques, offering a more enjoyable user experience.

However, these early websites were designed to be viewed on desktop computers, with monitors that were much larger than the screens on mobile phones. As a result, when the iPhone was launched in 2007 and mobile web browsing became possible, these websites looked terrible. Text was illegible, images were distorted, and interactive elements were impossible to use. Clearly, a new approach to web design was needed.

In the next decade after the iPhone was released, web design underwent a radical transformation, with a focus on mobile-friendliness and usability. Designers created websites that were touch-friendly and easy to use on small screens. As mobile phones became more and more popular, websites had to keep up.

Today, mobile traffic accounts for more than half of all internet traffic, and the importance of mobile-friendly design is clear. Websites that are not optimized for mobile devices risk losing traffic and revenue.

Throughout this decade of change, one principle has remained constant in good website design: the need to create a seamless user experience. From the early days of the web to the present day, websites that are easy to use and navigate have always been popular with users. As technology continues to evolve, we can expect to see even more innovative and intuitive website designs in the future.

Tata Steel aims to cut up to 15,000 jobs in Britain over the next decade as part of a restructuring plan.

The company, which employs about 20,000 people in the UK, said it had begun consultations that could lead to compulsory redundancies.

Unions said they were "disappointed" and called on the company to improve its offer on jobs and investment.

As part of the plans, Tata Steel is also selling its specialty steel making operation in South Yorkshire. It employs about 1,000 people and the potential buyer has until early October to submit a proposal.

The steelmaker has been hit by the coronavirus pandemic, as well as high energy prices and the closure of its main blast furnace at Port Talbot in south Wales last year.

Port Talbot's future was secured in March when Tata Steel signed a deal with the Welsh government to stay open.

As part of the latest plans, the company is aiming to deliver another £50-65m of annual savings to its European operations by the end of March 2026, on top of the £65m it aims to achieve this year.

Its British operations have been losing £1m a day, with steel demand hit by the recession triggered by the pandemic and global steel over-capacity.

The company said it had begun a consultation with union representatives on proposals that would see it lose a further 7,000 jobs in the UK by the end of the decade, on top of the 8,000 it has already cut over the last 10 years.

Unions have called for the UK government to take action to support the industry.

BBC news article - Domain system scam fear - by Andrew Jennings in Moscow Thursday 4 February 2010 GENERAL LISTINGS Check the general listings in your domain name registrar's control panel. If you find a mysterious entry, it could be a sign that someone has gained access to your account and adjusted your settings. It may be that the original owner set up the entry as a forward to another website, perhaps on behalf of a client. But it could also be a red flag. Forwarding to a dodgy site can harm your reputation and your search rankings, so it's always good to check. BEWARE OF DOMAIN NAME SYSTEM HIJACKS Be aware that the domain name system can be hijacked in order to redirect users to scam sites. It's unlikely that your domain name system (or nameserver) settings will be changed without your knowledge. But if a hacker does get access, this is one of the things they can do. This is a serious risk as it can affect your whole online presence. Make sure you have your registrar's emergency contact details to hand so you can call quickly in case your site suddenly goes down. ALSO READ - How to protect your website from hackers DON'T AUTOMATICALLY RENEW DOMAIN NAMES Automatic renewal is convenient, but it can lead to disaster. If you forget to cancel the renewal of a domain name you no longer want, you may end up paying for two, or even more if the scammer has forwarded the extra domains to their site. Check your domains one by one and decide whether you really need them. If you no longer require a domain, cancel the renewal. If you're not sure, hang on to it for now, but be aware that you may be charged for two years' renewal. ALWAYS CHECK YOUR BILL You will normally receive an annual bill for your domain name renewals well in advance of the expiry date. Make sure you recognise all the domains on it and that the bill is in the correct amount. If you are suspicious, contact your registrar immediately. If someone has forwarded your domain to another site, you should receive an email alerting you to the change. CHECK YOUR CONTACT DETAILS Make sure the contact details on your whois listing are up to date. If you fail to keep your email address current, you may not receive important alerts from your registrar. ANDREW JENNINGS http://www.bbc.co.uk/news/business-115114568

The BBC has learned that thousands of acres of land in the UK have been fraudulently sold to secretive offshore companies, in a scam that has cost taxpayers millions of pounds. The land, in some of the most desirable areas of the country, is sold for a fraction of its worth before being resold to innocent buyers for a huge profit. 

The scam works like this. Fraudsters first target public sector workers, tricking them into signing up to seminars and buying overpriced goods. They then use the information they have gathered to create fake identities, often of retired public sector workers, and use these to set up companies. This can involve the use of false passports and other forged documents. 

The companies are then used to register the land in the victims' names. They target land owned by local councils, the NHS, and the Ministry of Defence, as well as universities and other public bodies. The land is often near valuable infrastructure, such as train stations and schools. 

Once the land has been registered, it is sold on to other companies, often based in offshore tax havens such as the British Virgin Islands, Gibraltar, and Guernsey. These companies then sell the land on to innocent buyers, often for a huge profit. The scam has been running for years and is thought to have cost UK taxpayers millions of pounds. 

A BBC investigation has identified over 500 plots of land that have been targeted by the scam. The total area of land is estimated to be worth over £200m. The true cost to the UK taxpayer is believed to be much higher, as the scam also involves the fraudulent sale of land in Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland.

The BBC has learned that the National Crime Agency (NCA) is investigating the scam. It has made a number of arrests and is working to recover the stolen land. The NCA has also issued a warning to the public, urging them to be wary of investing in land that has been sold by a company with an offshore connection.

Petrol and diesel duty will be frozen for the remainder of 2022/23, the Chancellor has said.

Rishi Sunak told MPs that the measure would help cut costs for motorists. It follows a similar freeze in January, which the chancellor said would save average car drivers £1,900 over the next 12 months.

The announcement was among a series of measures in the chancellor's spring statement, which also included an end to the public sector pay freeze and an increase in the minimum wage.

Labour said the measures did not go far enough to help working people, while the Liberal Democrats said the chancellor had "failed on housing".

The spring statement is a mid-year update on the state of the economy and the government's plans for taxes and spending.

Mr Sunak said the decision to freeze fuel duty would save drivers £5 per tank, or around £100 per year. It means the price of petrol and diesel will remain at £1.71 and £1.81 per litre respectively.

The chancellor said the government had made decisions that would affect "every household in the country" and announced a "new age of optimism".

'Not enough'

Shadow chancellor Rachel Reeves said the chancellor had "failed on housing and childcare".

She added: "Working people across the country will not be convinced by this statement, because although Rishi Sunak has pointed in the right direction, he has not gone far enough.

"Because of the prime minister's incompetence and broken promises, this chancellor has had to row back on his own economic credibility with hikes in taxes on ordinary families."

Lib Dem leader Ed Davey said: "Rishi Sunak's failure to tackle the cost of living crisis means that millions of people are struggling to make ends meet.

"Instead of delivering a spring statement fit for a cost of living crisis, the chancellor has simply made more promises with no immediate relief in sight."

The price of petrol has been frozen for the twelfth month in a row, the chancellor has said.

Rishi Sunak said he would exercise his power to delay the inevitable increase in line with inflation until March next year. The move will save motorists an average of £1.30 per litre, or £19 per tank.

The chancellor said the measure, which will apply to diesel and petrol, was part of the government's plan to help people with the cost of living.

Mr Sunak said: "We know that people are worried about the cost of living, so to help with that we're freezing duty on petrol," he said.

The decision mirrors last year's freeze, which was also announced in November and lasted until March.

The announcement was met with a mixed reaction from motoring groups.

The RAC said the move would provide some relief from record prices, but added it was "only a temporary solution".

"We need to encourage drivers to swap to electric cars, by improving charging infrastructure and offering financial incentives," said RAC fuel spokesman Simon Williams.

"But upfront costs need to be reduced too, especially as inflation is now starting to bite into household income."

However, the AA said the freeze would help consumers amid the "cost of living catastrophe".

"This move will help consumers when they most need it," said Luke Bosdet, the AA's fuel price spokesman.

"But freezing duty isn't a long-term fix. The cost of filling up is largely determined by global oil prices, which showed little sign of easing as the chancellor spoke."

The announcement came as part of the chancellor's autumn statement, which included a package of measures to help with the cost of living.

This included a £2bn help package for households in England, comprising a £150 council tax rebate and £400 energy bill discount.

The UK's biggest business group has told the government it should set out a "clear plan" for tax rises in the coming months, ahead of the autumn budget.

The Confederation of British Industry (CBI) said the cost of living crisis and war in Ukraine meant the government could "no longer put off tough decisions".

It said it was "unrealistic" to believe that tax rises could be avoided altogether - but that they should be "fair, reasonable and proportionate".

The government has promised to tackle a £7bn shortfall in tax revenues after it ditched more than 30 taxes last year.

In its submission to the government ahead of the budget, due on 15 November, the CBI said it understood the "challenging context" facing Chancellor Jeremy Hunt, but that now was "not the time to be shy" about explaining the tax rises that would be needed.

"The overwhelming majority of firms accept that fair tax contributions are vital for public services - but they need confidence that taxes will be fair, reasonable and proportionate," said CBI director-general Tony Danker.

"Business needs a clear plan from the government on how they will balance the books, so companies can invest and grow with confidence. With the right plan, the budget can be a stepping stone to growth."

The CBI also warned that increasing taxes on businesses would make the UK less attractive to foreign investors and lead to lower economic growth.

Earlier this month, the independent Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) said the chancellor would have to raise taxes by £72bn over the next five years to help plug the gap in the finances.

That would mean an average £3,000 rise in taxes for every UK household, the OBR said.

In his Budget speech, Mr Hunt will also need to find ways to help households cope with the cost of living crisis, with inflation still running at double-digit levels.

The CBI said it accepted that this would require "tough decisions" on tax and spending, but that the government should focus any tax rises on those best able to pay.

It called for a review of the current "outdated" business rates system which taxes property values, and for a faster reduction in emissions to help keep costs down for businesses.

The business group also said the government should allow more skilled workers into the UK to help grow the economy.

Britain is set to vote in a general election for the third time in five years on Thursday. The governing Conservatives have been campaigning hard on the message that the country risks being stuck in a perpetual cycle of elections if Labour wins and fails to get its Brexit plan through Parliament. 

At the same time, the main opposition party has been warning that the Conservatives would put the NHS at risk by signing up to a trade deal with the US that would allow private healthcare companies to bid for contracts. Labour has also been attacking the government over its record on tackling crime, promising to hire 10,000 more police officers if it wins. 

This has been the nastiest campaign of the three elections, with both major parties trading blows over which of them has done more for the NHS and whether the leader of the opposition is fit to be prime minister. One poll put the Conservatives seven points ahead of Labour, giving the party a healthy cushion over its main rival. But another survey suggested that voters think neither party will win a majority, forcing another election.

A row over visas for Chinese musicians has prevented the BBC's music director, Sir John Eliot Gardiner, from travelling to China for this week's BBC Proms.

Sir John had been due to conduct the BBC National Orchestra of Wales in four concerts in China this month as part of the BBC's ongoing centenary celebrations.

But the BBC said the Chinese musicians' visas had not been issued in time.

Instead, the concerts will be conducted by Thomas Søndergård, the orchestra's principal guest conductor.

In a statement, the BBC said it was "extremely disappointed" at the last-minute cancellation of Sir John's visits.

"The BBC had been in discussions with the relevant authorities in China for many months to try to ensure the visas would be granted," the statement added.

"Despite regular and positive discussions with Chinese officials, an issue has arisen at the last minute relating to the visa process for some members of the BBC National Orchestra of Wales. As a result, the relevant Chinese authorities have not issued some of the visas in time for the tour to go ahead as planned."

The statement added that as the four concerts - scheduled for this week in the cities of Shanghai, Beijing, Nanjing and Tianjin - were part of the BBC's "significant" centenary celebrations, "it is essential that they go ahead as planned".

"We have therefore taken the difficult decision to recast the programmes with a different conductor and some different music," the statement said.

The Chinese foreign ministry said on Tuesday that it had "recently received applications from the BBC National Orchestra of Wales, and is processing them in accordance with procedures".

The BBC's statement added: "The BBC has a strong track record of working with Chinese artists and we have recently undertaken a number of successful tours to China with other BBC orchestras.

"We value our relationship with China and are committed to working together to make these important centenary celebrations a success."

Sir John, who is also the founder and artistic director of the Monteverdi Choir, has described the Proms as "the world's largest music festival".

This year's Proms series, which runs from 30 July to 18 September, marks five years since the BBC Last Night of the Proms returned to its traditional home at London's Albert Hall.

The BBC can reveal that Sir John Barrow, the recently appointed head of the BBC's Chinese language services, has had his application for a visa to work in China rejected.

The BBC has learnt that Sir John, a former ambassador to China, has been refused entry to the country. This comes after the BBC announced plans to launch a permanent presence in China earlier this year.

Our reporter John Sudworth has been investigating why.

China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs has given no official reason for the decision, but a letter from the embassy in London seen by the BBC says Sir John has been banned because of his "speech and behaviour in public space".

The letter cites articles he wrote in 2020 and 2021 in The Telegraph and The Times newspapers in which he criticised the Chinese government's handling of the Covid-19 outbreak.

Sir John was appointed as the BBC's international China editor in November 2021. The role was retitled head of BBC Chinese in September this year, following a recruitment process.

The BBC has not yet commented.

But minutes of a meeting about the referendum seen by the BBC show ministers discussed whether the public should be asked to vote explicitly for leaving the EU - or for staying in.

The debate - between ministers including Prime Minister David Cameron - is not recorded in the official minutes released by the Cabinet Office.

The question was agreed on the basis that those in favour of leaving would answer "leave", those in favour of staying in the EU would answer "remain", and that those who did not wish to answer, or who invalidly answered, would be allocated to the "remain" vote, the minutes state.

The discussion, revealed in documents obtained under the Freedom of Information Act, suggests ministers were aware that the question's formulation could affect the result.

The issue was raised by Education Secretary Nicky Morgan, who warned that the referendum would be "tight" and that the outcome could depend on how the question was worded.

In the event, she said, if voters were asked: "Do you want to leave the EU?", and the answer was yes, that would be a vote to leave.

But if the question was: "Do you want to remain a member of the EU?", and the answer was yes, that would be a vote to stay, she said.

Ms Morgan said she had received legal advice that there was no obligation to ask the "remain" question, but that her personal view was that the referendum would be "fairer" if the "remain" option was included.

The Cabinet minutes state: "The prime minister said that he was not persuaded by this [advice] and that there was a strong argument that only asking the 'leave' question was simpler and clearer."

The documents also show that ministers agreed the referendum question should be included in the Cabinet minutes - but that the discussion of how it should be answered was not.

The Cabinet Office has not responded to the BBC's enquiries about why the discussion is not recorded in the minutes released to the public.

Norwegian file-sharing website Megaupload has won a landmark case challenging whether internet service providers (ISPs) can be held responsible for content uploaded by users.

The nation's highest court ruled that the ISP was not liable for copyright breaches carried out by its customers.

The decision could have a major impact on the way in which copyright laws are enforced online.

The entertainment industry has argued that ISPs should be responsible for banning access to sites offering illegal content.

Megaupload was sued in Norway by the International Federation of the Phonographic Industry (IFPI) and Norwegian collection society Tono for allowing users to share songs online.

The lower courts had ruled that the ISP was liable for the actions of its customers.

But the Norwegian Supreme Court ruled on Thursday that the ISP was not liable for direct copyright infringement carried out by its customers.

The court said that indirect infringement - for example, failure to take down copyrighted content - was not sufficient to hold the ISP responsible.

The case turned on whether the ISP could be said to have "authorized" the copyright breaches.

"File-sharing services have argued that they are unable to monitor all the content that is being uploaded and downloaded, and that any obligation on their part to remove copyright violations or make sure that they do not appear would be impractical and unreasonably costly," the court said in its decision.

The ruling said that copyright holders instead should target the individuals who commit the breaches.

Megaupload was represented by lawyer Jon Wessel Tonning.

He said the ruling was a victory for ISPs who did not want to be held responsible for the actions of customers.

"They [the ISPs] have the responsibility to provide access to a network, but they should not be responsible for the information that is transmitted," he told the BBC.

The case is the latest in a series of legal battles over online copyright.

Last year, the US Supreme Court ruled that ISPs could be held responsible for copyright breaches carried out by customers.

That case, which involved college students who had shared music online, reversed a ruling that said the ISP could not be held responsible.

And in a recent case in the UK, the High Court ordered British ISPs to block access to file-sharing website The Pirate Bay.

Norway's highest court has upheld a ruling that found the country's largest Internet service provider guilty of violating copyright law by allowing its customers to download music from the Kazaa file-sharing service.

The Norwegian Supreme Court ruled that Telenor ASA breached copyright law with its sluggish response in closing down the accounts of customers who used Kazaa to download music illegally.

The case was brought by the International Federation of the Phonographic Industry (IFPI), which argued that Telenor failed to take reasonable measures to prevent subscribers from using its network for illegal file sharing.

The Oslo District Court ruled in 2015 that Telenor was liable for damages totaling $14.5 million for around 17,000 songs. The court said each song downloaded illegally was liable for between $852 and $3,047 in compensation.

Telenor, which has more than two million customers, appealed the decision, but Norway's top court upheld the 2015 ruling on Tuesday.

The Labour Party has been accused of using European Union propaganda.

The party has distributed a leaflet to households across the UK highlighting the UK's "£100 billion" annual payment to the EU.

The leaflet, entitled "the truth about the EU", also claims Britain's economic growth is "hampered" by the EU.

The BBC's Norman Smith said the leaflet was "much more sceptical" than previous ones.

The Liberal Democrats said Labour was "selling Brexit as if it was a Christmas present".

The leaflet says "the EU is failing" on immigration, the single market, and the euro.

It adds that leaving the EU offers the chance to "reshape our economy to tackle the real issues".

Labour said the leaflet presented "facts" and was not party political.
