Labour has been accused of creating "EU propaganda" for British citizens after it released a video urging people to vote to remain in the bloc.

The party's deputy leader, Angela Rayner, said the clip - which highlights the benefits of EU membership - was intended to "set the record straight" on the impact of Brexit.

But Conservative MP Alberto Costa called it "very misleading" and urged Twitter to remove it.

The video, released on Thursday, lists advantages of EU membership including cheaper phone bills, the right to live and work across Europe, and visa-free travel.

The voiceover says Labour is making the case to "defend our European future".

But in an letter to Twitter chief executive Jack Dorsey, Mr Costa, a Conservative MP for South Leicestershire, called for it to be taken down.

He said the video - which has been seen more than 120,000 times - was "very misleading" and broke the social network's rules on "misleading information".

"This is not the first time that Labour have pushed out this sort of propaganda and I strongly urge you to take immediate action in removing this video and to investigate Labour's behaviour in this matter," he wrote.

Ms Rayner said the video was intended to "set the record straight on the benefits of being in the EU".

"There are lots of benefits to being in the EU but the Tories want to deny that and just talk about immigration," she told the BBC's Newsnight.

"We're not going to let them get away with that. We're going to talk about the benefits as well as the control and the security as well."

The video was also criticised by the pro-Brexit campaign group Leave Means Leave, which said it was an "attempt to brainwash people".

"With just five days to go until the referendum, we are clearly seeing the fear campaign from the Remain camp stepping up a gear," a spokesman said.

"It is frankly disgusting that Labour are now resorting to trying to brainwash people with this propaganda."

On Saturday, Labour's leader Jeremy Corbyn accused Prime Minister Boris Johnson of using "fear and lies" to make his case for Brexit.

The Labour leader said: "The Tories' campaign of fear and lies is exposing the worst of their corrupt, deceitful and undemocratic nature."

Berlin hails European cinema

Movie makers from across the continent have descended on the German capital for the European Film Awards.

The winners of the Euromedia awards, which honour the best in European cinema, were announced at a glitzy ceremony in Berlin on Saturday.

The UK's Emily Blunt took the best actress award for her role in the drama The Girl in the Café, while the best actor award went to Spain's Javier Bardem for his part in the political thriller Mondays in the Sun.

The best film award went to Russian entry The Captain's Daughter, while the best documentary was given to the Danish/Swedish/Norwegian co-production The Swenkas.

The event was hosted by German actor Christian Ulmen and more than 500 guests attended.

They included renowned film-makers such as Britain's Mike Leigh and Terry Gilliam and Ireland's Jim Sheridan.

The awards are given out by the European Film Academy, which is made up of more than 2,000 film professionals from across the continent.

The academy says it aims to "promote and award the best in European cinema".

Its president, German director Wim Wenders, said this year's entries showed that European cinema was "as diverse, inventive and seductive as ever".

He added: "Even though national film funding is increasingly under threat, European cinema proves it has never been more needed and wanted by audiences all over the world."

The celebrations in Berlin on Saturday night reached a climax with the annual presentation of the Golden Bear trophies to the best films in the festival's competition sections. For the first time in nearly three decades, a documentary won the top prize, with the Golden Bear going to "All Quiet on the Western Front" by Edward Berger. The film, which is based on the classic novel by Erich Maria Remarque and tells the story of German soldiers in World War I, was praised by the festival for its "powerful and contemporary" portrayal of the horrors of war. "It reminds us that peace can never be taken for granted and must always be defended with determination," the festival said in its official statement.

The Silver Bear for best director was awarded to Wes Anderson for his new film "The French Dispatch", which stars Timothée Chalamet, Benicio del Toro, and Tilda Swinton. The film is a love letter to journalism and is full of Anderson's trademark eccentricity and quirkiness. The Silver Bear for best actress went to Joanna Kulig for her performance in "The Wedding", while the Silver Bear for best actor was awarded to Mads Mikkelsen for his performance in "Another Round". 

The festival also awarded a special bear to celebrate the career of German actor Michael Gwisdek, who died last year. Gwisdek was a frequent collaborator with director Christian Petzold and appeared in films such as "Barbara" and "Phoenix".  The festival concluded with a fireworks display over the Berlin skyline, marking the end of 11 days of film celebrations.

The UK government has said the country's next budget will be delivered on Wednesday, 16 March.
Prime Minister Rishi Sunak made the announcement as he opened the annual Conservative Party conference in Birmingham.
He said he would use the speech to "set out our plan for the future of the British people".

Nasdaq has announced plans to raise $100m (£85m) in a share sale.

The stock market operator said it planned to sell 7.1 million shares - about 5% of its total outstanding shares - to fund a variety of initiatives.

The sale could dilute existing shareholders' stakes in Nasdaq by about 5%.

In afternoon trading on Tuesday, Nasdaq was down 1.4% at $64.87 per share.

"The proceeds from this offering will be used for general corporate purposes, including, but not limited to, investments in existing and new businesses and strategic acquisitions, repayment of debt, and share repurchases," Nasdaq said in a statement.

Nasdaq's main rivals, the New York Stock Exchange and Intercontinental Exchange, have both undertaken major acquisitions in recent years as they seek to expand their businesses.

The Nasdaq exchange is planning a share sale that could raise around $100m (£85m) for its parent company Nasdaq Inc, according to reports.

The exchange operator is said to be considering a sale of around 10 million shares, which could increase its free float to nearly 20%.

If successful, it would be the first time Nasdaq has sold shares since it went public in 2002.

Nasdaq's parent company is currently owned by a group of investors including Silver Lake Partners, Bain Capital, and the Ontario Teachers' Pension Plan.

The news comes as the Nasdaq Composite index has risen more than 13% so far this year, due in part to the surge in technology stocks.

Last year, Nasdaq generated around $2.2bn in annual revenue, down from $3.4bn in 2019 before the pandemic.

The mountains and jungles of Peru have long been treacherous for internet service providers hoping to connect the country's far-flung regions.

But a project to beam internet via satellite is providing cheap, reliable connections to areas that until recently had none.

Among those benefiting is coffee farmer Leonor Choque.

"I get news from my children who live in other provinces, I learn about the prices for coffee and I see recipes for cooking," she says, as chickens peck the ground around her.

Ms Choque is one of about 4,000 people in the Peruvian province of San Martín who are using the service.

It is among a number of initiatives aimed at connecting the two-thirds of Peruvians who do not have internet access.

It sounds like a joke but it is a serious piece of malware which security experts say has caught thousands of people out.

The "joke" e-mail virus hides inside an attachment which claims to be a graphic image of a puppy or a kitten.

But the image is actually an executable file and opening it will launch the virus.

The attachment has a name like "cute_kitten.vbs". Users should be suspicious of files with ".vbs" extensions as they are often used by viruses, security experts said.

The e-mail comes with a subject line such as "Look at this cute kitten!"

Once launched, the virus sends a copy of itself to all the people in the victim's address book.

It also disables several security features on the victim's machine and may make it vulnerable to further attacks.

The virus, which security experts have called "Funlove", appears to have been created by the same group which developed the "I love you" virus.

That was one of the most damaging viruses ever, which spread rapidly through e-mails with subjects like "I love you baby" or "Hello baby".

Experts believe the new virus is likely to spread rapidly in the next few days as people return to their desks after the Easter holiday weekend.

The committee voted 18 to eight, with one abstention, in favour of the package, but a number of MEPs expressed reservations about the outcome.

"The EPLS will create a new court system without any control by the European Parliament," Austrian Green MEP Elisabeth Koestinger warned.

"Furthermore, the proposed legislation risks undermining the court system in Europe, and threatens to make the patent system more expensive, less transparent and unpredictable," she added.

The committee vote is not the end of the road for the legislation, as the full Parliament will now have to vote at the July plenary session in Strasbourg.

The legislation has already been approved by the European Council.

If the Parliament's vote in July ends up backing the patent package, the regulations will be officially adopted, and will enter into force 20 days after their publication in the EU Official Journal.

The EU is to create a unified patent system, making it easier for businesses to gain protection for their inventions in multiple countries. But the UK will not be a part of the scheme despite Brexit, leading to concerns over extra red tape for British firms. The new system is set to launch on 1 June this year and will be open to all member states of the European Patent Convention, including the UK. But Britain will not be part of the unitary patent system, which would have given inventors protection across the whole of the EU. It means UK businesses will have to use the new system alongside national patents to secure protection for their inventions in Europe. 

The unitary patent would have been valid in all EU countries and would have required applicants to choose a court in one of three countries to hear disputes. Britain would have been able to choose a court in either England, Germany or France to hear disputes. More than 70% of the top 10 European companies that filed the most European patent applications in 2019 were from the UK. Officials said the UK's absence from the unitary patent system would not affect British businesses that want protection in the EU because they can still use the new system. But it means they will have to follow national laws in each EU country they want protection in.

Adam Halsall, a partner at law firm Allen & Overy, said: "The consequence of this is that companies will have to continue to search for patents that give them protection in each country individually. "As such, the cost of obtaining broader protection for their inventions across Europe will be greater than it would have been under the unitary patent system."

The government said the UK is already a "world-leading innovator" and the new system "will not directly affect the UK". It said Britain has a "strong and well-respected patent framework". It began to be marketed in the US as a consumer product in 2017, and can be found in anything from chewing gum to beauty products.

Cannabis is classified as an illegal or controlled substance in much of the world. But as the evidence of its medical benefits has grown, so too have attempts to legalise it.

Last year, Canada became the second country after Uruguay to legalise it for recreational use.

Financial services group MetLife has agreed to buy the life insurance division of Citigroup for $12.5bn (£7.4bn).

The deal includes the sale of Citigroup's interest in the joint venture, Citigroup Insurance Holdings, as well as the sale of Metropolitan Insurance & Annuity Company, and MetLife Asia.

The transaction excludes Citigroup's foreign insurance businesses in Korea, India, and Japan.

New York-based MetLife is the largest life insurer in the US. It has about 70 million customers in nearly 50 countries.

Citigroup's insurance division, which offers life insurance, annuities and asset management, has about 130 million customers in North America, Japan and other parts of Asia.

MetLife said the deal would increase its presence in Asia and add to its portfolio of individual life insurance products in the US. It added the acquisition would make it "one of the world's leading insurance and financial services companies".

"MetLife and Citigroup's insurance businesses have highly complementary franchises, and this acquisition demonstrates our commitment to our clients and shareholders," said MetLife chief executive Steven A. Kandarian.

"This transaction offers substantial long-term value for our shareholders, with the strategic and financial benefits of size and scale, improved financial flexibility due to the lower amount of capital required to support the business, and the opportunity to realize approximately $1.5 billion of value over time through the monetization of the tax benefits generated by the transaction," he added.

MetLife is funding the deal with the cash it holds overseas as well as by issuing stock. The deal is expected to close in the first half of 2016, subject to regulatory approval.

MetLife, the largest life insurer in the United States, has agreed to buy the life insurance division of Citigroup for about $12.5 billion in cash. The deal will allow MetLife to expand its consumer finance business and provide Citigroup with much-needed capital. 

MetLife will acquire Citigroup's retail life insurance and annuity businesses, which operate in 52 countries and serve about 9 million customers. The deal does not include Citigroup's institutional retirement businesses or life reinsurance operations. 

The acquisition is expected to close by the end of 2023, pending regulatory approval. MetLife said it does not expect the deal to have a material impact on its earnings per share in the first year after closing. 

Under the terms of the deal, MetLife will pay $2.5 billion in cash and issue about 157 million new shares to Citigroup. The transaction is expected to reduce MetLife's common equity tier 1 capital ratio by about 170 basis points, the company said in a statement. 

MetLife also said it plans to cut about $1.3 billion in annual expenses from the acquisition, with about $870 million of those coming from eliminating duplicate and overlapping expenses between the two companies.

The dollar jumped and US bond yields surged on Thursday after data showed that the US economy added far more jobs than expected in January, while wages recorded their largest annual increase in four decades, sparking worries about inflation. The employment report added to indications that the world's biggest economy is recovering from the coronavirus pandemic, but it also raised the prospect of sharply higher interest rates coming sooner than thought. Financial markets had been expecting several interest rate rises this year, but the strong jobs data pointed to the need for tighter monetary policy, which tends to push up bond yields and boost the dollar.

The figures raised concerns because the large increase in wages could fuel inflation, as companies may have to pay more to hire workers. Annual wage growth accelerated to 5.7% in January from 4.4% in December, the largest increase since June 1982, the Labour Department said. But the data was collected before Russia's invasion of Ukraine, which has driven up oil prices and added to concerns about inflation. The strong jobs report could make the Federal Reserve, the US central bank, even more hawkish, analysts said.

"This is going to be rocket fuel for Fed tightening expectations," said Brian Coulton, an economist at Fitch Ratings. The prospect of faster rate rises pushed up the dollar's value against other major currencies, as it tends to attract investors seeking a higher return on their money. The dollar index, which measures the currency against six major rivals, was up 0.8% on the day.

The 10-year US Treasury yield, which tends to move in the opposite direction to the price, was up sharply at 2.14% compared with just 1.92% late on Tuesday. The two-year yield, which is more sensitive to interest rate expectations, also jumped, rising to 1.62% from 1.44% on Tuesday.

The latest data showing inflation in the US is running at its highest level since the early 1980s has sparked worries among economists and policymakers about the potential impact on the economy. The consumer price index (CPI), which measures the cost of a wide-ranging basket of goods and services, rose to 6.8% in November from 6.2% in October, marking the fastest pace since June 1982. The rise was driven by increases in the cost of shelter, used cars and trucks, and household furnishings, among other things.

The Federal Reserve, the US central bank, has been trying to curb inflation by raising interest rates, but the latest data suggests that these efforts have so far had little effect. Some economists are now predicting that the Fed will have to raise rates even higher in order to bring inflation under control, which could lead to a recession.

Others are calling for a more balanced approach, arguing that high interest rates could actually hurt the economy by slowing down consumer spending and business investment. They say that the Fed should focus on targeting inflation in a more targeted way, rather than raising rates across the board.

Whatever course the Fed chooses, it will need to act quickly in order to get a handle on inflation. With prices rising at such a rapid pace, the gap between the rich and the poor is widening, and the cost of living is becoming increasingly unaffordable for many Americans. For now, the data suggests that the US economy is in for a rocky few months, and the coming year could be a challenging one.

The bank's rate-setting council voted 8-1 to keep the rate on hold
It was the first time in a decade that a majority of members voted for no change
The Bank of England has kept interest rates on hold, following a split decision by its rate-setting committee.

It marked the first time in more than a decade that the majority of the Bank's Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) voted to keep rates on hold rather than to cut them.

The bank's rate-setting council voted 8-1 to keep the rate on hold at 0.5%, amid signs that the UK economy is recovering from a Brexit-induced slump.

Only last month, the MPC reduced the base rate from 0.75% to 0.5% in response to a global economic slowdown and no-deal Brexit fears.

But data released since then appears to show that the UK economy is weathering the Brexit storm better than expected, and that employers are still hiring.

'No need to panic'
The MPC's decision was welcomed by businesses, with the Confederation of British Industry saying it would help to keep "confidence high".

"The Bank of England's decision to hold rates is important for businesses as it signals no need to panic over the economy," said CBI chief economist Rain Newton-Smith.

"Although we face challenges, the lower base rate and reduced uncertainty about the UK's future relationship with the EU have helped make our exports more competitive."

However, Ian Wright, chief economist at Britain's biggest business group, the Federation of Small Businesses (FSB), said that "many small firms will be disappointed" by the decision.

"The majority of firms would have liked to see the base rate cut to 0.25% to help them tackle the upfront costs of complying with Brexit," he said.

Low inflation
The MPC's decision was based on its assessment that inflation was likely to stay low, and that there was no need for a rate cut to help the economy as a whole.

However, it did acknowledge that the UK's departure from the EU was proving to be a drag on growth, and that the outlook for the economy was uncertain.

"The monetary policy response to Brexit, while significant, has been limited thus far, and remains contingent on the outlook for activity, inflation and the exchange rate," the MPC said in a statement.

"The Committee stands ready to adjust monetary policy accordingly as economic circumstances evolve."

The Bank of England has kept the base rate at 0.5% for the 18th consecutive meeting after voting 8-1 to make no change.

The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) voted unanimously to keep the base rate at 0.5% back in July, but this was the first meeting since then where external member Catherine Mann was in attendance.

This is the last meeting of the MPC that Sir Dave Ramsden will attend as deputy governor for markets and banking, as he steps down from the Bank at the end of the month.

The Bank's decision comes as inflation looks like it may be close to its peak, and economic activity has slowed.

The MPC said in its policy statement that the slowdown in growth in October was "especially pronounced" and that the outlook for the UK economy had "weakened" since its last meeting.

It cited slower growth in China and the government's "recent change in fiscal policy" as reasons for the weaker outlook.

The committee also said that inflation had "peaked" at 11% in October, but that it would remain "elevated" in the coming months.

However, it said that the effects of the government's fiscal policy were "uncertain" and that the "net effect on demand was unclear".

The MPC voted 8-1 to keep the base rate at 0.5%, with Catherine Mann voting to raise rates by 15 basis points to 0.75%.

This was the first time she had voted to raise rates since she joined the MPC in June.

Mann said in a statement that she had voted to raise rates because she was "particularly concerned" about the risks of " entrenched expectations" of low inflation among the public and firms.

A US court has sentenced two men to four years in prison for scamming people through robocalls.

Jonathan R. Taylor and David A. Weiss admitted to their roles in a robocall scam that defrauded millions of dollars from victims.

The duo pleaded guilty in November 2021 to one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud and one count of wire fraud.

US District Judge Cecilia Altonaga sentenced them on Wednesday.

According to the US Justice Department, the men and their conspirators made more than a billion spoofed robocalls between 2019 and 2020.

The department said the men had made calls about vehicle warranties, debt reduction services, and fake charities.

In reality, there was no vehicle warranty and the "debt reduction" was simply a scheme to get people on the phone and sell them various products.

The US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) had called the case "robocall fraud on a massive scale".

The two men sentenced on Wednesday were "integral to the fraud", the FTC said.

Judge Altonaga also ordered them to pay $8m in damages.

According to the Department of Justice, David Weiss operated several businesses that made the robocalls.

He then sold the calls to Jonathan Taylor and his businesses, which completed the frauds.

In 2019, the FTC filed a complaint against Jonathan Taylor, David Weiss and others alleging that they had made millions of illegal robocalls and violated the FTC's Do Not Call Policy.

The pair pleaded guilty to both counts in November 2021.

In addition to the prison sentence, Jonathan Taylor was also sentenced to three years of supervised release and David Weiss was sentenced to five years of supervised release.

Jonathan Buck, 35, and Daniel Krugler, 23, pleaded guilty in September to fraud and forgery charges for their part in an e-mail scam that harvested personal data from vulnerable computer users.

The pair, from Scottsdale in Arizona, sent more than 70,000 e-mails through a "spam farm" in India, offering victims a chance to make money by working at home.

When victims responded, they were sent a forged letter appearing to be from Microsoft, claiming that viruses had been detected on their computers.

The victims were then instructed to telephone a toll-free number, at a cost of $1.20 per minute, for assistance in removing the viruses.

The scam - believed to have been operated by a criminal gang in India - raked in at least $200,000 before it was shut down in March by federal investigators.

As part of the plea bargain, Buck and Krugler each surrendered a laptop, a computer server and a list of e-mail addresses of their customers.

They were also forced to hand over $42,000 in profits. "This is a new kind of crime," said Thomas Collins, the attorney for Arizona.

"These are the first people in the US to be charged under state law with fraud for spamming."

Buck and Krugler could have faced up to 8.75 years in prison and $350,000 in fines. But the judge imposed a more lenient sentence, saying that the pair had cooperated with the investigation.

The pair had been charged with forgery, computer tampering and conducting a scheme to defraud.

Buck pleaded guilty to all charges, while Krugler pleaded guilty to one count of forgery.

Judge Warren Granville told the pair that they had violated the public's trust by sending out spam.

"You sent out e-mails to hundreds of thousands of people who didn't want them," he said. "It undermines the effectiveness of e-mail."

He added that the crime was "very serious" because some of the victims had spent large amounts of money on phone calls to the scam's helpline.

EU ministers to mull jet fuel tax

Brussels has rejected a proposal to include aviation in the EU's carbon trading scheme, instead tasking a group of officials with drawing up reports on alternative measures, including a kerosene tax.

The European Commission proposed including aviation in the EU's carbon market as part of its strategy for reducing greenhouse gas emissions.

But it was met with opposition from member states, which will now ask a group of officials to draw up reports on alternative measures, which will include increasing the price of kerosene.

The UK government welcomed the development, having previously expressed concerns that including aviation in the carbon market could hurt economic growth.

"We have always been clear that we want to see the aviation industry playing its part in reducing emissions, but that this must be done in a fair and sustainable way," a spokesperson for the Department for Transport said.

"We will continue to work with our European partners to ensure the aviation sector meets its environmental obligations."

Green groups expressed disappointment at the decision not to include aviation in the carbon market, saying it was a setback for efforts to reduce emissions.

"The Commission's original proposal to include aviation in the EU ETS (Emissions Trading Scheme) was the most cost-effective and efficient solution for tackling rising emissions from the sector," said Bill Hemmings, aviation director at the Transport & Environment (T&E) campaign group.

"All other options, such as a kerosene tax, are either ineffective or unfair."

The officials' reports will also examine whether revenues from any new measure could be used to lower taxes elsewhere, for example on income or profits.

The committee of officials from member states will submit its first report by the end of March next year.

The development comes ahead of a crucial United Nations climate change conference, Cop27, which will be held in Egypt in November.

Aviation emissions are currently growing at a rate of around 5% per year, according to the International Air Transport Association (Iata), and the sector accounts for about 6% of all greenhouse gas emissions.

The EU's carbon market currently covers about 40% of total carbon emissions from the 27-nation bloc.

It puts a cap on emissions from large industrial plants and power stations and forces them to buy permits if they want to emit more carbon dioxide.

The price of carbon has rocketed in recent months, reaching a record high of more than €90 per tonne

BRUSSELS (Reuters) - European Union ministers will discuss plans to impose a tax on kerosene used in commercial aviation on Wednesday, despite strong opposition from the airline industry and some member states.
The proposal, which was initially agreed by the EU's 27 member states in March, came under fresh criticism last week after Germany said it would not back the plan.
Aviation charities and the EU's two leading environmental groups have called on the bloc to go ahead with the tax to help mitigate the climate impact of air travel.
The proposal is for a kerosene tax that would start at €1.50 ($1.61) per litre, according to a document seen by Reuters. The tax would rise to €2.05 per litre by 2030.
The aim is to raise €6.6 billion per year by 2030, equivalent to around 4% of the EU's total climate spending plan for the next decade.
The measure would be imposed on all commercial aviation operating within the EU, irrespective of where the aircraft is registered.

Iraqi voters turn to economic issues

Economic reform has topped the agenda as Iraqis vote in the country's first parliamentary elections since 2018.

For the past two days, voters in Iraq have been going to the polls to elect 329 members of parliament, as well as a new president.

Sunday saw a relatively low turnout, but queues were seen outside polling stations on the final day of voting on Wednesday.

The election is seen as a test for the country's outgoing Prime Minister, Mustafa al-Kadhimi, who has been accused of failing to improve the country's economic situation.

Desperate for change amid the economic crisis, Iraqi voters are looking for candidates who can offer some form of economic reform.

The Iraqi people have voted for a new parliament, in hopes that it will address the economic crisis facing the country. The election was marked by a low turnout, with only 41% of voters participating. The results are expected to be known in the coming days.

The economic crisis has been a major issue for the Iraqi people, with the country's currency plummeting and basic goods becoming unaffordable. The outgoing government has been unable to address the crisis, and voters are hoping that the new government will be able to find a solution. Many are skeptical, however, and believe that the new government will not be able to make the necessary changes.

Britain must achieve "prosperity with a purpose", using the power of the world's fifth largest economy to help solve the planet's problems, former Prime Minister Tony Blair has said.

In his first major speech since ending his decade-long premiership, Mr Blair said only radical action would defeat global challenges.

And he called on the West to embrace religion rather than regard it as a source of conflict.

The speech in Chicago was well received by an audience of about 400 people, including politicians and diplomats.

But he was confronted by protesters both outside and inside the conference venue, with one man arrested for disorderly conduct.

Mr Blair, who led the Labour Party for more than a decade, stepped down as prime minister in June and was replaced by his chancellor, Gordon Brown.

The former prime minister has since taken up the role of Middle East peace envoy, and has been appointed special envoy to Africa by the African Union.

In his speech on Tuesday, Mr Blair outlined eight areas of what he called "interdependent" action needed to solve the world's problems.

They ranged from climate change and poverty in the world's poorest countries, to infectious diseases and the threat of nuclear terrorism.

Other goals included ensuring every child in the world went to school, and increasing the number of women in politics and business.

"Prosperity is not an end in itself, but a means of increasing our ability to address these challenges," he said.

"It is a means of bringing hope to more people, of extending the boundaries of human possibility, of improving the lives of people everywhere and, in doing so, improving our own."

Mr Blair said the G8 rich nations must deliver on their promises to increase aid to the developing world, and develop new green technologies to help combat climate change.

And he called on the West to work with, rather than against, Islamic countries, to help eradicate poverty and disease.

"We in the West like to see ourselves as the authors of our own fortunes. But in today's world, that is simply not good enough," he said.

"We did not create the modern world, nor did we create the opportunities that flow from it - though we have done more to benefit from them than any other part of the world.

"And, it is no good pretending that the Enlightenment ideals of reason and science alone can provide the answers to the questions of our time.

Former British Prime Minister Tony Blair has said the UK is no longer prosperous enough to take its prosperity for granted.

In a speech on the fringes of the Labour Party conference, he said other countries were "snapping at our heels" as they aimed to match Britain's economic success.

Mr Blair said the country needed to pursue pro-growth policies and harness the power of the state to deliver change.

He praised the government's decision to invest in infrastructure and training, but warned that "the jury is out" on whether it would deliver.

The former prime minister said he was in favour of constitutional change to bring the English regions and Scotland together in a federal system.

Mr Blair argued that the first step should be the creation of English regional assemblies, with powers over transport, training and economic development.

The assemblies would be given real power over time, as the public became used to the new system, he said.

Inevitably, perhaps, it was the captain who made the difference as Scotland progressed to the knockout stages of the Euros with a tough 2-0 win over Croatia. Callum McGregor's header just before half-time broke the deadlock in a tightly-contested match, with John McGinn adding a second just after the hour to ensure progress to the last 16 as one of the best third-placed teams. 

There were loud cheers at Hampden Park when the final whistle confirmed the result, with Scottish fans delighted at the prospect of a trip to Copenhagen to face the world's number one team, Belgium, on Saturday. And for Steve Clarke, the Scotland manager, it vindicates his bold move to change the system against the Czechs and play with three centre-backs behind a disciplined midfield.

There were echoes of Scotland's 2-0 win over England in 1977, with Clarke's team wearing the dark blue of Scotland and relying on two set-piece goals rather than the free-flowing performance that gave away nations a shock in the group stages of that year's World Cup.

"We can be proud of everybody, they are a great group and they have given the Scottish nation a lift," said Clarke. "We can look forward to the game against Belgium with a lot of excitement."

Scotland have been rewarded for their efforts with a meeting against the world's number one-ranked side, with Belgium's golden generation including Eden Hazard, Romelu Lukaku and Kevin De Bruyne. But Clarke insists his team will not be afraid, with Scotland aiming to emulate the performances of Wales and the Czech Republic, who both produced shock wins in the last 16.

"We will go into the game with a plan, and we will try to execute the plan," said Clarke. "We will not be afraid, we will be positive and go for the game."

It is 25 years since Scotland last appeared at a major tournament, and the win over Croatia means they have now reached the knockout stages in two of their three major tournaments – doing so at the World Cup in 1954 and at Euro 2020.

And former Scotland midfielder Graeme Souness, who was part of the team that reached the World Cup semifinals in 1990, was thrilled with the win over Croatia. 

"It's a magnificent result," he told the BBC. "To go into the game knowing that you have got to win, and to have the fortitude and the quality to do it

Japan has avoided a technical recession after recording better-than-expected growth in the final quarter of 2022, according to official data.

Quarter-on-quarter GDP data showed the economy expanded by an annualised 1.1%, beating estimates of a 0.5% contraction.

It comes after a slump in the summer when the economy contracted by 0.8% amid a surge in Covid cases.

However, economists warn that the recovery is fragile due to the prolonged impact of inflation and interest rate rises.

The data showed a modest pickup in consumer spending, which contributed to the better-than-expected expansion.

But it also revealed a decline in business investment and a slowdown in exports, especially to China.

Japan's central bank has kept its key interest rate at a record low of minus 0.1% despite rising consumer prices.

But the bank has signalled that it will take further steps to curb inflation as the yen continues to weaken against the US dollar.

Many countries are battling inflation as they emerge from the Covid pandemic, although price rises have been particularly acute in Japan, causing a cost-of-living crisis.

The government has introduced cash handouts and a pledge to cap electricity bills to help households struggling with the rising cost of living.

Japan has narrowly avoided slipping into a technical recession, with data showing the economy grew at a 1.2% annual rate in the last quarter.

The world's third-biggest economy contracted by an annualised 2.3% in the third quarter, meaning the latest data represent a rebound.

However, analysts warned that the recovery was fragile given the sharp fall in exports.

And they said the rebound owed much to stock rebuilding after low inventory levels, which could not be sustained in the coming quarters.

Japan's central bank has kept its key interest rate at -0.1% as it holds out hope that the slide in oil prices will finally push up consumer prices after years of deflation.

But it warned that slowing growth in China - a major trading partner - and the Ukraine war posed risks to the outlook.

African-American rapper Curtis Jackson, aka 50 Cent, has achieved the rare feat of occupying the top five positions on Billboard's digital songs chart.

The rapper, who has reigned the rap charts for the past decade, achieved the impressive sweep with individual songs from his recently released album "Animal Ambition."

The album, released in April, was his fifth studio recording and the first in three years.

All 10 tracks from the album made the chart, including the title track "Animal Ambition" at number six, "Smoke" at number seven and "9 shots" at number 10.

Only one other artist has come close to achieving the top-five sweep.

In 2009, The Beatles occupied the top six spots on the digital song chart following the release of their best-selling album "The Beatles: Rock Band."

The 50-year-old rapper, who started his career in 2000, has sold more than 30 million albums worldwide.

He has also acted in films including 2005's "Get Rich or Die Tryin'" and the television series "Power."

Introducing the man with the midas touch.

American rapper 50 Cent has scored his very first chart debut with his recent album, "Black Mafia Family".

The album, which was released on 26 March, made it to the top of the charts in the US, giving the rapper his first ever number one.

Not only that, but all of the album's 18 songs also made it onto the Billboard Hot 100 chart, meaning the album achieved a feat that not even the likes of The Beatles and Drake have managed to achieve.

The rapper, who is 41 years old and whose real name is Curtis Jackson, has had huge success in the past, with multiple number one singles and albums, however, he has never achieved a chart-topping debut for one of his albums.

'Black Mafia Family' is based on the television crime drama of the same name that he stars in and produces.
The album features some well-known names in the rap industry, such as Eminem and Lil Wayne.

The huge success comes 19 years after Jackson released his debut album, 'Power of the Dollar', in 2014.

The first Academy Awards ceremony took place on 16 May 1929 at the Hollywood Roosevelt Hotel. About 270 people attended. There were no television broadcasts then, and only local radio stations reported the event.

It was a low-key affair compared with today's extravaganza - and there were no best picture, best director or best actor awards.

The Oscars have been hosted by a wide range of celebrities - from Bob Hope to Whoopi Goldberg and Seth MacFarlane.

The first host was actor Douglas Fairbanks Sr., who appeared on stage with his wife, actress Mary Pickford. Together, they presented the best actor and best actress awards.

The Oscars were scheduled for 18 March this year but have been postponed until 25 April, seven weeks later than originally planned.

The ceremony often exceeds four hours and critics say it has become too long. Changes to the voting system and a tightening of rules around the acceptance speeches have been suggested as ways to save time. 

The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences - which organises the event - has said it is reviewing how to "enhance" the show.

The Academy Awards, also known as the Oscars, is one of the most prominent award ceremonies in the world. The first award ceremony took place in 1929 and since then has been held annually. The Oscars is an important event in the film industry, with many seeing it as the highest honour that can be awarded to a filmmaker or actor.

Throughout the years, the Academy Awards have undergone many changes and transformations. Initially, only male actors were permitted to be nominated and win an award. Despite women making significant contributions to the film industry since the early days, they were not recognised by the Academy. It was not until the 1980s when the Academy began to recognise the achievements of female filmmakers and actors by introducing the Best Actress award. 

The Academy Awards have also been criticised for not representing enough diversity on the screen. Over the years, the Academy has tried to address this issue by introducing new categories and making changes to the voting process. These changes have led to an increase in the number of diverse nominees and winners.

Despite the challenges it has faced, the Academy Awards remain one of the most prestigious and well-known award ceremonies in the world. It has continued to recognise and honour the achievements of filmmakers and actors, and has played a significant role in shaping the film industry.

The US government is to raise maximum fines for television programmes that air indecent material, media reports say.

The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) will now fine stations up to $325,000 for a single incident, up from $325,000 currently, and up to $3.25m for multiple violations.

The five-member commission voted along party lines on the plan, with the three Republican commissioners backing it and the two Democrats opposing it.

The FCC has fined several television stations in recent years for airing indecent material during the watershed hours of 08:00 to 17:00.

They include a rock concert by the band Nine Inch Nails, an episode of the popular sitcom South Park, and a celebrity boxing match.

But some fines were overturned in court because they were deemed to be excessive.

The US government first introduced fines for TV indecency in 1987, and raised the cap on them most recently in 2000.

Wednesday's vote means the FCC has aligned its cap on fines with a congressional vote last year to raise the cap.

The US government is to raise the cap on the fines imposed on television networks that air indecent material, officials say.

The move is part of a plan to make it easier for the authorities to penalise broadcasters who show objectionable material.

The head of the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said the increase - from $325,000 to $550,000 - would be "conservative".

Nicholas Johnson said it was "better" to raise the cap now than "later", adding that any future raise could be "substantial".

Actor Philip Seymour Hoffman has criticised the modern movie industry for making films which are "too fast" and lacking in depth.

The 46-year-old Oscar-winning star said studios were more interested in making money than producing good films.

"It's too bad that it's just about dollars and cents," he said. "Art house is dying, which is too bad - that's what I grew up with."

Hoffman was speaking at the Sundance film festival, where his latest movie A Most Wanted Man opened the event.

The film, which is based on a novel by John le Carre, focuses on intelligence surveillance after the September 11 attacks.

Hoffman, who starred in The Master, Capote and Boogie Nights, said the new film was "something different" for him.

"It's not an action film or a comic book adaptation," he said. "It's not Marvel - they're making movies for other reasons these days.

"It's too bad that the studios don't have enough faith in mature audiences to make challenging films."

Hoffman also criticised 3D films, saying he did not think the extra dimension added much to the movie-going experience.

"It just seems like a waste of money to me," he said. "The film business is changing - it's too fast.

"Things go up and they come down. I remember when musical theatre was huge and then it disappeared for a while.

"Things go in cycles and eventually things balance out."

Hoffman said he was not sure if he would make another film, adding that he was proud of the work he had done.

"Maybe I'll just be a carpenter," he said. "Maybe I'll just retire.

"I'm pretty fortunate. I've had a great career and a great life doing what I love - to have a job where you get to live your dreams, that's pretty rare."

The renowned actor Philip Hoffman has criticized the modern film industry for its overuse of computer-generated imagery (CGI), which he says is a "distraction" from the acting.

Speaking at the BFI Southbank, Hoffman, who has appeared in a number of classic films including 'Rain Man' and 'Quantum of Solace', said that CGI has taken the focus away from acting.

"I think it's a disgrace how all of these films are made now with no acting and all of the acting is done by computers," he said.

"It's a total distraction that takes away from the acting."

Hoffman cited the film 'Gravity' as an example of a film that relied too heavily on CGI, saying that the acting was "forgotten" about. 

However, despite his criticism of the modern film industry, Hoffman did praise the film '1917' for its combination of acting and special effects.

"That was acting and special effects combined the way they should be," he said.

Prime Minister Boris Johnson has said the return of school sports days will help tackle obesity and improve children's mental health.

Speaking at a Downing Street news conference, he said sport had been "forgotten" in schools and that pupils had lost out by being indoors.

Mr Johnson said PE lessons and after-school clubs would help pupils become "stronger and healthier".

The prime minister said the government would "enthuse" pupils to take part in sport, as research suggests an increase in obesity during the pandemic.

Mr Johnson was answering a question from journalist Robert Jenrick, the MP for Newark, who raised concerns about the impact of Covid on children's health.

"One consequence of lockdown that worries me is the rise in obesity among our young people," Mr Jenrick told the prime minister.

Mr Johnson said: "It's very interesting you should say that. One of the things that we've forgotten I think in the last 18 months is the importance of sport.

"And frankly, I think that the youngsters of this country have lost out, because sport is so vital for children's mental health, and of course their physical health.

"So what we're going to be doing is working with schools, working with teachers, making sure that PE lessons are reinstated, that after-school clubs are kicking into action, that we're enthusing youngsters about the importance of sport, both in school and in leisure time."

Sport in schools has "roared back" with children across the country now able to enjoy activities on a regular basis, Prime Minister Boris Johnson has said.

Speaking at a rugby club in London, Mr Johnson said he was "very cheerfully" supporting plans for a new national lottery fund to boost school sport.

The prime minister - a former chairman of Westminster Rugby Club - also praised the benefits of sport in tackling childhood obesity.

Speaking at the rugby club, he said: "I'm delighted that sport is finally back in schools properly.

"It has been one of the hardest parts of the pandemic, the effective cancellation, for almost two years, of school sport."

Mr Johnson said the government was "putting a lot of money into assemblies and getting aftercare going".

He added it was important to get children active because "it is so vital for their mental health".

The processor that will power Sony's PlayStation 3 has been unveiled in Japan.

It is the first chip to use IBM's new "cell" architecture - a design that aims to balance power and cost.

The new processor has nine "cores" that can work together or be split up to perform different tasks.

Sony said the chip would allow the PlayStation 3 to deliver ultra-realistic graphics and other multimedia capabilities.

Details of the chip, made by IBM and Toshiba, were unveiled at the Ceatec exhibition near Tokyo.

Sony's PlayStation 3 must succeed

The new machine is due to go on sale at the end of 2006. It will be powered by a processor chip that is the equivalent of three million transistors.

This is more than twice the number in the chip that powers Microsoft's Xbox 360, and roughly on a par with the chip powering Apple's G5 computer.

"By using the cell processor, PlayStation 3 will deliver a high performance, visually complex gaming and digital entertainment experience," said Sony's chief technical officer, Masayasu Ito, at the exhibition.

"With its breakthrough architecture, the cell processor does what existing processors can't even dream of," he added.

The chip is designed to improve the way computers handle the huge amounts of data needed to process high-quality graphics and video.

Most computer processors only have a single core, but the cell chip has nine.

Eight of these are for general processing, while the ninth is dedicated to manipulating video data.

This allows the chip to juggle many different tasks at the same time, such as sending graphics to a screen while simultaneously decoding digital music and handling other computing tasks.

Each of the eight main processor cores can also be split into two "threads", meaning up to 32 different processing tasks can be carried out at once.

This should allow the PlayStation 3 to take on the increasingly complex processing tasks needed to deliver high-quality graphics, digital music and video.

The chip will also be able to connect to other processors, meaning that as computing power increases, the PlayStation 3 should be able to take advantage of it.

Sony has also developed a new, simplified controller to go with the PlayStation 3.

The new controller features a touch pad, as well as more basic buttons.

Microsoft unveiled its new Xbox 360 games console in the US last week.

The machine will go on sale in the US on 22 November

The BBC has learned that Sony has sold more than 30m PlayStation 3 (PS3) games and entertainment devices since its launch in March. 

The news comes as Sony unveils a new, faster processor for the device in an attempt to keep up with the best selling Wii console from Nintendo. The new 80GB version of the PS3 will go on sale in Europe on 20 October, priced at £425. It will have a new, faster processor, and a bigger, higher capacity hard disk drive. 

The move comes after Nintendo announced a lower price for the Wii, and the imminent release of the Microsoft Xbox 360, due out next week. All three devices are vying for position as the must-have games console this Christmas. 

The new PS3 will have a Cell processor running at 3.2GHz, up from the current 3.0GHz, and the RAM memory has been boosted from 256MB to 384MB. The new, larger hard disk drive will be able to store more games, music, videos and other data. 

Sony said the new PS3 will have a quicker response time, enhanced high-definition graphics, and improved picture quality. It will also be able to run the increasingly popular digital television service, BBC iPlayer. 

The current 60GB PS3 sells for £425, compared with £179 for the Wii, and £279 for the Xbox 360.

Portishead have announced their return with a new album and some live dates this summer, including two nights at Bristol's Harbourside.

The announcement comes after a long social media campaign, in which the trio built anticipation with a series of short clips.

'Ultra Mono' is the band's first full-length album since 2010's 'Portishead', and is out on March 16.

The first track from the album - ' Athletico - Boy vs Machine' - is available now.

The band will play a string of festival shows this summer, including Latitude and Nos Alive, as well as their aforementioned hometown dates in August.

It will be the first time the trio have performed together since they played a charity concert in 2011.

Portishead released their self-titled debut album in 1994, followed by 'Portishead' in 1997 and 'Third' in 2008.

Portishead return with their first album in eight years. It's been a long time coming for Portishead, the trip-hop pioneers who released their last album, 'Third', back in 2008. Their return has been heralded by a new track, 'Where We Go', featuring vocals from Mercury Prize nominee Kakuta. The release of 'Where We Go' marks the band's first new material in over a decade, and comes ahead of their long-awaited fifth studio album, 'Ultra Mono', which is set for release in June. 

'Where We Go' is a markedly different sound for the band, fusing their trademark trip-hop sound with elements of ambient and industrial music. The result is a brooding, atmospheric track that is both haunting and beautiful. The new album 'Ultra Mono' is said to be a return to Portishead's roots, with the band's trademark sound of trip-hop, jazz, and other influences. It's a welcome return for one of the most innovative and influential bands of the past few decades. 

In other news, Portishead frontman Geoff Barrow has debuted a new solo album under the name of Sweet Billy. 'Fear Stories' features vocals from Ben Sedgemore of fellow trip-hop pioneers, Moloko.

When Kerry Sutcliffe became unable to work due to an autoimmune disease, she turned to meditation to help her relax. But the London-based journalist and PR consultant struggled to find the time to fit it into her schedule.

Then, during the first UK lockdown in 2020, she had an idea. Why not use the spare bedroom in her flat as a meditation space, and make herself available to others who were also craving some mental headspace?

"I knew a lot of friends who were struggling with not being able to get to classes or retreats," she says. "So I thought, why not deliver that service?"

Ms Sutcliffe started searching for a platform to help her do this, and found Hemma, a "virtual retreat space" that allows users to create online rooms where meditation can be practised remotely.

It was, she says, "a eureka moment". Within a month, she'd quit her job, and Meditational, her online meditation business, was up and running.

Ms Sutcliffe is not the only one who has pivoted to the digital wellness space during the pandemic.

According to a report by wellness app Mindbody, digital fitness and wellness apps saw a 50% year-on-year increase in revenue in 2020, with an estimated 62 million users worldwide.

The same report revealed that digital fitness classes and on-demand workouts accounted for 27% of total fitness consumer spend - up from 20% in 2019.

Forging in-person connections has been key to building her client base, says Ms Sutcliffe, who has hosted retreats in the UK and Europe, where participants have practiced meditation and taken part in yoga and sound baths.

She also runs a monthly meditation class at London's contemporary art gallery, the Serpentine. Here, she introduces meditation to those who are new to the practice, or who have found the pace of everyday life "a bit full-on" recently.

The future of healthcare lies in personalized, precision medicine. By leveraging technology, healthcare providers can offer patients tailored treatments and targeted therapies based on their unique genetic makeup, lifestyle, and environment.

One area where technology is making a significant impact is in the field of genomics, the study of the human genome. Through advances in sequencing technology, scientists can now analyze a patient's entire genetic sequence, allowing for the identification of genetic variations that may contribute to disease. This information can be used to develop targeted therapies, such as personalized cancer treatments, that are more effective and have fewer side effects than traditional treatments.

Another area where technology is making a difference is in the field of wearable devices and health tracking apps. These devices and apps allow patients to monitor their health and fitness, and provide data to healthcare providers that can be used to make more informed decisions about their care. For example, a patient with a heart condition can use a wearable device to monitor their heart rate and provide data to their doctor that can be used to adjust their treatment plan.

In addition to these examples, technology is also being used to improve the accuracy and speed of diagnoses, develop new treatments for diseases, and improve the overall quality of care. As technology continues to advance, it is likely that we will see even more personalized and precision medicine, which will lead to better outcomes for patients and a more efficient healthcare system.

Nasdaq has announced plans to raise $100m through a share sale as the exchange prepares to host the first Bitcoin futures on its platform.

The Nasdaq announcement came on the same day that rival exchange operator Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) revealed it would launch a physically-delivered Bitcoin futures product, rather than one based on derivatives, in the first half of 2020.

Maeda was again involved before playing in O'Riley, who provided an excellent first-time ball across the face of goal for Abada to tap in at the back post. It was a simple finish, but a superb team move created the opportunity. That was the last action of the game, as Celtic saw out the remainder of the match comfortably.

Labour plans to increase maternity pay to £260 a week, benefiting around 130,000 new parents if the party wins the general election.

The pledge would see statutory maternity pay rise to the level of median earnings for full-time employees - currently £260 - from April 2023.

Statutory maternity pay stands at £151 per week, but many employers offer more.

The plan was revealed ahead of Labour's spring conference which begins on Friday.

The Labour Party is to pledge to give mothers six months of paid maternity leave, doubling the amount currently offered in Britain.

The party said the change would benefit about 60,000 new mothers a year and cost £730m annually.

Labour's plans would bring the UK in line with Labour-led countries like Australia, Canada and New Zealand. The party has already pledged to increase corporation tax to help fund the rise.

The party's election manifesto will promise to give mothers "the longest and most progressive system" in the G7 group of countries.

In the UK, mothers currently get six weeks of paid leave at 90% of their salary or 33 weeks at £151 per week, whichever is lower.

The plans were welcomed by the Institute for Fiscal Studies think tank, which said the current system was "one of the least generous" in the OECD group of countries.

The government plans to introduce ID cards with "biometric data" - such as fingerprints and iris scans - despite a concerted campaign against the idea by Conservative MPs.

The idea was rejected in a vote by the Commons in 2006 and several of its supporters - including the then leader Michael Howard - resigned over the issue.

But in a U-turn, the new leader, David Cameron, said on Wednesday the Tories would support the plan in government.

The Conservative leader told the BBC it was "a price worth paying" to combat illegal immigration and terrorism.

He said biometrics - technical term for biological data - were "essential" to the cards.

ID cards were "an important part, with passports, of tackling illegal immigration", he added.

But Labour MPs warned the Conservatives against "posing for cameras" over the issue, with one describing it as a "stunt".

The announcement was also criticised by civil liberties groups.

The BBC's political editor Nick Robinson said the move was a "calculated gamble" that indicated how the Conservatives calculated they could now win votes on the issue.

One Tory backbencher said it was clear the party had decided to "go for broke" on immigration, telling the BBC: "You cannot be a serious party of government and not have an immigration policy."

Another said it was clear the Conservatives were "prepared to be tough to win back votes from UKIP".

The announcement came as the latest YouGov poll for the Sun put the party on 40%, its highest rating for nearly two years.

The same poll also put UKIP on 18%, level with the Liberal Democrats, who have slumped in the wake of their poor showing in the European elections.

The Conservatives have made a series of U-turns on the issue of ID cards.

In 2005, then-leader Michael Howard said the party was "totally opposed" to the idea, before deciding to support them a year later - a move which helped to trigger the resignation of his immigration spokesman, Mark Harper.

The scheme requires people to hand over biometric data - such as fingerprints and an iris scan - in order to verify their identity.

The information will be stored on a database - the National Identity Register - which opponents say will be a "honeypot" for hackers and terrorists.
