The government plans to reintroduce identity cards for all British citizens, reversing a decade-long ban on the cards, according to reports.

Ministers believe the cards, which would be used to verify people's identities and help combat fraud, could be introduced as part of the Brexit adjustment.

It is believed a bill to enact the change could be included in the Queen's Speech next year.

The proposal is said to have the backing of Cabinet ministers including Home Secretary Priti Patel.

Chinese engineers have started work on a controversial dam project that Beijing had tried to stop, according to a state-run newspaper.

Work began last week on the Xiaonanhai dam, on the border of Sichuan and Yunnan provinces, despite an official instruction from Beijing to suspend the project, the Securities Times said.

It said the instruction, issued in March, was ignored by engineers and local officials who felt that the dam should go ahead for "political" reasons.

"Some in the local region feel that the suspension of the project would bring about political consequences, and this has overridden the actual will of the central government," the newspaper quoted an unnamed official as saying.

The $1.6bn (£980m) project, which is owned by China's largest hydropower firm, China Three Gorges Corporation (CTGC), was suspended in March amid protests over resettlement issues.

But the Securities Times said that CTGC had got round the suspension by forming a subsidiary to take over the project, and that work was continuing under the new name of the Xiluodu hydropower station.

It said that the local government in Yunnan had asked the subsidiary to "speed up" construction.

Work on the dam was "defying the central government's instruction and representing the actual situation that 'the local region is governing the central government'," it added.

The Three Gorges Corporation had no comment on the report when contacted by the BBC.

The company suspended work on the project in March, after thousands of people in the region protested over plans to relocate them because of the dam.

There were also concerns that the dam, which will be 315m (1,033ft) high and sit on the Yangtze river, would be unstable because it is being built in an earthquake-prone region.

The suspension order was issued by the Ministry of Environmental Protection days after the protests began.

But the Securities Times report suggests that the order may never have been officially issued, despite confirmation from the company at the time that it had received it.

It said that the ministry had told CTGC to report back on issues relating to the relocation, and that this had been misinterpreted as an official suspension order.

A controversial dam project in eastern Tibet that has sparked concern among environmentalists and activists could be the first test of the Chinese government's promise to respect the rights of ethnic minorities, according to a report by the BBC.

The Chinese government has been promoting the Tibet Hydropower Development Project, a series of dams on the Brahmaputra River, as a way to develop the region and provide much-needed electricity to the sprawling Tibetan plateau. The project has been strongly opposed by environmentalists and activists who say it will disrupt the river's ecosystem and the lives of people who live along its banks.

The BBC spoke with Tsering Dorjee, an activist with the Tibetan Youth Congress, who said the project is a test of whether the Chinese government will respect the rights of Tibetans.

"If they really care about the Tibetan people, they should listen to our concerns and stop the project," he said. "This is a very important issue for us, because the environment is our life. If you destroy our environment, you destroy our future."

China has long been criticized for its treatment of Tibetans, including its suppression of their culture and religion. In recent years, the government has been trying to improve its image by promoting its investments in the region, including the dam project.

The Chinese Foreign Ministry did not respond to requests for comment, but officials have previously said the project is an "important part of a comprehensive plan to develop the region's economy and improve the lives of Tibetans."

The Brahmaputra River flows from Tibet into India and Bangladesh, and the dams could potentially affect the water supply for hundreds of millions of people.

China tightened the reins on its money supply in November, raising worries about the pace of economic growth.

Data from the central bank showed on Monday that the M2 money supply - a broad measure of the money supply - grew by 8.2% in November from a year earlier, compared with 8.6% in October.

The data also showed that China's new loans fell well short of expectations in November, as banks became more cautious about lending.

Some analysts said the move to tighten credit controls came as China's economy was showing signs of recovery.

"The credit data showed policy makers maintained a tight rein on credit growth in November as the economy continued to improve," said Zhang Zhiwei, chief China economist at Bank of New York Mellon.

"We expect credit growth to stay modest in the coming months as policymakers stick to their tight monetary policy stance."

The world's second-largest economy expanded by 7.8% in the third quarter, beating expectations and reversing a string of three consecutive quarterly declines.

But while the economy has been showing signs of recovery, China's leaders have moved to tighten credit controls in recent months to contain inflation and slow the rapid rise in property prices.

Data last week showed that China's consumer price index (CPI) rose to a 28-month high of 4.4% in November, driven by rising food and energy prices.

China's economy has been recovering from a soft patch earlier in the year, when it was hit by a downturn in its property market and a sharp fall in demand for its exports.

The government has set a growth target of around 7% for next year, but some analysts say that this may be difficult to achieve as policy makers continue to tighten credit controls.

China has kept a tight rein on credit in the last few months, with total social financing falling significantly compared to last year. Experts say the government is cautious about stoking inflation, and does not want to add to problems with the country's property sector. But economists say local governments and businesses are starved of cash, and China's economy is paying the price. The decline in social financing has been consistent despite four interest rate cuts since last year. In September, total social financing was down 22% from a year earlier, at 1.35 trillion yuan ($203 billion). Meanwhile, M2, a broad measure of money supply, is growing at its slowest pace in nearly three decades. 

China's economy is already suffering its slowest growth rate in nearly half a century. In the third quarter, GDP increased by 3.9% year-on-year, down from 7.9% in the same period the previous year. And the latest data suggests the economy is slowing further, with retail sales growing 2.5% in September from a year earlier, down from 8.5% in March. Meanwhile, industrial output grew by just 3.1% year on-year in September, down from 6.3% in March.

Most of the loans issued in September went to solvent firms, including property developers, according to central bank data. But economists say these companies are not keen on borrowing, as they already have cash tied up in projects that are not selling well. Many local governments are also under pressure after lavish spending on infrastructure projects in past years. 

Experts say the central bank is being very cautious about pumping more money into the economy, for fear of stoking inflation. Rising prices are a political sensitive issue for the government, as households have seen their cost of living rise rapidly in the last few months. Food prices have climbed as a result of the Russia-Ukraine war, and consumers are also feeling the pinch from rising energy and transport costs.

The property sector has been a major driver of China's economic growth in recent years, but the government has introduced a string of measures to curb speculation and slow the sector's growth. Real estate loans made up just 6.9% of all loans issued in September, down from 12.3% last year, according to the central bank. 

The government has also been trying to reduce its reliance on real estate, and promote other sectors, including consumption and services. But experts say these sectors are not yet strong enough to drive the economy forward.

The doping probe into British cycling star Chris Froome has been dropped, according to his lawyer.

Hugh Robertson said the International Cycling Union (UCI) had informed him via email that the investigation into Froome had been closed.

The four-time Tour de France winner has battled back from a career-threatening crash to compete at the 2023 event, which began in Jerusalem on Sunday.

The UCI said it was unable to comment on the "confidential" matter.

In a statement, Mr Robertson said: "I can confirm that the UCI has advised via email today that the investigation into Chris Froome has been closed and that no further action will be taken.

"It has taken lengthy negotiations to resolve this matter, but this decision finally closes that chapter."

Froome, 36, has battled back from a career-threatening crash in 2019 to compete at this year's Tour.

He has won the prestigious race on seven occasions - making him one of the most successful riders in the 110-year history of the competition.

The UCI opened an investigation into Froome in 2019 following a report by the Fancy Bears hacking group which claimed the athlete had tested positive for the asthma drug salbutamol during his career.

Salbutamol is permitted under World Anti-Doping Agency (Wada) rules, but only in certain circumstances.

At the time, Froome said he had "followed the administration of my medications consistently and precisely as prescribed by my doctors".

The UCI's decision to close the case is the end of a long legal battle which has rumbled on since the initial investigation opened.

In 2020, the UCI said the rider risked a potential ban if he missed the deadline to provide all medical information related to his asthma medication.

Froome - who has earned more than £3.5m in prize money - was also accused of using the banned substance ritalinic acid, but Wada said in 2020 there was "no evidence" of any violation.

The UCI had been expected to decide whether to open disciplinary proceedings against Froome by the end of 2021 but, in December that year, Froome's legal team said the rider had been "cleared of any wrongdoing" and that the UCI had agreed to close the case.

The cycling's governing body then went back on that decision, claiming the decision had been "premature" because it had not yet received the results of a second sample taken

The doping probe into British Cycling and Team Sky began today, with a detailed examination of medical records and data at the British Cycling headquarters in Manchester. The investigation, commissioned by the UK Anti-Doping agency and headed by Richard Freeman, will look at whether the team used banned substances. The probe will focus on rider Sir Bradley Wiggins, a five-time Olympic gold medallist and the first Briton to win the Tour de France. In a statement, UKAD said "it is fair to say the sport of cycling, and more specifically the GB cycling team, has never been bigger than it is now in this country. That is why it is essential that British cycling, a leading light in the sport, is not only winning clean, but is seen to be winning clean."

Ferguson, the singer and guitarist with rock band No Doubt, is "facing eviction" from his $1.5m Los Angeles home.
A lawyer for Ferguson's landlord said the musician had not paid rent for 2015.
Ferguson's lawyer denied the singer was being evicted, saying the issue would be resolved shortly.
The singer has lived in the hilltop home since 2004.

The house features in the video for No Doubt's hit single Looking Hot.

Lawyer Alan Brimer said Ferguson, whose full name is Tom Dumont, was "current on his rent".

"Tom Dumont has lived at this property for more than a decade, and intends to stay there," he said.

"There is no eviction pending. These are routine requests that are part of the lease and it will be resolved shortly."

The two-storey, 4,102-square-foot home features four bedrooms, four bathrooms, a pool and panoramic views of Los Angeles.

Ferguson, 43, formed No Doubt with Gwen Stefani, Tony Kanal, and Adrian Young in Anaheim, California, in 1986.

The band achieved mainstream success with their breakthrough album Tragic Kingdom in 1995.

Singer Jamie Ferguson is "facing eviction" from his £2m London home, according to his neighbours. The residence is allegedly being sold to a developer, with the singer's flat set to be converted into a series of luxury apartments. Ferguson, 65, known for his 1985 hit single "Parachute", purchased the property in 2017 for £1.35m. His neighbours, including comedian Harry Enfield, expressed their concerns about the singer's eviction to the local council in a letter that describes the situation as "an injustice".

Former Banco Santander executive Alfredo Saenz faces a charge of fraud in a trial that finally got under way in Madrid on Monday after years of legal battles.

The case centres on the alleged diversion of 1.4 billion euros ($1.7 billion) from the bank's subsidiary, Banif, to a company owned by Saenz's former business partner, Miguel Blesa, who is also accused of tax fraud.

Saenz has denied any wrongdoing.

The defendant arrived at the court in a black van, wearing a dark suit and red tie, and was met by his wife and other relatives.

After years of preparation, the trial finally got under way nearly 12 years after the start of the financial crisis.

Spanish authorities had been investigating the case since 2012, but a judge ruled in 2017 that there was not enough evidence to send Saenz to trial.

That decision was overturned in 2018 by Spain's highest court, which ordered a trial be held.

Saenz stepped down from his role as a member of the board of directors of Banco Santander in 2015.
He has always denied any wrongdoing.

Also on trial is Guillermo Schulz, the former head of Santander's legal department, who is accused of knowing about the alleged fraud.
He too has denied any wrongdoing.

The trial has begun in Spain of the country's top banker, who is accused of fraud and misusing public funds in a case that has shocked Spaniards and shamed the government.

The court in Madrid is hearing the case against Rodrigo Rato, who was the chairman of the Spanish bank Bankia when it collapsed in 2012.

He faces up to eight years in prison for alleged crimes committed when he was at the helm of the bank.

The case has become a cause celebre in Spain, where many people are furious that the country's top bankers have not been held to account for their role in the financial crisis.

Mr Rato, who is 62, has denied the charges against him.

Geraint Thomas will not ride for Wales in March's UCI Road World Championships as he focuses on preparing for the Giro d'Italia in May, his team Ineos Grenadiers said.

The 36-year-old British rider won the Giro in 2020 and the Tour de France in 2018 and 2019.

He will be part of a strong Ineos team for the Giro which will also include the Colombian duo of Egan Bernal and Daniel Martinez, who will target the overall win.

"I want to go to the Giro d'Italia in the best condition possible," Thomas said.

"After the Olympics last year I felt I'd be up for the World Championships but that changed after the Tour de France."

Thomas' place in the Wales team for the road world championships, to be held in Birmingham, will be taken by the Ineos Grenadiers' newest recruit, Luke Rowe.

Rowe recently returned to training after a serious leg injury suffered in an accident in November.

The 31-year-old had successful surgery after the accident, which happened in Spain, and has been training on the indoor trainer and is expected to return to the road next month.

"It's brilliant news that Luke is back on the mend and we're all delighted to see him making such good progress," Ineos Grenadiers team principal Dave Brailsford said.

"Taking part in the World Championships is a great target for Luke as he continues his return to full fitness."

Rowe won the team pursuit on the track at the 2010 Commonwealth Games in Delhi, India.

But his career has been disrupted on a number of occasions by injury, including a serious knee problem in 2015.

"It's a huge honour to be selected to represent Wales at the World Championships in Birmingham," Rowe said.

"I've been on the rehab train for the last few months and I'm buzzing that my form is heading in the right direction, I'm confident that come March I'll be in the best possible shape to represent Wales in the road race."

While Thomas will not ride for Wales in Birmingham, he is expected to compete in the national time trial championship in June.

He will be looking to win his seventh title - and fourth in a row - in the event, as he targets a place in the time trial at the 2024 Paris Olympics.

"I'd like to wish the Welsh team all the best for the World Championships," Thomas added.

Ed Collins will compete in the 100m breaststroke SB6 final tonight, after a challenging year. The classification will make its debut at the Birmingham 2022 Commonwealth Games. He will be up against fellow Englishman Tobias Pollap, who has a hearing impairment.

Collins, who suffered from testicular cancer last year, had successful surgery to remove it. However, the treatment left him with drop foot as a side effect. This causes his foot to drop when he tries to walk, and requires him to wear a brace on his right leg. He is still undergoing rehabilitation for the condition, but hopes to be able to walk again without a brace by the end of the year.

Despite this, the 24-year-old from Plymouth is determined to continue his career as a professional swimmer. He previously competed in the 200m breaststroke at the 2018 Commonwealth Games, and the 100m breaststroke at the 2019 World Aquatic Championships.

Collins said: "It's going to be a tough race but I'm looking forward to it. I've been working hard in training and I'm feeling confident."

The 100m breaststroke SB6 final will take place at Birmingham's NEC Arena on Friday evening.

Britain's terror laws are "absolutely necessary" to cope with the threat from al-Qaeda, former prime minister Tony Blair has said.

Speaking on the 10th anniversary of the 7/7 London bombings, Mr Blair said he had no doubt the legislation had saved lives.

The Labour ex-leader admitted aspects of the legislation - including some which had caused public concern - were "difficult".

But he said no government had "any alternative but to take the action we did".

The London bombings, in which 52 people were killed, prompted a revamp of the UK's anti-terror laws.

Speaking on BBC One's Breakfast show, Mr Blair - who was prime minister at the time of the bombings - said he had "no doubt at all" that the actions taken had saved lives.

"I believe the legislation we introduced has helped us to protect the British public but, as I say, it's not perfect and we need to keep improving it," he added.

Mr Blair said he had always tried to "balance" the human rights of individuals with the need to protect the public.

But he accepted that some of the measures - such as those allowing the detention without trial of suspects and the use of intercept evidence in court - had caused concern.

"I think any government has got to balance the need to protect the security of the public with the individual rights and that's what we did," he said.

"I think it's difficult, all of these things. Every step of the way there's a balance to be struck and, yes, you do make difficult decisions.

"It's not easy to strike that balance but it's absolutely necessary."

The former Prime Minister has argued that changes to the UK's terrorism laws have helped maintain a balance between security and civil liberties. Speaking a decade after the Prevention of Terrorism Act was introduced, Blair argued that the legislation had been essential in tackling the threat posed by al-Qaeda. However, he admitted that the threat had changed over the last ten years and that the legislation would need to be updated to reflect this.

The Labour leader said that the war on terror had fundamentally changed since the law was introduced, with the threat moving from al-Qaeda to Isis. Speaking at the Chatham House think tank, he said that whilst the legislation had been necessary and right a decade ago, it needed to be updated in order to maintain a balance between security and civil liberties.

The Prevention of Terrorism Act was introduced in 2001 in response to the terrorist attacks on the United States in September of that year. It gave the police powers to detain suspects without charge for up to 28 days and to restrict their freedom of movement with anti-terrorist prevention orders. 

Speaking about the need to update the legislation, Blair said that the government needed to ensure that the police had the powers they needed to tackle the terrorist threat, but that this needed to be balanced by safeguards to protect civil liberties. He said that the legislation also needed to take into account the changing nature of the terrorist threat, which had moved from al-Qaeda to Isis and away from the traditional security threats that the legislation had been designed to address.

Scotland's pubs, restaurants and other licensed premises will have to enforce a smoking ban from spring 2006, the Scottish Executive said on Wednesday.

Detailed plans for the prohibition were unveiled, with ministers saying the move had the backing of the public.

And they promised a "sensible" transition period for licensees to adapt.

First Minister Jack McConnell said the ban would come into force from April 2006, following a consultation exercise.

He said: "This legislation has widespread public support and its introduction next year will help improve the health of Scotland's citizens.

"It will also send a clear message to young people that smoking is not acceptable."

The ban will cover all enclosed and substantially enclosed areas of premises covered by the current licensing regime.

This includes pubs, clubs, restaurants and hotels, but not private homes or cars.

Mr McConnell said the government had listened to the concerns of the licensing industry and would introduce the ban in a "sensible and balanced way".

This would include a transition period for licensees to adapt, and further discussions on the practicalities of the new regime, said the first minister.

Ministers also want to cut the number of young people taking up smoking by at least 800 a year, and are launching a national awareness campaign.

They will ask for views on the best way to enforce the ban, and on potential exemptions for pavements outside premises.

The Scottish Executive said its plans were based on legislation in place in Ireland, which reduced the number of smokers there by 100,000 in the first year.

The ban was announced in Mr McConnell's keynote speech to the SNP conference in October, when he said it would be introduced in April 2006.

The Scottish Tobacco Manufacturers' Alliance has said the ban will cost 2,000 jobs and result in criminalising responsible smokers.

But public health minister Susan Deacon said the ban would not criminalise smokers, but would create a "more healthy environment for all".

She said: "This is a very important step for the health of Scotland.

"We know that almost half the deaths from coronary heart disease are attributable to smoking and thousands of people die every year from smoking-related illness."

The announcement was welcomed by health campaigners.

Action on Smoking and Health (Ash) Scotland said the ban would help protect workers and the public from the dangers of passive smoking.

Spokeswoman Anne Jones said: "This is a great day for

A smoking ban being planned by the Scottish government for next year will be widened to include hospitals, care homes, and school grounds, ministers have said. The original plan was to ban smoking in playgrounds and outdoor areas of cafes, pubs and restaurants. 

Health Secretary Humza Yousaf said the phased ban would not come into force until next spring at the earliest. The Scottish government aims to bring "smoking-free" standards to hospitals, care homes and schools by April 2024. This will require NHS boards to create smoke-free policies, and care homes and schools will need to have smoke-free policies in place by April 2022. 

Ministers expect most hospitals to prevent smoking on their grounds, with exceptions in specialised circumstances, by April 2023.

Tate & Lyle's chief executive has been named the most influential person in the world of sugar.

Jim Turner received the award at the World Sugar Conference in New York.

He saw off competition from the heads of top sugar firms and industry experts to win the title.

Mr Turner has led London-based Tate & Lyle's sugar division since 2016.

The award's organisers said he had played a pivotal role in the industry over many years.

Tate & Lyle, which is listed on the London Stock Exchange, is one of the world's largest producers of sugar and starch products.

Its products are used by food manufacturers, restaurants and bars, and in products such as fabrics and pharmaceuticals.

The firm's revenues reached £1.2bn in the six months to 31 March 2022, an increase of 14% on the same period the previous year.

The World Sugar Conference is an annual industry event which brings together key players from more than 70 countries.

As well as the top gong, awards were also given out in eight separate categories, including best sugar trader and best sugar analyst.

Sir Charles Bowman has been named the most influential person in the global sugar industry for a fourth consecutive year. The chairman and chief executive of British sugar maker Tate & Lyle received the award from Sugaronews, a sugar industry publication, for his work in driving the company forward and his involvement in industry debates. Sir Charles said it had been “an eventful year” for the industry and that he was “very proud” to receive the award. He also paid tribute to his colleagues and the company’s “strong culture and values”.

Tate & Lyle has had a difficult year, with the sugar market hit by inflation and rising energy prices, and the firm was forced to cut jobs at its plant in Liverpool. However, Sir Charles said that the company was well-placed to face the challenges as it begins work on a major renewable energy project in Scotland.

The award comes after Sir Charles was named the most influential person in the UK food industry by The Sunday Times in September. Tate & Lyle has also been recognized as one of the UK’s leading employers for women by the Women’s Business Council. In addition, the firm has recently been awarded the Queen’s Award for Enterprise in International Trade.

Grease is the word at the US box office this weekend, as the revival of the beloved musical scored the biggest opening of the year so far.

The reboot of the classic romantic musical, starring Julianne Hough and Vanessa Hudgens, took $8.1m on its first day of release.

Competition from non-musical films was muted. The number two film was Michael Douglas' financial thriller, Beyond a Reasonable Doubt, which opened in second place with $6.6m.

The top 12 films this weekend all played in wide release, bypassing the traditional platform release model that has launched many Covid-hit films including Spencer and King Richard.

They included Denzel Washington's A Journal for Jordan, which made $4.2m for a total of $9.4m after two weeks.

Both Beyond a Reasonable Doubt and A Journal for Jordan were released by Sony's Columbia Pictures, and were accompanied by expansion for the studio's critically acclaimed musical, Cyrano.

It features a song-and-dance number performed by Peter Dinklage, who has been nominated for best actor at both the Golden Globes and the Screen Actors Guild awards.

And popcorn movie staple Spider-Man: No Way Home continued its spectacular run, taking $1.8m for a sixth week of release and a domestic total of $668m.

It has now officially passed the $668m total gross of 2015's Star Wars: The Force Awakens to become the fourth highest-grossing release ever at the US box office.

No other film has come close to matching the might of Spider-Man, whose $668m six-week total is more than the annual grosses of all but a handful of movies, including La La Land, which made $446m in 2016.

The US box office has been led by Hollywood heavyweight Robert De Niro, whose film about a mob hitman starting a new life in the country has struck a chord with audiences.

The iconic actor stars in "The Irishman", which opened on limited release in the US last week.

The movie is reportedly on course to make $29m (£23m) so far, according to studio Netflix.

"The Irishman" follows De Niro's character as he reflects on his involvement in the 1975 disappearance of Jimmy Hoffa, a powerful union leader.

The film also features Al Pacino and Joe Pesci, and is directed by Martin Scorsese.

The family of President George H W Bush has blocked public access to his Texas coastal home, after a man drove his vehicle into a crowd of visitors.

Police in Houston said the driver was arrested and charged with aggravated assault.

The Bush family said the attack was "horrific" and "shameful", and described the block as a "security measure".

The home is in Houston, Texas, and is a national monument managed by the National Park Service.

Police were called to the Bush home, known as Prairie Chapel Ranch, at about 11:20 local time (17:20 GMT) on Wednesday.

"Upon arrival, a man in a pickup truck had entered the grounds of the Bush home after crashing through the gated entrance," Constable Mark Herman said in a statement.

"Investigators determined that the male suspect had intentionally driven his truck into a crowd of visitors," Constable Herman added.

A statement from the Bush family said: "We are devastated by the horrific attack on Mrs Bush's 92nd birthday party yesterday.

"Our family offers its deepest apologies to all those hurt by this shameful act.

"We are grateful for the prompt response of law enforcement and appreciate the efforts of those who jumped into action to assist."

The incident occurred two days after the 40th anniversary of when George HW Bush, who served as the 41st US president, married Barbara Pierce.

Mrs Bush, the former first lady, turned 92 on Sunday. She is now the oldest living first lady.

The site of a former US embassy in Libya's capital has been closed off following an attack that killed two police officers.

The British Embassy had been located in the same compound in Tripoli before the UK closed its mission in Libya in 2014.

The compound was unoccupied at the time of the attack.

Local reports say the site was targeted by gunmen arriving in several vehicles. There has been no claim of responsibility.

The British Foreign Office (FCO) confirmed that an attack took place but did not comment on the deaths.

It added that the security of its staff and premises was of "paramount importance".

The FCO also advised against all travel to Libya, except for urgent business.

The US closed its embassy in Libya in July 2014 and pulled out its staff because of violence and unrest.

Drink driving 'a diversion' from dangerous drugs

A public health expert has said that enforcing laws against drink driving is "a diversion" from dealing with the much greater dangers posed by drugs.

Prof David Nutt said that the focus on drink driving "distorts" public awareness of the risks on the roads.

He said most accidents were caused by drivers on legal drugs, particularly benzodiazepines, found in prescription drugs such as Valium.

The professor of neuropsychopharmacology said traffic officers should "start looking for drugs in the same way" as they do for alcohol.

Prof Nutt's comments come after a man was arrested this week for allegedly driving whilst over the legal limit for cannabis.

The Cuban detention centre has been used by the US government to hold suspects in the "war on terror" since it opened in January 2002.

The facility has been a source of international criticism for its alleged human rights abuses - with many detainees held for years without trial.

Mr Tutu's letter, written on South African Parliament notepaper, said: "The continued operation of Guantanamo Bay is a blight on the reputation of both the United States and the United Kingdom.

"Given our countries' shared commitment to human rights, I am confident that you will agree with me that the time has come for Guantanamo Bay to close."

The Nobel Peace Prize winner, who died in Cape Town, South Africa, continued: "I hope that you will agree to work with President Obama to ensure that Guantanamo Bay is closed permanently and that the prisoners remaining there are released either to stand trial or to be repatriated."

He said it would be a "disgrace" if the UK government did not step in to offer asylum to former inmates "who have been cleared of wrongdoing".

Mr Cameron declined to publish the letter, citing national security concerns. A government spokesperson said at the time that the prime minister "regularly corresponded with faith leaders".

The letter was shared with the BBC by the charity Reprieve, which campaigns for the closure of Guantanamo Bay.

Its director, Maya Foa, said: "It is a great tragedy that Archbishop Tutu did not live to see the closure of Guantanamo - a place he described as 'the epicentre of evil' - but his words will remain an urgent call to action."

Ministers lose slopping out case

Ministers have lost a court battle to force three asylum seekers to live on £5 a day.

They had sought to have the men, known as AP, DP and MP, returned to detention on the grounds they had violated their immigration detention licenses by not observing a curfew and leaving their accommodation.

But the Court of Appeal ruled against them, saying the men had a right to a fair hearing.

The Home Office has not said if it will seek to appeal.

The three men, from Sudan, Zimbabwe and Albania, are being supported by the charity Detention Action.

They had been living in a house in Hampshire provided by the charity while their cases were being heard.

But in July the Home Office served them with papers saying it planned to deport them and accused them of breaking their curfews and asked the court to revoke their licenses.

If their licenses had been revoked, the men would have been detained ahead of possible deportation.

They would have qualified for support worth £5.39 per day, rather than the more generous support provided to people who have been released from detention.

The men argued they had been given incorrect curfews by the Home Office and said they had done nothing wrong.

Lord Justice Singh, Lord Justice Patten and Lady Justice King concluded the men did not receive a fair hearing and ruled against the Home Office.

They said the decision to serve the men with deportation notices, which led to the revocation of their licenses, was a "classic case" of a decision being taken for "improper purposes" in that it was a "consequence" of the men launching judicial reviews of their cases.

Lady Justice King said the men should be given permission to apply for judicial reviews of their cases and the Home Office should pay their legal costs.

Detention Action welcomed the decision.

Policy director Bella Sankey said: "We are thrilled that the court has agreed that these men were unfairly treated and that justice has been done.

"No-one should be punished for trying to establish their right to remain in the UK.

"We hope that the home secretary will take this opportunity to overhaul the degrading and inhumane detention system which causes so much misery."

A Home Office spokesperson said: "The court has carefully considered the details of this case and we are pleased with the outcome.

The Supreme Court has ruled that ministers must give prisoners who want to be able to prepare their own meals with the necessary equipment to do so. The decision has been made under the European Convention on Human Rights, which guarantees the right to respect for private and family life, and cannot be overridden by legislation. 
There are 15,000 prisoners across England and Wales who are currently required to slop out – or empty – their chamber pots rather than being given access to flushing toilets. In 2013, three prisoners filed a legal case arguing that this constituted inhuman and degrading treatment, and that it violated their human rights. 

The Ministry of Justice had argued that the current system, in place in British prisons since the 1830s, was necessary for security and good order. Lord Reed, president of the Supreme Court, dismissed this argument, saying that the ministry had not provided sufficient evidence to support it.

The ruling could cost the ministry up to £40m per year to implement, however, campaigners have criticised the ruling for not going far enough. A recent inspection found that not a single prison in England and Wales was adequately prepared for the upcoming ban on slopping out.

The European Central Bank has held its main interest rate at a record low to support the eurozone's post-pandemic recovery, despite inflation reaching a record high.

The ECB's governing council left the rate on its main refinancing operations at 0%, while the rate on its marginal lending facility remained at 0.25%.

The ECB also said it would accelerate its bond purchases under its 1.85 trillion euro ($2.1 trillion) pandemic emergency purchase programme (Pepp).

The moves came as inflation in the eurozone hit a record high of 5% in December, well ahead of the ECB's 2% target.

The central bank had already said it expected inflation to be higher for longer and that it would keep rates at their current, or lower levels until it saw inflation reaching 2% consistently.

Portugal's central bank chief, Mario Centeno, who is also the ECB's governor, said: "We are witnessing a phenomenon that is not a generalised inflationary spiral in the euro area."

He said that the ECB did not want to "surprise" markets by changing its policy stance prematurely and that any exit from its current policies would be gradual.

The Pepp is due to run until March, but the ECB has said it would assess whether its duration should be extended in light of the continued uncertainty over the outlook for the economy.

It has also said it would create a new tool to cope with government bond yields that "deviate substantially, and persistently" from their levels seen before the Russian invasion of Ukraine.

The ECB's move came on the same day as the US Federal Reserve increased its key interest rate by 0.25% to a target range of 4.5% to 4.75%, its highest level since 2007.

In the UK, the Bank of England also increased interest rates, raising them to 4% from 3.5%, their highest level in over a decade.

The European Central Bank has held interest rates steady in its latest policy meeting, despite mounting fears over soaring inflation and the risks of a recession.

The central bank said it would continue its bond-buying programme, but at a slower pace, and keep rates at their current levels "until it sees inflation reaching 2% consistently".

The ECB has come under pressure to raise rates, with inflation in the eurozone running at almost double its target. But it said the economy was "weakening considerably".

The bank said it would buy bonds worth €15bn a month under its pandemic emergency purchase programme (Pemp), compared with €19bn a month previously. It will also continue its reinvestment of funds from maturing bonds.

The ECB also said it would provide further support for the eurozone by making loans available to banks at cheaper rates. This so-called targeted longer-term refinancing operation (Tltro) will continue at a significantly higher volume than in the previous round.

The ECB said the "substantially higher" demand for the loans showed that the measure was needed to help the banks to continue supporting the economy.

The decision comes after a string of regional central banks raised interest rates, including the US Federal Reserve, the Bank of England, and the Swiss National Bank.

But the ECB has faced particular pressure over its dovish stance, with Governor Christine Lagarde repeatedly arguing that raising rates would not address the root causes of inflation, and that the ECB needed to remain "patient and persistent" in its efforts to boost inflation.

The deal is subject to regulatory approval and is expected to close in the first half of next year. If successful, the merger would result in the creation of the largest stock exchange in Europe, with a market capitalization of over £130 billion.

The LSE has also been in talks with the Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Ltd (HKEX) about a potential merger. However, those discussions have been put on hold while the LSE considers the Deutsche Boerse offer. 

The battle for the LSE has been ongoing for several months and is not expected to end anytime soon. With three major players vying for control of the LSE, shareholders can expect more offers and counteroffers in the coming months.

Aid agencies fighting one of the world's worst humanitarian disasters are using satellite maps of Sudan's Darfur region to help them decide where to distribute relief.

The maps, produced by American company DigitalGlobe, are updated every two weeks and are being distributed free of charge.

They are already being used by 10 organisations, including Unicef, the UN's children's fund, and Oxfam.

Oxfam uses the maps to assess the needs of displaced people in camps and to plan where to place water points.

"The current humanitarian crisis in Darfur is one of the most challenging situations facing the international community today," DigitalGlobe's chairman, Jeffrey R. Tarr, said in a statement.

"DigitalGlobe recognises the critical role that accurate geospatial information plays in helping the relief community to provide the necessary support to the people of Sudan."

The firm's satellites can image up to one million square km of the Earth every day and the maps it produces can be zoomed in up to 30m (98ft).

The firm has also made public additional high-resolution satellite imagery of the region dating back to early 2004.

This can be used to create a historical record of the destruction in Darfur and could be used in future war crime trials, analysts say.

DigitalGlobe, which is based in Colorado, says it is the only commercial provider of high-resolution satellite imagery and geospatial solutions.

Its clients include Nasa, defence and intelligence agencies and mapping companies.

The firm recently launched a satellite - called WorldView-2 - that can photograph objects as small as 0.7m anywhere on Earth.

Darfur crisis

The Darfur region has been devastated by violence between ethnic Africans and Arabs since 2003, when the Sudan government launched a counter-insurgency campaign against rebels.

The fighting has killed an estimated 200,000 people and forced 2.5 million from their homes.

The UN says the conflict has created the world's fastest-growing refugee crisis and the world's largest humanitarian operation.

The suffering of the people in Sudan's Darfur region has been much documented in recent years, but the latest technology now promises to help alleviate their plight. In an impressive example of international cooperation, a consortium of public and private organizations has launched an initiative to map the entire region using satellite imagery.
 
The project, which was spearheaded by the World Bank and the European Space Agency, will create a detailed map of Darfur that will serve as an invaluable tool for relief organizations operating in the region. The map will include detailed information on the location of villages, roads, and other infrastructure, as well as the extent of damage caused by the ongoing conflict. This information will help relief organizations to better target their resources and plan their operations more effectively.
 
"This is an excellent example of how space technology can be used for humanitarian purposes," said Simon Gray, the European Space Agency's project manager for the initiative. "We are very pleased to be able to contribute to the effort to help the people of Darfur."
 
The project has already received widespread acclaim for its potential to improve the lives of the people of Darfur. 

"This is an incredibly important project," said John Holmes, the United Nations' Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs. "The detailed mapping of Darfur will be a valuable tool for relief organizations working to improve the situation in the region."
 
The initiative is also being praised for its potential to strengthen the peace process in Darfur. By providing a detailed map of the region, the project will help to resolve territorial disputes between the various factions involved in the conflict. 

"This is a very positive step towards improving the situation in Darfur," said Mohamed Ahmed, the Secretary-General of the Liberation and Justice Movement, one of the main factions in the conflict. "We welcome any effort that will help to bring peace to our region." 

With the initial phase of the project now complete, the consortium is turning its attention to the next step: creating a digital elevation model of the region. This will involve collecting additional satellite imagery to supplement the data already acquired.

BBC news article - Wales 'must learn health lessons'

Health experts in Wales have called for radical changes to accelerate improvements in public health.

The Welsh government's Public Health Act, which came into force in April, allows ministers to intervene in the nation's poorest areas.

But a new report by the Future Generations Commissioner for Wales questions whether public health is sufficiently high on the agenda.

The report calls on local and national government to work closer together.

Public health is the art and science of preventing disease, prolonging life and promoting health through the organized efforts of society.

It is a response to the epidemic of non-communicable diseases, the growth of multi-morbidity and the rising health inequalities affecting nations worldwide.

It addresses the wider determinants of health and focuses on the well-being of the whole population.

In Wales, public health is delivered by 22 local authorities, with national support from Public Health Wales.

The Welsh government's Public Health Act places a legal obligation on local and national government to work together to improve the health of the people of Wales.

It allows ministers to direct local authorities to take specific actions to protect public health, such as restricting the number of fast food outlets near schools.

But the Future Generations Commissioner for Wales, Sophie Howe, has called for a more holistic approach, bringing together health, education, transport and planning policies.

Her report, called Generation Demand, says the impact of adverse childhood experiences can lead to health problems in later life, including heart disease and mental health issues.

Ms. Howe said: "As a society we need to ensure that public services are designed to help prevent these experiences, and that where they do occur, support is put in place as early as possible to help children and families cope with the impact."

She added that "radical changes" were needed to protect the health of future generations.

"This means moving away from the current fragmented approach and taking a more holistic approach to policy across all sectors.

Viewers can also opt to receive the channels as a continuous broadcast, like conventional TV, or they can choose the programmes they want to watch from an archive of content updated every hour.

"I think we have a trend-setting product on our hands, a product that delivers television over the internet and, at the same time, makes use of the possibilities of interactive television," he said.

DVD review: Spider-Man 2

Released: 26 April 2004
Director: Sam Raimi
Stars: Tobey Maguire, Kirsten Dunst, Alfred Molina

In this eagerly awaited sequel, Spider-Man (Maguire) is struggling to come to terms with his dual life as a super hero and as Peter Parker, ordinary teenager. Things look promising when he meets up with M.J. (Kirsten Dunst) at a party but his hopes are dashed when she fails to show up at the next couple of meetings. It becomes apparent that she is being forced by her possessive and controlling father (Alfred Molina) to end the relationship. This is the least of Spider-Man's problems, as he faces a powerful new foe, Doctor Octopus (Molina again), who has harnessed the power of four genetically modified tentacles that he controls with his mind. The good doctor is plotting to steal a cache of missiles from the launch site at Coney Island and bring them into the city. As Spider-Man battles to save innocent lives, he is forced to ask himself what it is that really matters: his dedication to being a super hero, or his love for M.J.

This is a hugely enjoyable adventure, with breathtaking action sequences and a genuine emotional core. The spider suit has been redesigned and allows for even more flexibility than before, while the introduction of organic web shooters is a welcome addition. Doctor Octopus is an awesome opponent, and the climactic battle between the two in an arena of swinging chains is a masterpiece of special effects. The dialogue is snappy, and there are some nice comic touches, as when Spider-Man wraps a subway robber in web and gives him a hug, telling him to "take a chill pill". Maguire makes an engaging hero, investing Peter Parker with humility and self-doubt, and there is strong support from Dunst, who manages to overcome the clunky script and deliver a credible performance as M.J. However, it is Molina who really stands out, investing the doctor with a malevolence that is genuinely chilling.

The disk includes a number of interesting featurettes, including a look at the development of the story and the effects, a tour of the Spider-Man exhibit at Universal Studios, and a piece on the music. There is also a trailer for the next installment, Spider-Man 3. While this is unlikely to convert the sceptics, for fans of the web slinger this is essential viewing.

Spider-Man 2 is much bigger than its predecessor, but that doesn't necessarily make it better. Although it boasts a few memorable action scenes, the film is largely devoid of the humour and heart that made the first film so appealing.

One of the biggest problems is the film's lack of a clear villain. Doctor Octopus (Alfred Molina) is a fine actor, but his character is frustratingly underdeveloped. Likewise, the film's other villain, Sandman (Thomas Haden Church), is given short shrift. 

The film also suffers from a confusing plot. The story is presented as a race between Spider-Man and Doc Ock to retrieve a piece of technology from Harry Osborn that will allow one of them to control a group of New York City's omnipresent security robots. However, this MacGuffin is never adequately explained and the robots aren't even shown until the final act of the film.

There are some bright spots in the film. The action scenes are well-choreographed, and the film's visual effects are impressive for a film that was made in 2004. Additionally, the film's cast is excellent, with Tobey Maguire, Kirsten Dunst, and Alfred Molina all turning in strong performances.

Overall, Spider-Man 2 is a disappointing follow-up to a much-loved film. While it has some memorable moments, it is largely a forgettable entry in the Spider-Man franchise.

Britain's longest-serving Prime Minister in the 21st century announced his resignation yesterday, warning that the country's "darkest hour" lay ahead.

In a speech drawn up ahead of Sunday's fifth anniversary of the Brexit vote, Boris Johnson urged MPs to get behind the government's Plan B Covid restrictions, saying that the country owed it to the nurses who were "working flat out" to combat the Omicron variant.

And in an indication that he will not be leading the Tories into the next general election, due by 2024, he said it was time for the "party of low tax" to prove it could clear up the "congestion" of regulations introduced by Labour.

In a statement released after midnight, he said that it was "time for me to make an honest assessment" of the situation facing the government.

"I have concluded that we should not be asking people in this country to accept a higher level of taxation," he said.

"I passionately believe that this country should be a place where opportunity is equal for everyone, where everyone can go as far as their talents will take them, and where every child, whatever their background, can aspire to succeed and to be judged on their merits.

"But unless we take immediate action to get debt under control, we are going to go on creating problems for future generations. That's not what I came into politics to do."

Mr Johnson said that he hoped a new leader would be in place by the party conference in October.

The pound rose slightly on the news, which came after a tumultuous week in Westminster that saw 100 Tory MPs defy Mr Johnson in a vote on Tuesday.

Ministers had said they expected the PM to stay in post until the last possible moment before the next election, due on or before 2 June 2024.

But Mr Johnson said it was "not where I think we should be aiming to go" at the next election, although he added that he was proud of what had been achieved in "stopping Corbyn" and delivering the " Brexit people voted for".

The PM's announcement came after a cabinet meeting at which ministers discussed possible tax rises to pay for the NHS and social care.

Mr Johnson is expected to remain in post until the Conservative Party chooses a new leader, a process that could take up to two months.

Mr Berdimuhamedow added that "despite difficult circumstances", Turkmenistan would "do everything possible" to provide Ukraine with gas.

"This shows that Ukraine is a reliable partner, and Turkmenistan is a reliable gas supplier," he said.

Ukraine had been one of the most important routes for Russian gas to Europe, but Moscow has been forced to sell its gas to Europe via other routes since the invasion of Ukraine.

House prices suffered a festive fall as inflation and rising interest rates put the brakes on the property market, according to an industry survey.

The Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors (Rics) said its monthly price balance fell to -44 in December, its lowest level since May 2020.

It said that demand from potential buyers and the number of properties on the market were also flat.

The survey comes a day after data from lender Nationwide showed a surprise pick-up in UK house prices in November, but that was before the Bank of England's recent interest rate rises.

Rics said that, taking into account its monthly data going back to 2006, house prices were now close to "peak-to-trough" trends.

The organisation's chief economist, Simon Rubin, said the market had seen a "significant shift" in the last three months.

"Following a long period of imbalance between demand and supply, the recent rise in interest rates has helped tilt the balance more towards homeowners," he said.

"Going forward, we expect that trend to continue, but it remains too early to say if this will be reflected in a material decline in house prices."

The trend was reflected in all parts of the UK, with London seeing a particularly sharp drop, the survey suggested.

Mr Rubin said that, in the capital, prices were falling at a faster pace than elsewhere in the country "due to the combination of base rate hikes and a shift in investor activity".

He said that, while London house prices had surged in the years after the global financial crisis due to demand from investors, that had now changed.

"Following a trend which began last year, investor demand has now turned into a negative, dragging down activity levels and prices," he added.

But estate agents also reported that buyers were still in the market in December, despite the traditional Christmas slowdown.

The report said that 44% of respondents had seen an increase in the number of properties for sale, while 11% said that figure had decreased.

That was the lowest proportion of respondents reporting a fall in supply since January 2015, it said.

The average price of a UK home has fallen by £5,000 this month, to £296,000, according to a leading property website.

It said the market had "slowed down" following the festive period and buyers were "holding back" due to higher rates and inflation.

Rightmove said it was a reversal of the trend over the last few months, when prices rose.

The company's property expert said 2023 was "set to be the year of price corrections".

However, analysts said the falls were not as great as they first appeared, due to the time of year.

Rightmove's monthly house price index tracks asking prices for property advertised on its website.

It found that the average price of property advertised between 2 and 8 January was £296,000, down by 0.9% from £301,000 in the same period the month before.

The company said it was the first time in a year that prices had fallen month-on-month. However, they were up by 6.3% on the same time last year.

"The market has slowed down following the frenzy of activity we saw on the back of the mini-budget, and the festive period is always a quieter time for trading, with buyers holding back ahead of New Year, which is compounded this year by the hike in interest rates and the impact of inflation on household budgets," said Tim Bannister, Rightmove's property expert.

" 2023 is set to be the year of price corrections, and the start of it has seen a re-balancing of asking prices, with some sellers being forced to adjust their asking price in order to effect a sale, and others deciding to take their property off the market for now and reassess later in the year.

"Those who have been through the buying and selling process a few times are familiar with the ebb and flow of the market, but first-time sellers can find it frustrating when prices aren't rising fast, as they were last year."

Nicky Stevenson, managing director at estate agent Fine & Country, said: "The monthly fall in the Rightmove index is not as significant as it first appears, as the market slows down over the Christmas holiday, making it difficult to accurately assess true pricing trends at this time of year.

"However the market has seen a significant shift in the last three months, and asking prices are now more likely to reflect realistic current values."

Iranian authorities have arrested and sentenced a prominent feminist blogger to more than a decade in prison on charges of harming the country's "cultural heritage" through her social media posts.

The reformist news website Kalame reported that Nazanin Serajeddini, better known as Nazanin Satrapi, was sentenced to 14 years in prison.

Ms Serajeddini had been detained since October 2021.

She is best known for her blog Girl in Red which she used to advocate for women's rights and against sexual harassment.

Her blog and posts on social media were highly critical of the Islamic Republic establishment and she supported the large protests that rocked Iran in 2017-18.

Ms Serajeddini, 39, faced a charge of "publishing obscene content" - a crime under Iran's cyber-crimes law - and three counts of "insulting Islamic sanctities" through her online work.

The blogger had also been vocal about the country's handling of the coronavirus pandemic.

Her mother, Fatemeh Satrapi, told the BBC's Service Persian that the blogger had been denied medical help for acute leukaemia during her time in detention.

Ms Satrapi said her daughter's prison sentence could be appealed against within 20 days.

Human rights activists have accused the Iranian government of using controversial cyber-crime laws to stifle dissent online.

Iran has been ranked among the top 10 prisons for women in the world, according to a report published in September by the London-based rights group Article 19.

The Iranian judiciary on Sunday sentenced a prominent activist and blogger to 14 years in prison on security charges, a rights group said.

Narges Mohammadi, 57, was convicted of "conspiring to commit crimes against national security", her lawyer said.

Ms Mohammadi has campaigned for peace and women's rights and was already serving a sentence of 16 years, imposed in 2019.

She was detained last year after speaking at a conference on women's rights in Iran.

Her latest sentence, which comes amid a crackdown on anti-government activists, has been widely criticised by the United Nations and rights groups.

"This is the worst time to be a defender of human rights in Iran," said Michael Page, deputy Middle East director at Human Rights Watch.

"The authorities seem determined to use every tool available to them to criminalise activism and silence any dissent."

Ms Mohammadi, who is in poor health, was unable to attend her own trial because she was unable to walk, her lawyer said.
She has been held in Tehran's Evin prison, where she has gone on hunger strike several times to protest against her detention and the harassment of her family.

Her husband, Taghi Rahmani, who lives in France, told the BBC he was extremely worried about her well-being.

"I don't think she will be able to survive this imprisonment," he said.

"Her health condition is very critical… she has asthma and her lungs are damaged because of the imprisonment and the harassment of the security forces."

Ms Mohammadi was first arrested in 1998 for campaigning for the abolition of the death penalty.
She was arrested again in 2010 and served a sentence of six years in prison, after which she was placed under house arrest.

The economy has been dubbed "strong" by ministers and independent forecasters alike, as the UK enjoys its longest period of continuous growth for nearly 200 years.

The question now is whether that strength will continue as the cost of living crisis begins to bite.

The economy grew by 6.7% in 2021 as it recovered from the Covid pandemic, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

But in 2022, despite fears of a slowdown, it is estimated that the UK economy grew by around 6.5% compared with 2021.

That makes it one of the fastest growing in the world, although there are concerns that other leading economies are growing more quickly.

The UK's independent forecaster, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), says the economy will grow by about 2.5% in 2023, slowing to 1.8% in 2024 and 1.1% in 2025.

But it has downgraded its predictions previously, indicating that there are significant headwinds facing the UK economy.

This includes a cost of living crisis driven by high energy prices, which have been pushed up significantly since the Russian invasion of Ukraine.

The ONS said that in the three months to September 2022, the UK economy grew by 0.2% compared with the three months to June, the lowest growth since the three months to February 2022.

At the same time, inflation is predicted to have fallen from a peak of 11.1% in October to around 7% by the end of the year.

That is well above the government's target of 2%, but it is also a dramatic fall from the peaks hit earlier in the year.

The Resolution Foundation think tank predicts that living standards will still be lower next year compared with pre-pandemic levels.

"The economy may be heading in the right direction but too many families will still feel like they're going in the opposite direction next year, with incomes set to fall well short of pre-pandemic levels," said Torsten Bell, chief executive of the Resolution Foundation.

The think tank has predicted that median household income will not recover to pre-pandemic levels until the end of 2024.

But ministers say that the economy is now stronger than before the pandemic, with the unemployment rate at a record low and more people in work than ever before.

T in the Park has sold out in record time this year.

Organisers of the Scottish music festival have announced this year's event is completely sold out.

All 150,000 tickets to the festival have been snapped up in four days.

It beats the previous record of seven days set in 2008 and repeated in 2011, 2013 and 2014.

This year's festival will be the last to be held at Scotland's disused Balado airfield, near Kinross.

It will be staged for the final time at the Perthshire venue in July with performances from To Use An Idiom, Foo Fighters, The 1975 and Primal Scream.

Last month it was announced that the festival was being moved to a new, as yet undisclosed, location in Perthshire following the demise of its longstanding home.

The 3,000-acre (1,200 hectare) site at Balado, formerly an RAF base, was originally leased for 20 years when the festival first moved there in 1997.

 organisers said the new site - likely to be in the same area - will be "bespoke" and "purpose-built".

A statement from organisers DF Concerts said: "We are thrilled that in this, the final year at Balado, fans have grabbed the last chance to see an event at the site as quick as they have.

"We now can't wait to reveal all about the amazing site we have secured for the next chapter in the story of T in the Park."

Scotland's biggest music festival, T in the Park, has sold out for the first time in three years. 

All tickets for the festival, which takes place in Perthshire in July, were snapped up in about two days. 

Organisers said the "speed of sale" had been unprecedented.

Last year the three-day event was called off because of Covid-19. 

This year's festival will feature performances from the likes of Lewis Capaldi, Headline, and Stormzy.

Organisers said this year's event would be the last to be held at Scotland's rural Strathallan site.

They have requested permission to move the festival to a smaller location in nearby Perthshire.

In a statement, organisers said the relocation plan involved "a much-reduced capacity and numerous other changes that would make the festival a very different animal to the T in the Park fans know and love".

They said this meant it was "not suitable" to continue trading under the T in the Park name.

However, they added they were "confident" they can deliver a "fantastic" last festival at Strathallan.

The vast majority of the UK's mobile phones go online, with an average of 1.4 phones for every man, woman and child, official statistics have revealed. Nearly every adult owns a smartphone, with 97% of people aged 25 to 34 owning one, as well as 96% of those aged 16 to 24. Some 55% of adults aged 55 to 64 own a smartphone, as do more than 70% of those aged 65 and over.

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) figures show that 96% of 16 to 44-year-olds in the UK have used the internet on a mobile device. Overall, the majority of the population has access to the internet on the move. However, a persistent digital divide remains when it comes to accessing the internet on a laptop or desktop computer.

Some 81% of 25 to 34-year-olds use a desktop, laptop or tablet to go online, as do 79% of 16 to 24-year-olds. But only 57% of 55 to 64-year-olds do so, as do 49% of those aged 65 and over. When it comes to going online overall, 98% of 16 to 44-year-olds say they do so. This compares with 97% of 45 to 54-year-olds, 89% of 55 to 64-year-olds and 82% of those aged 65 and over.

The figures are compiled from surveys carried out in November 2021. The ONS rounded percentages to the nearest whole number, which means that not all percentages add up to 100%.

Earlier this month, UK statistics office the ONS revealed that nearly 98% of adults in Britain had gone online in the past three months. Separate figures from industry body Ofcom suggested that nearly 40% of households could be described as "super-connected". These are homes with access to a comprehensive range of internet-based services, including high-speed broadband, 4G mobile coverage, and a range of digital television services.

The BBC has learnt that half of the UK's smartphones are now capable of connecting to the mobile internet.

According to industry body, the GSMA, there are now more than 33 million devices capable of browsing the web on the move.

That means half of all UK mobile users now have smartphones capable of going online.

The figures are based on GSMA analyses of UK operator data.

Smartphones are increasingly taking over from other devices, such as laptops, as the primary means of going online, the GSMA said.

In the UK, for example, 35% of internet page views are now served to mobile devices, a figure that rises to 60% in several southern European countries.

Ministers are to announce plans to criminalise psychological abuse of partners and toughen the law on access to children in response to the case of a woman who was stabbed to death by her former partner as she dropped off their daughter at school.

The government will establish a new statutory definition of what constitutes "psychological abuse" in relationships to bring the law up to date with evolving abusive practices.

The proposed changes to child access legislation will make it a criminal offence for a parent to cross the agreed boundaries of contact with their children - for example, by turning up at a child's school without permission.

The announcements follow a review of the law on dangerous and abusive relationships by the former Conservative minister Caroline Dinenage.

Ministers are expected to say that the existing law is "inadequate" for dealing with psychological abuse, which includes controlling behaviour such as isolating a partner from family and friends, and monitoring their daily movements and communications.

The new legislation will make it a standalone crime to commit psychological abuse, with police given the power to arrest and charge offenders.

In addition, the government will amend existing child custody laws to introduce a new "safety clause" which will allow a judge to restrict a parent's contact with their children if there is a risk of abuse or harm.

The government will also consider whether to impose a legal duty on councils to provide safe accommodation for victims of domestic abuse and their children. At the moment, provision of safe housing is discretionary.

The announcements will be made by the Ministry of Justice and the Home Office on Tuesday.

Mrs Dinenage's review was commissioned after the killing of Fiona Pilkington, whose suicide note blamed the "controlling, coercive and abusive" behaviour of her former partner, Marcus Joyce.

Mrs Pilkington, 39, died along with her daughter France, 8, and son Patrick, 6, when she drove her car at a tree in October 2009.

The government said Mrs Dinenage's review had concluded "decisively" that a new definition of psychological abuse was needed.

The government is to change the law to allow judges to strip people who flout child access orders of their passports and driving licences. The move is designed to stop so-called “parental abductions”, where one parent takes a child against the wishes of the other.

At present, the courts can only issue orders to stop a parent taking a child if there is already evidence they have done so – for example, if they have crossed a border.

But ministers believe the current system is too slow and that it is better to head off such incidents before they happen.

The plan is to give the courts the power to impose financial penalties and strip parental rights, such as the right to a passport, if a parent is not complying with an access order.

The Ministry of Justice said the move would send a strong message to parents who flout court orders.

Ministers will also consider whether to introduce a specific offence of parental abduction, which could result in prison sentences. at present, cases are dealt with under the general offence of child abduction.

The proposals, which will be announced by Justice Secretary Dominic Raab on Monday, follow a campaign by a charity, the Domestic Abuse Legal Fund, and come after a rise in parental order breaches during the pandemic.

The charity’s founder, Jane Robey, whose daughter was abducted by her father 14 years ago when she was 12, welcomed the move.

“When a child is abducted it is often the start of a campaign of coercive control – it is the first step in removing the child from all they know and often from the other parent too,” she said.

“These changes… will give courts the tools they need to deter and tackle parental abduction at the outset, providing better protection for children and hope for parents who find themselves facing this terrible situation.”

Johan Cruyff's former coach Rinus Michels has died at the age of 88.

The Dutchman won league titles with Ajax in Holland, Bayern Munich in Germany and Barcelona in Spain.

Michels won three Dutch titles with Ajax between 1971 and 1976 before moving to Barcelona where he won the Spanish title in his first season in charge.

He guided the club to their first European Cup in 1978 by virtue of a 1-0 win over Juventus in the final.

Bayern Munich then lured him away to succeed Udo Lattek and he won the Bundesliga and the European Cup Winners' Cup with the Bavarian club in his first season.

He also guided the Netherlands to the World Cup final in 1978 and was in charge of the Dutch national team at two more major tournaments.

The football world is mourning the death of legendary Dutch boss Rinus Michels, who has passed away at the age of 88. Michels was a pioneer of the game, most famous for his role in developing the revolutionary "total football" system at Ajax in the 1960s. He went on to manage some of the biggest clubs in Europe, including Barcelona and Bayern Munich, and led the Dutch national team to the World Cup final in 1978. 

Michels was a true visionary, and his influence on the game is still felt today. He was a pioneer of attacking, passing football, and his teams were known for their fluid, attacking play. He was also a strong believer in developing young players, and his work at Ajax in the 1960s helped to produce some of the most talented players of their generation, including Johan Cruyff, Johan Neeskens, and Piet Keizer. 

Despite never winning a major trophy as a manager, Michels is widely regarded as one of the greatest coaches of all time. He was inducted into the FIFA Hall of Fame in 1991, and his work has influenced countless managers and players. 

The football world has lost a true legend with the passing of Rinus Michels. His contributions to the game will be remembered for years to come. Rest in peace.

Plans to create a "super union" for journalists in the UK have been touted as a way to tackle the growing power of tech giants like Google and Facebook, following the collapse of the industry's regulator.

The News Media Association (NMA), which represents UK news media outlets, made the proposal to merge the National Union of Journalists (NUJ) and the Broadcasting, Entertainment, Communications and Theatre Union (BECTU) at the weekend.

The plan would create a union of more than 40,000 journalists, making it the largest journalists' union in the world and one of the biggest in the UK.

It comes after the collapse of the News Media Association's regulatory body, the Independent Press Standards Organisation (IPSO), following the departure of a number of major publishers including the Guardian, the Financial Times and the Daily Mail.

IPSO's demise has led to calls for a new system of independent press regulation, with some arguing that the UK needs a "super regulator" to tackle the dominance of tech giants like Google and Facebook, which have been accused of using their dominance to exploit news publishers.

The NMA's proposal for a "super union" would give journalists more power in negotiations with publishers and help them fight for better wages and conditions.

It could also give journalists a stronger voice in the debate over press regulation and help them campaign for a new system that is independent of both the government and the industry.

The idea of a "super union" has been welcomed by some journalists, with one NUJ member saying it was a "great idea" that would give journalists "more clout".

However, others have expressed concern that it could lead to a dilution of the NUJ's core values and a loss of its unique identity.

The NUJ's general secretary, Michelle Stanistreet, said the union would "consider any proposal that enhances our ability to better defend journalists and our industry".

BECTU's general secretary, Gerry Morrissey, said the union would "engage in constructive discussions" with the NUJ about the proposal.

It is not clear how the plan would be funded or how the two unions would merge their operations.

The idea of a "super union" between the BBC, ITV and Channel 4 has been raised again by a senior BBC figure.

Director-General Tim Davie said such an approach could protect the firms from internet giants such as Google and Facebook.

The BBC's new charter - its mission statement - sets out a desire for "collaboration".

ITV and Channel 4 said they would work together where there were benefits to do so.

In a speech to BBC staff, Mr Davie said the UK's public service broadcasters had a "bright future" but needed to consolidate to survive.

"We need to recognise the world is changing fast and we need to adapt to it," he said.

"Other European countries have created super broadcasters or platforms to meet this challenge.

"A 'super union' of the UK's public service broadcasters could be a solution."

Mr Davie said the BBC could work with ITV and Channel 4 to "create a stronger voice for UK creativity".

"The super union idea is apparently being discussed at the highest levels of the BBC," he told BBC staff in an email.

"The BBC, ITV and Channel 4 have so much in common, including our longstanding commitments to distinctive, high-quality content for all UK audiences.

"We have always worked well together and will continue to do so where it is right for viewers and listeners."

ITV chief executive Carolyn McCall said: "The UK's creative sector is the best in the world and pays for itself twice over - as a world-leading cultural and economic force.

"We have a long history of working together where it makes sense for our viewers, and we have deeply collaborative partnerships on a wide range of initiatives from News to Sport and of course our world-class ITV Studios, which makes many of the BBC's most popular shows.

"The whole industry - both on and off-screen - needs to work together to rise to the challenges of increased international competition and the rapid pace of change in our industry, ensuring we continue to reap the benefits of our world-class creative sector for the British economy and audiences."

The Ireland centre, 35, was injured in the warm-up before Saturday's 19-9 win over England at Twickenham.

"Brian won't be considered for selection this week," said Kearney.
"He's still getting treatment. It's very frustrating for him."
