Prime Minister Volodymyr Groysman announced the new programme as he presented his government's programme for 2017 in parliament.

There are around 3,500 state-owned companies in Ukraine. Previous efforts to sell them off have often been hampered by corruption.

Mr Groysman said the government would sell "at least" 100 of the companies this year. They include aircraft maker Antonov and the state's stake in Ukraine's largest bank, Privatbank.

Fined but not banned, Mourinho happy with FA decision

The Football Association has decided not to punish Chelsea manager Jose Mourinho for his behaviour during a match against Southampton last month.

"The commission decided that the breach was inadvertent and intended no malice," said an FA statement.

"I'm happy with the decision. I knew from the beginning that I would not be punished," he said.

The Federal Reserve said it would begin tapering its portfolio of bonds in February, reducing its balance sheet by $30bn a month, at twice the pace it used during a similar process in 2017 and 2018. The US government has sued a man over the massive spam email and text messaging scheme that bombarded tens of millions of cell phone users with unsolicited advertisements.

It is the first lawsuit brought under the nation's new anti-spam law.

The lawsuit accuses Eric L. Jones of being the "principal architect" of a spamming operation that sent tens of millions of illegal spam messages advertising diet pills, cheap cigarettes and online porn.

The Federal Trade Commission (FTC), which filed the lawsuit, said Jones operated through two companies he controlled, Affordable Media and The Public Group.

The FTC said Jones' operation has generated at least $1.8m (£1.1m) in revenue since November 2003.

"This lawsuit sends a strong message to spammers that they cannot hide behind their computers," said FTC Chairman Timothy J. Muris.

"We will track them down and hold them accountable."

The lawsuit was filed on Tuesday in US District Court in Las Vegas.
The court issued a temporary restraining order against Jones, Affordable Media and The Public Group, and froze their assets.

Jones could not be reached for comment.

The US Can-Spam Act, which took effect on January 1, 2004, prohibits the sending of unsolicited commercial email and allows state attorneys general and the FTC to enforce the law.

Spam is unsolicited email that is sent in bulk.

It has become a major headache for Internet services providers, which have struggled to find effective ways of dealing with the flood of unwanted messages.

The US government has enforced a set of regulations aimed at curbing the flood of unsolicited e-mail, but early indications are that spam continues to grow.

The regulations, which came into effect on Friday, require that all mass-mailings include an option for recipients to opt out of receiving future e-mails from the sender.

But many spammers use web-based e-mail accounts to send their messages, making it difficult for law enforcement officials to track them down.

In addition, many spam e-mails are now being sent from legitimate servers that have been compromised by hackers, making it difficult to distinguish between legitimate and unwanted e-mail.

Despite these challenges, the US government is considering further regulations, including a requirement that all e-mail messages include a valid return address.

The government is also planning to increase its efforts to crack down on spam, and is working with Internet service providers to identify and block spam before it reaches consumers' inboxes.

Wal-Mart Stores Inc has agreed to pay $14m to survivors of a 2012 shooting in Colorado in which a man using an assault-style rifle killed three people and wounded nine.

The agreement between the retailer and survivors of the attack in the town of Aurora concludes a liability lawsuit against the US's largest retailer.

The lawsuit alleged that Wal-Mart violated state and federal laws by failing to properly secure its firearms inventory.

It also alleged that the retailer violated local laws by failing to warn police that the shooter had bought an AR-15 rifle and large quantity of ammunition just a few days earlier.

The gunman, who died in the attack, bought the rifle over the counter at a Wal-Mart store in Thornton, Colorado, on 15 December, 2012.

He killed two people when he opened fire at a crowded screening of a Batman film. 

Nine others were wounded.

"While no amount of money can adequately compensate them for their injuries, we believe this settlement makes good on our promise to support them and honours the memory of those they lost," Wal-Mart said in a statement. 

The company's shares rose 60 cents to $69.89 in New York Stock Exchange trading on Thursday.

Wal-Mart has agreed to pay $14m to settle a lawsuit that accused the retailer of failing to protect shoppers from a mass shooter at a store in El Paso, Texas.

The BBC is developing a way for people to watch television on their phones without eating into their mobile data caps.

Media player BBC iPlayer is to launch a new "data-free" iPlayer Radio app, offering listeners unlimited access to the BBC's radio output without it counting towards their data usage.

The app will automatically switch to using Wi-Fi networks if they are available, and will only use a mobile network if Wi-Fi is not available.

The BBC said the move would make its radio "more accessible than ever".

The app has been developed in partnership with mobile network operator EE, and will be available on iOS and Android phones.

The app will be available to all EE customers, as well as customers of BT and TalkTalk, which both use EE's network.

The app is not entirely data-free, however.

EE customers who use the app when they have run out of data or are not on an EE plan will have their data usage counted.

Customers of other networks will be charged for data usage if they have not bought a data add-on or are not on an unlimited plan.

The app is available to download now from the Google Play and Apple app stores.

A BBC spokesman said: "Data-free listening has been made possible following a deal between the BBC and EE, part of BT Group, to enable customers on EE, BT Mobile and TalkTalk Mobile to listen to BBC radio without impacting their monthly data allowance.

"The data-free version of the BBC iPlayer Radio app is the result of a groundbreaking partnership between the BBC and EE.

"EE has made it possible for its customers to use the app in a data-free way and the BBC has developed the technology that makes this possible."

Last month the BBC launched a "data-saving" version of its main iPlayer app, which reduces the amount of data used when people watch TV on their phones.

At the time, the BBC said it wanted to help people cut down on unexpected data charges.

The BBC's new "groundbreaking" technology has the potential to transform the television industry. The broadcaster is experimenting with a new way of transmitting television signals, using the phone line instead of the satellite or broadband. The technology, known as "ultra-fast" or "full-fibre" broadband, is capable of speeds of up to 1,000 Mbps. This is significantly faster than the average home broadband speed in the UK, which is currently around 63 Mbps.

The BBC's new technology would allow viewers to watch television without the need for a satellite dish or a broadband connection. Instead, the signal would be transmitted through the phone line, using the existing infrastructure. This would make it much easier for people to access television, particularly in rural areas where broadband coverage is limited.

The technology would also allow the BBC to provide a more personalized service to viewers. Using artificial intelligence, the broadcaster could tailor the content to the individual user, based on their preferences and viewing history. This could include recommending shows to watch, or even creating personalized playlists of content.

The BBC is currently in the process of testing the technology, and it is expected to be rolled out to the public in the coming years. It is hoped that it will provide a more reliable and resilient service for viewers, and could potentially revolutionize the way we watch television.

Text messages have become a key tool for relief agencies working to help victims of natural disasters such as earthquakes and floods.

Organisations such as the Red Cross and the United Nations use short messaging service (SMS) to coordinate relief efforts and to provide information to people in affected areas.

The use of SMS has proved particularly valuable in the aftermath of the earthquake in Haiti in January.

The country's damaged communications network made it difficult for aid agencies to co-ordinate their activities. But a text messaging system set up by the UN enabled relief workers to communicate quickly and effectively.

"It's immediate, you don't have to go and knock on doors, you don't have to worry about whether or not the infrastructure has collapsed, because everybody's got a mobile phone nowadays," he says.

"So it's probably the most effective way of getting messages to people in a hurry."

However, Mr Dalby says there are limitations to the technology.

Many people in disaster zones will have had their phones damaged or run out of charge, while network congestion can also be a problem.

And despite the widespread use of mobile phones in developing countries, many people still do not own one.

"It's definitely no panacea, it's no silver bullet, but I think it's an important part of the toolkit for communicating with people in disasters," says Mr Dalby.

In a statement, Carnival said that, following discussions with the administrators, it was "pleased to have reached this settlement, which provides a positive outcome for former Britannia customers".

The settlement includes an agreement that Smith & Williamson will handle all future customer enquiries relating to Britannia.

Britannia went into liquidation on 15 September, after talks with creditors failed to save the company.

More than 6,000 holidays on Britannia ships, including the Aurora, Braemar, Caribbean, Island Princess and Ocean Village, were cancelled.

At the time, about 160,000 passengers were affected.

The members of Britannia have been blessed with a £42m windfall. The group, whose hits include "I Wish It Would Rain" and "Baby Come Back", secured the cash after selling their catalogue of songs. The money will be shared between the four band members and their former manager. 

They sold nearly 400 songs, including some of their biggest hits, to music publishing company Hipgnosis. The price tag was disclosed in accounts filed by Hipgnosis at Companies House. 

The deal marks the latest in a string of acquisitions for Hipgnosis. It has also bought the rights to songs by Chic, TLC, and Motörhead. The company, which is run by former music manager Merck Mercuriadis, has built up a portfolio of more than 79,000 songs. 

The band said the deal will allow their music to be preserved. 

"We want to protect the legacy and also we want to protect the members, our kids, our grandkids," said band member Horace Panter. "This was a way of doing it because the money is in the songs. The music is worth more than any of us as individuals." 

The group also plans to release a new album next year.

Russian energy giant Gazprom has made a $36m back-tax claim against Ukraine, citing what it calls improper charges.

Gazprom said "extraordinary" charges worth $11.4m were imposed by Ukraine's gas transmission operator in June.

It said this had been followed by another $24.5m in charges for July and August.

Ukraine's economy minister said the Russian firm was trying to exert "political pressure" on Kyiv.

Oleg Ustenko said the government would "defend its interests".

Gazprom is the world's largest gas firm and a major supplier to Europe.

Relations between Moscow and Kyiv have been strained since Russia's annexation of Crimea and support for pro-Russian separatists in eastern Ukraine.

Gazprom said the charges raised by Ukrainian firm Ukrtransgaz were "groundless".

"The practice of making extraordinary charges is yet another example of the unfriendly actions of the Ukrainian transmission company, which raises barriers to Russian gas supplies to Europe," the Russian firm said in a statement.

Relations between the two countries have been particularly strained since Russia annexed Crimea in March 2014 and supporters of Moscow launched a rebellion in eastern Ukraine.

Washington and Brussels have imposed sanctions on Russia over the crisis while Moscow has restricted gas supplies to Ukraine.

Last year, Gazprom charged Ukraine $1.455bn for gas, up from $1.378bn in 2013, according to its website.

Gazprom, the Russian state-controlled energy company, has been accused of avoiding more than $36m in taxes in Moldova, according to the country's prosecutor general. The claim relates to the period when Gazprom controlled the gas transmitted through Moldova towards Europe. It is the latest in a number of disputes between the company and European countries. 

The prosecutor's office said in a statement that an investigation had found that Gazprom had been transporting gas across Moldova "without observing the formalities of customs clearance" at the southern endpoint of the pipeline that goes through the country. 

The statement added that the company had failed to comply with "the requirements of Moldovan tax legislation... for the payment of excise duties and VAT" for the five years from 2014 to 2019. The total amount of back taxes claimed is 7.2 billion lei ($1.35bn; £1.06bn). 

The company has been in dispute with a number of European countries over supplies of gas. It has reduced or completely cut off supplies to countries including Poland, Bulgaria and Finland after they approved plans to diversify their energy sources away from Russia. 

In October, the company stopped sending gas through the Nord Stream 1 pipeline running under the Baltic Sea to Germany, saying it needed urgent repairs. Germany rejected this explanation and accused Russia of using gas as a political weapon.

The stars have arrived on the red carpet for the British Academy Film Awards. Among the leading nominees is Brendan Fraser, who is up for best actor for his role in The Whale. He told BBC News he was proud his "unconventional" role was getting recognition. "It's gratifying to be nominated but honestly, this journey has been one of great gratitude," he said. "It's unconventional in terms of lead casting and I'm thrilled that Fraser is alive and well and thriving."

The Whale tells the story of a reclusive English teacher suffering from obesity who plans a trip to reconnect with his daughter. It has been nominated in five categories.

Fraser's co-star, Hong Chau, who plays his friend in the film, said she was happy to be back on the red carpet. "It's so nice to see familiar faces," she said. "I love walking the carpet, taking pictures and seeing friends."

She admitted she didn't think she would be recognised in her own right. "It's because I haven't made that many movies," the US actress said. "But it's getting better because people have seen The Whale."

Meanwhile, Bradley Cooper - who is nominated for best director for Leonardi Di Caprio's star vehicle, Killers of The Flower Moon - said it was "an honour" to be nominated. "It's always an honour," he said. "You always hope you get recognised by your peers. "It's nice to be acknowledged for all the hard work you do. As a creative person, you always put everything you have into it and sometimes it's acknowledged and sometimes it's not."

Cooper, who also produced and starred in the film, added that despite the hard work, he "loved every minute" of making it.

He wasn't the only director recognised by the British Academy.

All five directors of the documentary film, All the Beauty and the Bloodshed, were nominated. Laura Poitras, Howard Fischer, John Powers Middleton, Nan Goldin and Yael Bartana all walked the red carpet together.

Poitras said: "It's really exciting because it's our first film we've done all together as co-directors and it's nice to be here together."

She added they were "honoured" to be nominated for "a film that is important to us and hopes it can make an impact on the world".

The Conservative government will announce the end of more than 100 quangos, it is reported. The Sunday Telegraph says the plans will be announced in Wednesday's Queen's Speech. The newspaper claims the quangos - set up to oversee areas such as crime, drugs, pensions, and training - will be axed to save £650m a year. It also says the number of government departments will be cut from 12 to eight. And it reports that Cabinet ministers are set to lose the power to appoint their own advisers. The newspaper quotes a source close to Deputy Prime Minister Nick Clegg as saying the Liberal Democrats were prepared to "sacrifice" some of their policies to stop the Conservatives winning an overall majority at the next election.

Source: Tories unveil quango blitz plans by Mark Norman - BBC News (bbc.com)

The government has announced plans to streamline quangos, following a review by the Cabinet Office. The review recommended eliminating 157 out of 457 public bodies, with a further 91 undergoing reform.  The review claims the changes will result in an estimated £1.5 billion in savings for the taxpayer, and that the reforms will enhance the government's response to Brexit and the COVID-19 pandemic. 
The plans have been welcomed by some, but others have expressed concern that the reforms could result in the loss of expertise and experience. It is unclear whether the planned reforms will result in the desired savings, or whether they will have the intended effects on the government's response to Brexit and the COVID-19 pandemic.

Chelsea have beaten Liverpool 6-5 on penalties to win the FA Cup final after a thrilling contest ended 2-2 after extra time at Wembley.

The game appeared to be heading for a penalty shootout until Liverpool's Mohamed Salah scored a fine individual goal to equalise in the 70th minute - shortly after Eden Hazard had put Chelsea 2-1 ahead.

Hazard gave Chelsea the perfect start with a clinical finish after just five minutes, but Liverpool struck back quickly through Sadio Mane's equaliser.

Both sides had chances to win the game in normal time, with Liverpool's Loris Karius making a wonderful save to deny Chelsea's David Luiz and Willian hitting the post for the Blues.

The game turned on a bizarre goal two minutes into extra time, when Mane scored a own goal from an attempted clearance, but Salah's moment of magic took the game to the shootout.

Both teams scored their first four penalties, with Luiz hitting the post with Chelsea's fourth, but when Karius saved from Hazard, the chance fell to Mane to win it for Liverpool - only for him to blast his effort against the post.

That left Chelsea's spot-kick specialist Olivier Giroud to win it for the Blues and he made no mistake, sending Karius the wrong way to seal a fifth FA Cup triumph for the west London club.

Chelsea have beaten Arsenal 3-1 in the final of the FA Cup to clinch the first major trophy of the Roman Abramovich era. 

The match at Wembley was goalless at half-time but turned into a thriller after Blues striker Eddie Newton scored early in the second period. 

The Gunners equalised through a rare goal from defender Steve Bould before second-half substitute Gus Poyet hit the winner with a spectacular strike from 35 yards. 

It was Chelsea's first FA Cup final triumph for twenty-two years and came just three days after the club had secured a place in next season's Champions League by finishing fourth in the Premiership.

Hollywood studios have launched a campaign to press websites to remove links to pirate sites.

The six major film studios behind the campaign - Warner Bros, Fox, Disney, Paramount, Sony and Universal - have written to the largest US internet service providers (ISPs) asking them to forward the letter to their subscribers.

The movie industry has been fighting a losing battle against piracy for years.

The letter informs internet users that they are "visiting a website that illegally distributes copyrighted content". It appeals to their "better nature" and informs them that people who download copyrighted material are "breaking the law".

It then provides subscribers with a list of legitimate websites where they can watch movies and TV shows, and appeals for them to contact the film studios if they come across a website that offers illegal content.

"We believe that the people who run these sites are engaged in theft," said Rick Genow, chairman and chief operating officer of the Motion Picture Association of America (MPAA).

"They steal from the artists who create the movies, they steal from the studios that invest in and market the movies, and they steal from the hardworking people who play the movies in theatres," he added.

The MPAA, which is representing the film studios, has created a website where people can report pirate sites. It has also produced a list of frequently asked questions on its site, which addresses the issue of internet security.

The film studios said they planned to launch the campaign in other countries soon.

The initiative comes after the US government seized the domain names of several sites, including KickassTorrents, that offered illegal downloads.

In response, the music industry launched a similar campaign to the one announced by the film studios on Thursday.

The Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA) said it was "working to ensure that the internet remains a viable marketplace for the legal sale of music".

Hollywood studios have launched a campaign to stop websites from pirating their content. The studios behind the Harry Potter, Lord of the Rings and The Matrix movies are supporting the initiative. The campaign will target popular websites that are known to infringe copyright, and will ask internet service providers to take action against them. It will also target advertising networks, asking them to stop selling space on pirating websites. The move comes as the movie industry continues to struggle with online piracy. Studies have shown that millions of people worldwide download pirated movies and TV shows, costing the industry billions of dollars in lost revenue.

The US has been accused of "hypocrisy" and "double standards" over its criticism of Sri Lanka for welcoming asylum seekers arriving by boat.

US State Department spokesman Ned Price said offers of asylum were "not appropriate" and called for the "immediate return" of those who did not qualify.

India - which has itself been criticised for failing to offer refuge to those fleeing the Taliban in Afghanistan - described the US comments as "ill-timed and misdirected".

Sri Lanka's foreign ministry said the government was giving shelter to those in need on the basis of "international conventions and norms".

And MPs from the ruling party accused the US of double standards, saying America had been built on immigration.

They also pointed to the failure of the US to offer refuge to Muslims from the minority Rohingya community, who have fled Myanmar, formerly known as Burma.

Tens of thousands of Rohingya Muslims have fled Myanmar by boat after a military crackdown, which the US has condemned.

But the US has not offered asylum to them, instead pushing for their return.

Sri Lanka announced this week that it was setting up a special task force to manage the arrival of more than 300 would-be refugees.

The UN says about three dozen people have already died on board the vessels, which have been drifting in the Indian Ocean for months.

India said on Thursday that it had "consented" to allow the vessels to enter its waters, and that it had offered "diplomatic, logistical and medical assistance" to the stranded migrants.

But the government has made it clear that it will not offer asylum, with officials saying that the "primary onus" is on the countries the migrants came from.

The issue has put India - which is governed by a right-wing government that enjoys an electoral majority in parliament - under considerable domestic political pressure.

While India has been offering foreign aid and assistance to countries from Africa to the Pacific, as well as to neighbours such as Nepal and Bangladesh, it has maintained a tough stance on asylum seekers.

The government has argued that India is a democracy with a vibrant judiciary, and that refugees should go through proper channels to seek asylum.

But activists say that the government has not put in place a proper system to handle refugee requests, and that the views of the authorities are influenced by anti-migrant sentiments.

The US has been accused of holding up a £1.6bn ($2bn) package of aid for tsunami-hit Indonesia and Thailand.

The package - mainly from the UK, Japan and Australia - was due to be distributed at a donors' meeting in Bali on Tuesday.

But the US wanted the package to include debt relief, correspondents say. The US denied this.

The UK's International Development Secretary, Hilary Benn, said if the US did block the aid, it would be "completely unacceptable".

The massive Boxing Day tsunami last year killed about 220,000 people in 14 countries.

The UK has already given £400m in aid to the affected countries since the disaster.

And earlier this year, Gordon Brown announced that £1.6bn of debt would be written off by international creditors for the countries affected by the tsunami.

These include Indonesia, Thailand, Sri Lanka, India and Maldives. The debt relief will be implemented over 10 years.

Brazil plays down Varig rescue

Brazilian airline Varig's rescue has been played down by the country's new left-wing government.

The administration of President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva said the restart of operations by the restructured company was a mere "technicality".

Varig's administrator, Alex Vargas do Amaral, announced on Monday that commercial flights would resume on 12 April.

But the civil aviation agency, Anac, said it would investigate whether the airline had violated terms of its judicial recovery.

On Tuesday, Anac said it had not been consulted about the restart of flights, and that Varig had defaulted on a bank loan.

Varig, Brazil's biggest private airline, was grounded in July 2005 after it collapsed with debts of $6.7bn.

In early 2006, a Brazilian judge put the company into judicial recovery, and granted it permission to fly again.

The administrator said on Monday that Varig would fly to 17 Brazilian cities and also to Miami and Lisbon.

He said the renewed Varig would offer "competitive" prices and "better service".

But Brazil's new left-wing government, which came to power last month, played down the development.

A spokeswoman for the presidency's press office said: "Resuming flights is a mere technicality in the recovery process under way since Varig filed for bankruptcy protection.

"The important thing is that flights resume when the company is completely ready to do so," she added.

The BBC News article "Brazil plays down Varig rescue" discusses how the Brazilian government has been criticized for its handling of a recent rescue operation of a commercial airplane that crashed in the Amazon. The plane, which was owned by the Brazilian airline Varig, was flying from Rio de Janeiro to Belém when it crashed, killing all 97 people on board. The Brazilian government has been accused of not providing enough resources and support to the rescue operation, which was conducted by the military. The government has played down the significance of the crash, with the president, Jair Bolsonaro, claiming that the media is exaggerating the story. The crash has raised concerns about the safety of air travel in Brazil, as Varig has had a history of crashes and safety issues. It has also called into question the government's ability to respond to emergencies and crises.

BBC Sport's football expert Mark Lawrenson takes on singer-songwriter James Bay in this week's Premier League predictions.

This week they're joined by Arsenal fan and comedian Eddie Izard.

Together they look ahead to Friday's match between Manchester United and Arsenal and Saturday's London derby between Tottenham and Chelsea.

Lawro got four results correct last week and has another go this weekend as the Premier League returns after the third round of the FA Cup.

He is up against Bay, whose new album, "Chaos and the Calm", is released on Monday.

Bay is a big Arsenal fan but is not confident about his team's chances against United at Old Trafford.

Phil Dawson has been recalled to the England squad as cover for the injured Jamie Carragher. The 32-year-old, who has won seven caps, has not been selected since 2008. Manchester City's Joleon Lescott has also been called up by manager Roy Hodgson. Carragher, who has been ever-present in Hodgson's defence this season, injured his hamstring against Uruguay in England's final friendly before the crucial Euro 2016 qualifier in Ukraine next week. Hodgson said he had "no hesitation" in calling up Dawson, who has struggled for first-team opportunities at Hull this season. "I have been impressed with his form for Hull this season." Dawson joined Hull from Bolton in July and has made just eight appearances, with his only Premier League start coming in the 2-2 draw with Everton in September.

Triple triumph for Little Britain

Three people from Hull have repeated a charity's earlier success in crossing the Humber Bridge in their underwear.

Steve Clarkson, 44, Deborah Morgan, 40, and Andy Swift, 45, all from the city, took part in the challenge wearing only socks, shoes and hats. They raised £400 for charity. Steve Clarkson

They followed in the footsteps of the "Humber Bridge Three" who staged a similar stunt in 1992. It raised £250,000 for charity.

The latest trio were cheered on by hundreds of supporters as they made their way over the 1.5 mile (2.4km) bridge on Wednesday.

Mr Clarkson said: "Knowing there were lots of people supporting us, and knowing the reason we were doing it, made it easier."

He said the charity donations were an incentive to "keep going".

"We were freezing. It was really cold but we had to keep going. There was no chance to stop," he said.

The group chose to support the Teenage Cancer Trust, Macmillan Cancer Support and the Harry Potter-themed children's hospital in Birmingham.

Mr Clarkson said about £120 of the money was raised by an 11-year-old boy, who had heard about their challenge on the radio.

He said the three were "very relieved" to have completed the challenge.

"We feel elated. It's a great sense of achievement. We've had some lovely messages from people," he added.

The group's effort has been dubbed the "Little Britain" challenge, after the comedy show of the same name.

Why did they do it?

The group repeated a charity challenge which three people known as the Humber Bridge Three carried out in 1992.

They raised £250,000 for charity when they walked over the Humber Bridge near Hull in just their underwear.

That group - Dave Jones, Nigel Brown and Garry Wilkinson - were honoured with an MBE for their efforts.

Mr Clarkson said his group chose to reprise the challenge because "it has been talked about for years and we wanted to bring it back".

Britain has had its first triple triumph at the Winter Olympics with an impressive 1-2-3 in the women's skeleton bobsleigh.

The BBC's Nick Hope at the Olympics in Turin, Italy, says the medal winners were expected to be the same three who took gold, silver and bronze at the world championships last month.

But it was still a massive achievement for Shelley Rudman, who became the first British athlete to win a skeleton bobsleigh event at a Winter Olympics.

Her teammates, Amy Williams and number one pilot Heather Moyse, took the silver and bronze.

Deutsche Boerse has reported a record first-quarter net profit of 699m euros ($807m; £626m), as volatility related to Russia's invasion of Ukraine drove up revenues.

The German stock exchange's quarterly result was up by nearly a third on the same period a year earlier.

Chief executive Theodor Weimer said the firm was boosting its dividend by 23% due to the strong performance.

Shares in the group, which owns the Frankfurt Stock Exchange, rose 2.5% on the news.

The exchange has benefited from trading surges since Russia's invasion, as investors have reacted to the resulting economic uncertainty.

Volumes on Deutsche Boerse's Eurex derivatives exchange, where investors can bet on price movements in shares, bonds or indexes, were up 41% on the year earlier.

EBIT, which strips out exceptional items and financial derivatives, rose to 723m euros from 570m euros a year earlier.

The company, which in March reached a $5.2bn deal to buy the London Stock Exchange Group, said it was sticking to its full-year guidance.

German stock exchange operator Deutsche Boerse has raised its dividend for the first time in three years after increasing profits, with chief executive Theodor Weimer saying the company is “back on track”.

The group – which owns the Frankfurt Stock Exchange, among others – increased its dividend for the fiscal year 2022 to 70 euro cents ($73 cents) per share, up from 50 euro cents the previous year, with the company saying it was resuming “its normal dividend policy”.

The move comes after Deutsche Boerse reported a 14% increase in its annual profits, with earnings reaching 727 million euros ($790 million) – helped by increased revenue from its clearing and settlement business.

“We exited the transformation phase with our data and analytics business and are back on track with a strong set of annual results,” Deutsche Boerse CEO Theodor Weimer said. “All our businesses contributed to this success.”

The company reported that its revenue from its “data, analytics and index business” – which includes its Refinitiv platform – increased by 10% to 1.17 billion euros, with the company noting that it had achieved its goal of increasing recurring revenues to 65% of the unit’s total revenue.

Deutsche Boerse also reported increases in its revenue from its cash and derivatives markets, as well as its clearing and settlement business, with the company saying that it was benefiting from “increased client activity and higher revenues from partner workflows”.

However, the company said that it had incurred “significantly higher costs” in the fourth quarter of 2022, with Deutsche Boerse saying that it had invested in its “IT infrastructure as well as in the build-out of the new data centre in Frankfurt”.

Nevertheless, the company said that it was confident that it could continue to increase its profits in the future, with Mr Weimer saying: “We enter the new fiscal year with confidence.

“Our strong performance gives us comfort in reiterating our medium-term guidance of low to mid-single digit organic revenue growth and consistent annual increases in the dividend per share.”

Nathan Owen is set to continue as skipper of the Wales Sevens team.

The 29-year-old Cardiff Blues player has led his country since 2019.

Owen will be part of a seven-strong squad for the upcoming World Sevens Series tournaments in Dubai.

Ben Roach, 24, and Joe Jones, 22, are also named in the squad.

They will be joined by experienced players in Luke Morgan, Owen Jenkins, and Tom Williams.

The World Series begins on Thursday with Dubai Sevens, continuing on Friday and Saturday.

All six rounds of the World Series will be shown live on BBC television and online.

Britain's Luke Owen is set to be named captain of the GB Rowing eight for the 2024 season.
The announcement is expected later this week.
The 29-year-old, who won gold in the eight at the 2022 World Championships, takes over from Matt Rossiter, who retired after London 2022.

Owen - who won bronze in the four at the 2016 Olympics in Rio - has been encouraged by the progress the crew has made in recent months.

"We're moving in the right direction," he said.

"We're not there yet but we're getting there. We're excited about where we are and where we're going."

Great Britain already have a formidable history in the men's eight, with gold at the Olympics in Sydney 2000, Athens 2004 and London 2012, and bronze in Beijing 2008.

They also won the championship title every year from 1981 to 1996, with GB taking silver behind the United States at the last two World Championships.

The Beatles may be coming to iTunes, but for now, downloads are still ruled by the King. Elvis Presley's classic 1960s singles collection Elvis Presley Singles Collection: Volume 1 is this week's top-selling download album, according to Nielsen SoundScan, bumping the Beatles' greatest hits collection from the top of the chart after just one week.

Presley collected three new downloads this week from the album, for a total of 7,000, while the Beatles' album sold 6,000, for a two-week total of 63,000.

Sales of individual downloads were led by Justin Timberlake's "LoveStoned/I Think She Knows," which moved 172,000 downloads, according to SoundScan. That's just ahead of Presley's "A Little Less Conversation," which sold 169,000 downloads.

Downloads are a growing part of the music business. According to Nielsen, digital sales accounted for 20 percent of the overall market last year, and grew by 30 percent in 2007.

This is the first time downloads have shown up in the Billboard singles chart. Billboard plans to include downloads in the Hot 100 singles chart beginning in 2012.

This week's other top downloads included Josh Groban's "You Raise Me Up" at number three, followed by Journey's "Don't Stop Believin'," Glen Campbell's "Rhinestone Cowboy," and Johnny Cash's "Man in Black." Rounding out the top 10 were Eagle-Eye Cherry's "Save Tonight," Simon & Garfunkel's "Bridge Over Troubled Water," Guns N' Roses' "Sweet Child O' Mine," and Black Sabbath's "Iron Man."

Overall album sales were led by the soundtrack to the film "Dreamgirls," which sold more than 140,000 copies to top Billboard's list. That was followed by the Eagles' Long Road Out of Eden, Presley's classic hits collection Elvis 30 #1 Hits, and the soundtrack to "Now That's What I Call Christmas." Rounding out the top five were the Def Leppard/Poison collection Def Leppard/Poison – Best Of, and Radiohead's 2007 release In Rainbows.

In other music news, Coldplay scored its fifth straight number one album this week, as Viva La Vida moved more than 302,000 copies, according to SoundScan.

Downloads have entered the US singles chart for the first time ever, in a groundbreaking move for the music industry. The change, which was announced by Billboard, the company that compiles the chart, is the result of a dramatic shift in how people listen to music and reflects the growing dominance of streaming services such as Spotify and Apple Music.

Until now, the US Hot 100, the most influential music chart in the country, has been based on sales and radio play. But from now on, streaming will account for 50% of the chart, with sales and radio play making up the other 50%.

The move is significant because it means that songs will now be able to reach a far wider audience than ever before. Whereas before a song had to be purchased or played on the radio to chart, now all it takes is for enough people to stream it. This means that artists who might not have been able to get radio play or sell enough copies of their songs to chart can now find themselves in the upper echelons of the chart simply by gaining a strong streaming presence.

It also means that the chart will now be more reflective of the way that people listen to music today. More and more people are turning to streaming services as their primary means of music consumption, and this move by Billboard reflects that shift.

Some industry experts, however, have voiced concerns about the impact of streaming on the music industry. They argue that it is already difficult for new artists to achieve success in a market dominated by a few major labels, and that the new chart could make it even harder for them to break through.

Nevertheless, the move is likely to be welcomed by many artists and industry figures, who see it as a way of reflecting the changing landscape of the music industry and giving a platform to a wider range of artists. It remains to be seen whether the new chart will lead to any major changes in the type of music that is successful in the US, but it certainly marks a significant moment in the history of the music industry.

Wal-Mart has fought back against accusations of sexism, saying that it has already done much to promote women.

The retailer issued a report entitled Women in America which outlines its efforts to date and future plans on the issue.

It also commissioned a survey on American women which it says shows most are satisfied with their lives.

Wal-Mart has been one of several major firms targeted in the "war on women" debate.

Its report Thursday emphasized the opportunities it offers women, from flexible hours to training, and noted that 57% of its management team are women.

"At Wal-Mart we're proud of what we've done to support women... and we're not done yet," Wal-Mart's chief executive Mike Duke said in the report.

"We have always tried to provide opportunities for women... so they can achieve their dreams and goals," he added.

The report also detailed a number of initiatives aimed at helping women, such as providing more maternal and infant healthcare services at its stores and donating money to women's shelters.

Wal-Mart also commissioned a survey on 1,000 American women, which it says shows that women overall are generally happy with their lives, though their happiness levels vary significantly by age and by ethnicity.

The happiest women were those aged 65 and older, while the least happy were women aged 18 to 34, the survey found.

African-American women reported being much happier than Hispanic or white women, it found.

The survey also found that married women are happier than single or divorced women, and that working women are happier than stay-at-home mothers.

Wal-Mart has been an active player in the "war on women" debate, one of several corporations, including Google and Yahoo, to be named in the discussion.

Activist groups such as the Feminist Majority have accused firms such as Wal-Mart of paying women less than men, being slow to promote women and being unfriendly to mothers.

Wal-Mart has denied the accusations, saying that it provides opportunities for women that go beyond just pay and promotion.

Fighting back against accusations of sexism, racism and greed, Wal-Mart Stores Inc. has launched a campaign stressing its benefits to society.

The nation's largest retailer is putting a new spin on its reputation as a low-cost leader by calling itself "the nation's largest private employer of women" and "the most diverse company in America."

Wal-Mart has long been criticized by labor unions and women's groups for its pay and promotion policies. Company officials say they hope to head off such criticism with their new campaign. 

"This company feeds and clothes America and gives working families the chance to send their kids to college and retire with security," Chairman Rob Walton said in a statement.

The Iranian government has approved next year's budget, which has been described as the country's most "social" budget yet.

The budget, worth about $40bn (£28bn), will not impose any new taxes and promises to create more than 800,000 new jobs.

It also plans to sell off hundreds of loss-making state companies.

Iran's economy has been hit by years of sanctions over its nuclear programme and the fall in oil prices.

Oil revenues make up about 80% of the Iranian government's budget.

Tehran has been trying to tackle its economic problems, including high unemployment and inflation, by boosting its exports and cutting back on its reliance on oil.

The 2015 nuclear deal between Iran and the six world powers - UK, US, France, Germany, Russia and China - lifted some economic sanctions in exchange for Tehran curbing its nuclear activities.

But Iran's economy has yet to recover, in part because of the US's withdrawal last year from the nuclear deal and its decision to reimpose sanctions.

Who approved next year's budget?
The Iranian government approved next year's budget.

The budget proposed by Iran's conservative president, Ebrahim Raisi, on Tuesday, seeks to raise money by selling off state-owned companies and deepening a reformist drive to privatize. The budget, the first since Iran's September election, is aimed at helping to revive an economy battered by sanctions and the COVID-19 pandemic.

Iran has faced decades of isolation due to its contested nuclear program and is cut off from the global financial system, impeding efforts to rescue its economy.

Raisi's budget predicts economic growth of 6.2% for the next Iranian year, which begins on March 21, 2023, and a record high annual inflation rate of 39.8%. The budget is for the Iranian year 94, which begins on March 20, 2024.

To achieve this growth, the state will sell shares in more than 100 companies on the Tehran Stock Exchange this Iranian year, according to the budget. Iran has gradually been selling off state-owned companies since the 1990s.

The budget also allocates about $650 million for a "rainy day" reserve fund, which economists said shows the government's concern about being able to fund its budget deficit from abroad due to the return of sanctions.

The reserve could be used to control inflation, which is forecast to surge following a sharp decline in living standards. The budget also plans to provide basic goods at affordable prices.

Halo 2 has sold five million copies in its first week on the shelves in the US, according to its maker Microsoft.

The company said it was "the biggest entertainment launch ever".

The game, in which players battle aliens, went on sale on 9 November.

It has been so popular that Microsoft has struggled to supply enough consoles to play it on.

"We are making progress restock ing retailers with Xbox 360 consoles," Microsoft said in a statement.

Halo 2 is the sequel to the widely popular 2001 computer game Halo: Combat Evolved, and the second part of a trilogy.

The game was developed by Bungie, which was recently bought by Microsoft, and is published by Microsoft Game Studios.

It was launched simultaneously in Australia, Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Mexico, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, Portugal, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland and the UK as well as the US.

Microsoft has said it will release Halo 2 in Japan in February.

Halo 2 has become the fastest selling video game in history, racking up sales of more than $125m in just two days.

The figure includes pre-orders for the highly anticipated Microsoft video game. It beat the previous record held by Halo: Combat Evolved, the first game in the best-selling franchise, which grossed $100m in its first day.

"It's a great day for gamers," said Microsoft's Xbox chief, Robbie Bach. "This is the biggest entertainment launch ever."

Halo 2 is the sequel to the 2001 hit game, and goes on sale in the US on Monday. It is expected to be one of this year's biggest blockbuster releases.

The game, in which players battle aliens, has been seven years in the making and cost an estimated $30m to develop. It was created by Microsoft's in-house studio, Bungie, and will only be available on the Xbox 360 games console.

More than 2.4 million gamers pre-ordered a copy of the game at retail stores across the US, industry analysts NPD Funworld said on Saturday.

Strong pre-orders suggest Halo 2 could be one of the biggest entertainment launches of all time, behind only Spiderman and Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix, which sold a record breaking 4.7 million copies in their first days on shelves.

Halo 2 got off to a roaring start last week when more than 225,000 gamers logged on to Xbox Live, Microsoft's online gaming service, to play the game in a three-day beta test.

The game will go on sale in Europe on Friday.

The latest version of the Opera web browser can now read aloud any news article or website you visit.

The Norwegian software firm behind Opera said the feature was introduced to make surfing the web more accessible.

The browser can also be given commands verbally, making it possible to browse the web without touching the keyboard.

"This introduces a new way of interacting with browsers, making web content more accessible and bridging the gap between sites and applications," said Håkon Wium, the company's chief technology officer.

"It makes the desktop web experience a lot more like using a tablet or smartphone."

To read text out loud, users simply need to select it with their mouse and click on a speaker icon that appears in the browser's address bar.

They can also click on any link and have the content read aloud without leaving the page they are on.

Opera's "native speech" technology is based on the same browser engine that is used by Google's Chrome browser, but Wium said Opera was the first to make use of it in this way.

"We are trying to make the PC experience more like how tablets work, where you can enjoy the web without having to stare at the screen all the time," he said.

"This is an important step towards that."

However, the speech function does not work with all websites because it relies on them to be written in a way that is compatible with the speech API in Opera.

At the moment, it works best with news articles and stories on e-commerce websites, Wium said.

"We support the W3C's speech API, but not all sites implement this API," he said.

"As this technology advances, we expect more sites to implement it, making more web content accessible."

Opera's new browser, version 15, is available as a free download for Windows and Mac computers.

The latest version of the Opera browser for Android has an optional built-in feature that can read aloud any article or website that you view.

It's an intriguing idea, and one that could be useful for anyone who has vision impairments or finds it easier to listen to articles when they're multitasking. 

To activate the new feature, you'll need to browse to the website you want to read, then tap the speedometer icon at the bottom right of the screen. On the menu that appears, select "Speak" and the browser will read the text on the page out loud. 

You can adjust the speech rate and change the language it's spoken in, and even have Opera read aloud a simplified version of the text, which is useful for tackling complex topics. There's also a "Night Mode" available for low-light reading. 

Opera's new speak function is available in the latest version of the browser for Android, which you can download now from the Google Play store. There's no word yet on if or when the feature will arrive on the desktop versions of Opera.

The 58-year-old star made the comment at the press conference for his new film Killing Them Softly.

Military officials in Ukraine are hoping that a giant ring of steel will help protect the country's capital, Kyiv, from further Russian attacks.

The steel structure is described as a "mega-dam" by Ukrainian officials and is being assembled near the capital.

It is hoped it will help protect the city from flooding as well as from Russian military attacks.

Work on the 25km (15 mile) structure began in August.

It is being constructed in stages, with the first section - almost 6km long - due to be completed by the end of the year.

The structure does not encircle Kyiv itself, but closes off a stretch of the Dnipro river to the east of the city.

Ukrainian officials say the barrier is necessary because of the low water level in the river, which makes it difficult to use floodplains as a defence against Russian troops.

"If the enemy succeeds in blowing up the dam, Kyiv will be flooded," said President Volodymyr Zelensky.

"That's why we are building a strong anti-flood barrier, a dam, which provides protection against floods and, importantly, against enemy shells and missiles."

The structure, which is being built by the Ministry of Infrastructure, is made up of more than 1,000 concrete elements, some of which are more than 6m high.

Once the first section is complete, work will begin on the next phase of the project, with a target completion date of 1 May.

Ukrainian officials have not revealed how much the project costs, but say that funds have been allocated from the state budget.

The UK government is planning to erect temporary barbed wire barriers and concrete blocks to protect public spaces and landmarks in London from terror attacks, similar to the barriers that surround the White House in Washington. 

The £5 million scheme, which is known as Project Servator, involves scanning vehicles for explosives and deploying armed officers and dogs to patrol areas. The Metropolitan Police, which is responsible for security in the capital, launched the scheme in 2016 and it has been tested at the Natural History Museum, London Zoo, Madame Tussauds, and Buckingham Palace. 

It is now being rolled out to other locations, including Manchester, where barriers have been erected around Manchester Arena, and Birmingham, where similar barriers have been installed at the Bullring shopping center.

The UK government says the barriers are needed to protect the public from the threat of terrorism, while critics argue that they do not address the root causes of terrorism and may actually increase the risk of attacks.

Barriers have also been erected around other landmarks in recent years, including the Eiffel Tower in Paris and the Colosseum in Rome.

Tech giant Google's parent company Alphabet has seen its shares drop 2.3% after its employees were offered the chance to sell shares worth up to $45,000 each.

The sale came as part of a pre-arranged trading plan, which lets staff sell a certain number of shares at pre-set times.

It comes as several tech firms, including Google, face challenges due to the economic crisis sparked by the Covid-19 pandemic and changing consumer habits.

Alphabet's shares were down ($15.90) to $695.85 in afternoon trading in New York.

The stock has fallen substantially from last year when it was trading above $1,300.

"That's a reflection of the broader sell-off in tech stocks that we've seen this year," said Greg Martin, co-founder of Alphabet employee advocacy group MOVE.

He added that the trading plan had been in place for a while and was not a result of current economic conditions.

In a note to employees, Alphabet and Google's chief financial officer Ruth Porat said that staff need to exercise caution when trading shares, "given the volatility in the stock market".

"While we are in a period of uncertainty, it's important to remember that our business fundamentals remain strong," she wrote.

The drop in Alphabet's share price has been driven partly by the advertising market being hit by the pandemic as companies cut marketing budgets.

Google makes the majority of its money from advertising and like much of the tech sector is facing questions over its business practices.

The company has been the subject of antitrust lawsuits from the US government and regulators in India and Europe, who say it has abused its dominance in search and other areas.

The company's YouTube subsidiary is also facing questions over its role in political campaigning ahead of the US presidential election in November.

Last week, US President Donald Trump accused the video-sharing platform of "tying" political ad placements to favourable news coverage.

YouTube rejected the claim and said it had introduced measures to protect against misinformation in political ads.

In the wake of the news that Google's parent company, Alphabet, has seen its market capitalisation drop below $1 trillion, analysts have observed a correlation between the selloff of tech stocks and the large number of employees who have exercised their stock options this year. 

Data collected by Bloomberg shows that Alphabet and Microsoft Corp have lost about $84 billion in market value since the beginning of October, a period during which tech employees have sold twice as many shares as they did in the first nine months of the year. The selloff has accelerated in recent days, with "a flood of trades" executed by employees following Alphabet's decision to cut its workforce by around 6% - or around 20,000 jobs. 

The dip in share price has also been attributed to the Federal Reserve's continued interest rate hikes, which are expected to continue into next year, and growing concerns over the economic outlook. 

The dip in share prices began in October, when Amazon announced it was laying off around 18,000 staff, and Meta announced its first-ever year-on-year decline in advertising revenue. This was followed by Google's announcement of its own layoffs. It is thought that the announcements of mass redundancies within the tech sector have triggered the selloff, with employees seeking to cash in their stocks before they lose their value. 

Some analysts have said that the selloff is not surprising, given the scale of the layoffs in the tech sector and how expensive tech stocks have been in recent years. 

Will Straf, a manager of Boston Consulting Group's U.S. innovation fund, said: "That was the bubble: valuations that didn't reflect the underlying fundamentals and a lot of expectations about perpetual growth." 

However, others have argued that the selloff is an overreaction, with some analysts claiming that the redundancies represent a reset, rather than a sign of enduring economic pain. 

A former Wall Street analyst, Eric Schiffer, said: "Stock price declines are necessary and a good thing as money shifts from overpriced and speculative back to safety and quality, where it should be." 

As well as the selloff from employees, a large number of institutional investors have also sold off their tech stocks in recent days. It is thought that investors are moving to other sectors in order to mitigate risk in the event of a recession. 

Alphabet's current market capitalisation is around $913 billion.

The award for best novel has gone to Lev AC Rosenfeld for his adventure story, "Tom Clancy Hero."

Cyber criminals are stepping up their efforts to exploit vulnerabilities exposed by the Covid-19 pandemic, the EU's law enforcement agency has said.

In its latest report, Europol said that since February 2021, when mass vaccination programmes were rolled out, "spam campaigns, phishing and smishing attacks, malware attacks and scams" have been on the rise.

"Initial forecasts show an increase in cybercrime of around 20% in 2020 compared to 2019," Europol said in a statement.

The agency said that cyber criminals had adopted new tactics and techniques since the pandemic began.

"At the beginning of the pandemic, cyber criminals reacted quickly to exploit the fear and uncertainty of citizens," Europol's executive director, Catherine De Bolle, said.

"Criminals adapted quickly to fulfil their economic and practical needs, considering the new working-from-home environment, and they were able to achieve this by playing on people's fears," she added.

The pace of cyber attacks has accelerated in recent months, with criminals exploiting vulnerabilities in computer systems and launching more sophisticated campaigns.

The rise in cyber attacks has been driven by a number of factors, including the increasing use of technology in everyday life, the growing number of devices connected to the internet, and the lack of adequate security measures in many systems.

The most common types of cyber attacks include phishing, malware, and ransomware. Phishing attacks involve sending fake emails or messages that trick people into revealing their personal information or downloading malware. Malware is software that is designed to damage or disrupt computer systems, while ransomware is a type of malware that encrypts a user's files and demands payment in return for the decryption key.

The impact of cyber attacks can be severe, with victims often facing financial losses, data breaches, and damage to their reputation. In some cases, cyber attacks have even resulted in physical damage, such as the 2017 NotPetya attack on Ukrainian infrastructure that caused power outages and disrupted transportation.

To protect against cyber attacks, it is important to have strong security measures in place, such as firewalls, antivirus software, and password management tools. It is also important to stay informed about the latest threats and to take steps to protect your personal information, such as not clicking on suspicious links or downloading files from unknown sources.

Sony has said it sold 3.5 million PlayStation 5 consoles during the device's first fiscal year - racking up a total profit of $157m.

The Japanese electronics giant had sold 30% more PS5s than the number of PS4s sold at the same point in its lifecycle.

But it sold fewer PS5 games, causing PlayStation's profit to fall short of management's expectations.

Sony blamed the global chip shortage, which it said had impacted sales.

The results covered the three months to 30 June 2021.

During that period, Sony sold 3.3 million PS5 consoles, taking the total number of consoles sold since launch to 3.5 million.

That compares to 10 million PS4s sold in the three months after it was launched in November 2013.

Sony said it had secured more PS5 units for the year to March 2022, and expected to sell more than seven million consoles during that period.

It also announced that its upcoming PlayStation VR2 virtual reality headset would launch in February, with pre-orders opening on 11 November.

Sony's overall game and network services division, which includes PlayStation, recorded revenue of $25.5bn for the year, up 27% year-on-year.

That was driven by strong sales of PlayStation 5 and PlayStation 4 software, as well as an increase in subscribers to PlayStation Plus, its subscription service.

Sony has 49 million subscribers to PlayStation Plus, game streaming and membership service PlayStation Now, and its PlayStation Vue television service.

While the gaming division performed well, Sony's overall profit fell short of its expectations.

It recorded a profit of $157m - far short of the $548m it expected to make.

The company blamed the shortfall on the cost of selling the PS5 at a loss due to the global chip shortage, as well as its decision to sell the PlayStation 4 at a lower price to shift excess inventory.

It also cited the impact of Covid-19 lockdowns in China on its semiconductor manufacturing.

The news comes as Sony revealed that a slimmer version of the PlayStation 4, which launched in September, had driven a spike in sales. The new version of the console is 40% smaller than the original and includes a 500GB hard drive, HDMI 2.0 port, and improved graphics.

Sony said that the PlayStation 4's sales had exceeded its expectations and that it was grateful for the continued support from its fans. MANCHESTER UNITED cruised into the semi-finals of the League Cup with a comfortable victory over Nottingham Forest at Old Trafford.

First-half goals from Antony and Marcus Rashford and a late third from substitute Fred sealed United's victory and set up a last-four meeting with Nottingham Forest's East Midlands rivals Leicester City.

United dominated throughout, but struggled to find a way past a resolute Forest defence for the first 25 minutes.

The visitors survived an early scare when Tyrell Malacia's cross was inches away from curling into the far corner, with Anthony Martial unable to get a touch on it.

Moments later, Forest's Jason Cummings headed a cross narrowly wide from the left, but that was as close as the visitors came to scoring.

United took the lead a minute before the half-hour mark when Rashford cut the ball back for Antony, who produced a clinical finish to find the far corner from 18 yards.

And the hosts doubled their lead five minutes later when Rashford produced a fine finish from 10 yards out following a defensive mix-up.

Forest's best chance to get back into the game came five minutes into the second half when Cummings was played through on goal, but the forward's chip was too weak and easily saved by David de Gea.

United put the game beyond doubt with four minutes left when substitute Fred scored with a first-time finish from 20 yards out following a lay-off from another substitute, Jesse Lingard.

United could have added a fourth in the final moments, but Rashford's effort was too close to Forest goalkeeper Wayne Hennessey, who made the save.

Rashford opened the scoring in the 17th minute with a cool finish from 10 yards out after being played in by Anthony Martial.

United could have added to their lead in the second half, but Forest managed to hold on for a clean sheet.

Ethiopia's crop production up 24% 

Ethiopia - where a famine 30 years ago led to a global fundraising effort - has recorded a 24% rise in crop production, officials say.

The increase has been linked to good weather and agricultural reforms in Africa's second most populous nation.

Officials said the country had prevented food shortages by investing in irrigation and transportation.

The famine in 1983 led to a global fundraising effort - led by singer Bob Geldof - which raised millions of dollars for Ethiopia.

The country again faced a crisis in 2015-16 when drought caused a severe food shortage.

This time, the government refused offers of international aid, saying it had the situation under control. It urged citizens to donate money and time to the effort instead.

Officials said that efforts over the last few years to improve Ethiopia's agriculture had paid off.

"Reforms in the agriculture sector, together with favourable weather conditions, have led to a significant boost in production," said Eyob Tekalegn, a senior official at the Agriculture Ministry.

"We have so far harvested 327 million tonnes of crops from 12 million hectares of land," he was quoted as saying by the state-run Ethiopian News Agency.

Mr Eyob said the government was now working to meet its goal of becoming a middle-income country by 2025.

Ethiopia is often cited as an example of economic progress in Africa.

It has seen strong economic growth over the past decade, recently reaching 11% - one of the fastest growing economies in the region.

Ethiopia's crop production has increased by 24% this year, according to the country's Ministry of Agriculture, which released data for the entire 2021-22 harvest year.

The total harvest was 38.2 million tonnes, comprising field crops such as wheat, barley, sorghum and maize, and vegetables and fruits.

The increase is a significant boost for the country, which has been struggling with hunger and food shortages. It is good news for the government, which has been implementing reforms to boost the country's agriculture sector.

The ministry attributed the increase to favourable weather conditions, an expansion of irrigation facilities, and the introduction of high-yielding crop varieties. 

It also said that the government's efforts to improve the country's road network had helped to transport crops more efficiently.

However, the ministry also warned that the country still faced challenges in terms of food security. It said that the number of food-insecure people had increased from 16 million to 20 million this year, due to the impact of the war in the northern region of Tigray and the COVID-19 pandemic.

Fiat is considering floating 10% of its iconic supercar brand Ferrari, in what would be the Italian car maker's latest effort to trim its debt. 

The proposal could value Ferrari, known for its sleek sports cars, at between $7.6bn and $10bn, and follows a failed attempt in 2008 to sell Ferrari outright. 

Fiat and Ferrari are both controlled by the Agnelli family's Exor investment vehicle. 

At the end of March, Fiat said it planned to spin off Ferrari within two years, and list it in New York. 

The group had also been considering floating part of its automotive business on the Milan stock exchange, but said in April that a listing of Ferrari would "create greater value" for the group. 

Fiat said in a statement on Saturday that "various options" for Ferrari's IPO were "being analysed". 

"A decision in principle is expected to be made in the next few months," it said. 

The spin-off of Ferrari would be the latest in a series of moves by Fiat to raise money and cut debt built up by its unsuccessful takeover of Chrysler Group. 

The US car maker has not yet returned to profit, and Fiat has had to pump money into the company. 

In an earlier effort to reduce debt, Fiat sold a 19% stake in Ferrari in an IPO in October 2015.

At that time, Ferrari said it planned to raise up to $893m in capital, in what was then the biggest initial public offering in Italy in nine years.

Fiat said on Sunday it was considering listing its Ferrari supercar brand to raise money for a new industrial plan, taking advantage of the luxury carmaker's strong recent performance.

The announcement comes ahead of Fiat's five-year plan presentation on Tuesday, where the carmaker is expected to lay out strategies for its automotive business, following the completion of its separation from truck and agricultural machinery maker CNH Industrial last year.

"This would enable Ferrari to have more resources to invest in its industrial plan," Fiat said in a statement, referring to the potential listing.

Fiat has already spun off 10% of Ferrari into a public vehicle via a listing in New York in October 2015, raising $893 million.

The company said it could sell additional shares through a public offering or private placement.

The market debut of Ferrari would be the latest move by Fiat boss Sergio Marchionne to unlock the value of the company's assets.

Last year, Fiat spun off CNH Industrial, its truckmaker, and spun off and then merged its tractor business with that of agricultural equipment maker Agco.

Marchionne has also tried to merge with GM and has laid out a plan to spin off the company's automotive division from its financing arm, Fiat Chrysler Automobiles (FCA).

In Sunday's statement, Fiat said it was considering the possibility of a merger between FCA and Ferrari.

Fiat said it would hold a board meeting on Wednesday to approve the 2018 results and the 2018-2022 business plan.

Orange colour clash set for court

One of the world's biggest furniture retailers has been ordered to change the colour of its shop fronts in the UK.

Ikea was told by a UK court it must change the yellow and orange colouring of three of its London stores.

The company has been given two months to comply with the ruling, which was made on Friday.

Ikea said it was "disappointed" with the decision and was considering its response.

The company has been involved in a long-running dispute with the local authority in the London borough of Greenwich over the shops in and around the area of Charlton.

Shop fronts currently have yellow and orange facades but the local council objected to plans for the new IKEA Greenwich store, which opened in February, arguing that the proposed colours would adversely affect the area.

Rotherhithe councillor David Gardner said: "We welcome the decision of the judge.

"It is, I think, a very sensible decision. Yellow and orange do not complement each other - it is not a question of taste.

"It will be a relief to many local people that this well-known brand will soon be reflecting the natural environment which is so distinctive to our part of London."

Ikea previously said that it was keen to work with the local council to reach an agreement.
The company has until 24 June to appeal against the decision.

In a statement, IKEA said: "We are naturally disappointed with the decision and are considering our response.

"We have always wanted to be a good neighbour and invest in the local area, including creating jobs, opportunities for local businesses and educating children on the importance of a healthy lifestyle."

The legal battle over the orange colour has begun in the UK's highest court. Kraft Foods, the makers of Cheetos, are suing Sainsbury's for using orange in the packaging of their own "Tiger" brand snacks. Kraft claims that the colour is exclusive to Cheetos and that Sainsbury's have breached an array of laws in its use. Sainsbury's, in turn, claim that the colour is universally available to all and that Kraft's case is ridiculous. The case is being heard in the Supreme Court.

The romantic comedy, starring Will Smith, was narrowly ahead of new film "The Perfect Storm", which took $30m in its first week.

Third place went to "The Sixth Sense", which took $13.2m, pushing its total to $245.7m after seven weeks.

Newcomer "The Perfect Storm" is a disaster film, based on a best-selling novel about a fishing boat lost in the Atlantic.

It stars George Clooney, Mark Wahlberg and John C. Reilly and was directed by Wolfgang Petersen, who also made "Das Boot" and "In The Line Of Fire".

"The Perfect Storm" scored well with critics and was number one at the box office in Britain, but industry experts said its US performance was underwhelming.

"It's a decent opening, but it didn't spark on the weekend," said Rick Moses of Box Office Guru.

"It may be because of the lousy weather across the country, with all that rain, and people just didn't feel like going out."

The other big new film of the week was "The Crow: Wicked Prayer", a sequel to the 1994 gothic thriller, which took $8.7m for fifth place.

The film, starring Edward Furlong, is based on the comic book character created by James O'Barr.

The top 12 films took $112.5m, which was 11% down on the same weekend last year.

However, year-to-date business is still up by about 2% on 1999, and industry experts said they were optimistic that a strong autumn line-up would maintain the box office momentum.

The latest film starring Will Smith as the titular character, Hitch, maintained its number one position at the US box office for the second week in a row. Hitch, which co-stars Eva Mendes, has earned $76 million since its release two weeks ago.

The animated feature The Polar Express maintained its position at number two for the second week in a row. Rounding out the top three is the latest James Bond installment, Die Another Day, starring Pierce Brosnan in his fourth, and final, turn as the world's greatest secret agent. 

Overall, it was a quiet week at the box office, with no new releases making waves. The week's biggest opener, Jack Frost, opened in the number eight spot with a mere $4 million. It was the year that search engines became infinitely more useful – as personal assistants for the pocket, purse or wrist. 

Five years after Google launched Voice Search on its android platform, the rush to make our machines understand our spoken words hit full stride. Apple joined the fray, Microsoft beefed up Bing and Amazon's Alexa took voice recognition out of our hands and into our homes. 

Voice recognition has been a mainstay of science fiction for decades. But 2015 was the year that the technology broke into the mainstream, transforming the way we interact with machines. 

Voice recognition has been possible in one form or another since the 1980s. But it has taken massive improvements in the accuracy of speech recognition software, the rise of powerful mobile processors, and the arrival of always-on personal assistants for the technology to become part of our daily lives. 

In 2015, these three factors combined to create a perfect storm for voice recognition.

The launch of Apple's Siri on the iPhone in 2011 began the popularization of voice recognition. But Siri's limited capabilities, and the fact that it was primarily a novelty, meant that voice recognition remained a niche technology. 

All that changed in 2015 when Google launched Voice Search on Android. With Google's massive investments in machine learning and speech recognition, Voice Search was incredibly accurate. And with Android's growing market share, it quickly became one of the most widely used voice recognition services.

Voice Search wasn't the only game in town. Microsoft beefed up Bing's voice recognition capabilities, while Amazon's Alexa took the technology out of our hands and into our homes. Alexa became the voice-controlled brain behind the Amazon Echo, a always-on, always listening speaker that acts as a personal assistant and smart home hub.

The impact of these developments is hard to overstate. Voice recognition has transformed the way we interact with machines, moving from a keyboard and mouse to spoken words. It has made our devices more accessible, not just to people with disabilities but to anyone who wants a more intuitive way to use technology. 

And it has opened up new possibilities for how we use technology, from smart homes to wearable devices. It's not too much of a stretch to imagine a future where voice recognition is the primary way we interact with machines. 

2015 was the year that search became personal. And it's a safe bet that voice recognition will continue to play a central role in how we search for information in the years to come.

The year 2023 has been a landmark for personalization on the web. From shopping to education, more and more of our digital experiences are being tailored to our individual needs and preferences. This shift has been driven by advances in artificial intelligence and data analytics, which have made it possible for companies to gain deeper insights into their customers and deliver more tailored experiences.

One of the most significant examples of this trend has been the growth of personalized search engines. While traditional search engines rely on algorithms to determine the relevance of results, personalized search engines use machine learning to understand the unique needs and preferences of individual users. This allows them to deliver more relevant and useful results, which can improve the user experience and make it easier to find the information they need.

Another area where personalization has become increasingly prominent is online shopping. More and more retailers are using AI to recommend products to customers based on their past purchases and browsing history. This not only helps customers find the products they need more easily, but it can also help retailers increase sales and improve customer satisfaction.

Personalization also has the potential to transform education by delivering tailored learning experiences to students. AI-powered learning platforms can adapt to the needs of individual students, providing personalized content and support to help them learn more effectively.

Despite these benefits, there are also concerns about the growing role of personalization in our digital experiences. Some worry that personalization could lead to the reinforcement of biases and the creation of echo chambers, where people are only exposed to information that aligns with their existing beliefs. Others are concerned about the potential for misuse of personal data, which could be used to manipulate consumers or for other malicious purposes.

As we move into 2024, it's clear that personalization will continue to play a major role in our digital experiences. As we navigate this new landscape, it will be important to consider both the benefits and the potential risks of this powerful technology.
