Oil company Yukos has lost its bankruptcy battle in a US court, leaving its former owners with nothing.

The former Russian oil giant had been appealing against a court ruling last year that cleared the way for its assets to be sold off to pay off debt.

The Texas court rejected the appeal, saying Yukos had filed too late and failed to provide sufficient evidence.

Former Yukos shareholders including its former chief executive Mikhail Khodorkovsky had hoped to share in the proceeds.

The case dates back to 2004 when Yukos was broken up and its main production unit was sold to state-owned gas giant Gazprom for $9.35bn (£5.8bn).

Last year, a US court ruled that the sale of Yukos' main production unit could go ahead, clearing the way for its assets to be sold off to pay off debt.

Yukos had argued that the sale was merely an attempt by the Russian government to seize its assets and that it was politically motivated.

However, the US court rejected this argument, saying that there was "sufficient evidence" that Yukos had filed its appeal too late.

The former shareholders plan to appeal on Monday.

Yukos filed for bankruptcy in August 2006, leaving many investors from the US, Europe and Asia owed huge sums.

US bankruptcy judge Robert Drain approved a settlement proposed by Yukos' primary secured creditor, the Russian Deposit Insurance Agency, and the company's management.

It will see the agency convert its $3.5bn debt into 99.4% of Yukos' stock.

The plan does not allow for any money to be paid out to unsecured creditors, such as investors who bought Yukos' international bonds.

The decision leaves Russia as the sole jurisdiction in which Yukos investors can pursue claims for their losses.

Consumers in the UK are expected to return to pre-pandemic spending levels on gifts this Christmas, or even spend more, according to retail analysts.

People are planning to spend an average of 726 pounds on gifts, nearly 10 percent more than in 2021, a survey from Deloitte found.

It marks a return to spending levels seen before the pandemic, when people were spending around 720 pounds.

Deloitte's annual survey of Christmas shopping habits found that nearly a quarter (24 percent) of consumers were planning to spend more this year, while only 10 percent were expecting to spend less.

This suggests that concerns over the cost of living have not deterred people from indulging in a festive shopping spree.

Consumers are planning to shop across a range of channels, but demand for high street stores is notably down, with just over half (52 percent) of shoppers planning to visit them, compared with 61 percent in 2021.

This compares with 72 percent who plan to use online retailers, and 46 percent who plan to shop at discount stores.

People are also planning to spend more on experiences such as going out for meals, with average planned spending of 286 pounds, up by more than a third (38 percent) compared with last year.

Consumers are planning to spend more on their children (average of 338 pounds), and also on their partners (167 pounds) and other family members.

People in London are planning to spend the most overall (average planned spend of 908 pounds), followed by those in the south-east (751 pounds) and the east of England (709 pounds).

Those in Wales are planning to spend the least (average planned spend of 502 pounds), followed by those in the north (553 pounds) and the Midlands (570 pounds).

Deloitte's Emma Ward said that Christmas shopping was "back with a bang" this year.

"Consumers plan to spend more on gifts as they return to pre-pandemic spending levels plus more," she added.

"Shoppers are also planning to spend more on experiences, such as eating out, as they catch up with friends and family they may not have seen as much due to the pandemic.

"This year consumers are planning to spend more on their children, as well as their partners and other family members."

It was seemingly inevitable that the internet would transform the way we give and receive presents but the extent of that change is surprising. Seven out of every 10 pounds spent on UK Christmas gifts now originates online, a proportion that has doubled over the past decade, according to the Centre for Retail Research.

This shift has produced a boom in the fortunes of online retailers, yet another example of the upheaval in "the high street" as traditional retailers struggle to keep pace with the move to smartphones, tablets and computers.

The research, which was commissioned by payment services provider Worldpay, found that £19.3bn was spent online on Christmas gifts in the UK last year, a rise of more than £2bn on the year before.

Much of that growth is being driven by the rise of mobile phones as shopping devices. Worldpay chief executive Philip Jansen said: "Over the past few years we have seen a significant increase in the use of mobile phones for online shopping, accounting for 52% of online sales in 2017, compared with 39% in 2015."

John Baulch, a director at the Centre for Retail Research, said: "The high street is changing from what it was 10 years ago. It is all about experiences: you can go and have your hair done, you can have a coffee, you can meet your friends.

It's the game Star Wars fans have been waiting for, but that doesn't mean it's perfect.

Star Wars Battlefront 2 has plenty of bugs and some confusing design decisions, but if you can look past those there's plenty here to love.

It's taken three years and a change of developer, but we finally have a proper successor to the original Star Wars Battlefront games.

They're online multiplayer shooters, but with a Star Wars skin.

The original Battlefront games were essentially Battlefield games in disguise, and that's still true here.

The highlight is definitely the multiplayer modes - preferably played with a friend.

The meat of the multiplayer is made up of three different modes - Galactic Assault, Starfighter Assault and Strike.

They're basically your standard team deathmatch, vehicle deathmatch and conquest modes, but with a Star Wars skin.

They're simple, but still pretty exhilarating, especially when playing as or against iconic Star Wars characters and vehicles.

The controls are fairly simple, but it takes a while to get used to the floaty cover system.

The lack of a proper single player campaign is still pretty baffling though, and the one included here doesn't even come close to filling that void.

The campaign is a series of battles against the Empire, essentially a prolonged tutorial.

It's not particularly engaging, but at least it's short - lasting around two hours.

Battlefront 2 has some frustrating design decisions, but it has heart.

It looks gorgeous, and sounds amazing, but a lack of content and some baffling design decisions hold it back.

The original Battlefront games had a seemingly endless number of modes, but this one feels sparse in comparison.

The lack of a single player campaign is also confusing, especially when the one included here is so lacklustre.

But if you can look past those issues there's still a lot of fun to be had - especially when playing as a Jedi.

Napster has launched a subscription service offering access to millions of songs for a monthly fee.

The service, Napster Unlimited, is priced at $5 a month for broadband subscribers.

Napster, originally a free music file-sharing service, was shut down in 2001.

It was bought by Roxio, now known as Roxio/Napster, which hopes the new service will help it compete with market leader iTunes.

The service was announced at the Consumer Electronics Show (CES) in Las Vegas.

Napster Unlimited offers unlimited access to Napster's library of more than eight million songs. Users will be able to play songs on up to three computers and burn up to three songs a day onto CDs.

The service will be available in the US before the end of January, with a UK launch to follow shortly afterwards, a Napster spokeswoman said.

Roxio competitor iTunes offers a subscription service in conjunction with phone company Verizon, but it is only available to Verizon broadband subscribers and is more expensive than Napster Unlimited.

iTunes is the market leader in legal digital music sales. It sold more than 70 million songs in 2004 and accounts for more than 70% of online music sales, according to media analyst firm Nielsen SoundScan.

Roxio has struggled to compete. It sold just over two million songs last year, according to Nielsen SoundScan.

Roxio's chief executive, Chris Gorog, said Napster Unlimited would "create a new model for digital music".

"It is perfect for people who love music, it is affordable, and it provides unlimited access to a massive library of music," he said.

In addition to the monthly subscription fee, users will have to pay a one-off $0.99 fee to register their computers. Each song downloaded will come with "digital rights management" software that limits its use.

The new Napster service will be available in the US through such broadband providers as Comcast, Time Warner, and Cox.

Comcast executive vice-president David Cohen said the partnership offered customers "a great new way to access a broad array of music".

Music fans will soon be able to rent downloads from Napster, the digital music service that is being rebuilt by Best Buy.

The service has launched a range of rental options in the US, offering downloads from its eight million track strong catalogue for between two and 30 days. Rentals will initially be offered on a promotional basis, but could become a permanent feature if the trial is successful.

Napster chief executive Chris Gorog said the service would "add a new dimension to the way people experience and enjoy music".

Users will be able to rent albums for a day, week or month, and can rent music videos for up to 30 days. They can also rent a la carte tracks for two days, or for a month for the price of two downloads.

Industry observers said the rental strategy made sense because it answered the problem of what do once the download has been bought and was lying on a computer somewhere.

"Once you've bought a download it doesn't offer much unless you have an unlimited subscription to listen to it as often as you like," said Mark Mulligan, a media analyst with Forrester.

"This is an attempt to bring some of the flexibility of the old rental model to digital music and give people more options."

Napster, which was launched in 1999 and popularised digital music, has struggled in recent years in the face of competition from Apple's market-leading iTunes service.

Best Buy, the US electronics retailer, bought Napster for an undisclosed sum in September.

It is thought that spam e-mails often originate from computers that have been infected with malware.

But researchers at the University of California, San Diego, and the International Computer Science Institute have found that many spam emails are sent by regular users who simply fail to maintain their email addresses.

The researchers said that the lack of maintenance often allows spammers to use email accounts as they wish.

The team analyzed two large datasets of spam emails. The first represented global spam levels in the early 2000s, and the second represented spam levels in 2008.

They found that in 2008 more than half of spam emails were sent from email accounts that were maintained by their owners in such a way as to allow spammers to use them. In the earlier dataset, only about 20 percent of spam emails were sent from accounts that were maintained in such a fashion.

The researchers said that more than half of the spam they analyzed in 2008 was sent using accounts that had been registered with fake information. But of the spam that came from accounts with real information, about 60 percent were sent from accounts that were being maintained in such a way as to allow spammers to send messages.

They found that people tended to use single email addresses for long periods of time, and tended not to cancel email accounts even when they were no longer active.

The team found evidence that spammers were taking advantage of this by searching through old email accounts for ones that were still active, and then using them.

"People do a poor job of unsubscribing from things they no longer find valuable," said Eric Zielinski, one of the researchers. "That leaves open a small window that spammers use to keep these accounts alive."

The team found that spammers were able to keep using email accounts because people often did not notice small changes in the emails they received, such as a slight change in the sender's name.

Zielinski said that people should be more careful to maintain their email accounts, and that email providers should do more to alert people to potential problems.

"Email is universally used, and yet it's the one place where people don't apply the same practices they use everywhere else on the internet," he said.

Are you guilty of any of these?

Not including an unsubscribe link: If you're sending an email to a list of people, you should always include an unsubscribe link. If someone doesn't want to receive your emails, they should be able to easily opt-out. This is a legal requirement in many countries.

Not getting permission: If you're sending an email to someone, make sure they've given you permission to do so. Don't buy email lists or send emails to people who haven't opted in to receive them. This is the best way to get marked as spam.

Not using a real email address: If you're sending an email, use a real email address that people can reply to. Don't use a fake or anonymous email address. This just looks suspicious and can get your email marked as spam.

Not including a signature: If you're sending an email, include a signature with your name, title, and contact information. This helps people identify who you are and why they're receiving an email from you.

Not proofreading: Before you hit send, make sure you proofread your email for any spelling or grammar mistakes. A professional email should be free of errors.

Not using proper formatting: Use proper formatting, such as paragraphs and bullet points, to make your email easier to read. Don't use all caps or excessive punctuation.

Not considering the recipient's time zone: Make sure you consider the recipient's time zone when sending an email. You don't want to wake someone up with an email at 3 am their time.

Not using email tracking: If you're sending an important email, consider using email tracking to see if the recipient has opened it. This can help you follow up appropriately.

Not using a professional email address: Use a professional email address, such as your name@company.com, rather than a personal email address, such as yourname123@gmail.com.

If you can avoid these bad habits, you'll be on your way to better email etiquette and more effective communication.

US industrial output growth eases in November

The value of the goods and services produced by the US economy increased slightly in November, by 0.2%.

The figure, released by the Federal Reserve, was well below the 0.6% growth rate that economists had been expecting. It followed an upwardly revised 1.1% gain in October.

Output from the nation's factories, mines and utilities rose by 0.2% last month, less than the 0.5% increase that had been anticipated.

There was better news on the employment front, as the jobless rate fell to 4.2%, the lowest level since February 2008.

Non-farm payrolls increased by 211,000, easily beating the forecast of 200,000.

The November report showed that the manufacturing of computers and electronics products drove much of the industrial output growth.

There was also an increase in the production of home electronics. Output in the mining sector - which includes the oil and gas industry - was unchanged.

Utility output fell by 0.4% as unseasonably warm weather reduced the need for heating.

"The November report was a bit of a mixed bag," said Ryan Sweet, a senior economist at Moody's Analytics in West Chester, Pennsylvania.

"The drop in utility output due to warm weather is a bit of a one-off that won't be repeated in coming months.

"And the rise in manufacturing is a good sign that the sector continues to expand, albeit at a slow pace."

However, there was a note of caution about the jobs data.

The retail sector cut more than 20,000 jobs in November, the biggest drop since 2009.

And manufacturing employment actually fell by 10,000, the first decline since July.

"The fall in retail jobs is a warning sign that the sector is still struggling, despite the strong holiday shopping season," said Gus Faucher, chief economist at PNC Financial Services Group.

"And the decline in manufacturing jobs shows that factories are still having trouble finding enough workers to fill open positions."

Earlier this week, data showed that China's economy grew at a rate of 6.9% in the three months to the end of September, its slowest pace since the financial crisis.

On Thursday, the Bank of England kept interest rates on hold, but two policymakers voted for a rate hike, the first time since July that a split vote has occurred.

US industrial output growth eased in September, with the overall capacity utilization rate falling to the lowest level since November 2021, the Federal Reserve said.

Production at factories, mines and utilities increased by 0.1% in September, down from a 0.4% growth in August, the central bank said.

Economists had expected a 0.4% growth in output.

Capacity utilization, which measures the amount of available resources being used, fell to 76.4% in September from 76.8% in August. This was the lowest level since November 2021.

Seven English clubs will be playing in the last 32 of the Uefa Champions League and Europa League knockout stages for the first time in history. Uefa president Aleksander Ceferin said he was delighted by the English involvement. The following day he wrote to her again saying he had "checked and can confirm I have no data from you".

The county cricket system faces a "real risk of collapse", with the future of the domestic game under threat, warns former England captain Sir Alastair Cook.

Speaking to the BBC's Political Programme, Sports Minister Stuart Andrew said the future of the County Championship was secured provided the counties "accept there may be a different format".

The 12 first-class counties receive their main income from hosting international matches - mainly Test matches and limited-overs games - at their grounds.

But the coronavirus pandemic has led to the International Cricket Council extending the World Test Championship to 2023, which will affect the number of Tests England play and where.

Most counties have also had to borrow money from the England and Wales Cricket Board after being forced to refund around £35m in ticket sales and hospitality for international matches that were cancelled this year.

And former Essex and England batsman Cook believes the game could be about to change beyond all recognition.

"There is a real risk of collapse," he added. "I think we are going to lose some counties. I think that is a reality.

"The majority of counties are going to have to borrow more money from the ECB just to survive the next six months.

"So when you add that to the counties not being able to make money from gates - because there are not going to be as many international games and the ones that do take place are going to be behind closed doors - it is a scary future."

Cook - who played 161 Tests before retiring in 2018 - said the loss of county cricket would be "a sad day for English cricket".

"It would be absolutely devastating for the game," he added. "County cricket is the lifeblood of the game in this country.

"There are so many great players who have come out of county cricket and it would be a sad, sad day if that were to not exist in the way it does at the moment."

Andrew, the sports minister, said he had spoken to ECB chairman Ian Watmore and predicted a brighter future.

Italy suffered a second successive defeat in the Women's Six Nations as their injury woes continued with a 17-28 loss to Ireland.

The hosts, who lost their opening match to England, named an unchanged side while Ireland made six changes to their team.

Italy dominated the first half but only had a single penalty from Veronica Madia to show for their efforts.

Ireland, who beat Scotland in their opener, scored three tries in the second half through Amee-Leigh Murphy Crowe, Anne-Marie O'Hora and Eimear Considine.

Two of those tries came while Italy were down to 14 players as Sara Tounesi and Ilaria Arrighetti were shown yellow cards.

Italy have now lost their last 10 Six Nations matches since their victory over Scotland in March 2015.

Italy produced a spectacular second-half show to score seven tries in a 41-19 victory over Ireland in Rome on Saturday.

The hosts led 19-17 at half-time but were pulled apart in the second half as Italy scored four tries in a magnificent 12-minute spell.

Italy have now won three of their five matches in this year's Six Nations Championship.

They began brightly and took the lead when Edoardo Padovani scored in the left corner after a brilliant solo run in which he beat three Irish defenders.

Ireland struck back with a try from winger Keith Earls, who produced a superb finish in the right corner after a fine pass from Conor Murray.

Italy went back in front when Angelo Esposito scored a superb try, running across the pitch before diving under the posts.

The hosts continued to pressure Ireland and were rewarded with a penalty try as Murray was tackled without the ball after a quick tap penalty.

Ireland came close to scoring their third try when Jamie Heaslip was brought down just short of the line. 

Italy went in at the break trailing by two points after Tommaso Allan landed a late penalty.

The result ended a run of 20 consecutive defeats in the Six Nations for Italy, whose last victory in the competition came against Scotland in March 2015.

The FTSE 100 index has touched new records in recent sessions. But the euphoria is not shared by everyone.

"Every day when I open the papers and see the markets are booming, I feel sick," one reader told us.

"How can they be booming when the rest of us are struggling to make ends meet?"

So, as the FTSE 100 index touched a new intra-day high of 7,903.88 on Wednesday, we asked four market experts whether the boom is good news.

It is important to recognise that a buoyant stock market is not a guarantee of economic health.

In fact, share prices often lead the economy by several months.

That means the stock market can peak before the economy does. And it can keep rising even as the economy sinks.

Take the dotcom bubble of the early 2000s or the sub-prime mortgage crisis of 2008, for example.

However, over the long-term, there is usually a close correlation between the two.

That suggests that a booming stock market could be a good pointer to economic growth in the coming months and years.

"It is a good thing when share prices go up," says Richard Hunter, head of markets at Interactive Investor.

"It means that companies are more profitable and investors are getting a return on their investments."

When a company floats on the stock market, it is usually to raise money from investors.

That money is then used to invest in new plants and machinery, expand the business, and - hopefully - make more profit.

So, a booming stock market is good for businesses and good for investors.

Profits are - eventually - good for everyone, says Mr Hunter.

"The idea that only the rich benefit from a rising stock market is a complete fallacy. It's a broad church."

But it can take time for the benefits to trickle down.

In the meantime, the rich - who are more likely to own shares - do get a boost.

"The trouble is that the benefits of a rising stock market like this can take a long time to filter through to the economy," says Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell.

"The wealthy tend to be the ones who own shares. If the value of their shares goes up, then their wealth goes up.

Although the bank's economists believe that the US Federal Reserve will succeed in bringing down inflation from the current level of around 8% to 4% by the middle of next year, they say that this will be achieved by "crushing" economic growth.

HSBC predicts that the US will slip into recession during the first half of next year, with the Eurozone following suit in the second half.

The gloomy forecast comes as major stock markets around the world enjoy a boom, with the latest example being the London Stock Exchange which earlier this week hit a new record high.

Last week, the chief economist at Goldman Sachs said that the US stock market was "overvalued" by 10-15%, based on comparisons with historical averages.

According to the Bank of America, current stock market levels are among the most overvalued ever, when compared to corporate earnings.

Television is changing. Not only what we watch, but how we watch it. Regular television is becoming increasingly irrelevant as more and more people turn to streaming services such as Netflix, Disney Plus, and Amazon Prime for their fix. There are benefits to streaming services: the unskippable ads that annoy us on regular TV don't exist on streaming platforms, and we no longer need to wait a week to see the next episode of our favorite show. Streaming services provide on-demand entertainment, and this is something that viewers are clearly lapping up: in 2020, 46 million households in the US paid for at least one streaming service.

However, the downside is the cost. Streaming services quickly eat into your finances, with Netflix's most expensive plan costing $20 per month and HBO Max costing $15 per month. With the rising cost of living, many are forgoing these luxuries. But what if you could be paid to watch TV?

The BBC wants to take a leaf out of streaming services' books and pioneer a new way of watching TV. The British broadcaster is seeking to make its programs more "personalized and data-driven," according to its annual plan for the next year published Thursday. The BBC wants to serve its audiences "better, wherever they are," by using "data to get closer to audiences." It also plans to "increase [its] understanding of how different types of content perform on different platforms" and "use data to benchmark the popularity of different genres and types of programs." In short, the BBC wants to experiment with its programming to see what works and what doesn't.

To achieve this, the BBC wants to harness two of its most popular services: iPlayer and Sounds. The plan is that these services will personalize their offerings depending on a user's listening and watching history. The BBC also plans to create a "single, simplified data architecture" to "support personalized consumer journeys across all our products and services." in simpler terms, the BBC wants to get serious about data.

The idea is that the BBC will have a better idea of what its audiences like and don't like. It can then use this information to create programs that more people will watch. This may seem like a simple idea, but it's a significant shift for the BBC. The broadcaster has never been in the business of creating programs to order. The German economy has avoided a recession after official data showed it grew by 1% in the third quarter of this year.

Quarter-on-quarter growth was 0.5% in the three months to September, beating expectations of a 0.4% contraction.

It comes after Germany's economy shrank by 0.2% in the three months to June, and by 1.2% in the second quarter.

The data provided a boost to the new German government, which has been in office for just over a week.

One factor in the rebound was likely the reduction in VAT - Germany's version of sales tax - which took effect in July, experts said.

The reduction in VAT - from 19% to 16% - was part of a package of measures announced in September to help protect Germany's economy as it faces soaring energy prices and supply chain problems.

While the tax cut gave a short-term boost, it will start to reverse next year, and Germany faces a long-term challenge of adapting its economy as it moves away from coal and towards green energy.

In response to the data, Chancellor Olaf Scholz - who took office last week - said the recession had been averted "despite major challenges".

"We have managed to achieve positive growth in both industry and private consumption," he added.

Mr Scholz also said that his government would "do everything necessary" to ensure the German economy continues to recover.

The German economy has rebounded sharply after a downturn caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, with GDP expected to grow by 2.7% in 2022. This strong performance is driven by a number of factors, including the country's robust manufacturing and export sector, as well as its strong domestic demand.

The German manufacturing and export sector has been a key driver of the country's economic growth in recent years. The sector has benefited from the country's strong trade ties with other European countries, as well as its reputation for producing high-quality products. This has helped to keep the German economy resilient in the face of global trade tensions and other economic challenges.

The German domestic market has also been a major driver of economic growth, with consumer spending and investment in construction and equipment driving the recovery. This has been supported by the country's strong employment market, which has helped to keep wages and consumer spending high.

Looking ahead, the German economy is expected to continue growing at a steady pace, with GDP expected to expand by 1.4% in 2023. This growth will be supported by continued strength in the manufacturing and export sector, as well as sustained consumer spending and investment in the domestic market.

However, there are some challenges on the horizon, including the potential for global trade tensions to flare up again and the possibility of a slowdown in the European economy. If these challenges materialize, they could impact the German economy's growth prospects in the coming years.

House prices in Britain have fallen for the sixth month in a row, according to a survey. The average price of a home was £286,079 in November, which was £24,163 less than a year earlier, according to the mortgage lender Halifax. It said a lack of affordability, coupled with the impact of higher interest rates and inflation, had "cooled" the market. The average price of a detached property is now £372,077, while the average price for a flat or a bungalow is £257,965.

The figures come after a survey for the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors (Rics) last week found that demand for homes had slid to its lowest level for 20 years, as the cost of living crisis put off potential buyers. Rics described the market as "stagnant".

But Halifax said that despite the drop in house prices in November, prices had risen by almost £16,000 since April, when they averaged £270,817.

"In the face of rising living costs and higher interest rates, there's no doubt that buyers are re-evaluating their affordability," said Russell Galley, managing director of Halifax.

"As we enter the new year, we expect house prices to continue to soften, with unemployment set to rise and earnings growth failing to keep up with inflation, and the cost of living crisis expected to get worse before it gets better," he added.

However, estate agents Savills said average UK house prices were up by 6.8% in the six months to November, compared with the same period a year earlier.

It said prices had been pushed up by a shortage of properties on the market and that the trend was likely to continue in the coming months.

"While this supply-demand dynamic will continue to support prices in the face of a challenging economic backdrop, it cannot shield the market from the impact of higher interest rates and widespread cost of living pressures," said Lucian Cook, head of residential research at Savills.

"We therefore expect price growth to slow considerably over the next year, with a forecast price decline of 5% in 2023," he added.

Sales and prices of homes in Britain have fallen for the first time since the pandemic began, industry figures show. The price of a typical UK property fell by 0.9% in September, compared with a 0.4% rise in August, according to building society Nationwide. It said the market had "lost some momentum" as lenders worried about the economic headwinds facing the country. The number of mortgages approved for house purchases fell to their lowest level since April 2021, according to banking body UK Finance. It does not expect the market to return to record levels seen earlier this year. The trend is the same in London, where prices have fallen by 1.2% in September, compared with a 0.5% rise in August, according to the Nationwide figures. The capital saw the biggest fall in activity, with the number of mortgages approved for house purchases in London dropping to its lowest level since December 2000. Activity has slowed despite the government's recent decision to pause the imposition of a 1.25% tax on the value of people's homes in England that would have come into effect next month. From next year, people buying a property in England worth more than £250,000 will have to pay an extra 2% in stamp duty, on top of the 3% they already pay. But the tax holiday on the first £250,000 of any property purchase in England, which was due to end on 30 September, will continue until March next year. The US has approved the sale of advanced armed drones to Turkey, in a move that critics call a dangerous escalation with Russia and Syria.

The deal for up to 13 armed Predator drones, worth almost $70m, comes as Turkey presses its assault on Kurdish fighters in Syria and Russia threatens to intervene.

US officials insist the drones are meant to help Turkey fight ISIS.

But Rachel Stohl, of the Stimson Center think-tank in Washington, said the sale would likely have a chilling effect.

She said it would send a message to Russia, Syria and any other state operating in the region that the US "is willing to sell Turkey these drones which can conduct strikes well inside Syria".

"It raises the possibility of a confrontation between the Russians and the Turks, with the US essentially enabling that confrontation through the transfer of these drones," she said.

Michael Clarke, an associate professor at the National Defense University in Washington, said he was concerned that the sale could put the US in an awkward position.

The US insists that Turkey has not bought armed drones before, but the Turks have converted their existing surveillance drones to strike aircraft.

Michael Boyle, a former Pentagon official and expert on non-proliferation, said that the US was playing with fire by making the sale.

"This is a theocratic dictatorship with a terrible human rights record and an interventionist foreign policy, and it's a NATO ally," he said.

"To give them these drones is essentially to invite them to play in the sandbox in ways that they've not been able to do before. It's a very, very bad idea."

Mr Boyle said that the sale risked undermining America's alliances with Turkey's Kurdish allies, who will feel "undermined and vulnerable" by the increased Turkish capabilities.

The deal, signed on Friday in Oslo, aims to boost economic and military cooperation.

It comes after a dispute between the two countries last year over their opposition to Finland and Sweden joining NATO.

Turkey accused Norway of supporting Kurdish militants, while Norway accused Turkey of violating the human rights of its political opponents.

Ms Truss said the deal would bring the two countries "closer together" and help "maintain peace and stability in Europe".

She added that it would allow the two countries to work together to address some of the "biggest challenges facing the world today".

The deal follows a visit by Ms Truss to Norway last week, during which she discussed the importance of the two countries working together to address global issues, including the threat posed by Russia to Europe's security.

The foreign secretary has been touring European countries to promote Britain's global role as a diplomatic and military power following the completion of its exit from the European Union.

Sales of gadgets such as smartphones, tablets and laptops are expected to rise to record levels this year.

The figure for overall sales of electronic gadgets is put at more than $830bn (£489bn) for 2013.

One expert said the growth in demand for gadgets was "absolutely insane".

Environmental group Greenpeace said the rise in sales demonstrated the need for recycling.

"There's an explosion of gadgets coming onto the market, the pace of change is rapidly increasing, and that's causing a lot of stress on behalf of consumers," said Gary Cook, a senior IT analyst at Greenpeace.

"Many of us are struggling to keep up with the latest trends and device, and that means that we're discarding our electronics quicker than ever before," he said.

The figures, from the US-based analyst firm Gartner, show that mobile phones will account for almost half of all gadget sales this year.

Smartphones are expected to sell particularly well, with sales up by nearly a third compared with last year.

Tablets are also selling fast, with more than 200 million expected to be sold this year, double the number in 2012. And sales of traditional PCs, including laptops, are also expected to grow this year.

One of the factors driving the demand for gadgets, particularly smartphones and tablets, is the rapid development of cheaper devices, particularly in Asia.

And the rise of mobile broadband has made it possible for many people to go online on a smartphone or tablet instead of a PC.

"The growth is pretty much across the board, but what's driving it is the 'phablet' - a smartphone with a larger screen - in emerging markets, and also the traditional tablet and laptop markets," said Ranjit Atwal, a research director at Gartner.

"In emerging markets, the majority of people either can't afford or don't see the need for both a PC and a tablet, so they're opting for a smartphone with a larger screen.

"That's the biggest trend we've seen this year, and it's pretty much driven by the rise of the middle classes in countries like China, and to some extent India."

Sales of consumer electronics are expected to rise by more than 10% this year, the biggest increase since 2017.

But figures from OMDIA, a research consultancy, suggest that the boom could lead to a sharp rise in toxic waste.

It estimates that 57 million tonnes of waste electronic and electrical equipment (WEEE) was generated in 2021, up from 53.6 million tonnes in 2020.

Most of the waste - about 70% - came from small devices including smartphones, tablets, and headphones. The remainder was made up of large household devices such as fridges, washing machines, and TVs.

Under the Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment (WEEE) Directive, consumers are entitled to dispose of old electronics free of charge at designated collection points.

But the Local Government Association, which represents councils in England and Wales, said that in some areas, household recycling sites were so full that they had to turn away people with electronic waste.

"Increased producer responsibility - making brands that produce electronic goods contribute to towards the cost of disposal - would help alleviate the financial burden on councils and encourage manufacturers to take more responsibility for the lifespan of their products," he added.

The government said it was consulting on a new Waste Prevention and Recycling (WPR) framework, which would consider "how we could further reduce waste, increase recycling and move towards a more circular economy".

Jane Gardner, the chair of the Environment Services Association, which represents the UK's recycling and waste management industry, said there was a need for a more "joined-up" approach.

"You've got a fast-growing market in electrical goods and, as citizens, we're entitled to dispose of these items free of charge," she said.

"There needs to be a joined-up system between government, local authorities, and producers of these products to make sure that the system can cope with this growth," she added.

Mumbai fighter Moya beats Indian champion to earn national title

Police should "protect" people who have a "reasonable" reason to be in the UK, Boris Johnson has said.

The prime minister promised to change the law to make it clear that police should not arrest people at demonstrations if their only offence is allegedly breaking Covid rules.

He said his government would make changes to the Public Order Act, which he argued were needed to "restore balance" to protesters' and the police's rights.

The prime minister's comments came as the Conservative Party launched an election manifesto containing plans to outlaw disruptive protests.

Labour accused Mr Johnson of "trying to distract" from his failures by "picking a fight with protesters".

The party's manifesto, launched in Telford, also includes a promise to recruit more police officers and increase officer numbers by 10,000 - partly by training more former military personnel.

The document says the party would give officers "the powers, equipment and resources you need to keep us safe".

The manifesto does not contain a pledge to increase police officer numbers by 20,000 - a promise made by the prime minister in April.

Instead, it says the aim is to "increase total officer numbers by 10,000" - including 1,000 protection officers and 300 armed officers.

The other 8,700 officers would be recruited "over the next three years", it said.

The manifesto adds that, as part of the promise to recruit more police officers, the party would increase the number of PCSOs - police community support officers - in England and Wales.

The party also said it would introduce a new law to stop noisy protests "lasting for hours on end, blocking roads and causing disruption to businesses and residents".

If they are convicted, protesters would face "much higher" fines and courts would be given the power to impose "much longer" sentences.

The proposed law change - described by ministers as the "biggest change in police powers in a generation" - would amend the Public Order Act.

Labour's shadow policing minister Sarah Jones said the Conservatives had "shown their true colours" by including the plan in their manifesto.

"Rather than tackling crime and keeping us safe, this is a cynical attempt by the prime minister to distract from his failures and pick a fight with protesters," she said.

The Conservative government has promised to give police forces more power to enforce coronavirus rules as pubs and restaurants reopen in England.

Justice Secretary Robert Buckland said coronavirus restrictions were "here to stay" for the foreseeable future.

Mr Buckland said testing would also be increased to make sure local outbreaks were tracked and isolated.

The government's coronavirus recovery strategy aims to ease lockdown restrictions in a gradual, phased approach with the aim of returning to normal life by the end of the year. 

The next planned easing - allowing pubs, restaurants and hairdressers to reopen - is scheduled for Saturday, provided coronavirus cases continue to fall.

Five million Germans out of work:

Germany has seen its biggest annual rise in unemployment for 25 years. The number of people out of work rose by 130,000 to 5.1 million in February, the biggest monthly increase since November 2002, officials said.

The unemployment rate rose to 11.3% from 11.1% in January. Youth unemployment stood at 18.2% from 17.7% in the previous month.

The strong rise in unemployment has been attributed to Germany's steep coronavirus lockdown, with economists saying that without the restrictions in place the figure might have been closer to 4.8 million. The lockdown is due to be relaxed gradually over the next few months.

Germany has been less affected by the coronavirus pandemic than some other European countries, with its total official death toll standing at 69,000, according to data from the Johns Hopkins University.

The UK, for example, has recorded more than 150,000 deaths, and Spain has seen more than 120,000 deaths. However, as in other countries, the real death toll is believed to be significantly higher.

The country's statistics office said the impact of the pandemic became evident in the second quarter of the year, when the economy contracted by 10.1%. It said the decline in the fourth quarter was smaller, at 1.3%, following a rebound in activity in the summer and autumn.

The German government has predicted that the economy will grow by 4.2% this year, and the country's central bank says it could expand by as much as 5.2%.

Robert M. Bell, the chief executive of McDonald's who helped transform the hamburger chain into one of the world's most successful corporations, died on Monday at his home in Chicago. He was 44.

Mr. Bell took over as C.E.O. of McDonald's in November 2002, and over the next three years he oversaw a dramatic increase in sales and profits at the world's biggest fast-food company.

When he took charge, McDonald's was struggling to overcome a perception among many consumers that it was a mediocre company whose food was of poor quality. Under Mr. Bell's leadership, McDonald's introduced a new slogan, ''I'm lovin' it,'' changed its advertising strategy and expanded its menu to include newer, trendier items like chicken sandwiches and smoothies.

The changes appear to have paid off. For the first three quarters of this year, McDonald's posted record profits in the United States and overseas, in spite of a sluggish economy.

Mr. Bell joined McDonald's in 1982 as a financial analyst, and worked his way up through the company, holding a variety of positions in Europe and Asia.

He became a favorite of McDonald's founder, Ray Kroc, and was seen as a likely successor to him after he died in 1984. But Mr. Bell left the company not long after, and went on to work for the Rockport Company, a footwear maker, and Waste Management, the giant trash collector.

He returned to McDonald's in early 2002, and about a year later, he was named C.E.O., becoming the first African-American to run the company.

Mr. Bell is survived by his wife, Cheryl, and three children.

Venezuela's interim president, Juan Guaidó, has suffered a shock defeat in his home state of Vargas.

Opposition activists said they were cheated in Sunday's regional election, in which candidates backed by the government won a clear majority of votes.

The outcome is a major blow for Mr Guaidó, who had hoped to make gains in the election.

The electoral authority, however, said the vote took place normally.

"We won't recognise the results of a rigged election," Mr Guaidó tweeted, moments after the electoral authority announced that the government-backed candidates had won in most states. "They stole the election from the Venezuelan people."

The vote was held amid mounting tensions between the government and the opposition, with the two sides trading recriminations following the arrest of key opposition figures.

Government loyalists said the opposition had plotted a coup, while the opposition said that President Nicolás Maduro was using politics as a smokescreen for corruption and economic mismanagement.

The regional elections were themselves a product of a long period of wrangling and negotiation between the two sides, and came about after strong pressure from the international community, led by the US.

The elections were supposed to give a much-needed boost to Mr Guaidó, who has been recognised by more than 50 countries as the legitimate interim leader of Venezuela, and not to Mr Maduro, who retains the support of Russia and China.

The opposition had hoped to capitalise on anger at the government's mishandling of the Covid-19 pandemic, with the country suffering the highest death rate per capita in the world.

But analysts say the election results have defied the opposition's expectations and revealed the waning support for Mr Guaidó.

The result in Vargas state was particularly disappointing for the opposition as Mr Guaidó's brother, Carlos, was standing as a candidate.

With almost all the votes counted, preliminary results showed that Carlos Guaidó secured just 32% of the vote, while the government's candidate, José Manuel Suárez, obtained 47%.

Police in England and Wales have started naming and shaming "yobs" - as part of a new strategy to curb antisocial behaviour.

For too long the police have been "playing whack-a-mole" with individuals who persist in antisocial behaviour, Britain's biggest police officer said.

Now they are naming and shaming the "small minority" of offenders who play "a disproportionate part" in crime, said Chief Constable David Cameron of the Cambridgeshire force.

The first eight names and photographs were published on Tuesday on a new website - www.crimedesktop.com - developed by the Eastern Region Special Operations Unit.

They include a man charged with assaulting a police officer, and another accused of spraying graffiti on a church.

The website will be regularly updated with the names and photographs of people charged with six specified antisocial behaviour offences, including criminal damage and public order offences.

They have been chosen because they are "high volume" crimes, committed by a small minority, that blight people's quality of life.

Mr Cameron said the move was a world first and a "significant step".

He added: "For too long the police service has been playing whack-a-mole with these individuals who persist in antisocial behaviour and commit a high volume of crime.

"They are often known to police and are engaged in an ongoing cycle of disorderly behaviour, crime and reoffending.

"The impact on local communities is huge."

He said the new strategy, developed with local councils and the Crown Prosecution Service, was aimed at breaking the cycle.

The strategy, which has been trialled in Cambridge, will be rolled out across the Eastern region in the next few weeks.

Mr Cameron said: "It is designed to have a deterrent effect both on the individuals named, and, I hope, anyone else who considers engaging in this behaviour.

"Ultimately, it is designed to make our communities safer and improve people's quality of life."

He said the "vast majority" of people would welcome the move.

But the BBC's crime editor, Dominic Casciani, said there was a risk that it would lead to complaints that people had been named unfairly.

He added that some might question whether policing should be adopting a strategy more associated with tabloid newspapers.

The National Policing Improvement Agency, which developed the website, said it was a world first.

What high-definition will do to DVDs

If you have a library of DVDs, you might want to think about transferring them to a hard drive before the discs become obsolete.

It's happening already.

Even a modestly-sized HD television will reveal dust particles on the DVD and the blocks of pixels that make up the image.

The picture is often blurred, and there's a softness to the image that is absent from high-definition (HD).

This is not the fault of the DVD format, which is of excellent quality, particularly for the standard definition (SD) television sets for which they were designed.

It's the television that is at fault.

The picture information stored on a DVD is a series of dots, known in the trade as pixels.

In SD, there are 352,000 pixels, or blocks of colour, across the screen, while in HD there are 1,920,000.

That's more than five times as many.

A DVD player sends the information on the disc to a television at a constant rate of 25 megabits per second.

This information includes not only the pixels but also other data, such as sound.

To accommodate all this information, the data is compressed.

When it is decompressed inside the television, the picture is reconstructed from the dots.

Each dot relates to a point on the screen where a beam of light - a pixel - is required.

The position of the pixel and its colour is calculated from the dot.

That's fine for SD television, which has fewer pixels and therefore less information to handle.

But with HD, the television has to calculate almost six times as many positions for the pixels on the screen, and thus needs much more information, or data, from the disc.

The result is that a DVD will not give you a high-definition picture, however good the disc might be.

Some new machines are advertised as up-converting your DVDs, giving you a higher resolution picture.

In fact, they are simply sharpening the image, and the result is often disappointing.

A sharp, crisp HD image is a beauty to behold - but it needs a lot of data.

To get it, you will need to think about copying your DVDs on to a hard drive and compressing them to a format that can be played back through an HD television set.

Brits lost £768m to so-called "phantom goods" scams in 2021, with fashion items, mobile phones, and electronics among the most popular targets for fraudsters, a report has found.

Action Fraud, the UK's national reporting centre for fraud and cyber crime, received 17,405 reports of these scams in 2021, with victims losing an average of £43.10 each.

The report found that fraudsters most commonly lured victims in with offers for Nike and Adidas trainers, as well as Apple products like iPhones and AirPods.

Electronics in general were the most likely to prompt victims to make a report, with nearly a quarter (24%) of all reports referencing this kind of item.

Second-hand goods were the most popular proposition - fraudsters offered these items at suspiciously low prices in order to incentivise quick sales.

Many victims reported being initially hesitant, but were then pressured by the scammer into going through with the purchase.

One victim told the BBC that they had lost £300 to a scammer, having found a supposedly rare pair of trainers being sold for a significantly lower price than usual.

They paid using PayPal, but never received the goods. When they tried to contact the seller they found that the phone number had been disconnected.

PayPal refused to refund their money, and told the victim that they should have realised that the seller's account was fake.

"It's a hard lesson learned, but glad it was only £300 and not a mortgage payment or something else expensive," they said.

Fraudsters often asked victims to pay for items through online payment methods such as PayPal, bank transfer or with a virtual currency.

One victim told the BBC that they lost more than £1,000 after buying a car through eBay, which turned out to be nonexistent.

They were asked to pay via bank transfer and never received the vehicle. In this case, their bank was able to recover the lost funds.

The MP said current estimates of the cost of fraud in the UK, which stand at about £130bn a year, were likely an "understatement" because victims often failed to report incidents.

Sarah Clarke, chair of the APPG said: "We're shocked by the case of the 90-year-old woman who lost her life savings and the frequent examples of repeat victims."

The cross-party group has called on the government to adopt its recommendations in full within six months.

Andy Murray's hopes of a fairytale finish at SW19 came to an end as he was knocked out of Wimbledon in the third round by big-serving American John Isner.

The former world number one, who had knee surgery in February, was unable to convert any of his eight break points as Isner won 6-4 7-6 6-7 7-6.

It was a typically tough encounter on Centre Court between two players who have never lost a match on the Grand Slam stage when taking the tie-break to a third set.

But it was the American who emerged victorious to set up a last-16 meeting with Canada's Felix Auger-Aliassime.

Isner, who served a record 113 aces in his first-round match, fired down 25 aces against Murray and made only nine unforced errors on his way to victory.

Isner has now reached the fourth round at Wimbledon for the sixth time in his career, with his best result a run to the semi-finals in 2018.

Murray, who has been struggling with his movement, was unable to pressurise Isner's serve and make the most of his own potent weapon - his forehand.

The Scot has worked tirelessly to get fit for Wimbledon after undergoing surgery on his troublesome right knee, but he has struggled to find his best form.

A court in Portugal has heard testimony from a Greek brother and sister who say they were tricked into smuggling cocaine.

The pair say they were headed to Lisbon for a better life when they were forced to carry the bags at Athens airport.

They were arrested at Lisbon airport in November 2016 with 6kg (13lb) of cocaine worth about €260,000 ($300,000).

They had each been sentenced to seven years in prison.

The court in the Portuguese capital is hearing the case after the pair appealed against their conviction. They deny any knowledge of the drugs.

Their appeal was based on the premise that they had been victims of organised crime.

In testimony on Monday, the siblings said they wanted to start a new life in Lisbon, where they had relatives.

They said they had been offered a place to stay and had simply intended to renew their passports in Greece and then travel on to Portugal.

Their lawyer, Manuel Magalhaes e Silva, told the court that his clients had been "tricked" into taking the drugs by a network of drug traffickers.

The court heard how the sister had been approached by a woman at the airport who asked her to take a bag to Portugal.

She accepted and was then approached by a man who gave her a bag claiming it contained clothes.

The man then led her to a bathroom where he told her to cut open the lining of the bag and replace the clothes with the drugs, which were hidden in a box.

Her brother was approached by a man with the same story shortly afterwards at the airport.

The pair were arrested after customs officials found the drugs during a scan of their bags.

The court is expected to deliver its verdict on 23 October.

The pair, who are both aged 32, were arrested earlier this year after police raided a flat in the northern city of Thessaloniki. Authorities say they found drugs and weapons in the apartment.

The two men appeared in court on Friday. They denied the charges against them. 

The court decided to adjourn the trial until March. The two men were released pending trial, but must attend the next hearing.

Two more senior executives have resigned from Fannie Mae, the US mortgage finance giant, as it continues to suffer heavy losses.

The firm has now lost more than $14bn over the past year.

The US government took over the firm in September 2008 after it suffered heavy losses on its mortgage loans.

Fannie Mae's chief executive, Michael Williams, resigned in March.

On Thursday, the firm's chief business officer, Stephen Swad, and its chief risk officer, Rob Van der Straeten, said they would leave Fannie Mae.

In a statement, the company said that Mr Swad, who had been with Fannie Mae for more than 16 years, was leaving to "pursue other opportunities".

Mr Van der Straeten said he wanted to "pursue opportunities in the risk management field".

Fannie Mae said its first-quarter losses included a $1.7bn pretax charge to reflect "deteriorating economic conditions" that have led to increasing levels of mortgage delinquencies and foreclosures.

The firm also said it would need about $6bn in additional federal funding this year on top of the $100bn it has already received from the US Treasury.

The US government has given the firm a total of about $188bn in aid.

Winter freeze keeps oil above $50

The US benchmark price for crude oil has stayed above $50 a barrel, as oilmen anticipate the impact of cold weather on supplies.

The price of West Texas Intermediate (WTI) for February delivery rose 73 cents to $50.49 on Monday, reports the Associated Press.

Supplies of natural gas, which is used to heat homes and generate electricity, are expected to be lower than normal as temperatures drop.

That is because natural gas is also used in the drilling and extraction of oil.

"Drilling basically shuts down in extreme cold," said Tom Kloza, chief oil analyst at the Oil Price Information Service.

As a result, oil supplies will drop and prices will rise, he said. "It's going to be nasty."

The forecast comes as US oil production has finally surpassed output from Saudi Arabia.

The US Energy Information Administration said that the US produced an average 11.6 million barrels a day in November, compared with Saudi Arabia's 11 million.

The figures are preliminary, but if they are confirmed, it would be the first time since October 2008 that the US has beat the Saudi kingdom in output.

The rise in US output has been driven by production from shale oil deposits, which are scattered across the country.

These deposits were once considered inaccessible, but advances in drilling technology, such as hydraulic fracturing ("fracking"), have made them viable.

The US oil boom has contributed to a global glut of oil, which has seen the price of crude fall from more than $100 a barrel in mid-2014 to less than $30 in early 2016.

However, prices have recovered to about $50 a barrel as output has slowed in countries such as Nigeria and Venezuela, and sanctions have been imposed on Iran.

Mr Kloza said that prices below $50 encourage US oil producers to drill more, which could send prices lower.

However, he said that prices above $50 ought to encourage producers to limit their output.

The winter freeze that has swept across the United States is keeping oil prices above $50 per barrel. The cold weather has forced many homes and businesses to heat their buildings, increasing the demand for energy. This increase in demand has caused the price of oil to rise, as supplies struggle to keep up with the sudden spike in consumption.

The rise in oil prices is likely to be a short-term trend, as the cold weather is expected to pass in the coming weeks. Once the weather warms up, the demand for energy is likely to decrease, and the price of oil should return to its pre-freeze levels. In the meantime, however, the elevated oil prices could pose a problem for consumers and businesses alike. Many people are facing higher heating bills this winter, and some businesses may have to pay more for the energy they need to operate.

It remains to be seen whether the winter freeze will have a lasting impact on oil prices. Some experts believe that the rise in prices is simply a result of the cold weather, and that oil prices will return to normal once the weather improves. Others, however, believe that the winter freeze could be the start of a more sustained increase in oil prices. Only time will tell which prediction proves to be correct.

The value of the Irish stock market has reached an all-time high, despite economic sanctions against Russia.

The Irish Stock Exchange's (ISE) main index, the ISEQ 20, ended 0.5% higher on Friday at a record 14,596.42.

It means the index has gained more than 22% since the start of the year, outperforming many of its European peers.

Darren McKinley, head of equity sales with broker Goodbody, said it had been "a phenomenal year" for the Irish stock market.

"We've had few IPOs (initial public offerings), but the big drivers have been the M&A (mergers and acquisitions) and the overseas investors looking to access the growth stories in the US and the bigger European markets," he said.

"There has been about €12bn invested in the Irish market in the last year."

Mr McKinley said the ISE was a beneficiary of global investors looking to reduce their exposure to Russian assets.

Europe is experiencing an unprecedented wave of bank withdrawals, with worried citizens withdrawing about $1.3 trillion in the last year alone.

This has led to an acute shortage of the largest denomination bank note - the €500 note - leading to worries that the very basis of the euro currency scheme could be threatened.

Many of the withdrawals are taking place in Greece, where a banking crisis has led to fears that the country could reintroduce its old currency, the drachma.

But other countries with high levels of non-cash payments, such as Denmark, Austria and the Netherlands, have also seen massive increases in the amount of cash being withdrawn.

The problem is set to be discussed at a meeting of central bankers from around the world in Washington DC on Friday.

"The sudden increase in demand… exceeds the capacity of the Eurosystem" said a paper prepared for the meeting by the European Central Bank, referring to the 19 central banks which together form the Eurosystem, and manage the euro.

The ECB has increased the number of €500 notes in circulation by more than 20% in the past year, but says it is still not enough.

And it is now asking central banks from outside the eurozone for help.

There are thought to be about 23 billion €500 notes in circulation, with a total value of about €1.1 trillion. But some central bankers say that the demand is now starting to exceed the rate of reproduction.

"Increasing production of euro notes and coins is not enough to compensate for the exceptionally high demand," said the ECB. "Consequently, inventories of euro notes and coins in some denominations are now at low levels and member banks may experience temporary shortages."

"That is why I am inviting national banks from non-euro area countries to make available their stocks of euro notes and coins," it added.

The extent of the shortage was demonstrated when the Dutch central bank put a limit on the number of €500 notes that could be withdrawn by individuals last month. It said that the notes were being withdrawn "at an alarming rate".

The problem is not just a question of the amount of notes in circulation. In many countries, banks are choosing to hold fewer notes in reserve, and are turning to other forms of deposit. This has reduced the amount of notes in the system.

And the withdrawal of so many €500 notes - the largest denomination bank note in the eurozone - is making it difficult to replace them.

The crisis over the euro intensified yesterday as a leading member of the European Central Bank issued a stark warning about the future of the single currency.

Stock markets fell sharply after figures showed that inflation in the eurozone hit a record high of 4.1% in the year to October, far above the ECB's target of below 2%.

Ms. Lagarde said that the bank would "monitor very closely" any signs that inflation was becoming embedded in the economy.

In Asia, countries with currencies linked to the euro were also feeling the impact of the crisis.

In Japan, the government said it would take "necessary measures" to protect the Japanese economy from the fallout from the euro crisis.

And in China, the central bank moved to reassure jittery investors by injecting $19.2 billion into the country's five largest banks.

The measures came as data showed that China's economy was growing at its slowest pace in nine years.

Media firms could be barred from making take-over bids for rivals in a bid to curb the dominance of a small number of players, the competition watchdog has said. The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) said it was considering the move as it launched an in-depth investigation into the £29.5bn ($43bn) merger between Discovery and BT Sport, which would give the US media giant control over more than half of the country's paid-for sports rights.

The CMA said on Thursday it was "concerned" the deal could result in higher prices, reduced quality or less innovation for viewers and sports fans. Discovery owns the Eurosport channel, which owns the rights to the Olympics and other sports, and has agreed to buy BT Sport as part of its move to create a global sports streaming service.

If the CMA decides to move ahead with an order banning companies from making takeover bids in cases of so-called "killer acquisitions", it would be the first of its kind in the UK. Such a move would be designed to stop firms getting too big, the CMA said.

The watchdog's intervention on the Discovery-BT Sport deal marks the latest attempt by regulators to curb the dominance of a small number of players in the media market. TalkTalk has already said it plans to challenge the merger in court, arguing that the CMA had "significantly underestimated" the deal's impact on competition.

The CMA said its investigation into the merger would conclude in January, with a final report due in the spring.

Its decision to launch an in-depth probe comes after the government announced plans to overhaul regulations governing the media industry to tackle a perceived lack of competition in the sector.

Last month, the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) launched a consultation on plans to introduce a "news quality obligation" and a "public interest test" for takeovers of media firms.

The government has said it is concerned about the dominance of a small number of players in the media market, and the potential impact on consumers and democracy.

The DCMS consultation comes after the CMA found that just five companies accounted for 79% of the total UK spend on acquiring sports rights, and that a merger between Discovery and BT Sport could "raise concerns".

The BBC plans to cut the number of words in each news story and make stories more accessible to listeners, viewers, and readers. A pilot program will start in Northern Ireland this year, aiming to streamline the language in news articles and broadcast scripts to make them easier to understand. The corporation believes that simplifying its language will make it more accessible to audiences and will help retain viewers and readers’ attention. The plan does not aim to dumbing down the news but to make the content as easy to digest as possible. 

The scheme is based on a theory developed by cognitive scientist Neil Burgess, who has helped the BBC train its journalists. He argues that the sheer volume of information means each story must be more succinct to stand out. He said: "Many of our audience find our speech and writing styles too complex, too ambiguous, and too long. They often cannot see why, where or when they should use a particular word or phrase, because they are not sure what they mean". 

The pilot will launch in March and will be assessed by an expert panel who will publish a report in the summer. The panel will include academic experts as well as representatives from other media organizations and charities that support people with cognitive disabilities. The aim is for the simplified language to be used across all BBC news programs and articles by the end of 2024.

Director Christopher Nolan has signed a major deal with Warner Bros., the studio behind the Harry Potter films.

The film will see the director return to the science-fiction genre for the first time since 2010's Inception.

The two-year campaign for the agreement ended on Friday with a breakthrough at the Rome summit of the World Intellectual Property Organisation (Wipo).

Wipo's director general, Kamil Idris, said the new agreement marked "a historic moment".

He said: "It signals a new era of intellectual property protection on the internet. It shows that multilateral organisations, such as Wipo, can adapt to the realities of the internet age."

However, many people have continued to download music, and the industry has recently stepped up its campaign for tougher measures.

It has also been pushing for the Wipo treaty, which it sees as a crucial step in ensuring that artists get paid for their work.

The agreement aims to make it easier for rights holders to monitor and manage their intellectual property on the internet.

It also aims to cut down on online piracy, by making it a criminal offence in many cases.

The agreement still has to be ratified by at least 30 countries before it can come into effect.

But observers say they expect it to be approved, as it is in the interests of both the music industry and internet service providers.

Manchester United have asked their supporters to stop wearing masks of former player Eric Cantona during matches.

The club say it is a safety issue as masks of any kind are not allowed in sporting events in the UK.

United have also warned their fans it is illegal to carry weapons into a match.

A statement from Old Trafford read: "Manchester United advises supporters that it is against club policy for any items that are deemed to be an imitation of weapons to be carried into matches at Old Trafford."

A number of fans have been seen wearing masks of Cantona - nicknamed 'King Eric' - during the opening matches of the season.

United returned to the Premier League with a 2-1 victory over Leicester on Friday night and host Southampton in their first home game of the campaign on Saturday.

Cantona, who retired in 1997, is regarded as one of United's greatest ever players and his mask is commonly worn by fans when they want to make a point about the club's success under his former manager Sir Alex Ferguson.

The BBC has learned that Buckingham Palace sent a letter to the Met Police on Friday asking for an investigation into the alleged unauthorized use of the image of King Charles. The letter, seen by the BBC, states that the image of the king in a Cantona mask was used without his consent and in violation of the Copyright, Designs, and Patents Act 1988. 

The image, which has been widely circulated on social media, shows King Charles as a Cantona mask alongside the caption “Faites vos jeux,” a reference to the Frenchman’s iconic goal celebration.

A spokesperson for the Duke and Duchess of Sussex said the couple found the use of the Cantona mask cartoon image of the king “offensive.” 

When approached for comment, a spokesperson for the king said: “We respect the rights of individuals to display images of members of the royal family, should they choose to do so, subject to the same rules as any other member of the public.”

A US woman has filed a lawsuit claiming that Apple's cartridges for its newly launched MagSafe battery pack are incompatible with third-party chargers.

Stephanie Mendez filed the lawsuit in California this week, according to multiple reports.

Ms Mendez, who says she lives in San Diego, alleges in the suit that Apple's $129 (£110) battery pack is "designed to only work with Apple's own charger and not with other comparable chargers that exist on the market".

Apple launched the MagSafe battery pack in July, alongside its iPhone 14 line-up. The charger attaches to iPhones via magnets, and charges the device wirelessly.

But Ms Mendez claims that Apple's use of a proprietary charging method is anticompetitive, and is seeking class action status for her lawsuit, which was filed in the US District Court for the Northern District of California.

She argues that Apple's conduct violates California's competition and unfair competition laws, and wants the company to sell its battery pack with a standard charger, or to licence its charging technology to third-party manufacturers.

Apple did not respond to a request for comment.

It is not the first time Apple has been accused of creating proprietary parts that are incompatible with third-party products.

The company faced a similar lawsuit in 2019 over its Lightning connector, a proprietary charging port used on iPhones since 2012.

Apple recently announced that it would be abandoning the Lightning connector in favour of the USB-C port, starting with this year's iPhone 14.

Tech firms should be held responsible for harmful content on their platforms, the EU's internal market commissioner has said.

Thierry Brighton said EU laws could be used to force tech companies to remove illegal content.

The UK government has proposed holding firms "directly accountable" for harmful content.

Mr Brighton said the EU had "all the tools in the toolbox" to make sure action was taken.

The BBC has learned that Mr Brighton made the comments in a private meeting with journalists on Friday.

In recent years, the EU has struggled to agree on how best to regulate online companies.

Speaking at the Internet Governance Forum in Berlin, Mr Brighton said the EU had three key tools at its disposal:

Mr Brighton's comments are significant because he is responsible for proposing new EU laws on the digital single market.

The digital single market is an EU initiative to regulate the online economy across the 27-member bloc.

"When it comes to the responsibility of platforms, I think platforms have a responsibility to behave better on illegal content, on hate speech, on terrorist content and on copyright infringement," Mr Brighton said.

"And I think they have a responsibility to analyse and assess the risks that are linked to the platforms themselves."
