The promise of a cheaper chip for smartphones has led to a surge in the shares of a US firm behind the technology.

Shares in NuCurrent jumped by nearly 40% after it said it had developed a cheaper way to etch chips for mobile phones.

The process, which it calls "printed microelectronics", could replace the more expensive lithography machines currently used.

The firm said it had filed a patent for the technology, which could be used in vehicles and medical devices.

NuCurrent's shares rose 41% to $6.80 in early trading in New York, but later settled down to close at $4.96, a gain of 22%.

The firm is a spin-off from Princeton University in New Jersey. It is based in Sterling, Virginia.

Chief executive Jeff Klembczyk said the process his company had developed could "print several types of metals in a single layer".

"Using our proprietary solution-based process which leverages printed microelectronics, we can reduce the costs for mobile phones to be less than one-tenth of the costs of current manufacturing, or about $2 per phone for the fab (fabrication) portion of the bill of materials," he said.

At the moment, making a smartphone chip involves using a lithography machine - which is a very expensive piece of kit.

Traditional chipmaking technology can also waste a lot of materials, which adds to the cost, says the BBC's North America technology reporter, Chris Price.

Mr Klembczyk said his firm's process was more environmentally friendly because it used just 1% of the materials of traditional chipmaking.

He said the process could be used to make "flexible and wearable" mobile phones, as well as electronic devices for vehicles and medical devices.

"For example, the process could be used in [internet of things] devices, medical devices, automotive applications, and consumer electronics, such as smartwatches," he said.

"Printed microelectronics can also enable new form factors and new functionalities for these categories of devices."

The new chip, designed to bring smartphone features to cheaper devices, was presented at the Competitive Carriers Conference in Las Vegas. It is part of a trend towards cheaper, simpler phones that can still perform complex tasks. The presentation was accompanied by a live demo of the device.

The chip, which has been in development for over a year, is a system on a chip (SoC) solution that integrates all the components needed to build a smartphone. It is designed to be cost-effective and simple to manufacture, making it ideal for use in cheaper devices. The chip has been created to be scalable, so it can be used in a range of devices from basic feature phones to more complex smartphones.

The presentation was well-received by the audience, who were impressed by the chip's potential to bring smartphone features to cheaper devices. The chip has been designed to be compatible with a range of devices, so it can be used in many different products. 

The creators of the chip believe that it has the potential to make a significant impact on the smartphone market, by making devices more affordable and accessible to a wider range of people. It has already been met with a positive response from potential customers and investors.

UK firms 'embracing e-commerce'

The UK's largest businesses have been slow to embrace e-commerce, according to a survey of website effectiveness.

The UK has the slowest websites in Europe, with an average download speed of just four kilobits per second (Kbps), said the report by IBM and the Boston Consulting Group.

Despite this apparent failure, a separate survey indicated that many firms are keen to continue doing business online.

In a survey by consultants Deloitte and Touche, 90% of the firms questioned said they either were developing or planned to develop e-commerce websites.

It appears many companies are trying to put the lessons of the past few years into practice.

"There is no point in replicating the high-street experience on the web," said Andrew Clarke, a director of Deloitte and Touche.

"That's what a lot of companies did when they first started trading online during the dot com boom, with disastrous results."

But, in a warning to investors, Mr Clarke added that many of the new breed of websites were "still only marginal" improvements on earlier versions.

The British Chambers of Commerce (BCC) says firms across the UK are "embracing e-commerce" and increasingly selling online to help boost their sales.

Halloween writer Debra Hill has died at the age of 65.

Hill, who wrote the 1978 horror classic alongside John Carpenter, died on Sunday at her home in Los Angeles, her publicist has confirmed.

Her other writing credits include the Steve Martin comedy The Man with Two Brains.

She also produced a string of Hill-related films including Escape from New York, Halloween III: Season of the Witch and The Funhouse.

Her publicist did not reveal a cause of death. 
Hill was born in Los Angeles in 1951. She studied theatre at the University of California and then embarked on a career as a writer and producer in Hollywood.

Her most famous screenplay was for Halloween, a low-budget slasher movie that has gone on to be a huge influence on the horror genre.

It starred Donald Pleasence and Jamie Lee Curtis and told the story of psychotic killer Michael Myers' revenge on Halloween night.

Hill was credited as Nancy Loomis, her mother's maiden name, on the film because the producers did not think a female screenwriter would be taken seriously, Hill told website IndieWire in 2018.

"It was a very different time," she said. "I really didn't care about credit, and I realise that might sound silly, but it's true. I was just happy to have a job and to be able to pay my rent."

Carpenter, who directed the film, told the website it was "one of the great partnerships in cinema history".

" Debra and I created the movie from nothing," he said. "It literally was a green-screen shot in Michigan in the middle of winter. So it was not only memorable, but it was mandatory that we be collaborative and creative because there was nothing else to fall back on."

Hill wrote the script for The Man with Two Brains with the movie's star Steve Martin, and they won a Saturn Award for best writing.

Her producing credits included House Arrest, starring Kevin Bacon, and The Big Green, featuring Walter Matthau.

In later years, she founded independent film company Medusa Productions and continued to write, most recently on the 2010 TV movie A Nightmare on Elm Street.

The writer of the classic horror film Halloween, Debra Hill, has died at the age of 65. 

Hill was the daughter of legendary producer Milton Delugg. She got her start in the industry by writing episodes for television shows but later transitioned to film, writing the 1978 horror classic Halloween, directed by John Carpenter. The film starred Jamie Lee Curtis as Laurie Strode and Donald Pleasence as Dr. Sam Loomis. The film also featured Nick Castle as Michael Myers, a masked figure who embarked on a killing spree on Halloween night. 

Hill worked again with Carpenter on his 1981 film Escape from New York. She also wrote and produced TV movies, such as The Girl, starring Brooke Shields, and Halloween II, the follow-up to the original Halloween. 

In 1993, Hill was awarded the Women in Film Crystal Award for outstanding women who, through their endurance and tenacity, have helped make it possible for women to achieve significant and valuable positions in the entertainment industry. 

Hill was remembered by friends and family as being "smart, witty, and brutally honest." She is survived by her daughter and her sister.

Courts in England and Wales have been given new guidance on how to handle cases where someone has been accused of burglary - with a particular focus on domestic burglary.

The Council of Circuit Judges issued the guidance - which includes urging judges to consider the psychological impact on victims.

It follows a campaign by the charity Victim Support and the Association of Police Officers.

Domestic burglary "has a profound and long-lasting effect on those left behind" the guidance says.

Judge David Rennie, who chaired the council, said the impact on victims was "often underrated".

The guidance says burglars who target people's homes "strike at the heart of the victim's privacy and security".

Judge Rennie said: "Victims of domestic burglary are, more often than not, deeply shocked and distressed by the invasion of their home; that intrusion is compounded by the fact the burglar usually enters the house when the occupant is in bed.

"This guidance recognises that fact and, I hope, will assist courts in ensuring that the impact of this particularly invasive crime is properly recognised when sentencing."

The guidance, which has been sent to all sentencing courts in England and Wales, gives examples of when judges might decide to impose a higher sentence - such as where the victim is particularly vulnerable, or where the burglar took steps to avoid being detected, such as wearing a mask or gloves.

It also reminds judges that older people are particularly vulnerable to burglary, and that these crimes often have a "devastating" impact on them.

Acting Deputy Chief Constable Paul Mills, who chairs the APCC Crime Prevention and Response Committee, said: "I very much welcome the publication of this guidance.

"It is vital that the impact of this invasive crime is properly recognised by the courts and that offenders are sentenced appropriately."

"It is vital that all victims of burglary receive the support they need to recover, which is why we also welcome the emphasis on the need for courts to consider the provision of restorative justice."

Time Warner has reported a big jump in profits for the fourth quarter of last year, thanks to strong ad sales and the lack of major hits for its Warner Bros studio.

The owner of CNN, HBO, and Warner Bros said its profits soared 41% to $1.7bn (£1.2bn), beating expectations.

Sales at its WarnerMedia unit, which includes HBO and cable networks such as TNT and TBS, rose by 15% to $11.1bn.

Time Warner's results are the last major set of earnings from a media firm before Disney's report on Thursday.

Disney has been the year's biggest media story because of its $71bn (£45bn) bid for most of 21st Century Fox's entertainment assets.

Time Warner's results showed that it was able to keep costs down and grow revenues despite the gloomy outlook for the pay-TV industry in the US.

Pay-TV subscribers in the US fell by more than 550,000 in the fourth quarter. But that was a smaller loss than in the same period a year earlier.

Profits at HBO, which is preparing to launch a stand-alone streaming service, were down 13% to $255m.

Revenue from the Warner Bros studio, which like other film studios has suffered from a lack of hits, was down 5% on the same period a year earlier at $1.7bn.

However, revenue from TV programming, including shows such as Riverdale and The Big Bang Theory, was up 8% at $7.4bn.

Time Warner's chief executive, Jeff Bewkes, said 2018 was a "strong year" for the company.

"Our outlook for 2019 is positive, and we are focused on executing our plans and serving our customers," he said.

Time Warner's shares rose 2.7% in after-hours trading on Wednesday.

Strong advertising sales and the lack of major programming costs helped Time Warner Inc. post a higher profit Thursday, beating Wall Street expectations.

Net income at the New York media company rose to $526 million ($2.14 a share) in the fourth quarter, compared with $348 million ($1.47 a share) a year ago. Revenue rose 6.5 percent to $7.57 billion.

The results were driven by strong performances at Time Warner's cable networks, including TNT and CNN, and its film studio, Warner Bros. The company also benefited from the weak dollar, which boosted the value of overseas sales.

The DVDs, often of films still in cinemas, were sold in India and as far away as the US and Europe.

Police found more than 700 pirated films when they raided his home in Mumbai earlier this year.

Judge R.D. Khade told the Mumbai court that Khan, a school dropout, was "not too bright" but had become wealthy from his crimes.

"It is astonishing how a person who is not too bright, who left studies after failing in the 10th standard (grade), could make so much money," the judge said, as quoted by the Press Trust of India news agency.

The judge added that Khan had made about 10 million rupees ($220,000; £135,000) from his illegal trade.

Khan was arrested in February after a complaint by the Indian Film Industry's trade body, Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FICCI).

The FICCI, which represents more than 700 producers in India, said that the bootleg film industry was causing it losses of about $1.5bn (£960m) a year.

Khan's lawyer told the court that his client had been encouraged to commit the crimes by a friend.

The friend had shown him "how to go about it", lawyer Nitin Satpute said, as quoted by the Indian Express newspaper.

A man who became the first person in the UK to be convicted of selling illegal Bollywood DVDs has been jailed.

Kabir Rashid, 31, of no known address, sold the films on his YouTube channel, using the alias "Reel Cinema".

The films were recorded in cinema halls in India and uploaded on to YouTube within days of their release.

Rashid was sentenced to three years and eight months in prison at Leicester Crown Court.

The court also heard that he sold more than 1,000 illegal DVDs over seven years and made more than £60,000.

Rashid had pleaded not guilty to all charges, claiming he was not responsible for the content on his YouTube channel. 

But the jury returned a guilty verdict on six counts of unauthorised copies of films, following a five-day trial. 

During his trial, the court heard how Rashid "deliberately targeted" audiences in the UK, India and Pakistan.

His YouTube channel was deleted in 2018 following a BBC investigation.

**Brando 'rejected Godfather role'** – Albert Finney, who has died at the age of 82, was one of a handful of great actors who withstood the lure of Hollywood to remain faithful to theatre and appeared on the stage in Britain and the US. He was also one of a handful who straddled respectability and box-office allure. His career had many peaks, and it weathered the occasional valley. 

In the early 1960s, he was offered the role of Michael Corleone in Francis Ford Coppola's classic movie, The Godfather. The story goes that he turned it down, thinking the script was poorly written. It won't be the last time a great actor passed on a part that would become iconic. But Finney was hardly a fool. He was well aware of the film's quality, having been impressed by a early draft of the script. 

According to his biographer, David Thompson, Finney believed that "the mob was so attractive as the villains that you would be doing a sort of James Bond thing, and he wasn't interested in doing that." It seems unlikely that he would have turned down the chance to play the lead in The Godfather if it had been offered to him. 

According to Thompson, Finney "would ring people up and say 'Have you read this script? It's the worst bunch of crap I've ever read.'" He later admitted that he had been wrong to turn it down. Oil prices have fallen back from their recent highs as fears of a global economic slowdown outweigh concerns about supply.

 Brent crude futures - the international benchmark for oil - were down 82 cents at $85.94 a barrel early on Tuesday.

US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures fell 89 cents to $80.35 a barrel.

Earlier this month, Brent crude touched its highest since early December 2014 at $86.71 a barrel, while WTI reached a seven-year high of $85.41.

But prices have dropped back in the last 10 days as analysts point to signs of weakening demand.

"The threat of demand destruction because of higher fuel prices is looming, with jet fuel demand already showing signs of weakening," said Louise Dickson, an analyst at Rystad Energy.

She added that higher prices, driven up in recent months by the Ukraine war, had also encouraged stronger output from outside the OPEC+ group of major oil producers.

The Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) and its allies, known as OPEC+, have been restricting supply to support prices for more than a year now.

However, the group decided to raise output by 400,000 barrels a day in December, with Russia's contribution being the biggest increase.

But as oil prices came off their highs at the start of the year, OPEC+ decided to stay with its current output plans, despite calls from the US and other nations to produce more oil.

Last week, US President Joe Biden urged OPEC+ to pump more oil in an effort to lower prices.

"While OPEC+ recently agreed to add production, uncertainties remain as to whether the group can actually reach its target," said Ms Dickson.

The country's health authorities have stuck to a policy of zero-COVID, involving lockdowns and mass testing, slamming the brakes on economic activity.

"The sell-off in oil markets is primarily due to demand concerns out of China," said Nishant Bhushan, chief business officer at oil analytics firm Vortexa.

"With China's zero-COVID strategy prompting fresh lockdowns, the concern is that this could impact demand by as much as nearly half a million barrels per day," he added.

Another factor weighing on oil prices was the stronger US dollar, which tends to weigh on commodities priced in the currency. A higher US dollar makes oil more expensive for buyers using other currencies.

The US dollar was boosted by a hawkish shift in tone from the US Federal Reserve, with the central bank likely to raise interest rates by 50 basis points next week after data showed wholesale prices rose 11% in November from a year earlier.

Investors were also awaiting fresh oil supply data from the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) and its allies, together known as OPEC+, on Tuesday. The group will likely stick to its plan for a modest output increase in February at its meeting.

Apple's shuffle is encased in aluminium and comes in three colours - platinum, blue and green.

It can be attached to clothing via a new range of lanyards and belts to be sold by Apple, and features the same "voiceover" feature found on Apple's other iPods that tells the user the name of the song and the artist.

Apple said the device could play up to 15 hours of music on a single battery charge.

The shuffle does not feature the displays found on Apple's other iPods, instead there are three buttons on the device to control the music - volume up, play/pause and volume down.

To select a song, the user presses the play/pause button and the device will randomly choose another track from the playlist.

The shuffle joins Apple's expanding iPod family, which includes the iPod mini, iPod, iPod photo and the iPod video.

Apple said it now had a 70% share of the digital music player market and sold more than 22 million iPods in 2005.

The company also said it sold more than 50 million songs through its iTunes online music store last year.

Apple introduced a new, cheaper iPod model on Monday, marking the first addition to the iPod product line in two and a half years. The new iPod classic, available in 40GB and 80GB sizes, joins the iPod nano and iPod shuffle in the company's digital music player lineup. "We're excited to bring the total iPod family to three great products," said Greg Joswiak, Apple's vice president of hardware product marketing. 

The new iPod classic gives customers around the world another option for enjoying their entire digital music collections, in addition to the market-leading iPod nano and iPod shuffle. Over 55 million iPods have been sold to date. "Customers are going to love the new iPod classic -- it's an incredible all-in-one digital music player with all the passion and all the heritage of the entire iPod family," Joswiak said.

The new iPod classic retains the original iPod's familiar scroll wheel and intuitive navigation. The larger, 80GB model holds up to 40,000 songs, or 200 hours of video, as well as thousands of photos. The 40GB model holds up to 20,000 songs or 100 hours of video, along with thousands of photos.

Both models offer audio controls for playing songs and podcasts, a Cover Flow™ viewing mode that allows users to scroll through album art and select an album by its cover, and the ability to easily create and edit playlists on the go. iPod classic users can also choose from a wide selection of accessories, including speakers, headphones, and carrying cases.

Scotland's elimination from the World Cup finals may work in Ireland's favour as they eye a place in the last 16, according to Irish manager Giovanni Trapattoni.

The Republic of Ireland drew 0-0 with Scotland in their opening group game, before beating Croatia 1-0 and losing 2-0 to Brazil.

The Scots have one point from their three games and are eliminated from the tournament whatever the result of their final group match against Brazil.

"It could be that Scotland's departure is a help for us," said Trapattoni.

"We have four points and we hope to reach seven.

"We are stronger than Scotland, Croatia and even Brazil."
Ireland face Croatia in their final group match on 18 June and a draw would see them through to the last 16 at Scotland's expense.

However, even if they lose in Rustenburg, Trapattoni believes they will still have a chance of going through as one of the four best third-placed teams.

"If we finish third in the group, we have four points and possibly a goal difference of zero or there abouts," added the Italian.

"There are other groups where the third-placed teams have one or two points and a negative goal difference.

"I believe we can qualify as third placed if we don't qualify as a second placed team."

Ireland manager Martin O'Neill has backed his side to win World Cup Group D despite a disappointing start to the campaign.
The Republic of Ireland were left with just a single point from their first two games after a late goal condemned them to a 1-0 defeat against Serbia in Dublin on Tuesday.

The result followed Friday's 0-0 draw with the Netherlands in Amsterdam and leaves the Irish facing an uphill struggle to qualify for the last 16.

But O'Neill believes his team can triumph in a group that also includes Sweden and Mexico.

Speaking at a news conference ahead of Monday's game against the Swedes in Dublin, O'Neill said: "We have always believed that we can win the group.

"Is it a tough group? Very much so. There is not a lot between the four teams if I am being honest.

"I think everyone is capable of beating everyone else, but we have to get ourselves up for the game tomorrow."

England centre Emily Scarratt will lead out the British and Irish Lions in Saturday's opening tour match against New Zealand, as original tour captain Sarah Hunter is ruled out through injury.

The Lions have called up Hunter's England team-mate Emily Robinson as a late replacement, while Scotland's Lyndsay O'Donnell also gets a late call.

England's Katy Daley-Mclean and Abbie Scott, and Ireland's Larissa Muldoon, have all been ruled out of the tournament.

England's Hunter had been set to lead the Lions in New Zealand but injured her shoulder in training, meaning Scarratt, who was named vice-captain, will lead the team out at Eden Park, Auckland.

"It's obviously a huge honour for me to captain the Lions and I'm thrilled to be leading the girls out on Saturday," Scarratt said.

"It's been a really positive build-up to the first Test and we've all been hugely excited about getting out there and showcasing women's rugby on the biggest stage."

The Women's Six Nations has suffered from a high number of injuries, with players from England, Scotland and Wales ruled out of the rest of the competition.

In addition to the five players already mentioned, Wales have lost Ffion Lewis and Laurie Harries, while Scotland's Helen Nelson and Sarah Bonar have also been ruled out.

England have also lost prop Detysha Harper for the rest of the tournament, with an ankle injury.

Ireland centre Muldoon has been ruled out of the remainder of the Women's Six Nations with a foot injury, returning to her province Ulster.

Her absence increases the chances of Robinson being involved in the tournament.

The England centre has been drafted in to replace Hunter, while Scotland's O'Donnell has been called up as cover for Daley-Mclean.

O'Donnell, who plays for Murrayfield Wanderers, can cover at full-back and fly-half and has been drafted in as cover for the remaining Six Nations matches, as well as the Lions tour.

England Women head coach Simon Middleton said: "It's really disappointing for Katy, Abbie and Detysha. All three have worked so hard for this campaign and it's such a shame they've been ruled out.

"We all wish them a speedy recovery and know they'll do everything they can to come back stronger."

England head coach Eddie Jones has confirmed that Owen Farrell will be his captain for the 2022/23 Six Nations Championship.

It comes after Jones left Ben Youngs, Jamie George and Maro Itoje out of his squad for the tournament, and also benched Farrell in England's record-breaking November win over Australia.

Farrell, 31, has been restored as captain after being replaced by Youngs for the Autumn Nations Series, with Jones keen to put the focus back on his squad's leaders after a difficult year.

"Having a captain is important, and having a leadership group is important, but it's important that leaders lead," Jones said.

England begin their campaign against Scotland on 4 February, followed by trips to Wales and France, before hosting Italy and Ireland in Twickenham.

All six matches will be broadcast live on BBC Radio 5 Live or BBC Sounds, with further coverage on BBC Sport website and app.

Search wars hit desktop PCs

Google and Microsoft are battling for desktop search supremacy -- but are desktop users ready for search?

That's the question both companies are hoping to answer with new desktop search applications designed to help users find anything stored on their PCs.

Google has introduced Google Desktop Search, a free application that scans the contents of a PC and displays find results in a Google-style page.

The application, which works on Windows machines, indexes the contents of a PC's hard drive, including email archives, and allows users to search them quickly.

Microsoft, which introduced its own desktop search tool, Windows Desktop Search, as a downloadable beta application last year, plans to release the final version of the product, also for Windows PCs, later this year.

Unlike Google's offering, Microsoft's will be integrated with the next version of Windows, code-named "Longhorn," due out sometime in 2006.

Google's move has raised the stakes in the ongoing battle between the two companies for search dominance.

Microsoft is still well ahead of Google in overall search share with more than 62% of searches conducted in the US performed on Microsoft sites, according to latest data from ComScore Networks.

But Google is nipping at its heels. In February, Google sites accounted for 34.6% of US searches, up from 30.5% a year ago, ComScore said.

Now the two companies are battling for search supremacy on the desktop.

Microsoft has had a desktop search tool since 1995, when it introduced Windows 95.

But Google's new tool is seen as a significant upgrade, since it allows users to search information stored in many different applications, including Outlook, Outlook Express, and Netscape Messenger, as well as PDF and Word files.

It also lets users search across multiple PCs -- a boon for businesses.

All of this has Microsoft scrambling to catch up.

"Google has jumped into the desktop search market in a way that is sure to get Microsoft's attention," said Matt Rosoff, an analyst with Directions on Microsoft, a research firm that tracks the software giant.

"It's clear that Google views desktop search as a platform, and Microsoft will have to respond," he added.

The desktop PC market is in turmoil. For the first time in more than a decade, worldwide desktop shipments are on the decline.

Figures from technology analysts IDC show an 8.3% drop in desktop PC shipments between Q2 2022 and Q2 2021.

IDC has attributed this decline to businesses and educational institutions continuing to shift to laptops and tablets, a trend which accelerated during the pandemic.

"The decline of the desktop PC market can be attributed to a few factors, including the increasing use of laptops and tablets in the workplace and educational institutions," said Tom Mainelli, group vice president for devices and intelligence at IDC.

"Furthermore, the surge in remote work and learning during the pandemic, combined with ongoing supply chain constraints and inflation, have pushed the desktop PC market into a state of flux."

However, there are some vendors that have managed to grow their shipments in the desktop PC market.

IDC noted that Dell Technologies maintained its top position in the global desktop market with 23.5% of shipments.

It was followed by Lenovo, which experienced a significant decline in desktop shipments compared to the previous year.

HP Inc and Apple occupied the third and fourth positions with 21.9% and 7.2% of the market share, respectively.

IDC reported that the gaming segment was one of the bright spots in the desktop market, with gaming desktop shipments up 8.2% year-over-year.

This is due to the release of new gaming PCs and the continued growth of the gaming market, according to IDC.

"Gaming continues to be a bright spot in the desktop market, with gaming desktop shipments up 8.2% year over year in Q2 2022," said Jitesh Ubrani, research manager for IDC's Mobile Device Trackers.

"This is due to the release of new gaming PCs and the continued growth of the gaming market, although gaming laptops remain the more popular choice among consumers."

In addition, IDC noted that the commercial desktop market was hit the hardest, with shipments down 10.4% year-over-year.

This was due to businesses and educational institutions continuing to shift to laptops and tablets, as well as ongoing supply chain constraints and inflation.

IDC does not expect the desktop PC market to recover any time soon, as it believes that the shift towards mobile devices will continue.

The total number of migrants who have entered the UK by landing on Scottish beaches has reached more than 2,000, according to new figures from Police Scotland.

The force released details of its response to "summer tide" after SNP MPs criticised what they described as a lack of information from the government.

The figures show that 2,079 people arrived between 1 April and 31 October.

Most of the landings were on the beaches of the Pentland Firth - a strait between Scotland's mainland and Orkney.

Police Scotland released the figures in response to a freedom of information request from the Press and Journal newspaper.

They include 1,172 men, 391 women and 366 "unknown" and were arrived on 206 separate days.

The statistics show that the majority of those who came to Scotland had travelled from Iran - with many also fleeing from Afghanistan, Iraq and Syria.

They were found on 40 different beaches in the Highlands and islands - many on the Orkney and Shetland coastlines.

The force launched its Operation Tide in response to the increase in people crossing the English Channel from France to England in small boats.

It involves officers from Police Scotland, the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service, the Coastguard, RNLI, Scottish Ambulance Service and the UK Border Agency.

The operation has been scaled back since September - with the UK government now responsible for arranging accommodation and "contingency" arrangements for those who are picked up.

Earlier this month, SNP MP Angus MacNeil - who chairs the House of Commons Committee on Transport - accused the government of being "in denial" about migrants arriving in Scotland.

He claimed that ministers had "no clue" about the scale of the issue as they had "no wish to know".

Mr MacNeil said at the time that he had been told by the UK government that 51 people had arrived in Scotland since the start of the year.

The SNP has called on the Scottish government to establish its own asylum processing system, separate from the UK.

MSP Joan McAlpine said the figures released by Police Scotland showed that the "summer tide" had been a "major crisis".

"People have been washing up on Scottish shores for months and the UK government's failure to respond is unacceptable," she added.

A UK government spokesperson said that people should not travel to the UK through dangerous and illegal routes and should instead claim asylum in the first safe country they arrive in.

"The government's

The Scottish First Minister Nicola Sturgeon has described a new wave toll for England as “shameful” and accused the UK government of being “totally insensitive”.

Her comments came after UK Transport Secretary Grant Shapps admitted that the estimated cost of the recent flooding in England was £1bn.

In Scotland, the cost of the storm which hit the west coast of the country over the New Year is estimated to be £200m.

Ms Sturgeon said this was “not an equal partnership” when she was asked if the Scottish Government could expect financial support from the UK government to recover from the storms.

The first minister was being interviewed on BBC Radio 4’s Today programme after Scottish Conservative leader Douglas Ross had also accused the UK government of being “totally insensitive” to the needs of Scottish fishermen who have suffered as a result of the storms.

Mr Shapps said that the UK government had “always” worked together with the Scottish Government. 

He added that “all the mechanisms” were in place for the two governments to discuss further help for Scotland following the storms.

Rory McIlroy will bid to win his home Irish Open for the first time in nearly 20 years after confirming his attendance at Mount Juliet in May.

The Northern Irishman, 32, won the last of his 19 European Tour titles to date in Spain in 2019.

He followed that victory at the HSBC Champions in Shanghai with victory at the WGC-HSBC Champions a few weeks later.

But the former world number one has struggled for form since golf's coronavirus-enforced shutdown in March 2020.

McIlroy secured his place at this year's Masters with a top-10 finish at last month's PGA Tour Championship in Florida.

He finished seventh at Sawgrass, with compatriot Shane Lowry collecting the trophy after a gripping final round in which he overcame Justin Thomas on the final green.

That performance ensured Lowry would return to the top of the world rankings with the victory - but McIlroy hopes to join him there by winning in Ireland.

"It's a tournament that's very close to my heart," said McIlroy, who won the Irish Open as an 18-year-old amateur in 2007.

"It's been a while since I've been able to contend in it and hopefully I can put up a good performance and kick off the summer with a win."

Rory McIlroy will seek a third victory in four starts on the European Tour when he leads the field at the Madrid Open on Friday.

The world number two has continued his superb early-season form after winning the Dubai Desert Classic in January and following that with a memorable victory in Saudi Arabia last week.

Now the Northern Irishman will aim to add a second Spanish title to his collection after winning the 2019 edition of the Andalucia Valderrama Masters - an event hosted by his close friend and Ryder Cup teammate Jon Rahm. 

McIlroy gets another opportunity to succeed in the country once again this week at Club de Golf Escorial, which will also host the Spanish Open next season as part of a run of three consecutive events on the European Tour. 

A field of strong competitors includes former Masters champion Patrick Reed and 2021 US Open winner Jon Rahm, who will attempt to defend his title after winning last year's event by one shot ahead of Tommy Fleetwood.

Who will triumph in Madrid? Will Rory McIlroy continue his dominance on the European Tour?

Film-maker Morgan Matthews says it is "difficult" to get investors interested in campaigns for social good.
His documentary about school bullying, Defiance, is one of five short films nominated for best live action short at this year's Oscars.
But he said it was "very difficult" to get backing for the project as it "didn't fit the model" of what investors usually backed.
Matthews, 34, said he had to "beg, borrow and almost steal" to get the film made.
His film tells the story of a young victim of bullying who brings her tormentor to justice.
It features an appearance from Game of Thrones star Peter Dinklage, who also voices the audiobook of Matthews' original novel on which the film is based.
Matthews, who previously directed the well-received documentary Life in a Day, said it was hard to "get the balance" right between "making a film that is entertaining and makes you think".
He added: "It seems absurd that you can make a film about bullying, which is a social issue, but you can't advertise it because of the issues around bullying - it's a Catch-22.
"Ultimately, it comes down to money. If you are campaigning for an issue like this, it is very difficult to get investors."
Matthews said he was "very proud" of the film, which has been shown at film festivals around the world, and is "hopeful" it might win an Oscar next month, even though he does not expect to be able to advertise the film properly if it does.
The 90-second advert for the Defiance campaign, which was released earlier this year, was banned by London's Transport for London (TfL) and Manchester's Transport for Greater Manchester (TfGM) for being "too graphic and not acceptable for a public service".
The Oscar nominations were announced on 10 January. The awards ceremony takes place in Los Angeles on 24 February.

The BBC has refused to run a trailer for Sam Taylor-Johnson's new film about the last days of Marilyn Monroe amid concerns that it could be seen as a violation of rules on political advertising. The film's distributors submitted a trailer for Passion, which depicts Monroe's fictionalization of her troubled private life, for inclusion on the BBC's main channels. However, the broadcaster decided that the trailer was politically biased and could be construed as an endorsement of Christianity. 

A BBC source said the broadcaster did not believe the trailer was "objective" because its narration contained the phrase "Jesus Christ". The source added: "It was decided that the trailer was political and, therefore, should not be broadcast. "It's not unusual for political trailers to be submitted for BBC broadcast, and equally it's not unusual for them not to be broadcast. "In this case, the trailer was deemed to be biased and, as such, it was not shown on our networks." The BBC's decision has sparked a debate about whether the corporation has taken an overtly political approach to the trailer.

Martin Freeman, the actor and comedian who is a supporter of the Conservative Party, criticized the decision on Twitter, saying: "Jesus Christ indeed, the BBC won't run the trailer for Passion because they think it's too political. "So essentially any reference to Jesus is political but the many references to Stalin in Wolf Hall are just part of the general historical context. Seems odd. 

Freeman's comments were criticized by some Twitter users, with one person writing: "Not sure you're qualified to comment on this, Martin. You're not an expert on everything, despite your many talents. Let the experts do their job." 

The BBC's decision comes after it was revealed that John Whittingdale, the Culture Secretary, had written to the broadcaster demanding that it improves its coverage of religion. In the letter, Whittingdale said the BBC's output on religion was "too narrow" and "should reflect a faith perspective". The trailer for Passion will still be shown on other channels, such as ITV and Channel 4.

The UK government should increase its support for manufacturing, or risk losing jobs to Europe, an industry group is warning.

The Manufacturing Technologies Association (MTA) said a "perfect storm" of factors meant investment in the sector was needed.

It said high energy prices, increased labour and raw material costs and a shortage of skilled engineers were combining to create a crisis.

The MTA, which represents 400 firms in the sector, said one-third of those firms were considering moving some operations abroad.

The call for action comes in the same week that car maker Nissan announced it was turning its UK plant into an electric vehicle (EV) hub.

It also comes ahead of the government's ongoing review of business rates, a tax paid on non-residential properties, which have added to the pressures facing firms.

The MTA's call was backed by engineering companies, including Siemens and Rolls-Royce.

 MTA chief executive James Selka said: "There is a perfect storm of problems impacting on the sector.

"High energy prices are making it extremely difficult for manufacturers to invest in increasing output in the UK, whilst increased labour and raw material costs are causing a crisis in the supply chain as suppliers are finding it difficult to absorb these costs and pass them on."

He added that a shortage of skilled engineers and a lack of investment in technology was "stopping our members from taking on new work and increasingly they are considering moving operations abroad".

"This is a very real concern that needs addressing urgently by the government," he added.

A government spokesperson said: "We are taking decisive action to support British manufacturers during these global price surges, including introducing a £5bn Energy Bill Relief Scheme that offers discounts on energy bills for eligible firms, and a £1bn programme to help businesses improve their energy efficiency.

"We are supporting firms with skills development and have recently expanded the eligibility for the annual investment allowance to help businesses invest in plant and machinery this year."

Manufacturing jobs are once again in the spotlight as the UK government faces increased pressure to save them. The call comes after a recent report showed a sharp decline in the number of people employed in the sector over the past year.

The report, by the Manufacturing Institute, found that the number of manufacturing jobs had fallen by 2.8% in the past year, with a sharp decline in the number of jobs in the automotive and aerospace industries. The report also found that the number of jobs in the sector was down by almost a quarter since the beginning of the pandemic.

The call to save manufacturing jobs has been supported by industry groups such as the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT), which has called for the government to take action to support the sector. The SMMT has said that the sector is facing a "perfect storm" of challenges, including the pandemic, Brexit, and changes in technology.

The government has said that it is committed to supporting the manufacturing sector and has pointed to the recent announcement of a new £1.5 billion investment in the sector as evidence of its support. However, industry groups have said that more needs to be done to protect jobs in the sector.

Ringtone sellers face tougher rules on what they can sell, following a spate of complaints from customers.

The Committee of Advertising Practice (CAP) has written to all major providers, telling them to stop selling ringtones as mobile content, and instead to treat them as premium rate telephone services.

The move follows a surge in complaints to the Advertising Standards Authority (ASA).

Customers have been unhappy with the cost and difficulty of getting refunds after they bought a ringtone by text message and did not receive it.

CAP claims some advertisers were not adhering to its code on telephone services.

In a letter to ringtone providers, CAP said that text messages to purchase ringtones should be considered as premium rate telephone services, and subject to the same rules.

These rules include ensuring that callers are informed of the price they will pay, that there is a simple mechanism for opting out, and that their telephone bill accurately reflects the service they have bought.

CAP claims that some advertisers were not adhering to these rules, and has told them to ensure that their advertising is completely transparent.

In July this year, the ASA received 69 complaints about a ringtone advertisement placed in a newspaper by a provider called Mviva.

Complainants said that the advertisement did not make it clear that they would be charged for the ringtone, and that the mechanism for opting out was difficult.

A spokesperson for the CAP said: "Given the ongoing level of complaints, we wrote to providers to remind them of their obligations and to ensure that they are adhering to the code."

Mviva was contacted for comment.

The Federal Trade Commission is cracking down on ringtone sellers that charge customers without their explicit consent. The FTC has issued a warning to companies that use text messages to gather phone numbers for ringtone downloads, telling them to get express consent from customers before charging them. The announcement comes after several cases were opened against companies accused of charging customers without consent. In one case, a company must pay nearly $50 million to customers who were charged for ringtones they did not want. 

The FTC's warning has ringtones sellers taking a closer look at their policies. Some companies are already making changes to ensure they're following the rules. Others are waiting to see how the situation plays out. The FCC is hoping that its move will protect consumers from unwanted charges and make it easier for them to get refunds when they do incur them.

Disney has given its support to Sony's new high definition DVD format, a move which is likely to give the format a huge boost.

The decision is a major boost for the Sony HD DVD format, which is competing with a rival offering from Toshiba.

Disney's support will give the HD DVD format a huge lift, as the company controls some of the most popular films, including Star Wars and Pixar animations.

The format war has been going on for nearly two years, ever since Toshiba launched its HD DVD format, backed by Microsoft and Intel.

Sony later launched its own version, and now seems to be winning the battle, with a growing number of supporters.

Last week, US retailer Best Buy said it would stock the HD DVD players and movies in its stores.

This week, US director James Cameron said he had tested both HD DVD and Blu-ray and decided the HD DVD was superior.

"HD DVD is winning the format war, hands down," he said.

However, not all supporters of Blu-ray have given up hope.

Apple chief executive Steve Jobs, a strong backer of the Blu-ray format, said he believed that Blu-ray had broader support among consumers and he was confident it would prevail.

In a posting on Apple's website, Mr Jobs said that in addition to Best Buy, electronics giants Samsung and LG had also thrown their support behind HD DVD.

But he said that of the top six US electronics retailers, five were supporting Blu-ray, and that in Japan seven of the top eight electronics makers were backing the format.

"We think Blu-ray will prevail, based on its superior feature set and the growing number of Blu-ray players and titles available," he said.

Disney has decided to support Sony's new DVD format, known as Blu-ray Disc. The decision comes after Disney spent months weighing up the pros and cons of the various next-generation DVD formats. Blu-ray is being developed by a group of companies including Sony, Philips, and Panasonic. The format boasts a capacity of up to 50 gigabytes, which is enough for a feature-length film in high definition. 

Disney has been heavily involved in the development of the Blu-ray format. The company has been a leading member of the Blu-ray Disc Association's steering committee. In a statement, Disney said it would release its films in the Blu-ray format starting later this year. 

While Disney's announcement is a major boost for Blu-ray, the format still faces competition from two other high-definition optical disc formats. One is being developed by Toshiba, called HD DVD, and the other is known as Advanced Optical Disc. Both of these formats have the support of major electronics manufacturers. It remains to be seen whether Blu-ray will become the standard for high-definition DVDs.

West Ham United goalkeeper Paul Robinson has backed his deputy Robert Green to step up if he has to miss the Carling Cup final against Manchester United on Sunday.

England international Robinson has recovered from a calf injury but the decision on who will start between the sticks has been taken out of his hands.

West Ham stated on Friday that Robinson had not been included in the party travelling to Cardiff and it is now certain that he will miss out.

That means Green, who has had an eventful season despite playing second fiddle to Robinson, will be in goal at the Millennium Stadium.

And Robinson has given his colleague a vote of confidence by revealing he has told Green he believes he is capable of playing in the final.

"Robert knows what a good goalkeeper he is," Robinson said. "I have told him that he can be a top-class goalkeeper.

"I have every confidence in him and if he plays in the final I know he will do well. He has saved us on numerous occasions this season.

"He has been brilliant professional, a good goalkeeper to work with and I wish him well for the final."

Italy goalkeeper Carlo Cudicini will miss the Carling Cup final against Arsenal on Sunday due to a shoulder injury. The 31-year-old was hurt in training on Tuesday and will be out for two weeks. Chelsea manager Jose Mourinho described the injury as "bad, very bad". He said he did not know who would replace Cudicini, but that he did not want to use 38-year-old reserve keeper Pete Cech, who has not played since he was injured in a car crash in October.

Cudicini has been in excellent form this season, keeping seven clean sheets in 12 games. He has been ever-present in the Chelsea side since Petr Cech was ruled out with a skull fracture. The keeper has been credited with playing a major role in the club's revival under Mourinho.

His injury comes as Chelsea face a crucial period in the season. As well as the Carling Cup final, they have a Champions League last-16 tie against former manager Avram Grant's Maccabi Tel Aviv and an FA Cup fourth-round replay against Watford. They are also chasing success in the Premier League, where they face title rivals Manchester United on Sunday, 20 February.

South African car demand surges

South Africa's new car market is booming, confounding economists' predictions that borrowing costs would choke off demand as the central bank tightened monetary policy to curb inflation.

They are predicting record sales this year of more than 150,000 units, with growth in the motor sector outpacing the economy's expansion.

The demand has been fuelled by low interest rates and people opting to buy instead of renting.

But some analysts are questioning how long the boom can last. 

Already, the used car market is showing signs of overheating.

And with interest rates expected to rise further - and economic growth likely to slow - the new car market is likely to cool off.

South Africa's car market is an important barometer of the country's economic health.

Not only does it employ about 14% of the country's workforce, but it is also a key indicator of the strength of consumer demand and confidence.

When the economy started to grow again after the 2009 recession, car sales took off, climbing by more than 70% in five years to 556,000 units in 2014, according to data from the National Association of Automobile Manufacturers of South Africa.

But economists had expected the boom to end when the South African Reserve Bank started raising interest rates in early 2014 to curb rising inflation - increasing them five times over the subsequent year-and-a-half.

However, instead of choking off demand, higher borrowing costs have so far had little impact on the appetite of South Africans to buy new cars.

Official figures show that total vehicle sales last year grew 5.2% to 152,488 units, with the new car market up by more than 8% to 136,385 units. 

The figures include sales of demonstration vehicles and pre-owned cars, but exclude sales to car rental companies.

Some in the industry believe the growth can be sustained.

"All the factors that drove sales in 2014 are still in place - low interest rates, good value for money, great model offerings, a growing economy and positive consumer sentiment," says Johan van Velden, the chairman of the National Association of Automobile Manufacturers of South Africa.

However, not everyone is so optimistic.

"The market is likely to cool off this year," says Arno van der Veen, a senior economist at RMB.

South African car demand surges in 2022, buoyed by strong consumer demand and increased investments in the automotive industry.

Sales of new vehicles in South Africa surged 43% year on year to 558,955 units in 2022, according to data from the National Association of Automotive Manufacturers of South Africa. This marks the first time since 2016 that the market has surpassed the 500,000-unit mark.

The strong performance was driven by a number of factors, including a recovery in consumer demand after the COVID-19 pandemic, as well as increased investments in the automotive industry, such as the announcement of a new Ford assembly plant in South Africa.

However, the industry still faces challenges, including the ongoing semiconductor chip shortage, which has limited the production of some models. In addition, the recent rise in interest rates in South Africa has also increased the cost of financing, which could impact demand in the coming months.

Despite these challenges, industry analysts remain optimistic about the outlook for the South African car market, with many expecting continued growth in the coming years.

Gamers could help unlock the secrets of a 500-year-old painting by Leonardo da Vinci
By designing virtual robots to scrub the surface of the painting in ultra-high definition, researchers aim to remove centuries of dirt and grime to reveal the masterpiece in all its glory

Experts hope the project will shed light on the techniques used by the Renaissance artist, and offer insights into the pigments he used

Gamers could help unlock the secrets of a €300m (£275m) Leonardo da Vinci painting newly unveiled at the Louvre.

French researchers are appealing to gamers to help clean up the surface of the restored Salvator Mundi by designing virtual robots to scrub the surface of the painting in ultra-high definition.

They hope the project will shed light on the techniques used by the Renaissance artist, and offer insights into the pigments he used, as well as the exact tone of the colours.

"There's never been a painting analysed in this way before," said Marc Vallière, the scientific director of the Opéra National de Paris, who is heading the initiative.

"We're going to scrub the surface of the painting in ultra-high definition and the painting itself is going to become a database," he told the BBC.

The project - which has been compared to Google's Street View - aims to remove centuries of dirt and grime that have built up on the surface of the painting, and could even help answer questions about its authenticity.

Over the past two years, the researchers have been examining the painting in minute detail - capturing everything from the cracks in the paint to the traces of restoration work carried out in the past.

They have created a digital replica of the painting, which has around 30 layers of tiny pixels - each one containing information about the colours used by the Italian master.

By comparing the replica with the original, the researchers hope to be able to scrub away the dirt and reveal the masterpiece in all its glory.

"We're going to clean the painting, not with solvents or any other material, but with pixels," said Mr Vallière.

The project - which has been described as "madness" by the Louvre - could also offer historians a chance to discover whether the painting has been tampered with over the centuries, and to find out more about how it was restored in the past.

"This is a painting that has been heavily restored, and so the underdrawing is not necessarily by Leonardo," said Mr Vallière.

 iPods dominate the market for portable music devices in the US, but they face growing competition from phones that play music and cheaper devices that play MP3 files.

Singapore's economy grew an estimated 8.1% in 2004, driven by the booming semiconductor industry and a rebound in tourism, the government said.

The announcement released by the Trade and Industry Ministry on Friday showed that the growth rate was higher than the government's initial forecast of 7.5%-8.5% made in February last year.

For 2005, the ministry forecast that the economy would grow 3% to 5%, down from an initial forecast of 5% to 7%.

"The growth momentum is expected to slow largely due to the high base of 2004 and the expected moderation in the global economy," the ministry said.

2005 growth will also be affected by the tightening of monetary policies by major economies, weakening consumer sentiment and the high value of the Singapore dollar, the ministry said.

The government said it would release detailed figures on the economy later this month.

Singapore's economy grew an estimated 8.1 percent in 2004, the highest growth rate in more than 30 years, on the back of strong exports and buoyant consumer spending, the government said on Thursday.

The growth rate was more than double the 3.5 percent expansion in 2003 and surpassed the previous record of 7.8 percent in 1980.

The island state's manufacturing output jumped 15.5 percent in 2004, accounting for nearly half the economy's growth, while the services sector expanded 7.5 percent, the Trade and Industry Ministry said.

The construction sector contracted 3.7 percent, however, as the government continued its policy of restricting foreign work visas to control the population.

'We have not seen such rapid growth in a long time,' Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong told parliament. 'But we must not be carried away by the figures. The underlying trends are more important.'

Gervais writing Simpsons episode

Ronald Reagan - the 40th American president - once noted: "The toughest job in the world is being president of the United States."

He was probably right. But being the first ever British prime minister on The Simpsons? That's got to be up there.

Writing exclusively for the BBC, Gervais has revealed that he has been asked to pen an episode of the long-running cartoon show.

"One of the many perks of my success is that I get to do stuff like this," he said. "I've always been a big fan of The Simpsons. It's a huge honour."

Gervais, who shot to fame as David Brent in BBC sitcom The Office, will voice-over an episode based on the life of British Prime Minister Tony Blair.

The script will be written by Richard Appel, who was behind the Emmy Award-winning instalment Homer's Phobia, in which Homer fears he has HIV.

"I'm working closely with Richard Appel, who wrote that HIV episode, which I thought was hilarious and very clever," said Gervais.

"It's odd to see Blair, Bush and Dole as animated characters, but they are incredibly accurate visually and in their speech and mannerisms."

Gervais, whose BBC Two series Extras returns for a second series next month, said working on The Simpsons was "a childhood dream come true".

"To be honest, I always thought that The Simpsons existed in a kind of alternative universe to the UK - a bit like Twin Peaks," he said.

"So it's weird to see the inside of the Oval Office and the White House in Springfield.

"But it's exciting. It's a brilliant show and I can't wait to see what David Silverman (executive producer) and the animators do with my script."

It is not known whether Blair - who is currently mired in the controversy over the Iraq war - will appear in the finished episode.

"I don't know if Blair will be in it," said Gervais. "They haven't told me if they're going to make any of the scenes I've written.

"It's not like I can ring Blair up and ask him to do voiceover work. I'm sure he's got enough on his plate."

The episode will be broadcast in May.

The London Stock Exchange has asked its shareholders to reject a £79bn ($104bn) bid from Deutsche Börse, saying it "very significantly" undervalues the business.

The LSE described the offer as "simply not credible" and said Deutsche had not carried out sufficient due diligence.

Shareholders in the German company have until 26 July to decide whether to approve the bid. 

Shares in the LSE closed on Friday at £76.85 while shares in Deutsche Börse were trading at €91.35.

The LSE's adviser, Goldman Sachs, is expected to report back before the end of July.

Shareholders in the LSE, which includes the London Stock Exchange Group and the Milan Stock Exchange, include BlackRock, Capital Group, Axa, Invesco and Lansdowne.

They have been urged by the LSE to take "no action" over the offer for the time being. 

In May, the LSE rejected an unsolicited £70bn offer from the owner of the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, CME, as "unsolicited, inadequate and substantially uncertain".

At the time, the LSE said that its board believed that the offer "very significantly" undervalued the business.

Last week, US exchange Nasdaq joined the fray with an £86bn bid for the LSE.

Like the Deutsche Börse offer, the Nasdaq bid is largely comprised of its own shares.

The London Stock Exchange has approached the UK's financial regulator to seek clearance for a complicated plan to buy the Deutsche Börse stock exchange.

The LSE made the request regarding its planned merger with Refinitiv, due to be completed next year.

It wants the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) to waive an obligation for it to sell its interest in MTS Group, an electronic trading platform.

The LSE has been forced to rethink its approach to the $14.8bn (£11bn) takeover of Deutsche Börse after the deal was blocked by the European Commission in February.

The commission said the merger would harm competition in the trading of bonds and repurchase agreements, known as repos.

The LSE has until early next year to submit a revised plan for the takeover.

In August, the LSE said it had entered into an agreement to buy the 37% of Refinitiv it does not already own, and had planned to fund the purchase by selling its holding in MTS.

However, the LSE said on Monday that its request to the FCA was unrelated to its plans to buy Refinitiv.

The LSE added: "There is no certainty that the FCA will agree to the waiver."

England centre Ben Wilkinson has been cleared to play against Edinburgh at Murrayfield on Saturday after returning to training following a head injury.

The 28-year-old Yorkshireman, who has scored 17 tries in 57 appearances for the Leeds-based club, was forced off after just two minutes of the opening match of the Six Nations against Scotland last weekend.

He was subsequently diagnosed with concussion and has followed the necessary return-to-play protocols this week.

It is a big boost for Dean Richards' side as they bid to arrest an eight-match losing sequence - their last victory was at home to Edinburgh at the end of last year.

The match will be shown live on BBC Two, with coverage starting at 19:30 GMT.

Eddie Wilkinson will make his 100th appearance for London Irish on Sunday if he comes through a fitness test on his injured calf. The versatile back, who can play at full-back or on the wing, has scored 62 points including two tries for the Exiles this season. He has scored seven tries in his 99 previous appearances for the club. Wilkinson said: "The milestone is a nice personal achievement but the most important thing is that we get back to winning ways tomorrow."

BBC Sport - Leeds United midfielder Adam Prutton has been charged with misconduct by the Football Association for his involvement in an alleged altercation with a fan after a match.

The FA has charged Prutton with "misconduct in relation to media and improper conduct".

If found guilty, the 28-year-old is facing a ban of up to six matches and a fine of £25,000.

Prutton, who has made 14 appearances for Leeds this season, has until 18:00 GMT on Wednesday, 18 March to respond to the charge.

In the FA's charge sheet, it is claimed that Prutton's "conduct in the vicinity of the tunnel at the end of the fixture was improper".

It is also claimed he breached FA Rule E3, which relates to "misconduct in relation to media".

Leeds United have confirmed they will be conducting their own investigation into the incident.

Declan Prutton has become the first referee to be charged with misconduct under a new FA rule after he admitted failing to report a breach of betting rules. The governing body confirmed that the 37-year-old official had been charged with two breaches of its rules on betting. Prutton admitted both charges and is likely to face a lengthy ban from the game.

The first charge relates to placing bets on the result, handicap and total number of goals in football matches. The second charge relates to disclosing information for betting purposes. Prutton has been refereeing professionally since 2013 and was due to take charge of League Two games this weekend. He has now been removed from all appointments.

The new rule was introduced by the FA in August. It prohibits any involvement in betting or any form of gambling on football. If found guilty, individuals face a minimum ban of four years and a maximum of 16 years. They would also be banned from attending football matches in the UK. 

In a statement, the FA said: "Declan Prutton has been charged with misconduct in relation to The FA Rules on Betting. He has admitted both charges and will have a disciplinary hearing. The date of the hearing will be set in due course."

Prutton is the assistant manager of Scottish Premiership club Kilmarnock. The former Scotland Under-21 international spent the majority of his playing career at Swindon Town. He also had spells with Norwich City, Leeds United and Prutton had two loan spells with Scottish club Rangers. 

Swindon Town said they were "disappointed" with Prutton's actions and confirmed they would be conducting their own investigation into the matter. In a statement, the League Two club said: "Swindon Town are aware of the recent FA charges brought against former player and current assistant manager Declan Prutton. The club are disappointed with this news and will be conducting their own investigation into the matter."

The UK government has pledged £1bn ($1.4bn) to the international effort to develop a vaccine for coronavirus.

The sum - for research and development - will be paid in UK aid, Chancellor Rishi Sunak announced in his budget on Wednesday.

Mr Sunak said the money would help "create a vaccine" for Covid-19 "that will ensure we can protect people here in the UK and around the world".

UK aid, the Department for International Development (DfID), will also provide £388m to help end the pandemic and distribute treatments and vaccines.

It will spend £300m on the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (Cepi), a global alliance working on Covid-19 vaccines.

Cepi has already funded three promising candidates, according to Mr Sunak.

Additionally, DfID will give £38m to the WHO to help distribute coronavirus vaccines, treatments and tests.

It will also spend £62m on research and development, including testing new treatments.

The budget also included £1.35bn to accelerate the rollout of coronavirus vaccines, including helping the NHS to become ready to distribute a vaccine next month.

This included £150m to fund 50 million doses of a vaccine, if one becomes available, Mr Sunak said.

The budget also pledged £5bn for testing and tracing over the next six months.

The UK has pledged to donate 100 million COVID-19 vaccines to developing countries in a bid to help stop the spread of the virus. 

The donation will comprise five million doses of the Pfizer vaccine and 95 million doses of the AstraZeneca vaccine. 

The pledge comes as part of the G7 summit, where leaders of the group of seven largest advanced economies pledged to send 1 billion vaccines to developing countries over the next 12 months. 

The UK's pledge is one of the most significant contributions to the vaccine effort made by a single country to date. 

The vaccines are expected to begin being delivered in the coming weeks, with five million doses expected to be sent to the Covax programme by the end of September. The remainder will be sent by the end of 2022. 

This initiative comes alongside the recent announcement that the UK will accept donations of surplus vaccines from wealthy countries in a bid to help vaccinate more people. 

The UK has been at the forefront of the vaccine effort, with a successful rollout of the vaccine to its population. The recent announcement demonstrates the UK's continued commitment to combating the pandemic and protecting the most vulnerable. 

This donation will play a significant role in helping to stop the spread of the virus and ending the pandemic.

A television station has refused to air a show about an animal shelter after it was told the organisers were against gay marriage.  The show's creators say the station refused to broadcast it in the US because of the organisers' religious beliefs.  Animal Planet postponed the show after being told the leaders of an animal shelter in Texas did not support same-sex marriage.  The show was scheduled to debut on 7 February, but the network said it had decided to "reassess" the programme in the light of the views of its hosts, who are Christians.  Animal Planet is owned by Discovery Communications. In a statement, it said: "Animal Planet believes in inclusive programming and strives for an inclusive environment for its employees, viewers and fans across all platforms."  But reality show producers, Huhman Productions, said the network wanted to "censor" the series because of the religious beliefs of its hosts, and was "denying their First Amendment rights".  The show's creators also complained that Animal Planet had not told them specifically what was "problematic" with the series, other than a memo that said hosts Steven and Debbie Anderson needed to issue a statement "supporting gay marriage".  "Asking them to do this is a denial of their First Amendment rights," the producers said in a statement. "Our position is that Animal Planet is censoring Steve and Debbie's show because of their religious beliefs on marriage, which has nothing to do with the show." The show's creators also said the Andersons had received death threats because of the controversy.  The show was originally scheduled to air on 7 February at 7pm Eastern Time.

The BBC has refused to air a documentary that offers an unflinching look at the adoption process in the UK, after two major charities pulled their support for the show.

The BBC said it had decided not to air the programme, called "The Baby Factory", because it was "not in the BBC's editorial standards". A BBC spokesperson added: "The programme was due to be broadcast on BBC One next month but it has become clear that, given the current discussions around the adoption process in the UK, we will not be able to broadcast it.

"The BBC has very high standards of impartiality and the programme does not meet these standards given significant public debate around the adoption process in the UK."

The BBC's decision comes after the British Association for Adoption and Fostering (BAAF) and Adoption UK pulled their support for the programme, which they had been advised would offer an "unflinching look at every aspect of the adoption process".

The BBC was due to air the programme, made by independent production company Dragonfly, as part of its "Real Story" series.

US charity anthem 'We Are The World' is re-released with some of the original artists and some new stars.

The single, re-recorded by a group of US artists to help raise money for the Haiti earthquake appeal, has entered the US singles chart at number two.

The song has raised $300,000 (£200,000) for the We Are The World Foundation, set up after the original was released in 1985 to help African famine relief.

Organizers hope that this year's version will raise $1 million in the next few months.

The song was originally recorded by a group of 45 artists including Michael Jackson, Cyndi Lauper, Bruce Springsteen and Madonna.

This year's line-up comprises of both original singers and new stars, including Jennifer Hudson, Miley Cyrus, and Justin Bieber.

The project was the idea of producer Randy Phillips, who wanted to re-record the song in order to raise money for the victims of the Haiti earthquake.

He said he wanted to "continue the legacy" of the original song and to "encourage today's generation to stand up and take action".

The song was made available for download on iTunes and other digital music services on 14 February.

The proceeds from the sales of the single will go to the We Are The World Foundation.
