A charity has warned that homes for vulnerable people are facing "uncertainty and confusion" over the government's new immigration rules, which could leave them without vital staff.

Changing rules for EU nationals working in health and social care could mean care homes, nurseries and home-care providers struggling to fill job vacancies.

The Refugee Council warned of "difficult choices" facing services that protect the UK's most vulnerable people.

The government said its new immigration system would be "fairer" and ensure people coming to the UK "have the skills we need".

The charity's warning comes after the government announced that from 2021, EU citizens, regardless of whether they have lived in the UK for years, will have to apply for work visas and prove they have the skills to get a job.

Social care providers are already facing a staffing crisis and the new immigration rules could prevent them from recruiting carers from Europe, whose services are often crucial.

The Refugee Council said the change in the law had caused "confusion and uncertainty" for its network of partners providing housing and support to vulnerable people, such as asylum seekers and refugees.

It said the government's current policy offered "no certainty" to EU nationals working in these areas that they will be able to remain in the UK.

This could lead to a loss of staff at a time when the charity said these services were already struggling to recruit and retain staff.

"We are hearing of difficult choices being made on whether to continue providing services at all," the Refugee Council said.

"This is at a time when the need for these services has never been greater."

The charity said the situation was "particularly acute" in rural areas where housing and support services were already struggling to find staff.

It said the loss of EU nationals would be "particularly felt" in these areas.

A government spokesperson said its new immigration system would be "fairer to all, with no preferential treatment for any one nationality".

"It will be open to talent from around the world and porous to all, as it has been for generations, reflecting our desire to continue to attract the people who have made this country what it is today," they added.

The work of a private research institute that has been linked to far-right activist and YouTuber Lauren Southern has been deemed "highly suspect" by an alliance of scientists. 

The Centre for Countering Digital Hate (CCDH) - which fights against hate speech online - obtained leaked documents showing that Southern, real name Kelly, worked for the Institute for Strategic Dialogue (ISD), an organisation focused on "the study of contemporary antisemitism". 

According to the CCDH, the ISD's work, like Southern's, is "highly suspect and frequently violates basic research ethics and journalistic standards". They obtained Google Drive and Dropbox links that they say show how the ISD works closely with Southern, who they describe as an "influencer and activist". 

The 25-year-old Canadian has a history of posting anti-Muslim and anti-immigrant content on social media and was deported from the UK last year after she planned to enter the country to film a documentary on sharia law. She was held by authorities for nine hours and subsequently denied entry to the UK. 

The ISD, which has links to the neocon think tank the Henry Jackson Society, was founded by strategic communications consultant Ed Husain. It has received funding from the US State Department, the UK's Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport, and the European Commission. It claims to have "worked on projects in over 50 countries". 

In a series of tweets, the CCDH said the leaked files show that the ISD shared work with Southern, who they claim "has promoted conspiracy theories and fabricated news". They also alleged that the ISD covered up its relationship with Southern and failed to disclose its ties to the Henry Jackson Society. 

The CCDH said it has passed the files to the academic community for verification. 

In response to the leak, an ISD spokesperson said the files had been "selectively leaked as part of an orchestrated campaign" and that the organisation "has never worked with or for Lauren Southern in any capacity". 

They added: "We completely refute the outrageous allegations that we have in any way covered up our work, or that it is 'highly suspect'. We are a independent think tank, producing independent research on a range of issues, including online hate, anti-Semitism, and extremism." 

The spokesperson also said the organisation had a "commitment to the highest standards of research integrity and transparency".

Newcastle boosted their Premier League survival hopes with a crucial 2-1 victory over Bolton at St James' Park.

The Magpies took the lead when Yohan Cabaye scored with a 25-yard drive early in the second half.

Midfielder Darren Pratley equalised for Bolton with a superb volley from 20 yards.

But Newcastle regained the lead when Papiss Cisse scored with an angled finish in the 82nd minute.

The win takes Newcastle out of the bottom three and to within two points of Bolton, who drop to 17th.

Before the game, Bolton manager Dougie Freedman had said a draw would be a good result for his side, who had not won away from home in the league since August.

And for large parts of the game it looked like that would be the case as Newcastle struggled to create chances against a resolute Bolton defence.

When Newcastle did break through they found Bolton keeper Adam Bogdan in inspired form. The Hungarian, who signed from Liverpool during the week, made a host of fine saves.

He did not have much to do in the first half as Newcastle produced little in the way of chances, but in the second half he made a fantastic one-handed save to deny Leon Best and prevented the home side from taking the lead.

Newcastle's goal finally came when Cabaye collected the ball just inside the Bolton half and drove towards the visiting defence.

The Frenchman moved inside Pratley and hit a low right-footed shot that flew past Bogdan and into the corner.

The visitors equalised with their first effort on target eight minutes later.

Pratley, who had scored just one goal this season, connected sweetly with a volley from the edge of the area after Tim Ream had headed a free-kick into his path.

Newcastle responded and Bogdan was forced into another good save to tip a Hatem Ben Arfa shot over the bar.

The Magpies kept pressing and finally broke through when Cisse scored with a clinical finish after being set up by Ben Arfa.

It was a crucial win for Newcastle, who moved above Bolton and out of the bottom three for the first time since October.

Newcastle secured their place in the fourth round of the EFL Cup after edging past League One side Bolton Wanderers on Tuesday night. The Magpies, who won the competition in 2022, scored all their goals in the first half through Daniel Burn and Joelinton. Bolton pulled one back through Dion Charles late on in the second half, but it was too little too late for the visitors.

Burn opened the scoring after two minutes with a header from a free kick before Joelinton doubled the host's lead after 34 minutes. It was the Brazilian's first goal since his move to St James' Park in July 2022.

Charles gave the visitors a glimmer of hope with a superb strike with just over 20 minutes to go, but it was not enough for Bolton, who were looking to cause another upset after beating Aston Villa in the previous round.

Newcastle, who named a strong side, survived a late Bolton onslaught to book their place in the last 16. The draw for the fourth round takes place on Wednesday.

Wales coach Warren Gatland has praised his side's second-half improvement in their 20-13 win over England in the Six Nations.

The Welsh struggled in a error-strewn first half but improved after the break at a rainy Millennium Stadium.

Wing George North scored Wales' only try, with the home side's 10 points coming from the boot of Dan Biggar.

England, who had defeated Wales in 10 of their past 11 meetings, managed two Owen Farrell penalties.

"The second half was a lot better, a lot more direction and a lot more discipline in our play," said Gatland.

"England are a quality side, they kept the ball for long periods and they made it difficult for us."

The win saw Wales leapfrog England in the Six Nations table, climbing to second behind leaders Ireland.

England boss Eddie Jones said his side were not "brave" enough in the crucial moments of the game.

"We didn't play with enough poise in the critical moments," he said. "There was too much desperation in our play, not enough bravery.

"When you play a side like Wales who are very physical, you have to play with more poise and control. We didn't do that well enough."

The Australian added that England had struggled to contain North, who was a constant threat with his searing pace and power.

"George North is a high-quality player and it is difficult to contain him when he is playing well and we didn't do that well enough," said Jones.

"When he gets the ball with a bit of space he is very dangerous and he caused us a lot of problems."

Wales coach Warren Gatland has praised his side's resilience in the face of a stern test as they beat Australia 29-25 in Cardiff to complete a autumn clean sweep.

The Wales captain, Alun Wyn Jones, scored the opening try for the hosts, who led 12-0 at half-time.

Australia, who had already lost to Scotland and England this month, scored three second-half tries through Michael Hooper, Samu Kerevi and Sean McMahon.

But the visitors were punished for their ill discipline, with Wales scoring nine points from penalties.

"It was a great test for us, we asked a lot of questions of each other and I'm really pleased with the win," said Gatland.

"We talked about getting some momentum and I thought some of our decisions and the way we played were outstanding.

"Australia are a quality side, they kept coming back at us and in the end we had to show a lot of character and resilience to see the game out."

It was a historic night for Wales and Gatland, who won his 100th game in charge of the nation, with this being his final autumn series in charge.

Gatland signed off with a win over South Africa in his final match in charge of Wales last year and this result maintained that sequence of significant victories.

"It was nice to get up to 100 wins and now I have a couple of days to relax and enjoy myself before the attention turns to the Six Nations," said Gatland.

"We've won four on the bounce now and we can enjoy the moment. There are a lot of positives to take from these four games."

Sir Paul McCartney appeals to the "groovy" crowds at the Super Bowl in Arizona.

The former Beatle told reporters he was thrilled to be playing at the event.

"It's a classic, it's fabulous," he said. "We're gonna do a lot of the hits."

Sir Paul and his band played a 12-minute set, including songs such as Lady Madonna and I Saw Her Standing There.

The 74-year-old singer was joined by former Eagles guitarist Don Felder for a version of Felder's hit Life in the Fast Lane.

Sir Paul ended the set with a tribute to the late George Harrison, playing Something in tribute to his former Beatles bandmate, before leading the crowd in a "peace" salute, reports the BBC's Lisa O'Carroll at the scene.

The rock legend had said before the gig that he was nervous about playing to such a large crowd - estimated at around 120,000 - in the University of Phoenix Stadium.

"I never thought I'd do it," said Sir Paul, speaking at a press conference.

"I've got a rock 'n' roll band and we can do it. We've played big places but this is special."

He said the crowds at the stadium had been "groovy", praising their attitude.

"I've been saying 'groovy' all week," he said. "People say, 'Why are you saying that?' But it's a cool word, it means cool."

The singer added that he was excited to be playing at the same event as Madonna, who performed at the half-time show.

"I love Madonna, I think she's brilliant," he said.

"I think she's inventive, she's not afraid to do things that people haven't seen before, so I'm looking forward to seeing her performance."

The seven-time Grammy winner also spoke about his career as a songwriter, and how he had never expected to be playing stadiums as a solo artist.

"When we were kids it was crazy enough to think of being in a band, never mind thinking of playing a stadium," he said.

Sir Paul McCartney appeals to the masses at Super Bowl LV

Half-time shows at the Super Bowl are often extravagant; the NFL is willing to throw millions of dollars behind some of the world's biggest artists to entertain a TV audience that often tops 100 million.

They are rarely understated. Sir Paul McCartney, 76, gave perhaps the most subdued performance of the night during the halftime show of Super Bowl LV.

There were no dancers, no costume changes, no pyrotechnics. Just McCartney and his band — consisting of two guitarists, a bassist, a drummer and a keyboard player — running through a set of some of the most beloved songs of all time.

From the moment he strutted onto the stage in a sequined jacket, it was clear that McCartney was there to have fun and bring the joy of rock 'n' roll to the crowd.

And despite the lack of lasers, fireworks and other arena rock staples, Sir Paul's set was a high-energy, joyous ride from start to finish — the kind of performance that could convert anyone into a fan.

McCartney, a living legend, seemed to revel in it, bouncing around the stage, throwing his head back and singing to the sky, clearly enjoying every moment. 

The crowd was on their feet for nearly the entire 12-minute set, with the attendees cheering and clapping along to songs like "Get Back" and "Hey Jude" that have been staples of McCartney's live show for decades.

The only time the crowd was quiet was during a brief snippet of "Blackbird," a song that McCartney wrote in 1968 about the civil rights movement. 

As the music switched to "Ob-La-Di, Ob-La-Da," the camera cut to celebrities like Jennifer Lopez, Ben Affleck and David Beckham singing along and dancing to the music.

By the end of the performance, McCartney had worked through more than a dozen songs in a brisk 12 minutes, capping off the set with the chorus to "Freedom" before launching into the resounding chorus of "Live and Let Die."

It was a remarkable performance that showed the enduring power of McCartney's songwriting and ability to entertain a massive crowd. 

There may not have been a more universally enjoyable moment in the entire Super Bowl.

Five US citizens have been convicted of running a pirate streaming site which allowed tens of thousands of people to watch film and TV shows for free.

The platform, known as Jetflix, had a library of more than 10,000 movies and TV series. It registered a million user accounts and earned estimated revenues of $1.5m.

US authorities described it as "one of the largest streaming services offering illegal movies and television shows".

The site was shut down in November 2020.

At a federal court in western Texas on Tuesday, Jetflix's five founders were found guilty of conspiracy to commit copyright infringement.

The evidence presented at the trial showed that the defendants were aware that copyrights were being infringed but took steps to conceal their involvement in the piracy, according to the US Attorney's Office for the Western District of Texas.

The defendants were also found guilty of laundering the money earned from the streaming service through bitcoin.

Each faces up to five years in prison and $250,000 in fines for the copyright charges and up to 20 years in prison and $500,000 in fines for the money laundering charges.

In a major breakthrough for the fight against software piracy, four Americans have been convicted of engaging in widespread copyright infringement by operating a pirate website. After a seven-day trial, a federal jury in Texas found Denelle Dixon, David Bodher, Jeff Lundqvist, and Matthew Smith all guilty of conspiracy to commit copyright infringement. 

The four defendants were the masterminds behind a popular peer-to-peer file-sharing website called "MegaUpload," which allowed users to store and share files, including copyrighted content such as movies, TV shows, music, and software, without permission from the copyright holders. The site was shut down by the FBI in 2012 following an investigation that revealed the massive scale of copyright infringement taking place on the site. 

The jury found that the defendants were aware of the widespread copyright infringement taking place on MegaUpload but took no meaningful action to prevent it. In a statement, the U.S. Attorney's Office said that the defendants "made a profit by encouraging, promoting, and assisting the widespread distribution of copyrighted materials without the permission of the copyright owners." 

The four defendants face a maximum sentence of five years in prison and significant financial penalties for their role in operating MegaUpload. The sentencing hearing is scheduled for later this year.

The promise of super-fast, always-on wireless internet has prompted fears of an "evil twin" syndrome stealing personal details, the founder of America's largest internet provider has said.

Donald Gilligan, of EarthLink, warned that the coming of higher-speed wireless technology known as WiMax would increase the threat from opportunistic computer hackers with "nothing better to do".

His comments came as US telecommunications regulator, the FCC, voted to adopt rules to permit fixed and mobile WiMax deployment.

"Every time we introduce a new, faster service there are people out there who are going to use it for either good or evil," Mr Gilligan told the BBC.

"There is a whole category of people out there who did not have anything better to do before and now they do - and they can cause problems," he added.

WiMax, or 802.16, is a standards-based, broadband wireless technology that provides high-throughput data coverage over distances of up to 30 miles.

It allows users to connect without wires to the internet and is expected to be used for a wide range of services, from providing broadband coverage in rural areas to delivering high-speed access in airports, coffee shops and other public places.

The technology can also help networks cope with spikes in data use, such as when thousands of people try to access the internet during major events, Mr Gilligan said.

But he added that the growth of high-speed wireless internet would also create new opportunities for cyber criminals.

"There are people out there who are going to want to try to pretend to be your WiMax access point and if you log on through them, they can then intercept everything you are doing on the internet," he said.

The hacker could then potentially access everything from credit card details to passwords and sensitive emails, he added.

Mr Gilligan said that WiMax technology included some "very good security" but that this would never be "good enough" to keep out a determined hacker.

The issue was further complicated by the growing popularity of Wi-Fi, or 802.11b, which allowed hackers to piggyback on networks from nearby locations, he said.

Hackers had recently begun using Wi-Fi to steal credit card numbers and personal details in Germany, France and the US, he added.

"The technologies overall are good but they are not perfect and we are going to have to continue to improve them," Mr Gill

The idea of an "evil twin" hacking wireless networks has security experts urging governments to take action. The concept involves an attacker setting up a fake wireless access point, often at a coffee shop, airport, or other public place. When unsuspecting users connect to what they think is a legitimate network, the attacker can then intercept passwords, credit card numbers, and other sensitive information. 

Some security experts argue that the only way to protect against this type of attack is to shift away from passwords altogether. Others argue that more needs to be done to educate the public about the risks of connecting to unknown networks. 

One thing is certain: as long as wireless networks remain vulnerable, "evil twin" attacks will continue to be a serious threat.

U2 have entered the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame - accepting their induction with a star-studded performance in Brooklyn.

The Irish rock band were honoured at the 18th annual Rock and Roll Hall of Fame induction ceremony in New York City on Monday.

Accepting the award, Bono said the band had dreamed of achieving such accolades since they were teenagers.

"When we started out as four boys from Dublin, Ireland, who had aspirations and romantic ideas of being in a band - of course we dreamed of these things," he said.

"But I never thought I'd be standing here. Inducting U2 into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame? I never thought we'd be able to get in the door."

Joining Bono and his bandmates, The Edge, Adam Clayton and Larry Mullen Jr., were musicians who have previously worked with the group, as well as those who were inspired by them.

Musical collaborators Bob Dylan, Patti Smith and Joan Baez were among those in attendance, as well as Madonna, who was brought on stage by U2 to perform their single, I Still Haven't Found What I'm Looking For.

Pharrell Williams and Haim were also among those to take the stage with the band, with the four musicians closing the show with their biggest hit, One.

U2 has been eligible for the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame since 2005, but this year marked their first year of induction.

The band joined other performers honoured at this year's ceremony, including Stevie Nicks, who became the first woman to be inducted into the Hall of Fame twice.

Other honourees included folk-rock duo Hall and Oates, as well as Eminem, who was honoured with the Founders Award.

Classic rockers Judas Priest were also inducted into the Hall of Fame, as well as British music icons the Cure.

This year's ceremony was held at the Barclays Center in Brooklyn and was hosted by comedian and Saturday Night Live cast member Adam Sandler.

Bono, The Edge, Adam Clayton, and Larry Mullen Jr. have been elected to the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame class of 2023.

The announcement caps a year in which the quartet celebrated the 50th anniversary of the release of their debut album, Boy. Although they have been eligible for induction since 2005, this is the first time the members of U2 have received enough votes for induction into the hall.

They will be inducted during an April ceremony in Los Angeles. 

Punk legends the Ramones, soul singer Roberta Flack, and folk-rock duo Simon & Garfunkel are also among the inductees. 

Eligibility for the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame requires artists to have released a commercial recording at least 25 years prior. Fans are able to contribute to the selection process, with this year marking the first time that voting was open to fans online. 

More than 650,000 fans cast votes, which counted as a single vote among the more than 1,000 general ballot voters.

British condom maker SSL International is waiting for firm bids ahead of tomorrow's deadline, as it tries to fend off a takeover from its largest shareholder.

The company, which makes the Durex brand, has been fighting a takeover approach from its biggest investor, Russia's Sputnik Group.

SSL, which has operations in more than 90 countries, is understood to have received several approaches.

But it has said that none of them have so far been sufficient to recommend to its shareholders.

The company has been in the spotlight since Sputnik built up a stake of more than 25% last year.

The approach came at a time when SSL was struggling, along with other condom makers, due to a decline in the birth rate and economic slowdown in Southern Europe, its biggest market.

Last month, SSL admitted it had received a cash injection from its owner, which it described as a "rescue transaction".

It said it had drawn down $24.8m (£17.2m) from its debt facility with Sputnik.

And in March, it agreed to a $135m (£96m) cash call - where shareholders are asked to pay more money into a company to improve its financial position.

Sputnik, which is owned by Russian businessman Sergey Studennikov, did not take up its entitlement under the cash call and said it did not "have any intention of making any further investments in the company".

SSL's shares have been suspended from trading on the London Stock Exchange because of the pending takeover talks.

British condom maker SSL International is awaiting a firm bid from a private equity firm for its Durex brand, which it hopes will value the business at about £1.7bn.

US firm Carlyle has made a preliminary offer for SSL, which has been spun off from former parent company Unilever.

In May, SSL hired Credit Suisse to carry out a review of options for the business, which also makes the Femidom and Scholl plasters brands.

Its private equity owners, which bought an initial majority stake in 2014, were expected to sell their remaining shares this year.

SSL said it had received "a number of indications of interest" in Durex and the rest of its business, and that these were being "evaluated".

"No decision has been taken with respect to any offer and there can be no certainty as to the outcome of this process," it added.

SSL, which has its headquarters in London and a presence in more than 20 countries, reported annual sales of £393m in 2022.

Durex, which was founded in 1932, is the world's leading condom brand, selling more than 200 million condoms every year in more than 100 countries.

South Korea's economy minister has announced a $30bn spending push to help revive the country's economy, which is suffering its worst annual growth in a decade.

The package - equivalent to about 8% of the country's GDP - will focus on boosting affordability for households, strengthening the country's industrial base, and fostering innovation in small and medium-sized enterprises.

The announcement comes as South Korea's central bank warned of risks facing the economy from slowing growth and high inflation.

The Bank of Korea (BOK) cut its outlook for economic growth this year to 2.7% from 3.1% - its third cut in five months.

South Korea's economy has been hit by a fall in exports, particularly to Covid-19-hit China, its biggest trading partner.

The BOK also raised its inflation forecast for this year to 3.1% from its previous prediction of 2.5%, above its target rate of 2%.

Announcing the spending package, Economy Minister Hong Nam-ki said it would be focused on boosting domestic demand, which has been hit by rising import prices driven by global supply chain problems and inflation.

"The government decided to concentrate the policy direction on the recovery of domestic demand," Mr Hong said.

The package includes measures to help households with parenting costs and incentives for electric car purchases.

Mr Hong said the government would "take a step further" to stabilise goods supply chains and secure key parts to help the country's manufacturers.

South Korea's government also said it would offer tax benefits and loans to small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and start-ups to foster innovation.

About $17bn of the spending will be funded by the government's surplus, while the rest will be financed through local bond sales, Mr Hong said.

The latest measures build on the government's $173bn recovery plan announced last year, which included grants for families and tax benefits for businesses hit by the pandemic.

The Korean government has announced a spending package worth $430bn as officials warned that without urgent measures, the economy would shrink by more than 1% next year and fall into a technical recession.

The announcement followed data showing that in the third quarter of 2022, the economy contracted by 0.4%. It added to concerns that the economy is slowing after growth slowed to 0.7% in the second quarter.

"The economy is facing serious challenges," said finance minister Choo Kyung-ho. "This package is a pre-emptive, transformational investment for the future."

The plan includes money for public sector pay rises, subsidies for heating costs, and a one-off payment for families with children.

There will also be funds available for small businesses struggling with the rise in interest rates, and extra government borrowing has been ruled out.

South Korea is a major player in the global economy as an exporter of semiconductors which are used in products ranging from smartphones to cars.

But its economy has been hit by the Covid-19 pandemic, the war in Ukraine, and a slowdown in China, one of its major trading partners.

The government has been reluctant to restore its pandemic stimulus measures for fear of adding to rising inflation.

The central bank has raised interest rates six times since August last year, with the latest hike coming last week when it lifted them to 2.5%.

Business groups have reacted with alarm to the news that Macy's owner, Atlas Holdings, has bought rival retailer Kohl's for $11bn.

The deal came as a surprise, as talks of a possible merger between the two retailers had previously broken down.

Atlas said it would pay $51 per share, representing a premium of about 32% to Kohl's closing price on Friday.

The companies said the transaction would result in annual cost savings of about $350m, and that the deal should close in the second quarter of next year.

"We are pleased to bring together two winning retailers in a transformative combination that will enable us to better serve our customers," said Atlas Chairman Antony Ressler.

"Kohl's and Macy's, as the clear leaders in US retail, have long held reputations for delivering customers the very best products, services, and experiences."

However, business groups questioned the wisdom of the move, given the already bleak outlook for the US retail sector.

The National Retail Federation (NRF) said the cost savings promised by the merger were unlikely to materialise.

"Retailers often promise synergies that may not be realised for years, if at all," said Matthew Shay, president and CEO of NRF.

"In order for this merger to be successful, it will require significant reinvestment in stores and employees to enhance the customer experience and improve operations."

Richard Hunter, head of markets at Interactive Investor, also expressed reservations.

"While the deal may afford short-term benefits, the underlying issues of store closures and consumer behaviour will still need to be tackled," he said.

"The market is likely to welcome the deal given the healthy premium on offer, but the real challenge will be in delivering the synergies."

The owner of Macy's has agreed to buy jewellery chain Tiffany for more than $11bn (£9bn), marking the latest attempt by the struggling retailer to turn its business around.

Silver Lake, which owns roughly 20% of Macy's, is expected to own more than 150 million shares in the company after the deal's completion, making it Macy's largest shareholder. 

The deal comes as Macy's, like other department stores, tries to adapt to changing consumer habits, which have included a shift towards online shopping. 

Tiffany, known for its luxury jewellery and engagement rings, has itself been hit by the shift to ecommerce.  In recent months, the retailer has also been hit by the collapse of the wedding industry during the pandemic, which has dented sales of rings and other jewellery. 

The company said it would cancel its plans to sell its shares on the stock market, which it announced in October.

England legend Lawrence Dallaglio believes he is fit enough to win a place on the Lions tour of South Africa.
The 36-year-old number eight has not played international rugby since 2005, but is "itching" to make a comeback.
The British and Irish Lions leave on 31 May for a month-long tour, playing four matches against Southern Hemisphere teams.
"If I get picked, it would be the pinnacle of my career," said the Wasps captain.
He added: "I'm as fit as I have ever been, and if I get the opportunity to play for the Lions I'll be very keen to take it."

England's former World Cup captain Lawrence Dallaglio is aiming to make his fourth Lions tour at the age of 40. "I have to earn the right to be involved in the tour and that starts here." The Lions face the three Test winners Australia in a one-off Test on 27 June before heading to New Zealand for a four-Test series against the world champions. The first Test begins in Auckland on 7 July, with the final match taking place in Auckland on 28 July.

Councils will be able to increase council tax by 5% without a vote from parliament, after the government dropped a clause from the Levelling Up Bill.

The change would save local authorities about £3bn in the next five years, ministers say.

But Labour, the Liberal Democrats and some Tory MPs criticised the move, saying it would hit poorer households.

The government said the change would give councils "certainty" and allow them to invest in services.

Under current rules, councils that want to raise taxes by more than a certain amount - this year 2% - must hold a referendum.

The government had proposed introducing a new upper limit on council tax increases of 2%, plus an additional 1% to fund social care.

But the plan, which was criticised by MPs on all sides of the House of Commons, was removed from the Levelling Up Bill last week.

Instead ministers introduced a new clause which would increase the existing 3% ceiling on council tax increases to 5%.

The change would mean councils could increase tax by an extra 2% without a vote - on top of this year's 2% rise.

Ministers said the change would save £2.3bn for councils over the next four years and £700m in the fifth year.

They said the savings would be equivalent to putting £170 back into the pockets of the average household by 2026.

But opposition parties have accused the government of putting money ahead of protecting the vulnerable.

Labour's shadow local government secretary, Steve Reed, said the change would have "far reaching consequences for councils and the services they provide".

He added: "Hard-up households will be dismayed that the government has sneaked out this change without any scrutiny, letting councils hike up council tax without a vote."

Lib Dem leader Ed Davey described the move as a "stealth tax bomb", while Tory MP Robert Halfon, who chairs the Commons education select committee, said it was "madness".

"Hard-working families are already feeling the pinch and it is unfair to ask them to pay even more," he added.

But local government minister Marcus Jones said the change would put councils on a "more stable financial footing".

"This gives councils the certainty they need to plan for the future, and the space to invest in their services and their local communities," he added.

Mr Blair said he would serve out his third term as Labour leader.

The BBC's political editor, Nick Robinson, said he had seen a letter in which Mr Blair promised to go at or before the next election.

But the prime minister's official spokesman said: "He hasn't made any decision on his future.

"He has always said that he will serve a full third term - that remains his position."

Mr Blair's spokesman accused the BBC of making "a very serious mistake" and said it had breached its own guidelines on accuracy.

The BBC has confirmed that the letter - dated April 2005 - was written by Mr Blair.

But it insists the report was not a "leak" and that the letter was shown to the corporation "in good faith" by someone who had no right to possess or show it.

In the letter, Mr Blair says he is "determined" to serve a full third term as prime minister - but accepts that he cannot serve a fourth.

The letter is addressed to Lord Levy, the Labour Party's fundraiser, whose wife Cherie is said by friends to have persuaded her husband to stay on until 2011.

Mr Blair wrote that he had "always intended" to serve a full third term but had "said repeatedly" that he could not serve a fourth.

"That remains my position," the prime minister wrote.

"I am determined to achieve [the goals set out in the government's agenda for public services], and to do so I am also determined to serve a full third term."

The letter is dated April 2005, around the time of the last election, and refers to "the coming years".

Mr Blair added: "I should also say - because I sometimes think people forget this - that in the end, it is for the party to decide who should be leader, just as it is for the party membership to decide who should be member of Parliament."

The prime minister's spokesman again attacked the BBC for publishing what he described as "a pretty fundamental error of judgment".

He said: "They [the BBC] have breached their own guidelines on serious factual errors and serious breaches of fairness.

"We have made it clear to the BBC that not only has information been released, but that it was released by the BBC themselves."

The spokesman would not be drawn on whether Mr Blair had ever considered stepping down before the end of a third term.

Former British Prime Minister Tony Blair has rejected claims that he was on the verge of quitting as Prime Minister in the wake of the suicide bomb attacks on London in 2005.

The former Labour leader told the BBC's Andrew Marr that he "never considered" quitting in the weeks after the 7 July bombings, which killed 52 people.

 Mr Blair told the BBC that the report was "complete nonsense".

A student who has been blind since birth can now see colours, following a groundbreaking surgery. The surgery involved a unique "tongue display" which stimulated the brain, enabling the patient to see colours.
The patient, who was born with a form of congenital blindness that affects 1 in every 10,000 people, underwent the experimental surgery in November last year.
The operation, which was led by Dr. Ron Pelias, assistant professor of ophthalmology at Stanford University, stimulated the tongue's nerve fibres, which in turn stimulated the brain's visual cortex, allowing the patient to perceive colours.
"We're trying to work out the neural mechanisms of colour vision by stimulating the brain in this very precise way," said Dr Pelias.
The patient can now see colours, but still does not have any form of visual acuity, meaning they can't see shapes or outlines.
The surgery was carried out on a patient with complete colour blindness and involves a small, 1.5mm square electrode, which is placed on the tongue.
The electrode is linked to a small, wearable computer, which transforms images from a camera into "tongue maps", consisting of eight different regions, each stimulated by a different colour.
When the patient looks at an object, the computer converts the image into a "tongue map", which stimulates the brain in such a way that the patient can perceive colours.
"We're trying to stimulate the brain so that it interprets stimuli as colour, by coaxing neurons in the brain to respond in a way that would normally only occur when a sighted person sees colour," said Dr Pelias.
The device needs to be calibrated against a "tongue colour chart", which the patient uses to tune the colours on the device, ensuring they are seeing the right colours.
So far, the patient has been able to identify colours in experiments, but the team is still working on improving the clarity of the images produced.
"This is a very early stage of the research. We're a long way from understanding how the brain encodes colour and even further from understanding how to restore that ability through electrical stimulation," Dr Pelias said.
"But it's a very exciting proof of concept that brings us a little bit closer to helping patients with congenital colour blindness."
The team hopes to carry out the procedure on other patients in the future and believes the technology could also be used to help people who have lost their sight to retinal degeneration.

A blind student from Bristol, UK, says he "hears in colour" after receiving a bionic eye. Tom Williams, 25, has only ever seen shadows and shapes – but now, after receiving the implant, he can identify colours in food and on clothes. Williams lost his sight gradually as a result of a genetic condition and had the implant 18 months ago. "I knew colours existed, but until you experience it for yourself, you don't believe it," he said. "When I saw red for the first time it was amazing – it was like I'd seen it before, but I hadn't, not in that way. It's a truly wonderful experience."

The bionic eye works by stimulating Williams' retina with pulses of electricity. It bypasses the part of the eye that doesn't work and sends signals to the brain. The colours appear in the mind's eye as waves of noise, which he can then interpret. Williams, who studies psychology at the University of Bristol, hopes to become a mental health nurse after graduation. "I want to use my experience to help others and show that even if you have a disability, there are often ways around it," he said. 

The bionic eye, called the Orion, was developed by the US-based company Second Sight. It was approved for use in the UK last year and costs £140,000. Several charities, including Blind Veterans UK and SeeAbility, have helped fund the device. Williams is one of three people in the UK who have had the bionic eye fitted. They can identify colours, detect motion and spot the difference between light and dark. Williams hopes to one day see shapes and, eventually, faces.

Should the government introduce a cap on the amount of money individuals can donate to political parties?

A cross-party committee has recommended that the government should consider introducing a limit on political donations.

The House of Lords Appointments Committee said the current system "threatens the integrity and confidence of our political system".

It said the government should consider introducing a cap on the overall amount that can be donated by individuals, as well as a lower cap on the amount which can be donated in a single donation.

The committee's report said: "We are not convinced that a better alternative system to cap donations would deliver the improvements to transparency, fairness and confidence which would be needed to address the corruption risk and improve public confidence."

It added: "A lower cap on single donations could also help prevent 'big money' from having excessive influence.

"This would not prevent wealthy individuals or organisations from aggregating funds to promote a particular cause or objective, but it would reduce the risk of corruption by any one donor."

Government guidance on citizenship for faith schools is “confusing and complacent” and risks creating second-class citizens, a report by a group of MPs has warned.

The report calls on the government to issue fresh guidance to help faith schools understand their legal duties around the subject.

And it urges local councils to be given stronger legal powers to intervene at faith schools where there are concerns over the quality of citizenship teaching.

The report's authors spoke to local authorities, schools, parents and civil society groups for their findings. 

Their report said some faith schools gave greater emphasis to religious citizenship, such as teaching pupils about religious texts, than to secular citizenship, such as the rules of voting.

It said this reflected a “lack of understanding” of what good citizenship teaching involves, and of the legal duties of all schools to teach citizenship.

The report adds that “confusing and complacent” government guidance does not reflect the legal requirements set out in the Education Act 2002.

Author of the report, MP Yasmin Qureshi, said: “Citizenship is the only subject that is meant to level the playing field, to integrate our schools and bring people together.

“But our research has found that some faith schools are failing to properly teach citizenship, and in some cases, undermining it. 

“The law needs to be strengthened to make this a legal requirement for all schools, and the government needs to reissue its guidance to make this clear.”

The report also found that some local authorities were unclear about their legal powers to assess, monitor and improve citizenship in faith schools.

The group is calling on the government to give local authorities the power to intervene in schools where concerns are raised over the quality of citizenship teaching.

“We have clear guidance available to help schools understand their responsibilities and further support will be provided to schools in the autumn.”

Swedish appliance maker Electrolux is to cut thousands of jobs in Europe over the next two years as it shifts production to Hungary and Thailand.

The company, which makes refrigerators, ovens and other appliances, said it would cut about 6,000 jobs in Europe, with about 1,700 of the positions expected to be eliminated in Sweden.

Electrolux, which is based in Stockholm, said it would close a refrigerator factory in Motala, Sweden, and consolidate production at a facility in Hungary. It also plans to move the production of oven doors to Thailand.

The company said it was taking the measures to adapt to changes in the market and improve its competitiveness.

Electrolux has about 51,000 employees worldwide, with about half of the jobs based in Europe.

The company's Swedish operations have been hit by a strong krona, which has increased the cost of its exports and made it difficult to compete with cheaper producers in Europe.

Electrolux has also been hit by a decline in the European market for appliances, as consumers hold on to their old appliances for longer and opt for cheaper models.

Still, the company has seen rising profits in recent months, thanks in part to strong sales in North America and Asia.

Electrolux has been active in Hungary since 2007 and has a factory in the town of Székesfehérvár making refrigerators and freezers. It also has a sales office in the capital, Budapest.

Swedish home appliances maker Electrolux announced that it is to export hundreds of jobs from Europe to Southeast Asia, affecting workers in Sweden, Italy and Poland.

The company, which makes refrigerators and other appliances under the Electrolux, AEG and Frigidaire brands, said it would cut about 700 jobs in Europe, with most of the positions moving to Thailand. The company employs about 85,000 people globally.

Electrolux has faced increased competition from cheaper Asian brands, as well as from American appliance giant Whirlpool, which has been able to keep costs down by producing in Mexico. 

The company said it had taken the decision to optimize its European operations, and that the move would help to ensure its long-term competitiveness. It added that it would help to "secure jobs in a sustainable way" in the long term. 

Electrolux has already started discussions with employee representatives in the three countries, with the aim of minimizing the impact of the moves on workers.

Canadian telecoms equipment maker Nortel Networks has posted a surprise profit of $300m for the second quarter of this year.

The company had warned in April that it would post a loss of $60m.

The profit revision followed the sale of Nortel's stronger businesses.

The company is now focused on patent and other intellectual property litigation.

In January, Nortel sold its CDMA (code division multiple access) business to US telecoms firm Ericsson for $1.13bn.

In April, it sold its metro Ethernet and optical networking businesses to US telecoms firm Ciena for $700m.

Both deals were funded by cash and debt.

At the end of the second quarter, Nortel had $1.4bn in cash and cash equivalents, down from $2bn in the first quarter.

It also had $1.3bn in long-term debt as of 30 June.

The company has been operating under bankruptcy protection since 2009.

In its patent litigation, Nortel is pursuing a number of defendants, including Microsoft, Google and Apple.

Last month, the company reached a deal with Samsung to settle all patent litigation between the two firms.

Nortel is also a party in a patent infringement case against Apple in the US.

The case, which also includes Microsoft and Motorola, is due to go to trial in 2014.

The Canadian telecoms equipment maker Nortel Networks has posted a surprise profit of $300m for the second quarter of 2004, prompting it to upwardly revise its full-year forecast.

The company said it had benefited from stronger-than-expected sales of wireless and internet equipment, as well as cost cuts.

It also said it had not been as affected by the strong dollar as it expected, given that most of its sales are in US dollars, but most of its costs are in Canadian dollars.

However, Nortel, the world's largest supplier of phone switches, said it remained cautious about its prospects for the second half of the year.

Despite the profit, the company said it would not be paying a dividend, and instead planned to use the money to invest in its business.

Nortel also said it had appointed a new chief financial officer, Peter Currie, who joins the company from the US telecoms firm AT&T.

The money - to be used to improve pay and conditions - comes on top of £5.4bn already planned for social care over the next two years.

Lord Kerslake, a former head of the Civil Service, said it was "nowhere near enough" and would not stop council care markets "disintegrating".

His predecessor, Matt Hancock, had promised to fix social care by the end of this year - but he resigned once it became clear he had broken Covid rules.

The government says the money - about £2 billion a year - will ensure stability in social care while it draws up a long-term plan.

The UK has been refusing asylum to some of the world's most vulnerable people almost every 11 minutes on average since the start of the pandemic, according to a leading charity.

Refugee Council analysis of government data obtained through a freedom of information request showed that between March 2020 and March 2022, the UK refused asylum to more than 43,000 people.

The charity said it amounted to a refusal every 11 minutes on average.

The figures also showed a sharp rise in the number of people who had successfully claimed asylum in the UK - rising from 2,283 in 2019-20 to 10,661 in 2020-21.

The Refugee Council said this showed that judge's decisions were being made "more quickly" and were "largely in favour" of asylum seekers.

The Home Office said it would not comment on the accuracy of the figures as it was due to reply to the freedom of information request shortly.

But it said it was important to distinguish between those making legitimate claims and those who attempted to "abuse the system".

"We have stopped criminals, people who've served a prison sentence or been convicted of a serious crime in their home country, travelling to the UK anonymously to claim asylum and bypassing normal security checks," it said in a statement.

"Last year we introduced major reforms to the asylum system to make it fairer and faster, including introducing a five-year time limit on asylum claims and providing certainty to those with successful claims to stay in the UK."

The charity's analysis showed that the largest group of people who had successfully claimed asylum in the UK were from Iran, with 4,551 granted permission to stay in 2020-21.

This was followed by Syria (2,730), Myanmar (1,510), Iraq (1,447) and Eritrea (1,081).

The figures also showed a sharp rise in the number of people who had their asylum claims rejected after attending a hearing - rising from 1,408 in 2019-20 to 8,429 in 2020-21.

The Refugee Council said its analysis showed "a high number of people who are given the right to remain in the UK are only given that right after a decision by a judge".

"Given how few people are arriving in the UK, it is clear the government can afford to give people the time to tell their stories and have their claims properly assessed," it added.

It is calling on the government to extend the health and care visa to the partners and children of all who work in the sector. The government has been urged to stop using the current immigration rules as an excuse not to change the policy and start listening to the voices of NHS staff.

The European Commission has recommended that member states should not impose cuts in 2023, and should instead aim for a modest fiscal expansion.

Many countries have been struggling with increased spending on energy support and rising interest rates as they battle inflation.

The recommendation represents a significant change in the EU's economic policy.

The commission said that its "economic outlook has deteriorated significantly" since it last made recommendations in July.

It said that "more ambitious" fiscal policies were needed to respond to "the unfolding energy crisis, persistent inflation, and the deteriorating economic activity".

Inflation in the eurozone is now lower than it was last year, but it is still very high by the standards of the last decade, with prices rising by 9.2% in December.

Energy prices have fallen from their peaks but are still nearly double what they were before the pandemic, and businesses and households are facing higher borrowing costs after the European Central Bank's recent interest rate rises.

The commission's recommendation to halt austerity is the first since 2010 when member states were battling the financial crisis.

It says countries with fiscal space, such as Germany and the Netherlands, should "take the lead" in spending to support the economy.

Those without that space, such as Italy, should use "all available means" to support households and companies, it adds.

Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said she would "study" the recommendations, adding that "we have always said that we are ready to do what is necessary to face the crisis".

The EU executive's advice is not binding, but it is used by the European Council to make its own recommendations, and by the Court of Justice to rule on whether national budgets are in line with EU rules.

The commission's President Ursula von der Leyen said "when times are tough, we must be tough".

"This is why we propose to our member states to suspend all fiscal rules and to revert to growth-friendly investments," she said.

The recommendation to halt austerity is likely to be welcomed by southern European countries, which have called for fiscal stimulus to help them through the energy crisis.

However, it is likely to be resisted by northern European countries, which have been pushing for continued spending discipline.

The commission's proposal will now go to the European Council for discussion at a meeting of finance ministers on 24 January.

The battle to keep the European Union’s deficit within limits may be over for now after governments agreed to stop punishing each other for breaching the bloc’s limits on government spending.

The decision, if approved, would cancel out most of the fines estimated at €83bn (£70bn) that the EU’s executive committee, the European Commission, had planned to impose on countries breaching the bloc’s ceiling of 3% of GDP for the deficit.

The fine regime, which has never been used, was due to come into force on Friday but will now be scrapped provided that countries with too-high deficits take action to correct their finances.

The about-face comes after a year of intense debate over the EU’s fiscal rules, which have been suspended for the past two years to allow members to spend without fear of punishment as they battled the economic impact of the Covid-19 pandemic.

The relaxation, known as the general escape clause, was due to expire this month, but the European Commission proposed extending it to the end of 2023, raising concerns among the more fiscally conservative countries, led by the Netherlands, that spending discipline was coming apart.

"It all happened quite quickly for me," he says. "From playing in National Two to training with the England Saxons and now potentially the Lions.

"It's been a crazy journey, but it's a great opportunity."

Dickenson comes from decent stock. His father Mike played for Penryn and Cornwall, and stood as a police officer in the line of fire during the London riots.

Brennan and his brother Dan, also a Penryn and Cornwall player, attended the same school as another prolific Cornish scorer - Tom Cowan-Dickie, the Exeter and England centre.

"We're good friends still," says Dickenson. "I went to school with him and his brother and then played with him at club level.

"We're pretty close and it's nice seeing him do so well. I'm proud of what he's achieved."

Senior NHS officials in England are urging staff to support the Conservative Party in the forthcoming general election, in a move described by Labour as a "full-frontal assault on the neutrality of the NHS".

The NHS Confederation, which represents organisations including hospital trusts, acute care providers and NHS partnerships, has emailed staff with links to Conservative policies and those of other parties.

It comes as a poll suggested the Conservatives had moved into a four-point lead over Labour.

In the email, the confederation stressed it was not telling NHS staff how to vote, but said it was "highlighting" policies that "will impact the NHS".

These include the Conservative promise to build 40 new hospitals and the Labour plan to recruit more staff.

It also pointed out that Labour had promised to bring in stronger regulation on the use of expensive drugs.

The email said there would be "significant financial consequences for the NHS" if Labour were elected because of "a high probability of significant tax rises".

It added that while the Conservatives had said they would increase funding for the NHS in England by £33.9bn ($43bn) by 2023/24, Labour had promised an extra £6.6bn.

In response, Labour said the move was "a full-frontal assault on the neutrality of the NHS".

It said that as chancellor, Rishi Sunak had "increased NHS funding every year he has been in office".

A spokesperson for the NHS Confederation said it was "an independent organisation, which represents the whole NHS, including those who deliver and receive care".

"As an organisation we will always speak up for the NHS, its people and patients on the big issues that affect it," they added.

"We have highlighted, in a neutral way, some of the key published policy offerings from the main political parties in the general election, as these will impact the NHS, its people and patients."

But Dr. Julia Grace, chief people officer at Sheffield Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, said: "As general elections are often a heated debate, I think it's a mistake for NHS organisations to be seen to be promoting the views of one party over another.

The report, entitled The Rising of Artificial Intelligence: Future Scenarios for International Relations, calls for a new "transdisciplinary" approach, bringing together experts from a wide range of backgrounds, to help make sense of the changes happening across society. 

"We need to open up the social sciences much more than we have done in the past," said Woolcock. "We should be looking to collaborate with people from all sorts of different disciplinary backgrounds." The report also warns that the increasing use of AI in the public sector and government could, in the long run, threaten the autonomy of social sciences. "If we are not careful, we could end up sleepwalking into a world where the engineering perspective dominates," said Woolcock.

The future of Rover looks uncertain as the company's owners, BMW, have given it until the middle of November to find a buyer.

The German car giant has agreed to continue funding Rover's loss-making Longbridge plant in Birmingham, central England, until then.

But the company has made it clear it will not do so indefinitely and has not ruled out closing the plant.

About 6,000 people work at Longbridge but only 2,000 are certain to keep their jobs until November.

The uncertainty over the future has prompted speculation that BMW may pull out before November if a buyer is not found.

'Improving competitiveness'

Rover has been seeking a partner to share the high costs of making cars and has had talks with a number of companies, including Honda, General Motors and Ford.

But these have not been successful and the company's managing director, Kevin Howe, said on Wednesday that it was now looking for a buyer.

In a statement, BMW said it was in talks with three possible partners but these had not progressed as far as it had hoped.

"Based on intensive analyses of all alternatives for the future of Rover, the BMW board has decided to explore the option of a sale of Rover," it said.

"This process will be carried out in parallel with ongoing efforts to improve the competitiveness of the Rover Group."

The statement said BMW would not fund losses at Rover indefinitely and the company's management would "continue to explore all options for the future of Rover".

This has led to speculation that BMW may pull the plug on Rover if a buyer is not found by November.

The German car maker bought Rover in 1994 for more than £800m but has failed to make a profit from its UK operations.

The company has made losses of more than £600m over the last three years and BMW has already spent more than £900m trying to turn Rover around.

The plan to replace the House of Lords with a elected Senate has been backed by more than 100 MPs from five different parties, in a cross-party push to reform the UK's upper chamber.

The proposal for a democratically elected Senate was put forward by the Labour MP Chuka Umunna and the Conservative MP Chris Skidmore.

The pair have won the support of MPs including Labour's shadow justice secretary, Shadow Chancellor John McDonnell and his predecessor as shadow chancellor, Rebecca Long-Bailey, the Conservative former foreign secretary Boris Johnson, and the SNP's Westminster leader Ian Blackford.

The proposal would see the House of Lords replaced with a Senate, with representatives from the nations and regions of the UK elected by the public.

The pair claim that the proposed change would stop the watering down of legislation as senators would be "responsible to the people".

They said: "A Senate of the Nations and Regions could provide a legitimate body, capable of challenging and scrutinising the executive, and protecting the rights and freedoms of the people it represents."

The proposal has been put forward at a time when all three major parties have pledged to reform the House of Lords.

The Liberal Democrats are currently campaigning for an elected Senate, replacing the current appointments system, while the Labour Party has pledged to replace the House of Lords with a "fully-elected second chamber".

The Conservative Party has promised to cut the number of Conservative peers, but has not said whether the House of Lords will be replaced.

No 10 said the government had no plans for a "major surgery" on the House of Lords, but was looking at ways to reduce the number of peers.

MPs have outlined plans to replace the House of Lords with a new assembly of elected representatives, as part of a wider reform of the UK's constitution. The government has promised to establish a commission to examine the issue but said any reform would take place over a number of years.

The issue of constitutional reform was one of the key items on the agenda at the Conservative Party conference in Birmingham. In his keynote speech, the prime minister, Boris Johnson, said he was "fed up" with the "ancient conventions" that he claimed were holding Britain back.

The government has promised to establish a constitutional reform commission, which would examine issues such as the future of the House of Lords. The BBC's political editor, Chris Mason, says any reform would be likely to take years to become a reality.

The existing House of Lords is made up of about 800 members - most of whom were appointed directly by the prime minister, or elected by fellow MPs to sit in the House of Lords. Former prime minister Tony Blair had hoped to reform the Lords by replacing it with a mainly elected chamber, but plans for reform were dropped after the Labour government lost power in 2010.

The film Aviator has been criticised for its historical inaccuracies, but it did win five Oscars including best picture.

The film's director, Martin Scorsese, was not nominated for his work on the film, but he did receive an honorary Oscar in 2007.

The maker of the controversial film, The Aviator, about the life of flying ace Howard Hughes, failed to win a single Oscar, despite receiving a leading 11 nominations.

The film, which starred Leonardo DiCaprio as the millionaire adventurer, and was directed by Martin Scorsese, did not even win best picture, the top Oscar, which went to Sideways.

It did, however, scoop five awards including best actor for Leonardo DiCaprio, and best supporting actress for Cate Blanchett.

"It's a little disappointing," Scorsese told a news conference as he collected his best director award for The Departed, which also won best picture.

"When you're in the middle of making a film, you live with these people six months, eight months, sometimes a year.

"You become close to them and then the film is over and you don't see them for a while and then you meet up at these events and it's great to see them and to catch up a little bit."

Despite The Aviator's snub, the Academy Awards ceremony did have a few historical references of its own.

Host Jon Stewart began the evening with a reference to one of the greatest directors of all time, Howard Hawks, creator of classic Hollywood films like Scarface and Bringing Up Baby.

And another past director made a cameo appearance - Alfred Hitchcock, appearing in a brief sketch about a shower scene.

The film industry's night of nights, the Oscars, have finally arrived. While the red carpet was graced by many, several big names were surprisingly missing. Aviator director Martin Scorsese was among them. The film, which stars Leonardo DiCaprio as pilot Howard Hughes, was a favorite to take out the award for Best Picture. But in a shock move, it was nowhere to be seen in the list of nominations. The film did however secure nominations for Best Actor, Best Costume Design, and Best Cinematography. So what went wrong? Is it possible that the Academy just didn't care for the direction of the film? Perhaps there was bias within the judging panel. Only time will tell.

Australian Prime Minister John Howard has said he will not be distracted by "outdated and offensive" comments from his opponent.

Mr Howard's centre-left opposition, the Labour Party, has accused him of using "dog-whistling" tactics in immigration policy.

Labour's immigration spokesman, Tony Burke, said the government's policy amounted to "pretending we're not a country of mongrel Australians".

In Australia, "mongrel" is a derogatory term for a person of mixed race.

Mr Howard, leader of the conservative Liberal Party, accused Labour of hypocrisy.

"As far as I'm concerned the Labor Party should be utterly ashamed of itself for using words like that," he said.

"It's offensive, it's outdated, but worse than that it demonstrates a complete lack of judgment on their part."

Mr Howard, who is visiting the US, said he would not "take a backward step" on immigration policy.

He has faced persistent criticism over his government's policy on asylum seekers, which includes turning back boats carrying would-be refugees.

The government argues the current policy is necessary to maintain what Mr Howard calls "one Australia".

Mr Burke accused the prime minister of using coded language on immigration to stir up fears within the community.

Using the term "dog-whistling", he said Mr Howard was "pretending we're not a country of mongrel Australians".

"He knows that the Australian people are a confident, proud people who are not going to be stirred by semantics about whether or not we're a Christian country or whether or not we're a multicultural country," Mr Burke said.

"What we want is to make sure that everyone in the world knows that there is a place called Australia and... that it's a place which is open to people who want to live by our values."

But Mr Howard said the Labour Party had used the "most offensive and derogatory terminology" possible.

"The Labour Party are now so desperate that they will throw around this type of terminology," he said.

The former Ausie test cricket captain Michael Howard has hit back at the mongrel jibe launched his way by English fast bowler Steve Harmison.

Speaking exclusively to BBC News, Howard said "It was a harmless remark, I hardly think it's worth commenting on."

"He's only said it because it's coming up to the Ashes and he's trying to get in the squad."

"I've seen this sort of thing happen before when a player is trying to grab the spotlight. It's not the first time someone has used the word mongrel against me and it certainly won't be the last. I let it go then and I'm certainly not going to let it bother me now."

"I can understand how he (Harmison) could use that word in a sporting context in a positive way but I don't think it's a good idea to be using it to describe people."

There are growing concerns that the English team are beginning to get distracted with both Andrew Flintoff and now Harmison saying controversial things.

The England and Wales Cricket board (ECB) are scheduled to meet on Monday to discuss the developments.

Laser beams carrying internet data can help connect remote areas where laying cables is challenging, researchers say.

Two teams of scientists have used lasers to transmit data at high speeds over long distances.

One team sent images and high-quality video between two mountain tops in Switzerland.

The other team connected two universities in Mexico, but eventually hopes to link a town to the internet.

Both projects are small-scale but could be used to deliver internet in places where laying fibre is too difficult or expensive.

"We are trying to find solutions for the last mile," said Prof Gerald Fabre from the University of Southampton, UK, who led the Mexican project.

"There are many remote areas, for example in the UK we have hundreds of kilometres of coastline where laying fibre is not easy," he told the BBC.

"There are also other applications where you don't want to have any physical contact - in the Arctic or Antarctic, for example."

Ordinarily, the "last mile" problem - the final leg of getting from a telecommunications hub to a user - is solved by laying fibre-optic cable, which can be slow and expensive.

But laser light in the mid-infrared range can be sent along tiny glass fibres, and carry far more data than current technologies.

The researchers in Mexico used a beam with a wavelength of 1,550 nanometres - a similar wavelength to that used in traditional fibre-optic cables - to send data at speeds of 2.89Gbps over a distance of 20km (12 miles) between the cities of Puebla and Toluca.

Their apparatus cost less than £2,000 ($2,730) - about 100 times less than a similar experiment a few years ago.

What's more, the laser they used was powered by the USB port of a laptop, and its energy use was negligible, said Prof Fabre.

In a separate project, researchers from the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology in Lausanne (EPFL) used a similar technique to send data over a record-breaking 143km.

Their low-power, wavelength-tunable laser sent information at speeds of up to 1.4Tbps through the air between the peaks of two mountains, at a distance of up to 120km.

From 2020, the EU began building a network of ultra-fast routes over land and water, to test out the potential of trains travelling at 350kph (220mph).

All the relevant infrastructure, including new bridges, tunnels and track, came with a catch - how do you make it all safe to use at high speed?

"If you want to have a safety system for a high-speed railway, you need to have some kind of sensor system providing you with information about the train, the track and everything around it," said Prof Klaus Hellmueller, who works on laser-based sensors at Birmingham University.

"To monitor track conditions, the current approach is to send people with measuring tools to walk the tracks at night, hoping they don't miss anything."

That is unlikely to find everything that could go wrong, he says - and it is too dangerous for staff to access some parts of the network during the day.

Prof Hellmueller's solution takes the form of a large, white box, a little under 2m (6ft) long, attached to the front of a train.

It fires a laser beam onto the track, which is reflected back onto a sensor. By analysing the signal returned, it can build a detailed picture of the track conditions - even through thick fog.

It can also detect any obstacles on the line, such as fallen trees, vehicles and even trespassers. This can all be done at speeds of up to 350kph (220mph).

The system has been developed in collaboration with rail infrastructure manager Network Rail and rolling stock owner Porterbrook, and is currently undergoing rigorous testing.

If all goes to plan, a similar, smaller device could soon be attached to the front of every train.

Network Rail's head of technology, Jeremy Mitchell, said the "game-changing" technology had the potential to protect the railway and give customers even more confidence in the safety of the network.

The system could also be used to monitor the state of the track and collect data on wear and tear.

That could enable engineers to spot and fix problems before they become dangerous, or even allow the network to be remotely monitored.

The UK economy grew faster than expected in the October-to-December quarter, despite worries about higher interest rates and falling consumer confidence.

Official data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) showed that economic growth accelerated to 0.2% in the final month of 2022, above analysts' forecasts of 0.1%.

For the whole quarter, economists had expected 0.2% growth, but official figures showed that the economy expanded by 0.3%.

It comes after the UK economy contracted in the third quarter as households cut back on spending.

The ONS said that warmer weather helped generate 0.3% growth in construction in the fourth quarter, while a weaker pound helped manufacturing to expand by the same amount.

However, retailers continued to struggle as sales fell by 0.5% in December, the biggest fall since January 2021.

Chancellor Jeremy Hunt said: "Today's GDP data shows that the fundamentals of our economy are strong with solid consumer spending and a resilient construction sector supporting growth, despite global challenges.

"However, I am not immune to the pressures facing households around the UK with the cost of living, and we are taking decisive action to support people in getting through the winter, with further support to come at the next Budget."

But the British Chambers of Commerce (BCC) warned that the cost of living crisis and soaring inflation was likely to drag on the UK's economic growth in 2023.

Suren Thiru, head of economics at the BCC, said: "The UK's economic growth surge at the end of 2022 was driven by the vagaries of the weather, the NHS backlog and the Omicron wave, rather than underlying strength.

"While these factors provided a significant boost to the economy in Q4, this is likely to be a one-off rather than a sustainable improvement. We expect growth to stagnate in the first quarter of 2023 as the UK economy slips into recession."

The UK economy ended the year with a spurt, growing faster than any other large advanced economy, as it recovered from the economic impact of the Covid pandemic.

According to preliminary estimates from the Office for National Statistics (ONS), gross domestic product (GDP) increased by 1.3% in the fourth quarter of 2022, compared to the same period a year earlier. This was higher than the 0.2% growth rate recorded in the third quarter.

The ONS said the growth was driven by a strong performance in the service sector, which accounts for about 80% of the UK economy, as well as a rebound in construction activity. However, manufacturing output fell slightly over the quarter.

UK government ministers have been "naive" in their response to allegations of corruption in the News International phone-hacking scandal, a senior Tory has said.

Lord Ashcroft said ministers had failed to realise the gravity of what had happened and called for a "full and fearless" investigation.

He also said the affair had been a "wake-up call" to the Conservative Party as a whole.

His comments are the most significant indication yet that the row has split the Tory leadership.

The peer, who funds the Conservative Party, will call for legislation to regulate the media, including a new system for accrediting journalists and a statutory regulator with teeth.
