The home secretary has accused her counterparts in other countries of being "naive" over reports that journalists at a prominent media organisation were hacked by authoritarian governments.

Suella Braverman said she had raised the issue of journalists at the BBC and other organisations being targeted by state actors "at the highest levels".

Her comments came after the BBC reported that the mobile phones of editors and correspondents, including in Westminster, were being targeted.

Last week the corporation said a small number of journalists had been hacked, and it was contacting those affected.

The corporation said it had no evidence the hacks had been carried out by the UK government, and MI5 said it had no involvement in such activity.

Speaking on a visit to a prison in Hertfordshire, Ms Braverman said she had "raised this at the highest levels with my counterparts, making clear that this is completely unacceptable".

She added: "I have expressed my deep concerns to ministers and senior officials around the world and made clear that this must stop."

The home secretary said the targeting of journalists was "something we all need to be extremely concerned about".

"It is threatening freedom of news, it's threatening freedom of expression, it's threatening people's privacy," she added.

Last week's BBC report said that in recent months, a number of journalists had had their phone messages accessed through hacking by "state actors".

They included reporters in China, Russia and Iran, as well as political correspondents in Westminster.

The corporation said it had not been notified by any state actor about the hacking, and its investigations into the breaches were continuing.

Foreign Secretary Liz Truss said the hacking of journalists was "completely unacceptable" and "a violation of freedom of expression".

"It is right that the UK and its allies stand up for journalists under attack in authoritarian regimes," she added.

The government has previously faced criticism for failing to act to prevent the hacking of MPs' phones during the 2016 Brexit referendum.

The cyber-attack, by a suspected Russian-backed actor, targeted the internal systems of Parliament, as well as the emails of MPs.

Last month the government announced that an official review into the cyber-attack on Parliament would begin next year.

The law governing the patenting of software in Europe faces being scrapped, following a warning from the European Commission.

The commission said the software patent directive, two years in the making, would be withdrawn because it was irreparably flawed.

The announcement was greeted with relief by open-source software developers and free software advocates, who had fought a high-profile campaign against the legislation.

But the news was a blow to companies who wanted patent protection for the software they develop.

Patents give an inventor exclusive rights to make or sell their invention, with the aim of stimulating more innovation.

The bill was aimed at harmonising patent laws across the EU, making it easier for companies to secure patents in multiple countries, and was seen as crucial to the future development of the software industry.

But the proposal ran into strong opposition, particularly in Europe's open-source software community which feared it would restrict programmers' ability to access and adapt software.

Open-source software, which includes Linux and Apache, is developed in a collaborative approach, with programmers able to build on each other's work.

The directive would have made it illegal to use certain types of software in Europe, said Benjamin Henrion, one of the leaders of the NoSoftwarePatents campaign.

"The directive would have made patents on software legal in Europe, and that would have stopped competition, stopped new entrants to the market, and stopped programmers from working on each other's code," he said.

The campaigners' objections were reinforced by several court rulings, most recently a decision by the European Court of Justice last July which said the draft law would have gone against European Union rules on intellectual property.

The commission said it wanted to press ahead with legislation on patents for software, but needed to withdraw the current bill to reconsider its approach.

"The commission is committed to creating a legal framework which encourages innovation in the software industry," it said in a statement.

"To this end, the commission will shortly be presenting proposals for a targeted approach which takes account of the particularities of the software sector while ensuring legal certainty," it said.

The announcement was welcomed by campaigners.

"The European Commission has listened to reason, and avoided making a terrible mistake which would have had serious consequences for innovation and competition in Europe," said Georg Greve, president of the Free Software Foundation Europe.

The EU parliament's legal affairs committee has voted to repeal the software patent law that came into force in January. The committee said the law would have created legal uncertainty and hampered innovation and competition. The issue now goes before the European Parliament for a vote in February.
   
The legislation in question was approved by EU governments and the European Parliament in 2003, and was designed to harmonise patent laws across the EU, clearing up a legal maze that has seen cases drag on for years.
   
But a report by the committee, drafted by British Liberal MEP Sarah Ludford, said the legislation would "have the effect of legalising software patents in a way which could lead to legal uncertainty, hinder competition and innovation, and create a barrier to free market access".
   
Ms Ludford said the laws would have allowed companies to patent "ideas which should never be monopolised".

Michael Collins has been banned from flying for five years after pleading guilty to flying his drone near an airport.

The decision, thought to be the first of its kind, was made by Dublin's District Court and comes into immediate effect.

The Irish pilot had pleaded guilty to charges of flying his drone in prohibited airspace.

Judge Grainne O'Neill imposed the ban after being told that Collins had been warned about flying his drone close to an airport before his prosecution.

She said the offence was so serious that she could not impose a fine and that a community service order would not be appropriate.

Her judgement comes amid increasing concerns in Ireland over the illegal use of drones. 

Judge O'Neill told Collins that his actions were reckless as he flew his drone within 4km (2.5 miles) of Dublin Airport, which is prohibited airspace.

She said the airport's safety was of "utmost importance" and that Collins' behaviour was unacceptable. 

Collins was also fined €1,000 (£850) and ordered to pay €500 (£420) in legal costs. 

He declined to comment as he left Dublin District Court.

The Football Association has banned former England manager Graham Taylor and cleared ex-defender David Collins of making racist comments to a teammate. The FA's ruling is a landmark case because it is the first time that an investigation into racism has reached the FA's judicial panel. In an emotional hearing, Collins fought back tears as he described being subjected to a "kangaroo court" and accused the FA of failing to provide proper evidence.

The case relates to allegations that Collins, 38, made a racist comment to fellow England player Sol Campbell during a training session in 1995. Campbell, who is of Jamaican descent, has always maintained that Collins made a racist comment towards him. The FA launched an investigation in 2008 but it was put on hold because Collins refused to co-operate. The FA reopened the case in 2013 and charged Collins with alleged misconduct.

In its decision, the FA judicial panel said the organisation had not received sufficient evidence to prove that Collins is guilty. However, it banned Taylor, who was England's manager at the time of the alleged incident, for eight weeks and fined him £170,000 for failing to ensure that his players conducted themselves in an orderly fashion. Taylor plans to appeal against the length of the ban, which is the largest ever given to an individual by the FA.

The Brian Farrell saga appears set to drag on, with the former Taoiseach's supporters vowing to contest the result of Saturday's Dublin West bye-election.

Fine Gael candidate Brian Murphy was elected to the Dáil after receiving more than 16,500 first-preference votes.

But Mr Farrell, an independent, said the vote had been "contaminated" by the decision to hold the by-election on the same day as the presidential election.

In a statement, he said he would not be making any comment on the result "until such time as all electoral irregularities have been fully investigated".

"This will be carried out in the next week," he said.

"In the meantime, I wish to state that I will be continuing my campaign to become a TD for Dublin West."

Mr Farrell has already indicated he will take legal action over an alleged breach of the Electoral Act, as he sought votes transfer from unsuccessful candidates.

The returning officer for the Dublin West by-election, Roger Conlon, told RTÉ that transfers could not be accepted from candidates who had withdrawn from the race.

This was confirmed in writing by the constituency returning officer, he said.

 RTÉ is reporting that four candidates who had withdrawn - Labour's Patrick Nulty, Socialist Party candidate Ruth Coppinger, and independents Vincent Brown and John DeLorean - did not sign the official paperwork to that effect.

Mr Nulty, who received just 407 first-preference votes, said he did not sign the form, because he was unaware of the need to do so.

The form was signed by the other six candidates, who received a total of about 12,500 votes between them.

The sports minister has stood by comments made by the Olympic champion Sir Mo Farah, who suggested that the reason why he and other British athletes were never accused of blood doping was because of his skin color. Iraqi intelligence officials have admitted that a 2017 air strike which killed 140 people was based on "wrong information" provided by a woman whose father was among the dead.

The woman - known by the initials HT - had told US and Iraqi forces that her father, Ali Fares, was an extremist.

But after the strike on the village of al-Faruq, she told investigators she had lied because she and her family had been harassed by Iraqi security forces.

The admission was made in a report by Iraq's Counter-Terrorism Service (CTS), which was obtained by the BBC.

The report also said that a second air strike on the village, two days later, which killed an additional 65 people, had been based on accurate information.

That strike was ordered in response to an IS suicide bombing in Baghdad on 12 February 2017, in which at least 78 people were killed. 

The admission sheds significant new light on an incident in which the US and its Iraqi allies were accused of killing large numbers of civilians during the battle against so-called Islamic State (IS). 

US and Iraqi officials say the strikes targeted IS militants - but survivors and local officials said most of those killed were civilians and not members of the group.

The CTS - which reports directly to Prime Minister Mustafa al-Kadhimi - began its investigation in April after one of the survivors filed a lawsuit against the intelligence apparatus. 

Its findings were shared with the prime minister and the cabinet late last month. 

The report said HT's father, Ali Fares, was an IS extremist and that she had witnessed him conducting military training for the group in the village square. 

But it added that after the first air strike she changed her story, saying she had been pressured by security forces to provide the information about her father because he was a Sunni Muslim and a former member of the Iraqi army.

The report also said that a second air strike two days later on the village of al-Faruq was based on accurate information about IS activity provided by three separate sources.

The father of a young Iraqi woman, who died in 2019 while attempting to join ISIS, has won a landmark court case, in a probe described by prosecutors as "the first of its kind". Rabia Kamil's father filed a criminal complaint in the French city of Rouen against the Islamic State group, as well as against his daughter's spouse and another man, who had helped prepare the couple's journey from Iraq to Syria. 

In a verdict delivered earlier this week, a judge ruled that the two men had facilitated Rabia Kamil's journey - an attempt to join ISIS - knowing that it risked her safety. The judge described her death as "foreseeable". 

The only defendant present at the trial, Rabia Kamil's husband, was sentenced to four years in prison, while the other man received a three-year term, both with suspended sentences. However, the judge did not find enough evidence to convict ISIS. 

The presiding judge said the group had "played on the couple's religious and ideological convictions" and that ISIS had deceived them. The judge added that ISIS had left them "to their fate". 

The couple's daughter, aged three, has been placed in the care of the French authorities. During the trial, Rabia Kamil's father asked for his grandchild to be placed in his care, but his request was denied. 

The head of the French prosecutors' office for the investigation of terrorist crimes, François Molins, said the case was "the first of its kind". 

"There have been other cases in France of course of young people who have died, or been killed, in Syria while trying to join ISIS, but this is the first time we have a death penalty for a youngster caused by indirect criminal liability," he said. 

In 2019, French prosecutors opened some 1,200 investigations into the activities of ISIS in France. About a quarter related to deaths in Syria or Iraq of people who had left France to join ISIS. To date, none has led to a trial.

Robot firms are constantly trying to out-do each other with claims of creating the fastest robot.

Hitachi has developed what it calls the "world's fastest robot".

The firm said the robot, called "Swift", can now pick up a variety of objects with greater speed and accuracy.

The company said it has sold about 200 of the robots since 2016. They are currently being tested by a number of companies ahead of a full rollout later this year.

"We're always focusing on speed and efficiency," said Hitachi's Hitoshi Okawa.

"But it's not just about picking things up quickly. The robot can also show where it is in the process of picking an item, and why it is holding a particular item in a particular way," he added.

Swift has a number of sensors and a digital camera, to help it identify the position and appearance of objects.

It can also use its sensors to "feel" its way around items that are not positioned quite right.

Mr Okawa said the firm had planned to launch the robot in 2020, but the pandemic had accelerated demand for automation.

"The need for robots in warehouses and the like has suddenly increased," he said. "We've had to speed up our plans."

Hitachi has built what it claims is the world's fastest robot. Together with the University of Tokyo and other partners, the Japanese electronics maker developed a robot that maneuvers by bouncing off walls and can clean a room in under 10 minutes. Unlike other speedy robots, which are typically wheeled, Hitachi's new robot—called Rapid Explored Rectified Orientation Tracking (REROT) Robot—has legs like a insect, enabling it to traverse uneven surfaces at speeds of up to 5.6 meters per second. According to Hitachi, that is the fastest speed achieved by a robot on legs. 

The robot measures approximately 5.1 inches long, 3.5 inches wide, and 2.7 inches tall. It navigates by keeping a wall about 1 to 2 feet to its left throughout its movement. Its two legs are modeled after those of an insect, and they enable the robot to traverse uneven surfaces at high speeds. Its unique leg movement is inspired by how a person would run on a slippery road, and the robot uses its legs to maintain balance as it moves. 

The REROT Robot can clean a room in under 10 minutes, which is significantly faster than the average household robot. It can also be used for various other applications, including transportation and inspection. As the robot can fit into tight spaces, it could potentially be used to search for survivors in the event of a disaster. 

Looking ahead, Hitachi hopes to increase the robot's speed by improving the control of its legs and developing an advanced collision avoidance system. It is also exploring the use of the REROT Robot in other applications, such as transportation and inspection.

The dollar has hit a new low, amid expectations that the Federal Reserve will push up interest rates faster than previously expected to tackle inflation.

The Australian dollar hit a fresh record high, while the Norwegian crown hit a new record versus the US currency.

"The dollar remains under persistent selling pressure, which only amplifies when US data prints disappointively, as was the case [on Wednesday]," said Karl Schamotta, chief market strategist at Corpay.

The dollar index, which measures it against currencies including the UK pound and the euro, stood at 102.92, having fallen to as low as 102.63 on Wednesday, the lowest since September 2020.

It has tumbled from a peak of 114.78 in October 2021.

A weaker dollar tends to boost commodities priced in the currency, making them more attractive to holders of other currencies.

This helps explain why the Australian dollar has been rising in recent months as the country is a major exporter of iron ore and other commodities.

The euro also hit a fresh 15-month high versus the dollar, amid optimism over the European Central Bank's economic outlook.

Market participants now await the Bank of England's interest rate decision and comments on the economic outlook on Thursday.

Market analysts said the dollar's decline - which has gathered pace since the start of the year - could hamper the US economy's recovery as it makes American goods more expensive to buy abroad. It also makes imports cheaper for Americans, potentially fueling inflation.

The dollar has been battered by the Fed's ultra-easy monetary policy, with the central bank already cutting rates once this year in an attempt to stave off a slowdown.

Many analysts now expect another rate cut this month, with some forecasting a further reduction before the end of the year.

The dollar's decline against the euro was its lowest since November 2002, with one euro now worth $1.267.

Against the Japanese yen, the dollar fell to a four-year low.

A new computer worm has been discovered that uses the classic Soviet arcade game, Tetris, as a way of infiltrating and taking over a user's PC. Researchers at California-based security firm, Kaspersky Lab, say the malware has so far been found only in Russia. It is the first known case of a game being used in this way. Experts believe the worm, which has been named Win32.Rmnet.12, is a test version of a tool that could be used for industrial espionage or other attacks. The game is used to trick the user into launching the malware by clicking on an executable file that appears to be a harmless screenshot from the game.

"The malware is written in a compiled language and lacks any debugging symbols, which suggests it may be distributed as a commercial product," a blog post on Kaspersky's website said. "There are a number of clues that suggest the authors are Russian speakers." The firm said the worm had been detected on a relatively small number of computers so far. It added that it was not yet being distributed via email and that the distribution method appeared to be "still a work in progress".

Researchers believe the worm is a test version of a larger piece of malware that could be used by criminal gangs or state-sponsored attackers. "The fact that this particular piece of malware has not been observed in the wild yet, and the fact that it carries a debugging symbol, suggests that it may be a prototype or possibly a test version," Kaspersky said.

The use of gaming elements in malware is not common. In 2010, the Storm Worm malware used images from the game, World of Warcraft, to deceive users. The Win32.Rmnet.12 malware is significant because it uses an executable file that appears to be a screenshot from the game Tetris, which is a recognised and trusted brand, researchers said.

It was one of the most bizarre and clever pieces of malware around: the Windows worm that travelled with Tetris. The self-replicating malware worm, known as Ramnit, would infect a computer. It would then wait until the victim used the Internet to search for Tetris – perhaps to while away the time during the lunch break or after hours. 

Once the victim had started up a game, Ramnit would take over the computer and start spamming out messages to contacts on the victim's instant messenger, sending them a link to the malware. In this way, the worm was able to spread from one computer to another, using a game of Tetris to entice victims to click on the link and, in effect, infect their own computers. 

But now researchers have announced that they have finally killed off this particular strain of Ramnit – although they expect a new version may emerge at some point. They have discovered a flaw in the worm, which they have managed to turn to their advantage.

The flaw means that the worm only replicates on computers with a specific configuration. By creating a piece of software that exploits this flaw, researchers can ensure that the worm only infects those types of machines and not others. In this way, they have been able to corral the worm and keep it under observation. 

"We were able to subdue it and keep it in a zoo, so to speak," said Brad Duncan, a security researcher at Palo Alto Networks, who led the research. "It can't hurt anybody any more." 

Duncan and his team have been observing the worm for the past six months to learn more about how it works and how it is able to replicate so quickly. They have also been able to work out where it came from. 

The researchers believe that Ramnit emerged from a single laptop that was infected with an earlier version of the worm, which was unearthed by Microsoft in 2010. The laptop in question was then used to write the code for an updated version, which went on to infect more than 2.5 million computers around the world. Its spread was helped by the fact that it was designed to replicate itself every 82 seconds. 

Duncan said that the researchers were now in a position to release details of the worm's vulnerabilities, in the hope that this will help other security experts to kill it off once and for all. Jones, who also wrote lyrics for The Monkees, died on Tuesday, his publicist said.

His songs were also performed by Frank Sinatra, Elvis Presley and Barbra Streisand.

The singer-songwriter died at his home in Los Angeles following a long illness, publicist Linda Petrie said.

Ring of Fire was a US chart-topping single for Johnny Cash in 1963 and received the Grammy Hall of Fame Award in 2014.

Jones co-wrote the song with husband-and-wife team Howard Greenfield and Sue Greenfield, known as the Greenfield Quartet.

Cash's version, about a love affair ending in betrayal and heartache, became one of the biggest hits of his career and saw him perform it in front of US President Lyndon B Johnson at the White House in 1968. It was also honoured with a Grammy Award for best country solo performance.

Jones also wrote The Monkees' theme song and other songs for the band, and penned Love Shack for the B-52's.

His other compositions were performed by Sinatra, Presley, Streisand, The Grass Roots, The Everly Brothers and The Beach Boys.

The co-writer of the Ring of Fire, one of the most successful songs in music history, has died at the age of 95. Lou Christie, a singer and songwriter who was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2018, passed away in his sleep on Sunday at his home in New Jersey, his publicist said. Ring of Fire, which Christie co-wrote with June Carter Cash and others, has sold more than 35 million copies worldwide and was recorded by more than 200 artists. A statement from his family said Christie's health had been failing recently, but the exact cause of his death was not immediately clear.

Christie's career spanned more than 60 years, and he recorded more than 40 albums. He was born in Philadelphia in 1929 and served in the US Army during the Korean War. He went on to become a disc jockey and is credited with introducing The Beatles to American audiences in 1964. He began recording music in the early 1960s, achieving success with the single Rhapsody in the Rain, which sold more than 25 million copies. He went on to work with other artists, including Elvis Presley, Frank Sinatra, and Barbra Streisand.

Christie was married to his wife Eileen for more than 50 years before her death in 2015. He is survived by his son, daughter, and four grandchildren. Finally, at the very bottom of the search results, there is a list of "other searches" with, again, a faint "ad" label.

Millions of users click on the top couple of results, where the ads are clearly labelled - and a similar number on the "related searches" where the ad label is fainter.

But virtually no-one clicks on the "other searches" ads at the very bottom, where the label is a grey font size 2 - even though these are often the most relevant ads to the search.

Google has run tests to check the ad labels' effectiveness. In one, the "other searches" ads were presented without the "ad" label at all - and users clicked on them more.

The company says the test proved that the existing labelling is working well, because few people click on the bottom ads even when the label is there.

The authority threatened formal enforcement action, which could ultimately lead to changes in how Google presents its ads. The company has until 30 September to make changes.

Google has already started testing a new label - a bold "sponsored" tag - for its top ads and plans to test a new format for presenting ads in the "related searches" box.

But it is unlikely to change the bottom ads, which Ms Bailey said have been shown in user testing to be understood by users.

A study carried out by the University of Texas showed that people were unable to correctly identify the sponsored advertisements on search engine results pages (SERPs). When shown screenshots of Google search results, participants pointed out advertisements as fewer than 25% of the time, despite the presence of cues like "Ad" or "Sponsored." 

One of the authors of the study, Amanda Broderick, commented on the low number of participants able to discern between ads and search results, noting that "just because something is labeled 'Ad' doesn't mean that people will notice that it's an advertisement."
